stories.title: ‘Land back’ on the table as part of Saugeen Ojibway nation land dispute
stories.summary: A provincial judge has dismissed a claim by the Canadian government to not allow land to be used as compensation for the government breaking an 1800’s treaty with the Saugeen Ojibway Nation.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A provincial judge has dismissed a claim by the Canadian government to not allow land to be used as compensation for the government breaking an 1800’s treaty with the Saugeen Ojibway Nation.

651 parcels of federally and provincially owned land, along the Bruce Peninsula including Bruce Peninsula National Park, are back on the table as possible compensation following the judge’s ruling.

In 2021, a judge ruled the Crown broke am 1836 treaty with Saugeen Ojibway Nation ancestors, to protect the Bruce Peninsula from settler development.

A trial slated for 2030, will determine what compensation the indigenous group is entitled to the broken promise.

Canada had argued that returning land to the Saugeen Ojibway Nation (S.O.N) was not in the spirit of the ruling, but a judge says land can be used as compensation in the case.

651 parcels of land, all owned by the federal or provincial government have been designated by S.O.N., as potentially being returned to them via a constructive trust which means the land would be held for the benefit of the Saugeen Ojibway Nation.

S.O.N. is also seeking $90 billion in compensation, from the two levels of government, for the broken treaty.

S.O.N says no private land is being sought as part of this land settlement.

651 parcels of federally and provincially owned land, along the Bruce Peninsula including Bruce Peninsula National Park, are back on the table as possible compensation following the judge’s ruling.
In 2021, a judge ruled the Crown broke am 1836 treaty with Saugeen Ojibway Nation ancestors, to protect the Bruce Peninsula from settler development.
A trial slated for 2030, will determine what compensation the indigenous group is entitled to the broken promise.
Canada had argued that returning land to the Saugeen Ojibway Nation (S.O.N) was not in the spirit of the ruling, but a judge says land can be used as compensation in the case.

651 parcels of land, all owned by the federal or provincial government have been designated by S.O.N., as potentially being returned to them via a constructive trust which means the land would be held for the benefit of the Saugeen Ojibway Nation.
S.O.N. is also seeking $90 billion in compensation, from the two levels of government, for the broken treaty.
S.O.N says no private land is being sought as part of this land settlement.

stories.title: Supreme Court reverses policy and reopens courtroom doors to intervenors
stories.summary: Lawyers had complained about Zoom-only rule for intervenors
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada is reopening its courtroom doors to some intervenors as of next spring, loosening an internal policy that had been criticized by lawyers.

The main parties at Supreme Court hearings present their oral arguments in person. Intervenors, groups that are not directly connected with a case but with views on the issues at stake, have only been allowed to appear by Zoom in recent years.

The Supreme Court had said this system improved access to justice, making it less expensive for intervenors to be involved in a case at the top court, but lawyers who often work for free representing intervenors objected. Many intervenors felt the impact of their oral advocacy was somewhat muted on Zoom, a point on which the court has previously disagreed.

On Thursday, Supreme Court Registrar Chantal Carbonneau announced that as of April 2027, the court will start a pilot project allowing intervenors to present arguments both in person or on Zoom. Intervenors, whether online or in person, generally get five minutes. In-person appearances will still have to be approved by the court.

Common intervenors at the Supreme Court include advocacy groups such as the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Criminal Lawyers’ Association, as well as provincial and federal attorneys-general. On Thursday, the court said that intervenor submissions, whether in writing only, in person or on Zoom “are given equal consideration.”

The Canadian Bar Association, the largest lawyers’ group in the country, applauded the shift to open the in-person option to intervenors.

“We have raised concerns about limiting intervenors to virtual participation, and we appreciate the Court’s openness to our members’ views,” association president Loreley Chekay said in a statement.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the court had allowed all parties to appear in person, but as the courtroom was fully reopened for in-person hearings in 2022, intervenors remained on Zoom.

Court spokeswoman Vanessa Racine said the new change is to provide greater flexibility to intervenors.

“As a pilot project, this initiative will allow the court to continue assessing and refining its practices to ensure they best serve the public interest,” Ms. Racine said in an e-mail.

In September 2025, ahead of the landmark hearing in March on the Quebec secularism law known as Bill 21 and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, provincial and federal attorneys-general had asked for a one-time exception to the intervenor-by-Zoom rule. Others thereafter also asked . The Supreme Court said no to all last December.

The Bill 21 hearing unfolded over four days. On the third and fourth days, the judges watched a parade of intervenors on Zoom, using individual monitors behind the bench and television screens mounted on the courtroom walls.

The hearing featured a record 38 outside intervenors and six attorneys-general. Most intervenors effectively sided with the six appellants, who had argued on the hearing’s opening day that the court should strike down Bill 21. Quebec had few allies beyond Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan.

On Thursday, Supreme Court also reiterated a 2021 internal policy regarding the role of intervenors. This May suggest the court will not allow every application to intervene in every case, as it usually has in recent years. “In considering applications to intervene, the court will be mindful of the need not to unduly imbalance the arguments before it,” the 2021 policy, which was restated Thursday, says.

Some top judges have spoken out about allowing too many intervenors in their courts. David Stratas, the longest-serving judge on the Federal Court of Appeal, turned down an intervenor application in a 2025 order. He spoke of “other courts” and stated: “It’s up to them whether they want to admit many on only one side of the courtroom and create the appearance of a court-sanctioned gang-up against the other side.”

The Supreme Court’s shift on the intervenor policy is the second time this year that the country’s top court appears to be responding to public calls for change.

Another issue cited by many lawyers in recent years was the number of cases the Supreme Court agrees to hear. Beyond a smaller number of criminal cases that the court automatically hears, all others must apply to have their appeal taken on by the top court.

From 2018 to 2025, under Chief Justice Richard Wagner, the court agreed to hear an average of 35 new cases each year – known as granting leave to appeal. During the previous eight years under former chief justice Beverley McLachlin, the average annual number of cases was 55. In that period, the McLachlin court said yes to 11 per cent of applications. The Wagner court, through to the end of 2025, said yes to an average of 7 per cent.

In 2026, the Wagner court has said yes to 13 per cent of applications, and on Thursday, it said yes to three more applications for new cases, bringing the annual total to 55 – the most since 2012.

stories.title: ‘Multiple trade issues’ outstanding in Canada, U.S. trade talks: Sources
stories.summary: According to sources present at a meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and Donald Trump in China, the biggest trade issue is the 25 per cent U.S. tariff on Canadian automobiles.
stories.author: Mackenzie Gray and Sergio Vargas
stories.content:
Canada’s chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, told a federal advisory committee that “multiple trade issues” remain outstanding with the United States and are preventing a deal, several sources who were briefed by the federal government have told Global News.

The biggest issue still outstanding is the 25 per cent U.S. tariff on Canadian automobiles, according to sources in the meeting. Negotiations around auto tariffs were a core reason trade talks between the Carney government and Trump administration fell apart in August.

Ottawa is attempting to get what it says is an “interim deal” that would provide tariff relief for Canadian businesses and resolve core trade irritants, ahead of Canada-U.S.-Mexico free trade renegotiation talks, according to individuals briefed by Ottawa.

This strategy has been employed by the Liberals since the Carney government took office, part of a three-pronged approach, according to government sources. The first step is to deal with outstanding trade issues with the Americans. Step two is to partner with the Americans in key areas, such as defence and energy, before finalizing a new free trade agreement.

The Carney government now believes there is a window to get a deal with the Trump administration by the end of the year, prior to the Democrats taking control of Congress . Despite multiple Democratic lawmakers publicly objecting to tariffs on Canada, sources in the meeting tell Global News the Liberals believe a friendlier Congress will not materially change negotiations with the Trump administration.

That view is not universally accepted by council members. One told Global News that Ottawa’s push for an agreement makes it appear “desperate for a deal.”

The federal government’s framework of an agreement with the U.S. remains broadly the same as the deal that fell apart in August: Ottawa would drop its counter-tariffs in exchange for the U.S. removing or reducing sweeping 50 per cent Section 338 tariffs on more than $20 billion of Canadian products, which were implemented on Aug. 22 after trade talks fell apart. Negotiators would also be looking to reduce the long-standing Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum, softwood lumber and autos.

Auto tariffs remain the core stumbling block, after they played a major role in ending the August talks. The Americans had offered to reduce tariffs from 25 per cent to 15 per cent on Canadian cars and parts, with no carve-out for Cusma-compliant products. The Carney government was poised to accept that deal, despite labour leaders, auto parts manufacturers and automakers that operate in Canada all telling the government a 15 per cent tariff level would cripple the industry in Canada.

The government readout of the meeting says discussions “also addressed the implementation of federal measures to support Canadian businesses and workers affected by U.S. tariffs, including the effectiveness of existing supports and opportunities to better respond to the needs of affected businesses.”

Sources say the government promised a more agile response to tariff relief, particularly on Section 338 tariffs imposed on Canadian goods in August after multiple members of the committee raised concerns over their impact on small businesses across the country.

While Donald Trump and Mark Carney recently met in China, they’re not the only ones talking.

Canada U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, who did not take questions from Global News on Parliament Hill Thursday, and Janice Charette, have been speaking with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer regularly.

The Liberals have crucially not labelled those conversations as negotiations with the Americans, which one member of the advisory council told Global News they believe is an attempt by the Liberals to play down expectations on the possibility of getting a deal.

stories.title: Six Canadian men sanctioned as powerful Mafia bosses with global reach by U.S. government
stories.summary: The men are accused of being leading members of a sophisticated transnational criminal Mafia network known as the ‘Ndrangheta
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The U.S. government designated six Toronto-area men as accused Mafia leaders who oversee a powerful global organized crime group, as well as sanctioned a network of Ontario funeral homes accused of being connected to the mob.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury accused the men of being leading members of a sophisticated transnational criminal Mafia network known as the ‘Ndrangheta that facilitates large-scale drug trafficking and money laundering.

Four of the six men are also accused of forming a board of control for ‘Ndrangheta activities in the Toronto region as leaders of three separate but cooperating clans within the ‘Ndrangheta.

Alongside the alleged Canada-based mafiosi, the Comancheros Motorcycle Club, an outlaw biker organization based in Australia, was also sanctioned. The two organizations are accused of providing essential logistical and operational support that help “terrorist cartels” expand and sustain global drug networks.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

Scott Bessent, the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, announced the designations and sanctions Thursday, saying: “Cartels do not operate in isolation. They rely on other criminal organizations like the Comancheros and ‘Ndrangheta to move drugs, launder illicit proceeds, and ultimately poison Americans with narcotics.”

The ‘Ndrangheta clans based in the Toronto area have grown in recent years, U.S. officials said, “becoming so powerful that they dictate events in Italy from across the ocean. In Canada, the ‘Ndrangheta is involved in drug trafficking, money laundering, murder and other crimes.”

Named as Mafia figure in Canada are Angelo Figliomeni, his brother Cosimo Figliomeni, Vincenzo DeMaria, Rocco Remo Commisso, Francesco Commisso and Luigi Vescio Sr.

The men are not criminally charged but face significant economic and financial sanctions by the U.S. government. The designations are not arrived at through a court process.

Cartels do not operate in isolation

Angelo Figliomeni, 64, of Vaughan, Ont., is named by the U.S. Treasury as the leader of the Toronto faction of the ‘Ndrangheta. He is listed as also being known as “Don Angelino.” His listing says he fled to Canada from Italy around 20 years ago to escape a sentence on weapons charges in his homeland. “Angelo’s power extends beyond Canada, stretching back to Italy. He has engaged in money laundering and other criminal activities on behalf of the ‘Ndrangheta,” the U.S. Treasury alleged.

He was arrested in 2019 by York Regional Police and accused of being the head of a Mafia clan, but charges were later stayed by a judge after court heard police investigators improperly monitored interactions between suspects and their lawyers.

Cosimo Figliomeni, 61, who is sometimes known as “Cosimino,” is named as joining his brother as a senior ‘Ndrangheta leader in Toronto and in the Figliomeni clan, and has also faced Mafia-linked criminal proceedings in Italy.

DeMaria, 72, of Mississauga, Ont., also known as Jimmy DeMaria, has long been named, but not proven, to be a Mafia boss in Canada as the federal government tried unsuccessfully to deport him for more than 40 years, since his murder conviction in 1982. U.S. officials called him “one of Toronto’s top ‘Ndrangheta bosses” and claim he “holds significant power in the ‘Ndrangheta.”

Rocco Remo Commisso, 80, who is frequently known by his middle name Remo, is accused by U.S. officials as an ‘Ndrangheta leader in charge of narcotics trafficking networks in the United States. He also has a serious criminal record: convicted in 1981 for three charges of conspiracy to commit murder and in 1984 for his involvement in a bombing that killed one person.

Francesco Commisso, 70, is also known as “U Scelto,” U.S. officials said, and is a relative of Rocco Remo Commisso. He faced allegations in Italy of being part of a Toronto oversight body that imposed disciplinary sanctions on members, among other tasks.

Vescio, 55, is the only one of the men named who was born in Canada. He runs a network of funeral homes, which provides an alleged nickname: “The Undertaker.” He is accused of being a senior ‘Ndrangheta member and an associate of Angelo Figliomeni and DeMaria. Vescio faced charges in Italy of Mafia association alongside the Figliomeni brothers and the Commissos in 2019.

Vincenzo “Jimmy” DeMaria being arrested in Toronto in April 2009. Peter J. Thompson/National Post

U.S. Treasury officials also designated the corporate network of Vescio for sanctions, including three large funeral home facilities and a luxury vehicle rental agency in Ontario.

The U.S. officials named Fratelli Vescio Funeral Homes in Woodbridge, and Vescio Funeral Homes in both Toronto and Maple. Also named is Phantom Limousine Services, a luxury limousine and high-end vehicle rental and private security company. Vescio is said to be president of all of the businesses.

Lawyers who have represented the Figliomenis and DeMaria in past proceedings did not return requests for comment Thursday afternoon prior to deadline. Two people who answered the phone at a Vescio funeral home hung up when asked about the allegations. The Commissos could not be reached prior to deadline.

All of the men are designated by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (Ofac) for “having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, ‘Ndrangheta.”

The Ofac said the agency’s actions were designed “to disrupt the flow of illicit drugs and dismantle the networks, facilitators and financial infrastructure that enable their production and distribution.”

The designations create significant economic problems for named people and companies. All property and interests that are in the U.S. are blocked. The designation prohibits financial transactions within the United States or with any U.S. citizen. Treasury officials warned that financial institutions — even foreign ones — May risk sanctions against them if they conduct certain transactions or activities with designated entities.

The ‘Ndrangheta controls a significant share of the European cocaine trade, while the Comancheros have helped open access to some of the world’s most lucrative illicit drug markets, Treasury officials said.

The ‘Ndrangheta is the traditional Mafia organization that formed in Italy’s Calabria region about 150 years ago. It is similar to the better-known Cosa Nostra that formed in neighbouring Sicily.

It expanded to other countries, with members who came to Canada, beginning in the 1950s, finding fertile soil and thriving to such as extent that investigators in Italy found it is often seen as a parallel leadership group rather than a mere branch plant.

“As one of the largest criminal organizations in the world, the ‘Ndrangheta’s primary business comes from drug trafficking, with some estimates stating that almost 80 per cent of the European cocaine trade is controlled by the ‘Ndrangheta. While primarily focused on the cocaine trade, Italian officials have stated that the ‘Ndrangheta have started expanding into the illicit fentanyl market,” the U.S. Treasury said.

The ‘Ndrangheta often partners with Mexican and South American cartels, including some of the largest and most feared.

“This faction of the ‘Ndrangheta uses the U.S. and Canadian financial systems to launder illicit proceeds,” the officials alleged.

U.S. Treasury officials said they worked with international law enforcement agencies, including Canada’s RCMP and York Regional Police, which were “instrumental in supporting today’s action.” National police forces in Italy, Australia and New Zealand are also named as supporting partners.

Adrian Humphreys, a founding journalist at National Post in 1998, is a senior national reporter focusing on crime, policing and justice stories, and investigative journalism. He is the author of three non-fiction bestsellers about organized crime, and runs a popular YouTube channel about global gangsters.

stories.title: Calls for government to crack down on wage theft after Motive Espresso shuttered
stories.summary: There are new developments in the case of a local coffee shop chain accused of not paying some staff all their wages. CTV News has learned that a second location of Motive Espresso has now closed, with the business having been evicted by the landlord.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
There are new developments in the case of a local coffee shop chain accused of not paying some staff all their wages. CTV News has learned that a second location of Motive Espresso has now closed, with the business having been evicted by the landlord.

This comes as workers’ advocacy organizations call on the provincial government to beef up enforcement of employers accused of wage theft.

“Every time we tried to reach out and ask, she would get a lawyer involved and claim we were harassing her. So, it probably took three months for us to get our money,” said Jaimee Parcels, a former employee at the Motive Espresso location at Pall Mall and Colborne in London.

She was among former workers who gathered Thursday to share their experiences working for the company.

Those who spoke with CTV News say they were either not paid their full wages, or they were paid off the books and with no proper paperwork such as pay-stubs or a record of employment.

“I’m owed 61 hours of labour, plus a correction on my Labour Day paycheck because she didn’t give me the time and a half, and I worked the Labour Day, which I think is kind of ironic,” said former employee Emma Brown.

“I was fired with no cause, and I was not given or paid out any kind of severance despite working for the company for over a year,” added former employee Crimsen De Santis.

The shop in Old North now sits empty - it’s furniture and equipment appear to have been removed. Former employees say this location closed within the last couple of weeks.

It wasn’t long after that the south location on Ridout Street in Old South would close. Notices in the window indicate the business was evicted last Friday, Nov. 13.

The non-profit Workers Action Centre says it surveyed hundreds of workers across Ontario. 60 per cent said they experienced at least one case of wage theft. More than 50 per cent said they did not get paid for all the hours they worked. 46 per cent reported they don’t get public holidays with pay.

“It has become easier for employers to steal workers’ wages and get away with it,” said Workers Action Centre executive director Deena Ladd.

Ladd appeared before the Queens Park Standing Committee on Finance this week, calling for more enforcement officers to investigate wage theft complaints.

“The use of proactive inspections has plummeted 87 per cent from 3,500 in 2018 to just 474 in 2025,” Ladd informed the committee.

Ladd says the lack of employment standards officers has resulted in $80 million in workers’ wages not being collected from 2014 to 2023.

The president of the Ontario Federation of Labour says the Motive Espresso workers are doing the right thing by banding together and bringing awareness to their situation.

But Laura Walton also has strong words for businesses that open without the ability to pay staff.

“But I also hope that this is a lesson to folks as they’re heading into business. It isn’t enough just to have a really great idea. There are rules and regulations around employees, and what the Employment Standards Act in Ontario requires you to do,” Walton said.

In the meantime, Ontario’s Ministry of Labour says it can’t comment on ongoing investigations related to Motive Espresso. It issued a statement, saying, in part:

“Our government has zero tolerance for wage theft and has put in place some of the strongest workplace protections and enforcement tools in the country. This includes doubling the maximum fine for individuals convicted under the Employment Standards Act to $100,000 and increasing administrative penalties for repeat offenders to $5,000 per employee…”

The former Motive Espresso workers say that’s all well and good, but they just want what they believe they earned.

“I’m just mad and sad. I hope some justice can be served because she’s hurting a lot of really good people,” said Jaimee Parcels.

We reached out to Motive Espresso owner Sarah Levine by email and phone. She did not respond to our messages by publish deadline.

It wasn’t long after that the south location on Ridout Street in Old South would close. Notices in the window indicate the business was evicted last Friday, Nov. 13.

content_blocks.alt: Wage theft graphic
content_blocks.caption: Wage theft graphic (Survey statistics from Workers Action Centre)

content_blocks.text: The non-profit Workers Action Centre says it surveyed hundreds of workers across Ontario. 60 per cent said they experienced at least one case of wage theft. More than 50 per cent said they did not get paid for all the hours they worked. 46 per cent reported they don’t get public holidays with pay.
“It has become easier for employers to steal workers’ wages and get away with it,” said Workers Action Centre executive director Deena Ladd.
Ladd appeared before the Queens Park Standing Committee on Finance this week, calling for more enforcement officers to investigate wage theft complaints.
“The use of proactive inspections has plummeted 87 per cent from 3,500 in 2018 to just 474 in 2025,” Ladd informed the committee.

content_blocks.alt: Former staff Motive Espresso
content_blocks.caption: Former staff Crimsen De Santis, Emma Brown, and Jaimee Parcels gather outside the now closed Motive Espresso location in Old North London. (Bryan Bicknell/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: Ladd says the lack of employment standards officers has resulted in $80 million in workers’ wages not being collected from 2014 to 2023.
The president of the Ontario Federation of Labour says the Motive Espresso workers are doing the right thing by banding together and bringing awareness to their situation.
But Laura Walton also has strong words for businesses that open without the ability to pay staff.

“But I also hope that this is a lesson to folks as they’re heading into business. It isn’t enough just to have a really great idea. There are rules and regulations around employees, and what the Employment Standards Act in Ontario requires you to do,” Walton said.
In the meantime, Ontario’s Ministry of Labour says it can’t comment on ongoing investigations related to Motive Espresso. It issued a statement, saying, in part:

“Our government has zero tolerance for wage theft and has put in place some of the strongest workplace protections and enforcement tools in the country. This includes doubling the maximum fine for individuals convicted under the Employment Standards Act to $100,000 and increasing administrative penalties for repeat offenders to $5,000 per employee…”
The former Motive Espresso workers say that’s all well and good, but they just want what they believe they earned.
“I’m just mad and sad. I hope some justice can be served because she’s hurting a lot of really good people,” said Jaimee Parcels.
We reached out to Motive Espresso owner Sarah Levine by email and phone. She did not respond to our messages by publish deadline.

stories.title: Why many Canadians now need higher incomes to get a mortgage even as home prices decline
stories.summary: Rising borrowing costs are offsetting savings for homebuyers in major Canadian cities, an analysis shows
stories.author: Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
Rising mortgage rates are eroding housing affordability in major Canadian cities despite falling home prices, according to an analysis by financial-products comparison site Ratehub.CA.

The report found homebuyers are facing bigger payments and higher income requirements to qualify for a mortgage even in cities where home prices have declined.

For example, the analysis found someone buying an average-priced home in Vancouver in October would pay $202 more in monthly mortgage costs, compared with purchasing in September. That’s despite the average home price in the city dropping by more than $7,000 to just under $1.07-million in the same period.

The same homebuyer would also need $6,650 more in household income to qualify for the government’s mortgage stress test in October, compared with September.

The increases in monthly mortgage payments were similar in Toronto, where housing prices also fell last month.

Meanwhile, some cities such as Hamilton and Montreal saw both housing prices and interest rates increase in October, a double blow to affordability.

The calculations are based on average available rates among Canada’s big banks for a five-year fixed insured mortgage, assuming a 25-year amortization and a 10-per-cent down payment.

That rate’s average has jumped to 4.99 per cent from 4.56 per cent between September and October, according to Ratehub.

“Rates faced constant upward pressure due to elevated bond yields, which were pushed higher by high oil prices and heightened inflation expectations,” said Clay Jarvis, a mortgage expert at Ratehub.

“While most cities saw home prices soften, the declines weren’t enough to offset the impact of higher mortgage rates.”

Mr. Jarvis added that home prices are dropping at a slow pace because sellers are reluctant to sell at a loss.

Meanwhile, mortgage rates face continued upward pressure.

Economists have observed that fixed rates are unusually low compared with current bond yields , as lenders compete for an unusually large cohort of renewals from the early-2020s housing boom.

Is a variable mortgage rate still worth considering after the Bank of Canada’s rate hike?

Renewals are expected to slow down during winter, and lenders could increase their rates as competition decreases, Daren King, senior economist at National Bank of Canada, said in October.

Variable-rate mortgages also became more expensive over the past month, after the Bank of Canada hiked rates by a quarter of a percentage point in October to tamp down inflation from rising gas prices.

Bond swap markets, which capture investor expectations around monetary policy, are currently pricing in three more rate hikes by October 2027.

stories.title: Trans Mountain oil shipments jump as upgrades boost pipeline capacity
stories.summary: High demand driven by production growth in Alberta and global energy crisis exacerbated by war in Iran
stories.author: Emma Graney
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

Shipments of crude oil from the British Columbia coast rose sharply in October, after Trans Mountain finished a project to boost capacity on its pipeline system two months ahead of schedule.

The pipeline, which can now carry 980,000 barrels a day of oil to the coast from Alberta, was also full in the summer , but dropped to 90 per cent of capacity in September, according to data from the federal Crown corporation. High demand for the line is being driven by production growth in Alberta and a global energy crisis exacerbated by the war in Iran.

Various international customers are “reimagining what their supply strategy should be” as the conflict drags on, said Jennifer Pierce, Trans Mountain’s chief administrative officer.

That’s particularly true in Asia, where Prime Minister Mark Carney this week pitched a business summit on the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline as a project that could feed growing demand in the region for Canadian crude. That conduit would run adjacent to the Trans Mountain system for much of its length.

Trans Mountain reported that it has loaded 722 tankers at the Westridge Marine Terminal in Burnaby, B.C., since its expanded system started operating in May 2024. More than 65 per cent of those travelled to Asia. Demand for Canadian heavy crude is particularly high among Chinese refineries, which have more than doubled their purchases.

Thirty oil tankers set sail from Westridge in October – the most counted yet and six more than in September, according to a Royal Bank of Canada analysis released Thursday.

Export volumes climbed to 15.9 million barrels, the analysis said. Asia-Pacific was the primary destination for tankers last month, with China receiving the lion’s share. Additionally, two tankers were bound for California (versus none in September), three for Washington state and one for Alaska.

Trans Mountain’s capacity-boosting project, completed in October, introduced drag-reducing agents into the pipeline system, reducing friction between the oil and the line itself. This increased capacity by roughly 90,000 barrels a day.

“We are seeing record production out of the basin, and we’re also seeing record demand coming in on the Pacific Coast,” Ms. Pierce said, adding that the company found “ways that we were able to complete that 2½ months ahead of schedule and put it into service.”

Growing demand has Trans Mountain looking to further increase the system’s capacity.

It has applied for approval for a second, larger optimization project to boost capacity by a further mainline 210,000 barrels a day. The project would add 30 kilometres of new 36-inch diameter pipe adjacent to the existing main line and 11 new pump stations along the route. It would also increase power to the system to make pump stations more effective.

If it’s approved, Trans Mountain will go ahead with an “open season,” in which oil companies commit volumes to the expanded line to make the commercial case for the project.

“We’re anticipating that we would have a regulatory decision on the technical aspects by April, and we need to have the commercial underpinnings for that to move forward with a final investment decision,” Ms. Pierce said.

The RBC analysis said the lack of space on Trans Mountain, persistent demand from Asian buyers for Canadian barrels and further supply growth expected from Alberta’s new Oil Sands Growth Program, announced last week , all reinforce the case for the Pacific Link pipeline.

Ottawa last month designated the proposal as a project of national interest. It was the first such official designation under the Building Canada Act, which provides an accelerated pathway through regulatory approvals with the support of the federal government.

stories.title: Toy mogul Ronnen Harary puts Western students to the test in No Experience Necessary Challenge
stories.summary: No Experience Necessary Challenge comes to Western, where Ronnen Harary awarded cash prizes to student founders to advance promising ideas
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
The entertainment visionary behind Spin Master, Canada’s biggest toy company and creator of PAW Patrol, brought his No Experience Necessary Challenge to Western University this week. Spin Master co-founder and Western alum Ronnen Harary, BA’94, is on a mission to inspire students to build their own business ventures while they’re young, offering initial funding and a shot at $25,000 for the most promising ideas.

Western University students (L to R) Finilayomi Betiku and Fifelayomi Betiku celebrate a successful pitch of their business TwinChin at Ronnen Harary’s No Experience Necessary Challenge in London, Ont. on Nov. 17, 2026. Harary said the sisters’ pitch was especially memorable for their energy and insight into an tapped market. (Morrissette Entrepreneurship)

Twenty-six aspiring Western founders took up his challenge to pitch their business idea in just 60 seconds, presenting to Harary outside a trailer decked out in entrepreneurial mottos from his new book, No Experience Necessary. Students with ideas he liked walked away with $500 that must be spent within a week to spark momentum in their venture.

“I want them to really push themselves over seven days of focused activity to make things happen they hadn’t imagined possible,” Harary said.

He offered feedback on the spot and workshopped ideas with students, including how they might best leverage $500 of initial funding. Students who receive it are asked to document their efforts over the week as they vie to win one of 10 grand prizes of $25,000.

“I can understand the entrepreneur really well by how they spend $500 over seven days. That informs the decision to award the $25,000,” Harary said.

One of the hopefuls was Piercen Di Berardo, a fifth-year computer science student. He and two other Western students created Axioma Scholar, a personalized learning platform for high school and post-secondary students struggling with math.

“Our product works because it’s unique for each learner,” Di Berardo said. “It took us two years to research and develop the platform’s complex, personalized algorithm based in neuroscience, machine learning and predictive math.”

At the No Experience Necessary Challenge at Western University Nov. 17, (L to R) Ronnen Harary, co-founder of Canadian toy giant Spin Master, congratulates computer science student Piercen DiBerardo after awarding him $500 for his team’s learning platform, Axioma Scholar. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

Di Berardo’s role is focused on writing code, not pitching, but he was thrown into the job of convincing Harary on short notice – both his teammates had a mandatory math class during the competition. That left him with just a week to prepare while juggling his midterm exams.

The unexpected pressure didn’t compromise the outcome. Di Berardo was one of nine students from four different faculties who received $500. He also got some advice. His team has been brainstorming options to rebrand their product, leaning toward ‘Axi Math’. Harary agreed a name change is needed and suggested “A Scholar” instead.

The pitch competition was just one of several events Harary took part in during Global Entrepreneurship Week, hosted by Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship in the Ronald D. Schmeichel Building for Entrepreneurship and Innovation. For Harary, the return to Western is homecoming.

Western University grads and Spin Master co-founders (L to R) Ronnen Harary and Anton Rabie, show off an Earth Buddy, the first product they launched after the company’s founding in 1994. (Spin Master)

He co-founded his first business here, Campus Faces, with childhood friend and Western classmate, Anton Rabie, Hba’94. Another Western student, Ben Varadi, Hba’94, joined the duo in founding Spin Master after graduation. The company went on to create best-selling toys, games and global franchises including PAW Patrol, a toy line and animated TV series that now airs in more than 160 countries.

“I recognized the critical moments in our path, like when we were only 25 years old and the now late CEO of Hasbro actually took our call. His attitude was, ‘Welcome to the toy industry,'” Harary recalled.

Being embraced as promising mentees rather than upstart competitors was a “lucky break” for Harary. He said it helped him recognize one of several advantages entrepreneurs can only seize when they’re young.

“When you’re in your 20s, everybody’s rooting for you. They just want you to win.”

A few decades on, Harary decided to pay it forward by writing No Experience Necessary: Why Betting on Yourself in Your Twenties Is the Best Decision You’ll Ever Make. His first 75,000-word draft was no easy feat.

“Growing up with a learning disability, you learn to grind. All that grinding made me believe anything is possible if you stick with it long enough.”

Over four years, Harary worked with several editors in succession to refine the manuscript, then found an agent to connect him with a writer to bring the book to the finish line. Securing a publisher brought another set of hurdles. Nineteen turned him down, before an editor at Crown Publishing championed the manuscript and helped him turn it into a published book that’s now earning positive reviews.

“It was my own ‘no experience necessary’ moment,” Harary said.

stories.title: Canadian producer Brian Ahern helped lay the groundwork for the Americana sound
stories.summary: Grammy winner was known for his fruitful collaborations with singers Emmylou Harris, to whom he was also married, and Anne Murray, whose earliest recordings he produced
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Record producer Brian Ahern, known for his work with Anne Murray and Emmylou Harris, often used strings players from the Toronto Symphony Orchestra to sweeten his recordings in the early 1970s. He found, however, that the assorted violinists, violists and cellists lacked enthusiasm in the studio compared with their more vigorous performances in concert.

To spark their passion, he booked a session at the city’s Massey Hall, then the orchestra’s venerable home, outside of which he parked his custom-made mobile studio, the 42-foot (13-metre) facility dubbed the Enactron Truck. Playing in familiar environs, the attitude of the string players drastically improved.

“They played their hearts out,” Mr. Ahern later told Mix Magazine. “That’s when I realized what magic I could work by having a mobile studio.”

His “control room on wheels” was a tractor-trailer converted with help from engineer Stuart Taylor and lined with a thin layer of lead to block exterior radio frequencies from interfering with the sound. In 1974, the Halifax native put the “mobile” in mobile studio when he moved it to Coldwater Canyon in Beverly Hills, Calif. There it sat next to a funky bungalow, with audio cables connecting the house to the truck’s console.

Willie Nelson fanatics know that harmonicist Mickey Raphael recorded his parts for the 1978 album Stardust , produced by Booker T. Jones, inside the house’s tiled bathroom shower.

Among the classic albums recorded there by Mr. Ahern was Ms. Harris’s breakthrough major-label debut Pieces of the Sky in 1974, with Elite Hotel and Luxury Liner to follow in short order.

“Brian’s first albums with Emmylou Harris were some of the greatest records made in my lifetime,” said musician and producer Colin Linden.

Mr. Ahern, an influential Grammy Award-winning country music producer and soft-spoken bear of a man whose early work with Ms. Harris helped lay the groundwork for the Americana genre, died of natural causes at his home on Nov. 9, in Duluth, Minn., according to his family. He was 81.

Mr. Ahern was inducted into the Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame in 2006 and was presented a Lifetime Achievement Award for Producer/Engineer at the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville four years later. He was invested as a member of the Order of Canada in 2022 for contributions to the musical landscape and for “recording with some of the finest artists of our times.”

Among the dozens of albums he produced, recorded or mixed were John Allan Cameron’s Get There by Dawn , Gene MacLellan’s eponymous debut, Johnny Cash’s Silver ( which included the country hit [Ghost] Riders in the Sky ), Jesse Winchester’s Nothing But a Breeze , Ricky Skaggs’s Solid Ground and a dozen long-players with Ms. Murray.

The 2013 collaborative album Old Yellow Moon by Ms. Harris and Rodney Crowell earned a Grammy Award . All told, he produced 11 solo albums with Ms. Harris, who was his wife from 1977 to 1984. After the death of her music partner Gram Parsons in 1973, Ms. Harris found herself in limbo artistically.

“Whatever vision I had was uninformed,” she told The Globe and Mail. “But Brian trusted my instincts before I did. He gave me the confidence as I grew and learned in the recording studio.”

Mr. Ahern’s other famous collaboration was with Ms. Murray. In 1965, she auditioned for CBC Television’s Halifax-produced Singalong Jubilee , with Mr. Ahern accompanying her on guitar. He later became the show’s music director and was newly relocated in Toronto when he sent a string of registered letters to Ms. Murray, urging her to record with him there.

She had graduated from the University of New Brunswick in 1966 with a bachelor of physical education and was teaching in Summerside, PEI.

“I knew how talented he was, you could see that,” Ms. Murray told The Globe. “I didn’t really know what he was doing in Toronto, though. It obviously wasn’t a whole lot, because he wasn’t making a lot of money.”

Ms. Murray got wind of his bank balance immediately upon her arrival in Toronto in 1967 when he asked her to get his guitars out of hock from a pawn shop.

“I had only been in Toronto once before,” Ms. Murray said. “It scared the living daylights out of me, but that’s how it all started.”

Ms. Murray’s debut album, What About Me , was released on Arc Records in 1968. The follow-up LP included the breakout hit Snowbird , written by PEI songwriter Mr. MacLellan. Mr. Ahern paid Ms. Murray back for the pawn ticket. He could afford it: The royalties from a song that reached No. 8 on the U.S. pop singles chart would have been a bonanza.

He could afford a shave and haircut, too, but never paid much attention to fancy grooming. The former football player at St. Mary’s University stood 6 feet 2 inches tall and dressed eccentrically, often with a bandana covering his head. He wore firemen’s boots with shorts and a shoulder bag, and typically donned sunglasses in the studio.

“He was a thinker,” Ms. Murray said. “I didn’t care what he looked like. We were there to make music.” Mr. Ahern, known by friends and family as “B.A.,” won four Juno Awards for the recordings with Ms. Murray.

He was cavalier about his image, lived outside the mainstream and was never concerned with outside approval or expectations. His manner was subdued, occasionally grumpy, with a dry sense of humour and a quietly imposing presence. His words were measured and meaningful, if hard to detect.

“My imitation of Brian talking is putting my hand over my mouth and mumbling,” said business partner Bob Hunka. “Brian spoke just clearly enough to make himself understood, and he was worth paying attention to.”

In 1991, Mr. Ahern moved to Nashville. By then he had established a reputation as a selfless producer and creative soul who earned the trust of elite artists.

For the duets album The Bradley Barn Sessions , he paired country legend George Jones with artists such as Marty Stuart, Keith Richards, Dolly Parton, Mark Knopfler and Mr. Jones’s ex-wife Tammy Wynette.

“Brian believed being a producer was more than gathering songs and performances,” said fellow producer Rick Clark, a mentee of Mr. Ahern. “It’s helping forge a chapter of an artist’s life, and Brian rose to that responsibility time and time again.”

Decades after Mr. Ahern’s divorce from Ms. Harris, the two reunited for the latter’s 2008 album All I Intended to Be , her first LP in five years. The record was judged one of the year’s 50 best by Q magazine and was nominated for a Grammy Award.

It included a pair of songs she co-wrote with Montreal sisters Kate and Anna McGarrigle. Though his career took him to Los Angeles and Nashville, Mr. Ahern promoted Canadian songwriters. One of his first domestic hits he produced was a version of Bobby Gimby’s Canada in 1967 by the Toronto sunshine-pop vocal group the Sugar Shoppe, featuring actor Victor Garber.

Ms. Murray’s first album featured songs written by emerging Canadians Joni Mitchell, Ken Tobias, David Wiffen and William Hawkins. In addition to recording Mr. MacLellan’s Snowbird , Ms. Murray also sang his gospel song Put Your Hand in the Hand . Mr. Ahern produced Ronnie Hawkins’s country-hit cover of Gordon Lightfoot’s Home from the Forest .

“At the time, Canada was gaining its autonomy, and there seemed to be a hunger for things Canadian to reinforce this whole idea,” Mr. Ahern told music journalist Jason Schneider for his book Whispering Pines . “It wasn’t anti-American or anti-anything, just pro-Canadian.”

He was born in Halifax on Jan. 8, 1945, one of six children in a musical Scottish-Irish household. His father, Terence Ahern, owned the Maritime Hobby Centre and was the choir director and organist at Saint Joseph’s Catholic Church; his mother, Teresa Ahern (née McKay), was a homemaker and progressive type who played piano, loved to dance and enjoyed a strong cup of tea.

His first guitar was a Harmony-made S.S. Stewart archtop, given to him after he was hospitalized for asthma. He strummed his way through Saint Patrick’s High School and the era’s folk music revival.

By 19, he was music director and band leader on Frank’s Bandstand , the Halifax segment of CBC TV’s national Music Hop series. One of the singers was Patrician Anne McKinnon, with whom Mr. Ahern was romantically involved. The relationship produced a daughter, Shannon Ahern. Ms. McKinnon’s sister was singer Catherine McKinnon; Mr. Ahern played guitar on her 1964 album The Voice of an Angel .

Before he devoted himself to producing records, Mr. Ahern spread his guitar talents among three groups, including the Offbeats. “I wore sunglasses in that band, because the lights annoyed me, but the image of the sunglasses became a very hip thing and generated lots of fan mail,” he said in 1996.

Another of his bands, the Nova Scotians, played Celtic jigs and reels. He changed his hairstyle and took off the sunglasses. “We wore plaid blazers and really itchy grey flannel pants,” he recalled.

On CBC’s Singalong Jubilee , he met Ms. Murray, a wholesome, honey-voiced native of Springhill, N.S. Though his career was thriving in Halifax, he grew bored with the scene. “I went to Toronto and starved for a while and talked Anne Murray into doing a really cheap album for $2,500,” he told Mix Magazine.

That album, What About Me , earned Ms. Murray a record deal with the U.S. label Capitol Records. Her 1973 album Danny’s Song , was partly recorded by Mr. Ahern live at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa and included the titular hit single written by Kenny Loggins. The follow-up LP Love Song included a cover of the Beatles’ You Won’t See Me , notable for the bassline by her bandleader Skip Beckwith.

“John Lennon came into my dressing room and said that version of You Won’t See Me was the greatest,” Ms. Murray said. “He just loved it, and it was Skip’s bassline.”

Mr. Beckwith presented Mr. Ahern with three songs written by the then unknown Nashville songwriter Mr. Crowell. One of them, Bluebird Wine , ended up as the lead track on Ms. Harris’s Pieces of the Sky album.

Ms. Harris and Mr. Ahern were married at his parents’ home on Jan. 9, 1977, one day after the record producer’s birthday. A snowstorm had delayed the arrival of guests flying in for the ceremony. It was the Alabama-born singer’s idea to get married in Halifax.

“I not only married Brian, I married his country,” Ms. Harris said. “I adored his mother, and I wanted to marry into his family.” The marriage produced a daughter, Meghann Robern.

Mr. Ahern produced Mr. Crowell’s debut 1978 album Ain’t Living Long Like This . “I called him ‘Bullseye,’” the Grammy Award-winning singer-songwriter said. “I knew it when I got into his creative zone. It might be a chuckle if I played the right note or sang the right thing. They were small gestures from Brian perceived in a large way.”

Mr. Ahern’s Enactron Truck is on display at the Musicians Hall of Fame & Museum in Nashville. He leaves his siblings Aileen Ahern, Nanci Ahern and Patrick Ahern; daughters, Shannon Ahern and Meghann Robern; and ex-wife, Emmylou Harris.

“He was a thinker,” Ms. Murray said. “I didn’t care what he looked like. We were there to make music.” Mr. Ahern, known by friends and family as “B.A.,” won four Juno Awards for the recordings with Ms. Murray.

He was cavalier about his image, lived outside the mainstream and was never concerned with outside approval or expectations. His manner was subdued, occasionally grumpy, with a dry sense of humour and a quietly imposing presence. His words were measured and meaningful, if hard to detect.

“My imitation of Brian talking is putting my hand over my mouth and mumbling,” said business partner Bob Hunka. “Brian spoke just clearly enough to make himself understood, and he was worth paying attention to.”
In 1991, Mr. Ahern moved to Nashville. By then he had established a reputation as a selfless producer and creative soul who earned the trust of elite artists.

For the duets album The Bradley Barn Sessions , he paired country legend George Jones with artists such as Marty Stuart, Keith Richards, Dolly Parton, Mark Knopfler and Mr. Jones’s ex-wife Tammy Wynette.

“Brian believed being a producer was more than gathering songs and performances,” said fellow producer Rick Clark, a mentee of Mr. Ahern. “It’s helping forge a chapter of an artist’s life, and Brian rose to that responsibility time and time again.”

Decades after Mr. Ahern’s divorce from Ms. Harris, the two reunited for the latter’s 2008 album All I Intended to Be , her first LP in five years. The record was judged one of the year’s 50 best by Q magazine and was nominated for a Grammy Award.

It included a pair of songs she co-wrote with Montreal sisters Kate and Anna McGarrigle. Though his career took him to Los Angeles and Nashville, Mr. Ahern promoted Canadian songwriters. One of his first domestic hits he produced was a version of Bobby Gimby’s Canada in 1967 by the Toronto sunshine-pop vocal group the Sugar Shoppe, featuring actor Victor Garber.

Ms. Murray’s first album featured songs written by emerging Canadians Joni Mitchell, Ken Tobias, David Wiffen and William Hawkins. In addition to recording Mr. MacLellan’s Snowbird , Ms. Murray also sang his gospel song Put Your Hand in the Hand . Mr. Ahern produced Ronnie Hawkins’s country-hit cover of Gordon Lightfoot’s Home from the Forest .

“At the time, Canada was gaining its autonomy, and there seemed to be a hunger for things Canadian to reinforce this whole idea,” Mr. Ahern told music journalist Jason Schneider for his book Whispering Pines . “It wasn’t anti-American or anti-anything, just pro-Canadian.”

He was born in Halifax on Jan. 8, 1945, one of six children in a musical Scottish-Irish household. His father, Terence Ahern, owned the Maritime Hobby Centre and was the choir director and organist at Saint Joseph’s Catholic Church; his mother, Teresa Ahern (née McKay), was a homemaker and progressive type who played piano, loved to dance and enjoyed a strong cup of tea.
His first guitar was a Harmony-made S.S. Stewart archtop, given to him after he was hospitalized for asthma. He strummed his way through Saint Patrick’s High School and the era’s folk music revival.

By 19, he was music director and band leader on Frank’s Bandstand , the Halifax segment of CBC TV’s national Music Hop series. One of the singers was Patrician Anne McKinnon, with whom Mr. Ahern was romantically involved. The relationship produced a daughter, Shannon Ahern. Ms. McKinnon’s sister was singer Catherine McKinnon; Mr. Ahern played guitar on her 1964 album The Voice of an Angel .

Before he devoted himself to producing records, Mr. Ahern spread his guitar talents among three groups, including the Offbeats. “I wore sunglasses in that band, because the lights annoyed me, but the image of the sunglasses became a very hip thing and generated lots of fan mail,” he said in 1996.
Another of his bands, the Nova Scotians, played Celtic jigs and reels. He changed his hairstyle and took off the sunglasses. “We wore plaid blazers and really itchy grey flannel pants,” he recalled.

On CBC’s Singalong Jubilee , he met Ms. Murray, a wholesome, honey-voiced native of Springhill, N.S. Though his career was thriving in Halifax, he grew bored with the scene. “I went to Toronto and starved for a while and talked Anne Murray into doing a really cheap album for $2,500,” he told Mix Magazine.

That album, What About Me , earned Ms. Murray a record deal with the U.S. label Capitol Records. Her 1973 album Danny’s Song , was partly recorded by Mr. Ahern live at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa and included the titular hit single written by Kenny Loggins. The follow-up LP Love Song included a cover of the Beatles’ You Won’t See Me , notable for the bassline by her bandleader Skip Beckwith.
“John Lennon came into my dressing room and said that version of You Won’t See Me was the greatest,” Ms. Murray said. “He just loved it, and it was Skip’s bassline.”

Mr. Beckwith presented Mr. Ahern with three songs written by the then unknown Nashville songwriter Mr. Crowell. One of them, Bluebird Wine , ended up as the lead track on Ms. Harris’s Pieces of the Sky album.

Ms. Harris and Mr. Ahern were married at his parents’ home on Jan. 9, 1977, one day after the record producer’s birthday. A snowstorm had delayed the arrival of guests flying in for the ceremony. It was the Alabama-born singer’s idea to get married in Halifax.
“I not only married Brian, I married his country,” Ms. Harris said. “I adored his mother, and I wanted to marry into his family.” The marriage produced a daughter, Meghann Robern.

Mr. Ahern produced Mr. Crowell’s debut 1978 album Ain’t Living Long Like This . “I called him ‘Bullseye,’” the Grammy Award-winning singer-songwriter said. “I knew it when I got into his creative zone. It might be a chuckle if I played the right note or sang the right thing. They were small gestures from Brian perceived in a large way.”

Mr. Ahern’s Enactron Truck is on display at the Musicians Hall of Fame & Museum in Nashville. He leaves his siblings Aileen Ahern, Nanci Ahern and Patrick Ahern; daughters, Shannon Ahern and Meghann Robern; and ex-wife, Emmylou Harris.

stories.title: Mother dead in Burlington, Ont., house fire that killed father and two children
stories.summary: Burlington, ONT. - The mayor of Burlington, Ont., says a mother has died in hospital after her husband and two of her children also died following a house fire over the weekend.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Burlington, ONT. - The mayor of Burlington, Ont., says a mother has died in hospital after her husband and two of her children also died following a house fire over the weekend.

Mayor Marianne Meed Ward says the fire is a “devastating tragedy” and her community has been deeply shaken by the loss of the four lives.

stories.title: Why is the federal government fighting to keep the Stellantis Brampton plant open? Ask our reporter
stories.summary: Transportation reporter Eric Atkins will answer reader questions on the sale, the government’s involvement and what could happen next
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
On Nov. 9, automaker Stellantis said it finalized the sale of its idled factory in Brampton, Ont. , to defence contractor Roshel Inc. for an undisclosed amount.

Stellantis idled the Brampton plant in 2023, laying off about 3,000 workers, with the intent of retooling for the Jeep Compass. But that work was halted after the U.S placed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars in early 2025. Stellantis, later that year, said the Jeep would not be built in Brampton, but at an idled plant in Illinois.

Since the announcement of the sale, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has been meeting with Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa in an effort to save the plant and thousands of Canadian jobs in the process.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24 at noon, transportation reporter Eric Atkins will be answering reader questions on the Stellantis sale, the government’s involvement and what could happen next.

By The Canadian Press

The court’s website says judges are to hear arguments from the province and UR Pride, a Regina LGBTQ group on March 22 and 23.

The judges are to hear arguments over whether courts can provide a declaratory judgment on a law if the notwithstanding clause was used.

stories.title: Stellantis workers left in limbo as car plant’s future is determined
stories.summary: The automobile manufacturer announced earlier this month that it sold its Brampton factory
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Samantha Lafave was pregnant with her second child and on maternity leave when she was laid off from her job at Stellantis NV’s Stla-N auto plant in Brampton, Ont., in 2023. Her husband, also a Stellantis employee, was laid off too.

Almost three years later, they are still off work, along with 2,200 other Stellantis employees who could only watch as their employer stopped retooling the plant in 2025, transferred the Jeep Compass planned for the plant to Belvidere, Ill., and then, ON Nov. 9, announced the factory was sold .

“Devastating,” is how Ms. Lafave, 34, described the news that could end 40 years of carmaking at the plant near Toronto.

She was watching TV with her family when the news of the plant’s sale broke. “A lot of tears were shed, and, you know, our children were a part of it,” Ms. Lafave said, describing “a great sense of loss and worry and stress and anxiety. Nothing good.”

Stellantis says Roshel Inc., a Brampton-based maker of armoured vehicles, has bought the plant for an undisclosed amount. The two companies say the plant could be used to make automotive and defence products, although they have provided no details.

The Unifor union and federal government accuse Stellantis of breaking commitments it made when it received $24-million in funding to refit the plant for the Jeep. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who failed last week to convince Stellantis to reverse the sale, is scheduled to meet on Friday with the chief executive officer of Stellantis, Antonio Filosa, along with Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor. Ms. Joly has said she is prepared to offer an “aggressive package” to save the plant.

Lou Ann Gosselin, a spokeswoman for Stellantis Canada, said in a statement it is “committed to engaging constructively” with the other parties at the Friday meeting.

“Our priority remains on working constructively with Unifor toward a fair, negotiated resolution that supports affected employees and recognizes their years of service,” Ms. Gosselin said.

Stellantis, which is struggling to make a profit and has excess global manufacturing capacity, has partly blamed the U.S. trade war for the closure and sale. Stellantis, formerly called Chrysler, makes Dodge, Fiat, Ram and several other brands. The company said it tried and failed to find a vehicle to build in Brampton. In the summer, the government and Unifor rejected Stellantis’s proposal to assemble Chinese cars from kits, saying the plan would create few jobs while contributing nothing to local supply chain.

Ms. Lafave worked at the plant for two years before being laid off. She worked in quality control, ON chassis assembly, as well as on the engine line, using an air ratchet to install parts. A new engine swung by every 90 seconds, and she performed the same task 450 times a shift, five days a week.

It was demanding, repetitive work, but she would go back in a second. She misses the closeness of her coworkers, whom she describes as like a family. She also misses the community work the union would do and aspired to a leadership role in Unifor.

“If I got the call tomorrow, I would go in and sweep the floor if I could,” she said. “I’m very [proud] of working where I was working. A lot of hard work goes into making cars.”

The Trump tariffs have devastated the Canadian car industry, centred in Southern Ontario. General Motors in 2025 idled its electric van plant in Ingersoll, and eliminated a shift at its Oshawa assembly plant this year. Stellantis’s Windsor plant, which makes minivans and muscle cars, has been closed for several weeks this fall, a move the company blames on sales and tariffs.

Industry observers say the Brampton sale is a serious blow to the Canadian economy, and a departure from the more patient moves by other car makers. GM has not sold its Ingersoll plant and has hung on to its Oshawa factory, which was closed for almost two years before reopening in 2021. Ford, meanwhile, stuck to its commitment to reopen the Oakville plant this fall, even after the U.S. tariffs went into effect.

Peter Frise, a University of Windsor professor, said the loss of an auto assembly plant is a “big deal.”

Every well-paying job at a car plant creates another seven to jobs in the community, Prof. Frise said. This extends well beyond the suppliers of car parts that are assembled at the plant.

“It’s the transport drivers who drive those parts back and forth between the plants. It’s the lady who works in the restaurant opposite all those factories where the workers have lunch or grab dinner before they go home, it’s the people who sell them work wear,” Prof. Frise said. “People will say, ‘Oh, who cares. It’s just one big plant.’ No, no, you don’t understand. This is the livelihood of whole communities.”

William Loseto, 59, is one of the Stellantis workers who has built a life around the plant. In 1987, he lined up with hundreds of others at an amusement park north Toronto to put in an application to the plant. He got hired by American Motors Corp., which had just opened the Brampton factory then sold it to Chrysler a few months later.

Mr. Loseto began in the body shop, welding panels for the AMC Eagle Premier. His starting wage was about $13 an hour, enough in those days to get married, buy a house in Brampton and raise a family.

“Everybody wanted these jobs,” Mr. Loseto said. “It was a fantastic wage then.”

The job still pays well, about $45 an hour, even as the cost of living and house prices have skyrocketed.

The laid-off Stellantis workers collect as much as 70 per cent of their wages in a settlement negotiated by Unifor.

Mr. Loseto agrees that’s not a bad wage to stay home, but said he and everyone else are still paying 100 per cent of their bills – car payments, mortgages and the rest. Everyone has had to cut back on their expenses amid all the uncertainty, he said.

“I’ve been lucky. The wife and I have made it work. The kids are older. They have jobs of their own. I’m in a good position. For others, unfortunately not, and I feel bad for those people,” Mr. Loseto said.

Mr. Loseto is baffled why Stellantis has sold the plant when other carmakers in Canada are still producing. “They made all kinds of mistakes and they’re blaming us,” he said. “Their bad decisions are costing us our future.”

He noted the plant in Belvidere to which Stellantis transferred the Jeep Compass is still idle, while the Brampton plant could be easily prepared to build again, with much of the new equipment in place.

“We’re more ready to build the Compass than they are,” he said.

The idled Belvidere plant is scheduled to reopen in 2028 and produce the Jeep Cherokee. Stellantis Canada referred questions about the Compass to its U.S. office, which declined to say when the car will be built in Belvidere.

A $250,000 award was announced for the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, commonly known as Goldy Brar and a high-ranking leader of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang

Members of the Bishnoi gang were among the 37 individuals charged by the F.B.I. on July 7 in a multi-year investigation into three India-based crime gangs. Jailed leader Lawrence Bishnoi is facing new charges, including in the 2023 murder of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada. So, who is the alleged crime boss of a gang accused of targeting Canada’s Sikh community? We spell it out.

November 19, 2026 at 5:16 p.m.

Bad guys can only hide for so long before someone spots them, Bolo (be on the lookout) program executive director, Max Langlois, said during a press conference at Toronto Police service headquarters Thursday morning.

His comments opened an announcement about the newest list of 25 most wanted fugitives in Canada. Langlois was joined by representatives of the Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Peel, Niagara and Waterloo regional police services.

“It is only a matter of time,” Langlois said. “Bad guys can only run for so long before police catch up … They can only be hidden for so long before someone decides their loyalties have changed.”

The Bolo Program was launched in May 2018 to amplify top-priority wanted notices issued by Canadian police services, Toronto police said.

The complete list of 25, with AI-generated animations of the fugitives, can be found here.

The announcement also included unusual AI-generated projections of life-size images of the most wanted, appearing like holograms as police service representatives spoke. “Today, not all fugitives could join us in person to attend, so we decided to invite them virtually to join us,” Langlois said.

Langlois began by focusing on the victim of the number two most wanted fugitive, Kyle Prouse, who is wanted for attempted murder.

His victim (unnamed during the announcement), shot earlier this year, was a member of the security team at a mall in Toronto, said Langois. “This is a man who has worked in the security and emergency management industry for many years. In that time, he has learned one thing to be true: it is only a matter of time,” said Langlois.

Speaking to Prouse directly, Langlois said the search for him has now widened beyond the police investigation. “Now you’ve got the Bolo Program. That means you’ve got the whole country, indeed the whole world, ON the lookout for you. Wherever you go, wherever you sleep, wherever you hide, it’s only a matter of time. Someone will spot you. Someone will call in that tip. Someone will turn against you, so get a lawyer and turn yourself in, because it only gets harder from here.”

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw followed Langlois to the podium.

“Since 2018, 19 of the 28 Toronto cases featured by Bolo have ended in an arrest, including the case that held last year’s number one spot,” Demkiw said.

Six Toronto most wanted cases are featured on the new top 25, the chief added, including two of the top three spots.

He stated that Bolo reward offered for Prouse’s arrest is up to $100,000.

Winnipeg Police Service Deputy Chief Cam MacKid spoke during the press conference about 32-year-old Satinderjeet Singh, who he said is more commonly known as Goldy Brar, and wanted on charges of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in relation to a shooting death in Winnipeg.

He sits at the top of the top 25 wanted list “and he’s there for a reason,” said MacKid. “The man is wanted for very serious crimes in three different countries, including ours … He’s known to have lived in California and various parts of Canada. His name and his face are already familiar to many people, including Canadian, U.S., and international law enforcement.”

At the time of the murder, said MacKid, he “was already widely recognized as a high-ranking leader of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang,” an India-based transnational organized crime syndicate, officially designated by the Canadian government as a terrorist entity in 2025.

“And we’re now asking all Canadians to be on the lookout for Goldy Brar. He should be considered extremely violent, armed, and dangerous,” he added, noting that Bolo is offering a reward of up to 250,000 Canadian dollars for information leading to his arrest in Canada or in the United States.

“This is the largest reward on today’s list … All he needs to be is arrested in our custody within Canada or the United States. If we put handcuffs on him, it’s worth $250,000 to the person who assists us with that. It’s that simple.”

The public was encouraged to read up on each of the 25 most wanted cases at the Bolo Program website.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.
