stories.title: Alleged high-ranking leader of Bishnoi gang wanted for ‘execution-style murder’ in Winnipeg is Canada’s top fugitive
stories.summary: A man described by police as a “high-ranking leader” of a terrorist organization and wanted for an “execution-style murder” in Winnipeg is the top fugitive in Canada. Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, has taken the top spot on the Bolo Program’s newly released list of Canada’s 25 most wanted fugitives. A reward of […]
stories.author: Kelsey Patterson
stories.content:
A man described by police as a “high-ranking leader” of a terrorist organization and wanted for an “execution-style murder” in Winnipeg is the top fugitive in Canada.

Satinderjeet Singh, more commonly known as Goldy Brar, has taken the top spot on the Bolo Program’s newly released list of Canada’s 25 most-wanted fugitives.

A reward of $250,000 is being offered for information leading to his arrest in Canada or the United States.

“The harm we believed he has caused and will continue to cause if he’s not caught extends well beyond one community, one city, or even one country. This is one extremely dangerous individual,” Winnipeg Police Service Deputy Chief Cam Mackid told the Bolo Program press conference.

According to authorities, Brar is an important member of the Lawrence Bishnoi group, a crime syndicate that was founded in India and listed as a terrorist entity by the Canadian government last year.

He’s wanted for the Sept. 20, 2023, murder of 39-year-old Sukhdool Singh Gill in the northwest Winnipeg neighbourhood of Castlebury Meadows.

Following what Winnipeg police have described as “one of the most complex, difficult investigations” the force has ever conducted — Project Krait — an arrest warrant for first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder was issued for Brar and his associate, 26-year-old Karanbir Singh, earlier this year.

“Both of these individuals remain at large, and we’re here today hoping to change that,” Mackid said.

Brar, who is believed to be evading arrest in Canada, is known to frequent Montreal and Brampton. He is described as six-feet tall, weighing 244 lbs., with dark hair, dark eyes and a medium build. He has tattoos on his right arm, including the face of his deceased cousin.

“He should be considered extremely violent, armed, and dangerous. He should not be approached,” said Mackid.

Brar has been charged in the U.S. for allegedly ordering the killing of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C., in 2023.

Brar, who police say first came to Canada on a student visa in 2017, is also wanted in India for a 2022 murder, and in the U.S. for racketeering. He has featured on the Fbi’s top-10 most-wanted fugitives list since September.

The FBI is offering a reward of up to US$1 million for information leading to his capture.

Other Winnipeg fugitives on the list are Paul Bonnick (No. 11) and Yusuf Abdulqadir Ali (No. 22).

Bonnick, 34, is wanted for second-degree murder in the May 23, 2025, fatal shooting of Ralph Moise, a member of the Sayisi Dene First Nation, in Winnipeg. Last October, Winnipeg police warned Bonnick May have fled to Ontario.

Ali, 31, is no stranger to Bolo’s list, having featured on it multiple times in the past. He’s wanted on two counts of attempted murder and several firearms offences in connection with attempted murders on Nov. 25, 2021, in Winnipeg’s West Broadway.

Police say two men sustained life-threatening gunshot wounds during the incident on Furby Street near Sara Avenue. Both victims were taken to hospital in critical condition, where they later recovered from their injuries.

Winnipeg police have said Ali is “gang-affiliated and involved in the drug subculture,” is considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

Bolo executive director Max Langlois issued a direct message to all the fugitives named on the list, saying increased public awareness makes it increasingly difficult for them to remain hidden.

“Every day you evade arrest is another day someone could recognize you,” Langlois said. “You have to be right every minute of every day. We, as a community, have to be right just once.”

The Bolo Program, also known as “be on the lookout,” is a national initiative that works alongside police services across Canada, using public awareness campaigns and cash rewards to help locate and apprehend some of the country’s most sought-after fugitives.

According to Bolo, its ranking system is based on factors including the seriousness of the alleged offence, the likelihood a fugitive is actively evading police, the amount of media attention generated by a case and the potential impact of public participation in locating the suspect.

–With files from Lucas Casaletto in Toronto

stories.title: Ottawa to study Divorce Act reform to address family violence
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal government says it's launching a study of ways to strengthen the Divorce Act, one day after critics condemned its handling of a private member’s bill that sought to curb parental alienation claims.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government says it’s launching a study of ways to strengthen the Divorce Act — one day after critics condemned its handling of a private member’s bill that sought to curb parental alienation claims.

The government said Thursday in a media release it is initiating a “cross-Canada, interdisciplinary study” of how to protect families affected by domestic violence.

“It is essential that Canada’s family justice system promotes the best interests of children, which includes responding effectively to family violence,” the release said.

On Wednesday, a women’s advocacy group said a parliamentary committee stripped private member’s bill C-223 of measures designed to protect women and children by removing clauses focused on parental alienation claims.

The National Association of Women and the Law says parental alienation claims can be used to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence, and to blame children’s fear of abusive fathers on parental alienation by mothers.

The government release, which doesn’t specifically mention parental alienation, says the study will build on “important issues” raised by Bill C-223.

It says the bill “generated significant discussion and feedback from individuals, organizations and experts, underscoring the importance of ensuring that the family justice system appropriately recognizes and responds to family violence.”

It also says more work is needed to determine where to go from here.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said in the release the study will “help build a family justice system that is more responsive to family violence and better meets the needs of children and families experiencing family violence across Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Ottawa — The federal government says it’s launching a study of ways to strengthen the Divorce Act — one day after critics condemned its handling of a private member’s bill that sought to curb parental alienation claims.
The government said Thursday in a media release it is initiating a “cross-Canada, interdisciplinary study” of how to protect families affected by domestic violence.
“It is essential that Canada’s family justice system promotes the best interests of children, which includes responding effectively to family violence,” the release said.

On Wednesday, a women’s advocacy group said a parliamentary committee stripped private member’s bill C-223 of measures designed to protect women and children by removing clauses focused on parental alienation claims.

The National Association of Women and the Law says parental alienation claims can be used to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence, and to blame children’s fear of abusive fathers on parental alienation by mothers.
The government release, which doesn’t specifically mention parental alienation, says the study will build on “important issues” raised by Bill C-223.

It says the bill “generated significant discussion and feedback from individuals, organizations and experts, underscoring the importance of ensuring that the family justice system appropriately recognizes and responds to family violence.”
It also says more work is needed to determine where to go from here.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said in the release the study will “help build a family justice system that is more responsive to family violence and better meets the needs of children and families experiencing family violence across Canada.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.
Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Olivia Chow turns down Toronto police board seat, sticks with deputy mayor roster
stories.summary: Ausma Malik will continue her role as Chow’s first deputy along with three other regional, nonstatutory deputy mayors
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mayor Olivia Chow shuffled her leadership team at city hall on Thursday, tapping a former Liberal MP to head up the housing committee and her Scarborough deputy as transit chair.

The appointments of Nate Erskine-Smith to housing and Paul Ainslie to transit were among the shakeups announced Thursday. Elsewhere, Chow opted for continuity with her last term, sticking to the same roster of deputy mayors and bringing back her budget chief.

“This is the team that will help deliver strong public services and take on the biggest challenges facing our city,” Chow said.

The mayor will look to take more direct control of the homelessness file by consolidating that work into her executive committee, Chow said. Her focus would go beyond temporary shelter, she said, to more lasting solutions with a goal to “significantly reduce” homelessness over the next four years.

“Other big cities have been able to deal with homelessness better than we have and there’s a lot of lessons that need to be learned there, and for me it’s a very, very high priority,” she said.

That work is expected to dovetail with the city’s housing committee, to be chaired by Erskine-Smith, who served briefly as a federal Liberal housing minister. He was elected to council after a failed bid earlier this year for the Ontario Liberal leadership, taking over the Beaches-East York seat vacated by Chow’s rival in the mayoral race, Brad Bradford.

Erskine-Smith, who earned a reputation as an independently minded Liberal on the party’s left flank, will lead the committee alongside vice-chair Diana Chan McNally, a former housing worker and advocate.

In a nod to Scarborough’s public transit frustrations, Chow tapped the area’s deputy mayor Ainslie to head up the transit board. A key issue for him will be advancing work on the Scarborough East LRT, a proposed 18-kilometre line, the mayor said.

Chow, who has overseen consecutive hikes to the police budget, turned down a seat on the police board, as she did in her first term. All post-amalgamation mayors have, at one time, delegated that position, but Chow was routinely criticized by rival Bradford for the move during the mayoral campaign.

It comes as the board is overseeing the service’s response to the explosive Project South scandal, which implicated several officers in a case tied to allegations of bribery, illegal searches and a murder plot.

Chow said the board and the chief had “been able to do good work to keep our city safe” but acknowledged “there’s always improvement.”

“I have confidence in how they have been managing in the last three years,” she said.

Newly elected Toronto Centre councillor Curran Stikuts will replace Lily Cheng on the board. In a statement, a spokesperson for Stikuts said the councillor “believes in transparent and accountable policing that is effective.”

“As a gay man who has spent most of his career working in the Church and Wellesley Village, the councillor is keenly aware of the work required to rebuild trust on our communities’ terms,” his chief of staff Nadine Tkatchevskaia wrote in a statement, which also referred to concerns raised by festival and street fair organizers about the rising policing costs.

Stikuts joins a board with returning councillors Amber Morley and Shelley Carroll.

Carroll expressed her openness on Thursday to return as board chair and is also set to reprise her role as Chow’s budget chief. As the mayor did in her inaugural speech, Carroll, a 23-year council veteran, alluded on Thursday to the city’s looming fiscal pressures. Officials have estimated a roughly $1 billion shortfall in the upcoming budget.

“We have a really tough budget coming this year, but it’s going to need the institutional memory. All the solutions that we’ve ever used are going to be employed here,” she said.

Affordable housing and provincial relations were at top of the mayor’s agenda during Thursday’s council meeting, two issues likely to figure prominently in her second term. Council advanced a program designed to give financial breaks to selected affordable rental housing developers and pushed back on proposed changes by Premier Doug Ford’s government to remove council’s representative from the Toronto Hydro board.

The provincial pushback at city hall Thursday went beyond proposed changes to Toronto Hydro. Mike Layton, newly minted chair of the infrastructure and environment committee, said one of his goals would be defending the city’s bike lane network from the province’s overhaul.

“Wasting taxpayer money was not the mandate that Mr. Ford was given,” said Layton, who sat on council for 12 years before stepping away in 2022 and then returning as University-Rosedale’s representative in last month’s election.

stories.title: Top court won't hear bid for class-action lawsuit on behalf of Indigenous children
stories.summary: The Supreme of Court of Canada will not hear a bid to certify a class-action lawsuit against Ottawa on behalf of Indigenous children who were taken from their families while living away from reserves and placed in non-Indigenous care.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme of Court of Canada will not hear a bid to certify a class-action lawsuit against Ottawa on behalf of Indigenous children who were taken from their families while living away from reserves and placed in non-Indigenous care.

The class-action claim is based on Canada’s duty to protect Indigenous children in care from harm, specifically as it relates to the loss of their identity.

The lawsuit challenges Canada’s role between Jan. 1, 1992 and Dec. 31, 2019 in allowing Indigenous children in state care to be placed in non-Indigenous homes.

In 2022, the Federal Court ruled the matter could go ahead as a class action for those affected in all provinces and territories.

Last year, the Federal Court of Appeal overturned that decision, saying Canada does not have possession, power or control over documents and information relevant to the claim.

The Court of Appeal also said the preferable course would be proceedings before courts that can compel the participation of provinces responsible for administration and delivery of child and family services to off-reserve Indigenous children.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Liberals expected to face House of Commons vote on Budget 2026 today
stories.summary: The federal Liberals are expected to face a vote in the House of Commons on their 2026 budget today. The budget, tabled Nov. 5, proposes billions of dollars in new borrowing and tax measures largely aimed at stimulating infrastructure construction and other capital projects. Because the Liberals now hold a majority of seats in the […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Members of Parliament have voted to pass the 2026 federal budget in the House of Commons.

Liberal MPs cheered and applauded as the Speaker announced the motion had passed with a vote of 162 to 151.

The budget, tabled Nov. 5, outlined billions of dollars in new borrowing and tax measures largely aimed at stimulating infrastructure construction and other capital projects.

Last year’s budget vote was a tense affair, as the minority Liberal government of the day needed members of other parties to either back its agenda or abstain from the vote to pass the spending plan.

Elizabeth May, then leader of the Green Party, cast the crucial vote that allowed Budget 2025 to pass, while two NDP and two Conservative MPs abstained or were absent.

Due to a series of byelections and floor-crossings over the last year, the Liberals now hold a majority of seats in the Commons, meaning the government can pass much of its agenda without the support of other parties.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has railed against the scale of the proposed borrowing in the budget, arguing it passes on costs to Canadians and fails to make life more affordable.

Parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan published a series of reports this week scrutinizing Budget 2026. She also raised red flags about the total amount of borrowing on the horizon but found the government is narrowly on track to maintain its fiscal anchors.

Improved revenues from better-than-expected economic results and a tailwind of tax dollars from higher global oil prices have improved the government’s bottom line since the spring.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the budget meets an uncertain moment by leveraging Canada’s relatively strong fiscal position to invest in its future.

Liberal members of Parliament clapped when Champagne voted in favour of the budget on Thursday, with the minister raising his arms in triumph.

“Confident countries invest,” Champagne told a Senate committee on Tuesday when asked why the government opted to spend much of its recent fiscal windfall rather than meaningfully paying down the deficit.

“We’re one of the very few countries in the G7 who can afford to do that, which is investing in the growth, but at the same time supporting Canadians at the time of need … with affordability measures,” he said.

Proposals in Budget 2026 such as the $36-billion productivity mega-deduction are aimed at convincing businesses to invest more in their own machinery and boost worker productivity.

Other budget measures would top up the Groceries and Essentials Benefit for lower-income families, offer support to Canada’s cultural sectors and ramp up efforts to eliminate homelessness.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis told reporters Thursday his party’s MPs would vote against the budget, which he argues caters to the needs of big business.

“Canadians need a budget that delivers real solutions to lower the cost of living: groceries, cellphones, housing and health care,” he said.

The budget’s title — “Maîtres Chez Nous,” or “Masters of our Destiny — borrows a phrase from Quebec’s Quiet Revolution, a period of rapid socio-economic change in the province.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet has criticized the Liberals’ use of the phrase, arguing the budget doesn’t give the province more control over its own affairs.

Even after a budget passes a vote, there are more hurdles to clear before its various proposals are enacted.

The government will go on to table one or more budget implementation bills. Those bills go through committee studies and votes and might be amended before passing into law.

The Liberals’ second budget implementation act for the 2025 budget wasn’t tabled until May of this year and is still working its way through Parliament. It includes provisions to deliver automatic federal benefits to low-income households and implement a framework for reporting cryptocurrency assets.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Other budget measures would top up the Groceries and Essentials Benefit for lower-income families, offer support to Canada’s cultural sectors and ramp up efforts to eliminate homelessness.
NDP Leader Avi Lewis told reporters Thursday his party’s MPs would vote against the budget, which he argues caters to the needs of big business.
“Canadians need a budget that delivers real solutions to lower the cost of living: groceries, cellphones, housing and health care,” he said.
The budget’s title — “Maîtres Chez Nous,” or “Masters of our Destiny — borrows a phrase from Quebec’s Quiet Revolution, a period of rapid socio-economic change in the province.
Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet has criticized the Liberals’ use of the phrase, arguing the budget doesn’t give the province more control over its own affairs.
Even after a budget passes a vote, there are more hurdles to clear before its various proposals are enacted.
The government will go on to table one or more budget implementation bills. Those bills go through committee studies and votes and might be amended before passing into law.

The Liberals’ second budget implementation act for the 2025 budget wasn’t tabled until May of this year and is still working its way through Parliament. It includes provisions to deliver automatic federal benefits to low-income households and implement a framework for reporting cryptocurrency assets.

stories.title: Nasa’s Voyager 1 is an awe-inspiring one light-day away from Earth
stories.summary: It is humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space
stories.author: Marcia Dunn
stories.content:
Nasa’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.

Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That’s how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 26 billion kilometres at the speed of light.

“Voyager 1 light-day distance confirmed ... Voyager 1 continues its journey into the unknown,” controller Nshan Kazaryan announced to cheers and applause.

For a spacecraft already loaded with historic firsts, it was an especially momentous milestone.

“Once again Voyager breaking records, breaking boundaries and taking humanity on a voyage,” Nasa’s science mission chief Nicky Fox said. “There’s no end for the Voyager mission.”

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our “Pale Blue Dot” in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.

Nasa could not confirm the newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory via the deep space telescope near Madrid. But that didn’t stop the space agency from wishing everyone a “Happy Voyager light-day … day!” via social media on Wednesday.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are Nasa’s longest-operating space missions, churning out data for nearly a half-century despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.

Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won’t reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.

Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 61,000 km/h with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.

Over the weekend, though, Voyager 1’s stream of science and engineering data came to an abrupt halt. The carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming in strong and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone. Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped. A similar problem three years ago was traced to an onboard computer.

Each Voyager carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase “Pale Blue Dot” for Voyager 1’s farewell glimpse of Earth.

Nasa expects the gold-plated phonographic records – time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them – to last more than 1 billion years.

“No matter how long it takes or how dark things get or what we think our limitations are, we should never stop shining and never stop reaching for the stars. For we never know how far we will go,” said deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University. “Shine on, Voyager, shine on.”

stories.title: Bradley Avenue extension opens, creating new east-west route in southwest London
stories.summary: A major road project in southwest London has reached a milestone with the opening of the Bradley Avenue extension between White Oak Road and Wharncliffe Road South.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A major road project in southwest London has reached a milestone with the opening of the Bradley Avenue extension between White Oak Road and Wharncliffe Road South.

The new stretch of road connects two previously separate sections of Bradley Avenue, creating a continuous route between Wonderland Road South and the White Oaks area.

The City of London expects Bradley Avenue to carry approximately 25,000 vehicles per day as southwest London continues to grow with new homes and businesses.

As part of the project, the existing section of Bradley Avenue between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard was widened from two lanes to four lanes to provide continuity along the corridor.

The project also included new sidewalks and cycling paths along the newly constructed roadway, as well as new cycling infrastructure beside existing sidewalks between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard.

A new traffic signal has been installed at Bradley Avenue and Wharncliffe Road South to improve traffic flow and make it easier for motorists to turn onto and off Bradley Avenue.

In addition to road improvements, the project included upgrades to underground water and sewer infrastructure to support existing and future development in the area.

Stormwater management work was also completed, including the creation of a new creek channel and wetland areas, improvements to drainage infrastructure and upgrades to a stormwater management pond. The city said the work is intended to improve water quality and help reduce the risk of flooding during heavy rainfall.

“Opening Bradley Avenue on schedule and before winter is an important achievement for the City and everyone involved. There was a lot happening beyond the road itself, and bringing all of that work together took coordination across the project. We’re excited to see people now using this new connection,” said Jennie Dann, director of construction and infrastructure services.

Construction on the project began in June 2025. The city said all major road work was completed on schedule, allowing the new section of Bradley Avenue to open to traffic in November 2026.

Crews are expected to return in spring 2027 to complete final asphalt paving, landscaping and remaining finishing work.

content_blocks.text: As part of the project, the existing section of Bradley Avenue between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard was widened from two lanes to four lanes to provide continuity along the corridor.

The project also included new sidewalks and cycling paths along the newly constructed roadway, as well as new cycling infrastructure beside existing sidewalks between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard.
A new traffic signal has been installed at Bradley Avenue and Wharncliffe Road South to improve traffic flow and make it easier for motorists to turn onto and off Bradley Avenue.

content_blocks.alt: Bradley Avenue - london - nov 2026
content_blocks.caption: A photo showing a new naturalized creek channel and wetland areas to support water quality and reduce flooding risk near the new Bradley Avenue extension. (Source: City of London)

content_blocks.text: In addition to road improvements, the project included upgrades to underground water and sewer infrastructure to support existing and future development in the area.

Stormwater management work was also completed, including the creation of a new creek channel and wetland areas, improvements to drainage infrastructure and upgrades to a stormwater management pond. The city said the work is intended to improve water quality and help reduce the risk of flooding during heavy rainfall.

“Opening Bradley Avenue on schedule and before winter is an important achievement for the City and everyone involved. There was a lot happening beyond the road itself, and bringing all of that work together took coordination across the project. We’re excited to see people now using this new connection,” said Jennie Dann, director of construction and infrastructure services.

content_blocks.alt: Bradley Avenue - london - nov 2026
content_blocks.caption: A photo showing the newly built road connecting Bradley Avenue between White Oak Road and Wharncliffe Road South, along with new cycling paths, and sidewalks. (Source: City of London)

content_blocks.text: Construction on the project began in June 2025. The city said all major road work was completed on schedule, allowing the new section of Bradley Avenue to open to traffic in November 2026.
Crews are expected to return in spring 2027 to complete final asphalt paving, landscaping and remaining finishing work.

stories.title: Staples plays with its business model in bid to resurrect Toys ‘R’ Us brand
stories.summary: Storied toy retailer, fresh out of creditor protection, is opening in 300 Staples stores in Canada
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
Standing in a back quadrant of a Staples Canada store north of Toronto in the city of Richmond Hill, Mike Rinaldi is at the centre of a child’s dreamscape.

Behind the company’s chief merchandising officer are rows of Hot Wheels, Barbies and dumpling-shaped squishies, alongside bins crammed with junk food-inspired plushies and bouncy balls. A giant Lego spaceship towers over him and birthday balloons are bobbing in the background.

The sprightly scene comes courtesy of Toys “R” Us Canada – the storied toy retailer freshly out of creditor protection and now connected to the U.S. firm behind Party City, Chia Pets and the Elvis Presley attraction, Graceland.

In a bid to bring back the beloved brand, Toys “R” Us and Parties “R” Us departments are moving into portions of 300 Staples Canada stores by the end of next year. The location Rinaldi is visiting, a short drive from Staples Canada’s headquarters, is the first to be transformed.

There’s a lot riding on the plan – for both retailers. Toys “R” Us Canada owner Next Century and affiliate Ad Populum will be testing just how many customers are sticking with the brand. Meanwhile, Staples Canada will be trying to convince shoppers it’s more than an office and school supplies mecca or the place you go when you need to print something.

Put simply, Rinaldi is trying to prove “Staples is evolving.”

It wants to be the place people can go to “get multiple things done in today’s world where everyone’s in a hurry,” he explained.

In keeping with that ethos, some of the retailer’s locations have welcomed workspaces, coffee shops and Service Ontario branches processing drivers’ licenses, health cards and vehicle permits in recent years. Many have drop-off points for Amazon returns, and others have growing travel departments selling suitcases, neck pillows and toiletry bags.

Now, it also wants to be a destination for birthdays, Christmas and any other occasion when shoppers May need puzzles or pinatas.

If you ask Rinaldi, it made sense to repurpose space already dedicated to kids and events to make room for the partnership. Staples Canada already sold toys, but they had more of an educational slant. The Toys “R” Us Canada partnership blows wide open that assortment under a brand name that carries a lot of nostalgia.

In fact, Rinaldi can’t help but grin while recalling buying wrestling figurines from the toy chain in the ’80s that he and his pals wrapped in newspaper to carry home during a rainstorm.

“The newspaper imprinted on the figures and the figures were destroyed, but I was so excited to get those,” he said.

That trip to Toys “R” Us would have been when the chain was in its infancy in Canada and quickly morphing into the go-to place for every kid’s wants.

Later, when Walmart WMT-Q , Costco Cost-Q and Amazon Amzn-Q started more aggressively cornering the market with lower prices, Toys “R” Us started to fumble. By the time it was bought by Ancaster, Ont., entrepreneur Doug Putman in 2021, the retailer’s death knell was already ringing.

The last few years brought inflation, rising labour costs, supply chain disruptions and a shift toward e-commerce – all factors Toys “R” Us Canada cited when it claimed insolvency in February and then, sold its trademarks to Ad Populum in June.

Staples Canada has not been immune to such pressures.

“Its core business – office supplies, paper, ink and printing – has been shrinking for years. Customer preferences keep evolving and remote work has only sped that up,” said Liza Amlani, the founder of consultancy company Retail Strategy Group, in an e-mail.

“When your core categories shrink, you either shrink the store or you give people new reasons to walk through the door. Staples is choosing the second option.”

While it takes time to get shoppers to connect longstanding retailers with new business segments like coffee or coworking areas, Amlani thinks toys are a worthy foray for Staples.

“Toys and party supplies speak to the same parent that shops back-to-school at Staples,” she said. “It extends the relationship and ... gives families a reason to come back beyond back-to-school.”

Plus, the toy business can be lucrative. Hook a customer when the child they’re buying for is very young and you might win their toy purchases for years to come.

However, there are many businesses vying for the same relationship. Amazon, Costco and Walmart have used their high sales volumes to offer bargain prices, squeezing competitors and luring in customers.

At the same time, big brands like Lego have aggressively expanded their own store footprints and the tariff war has spurred more Canadians to support small, local toy shops.

But perhaps the biggest challenge Staples will face is awareness, said Graham Heuman, retail insights lead at JC Williams Group.

“They’re going to be working pretty hard on just identifying that Staples is now going to be a place you can go for toys through Toys ‘R’ Us,” he said.

“Some consumers May be a little confused by the store-in-store concepts, if they’re not used to it.”

The company’s been trying to address the possible awareness gap by marketing itself on social media and the doors to the Richmond Hill Staples have a Geoffrey giraffe mascot popping through a pane that also reads “Toys ‘R’ Us lives here now!”

Step inside and it’s hard to miss the bright signage beckoning people to the toy department, where there are stations to test out Magna-Tiles and Kinetic Sand.

Rinaldi said the chain plans to draw in others by hosting crafting events and playtime sessions in partnership with Lego, Ravensburger and more.

But on a recent Tuesday afternoon, most seem to be there because of osmosis.

A woman who had visited the print centre chased after a toddler enthralled with the department, while an older fellow who’d previously browsed the electronics area rooted through a bin of stuffed animals shaped like pizza boxes and ramen bowls.

Rinaldi stopped to ask one man leaving the parcel drop-off area what he thought of the Toys “R” Us section.

“Are you going to put a Walmart in here?” the man asked as he sped toward the store’s exit. “What’s next?”

Rinaldi just nervously laughed.

stories.title: Two people taken to hospital after apartment fire on Kipps Lane
stories.summary: Fire investigators remain on scene and are working to determine the origin, cause and circumstances of the fire.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people have been taken to hospital, one in life-threatening condition, after an apartment fire in London on Thursday morning.

According to Deputy Chief Matt Hepditch, emergency crews responded to the fire in a fourth floor unit of a building in the 700 block of Kipps Lane.

Hepditch also said smoke alarms were working at the time crews arrived.

Witnesses told CTV News they could see CPR being performed on an elderly woman.

Fire investigators remain on scene and are working to determine the origin, cause and circumstances of the fire.

The Ontario Fire marshal’s office has also been called.

stories.title: Travel advisories can help assess China detention risk, Anand says
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says travel advisories can help Canadians assess whether they are at risk of arbitrary detention when visiting China
stories.author: Dylan Robertson

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says travel advisories can help Canadians assess whether they are at risk of arbitrary detention when visiting China , when asked whether it’s a safe country to visit.

“At Global Affairs Canada we have travel advisories. We are ensuring that those are always accurate,” said Anand, who would not specify whether Canadians are safe when they visit China.

“There is an initiative between our countries to ensure that the people-to-people ties can be stronger, and that includes through more flights,” she said, as well as more exchanges and China dropping a visa requirement for Canadian tourists.

She was speaking on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or Apec, in China’s tech megacity, Shenzhen.

This week, Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, and they announced renewed funding for university exchanges, and promised more partnerships for people-to-people ties, such as in cultural fields.

Jeff Nankivell, head of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, said it’s important to pursue deeper exchanges in spite of the risks.

This is why Global Affairs Canada puts resources into updating and verifying information in its travel advisories, he said.

Nankivell said detainment is a concern for China in particular because its justice system falls short of international standards, including in corruption and transparency.

“There are unusual risks for China that we do not see in other countries. And so you have to take the travel advisory quite seriously, and make your own assessment as to whether there are factors in your case that could put you at risk,” Nankivell said in an interview.

Canada’s travel advisory for China suggests visitors “exercise a high degree of caution,” which is the second-lowest risk level of the four Ottawa uses. Canadians visiting China face risks of arbitrary detention or not being able to leave the country, it says.

“Canadian business travellers have been detained and had their passport confiscated as a result of business disputes with their Chinese counterparts,” the travel advisory reads.

“Disputes are often costly and prolonged, and you May be subject to a travel ban restricting you from leaving the country until the matter is resolved.”

It adds that foreign drivers in China face “harsh penalties.”

“If you’re suspected of being responsible for road accidents, police officers can detain you until their case is closed, which can take years,” the advisory says.

The advisory warns that China can also withhold passports for foreigners suspected of a crime or detain them for up to 37 days without charges.

The advisory warns that Canadians detained on national security charges, such as “upsetting social order,” could face six months of detainment before formal arrest, and a trial in a closed court.

The advisory has particular warnings for China’s Xinjiang region, where the United Nations in 2022 reported that China had committed serious human rights violations against Uyghurs that could constitute crimes against humanity. China strongly disputes those findings.

“Chinese authorities are increasingly detaining ethnic and Muslim minorities in the region without due process. There are reports of extrajudicial internment and forced labour camps. Family members of Canadian citizens with Chinese citizenship have been detained,” the travel advisory reads.

Nankivell said someone in China on a student or faculty exchange, or on their first business trip to China, faces the constant risk of “serious consequences imposed in an arbitrary way” by authorities.

“One example would be someone, a university student who finds themselves in the wrong place at the wrong time, like they’re at a bar and a fight breaks out, and everyone at the bar gets detained,” he said.

“The highest risk these days is probably one that has existed for many years, which is if it’s something related to your business.

“That you’ve had a falling out with a local partner — or you have local partner you know who is a bad actor and has access to friends in the local justice system and is able to to get you detained.”

Nankivell said it’s unlikely Canada would face a full-blown diplomatic crisis in which a senior CEO is arrested, or something similar to the Two Michaels case in 2018, when China detained two Canadians for more than 1,000 days in response to the Vancouver house arrest of a tech executive facing U.S. charges.

He said the fact that it happened makes a repeat all the more likely.

Anand told reporters the safety of Canadians in China was among the issues she raised with her Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, at the start of their Tuesday meeting.

“I raised human rights, democratic principles including freedom of the press, the treatment of Canadians in China, transnational repression — and the importance of these fundamental principles to our country and to our people,” she said.

Anand argued that more dialogue with China helps deal with issues as they emerge, but wouldn’t say whether that lowers the risk of detainment from happening in the first place.

“You need to have the fortitude to sit at the table and to raise topics that you know have not historically (been) met with a welcome doormat — that you are able to sit across the table and raise these issues, because of the regularized communication channels that our systems are engaged in,” she said.

stories.title: One person taken to hospital after apartment fire on Kipps Lane
stories.summary: Fire investigators remain on scene and are working to determine the origin, cause and circumstances of the fire.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people have been taken to hospital after an apartment fire in London on Thursday morning.

Deputy Chief Matt Hepditch, emergency crews responded to the fire in a fourth floor unit of a building in the 700 block of Kipps Lane.

The extent of the injuries was not immediately known.

Witnesses told CTV News they could see CPR being performed on an elderly woman.

Fire investigators remain on scene and are working to determine the origin, cause and circumstances of the fire.

No further information has been released.

smoke detectors were operational when firefighters arrived

stories.title: Winnipeg Blue Bombers fire head coach Mike O’Shea after 12 seasons
stories.summary: Call of the Wilde: Montreal Canadiens rebound for an impressive win in New Jersey
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Winnipeg Blue Bombers have fired head coach Mark O’Shea, marking the end of a 12-season era that saw five straight Grey Cup appearances and back-to-back championships.

Wade Miller, president and CEO of the Winnipeg Football Club, made the announcement Thursday morning.

“A difficult day for the organization and we’re going to move in a new direction. (I) just have all the appreciation for an unbelievable coach that’s coached for 12 years and has just left a mark on the Winnipeg Football Club in such a positive way,” Miller said.

The Bombers finished the 2026 regular season with a 9-9 record and entered the playoffs as the East Division crossover team. The club defeated the Toronto Argonauts 25-22 in the East Division semifinal before losing 33-23 to the Montreal Alouettes in the East final.

Speaking with reporters, Miller said the Bombers, like every other CFL team, have the goal of winning a Grey Cup each season.

“(When) we don’t win the Grey Cup, you didn’t do what you set out to do,” Miller said, adding that parting ways with O’Shea was a “very difficult decision.”

“It’s just where I believe we need to go as an organization. And if it works out, which we believe it will, it’s great for the organization. If not, then it’s my responsibility.”

He said he met with O’Shea on Wednesday, but would not divulge the details of that conversation.

“The way he’s done everything in this organization, (he) did it with class. And he is just such a competitor and great individual,” Miller said.

Miller added that the club believes “it was the right time” after evaluating its future. He noted what that exactly looks like remains unclear.

The club president said the team hopes to bring in a new coach that will hold the standards O’Shea set and help to grow the organization.

“There’s candidates out there that are strong and we want to win next year, and we want to win in five years. And we’re going to look for the right candidate for that,” he said.

The successful candidate, he said, will be a knowledgeable “leader of men” with a passion for the sport.

Derek Taylor, voice of the Bombers on 680 Cjob, said he was not shocked by the news, but found the timing surprising. O’Shea signed a three-year extension with the Bombers last year .

“The Bombers, by doing this, have to eat the final two years of his contract, and I mean, that’s a significant sum of money,” Taylor told Global News.

“The fact that it happened, I don’t think surprises me because results have kind of diminished over the years. Fifteen wins to 14 to 11 to 10 to nine. They didn’t make the West playoffs in the last two years.”

Taylor said the locker room will feel the absence of the man who has loyally led them for the past dozen seasons. He recalled players saying they signed with Winnipeg to play for O’Shea, and others, he said, extended their contracts to stay loyal to their coach.

“I think some will miss him. I, honestly, wonder if guys who May have been on the fence about retiring, if this tips them toward retirement. Whether because they loved working with O’Shea or they don’t want to deal with a new regime in the final years of their career,” Taylor said

Now that O’Shea’s tenure at the head of the team has ended, Taylor said he will be beloved and missed by Bombers fans and remembered as the winningest coach in the team’s history thus far.

“Nobody has a tenure like this in pro sports anymore. Mike O’Shea was the fourth longest tenured coach in North American sports, before he was fired. His impact on this team has been profound,” Taylor added.

O’Shea leaves Winnipeg as the franchise’s all-time leader in coaching wins with a 126-86 regular-season record.

He led Winnipeg to five straight Grey Cup appearances, in 2019 and 2021-2024, and won back-to-back championships in 2019 and 2021.

O’Shea was named CFL coach of the year in 2021 and 2022.

The future looks bright for the Bombers, according to Taylor, who said he believes Miller must have a plan if he made the move to fire his coach.

“When you fire Mike O’Shea, I have to believe that Wade Miller at least has an idea of who he wants to be the head coach. And we could throw out a bunch of names,” Taylor said – pointing to the potential for hiring members of other CFL teams’ coaching staff, as well as in-house hires.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew thanked O’Shea on social media.

He said the two Grey Cups the coach brought to Winnipeg were “a true testament to his coaching, the players on the field, and the brass – including Wade Miller for building such an unforgettable team.”

— With files from The Canadian Press.

stories.title: Former top Mountie to be sentenced for assault on teen in B.C. court
stories.summary: A former senior RCMP officer who held a teenager off the floor by their neck while off duty is expected to be sentenced Thursday in a British Columbia provincial court.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A former senior RCMP officer who held a teenager off the floor by their neck while off duty is expected to be sentenced Thursday in a British Columbia provincial court.

David Teboul resigned as an RCMP assistant commissioner before pleading guilty on Oct. 28 to assaulting the 16-year-old at a lacrosse game that also involved the officer’s son.

The court heard in an agreed statement of facts that Teboul’s son got into a verbal altercation with the victim and Teboul intervened, holding the teen by the neck twice, first briefly, then bending the victim over a low wall for about 15 seconds.

Special prosecutor Andi MacKay told the court last month the attack was unprovoked and Teboul’s account of what happened was different than what security camera footage showed.

MacKay told the court Teboul declared he was an officer during the assault, which May have deterred the teen from fighting back, and she has asked the court to impose an 18-month suspended sentence.

Teboul’s lawyer has asked the court for a conditional discharge, meaning he would not have a criminal record if he abided by conditions imposed by the judge.

The RCMP said last month that Teboul voluntarily submitted his discharge document over the summer and retired after 29 years of service.

stories.title: New designer drug found in Toronto fentanyl supply
stories.summary: A new opioid part of an emerging class of designer drugs has been found in fentanyl samples in Toronto, according to a drug monitoring program.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
A new opioid part of an emerging class of designer drugs has been found in fentanyl samples in Toronto, according to a drug monitoring program.

It’s the sixth new substance to be found in the city’s fentanyl supply so far this year, as reported by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service, raising concerns about the ongoing contamination and ever-changing nature of the street supply driving Canada’s opioid overdose crisis.

Karen McDonald, executive director of the drug checking service that operates out of St. Michael’s Hospital, said little is known about the new drug that was first found in four fentanyl samples in October. It is so new, it doesn’t even have a generic name yet.

N’-Phenethyl-5-chloro nor-orphine or N’-Phenethyl-6-chloro nor-orphine — the two drugs are so chemically similar the drug checking service said it can’t currently differentiate between them — has also been detected in Vancouver.

The drug is part of the orphine class of opioids, a potent group of designer drugs that have increasingly been on the radar of global monitors.

Late last year, Toronto’s Drug Checking Service started finding cychlorphine, an orphine-class opioid believed to be about 10 times stronger than fentanyl, in the city’s illicit drug supply.

But with next to no available research, the strength and effects of the novel orphine found in Toronto and Vancouver in October is unknown, McDonald said.

“This is a really good example of what we’re dealing with, with the unregulated fentanyl supply. It is just evolving, and the substances that are presenting are incredibly novel,” she said.

Cristiana Stefan, a lab director and clinical biochemist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, has concerns about how the orphine May interact with other drugs.

“It’s never good news whenever there is something else in the supply,” she said.

Stefan and her team, who analyze and identify the drugs collected by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service, spent weeks trying to unmask the unknown substance they were seeing in October’s samples using instruments that blast molecules with intense energy until they break down into fragments.

The biochemist’s concern about the novel orphine’s interactions with other drugs is made all the more salient given that drugs sold as fentanyl in Toronto hardly come as advertised.

The vast majority of “fentanyl” samples collected by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service — 96 per cent in the service’s latest report — were cut with at least one non-opioid drug, usually a veterinary tranquillizer or benzodiazepine, a class of depressants that includes Xanax.

During the same period, 83 per cent of fentanyl samples were found to contain multiple high-potency opioids and more than a quarter contained all three — a high-potency opioid, a vet tranquillizer and a benzodiazepine.

The share of overdose deaths across Canada involving multiple substances has been on the rise, according to the latest data.

From 2018 to 2023, the Public Health Agency of Canada found the percentage of opioid or stimulant overdose deaths involving three or more substances rose to 42 per cent from from 20, representing 491 deaths in 2018 to more than 1,500 in 2023.

When Toronto’s Drug Checking Service first launched, the fentanyl supply was far less contaminated, McDonald said. She speculated there are a number of factors why the cocktail of substances sold as fentanyl is ever-changing.

The availability of precursor chemicals to synthesize opioids is affected by drug laws and scheduling, as governments across the globe attempt to keep up with emerging opioids and drug producers invent new ones to minimize risk and cost, McDonald said.

According to Dan Werb, a substance use epidemiologist and St. Michael’s Hospital Chair in Mental Health and Substance Use Disorders, the drug market has seen “absolute disruption” since fentanyl became the dominant opioid, taking over from heroin before it.

That’s when opioid production shifted from poppy fields in Southeast Asia, Afghanistan and parts of Western Mexico, to backyard laboratories across the world, Werb said. Suddenly, anyone with the right precursor chemicals and equipment could be an opioid producer.

Werb said drug producers also change their recipes in response to their clients.

“There’s an incentive for drug traffickers to produce these higher-potency opioid products. They test them, they introduce them, they see what happens. If too many people die, they remove them, maybe they reduce the potency and the cycle continues,” he said.

This vicious feedback loop played out with the rise and fall of carfentanil, an opioid about 100 times more potent than fentanyl.

According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, carfentanil was, at its peak, implicated in 20 per cent of apparent opioid overdose deaths in 2019 before gradually falling to three per cent in 2024.

Werb said drug producers lowering the potency of the illicit opioids they sell has been a driving factor in declining overdose deaths observed in Canada since 2023.

“What keeps me up at night is the fact that we do not control these markets. At any time, new products could be introduced. Now we’ve got orphine opioids, what people call now ultra-potent opioids,” Werb said.

“While we’ve seen these reductions really across most places in North America that have been previously hot spots of overdose mortality, that could change at any moment.”

stories.title: Chow to shuffle city hall leadership, decide whether to sit on Toronto police board
stories.summary: Olivia Chow is set to shuffle her leadership team at Toronto City Hall as new faces are set to be picked for high-profile committee roles.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Olivia Chow is set to shuffle her leadership team at Toronto City Hall as new faces are set to be picked for high-profile committee roles.

The striking committee will meet Thursday morning to finalize the picks to the city’s committees and boards.

Chow is expected to indicate whether she will join the police board, a seat reserved for the mayor but that she turned down during her first term.

The housing committee and transit board are guaranteed to see new leaders after Gord Perks retired and Jamaal Myers was defeated in last month’s election.

Chow will have seven new councillors to consider for appointments, including Mike Layton and housing advocate Diana Chan McNally.

Avi Lewis sees Montreal byelections as a crucial part of rebuilding the NDP

Ford says he won’t impose AI data centres on unwilling municipalities, bolstering municipal moratoriums

stories.title: As seen at the movies: The films that inspire our design senses
stories.summary: Design creatives talk about the movies that introduced them to the allure of a captivating environment
stories.author: Nathalie Atkinson
stories.content:
Movies are often a design lover’s introduction to the allure of a captivating environment. Ahead of the 2027 DesignTO Festival, Nathalie Atkinson asked design creatives to recommend their cinematic reference points

“When the characters are having an intimate conversation mediated through a piece of one-way glass, they are so close but so far apart. And the desert – where there’s no built environment. It’s more the absence of things that stuck with me: thinking about what’s not there is still part of an architectural imagination. There is space, there is landscape, and there is silence.” - Deborah Wang, artistic director of DesignTO and principal architect at dw/a

“People talk about The Godfather movies being operatic and dramatic but that’s underpinned by the restraint of their lighting and camerawork. There’s a lot of chiaroscuro and a lot of Caravaggio. Cinematographer Gordon Willis’s use of lighting is so intentional. The blacks from the shadows create architecture and negative space – an atmosphere. We don’t know that Willis ever read it but Tanizaki’s In Praise of Shadows is about allowing time to manifest itself in the house. He understood light as not just utility, but enough to create a psychological effect.” - Guido Costantino and Domenica Rodà, creative partners at Guido Costantino Projects

“Dogville brilliantly shows us how much of our behaviour and relationships are shaped by architecture, even when the architecture itself disappears. Walls are reduced to lines on the floor, but they still create privacy, security and boundaries. Our minds fill in the invisible almost immediately. Someone knocks on a door that isn’t there, and we accept that the door exists. We spend enormous effort constructing walls and boundaries, yet Dogville creates them with nothing but our imagination and a bit of social agreement. It makes me look at the world around me and wonder what else isn’t physically there but controls how I behave.” - Stanley Sun, co-founder and creative director of Mason Studio

“I love what I call ‘architecture of absolute intention’: the villain’s lair, the isolated modernist house or the sensual minimalist interior where nothing feels accidental. The house in Ex Machina is a perfect example. The architecture is seductive and elegant, and wholly sinister. Changes in level establish hierarchy. Circulation determines who can be seen and who disappears. Hidden spaces conceal. The architecture embodies the quieter villainy of class and removes us from the ordinary using scale, movement, concealment and revelation to influence how we feel.” - Jane Son, architect and co-founder of Casson Hardware

“ Blade Runner is apocalyptic but so atmospheric in the way it features people and neighbourhoods – the vibrancy of different street signs and streetscapes, like when Harrison Ford’s character Rick Deckard stops by the noodle bar. When you look at parts of Asia, like Singapore and Hong Kong, or even Istanbul, that compact, humane density is quite delightful. There’s a great restaurant in a back alley somewhere, or you can go vertically up the building to a great rooftop restaurant.” - Angie Jim Osman, designer and urbanist, and partner at Allies and Morrison

“Wings of Desire has always haunted me. Those big empty spaces, like the Berlin State Library, are amazing. But then these little intimate street scenes, like in front of the diner when Peter Falk is getting coffee. In his career, director Wim Wenders has been so fascinated with space. His newest movie is about Swiss architect Peter Zumthor. He has always loved architecture, and you really see it in the early films.” - Kyle Bergman, founder and director of the Architecture & Design Film Festival

“In the opening scene of Steve McQueen’s Lovers Rock , people come into a London home to set up a party. It’s 1980, so a lot of oranges, rugs and ornamental wallpaper that feel of that moment. The piece that really sits with me is the transformation of that room: they move the furniture, bring in the crates, set up the A/V. It becomes a social gathering, a dance floor. There’s something exciting about communities finding joy and community wherever they can, either by choice or because there’s no other place. It starts with the spirit of making space.” - Michael Nyarkoh, creative producer and cultural programmer

These interviews have been edited and condensed.

As part of The Globe and Mail’s programming during the DesignTO Festival, style and film columnist Nathalie Atkinson dissects the relationship between cinema and the work of designers at Toronto’s Revue Cinema on Jan. 26. The talk will be followed by a screening of Wes Anderson’s visually dazzling caper, The Grand Budapest Hotel. For more, visit designto.org.

content_blocks.text: Paris, Texas (1984)
content_blocks.html: Paris, Texas (1984)

content_blocks.text: “When the characters are having an intimate conversation mediated through a piece of one-way glass, they are so close but so far apart. And the desert – where there’s no built environment. It’s more the absence of things that stuck with me: thinking about what’s not there is still part of an architectural imagination. There is space, there is landscape, and there is silence.” - Deborah Wang, artistic director of DesignTO and principal architect at dw/a

content_blocks.text: The Godfather I & II
content_blocks.html: The Godfather I & II

content_blocks.text: “People talk about The Godfather movies being operatic and dramatic but that’s underpinned by the restraint of their lighting and camerawork. There’s a lot of chiaroscuro and a lot of Caravaggio. Cinematographer Gordon Willis’s use of lighting is so intentional. The blacks from the shadows create architecture and negative space – an atmosphere. We don’t know that Willis ever read it but Tanizaki’s In Praise of Shadows is about allowing time to manifest itself in the house. He understood light as not just utility, but enough to create a psychological effect.” - Guido Costantino and Domenica Rodà, creative partners at Guido Costantino Projects

content_blocks.text: Dogville (2003)
content_blocks.html: Dogville (2003)

content_blocks.text: “Dogville brilliantly shows us how much of our behaviour and relationships are shaped by architecture, even when the architecture itself disappears. Walls are reduced to lines on the floor, but they still create privacy, security and boundaries. Our minds fill in the invisible almost immediately. Someone knocks on a door that isn’t there, and we accept that the door exists. We spend enormous effort constructing walls and boundaries, yet Dogville creates them with nothing but our imagination and a bit of social agreement. It makes me look at the world around me and wonder what else isn’t physically there but controls how I behave.” - Stanley Sun, co-founder and creative director of Mason Studio

content_blocks.text: Ex Machina (2014)
content_blocks.html: Ex Machina (2014)

content_blocks.text: “I love what I call ‘architecture of absolute intention’: the villain’s lair, the isolated modernist house or the sensual minimalist interior where nothing feels accidental. The house in Ex Machina is a perfect example. The architecture is seductive and elegant, and wholly sinister. Changes in level establish hierarchy. Circulation determines who can be seen and who disappears. Hidden spaces conceal. The architecture embodies the quieter villainy of class and removes us from the ordinary using scale, movement, concealment and revelation to influence how we feel.” - Jane Son, architect and co-founder of Casson Hardware

content_blocks.text: Blade Runner (1982)
content_blocks.html: Blade Runner (1982)

content_blocks.text: “ Blade Runner is apocalyptic but so atmospheric in the way it features people and neighbourhoods – the vibrancy of different street signs and streetscapes, like when Harrison Ford’s character Rick Deckard stops by the noodle bar. When you look at parts of Asia, like Singapore and Hong Kong, or even Istanbul, that compact, humane density is quite delightful. There’s a great restaurant in a back alley somewhere, or you can go vertically up the building to a great rooftop restaurant.” - Angie Jim Osman, designer and urbanist, and partner at Allies and Morrison

content_blocks.text: Wings of Desire (1987)
content_blocks.html: Wings of Desire (1987)

content_blocks.text: “Wings of Desire has always haunted me. Those big empty spaces, like the Berlin State Library, are amazing. But then these little intimate street scenes, like in front of the diner when Peter Falk is getting coffee. In his career, director Wim Wenders has been so fascinated with space. His newest movie is about Swiss architect Peter Zumthor. He has always loved architecture, and you really see it in the early films.” - Kyle Bergman, founder and director of the Architecture & Design Film Festival

content_blocks.text: Lovers Rock (2020)
content_blocks.html: Lovers Rock (2020)

content_blocks.text: “In the opening scene of Steve McQueen’s Lovers Rock , people come into a London home to set up a party. It’s 1980, so a lot of oranges, rugs and ornamental wallpaper that feel of that moment. The piece that really sits with me is the transformation of that room: they move the furniture, bring in the crates, set up the A/V. It becomes a social gathering, a dance floor. There’s something exciting about communities finding joy and community wherever they can, either by choice or because there’s no other place. It starts with the spirit of making space.” - Michael Nyarkoh, creative producer and cultural programmer

stories.title: Bungalow’s low price a magnet for first-time buyers in Hamilton
stories.summary: This 577-square-foot bungalow sells for $400,000 after eight days on the market
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
67 Robins Ave., Hamilton, Ont.

Asking price: $409,000 (August 2026)

Selling price: $400,000 (September 2026)

Previous selling prices: $356,000 (May 2024); $200,000 (March 2017); $88,500 (June 2009)

Taxes: $2,382 (2026)

Days on the market: Eight

Listing agents: Michael St. Jean and Amrit Singh, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

The owners of this two-bedroom bungalow made some improvements after buying it for $356,000 in 2024. But, realizing they needed more space, they put their home on the market for a slight markup at $409,000 this summer. Buyers turned up at the first open house and throughout the rest of the week.

“It’s in a pretty attractive price bracket around $400,000,” said agent Michael St. Jean. “It’s move-in ready, and it’s in an in-demand area.

“There are a lot of first-time homebuyers trying to take advantage of more attractive price points and really considering Hamilton.”

As one of the few detached, single-storey options in the community, the home drew an offer just a week after launch. The sellers took it for $400,000.

“Bungalows are the least common of the house types you’d see downtown,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“People really do like the little bungalows; some people call them cottages. They’re cute, not huge, but you get everything you need.”

This bungalow, built more than 100 years ago, has 577 square feet of living space.

The last two owners replaced the roof, porch and back deck, and repaved the driveway on the 25- by 104-foot lot.

The kitchen and single bathroom were renovated. They added a sliding barn door to enclose a bedroom off the living room.

The basement was waterproofed.

“It’s 10 minutes, either by car or on foot, to pretty well everything you could want,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“Young families in the neighbourhood treat Halloween like they do Christmas with all the decorations and lights.

“It’s also close to the Hamilton field where the Hamilton Ticats play. People just walk to the game from their home.”

stories.title: Updated Toronto home sells above asking price in slower market
stories.summary: The semi-detached house received seven bids, down from 12 in 2023
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
495 Roxton Rd., Toronto

Asking price: $898,000 (October 2026)

Selling price: $1,125,495 (October 2026)

Previous selling prices: $1,115,000 (February 2023); $845,000 (May 2018); $440,000 (July 2008); $279,900 (July 2004); $137,000 (July 1997)

Taxes: $6,847 (2025)

Days on the market: Seven

Listing agents: Ken and Jaime Ramsay, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

Owners of this house near Christie Pits Park outbid 11 other house hunters to land the semi-detached in 2023. Since then, they have longed to move closer to family, even at the risk of selling their home at a loss in a quieter market. To guide them through the process, they brought back the same listing agents from 2023. They also chose the same low asking price of $898,000. This time, seven buyers made offers, the best of which came in at $10,495 over the purchase price of three years ago.

“The market overall is down substantially from when they purchased,” said agent Ken Ramsay.

“We surpassed their expectations because it sold for more than what they paid in early 2023.”

Co-listing agent Jaime Ramsay said generating a higher price from competing buyers is easier with turnkey properties. The last two owners of this nearly 130-year-old home made extensive upgrades, including a newly refinished basement recreation area and a freshly painted garage facing a laneway behind the 14- by 121-foot lot.

“The strategy does not work in every neighbourhood and on every type of house,” said Mrs. Ramsay. “They had a small gym at the back of the garage and were still able to park their car.

“As a housewarming gift, a sibling had a beautiful mural painted with a sea turtle.”

This two-storey house has 1,054 square feet of living space, including two bedrooms and two bathrooms.

There is a living room and an updated kitchen with quartz countertops.

The mud room has laundry machines and exits to a patio with a pergola.

“It’s a great condo or townhouse alternative,” said Mr. Ramsay.

“It’s walking distance to Bloor [Street] and Ossington station.”

stories.title: Canada’s tightrope walk with China
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the new Canada-China trade pact, and whether or not China is the right fit for Canadian diplomacy.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
The Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit is underway in Shenzhen, China, as some of the world’s biggest leaders meet to discuss trade, diplomacy and economic prosperity in the region.

Among those are Prime Minister Mark Carney, who’s met with both Chinese President, Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump to discuss our country’s trade relationship with the respective countries. Both of which carry very different tones.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Lynette Ong, director of China Governance Lab at the Munk School of Global affairs and public policy at the University of Toronto, and Michael Kovrig, a former diplomat who was detained in China for more than 1,000 days before being released in September of 2021. They discuss the new Canada-China trade pact, and whether or not China is the right fit for Canadian diplomacy.

stories.title: Jewish groups condemn Toronto conference set to host speakers such as Charlotte Kates, Khaled Barakat
stories.summary: 'An Iranian-backed, pro-terror conference in the heart of our country's largest city is a clear threat not only to our national security, but our democratic way of life'
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Jewish advocacy groups are urging the federal government to bar the U.S.-sanctioned Masar Badil from hosting a conference in Toronto later this month that will feature speakers such as Charlotte Kates, Khaled Barakat and Mohammed Khatib.

“An Iranian-backed, pro-terror conference in the heart of our country’s largest city is a clear threat not only to our national security, but our democratic way of life,” Max Robert, vice president of policy at the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, told National Post.

“Canada’s new National Security Strategy, the first in 20 years, warns that ‘threats once thought distant are now immediate and proximate.'”

Charlotte Kates, a co-founder of Vancouver-based Samidoun, which has been declared a terrorist entity by the Canadian government, at the funeral of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in Lebanon in February 2025. @charlottekates/X

On Thursday, Cija released a letter it sent earlier this month to Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, urging the government to stop the conference.

“The Minister is concerned by any gathering that May involve individuals associated with entities listed under Canada’s anti-terrorism laws,” David Taylor, a spokesperson for Anandasangaree, told National Post — although the statement did not mention the letter specifically.

“Law enforcement is responsible for investigating potential violations of the criminal law, including Canada’s anti-terrorism laws,” said Taylor in the statement. “If someone has relevant evidence, it should be provided to the police of jurisdiction.”

On Wednesday, the Association of Canadian Families of the Victims of October 7th released a statement, calling on the RCMP, Toronto police and the Canadian government to take action.

“I buried my child and now must watch the people who call his murder ‘courageous’ book a room in Toronto to hold a conference not just celebrating his death, but discussing what the path forward is to build on what happened on October 7th,” said Raquel Look. Her son, Alex, was murdered by Hamas terrorists in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

“This is not a protest or a debate about Israel. It is a victory party for terrorists, hosted in the country my son was a citizen of. Every official who has the power to stop it and does nothing needs to look our families in the eye and explain that choice.”

There are concerns over Kates, Khatib and Barakat, who are affiliated with Samidoun, also called the Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network, which is listed as a terrorist entity in Canada.

Kates was arrested by Vancouver police in 2024 after she praised the October 7 attacks. She has not been charged.

The U.S. Department of State called Samidoun “a sham charity that serves as an international fundraiser for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (Pflp) terrorist organization.” Barakat, a member of the Pflp’s leadership, was sanctioned by the U.S. in 2024.

Khaled Barakat shown in this undated photo. samidoun.net

B’nai Brith Canada, another Jewish advocacy group, said in a post on X that the conference was a “threat to our national security.”

The conference, set to take place on Nov. 28 and 29, is being organized by Masar Badil, or the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement.

The group operates as a front for the Pflp, the U.S. Department of the Treasury said in August 2026. The Pflp is designated in the U.S. as a foreign terrorist organization. Masar Badil is also “inextricably linked with Samidoun,” the department said.

On social media, the conference is described as a chance to “hear from liberated Palestinian prisoners, participants in the student intifada, journalists on-the-ground in West Asia, militant intellectuals and more,” according to organizers.

Another speaker being featured online by the group is Calla Walsh, who was reportedly placed on a U.S. government watch list. Masar Badil described her as co-founder of Palestine Action US, the American offshoot of the global direct action campaign against Israel-based Elbit Systems.

In mid-October, the Canadian arm of Palestine Action took responsibility for damaging a GeoSpectrum Technologies Inc. facility in Ontario. GeoSpectrum is a subsidiary of Elbit. The incident is being investigated by police as a hate crime.

In a September news release, Masar Badil said it would be proceeding in Toronto as planned after “Zionist attacks” and U.S. sanctions. It quoted Barakat, as an executive committee member, who said, “the Masar does not seek the approval of the colonizer, nor do we recognize their authority to define our struggle.”

“Our struggle is rooted in a continuous confrontation that will only end when imperialism is abolished and the Zionist entity is dismantled,” the news release said.

Masar Badil did not respond to National Post’s request for comment.

In Cija’s letter to Anandasangaree, it asked the federal government to put a stop to the conference to “demonstrate that Canada will not serve as a safe haven for Iran’s Islamic regime, terrorist organizations or their proxies.”

A spokesperson for Public Safety Canada told National Post in a statement that it does not “comment on specific organizations, individuals, or whether particular groups are subject to monitoring or assessment” in order to “protect the integrity of Canada’s national security.”

Cija recommended in its letter that individuals with documented ties to terrorist organizations be denied entry to Canada. It also asked that Masar Badil be labelled a terrorist entity.

“Listing an entity is an extensive process based on a high threshold that must be established through criminal or security intelligence reports,” Public Safety said in its statement. “Canada continues to assess additional entities that May pose a threat to people in Canada, Canadians abroad or Canada’s national security.”

Some speakers, Cija’s letter says, will be travelling from Iran and “have documented connections to the Islamic regime.”

Cija is especially concerned about the conference, considering Canadian security agencies have warned of a “realistic possibility” that Iran is behind a series of shootings targeting synagogues, businesses and the U.S. Consulate in Toronto, it said.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.
