stories.title: Grocery and drugstore retailer Loblaw reports Q3 profit and sales up from year ago
stories.summary: Brampton — Loblaw Cos. Ltd. reported its third-quarter profit rose compared with a year ago, boosted by the sale of its PC Financial business and retail sales growth.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Loblaw is in a bind as high fuel prices chip away at price-conscious consumers’ budgets, while large-scale suppliers push for price increases.

“We are still seeing a high increase from the big (consumer packaged goods companies) and we are pushing hard back on it because we don’t think it’s justified,” chief executive Per Bank told analysts on a conference call Thursday.

“We are seeing increases that are over and above the inflation rate right now. So, that’s going to be a big task for us to push back.”

Grocers have entered their typical period of price freezes ahead of the holiday season, meaning they will not accept any cost increases from suppliers between November and February, when consumers are more price sensitive.

But more requests are expected to trickle in when the freeze lifts early next year.

Richard Dufresne, Loblaw’s chief financial officer, said many vendors are locking in higher input costs going into the new year, compared to what they paid this year.

“This is sort of the noise that’s starting to filter through. So, we’re going to feel it more in 2027,” he said.

In an October report, Loblaw said the dollar value of proposed supplier increases rose 120 per cent in the fourth quarter from a year ago, even as the number of requests fell 35 per cent.

Meanwhile, consumers are buying less, as growth in the company’s food same-store sales — a key metric in the grocery industry — slowed to 0.6 per cent.

“Customers, they only have the dollars they have, and when they are forced to spend more on fuel, they have a budget left and an obvious place to go and save money is, of course, eating out, but it’s also groceries,” Bank said.

Dufresne said spending trends from PC Mastercard data showed consumer spending on fuel was up more than 20 per cent year-over-year between August and October.

“You can see that that’s where customers are forced to spend some of their money so that is definitely affecting retail sales throughout the country.”

The continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz stemming from the war in the Middle East has disrupted oil shipments from the Gulf region, keeping fuel prices higher and more volatile, while driving up overall inflation.

As headwinds mount, Loblaw is intensifying its bet on AI-backed chatbots to boost consumer loyalty.

The grocer announced on Wednesday it was partnering with Meta’s personal agent Muse to help shoppers plan meals or stay within a set grocery budget. Consumers can shop at Loblaw via ChatGPT already.

“It’s giving us more loyalty because we are one of the few where customers can shop like this,” Bank said.

But how much that drives up overall same-store sales is “really too early to tell,” he added.

Loblaw Cos. Ltd. reported its third-quarter profit rose compared with a year ago. It earned a profit attributable to common shareholders of $1.19 billion or $1.03 per diluted share for the quarter ended Oct. 10.

The result compared with a profit of $794 million or 66 cents per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

On an adjusted basis, Loblaw says it earned 74 cents per diluted share in its latest quarter, up from an adjusted profit of 68 cents per diluted share a year earlier.

Sales for the quarter totalled $19.86 billion, up from $19.16 billion in the same quarter last year.

Growing demand for generic weight-loss drugs, meanwhile, helped push drugstore retail same-store sales up 4.8 per cent. Pharmacy and health-care services same-store sales were up 7.6 per cent and front store same-store sales grew 1.6 per cent.

The company says 18 food and drugstores were opened and one drugstore was closed in its third quarter of 2026.

In July, EQB Inc. completed its acquisition of PC Financial, while adding two Loblaw nominees to its board.

Loblaw said the sale of PC Financial resulted in a gain, net of transaction costs, of $432 million, before income taxes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX: L)

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: The wild East Coast shores that draw surfers all year long
stories.summary: Just outside of Halifax, an unlikely surf scene is a delight – for those who can find it
stories.author: Carolina Andrade
stories.content:
Underexposed is a photojournalism series dedicated to shedding light on the unseen lives of Canadians in every province and territory. Learn more and share your thoughts with The Globe.

Surfing in Nova Scotia is a year-round affair.

On a recent mild November day at Lawrencetown Beach Provincial Park, a 45-minute drive east of Halifax, a car pulls up. The driver watches the ocean for a bit, then changes into a neoprene wetsuit, boots and gloves.

They grab a surfboard and head into the 10-degree water, paddling in search of a rideable wave. Meanwhile, a Sprinter van with Quebec plates arrives and two more surfers hop out.

Nova Scotia’s surf scene is a “hidden gem,” says Emily Hansen, who works at the nearby shop Lawrencetown Surf Co., a popular local hub for the community.

Surfers track swells generated by hurricanes along the Eastern Seaboard, following their path up to the Maritimes.

Unlike many other surf destinations, weather in Nova Scotia is not consistently sunny and calm. But the coastline here has its charm, and the people who love it really love it. Some surfers travel from as far as B.C. or California to catch North Atlantic swells.

“It’s not very predictable,” says Hansen, “and you appreciate the waves more because they are not as frequent.”

At his Dartmouth home, Toby Balch dries out his boots and gloves between sessions.

Local surfer Toby Balch is one of the founding members of the Surfing Association of Nova Scotia. His lifelong obsession began in 1983, when he was 17. Nowadays, surfers consult multiple apps to forecast swell conditions.

Balch has a collection of calendars that he’s used to manually record surf conditions. He checks them to track how the conditions have shifted from year to year.

Back when he started surfing, Balch remembers, he and a buddy used to phone the weather hotline, then climb a tree in Halifax with binoculars in hand to check for whitecaps 20 kilometres up the coast. “At the time, there were only about a dozen guys surfing in Nova Scotia,” he says.

In 1990, Balch was one of the first four Canadians to compete at the World Surfing Games in Niijima, Japan.

Now, he and his daughter, Juniper, 19, have a custom-made surfboard they can each use; Juniper chose the colour and Toby chose the dimensions with the help of a local surfboard shaper.

Rachel Barrett, a surfer, yogi and mother originally from New Brunswick, moved to the eastern shore of Nova Scotia to live by the ocean. She learned to swim as an adult, then did scuba diving, and finally felt ready to try surfing in her 20s. She’s never looked back.

She surfed while pregnant (twice) and has competed locally and internationally. She says she loves the sport for its healing aspects. “Being a Black surfer in Nova Scotia,” she notes, “is an honour and ode to the ancestors who did not have this same freedom on these shores.”

Montreal-based river surfers Alexis Roy and Phil Charest travelled to Nova Scotia for three days just to surf. They surfed any chance they got, bringing along a board made entirely from timber harvested in Quebec and shaped by Roy.

“There’s nothing quite like feeling a peeling wave unfold right in front of you – that’s exactly what we’re chasing in Nova Scotia,” says Charest.

Lawrencetown Surf Co.’s owners, Nico and Jill Manos, also run the East Coast Surf School, which is a draw for beginner surfers from all over the province and beyond.

The local surf community is “kind of built around just loving the sport and appreciating every wave that you get,” says Hansen.

Carolina Andrade is a Canadian-Chilean photojournalist, writer and surfer based in Halifax, Nova Scotia/Kjipuktuk Mi’kma’ki. She focuses her lens on the light within stories that invite compassion and remind us of our shared humanity. Her work can be found in The Globe and Mail, The New York Times, The Guardian and more.

stories.title: The Liberals tilt the table for Stellantis, again
stories.summary: Subsidies justify political meddling, which then is used to justify additional subsidies
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
In a different universe, the federal government would be celebrating the announcement that Stellantis plans to sell its idled Brampton, Ont. factory to defence contractor Roshel as a demonstration of the ability of the private sector to adapt to a rapidly changing global economy.

In that reality, Ottawa would also be pointing to the fact that Roshel would be creating jobs for some Stellantis workers laid off nearly three years ago, while buttressing Canada’s ability to manufacture military vehicles.

We do not live in that universe. Instead, we dwell in the one where Ottawa has a vested interest in deterring Stellantis and Roshel from a transaction that makes sense economically, but not politically.

Three years ago next month, Stellantis laid off 3,000 workers, with plans to retool the Brampton facility to produce electric vehicles. The company and the federal government had signed a deal in which Ottawa would hand over up to $529-million to convert plants in Brampton and Windsor. That was part of a broader strategy by the Trudeau (and then the Carney) government to commit tens of billions of taxpayer dollars to create an EV industry in Canada.

And it is that contract that Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has brandished in threatening Stellantis with legal action to recover “hundreds of millions” of dollars if it goes ahead with the planned sale to Roshel. (The company has said it will return the $24-million that it says it has received to date for the Brampton facility.)

Ms. Joly has not just brandished a cudgel; she has also waved carrots, holding out the prospect of additional subsidies to Stellantis to keep the plant open, and bring back the remaining 2,200 laid-off Stellantis workers. “Our goal is to make sure that we are able to protect the jobs, and so the government of Canada is willing to play its part to protect the jobs,” said Ms. Joly, who is to meet with Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa in Toronto on Friday.

There is a problem both with Ms. Joly’s cudgel, and with her carrot.

On the cudgel side of the ledger, despite the Industry Minister’s intimations, the contract signed with Stellantis has language that the company could point to in the event of a formal legal dispute. There is, as any prudent lawyer would hope, a boilerplate force majeure clause.

But the arrangement also contains a clause referring to the possibility of several factors – including “trade levies” – having a material impact on the completion of the conversion project, and obliging the parties to discuss amendments, and in doing so, to act reasonably. Has the government fulfilled that obligation? A lawsuit would certainly bring that question out for public consideration.

As for the carrot, well, there is the nub of the problem: Would Ms. Joly be so vigilant in her defence of those 2,200 jobs if not for the subsidies committed to the plant, and the political vulnerability that accompanies that largesse?

One can feel sympathy for every one of those workers, facing either unemployment or a reduced wage, and still ask: Why should Ottawa invest so much time and money in an attempt to preserve their jobs?

The Stellantis workers represent a fraction of the Canadians who lost their jobs to layoffs. As of October, 932,400 workers had been permanently laid off in the previous 12 months and had still not found a new job, according to Statistics Canada. Why is each of those Canadians’ jobs worth less of a fight? Where is Ms. Joly’s news conference where she advocates on their behalf? Which CEO does she propose to meet to force their rehiring?

The answer, of course, is that the Liberals are defending not just the jobs of those laid-off Stellantis workers, but also themselves. Throwing hundreds of millions of dollars at a foreign-owned firm is bad enough. Throwing hundreds of millions of dollars at a foreign-owned firm that then lays off workers looks a lot like a political fumble.

If nothing else, the episode underscores the essential folly of governments playing the subsidy game and attempting to tilt the table against market forces. All too often, economic circumstances change, and the table needs to be tilted even more, at greater expense.

Government ministers can swagger all they want about “saving jobs” – the jobs they are most concerned about are those that have a seat at the cabinet table.

stories.title: Strong mayor powers spark debate as London council selects committee chairs
stories.summary: A routine task became an early test of London’s newly-elected council, as the selection of councillors to sit as the chairs of three municipal standing committees sparked debate about how to best collaborate on decisions governed by strong mayor powers.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A routine task became an early test of London’s newly-elected council, as the selection of councillors to sit as the chairs of three municipal standing committees sparked debate about how to best collaborate on decisions governed by strong mayor powers.

On Wednesday, the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc) heard a motion from Coun. Elizabeth Peloza proposing a different approach to choosing the chairs and vice-chairs the Infrastructure and Corporate Services Committee (Icsc), the Planning and Environment Committee (PEC), and the Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee.

Peloza’s letter suggested that it would be more collaborative to have each standing committee nominate their own choices for the leadership roles, and forward them to Mayor Josh Morgan for appointment.

“This letter came from a conversation I had proactively and respectfully with the mayor,” Peloza explained to colleagues on Sppc.

However, Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis challenged whether the proposal could proceed because strong mayor powers provided by the provincial government include a requirement that the mayor appoint standing committee chairs, “It’s my opinion that this motion is actually out of order.”

After consulting with the city clerk, Deputy Mayor Corrine Rahman agreed that Peloza’s motion was out of order.

Instead, Mayor Josh Morgan sought council’s non-binding support for his selections: Lewis to chair the Icsc, Coun. Skylar Franke to chair PEC, and Coun. Hadleigh McAlister to chair Caps.

“There’s committee (meetings) starting on the 30th of November. This is a super tight timeframe at the start of the term,” the mayor reminded colleagues. “I’m totally open to lots of ways that we can improve the process for next year and the year after. But at the start here, I feel some level of obligation to get things set-up and going.”

The subsequent discussion exposed different views about whether every councillor is equally qualified to chair a standing committee.

“I feel very strongly, very strongly, that we should be rotating the positions of chairs and vice-chairs as much as possible, and that every member of council during a council term should have the opportunity, if they’re willing,” asserted Coun. Sam Trosow.

Lewis argued councillors require certain abilities to chair standing committees.

“Look around the (council) horseshoe. We don’t all come with equal skills and abilities. In different areas we have different skills and abilities. One of the key things for me in the selection of a chair is the people with the skills and abilities to chair a committee,” explained Lewis.

Budget Chair Steven Lehman supported Morgan’s choices, emphasizing the demands of running a meeting.

“It’s a challenging job to be a chair,” Lehman explained. “You’re listening to debate, but you’re also having to act as a referee in some regards, not only with committee people, but often with people in the gallery. I’m fully supportive of these three (nominees). I think they’ll do an ideal job.”

“I’m not a fan of strong mayor powers. I like the powers to rest with the people,” said Coun. Jason King at his first committee meeting. “Councillors should have as much opportunity to contribute and make decisions as much as possible, but on the other hand, I also appreciate the efficiency with which we need to move.”

Although Morgan said he would strongly consider the results of the vote, councillors on the committee were reminded that even if they rejected one or more of the mayor’s selections, responsibility for the appointments would still rest with him.

“I did receive that question earlier, and the answer to that was, it would be back in the mayor’s hands,” explained Deputy Mayor Corrine Rahman who chairs Sppc.

Council supported the three chairs by a vote of 13-2, Trosow and Peloza opposed.

Morgan maintained that seeking input was intended to make the process collaborative while meeting provincial requirements.

“I’m happy to engage with any member of council on alternative processes in future years. My intention is to appoint these individuals for one year, not for a longer term, which would allow for continued discussion on this approach,” Morgan said.

stories.title: Unseasonably warm weather continues through Saturday
stories.summary: Sunshine and unseasonably warm temperatures are expected across the region Thursday, with a high of 14 C, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.content:
Sunshine and unseasonably warm temperatures are expected across the region Thursday, with a high of 14 C, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

High pressure and southerly winds are bringing mild conditions, with sunshine expected to continue through Saturday.

Friday will be sunny with a high of 12 C, while temperatures could reach 14 C Saturday.

A cold front is expected to move through Sunday, bringing a 30 per cent chance of showers and cooler temperatures.

Daytime highs will drop to between 2 C and 4 C Monday through Wednesday, with a chance of lake-effect flurries Tuesday and Wednesday.

Atchison says residents should enjoy the sunshine while it lasts, with the warmer conditions expected to hold through Saturday.

stories.title: How chef Shane Harper found his way back to fine dining by learning to farm
stories.summary: After a rare autoimmune disorder stole his sense of taste, the star chef rethought his approach to food. That pivot led him to farm full-time at Pearl Morissette, widely considered Canada’s best restaurant
stories.author: Graham Isador
stories.content:
Before the age of 30, Shane Harper had earned a reputation as one of the top pastry chefs in the country. Achieving that goal cost him personal relationships, his physical and mental health.

“I love the idea of struggling to achieve something that you absolutely love,” said Harper. “It took an enormous amount of hard work and dedication to the craft to get to that point. But, man, I’m just interested in testing my capabilities as a human being.”

Cutting his teeth in high-end establishments, Harper recalls long, thankless, hours. Thrown dishes. Even physical violence. But his time in Toronto’s and New York’s best kitchens honed a sense of creativity and passion that was, in a word, undeniable.

Peers recall Harper measuring his desserts with a ruler, making sure every line of his rhubarb crisp was exactly the same distance apart. That kind of dedication and care were applied to even the most basic dish.

“Something as simple as a sticky toffee pudding became very iconic,” said Daniel Hadida, co-chef of Restaurant Pearl Morissette in Lincoln, Ont. Hadida first worked with Harper at Nota Bene, where the two began a long friendship. “I saw Shane as a leader in that space.”

“He’s also one of the smartest people I’ve ever met. Just completely engrossed and passionate about what he does,” said film director Sandy Chronopoulos. She spent months following Harper for Pirate Produce , an intimate portrait of the chef and his work. The documentary premiered in October at Devour! The Food Film Fest in Wolfville, N.S.

Harper had achieved the kind of career that people work their whole lives for. The fact that he’d been self-medicating with alcohol and a Lorazepam prescription – a drug generally used for anxiety attacks – didn’t seem like a problem. Neither did missed weddings and funerals or screaming matches with co-workers. Success was the only measure of his self-worth. And then Harper got sick.

Miller Fisher is a rare neurological disorder, a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome. The condition can come on after viral or bacterial infections. It causes your immune system to attack the nerves, with impacts usually starting in the face. For Harper, symptoms such as co-ordination and vision problems were frightening. But the biggest issue was the impact on his palate.

“I chose all of my adult life to pursue the manipulation of flavour,” said Harper. “By no means was there a career beyond the ability to taste.”

Symptoms started small. Working at the One Restaurant in the Hazelton Hotel Harper recalls having brain fog. Ingredients tasted off. He began to have trouble moving around. When the illness began affecting his eyesight, the chef reluctantly went to the hospital. Doctors came up empty. Harper was sent home, hoping things might improve with rest and Tylenol.

“I laid in my bed for three days, getting worse and worse. Finally somebody came from the restaurant to drive me back to the hospital,” he said. “I couldn’t walk at that point. Couldn’t see properly. Definitely couldn’t taste.”

When the official diagnosis finally came, the chef started to spiral. The sickness might mean completely reshaping how he worked. Maybe leaving the industry entirely.

Harper stayed in the hospital for a week. He spent a month off work. It took almost two years before he felt normal again.

Miller Fisher left him cross-eyed. Harper began wearing an eye patch to help the condition, something he still wears to this day. During early recovery, basic tasks such as opening doors or handling utensils felt difficult. The rehab forced a giant shift in his priorities.

“Miller Fisher syndrome changed everything for him. His life was about sacrifice,” said Chronopoulos. “I think being a perfectionist to that level can break you. You’re pushing yourself to the edge constantly to see how far you can go . . . the illness gave him a moment to actually stop for the first time in a decade.”

“You could tell how destabilized he was. Mentally. Physically,” said Hadida.

Part of finding a new stability for himself meant rethinking both his career and his approach to food.

As his taste returned, Harper began growing vegetables on his apartment balcony. He’d steal oversized buckets from the back of alleyways of the restaurants he used to frequent, weighing things down with rocks he’d pick up from Toronto beaches.

Gardening spoke to the bigger questions he’d been wrestling with. As a chef, he felt disillusioned only handling the “last five per cent” of an ingredient’s journey.

“How does flavour get to a restaurant? Flavour comes from the field. Well, who is growing these ingredients? Why are they grown this way?” said Harper. “It really solidified the next stage of what my life was going to look like, even though I didn’t know it at that time.”

The chef approached his crude attempts at growing tomatoes and carrots with the same passion, curiosity and dedication he’d used to make pastries. The vegetables were a reminder of how divorced we are from our food. Easing back into kitchens as his health returned, Harper found himself unmoored from his day-to-day activities.

“I’m having to order conventional strawberries and carrots, through distributors that don’t care about ingredients, through subsidized labour from coming from the United States,” he said.

Harper wanted to create flavours starting from the very beginning, down to the roots. He began looking for work on farming message boards and job sites such as Craigslist. In 2014 , Harper left Toronto to work as a farm manager at Holly Ray Farms, about a two-hour drive northeast of the city in the village of Stirling. Harper would live on the property and take care of a hundred chickens and six pigs. He’d create systems to help run the farm and grow plants.

Harper had no practical farming experience but the minuscule pay and physical labour meant there wasn’t a lot of competition for the gig. The chef recalls working sun up to sun down with no days off. It was impossibly hard work. It was also the most content he’d been in years.

Today, as Harper walks through the farm at Restaurant Pearl Morissette, he’s pointing out various plants and vegetables. Harper is funny and affable, speaking with a fast infectious energy, as if his words can barely keep up with the speed of his thoughts. There’s a depth and intelligence to how he talks about the food. He shows his passion by punctuating every second sentence with a curse.

This year marks his eighth season with Pearl Morissette, serving as the restaurant’s “chef de farm.” The restaurant is one of three establishments in Canada to earn two Michelin stars. Harper’s produce is one of the best tools in their arsenal.

“A strawberry, if it’s at its peak, cooked beautifully in the sun, and picked in a timely manner by individuals that love to grow these ingredients . . . that’s a two Michelin star dish with just a couple other things that go with it,” said Harper.

For Harper, the job of chef de farm is overseeing the evolution and ethos of what a farm means to a restaurant. A typical day sees Harper get up early to pick ingredients for service, move animals around the property and tend to the various growing needs in the field and the greenhouses. But it’s a position that almost didn’t happen at all.

“I knew that Shane had been working on farms. I reached out to him and don’t think he ever responded,” said Hadida. Eventually, the two ran into each other at a 10-year anniversary party for Nota Bene.

Harper was working the appetizers at the party, having picked up the gig during the farm off-season. “It troubled me that this person who had been in a leadership position in this kitchen and had a goal, purpose and focus in the agricultural world was not in a position that I thought he deserved,” said Hadida.

After the meeting at Nota Bene, Hadida finally convinced Harper to visit Pearl Morissette, no strings attached. Then, he offered him a year-round position to farm for the restaurant.

“The goal was to be able to remove the boundaries that separate the farm, the garden and the kitchen,” said Harper.

Reflecting on his journey, Harper steers any philosophizing about his transformational experience back toward the work. He hopes he’s a good mentor for other farmers wanting to learn the trade. He hopes the service industry can be less toxic than when he was coming up. He believes the approach they have to gardening at Pearl Morissette could be replicated at high-end restaurants across the world.

Asked where he’d be if he hadn’t gotten Miller Fisher, the chef is grateful for what was – in many ways – the worst experience of his life. “I feel as if it’s something that happened for me, not to me.”

For Harper, the job of chef de farm is overseeing the evolution and ethos of what a farm means to a restaurant. A typical day sees Harper get up early to pick ingredients for service, move animals around the property and tend to the various growing needs in the field and the greenhouses. But it’s a position that almost didn’t happen at all.

“I knew that Shane had been working on farms. I reached out to him and don’t think he ever responded,” said Hadida. Eventually, the two ran into each other at a 10-year anniversary party for Nota Bene.

Harper was working the appetizers at the party, having picked up the gig during the farm off-season. “It troubled me that this person who had been in a leadership position in this kitchen and had a goal, purpose and focus in the agricultural world was not in a position that I thought he deserved,” said Hadida.
After the meeting at Nota Bene, Hadida finally convinced Harper to visit Pearl Morissette, no strings attached. Then, he offered him a year-round position to farm for the restaurant.
“The goal was to be able to remove the boundaries that separate the farm, the garden and the kitchen,” said Harper.

Reflecting on his journey, Harper steers any philosophizing about his transformational experience back toward the work. He hopes he’s a good mentor for other farmers wanting to learn the trade. He hopes the service industry can be less toxic than when he was coming up. He believes the approach they have to gardening at Pearl Morissette could be replicated at high-end restaurants across the world.

Asked where he’d be if he hadn’t gotten Miller Fisher, the chef is grateful for what was – in many ways – the worst experience of his life. “I feel as if it’s something that happened for me, not to me.”

stories.title: US$582 million: Suspicious Epstein payments twice the amount previously reported, leaked Deutsche Bank records show
stories.summary: The German bank was eager to welcome the convicted sex offender but now 'regrets' the relationship
stories.author: Khadija Sharife, Emma Prest, Maria Fernanda Cruz Chaves, Brian Fitzpatrick, Sophia Baumann, Karina Shedrofsky, Jeremie Baruch, Investigative Journalism Bureau
stories.content:
In August 2026, Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, a senior member of the U.S. Senate Finance Committee, published a damning report called Looking the Other Way, which railed against financial institutions after concluding that their failures had enabled Jeffrey Epstein to operate.

Describing Deutsche Bank’s relationship with Epstein, Wyden told CNN: “For Deutsche Bank to be involved in the whitewashing business is absurd. They failed to promptly report to Treasury more than US$250 million in suspicious transactions that were tied to Epstein.”

“That is brand new information for the public,” Wyden said, as his extensive report recommended a criminal investigation into Epstein’s bankers. Deutsche Bank has not been charged in relation to any alleged offence.

Now a new set of leaked documents from inside Deutsche Bank reveal the suspicious Epstein payments are much bigger than even Wyden knew.

An internal document from Deutsche Bank’s U.S. Financial Crimes Intelligence Unit shows that the bank filed 21 suspicious activity reports, or SARs, involving 3,000 transactions between October 2013 and May 2019 relating to Epstein or his companies. In total, these transactions amounted to US$581.9 million.

In banking, a SAR is a confidential document filed with authorities when a bank identifies transactions or activities it suspects May involve financial crimes.

The internal document is part of more than 15 million files leaked by two whistleblowers to Indian author and journalist Josy Joseph, and South African investigative journalist Khadija Sharife. The whistleblowers, whose identities are being protected, say they copied the files and removed them from Deutsche Bank.

The files also provide more details of how the bank welcomed and kept a convicted sex offender whose accounts had been shut down by JP Morgan Chase. They also show the behind-the-scenes machinations as the bank grappled with a crisis of its own making.

U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR). Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

In a response, the bank said:

“Deutsche Bank notified Jeffrey Epstein in December 2018 that the Bank intended to close his accounts. The Bank worked to ensure that Epstein’s assets were transferred out of the Bank in the following months.”

The bank said it “acknowledges its error of onboarding Epstein in 2013 and regrets our historical connection with him. We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies and the U.S. Congress regarding their investigations and have been transparent in addressing these matters in parallel.”

“In recent years Deutsche Bank has made considerable investments in strengthening controls, including bolstering our anti-financial crime processes through technology, training and additional staff with dedicated expertise.”

The bank declined to comment on questions about the discrepancy between Wyden’s figures and its own internal documentation.

By the time Deutsche Bank accepted him as a client in August, 2013, Epstein’s crimes involving the sexual exploitation of a minor were a matter of public record.

Despite this, internal documents show the banking of Epstein at Deutsche Bank involved sign-off at the highest levels, including by the head of anti-financial crime and compliance, and the then-general counsel for Deutsche Bank America.

Documents show the bank maintained its relations with the “high-risk” Epstein from August, 2013 until informing him it would be closing his accounts in late 2018, a process that would take a further six months.

According to Wyden’s report, Deutsche Bank only filed SARs concerning Epstein after his July 2019 arrest on federal charges of sex trafficking of minors and conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of minors.

A road cleaning machine drives past the exterior of a Deutsche Bank AG branch in Berlin, Germany. Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg

In the leaked Deutsche Bank files, reporters discovered a report produced in 2020 by independent monitors. The monitors were tasked with tracking whether Deutsche Bank was complying with legally binding consent orders it had entered into with regulators — including one resulting from issues with its Epstein business.

In the document the monitors outline various red flags about Epstein that the bank knew about before taking him on board, such as “widely-known interactions with the legal system including a guilty plea and sentence for two prostitution crimes.”

Recounting how Epstein was first onboarded, the monitors wrote that, “Senior leaders in the WM (Wealth Management) Americas group were well aware of these issues at the time, but approved the relationship via email.”

In mid-2013, a former banker at JPMorgan Chase who had moved to Deutsche Bank rekindled a relationship with an ex-client whose name was already synonymous with predatory abuse: Jeffrey Epstein.

That year, JPMorgan Chase was winding down its banking relationship with Epstein; his 2008 guilty plea to prostitution-related charges involving a minor and his subsequent registration as a sex offender had made him a liability.

JP Morgan Chase did not respond to a request for comment.

But Deutsche Bank viewed Epstein as a financial whale, classifying him internally as an ultra-high-net-worth individual. A “know your customer” form for Epstein revealed an estimated net worth of between US$100 million and US$500 million.

Documents show that in August 2013, he began transferring his company accounts to Deutsche Bank. That month, the bank opened a corporate account for Southern Financial, one of his companies, based in the U.S. Virgin Islands. A document related to this lists his annual income from Southern Financial at about US$10 million.

Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s former partner and associate who is now imprisoned in the U.S., was a beneficiary of one of Epstein’s trusts.

Ghislaine Maxwell with Jeffrey Epstein. Handout/U.S. Department of Justice/AFP via Getty Images

In a 2015 email, the bank described her as an alleged “co-conspirator in Epstein’s illegal activities,” but allowed the arrangement to go ahead, concluding that because she was not a Deutsche Bank client, but only a beneficiary of the trust, they would allow it. The same email, titled “cleared,” saw an alert concerning Maxwell and the trust given a pass. The trust was given the all-clear from “a reputational and (anti-money-laundering) risk perspective.”

During Epstein’s relationship with Deutsche Bank, court documents surrounding the bank’s 2020 consent order show his accounts were used to make numerous payments to people who had been publicly identified as alleged co-conspirators in his abuses. The bank failed to adequately investigate or block these transactions, according to its records and financial regulators.

The monitoring report on the consent order, from later the same year, shows that Deutsche Bank had “continuously” expanded Epstein’s relationship with the bank “without appropriate documentation from the relevant controls.” Ultimately, according to New York regulators, Epstein, his entities and his associates would open more than 40 accounts with the bank.

In November 2018, Epstein was thrust back into the public spotlight by the Miami Herald’s landmark investigative series, Perversion of Justice, by journalist Julie K. Brown.

Brown exposed how Epstein had secured an extraordinary deal with federal prosecutors in 2007, allowing him to avoid federal sex-trafficking charges, leaving victims unaware of his sweetheart deal and receiving a lenient sentence in Florida.

Crucially, the investigation gave a voice to survivors who had been silenced for years, with Brown tracking down dozens of victims and persuading several to speak publicly.

In December 2018, Deutsche Bank informed Epstein that he would be offboarded.

By 2019, the scrutiny triggered by Brown’s story led to renewed law enforcement efforts, culminating in Epstein’s arrest on sex-trafficking charges in July of that year.

A March 2020 email titled “confidential,” copied to Deutsche Bank senior executives, stated that a Deutsche Bank staffer had sent foreign banks two letters of recommendation for Epstein’s investment companies in the spring of 2019, while his offboarding was in progress.

According to the email, the second letter had made “a specific representation that the relevant account had not experienced anti-money laundering problems.” The email went on to admit that the bank did not, by then, have a policy in place for writing “these types” of reference letters for clients.

Brown’s story triggered an awakening within Deutsche Bank. By August 2019, it appears that two investigations into Epstein were underway, including one in the U.K.

In September 2019, a summary from the internal U.K. investigation found at least, “112 high risk transactions,” including payments from Epstein’s corporate accounts. The investigation identified transactions that could potentially have been related to sexual abuse, the summary shows.

In an email the same month, multiple companies were identified for potentially enabling the abuse of minors, including at the infamous Zorro Ranch in Stanley, New Mexico. The investigation also identified a “shadowy” charitable organization through which Epstein May have laundered his money.

Three days after Epstein’s July, 2019 arrest, Deutsche Bank finally concluded its drawn out process of de-banking him, shutting down his two remaining accounts.

The two towers of Deutsche Bank headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany. Daniel Roland/AFP/Getty Images

In July 2020, Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing told colleagues that onboarding Epstein was a critical mistake and should never have happened.

U.S. court filings show Deutsche Bank had hoped to create US$2 million to US$4 million in revenue per year from the business relationship.

But even in a best-case scenario, these figures would be dwarfed by the bank’s eventual Epstein-related fines. In 2020, Deutsche Bank agreed to pay US$150 million to New York’s Department of Financial Services in connection with failures in dealing with Epstein, among other matters, and in 2023 it agreed to pay US$75 million to settle a class action lawsuit by victims who had alleged that Deutsche Bank knowingly benefited from and facilitated Epstein’s abuses.

Deutsche Bank’s high-stakes gamble with the financier never paid off. Epstein died by suicide in prison on Aug. 10, 2019.

Despite this, internal documents show the banking of Epstein at Deutsche Bank involved sign-off at the highest levels, including by the head of anti-financial crime and compliance, and the then-general counsel for Deutsche Bank America.

Documents show the bank maintained its relations with the “high-risk” Epstein from August, 2013 until informing him it would be closing his accounts in late 2018, a process that would take a further six months.

According to Wyden’s report, Deutsche Bank only filed SARs concerning Epstein after his July 2019 arrest on federal charges of sex trafficking of minors and conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of minors.
A road cleaning machine drives past the exterior of a Deutsche Bank AG branch in Berlin, Germany. Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg

In the leaked Deutsche Bank files, reporters discovered a report produced in 2020 by independent monitors. The monitors were tasked with tracking whether Deutsche Bank was complying with legally binding consent orders it had entered into with regulators — including one resulting from issues with its Epstein business.

In the document the monitors outline various red flags about Epstein that the bank knew about before taking him on board, such as “widely-known interactions with the legal system including a guilty plea and sentence for two prostitution crimes.”

Recounting how Epstein was first onboarded, the monitors wrote that, “Senior leaders in the WM (Wealth Management) Americas group were well aware of these issues at the time, but approved the relationship via email.”
In mid-2013, a former banker at JPMorgan Chase who had moved to Deutsche Bank rekindled a relationship with an ex-client whose name was already synonymous with predatory abuse: Jeffrey Epstein.

That year, JPMorgan Chase was winding down its banking relationship with Epstein; his 2008 guilty plea to prostitution-related charges involving a minor and his subsequent registration as a sex offender had made him a liability.
JP Morgan Chase did not respond to a request for comment.

But Deutsche Bank viewed Epstein as a financial whale, classifying him internally as an ultra-high-net-worth individual. A “know your customer” form for Epstein revealed an estimated net worth of between US$100 million and US$500 million.

Documents show that in August 2013, he began transferring his company accounts to Deutsche Bank. That month, the bank opened a corporate account for Southern Financial, one of his companies, based in the U.S. Virgin Islands. A document related to this lists his annual income from Southern Financial at about US$10 million.
Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s former partner and associate who is now imprisoned in the U.S., was a beneficiary of one of Epstein’s trusts.
Ghislaine Maxwell with Jeffrey Epstein. Handout/U.S. Department of Justice/AFP via Getty Images

In a 2015 email, the bank described her as an alleged “co-conspirator in Epstein’s illegal activities,” but allowed the arrangement to go ahead, concluding that because she was not a Deutsche Bank client, but only a beneficiary of the trust, they would allow it. During Epstein’s relationship with Deutsche Bank, court documents surrounding the bank’s 2020 consent order show his accounts were used to make numerous payments to people who had been publicly identified as alleged co-conspirators in his abuses. The bank failed to adequately investigate or block these transactions, according to its records and financial regulators.

The monitoring report on the consent order, from later the same year, shows that Deutsche Bank had “continuously” expanded Epstein’s relationship with the bank “without appropriate documentation from the relevant controls.” Ultimately, according to New York regulators, Epstein, his entities and his associates would open more than 40 accounts with the bank.
In November 2018, Epstein was thrust back into the public spotlight by the Miami Herald’s landmark investigative series, Perversion of Justice, by journalist Julie K. Brown.

Brown exposed how Epstein had secured an extraordinary deal with federal prosecutors in 2007, allowing him to avoid federal sex-trafficking charges, leaving victims unaware of his sweetheart deal and receiving a lenient sentence in Florida.
Crucially, the investigation gave a voice to survivors who had been silenced for years, with Brown tracking down dozens of victims and persuading several to speak publicly.
In December 2018, Deutsche Bank informed Epstein that he would be offboarded.
By 2019, the scrutiny triggered by Brown’s story led to renewed law enforcement efforts, culminating in Epstein’s arrest on sex-trafficking charges in July of that year.

Brown’s story triggered an awakening within Deutsche Bank. By August 2019, it appears that two investigations into Epstein were underway, including one in the U.K.

In an email the same month, multiple companies were identified for potentially enabling the abuse of minors, including at the infamous Zorro Ranch in Stanley, New Mexico. The investigation also identified a “shadowy” charitable organization through which Epstein May have laundered his money.
Three days after Epstein’s July, 2019 arrest, Deutsche Bank finally concluded its drawn out process of de-banking him, shutting down his two remaining accounts.
The two towers of Deutsche Bank headquarters in Frankfurt, Germany. Daniel Roland/AFP/Getty Images
In July 2020, Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing told colleagues that onboarding Epstein was a critical mistake and should never have happened.
U.S. court filings show Deutsche Bank had hoped to create US$2 million to US$4 million in revenue per year from the business relationship.

Deutsche Bank’s high-stakes gamble with the financier never paid off. Epstein died by suicide in prison on Aug. 10, 2019.

stories.title: Police to make announcement about Canada's most wanted fugitives Thursday morning
stories.summary: Investigators in Toronto and in several other Canadian regions, along with the Bolo Program, will hold a news conference at 10:30 a.m.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
An alleged high-ranking member of the notorious Lawrence Bishnoi gang , a man accused of shooting a Fairview Mall security guard during a brazen daytime theft and another wanted in a North York homicide.

These three men top the updated list of Canada’s 25 most wanted fugitives in the Bolo (Be On The Lookout) Program , unveiled Thursday morning at the Toronto Police College in Etobicoke.

Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw joined Bolo executive director Maxime Langlois and police representatives from across Canada and the United States to announce the names. AI-generated models of each fugitive were presented on a screen, occasionally moving and gesturing behind the speakers as they made their speeches on stage.

Six people wanted by Toronto police made the list, including Kyle Prouse at No. 2 and Cody Rudifo at No. 3.

Satinderjeet Singh, 32, also known as Goldy Brar, ranks first. He is wanted in the 2023 killing of Sukhdool Singh Gill in Winnipeg and is accused by U.S. prosecutors of ordering the killing of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C., that same year.

He is believed to be a high-ranking member of the Lawrence Bishnoi crime organization, which has been labelled a terrorist group by the Canadian government, authorities said.

Singh is also on the Fbi’s ten most wanted fugitives list. Bolo is offering up to $250,000 for information leading to his arrest in Canada or the United States.

Prouse, 53, of Montreal, is wanted on several charges, including attempted murder in connection with an April shooting and jewelry robbery at Fairview Mall in North York. A mall security guard was seriously injured after he was shot confronting the suspect.

Prouse has ties to Toronto and Vancouver, and investigators believe he is responsible for other armed robberies and break-ins at banks and jewelry stores in Ontario and Quebec dating back to 2023.

A statement from the victim in the mall shooting — who wasn’t named at the news conference — was read out by moderator Tamara Cherry.

From left, Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, Kyle Prouse and Cody Rudifo.

“The clock is ticking. For the past seven months, you’ve had a police service looking for you. Now, you’ve got the Bolo Program,” the statement said.

Rudifo, of Timmins, is wanted for first-degree murder in the death of 34-year-old Christopher Gordon in early October. Police say a disturbance was heard inside an apartment building before Gordon was found with traumatic injuries.

Demkiw said Prouse and Rudifo should be considered armed and dangerous. Bolo is offering up to $100,000 for information leading to Prouse’s arrest and up to $50,000 for Rudifo’s.

Demkiw also warned people against helping fugitives evade authorities.

“To anyone helping them with a place to stay, a ride or money, you are putting your communities at risk,” Demkiw said.

Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw joined Bolo executive director Maxime Langlois and police representatives from Canada and the United States to announce the names.

Two Peel police cases also made the list: Manpreet Singh, wanted for first-degree murder and attempted murder in a 2025 Brampton shooting, is ranked No. 8. Pedram Rabie, wanted for attempted murder, is ranked No. 20.

When asked how the Bolo program might’ve been affected by the large-scale Crime Stoppers data breach earlier this fall, Langlois said the program had stopped working Crime Stoppers well before those services suspended their tip lines.

Toronto police instead run a dedicated, 24-hour Bolo tip line at 416-808-0606 . “It’s not anonymous, it’s confidential,” Langlois said.

Langlois said a committee of eight investigators from across Canada who specialize in finding fugitives recommends which cases to prioritize. Bolo makes the final ranking decisions.

“Every day you evade arrest is another day someone could recognize you,” Langlois said.

A man was seriously injured after he confronted a jewelry store thief at the North York mall on

On Thursday afternoon, the 14th-ranked fugitive on the Bolo list was arrested by the RCMP and local police in Winnipeg, the OPP said in a news release.

Filmon Fesshaghirgis, 28, of London, Ont., faces three charges, including first-degree murder, in connection with a fatal shooting in Bolton, Ont., in January 2021.

Bolo launched in 2018 to draw public attention to priority cases from police services across Canada. Toronto police say 19 of the 28 Toronto cases featured by the program have resulted in arrests.

With files from Joshua Smith

stories.title: In a reversal, Ontario hospital CEO now part of decisions keeping patients locked up alone — for as long as 21 years and counting
stories.summary: The daily involvement of the CEO in seclusion decisions is part of the Six Core Strategies, which the hospital said it was already following.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
This story is part of 20 Years in Isolation , the Star’s ongoing investigation into the use of psychiatric seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. The Star’s reporting has been met with calls for an independent review of Ontario’s mental health system .

The CEO of Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital has started participating in decisions to keep patients in isolation, in what appears to mark a shift in practice compared to just a few months ago.

It was revealed last week during an Ontario Review Board hearing that Dr. Nadiya Sunderji has been attending “seclusion rounds” at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene. It’s during these daily rounds that a psychiatrist decides — without an in-person assessment — whether a patient should continue to be kept locked up alone in their room.

The hospital later confirmed to the Star that Sunderji attends rounds “periodically in (her) role of providing organizational oversight.” Waypoint refused to say when she began participating in the rounds or what exactly she does when she attends.

Previously, in May, Sunderji told the Star it would be inappropriate for her to be involved in seclusion decision-making “in keeping with provincial legislation and clinical standards in Ontario.”

Nadiya Sunderji, Waypoint’s president and CEO.

It’s a change that advocates attribute to the Star’s ongoing investigation, 20 Years in Isolation, which has revealed that Waypoint is keeping patients in seclusion for years , including Camelott Hamblett , who has now spent just over 21 years in isolation. This despite the fact that Waypoint’s own policy calls for seclusion to be the option of last resort, to be used for as brief a time as possible when dealing with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others.

The revelation about Sunderji’s involvement in seclusion decisions comes as the Ford government expressed confidence this week in the “clinical supervision” at Waypoint; the statement was made by the office of Associate Minister of Mental Health and Addictions Michelle Cooper, in an emailed reply to concerns from a constituent.

It marks the first time the government has weighed in on the Star’s investigation. The office of Health Minister Sylvia Jones has never responded to any requests for comment.

As the Star previously reported, the Tories have been aware of concerns about seclusion at Waypoint since 2018, but took little action in response .

“Our government remains confident in the clinical supervision provided at Waypoint and the decisions of the Ontario Review Board, and will continue to support the delivery of high-quality, specialized mental health care for individuals across Simcoe North and beyond,” Cooper’s office told the constituent this week.

The office did not return the Star’s request for comment.

The grounds of Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.

The daily involvement of the hospital CEO in seclusion decision-making is the first strategy in the Six Core Strategies , an internationally recognized set of best practices to reduce and eliminate the use of seclusion. The strategies are in use in hospitals across the continent, including other Ontario facilities.

The authors of the “six core strategies” say Dr. Nadiya Sunderji’s refusal to involve herself in Waypoint’s “highly unusual” use of psychiatric

Waypoint has said it has been implementing the strategies since 2023. However, Sunderji’s comments to the Star earlier this year prompted the strategies’ U.S.-based creators to conclude the hospital had failed to adopt their work .

The hospital confirmed to the Star this month that daily seclusion rounds have been in place since December 2023, and that “since implementing the practice,” a number of unnamed senior leaders and vice-presidents, as well as managers and directors, are involved.

The hospital declined to say when exactly vice-presidents began attending, or to provide specifics about Sunderji’s role in the rounds.

“We have nothing further to add at this time.”

The fact that Sunderji now participates to some degree brings her closer in line with the strategies, but it’s not nearly enough, said the creators, psychologist Janice LeBel and mental health nurse Kevin Ann Huckshorn.

“This seems more like ‘show’ than real commitment to change,” Huckshorn said.

The media scrutiny of Waypoint’s practices May be leading to change, “but it suggests that leadership participation in rounds May be a reactive response, not compelled by recognition that it is good clinical care and essential to prevent/reduce (restraint and seclusion),” LeBel said in an email.

She said she would want to see data showing what has changed because of leadership participation in the rounds, especially whether it has led to a drop in the use of seclusion. She would also want to know how Waypoint defines “oversight” in this context, and whether senior leaders are leading the seclusion rounds or merely participating.

Sunderji’s involvement in seclusion rounds came up last week at Camelott Hamblett’s annual Ontario Review Board hearing ; the board has oversight of patients detained in hospitals who have been found not criminally responsible due to a mental disorder or unfit to stand trial.

Hamblett, a 44-year-old Toronto man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, has spent half his life locked in a room alone at Waypoint due to what the hospital describes as aggressive behaviour caused by his hallucinations.

His treating psychiatrist, Dr. Stephanie Bouskill, explained at the hearing that the status of secluded patients is discussed at daily rounds at 11 a.m., when the on-call psychiatrist decides whether to renew the patient’s seclusion order after reviewing their file and talking with staff.

The patient is not assessed in person, and the psychiatrist’s reason for prolonging the seclusion is not always indicated in the file. Hamblett himself was ordered to remain in seclusion last Monday while he sat without incident in restraints in a boardroom at Waypoint watching his ORB hearing via Zoom for eight hours.

Camelott Hamblett, who has been locked in isolation at Waypoint for two decades, watched Monday’s hearing for eight hours without issue.

Bouskill said she has only participated in the rounds a handful of times because she’s not a full-time staff member at Waypoint, meaning she’s rarely been directly involved in the decision keeping her own patient in seclusion.

She was initially unaware of anyone more senior than a clinical manager participating in the seclusion rounds. But at the very end of the ORB hearing, Bouskill was recalled by Waypoint lawyer Julia Lefebvre to offer a “correction” to her testimony.

Bouskill then testified that Dr. Kevin Young, vice-president of medical affairs, and Chad Draper, vice-president of clinical services and chief nursing executive, attend the seclusion rounds on a daily basis.

Lefebvre pressed her: Anyone else?

“My other correction is that the CEO does attend,” Bouskill testified. “Not on a daily basis.”

Sunderji, a psychiatrist, became Waypoint’s president and CEO in 2022 after previously serving as vice-president of medical affairs and chief of staff.

According to Hamblett’s chart, the last time Sunderji attended his seclusion review was on Sept. 10, Bouskill said.

“The only logical conclusion that I can draw from it is that the public scrutiny has in fact lit a fire under them, such that they’re at least trying to figure out what they’re supposed to be doing in accordance with the six core strategies,” said Hamblett’s lawyer, Anita Szigeti, in an interview.

But Sunderji’s sporadic participation is “glaringly inconsistent” with the Six Core Strategies’ requirement for daily involvement by the CEO, Szigeti said. And she lamented that there was no evidence at the hearing about an actual hospital strategy to reduce and ultimately eliminate the use of seclusion.

Szigeti thought back to people asking her how someone like Camelott Hamblett can spend so long locked in isolation in hospital.

“It can only happen without the constant supervision, oversight and direct, hands-on involvement of the CEO and senior management,” she said. “That’s the only way it can happen.”

stories.title: From pork to online French usage: six take-aways from Carney’s tour of Asia, Ireland
stories.summary: Shenzhen — Prime Minister Mark Carney has left China to return to Ottawa after a whirlwind trip that took him to four summits in Ireland, the Philippines, Cambodia and the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Shenzhen — Prime Minister Mark Carney has left China to return to Ottawa after a whirlwind trip that took him to four summits in Ireland, the Philippines, Cambodia and the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

Here are some of the main take-aways from the trip, in chronological order.

1) Touching base on Ukraine peace talks

Carney started his trip last Wednesday in Dublin on the eve of the European Political Community summit, an informal gathering of leaders from around Europe that has occurred every six months since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended and briefed Carney and a dozen European leaders on the state of negotiations with Russia.

The Ukrainian leader discussed this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi with Russian officials organized by U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Those talks reportedly touched on Russia’s desire to change the security infrastructure that brought countries bordering Russia into a military alliance with other Europeans, the U.S. and Canada.

Carney later told a news conference that Canada would stand by its Nato allies and it’s up to the Europeans to craft arrangements to secure their continent.

2) Opening up trade

Carney and his Philippine counterpart concluded talks on a free-trade agreement in Manila and the deal is expected to be formally signed next year.

The news came on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

The deal looks to expand Canadian exports in agriculture, forestry, mining and energy, while shifting trade toward more advanced fields such as aerospace technology and artificial intelligence.

Canada is also pursuing a broader trade agreement with the Asean bloc, which includes the Philippines and 10 other countries such as Thailand.

The region hosts some of the world’s fastest-growing economies and is home to nearly 700 million people. Ottawa says the region is key to Carney’s goal of doubling exports to countries other than the U.S. by 2035.

Carney then flew to Cambodia for the Francophonie summit.

3) The first Plamondon meeting

In Cambodia, Carney met Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon for the first time since the province elected a sovereigntist government last month.

St-Pierre Plamondon has repeatedly raised his aspiration to have Quebec become an independent country.

The two were cordial in their meeting and focused on shared objectives, with Carney mentioning homelessness and St-Pierre Plamondon speaking about the use of the Francophonie for business investment.

“We will continue in a professional way — friendly but not necessarily a bromance. I have a wife,” Carney quipped in French.

The prime minister complimented St-Pierre Plamondon’s looks and the premier seemed bemused. They joked about who was the better goaltender for Oxford University’s hockey team, a role they both held.

Carney later said that while Quebec could engage with American counterparts on trade as a “stakeholder,” international agreements “are negotiated between federal governments.”

4) A vision for the French language

Carney closed his visit to Phnom Penh by defending the French language and urging leaders of French-speaking countries to band together against the forces of American big tech.

“Canada will always defend the French language and francophone cultures, including in the face of pressure from tech giants and our closest neighbour,” he said in French.

The prime minister said Canada wants to mobilize other countries to make sure American tech giants give French-language content a prominent place on online platforms.

Carney said French-language content should be easily retrievable, like a library catalogue — rather than an old warehouse of books with the lights turned off.

The prime minister was greeted by rousing applause from leaders at a formal plenary and an innovation event where many African countries were represented.

Carney said artificial intelligence risks leaving behind French speakers and flattening linguistic diversity. He also said French-speaking countries should partner with Canada on seeking economic gains through the responsible use of AI.

The Francophonie summit takes place every few years. Canada is set to host the next summit in 2028 in the Ottawa region. Carney says he wants to work with Quebec and New Brunswick — who are also full members — to have the summit focus on French in the digital age, youth and the economy.

Carney ended his brief Cambodia stay with a visit to the prime minister’s palace after laying wreaths at monuments surrounded by military officials. Between the two visits, Carney’s motorcade was greeted by groups of children holding flowers and Canadian flags.

5) Deeper relations with China

Carney travelled to Shenzhen late Monday, where he was greeted by dozens of synchronized dancers on the tarmac.

The next morning, Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping at a lavish guest house surrounded by lush, manicured gardens, nestled among skyscrapers in the high-tech metropolis.

The two agreed to drop trade restrictions on more goods at a bilateral meeting in China, with more access for Canadian agricultural products such as pork in exchange for more imports of Chinese steel and aluminum.

The pork sector hailed that as a big step in restoring some of the market access lost since bilateral relations hit a low point in late 2018.

The leaders noted progress in multiple fields since Carney visited Beijing in January.

Tuesday’s deal came ahead of Xi hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or Apec.

Carney said Shenzhen’s breakneck economic growth — “from a rustic fishing village to an innovation-forward megacity” — is a model for how Canada wants to speed up development by cutting red tape and investing in big projects.

6) Meeting with Trump

Carney met with Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit for a roughly 20-minute meeting that included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, among others.

Carney’s office said they discussed work on “a mutually beneficial trade agreement” that includes protections for the French language and a viable Canadian auto sector. The prime minister has said those issues derailed talks in August.

Anand told reporters the in-person meeting was the first in a while between Trump and Carney, aside from regular phone calls and text messages.

She said Canada would diversify its trade regardless of the results of this month’s U.S. midterm elections, which saw the Democrats take control of Congress for the rest of the Republican president’s term.

She called it a “lame-duck Congress.”

Carney’s recent agreements with China on trade have infuriated some of the people closest to Trump, notably trade adviser Peter Navarro.

Carney has said Canada is focused on exporting to China commodities such as iron and oil. He compared that to American trade with China, which he said involves sensitive and advanced technologies like superconductors.

Trump met Thursday with Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. That meeting has raised concerns about a possible deal to end to the war in Ukraine that would not protect Europe.

Carney and Anand have said they welcome any meeting that helps advance the cause of a just peace.

Before the three-way meeting began, the U.S. president had a separate one-on-one meeting with Xi lasting about an hour. Trump also sat down with Putin.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Anand says travel advisories can help Canadians assess China detention risk
stories.summary: Shenzhen - Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says travel advisories can help Canadians assess whether they are at risk of arbitrary detention when visiting China, when asked whether it's a safe country to visit.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Shenzhen - Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says travel advisories can help Canadians assess whether they are at risk of arbitrary detention when visiting China, when asked whether it’s a safe country to visit.

“At Global Affairs Canada we have travel advisories. We are ensuring that those are always accurate,” said Anand, who would not specify whether Canadians are safe when they visit China.

“There is an initiative between our countries to ensure that the people-to-people ties can be stronger, and that includes through more flights,” she said, as well as more exchanges and China dropping a visa requirement for Canadian tourists.

She was speaking on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or Apec, in China’s tech megacity, Shenzhen.

This week, Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, and they announced renewed funding for university exchanges, and promised more partnerships for people-to-people ties, such as in cultural fields.

Jeff Nankivell, head of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, said it’s important to pursue deeper exchanges in spite of the risks.

This is why Global Affairs Canada puts resources into updating and verifying information in its travel advisories, he said.

Nankivell said detainment is a concern for China in particular because its justice system falls short of international standards, including in corruption and transparency.

“There are unusual risks for China that we do not see in other countries. And so you have to take the travel advisory quite seriously, and make your own assessment as to whether there are factors in your case that could put you at risk,” Nankivell said in an interview.

Canada’s travel advisory for China suggests visitors “exercise a high degree of caution,” which is the second-lowest risk level of the four Ottawa uses. Canadians visiting China face risks of arbitrary detention or not being able to leave the country, it says.

“Canadian business travellers have been detained and had their passport confiscated as a result of business disputes with their Chinese counterparts,” the travel advisory reads.

“Disputes are often costly and prolonged, and you May be subject to a travel ban restricting you from leaving the country until the matter is resolved.”

It adds that foreign drivers in China face “harsh penalties.”

“If you’re suspected of being responsible for road accidents, police officers can detain you until their case is closed, which can take years,” the advisory says.

The advisory warns that China can also withhold passports for foreigners suspected of a crime or detain them for up to 37 days without charges.

The advisory warns that Canadians detained on national security charges, such as “upsetting social order,” could face six months of detainment before formal arrest, and a trial in a closed court.

The advisory has particular warnings for China’s Xinjiang region, where the United Nations in 2022 reported that China had committed serious human rights violations against Uyghurs that could constitute crimes against humanity. China strongly disputes those findings.

“Chinese authorities are increasingly detaining ethnic and Muslim minorities in the region without due process. There are reports of extrajudicial internment and forced labour camps. Family members of Canadian citizens with Chinese citizenship have been detained,” the travel advisory reads.

Nankivell said someone in China on a student or faculty exchange, or on their first business trip to China, faces the constant risk of “serious consequences imposed in an arbitrary way” by authorities.

“One example would be someone, a university student who finds themselves in the wrong place at the wrong time, like they’re at a bar and a fight breaks out, and everyone at the bar gets detained,” he said.

“The highest risk these days is probably one that has existed for many years, which is if it’s something related to your business.

“That you’ve had a falling out with a local partner — or you have local partner you know who is a bad actor and has access to friends in the local justice system and is able to to get you detained.”

Nankivell said it’s unlikely Canada would face a full-blown diplomatic crisis in which a senior CEO is arrested, or something similar to the Two Michaels case in 2018, when China detained two Canadians for more than 1,000 days in response to the Vancouver house arrest of a tech executive facing U.S. charges.

He said the fact that it happened makes a repeat all the more likely.

Anand told reporters the safety of Canadians in China was among the issues she raised with her Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, at the start of their Tuesday meeting.

“I raised human rights, democratic principles including freedom of the press, the treatment of Canadians in China, transnational repression — and the importance of these fundamental principles to our country and to our people,” she said.

Anand argued that more dialogue with China helps deal with issues as they emerge, but wouldn’t say whether that lowers the risk of detainment from happening in the first place.

“You need to have the fortitude to sit at the table and to raise topics that you know have not historically (been) met with a welcome doormat — that you are able to sit across the table and raise these issues, because of the regularized communication channels that our systems are engaged in,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.
