stories.title: Toys “R” Us partnership has Staples Canada playing around with its business model
stories.summary: Richmond Hill — Standing in a back quadrant of a Staples Canada store north of Toronto in the city of Richmond Hill, Mike Rinaldi is at the centre of a child's dreamscape.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Richmond Hill — Standing in a back quadrant of a Staples Canada store north of Toronto in the city of Richmond Hill, Mike Rinaldi is at the centre of a child’s dreamscape.

Behind the company’s chief merchandising officer are rows of Hot Wheels, Barbies and dumpling-shaped squishies, alongside bins crammed with junk food-inspired plushies and bouncy balls. A giant Lego spaceship towers over him and birthday balloons are bobbing in the background.

The sprightly scene comes courtesy of Toys “R” Us Canada — the storied toy retailer freshly out of creditor protection and now connected to the U.S. firm behind Chia Pets and the Elvis Presley attraction Graceland.

In a bid to bring back the beloved brand, Toys “R” Us and Parties “R” Us departments are moving into portions of 300 Staples Canada stores by the end of next year. The location Rinaldi is visiting, a short drive from Staples Canada’s headquarters, is the first to be transformed.

There’s a lot riding on the plan — for both retailers. Toys “R” Us Canada owner Next Century and affiliate Ad Populum will be testing just how many customers are sticking with the brand. Meanwhile, Staples Canada will be trying to convince shoppers it’s more than an office and school supplies mecca or the place you go when you need to print something.

Put simply, Rinaldi is trying to prove “Staples is evolving.”

It wants to be the place people can go to “get multiple things done in today’s world where everyone’s in a hurry,” he explained.

In keeping with that ethos, some of the retailer’s locations have welcomed workspaces, coffee shops and Service Ontario branches processing drivers’ licenses, health cards and vehicle permits in recent years. Many have dropoff points for Amazon returns, and others have growing travel departments selling suitcases, neck pillows and toiletry bags.

Now, it also wants to be a destination for birthdays, Christmas and any other occasion when shoppers May need puzzles or pinatas.

If you ask Rinaldi, it made sense to repurpose space already dedicated to kids and events to make room for the partnership. Staples Canada already sold toys, but they had more of an educational slant. The Toys “R” Us Canada partnership blows wide open that assortment under a brand name that carries a lot of nostalgia.

In fact, Rinaldi can’t help but grin while recalling buying wrestling figurines from the toy chain in the ’80s that he and his pals wrapped in newspaper to carry home during a rainstorm.

“The newspaper imprinted on the figures and the figures were destroyed, but I was so excited to get those,” he said.

That trip to Toys “R” Us would have been when the chain was in its infancy in Canada and quickly morphing into the go-to place for every kid’s wants.

Later, when Walmart, Costco and Amazon started more aggressively cornering the market with lower prices, Toys “R” Us started to fumble. By the time it was bought by Ancaster, Ont., entrepreneur Doug Putman in 2021, the retailer’s death knell was already ringing.

The last few years brought inflation, rising labour costs, supply chain disruptions and a shift toward e-commerce — all factors Toys “R” Us Canada cited when it claimed insolvency in February and then, sold its trademarks to Ad Populum in June.

Staples Canada has not been immune to such pressures.

“Its core business — office supplies, paper, ink and printing — has been shrinking for years. Customer preferences keep evolving and remote work has only sped that up,” said Liza Amlani, the founder of consultancy company Retail Strategy Group, in an email.

“When your core categories shrink, you either shrink the store or you give people new reasons to walk through the door. Staples is choosing the second option.”

While it takes time to get shoppers to connect longstanding retailers with new business segments like coffee or coworking areas, Amlani thinks toys are a worthy foray for Staples.

“Toys and party supplies speak to the same parent that shops back-to-school at Staples,” she said. “It extends the relationship and … gives families a reason to come back beyond back-to-school.”

Plus, the toy business can be lucrative. Hook a customer when the child they’re buying for is very young and you might win their toy purchases for years to come.

However, there are many businesses vying for the same relationship. Amazon, Costco and Walmart have used their high sales volumes to offer bargain prices, squeezing competitors and luring in customers.

At the same time, big brands like Lego have aggressively expanded their own store footprints and the tariff war has spurred more Canadians to support small, local toy shops.

But perhaps the biggest challenge Staples will face is awareness, said Graham Heuman, retail insights lead at JC Williams Group.

“They’re going to be working pretty hard on just identifying that Staples is now going to be a place you can go for toys through Toys ‘R’ Us,” he said.

“Some consumers May be a little confused by the store-in-store concepts, if they’re not used to it.”

The company’s been trying to address the possible awareness gap by marketing itself on social media and the doors to the Richmond Hill Staples have a Geoffrey giraffe mascot popping through a pane that also reads “Toys ‘R’ Us lives here now!”

Step inside and it’s hard to miss the bright signage beckoning people to the toy department, where there are stations to test out Magna-Tiles and Kinetic Sand.

Rinaldi said the chain plans to draw in others by hosting crafting events and playtime sessions in partnership with Lego, Ravensburger and more.

But on a recent Tuesday afternoon, most seem to be there because of osmosis.

A woman who had visited the print centre chased after a toddler enthralled with the department, while an older fellow who’d previously browsed the electronics area rooted through a bin of stuffed animals shaped like pizza boxes and ramen bowls.

Rinaldi stopped to ask one man leaving the parcel dropoff area what he thought of the Toys “R” Us section.

“Are you going to put a Walmart in here?” the man asked as he sped toward the store’s exit. “What’s next?”

Rinaldi just nervously laughed.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: How Netflix turned a Toronto mall into the set of its latest game show
stories.summary: Toronto — When Charles Wachter signed on as a showrunner for Netflix, he was tasked with a shopaholic's dream: visiting innumerable malls across North America to find the perfect set for his new reality competition show.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

Posted November 19, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 19, 2026 5:26 am.

TORONTO — When Charles Wachter signed on as a showrunner for Netflix, he was tasked with a shopaholic’s dream: visiting innumerable malls across North America to find the perfect set for his new reality competition show.

“Win the Mall” is high-concept: 10 teams of two move into a shopping mall and compete in a series of challenges to win “ownership” of different stores.

Each store comes with its own benefits (a luxury bedding boutique includes the most comfortable place to sleep; a fried chicken franchise features endless snacks during filming) and associated prizes ($40,000 worth of bling from a jewelry store; a year’s worth of makeup from a cosmetics store).

At the end of the season, the team that owns all the stores wins a million dollars.

It’s a “fantasy mall,” Wachter said on a recent video call. “It’s this sort of hyper-surreal experience.”

“Win the Mall” ups the ante on shows like “The Price is Right” and “Supermarket Sweep,” gamifying consumerism while glamorizing the shopping mall as a commercial oasis where dreams come true.

Bringing that concept to life required a very specific set of criteria and a lot of work, Wachter said.

“With a show like this — no one’s ever done it: a 400,000-square-foot set, 200 retailers. We had to do deals with everybody. So it was really complicated.”

FIND THE MALL

They considered building a set in an abandoned mall, but “it quickly became apparent that wasn’t a good idea because the amount of dressing and money to bring a mall to life is tens of millions of dollars,” he said.

“But at the same time, we couldn’t shoot in a mall all day because it’s full of people. We couldn’t shoot in a mall just at night because it’s a game about real people and real people get tired, just like producers get tired.”

What they needed was a unicorn — and they found it in Toronto.

“The irony of ironies is the perfect mall was the mall I actually grew up going to, because I’m from Toronto and I went to Sherway Gardens — it’s where my dentist was when I was a kid,” Wachter said.

The proverbial horn that set Sherway Gardens apart from all the horses was, as it happens, also one of the biggest changes to Canada’s retail landscape in recent memory: the closure of the Hudson’s Bay Company.

The 355-year-old company’s collapse left a gaping hole in one three-storey wing of the mall.

PREP THE MALL, FILM THE MALL

The team turned the former Hudson’s Bay location into “a cover set,” Wachter said.

The ground floor was the production hub; the second floor included a fabricated food court and several faux stores (including the bedding store that served as sleeping quarters for some of the contestants); the third floor is where they conducted interviews with contestants.

They’d start filming in that set at about 4 p.m., Wachter said, and they’d stay there “more or less until the mall closed.

“And then we’d rush out (into) the mall with all our cameras and people and shoot challenges.”

But filming in a real mall — even when closed — came with its own set of challenges.

There are roughly 200 stores in Sherway Gardens, which is owned and operated by Cadillac Fairview, and Wachter said his producers had to work out contracts with each of them.

That’s because brand deals are a massive part of the show.

“We had hundreds of brands to deal with — thousands, millions of dollars worth of retail and logos,” Wachter said.

The amount each brand paid for placement differed — more money meant more exposure, which affected how much of each storefront they could show.

“It was a huge department and a big part of the show and very complicated, honestly — the speed at which we had to close these deals and then figure out where to shoot.”

In some cases, they built whole storefronts for brand partners that don’t have a presence north of the border, such as an American guitar retailer.

In other cases, they convinced storefronts to keep their doors open and lights on after hours in case they showed up in the background of a shot.

They created a sort of war room to keep track of it all, Wachter said, pulling out a large, laminated map of the mall. As they closed deals, he said, they’d change the colour of the store on the map.

It was unlike anything the veteran producer — who was also showrunner of the first season of “Beast Games,” the Mr. Beast-helmed Prime Video series, and Netflix’s “Million Dollar Secret” — had done before.

“We’d be like, ‘OK, we can’t go there, but we can go here. We could shoot this; we have to do a (brand) integration here; we’ve gotta show logos there; we can’t show those logos but we can show the storefront; we can show storefront but we can’t use the product,'” he said.

“So we had this huge matrix of what we can and can’t do and a whole bunch of very organized people making sure that when we were filming, it was all making sense to what we had promised people.”

Ideally, he said, all of this will go unnoticed by the general viewing public.

“I think hopefully my producer friends are going to be like, ‘Wow.'”

CONSIDER THE MALL

Wachter is a defender of the mall as an institution.

While there may have been too much “build-out” in the 1980s and 1990s and some of the smaller malls didn’t survive, Wachter said scouting locations showed him that the shopping centre is alive and well.

“They’re going through a resurgence,” he said. “I think Gen Alpha and Gen Z have rediscovered how much fun it is to go to a place that’s full of life and full of people and products. And a lot of these malls are actually seeing a rebound.”

Likewise, he said, the closure of Hudson’s Bay isn’t representative of the fate of the mall as a whole.

“I would argue the Hudson’s Bay piece of it is a little bit more of that big private equity one-stop shop type of approach to shopping that’s gone away,” he said.

“But the malls that do it right … I think are finding that the crowds are showing up.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sixty-four B.C. Conservatives including premier-designate Doerkson take office oath
stories.summary: Victoria - Political change is coming to British Columbia as members of the incoming Conservative government are being sworn into office at the legislature today.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia voters have made it clear they want no excuses from their new legislators and the new government must deliver on the promises it made, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said.

He told the first batch of his 63 caucus members who were sworn in on Thursday that they can never lose sight of serving their constituents and must listen more than they speak, a message that he repeated during the second swearing-in ceremony.

Doerkson said his government will pursue an ambitious, unprecedented economic agenda, because it’s what the province needs.

“I want it made clear that I meant everything that I said in the campaign,” he said, referring to his promise to supercharge the economy.

“We are absolutely going to help those people who need it most and I promise that we will absolutely provide tax relief for low-income families and for seniors … and create jobs in this province like we have never seen before.”

The Conservative MLAs took the Oath of Allegiance to King Charles and his heirs and signed the historical parliamentary roll, which has been signed by all members of the legislature since 1917.

They will form B.C.‘s first Conservative majority government in nearly 100 years and the province’s largest majority caucus in 25 years almost two months after Premier David Eby visited Government House to trigger a snap election.

Doerkson told the members that they would experience some of the proudest moments of their lives working in the legislature.

“Our mandate from this election was clear that it is time for change,” he said.

“British Columbians have spoken quite clearly. Electing all of you in such massive numbers, they’ve also made it very clear to me and others that they want no excuses. This is a government that can bring the change that we promised and so now we absolutely must deliver.”

Doerkson’s included an anecdote about his late father, who told him on the occasion of his first swearing-in to be “honest, if it’s even to a fault” and to “do what you say you’re going to do.”

“That is exactly what we are going to do,” he said, drawing applause.

Doerkson, a former rodeo rider and newspaper publisher, drew his first round of applause when he entered the chamber after people had taken their seats.

“Hello everybody,” he said with a smile to the cheering and clapping crowd.

The remaining Conservatives took part in a second ceremony later Thursday, during which Doerkson thanked his mother Bev, who watched from inside the chamber.

“Mom, I just want to say this is amazing night. It is largely because of you,” he said.

“It looks like you have got a really good team working for you,” she said in response.

While Elections BC says the final results are 64 Conservatives, 27 New Democrats and two Greens, there are still two judicial recounts necessary in Kelowna-Centre and in Ladysmith-Oceanside with the counting expected to start on Nov. 23.

Conservative Kristina Loewen leads New Democrat Loyal Wooldridge by 43 votes following the final count in Kelowna-Centre, and incumbent New Democrat Stephanie Higginson leads Kris McNichol by 50 votes in Ladysmith-Oceanside.

Elected New Democrats and the two Green legislators will take their oath of office next week.

Eby said during the election campaign that his party’s one-seat majority prevented him from taking “big swings” on behalf of the province in responding to the economic attacks coming from the United States.

Instead, the election magnified the Ndp’s nine-year record in office with an accumulated $14-billion deficit, reducing the New Democrats to just 27 of 93 seats and forcing Eby to resign as the party leader shortly after the polls closed on Oct. 24.

Doerkson, who became his party’s interim leader just days before the election was called, will be sworn in as British Columbia’s 38th premier on Friday along with his Conservative cabinet.

Prior to Thursday’s ceremony, Conservative Cathie Ounsted, the MLA-elect for Saanich-South, said she was “really thrilled” to take the oath of office and work hard for her constituents.

Ounsted calls it an honour to be able to represent residents and said she’s “completely ready” for the work that lies ahead, while her “biggest learning curve” consists of finding her way around the building.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly said that 64 Conservatives will take the oath of office. In fact, 63 will take the oath.

stories.title: Anthropic needs rapid growth to keep up spending, as Canadian AI sector heats up
stories.summary: Halifax - A U.S. tech giant with plans to lease its first Canadian artificial intelligence data centre next year says it doesn't have enough customers or revenues to keep pace with more than US$900 million in spending commitments.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - A U.S. tech giant with plans to lease its first Canadian artificial intelligence data centre next year says it doesn’t have enough customers or revenues to keep pace with more than US$900 million in spending commitments.

The need for new revenues is among the risks highlighted in a prospectus for investors considering Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, which has become the biggest Wall Street debut of all time.

The company behind the Claude AI model said it is offering 980 million shares at US$83 each. Expected proceeds of US$81 billion put it ahead of the SpaceX, which raised about US$75 billion in June. Anthropic is now valued at about US$1.5 trillion.

Anthropic’s investor documents show it has committed to spend about US$901 billion on data centres by 2045, including US$70 billion by next September.

“Just to put it in perspective, US$900 billion is roughly Canada’s entire sovereign debt,” Joel Blit, economics professor at the University of Waterloo and co-founder of the Canadian AI Adoption Initiative, said in an interview.

Last month, Anthropic announced it had signed a 20-year lease for the first phase of EverWind Fuels’ proposed data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., which would be the Dario Amodei-led company’s first Canadian site.

EverWind has said it will build and own the 95-megawatt, 18,600-square metre data centre at a cost of $8 billion, with another $2 billion planned for wind farms to power the operation. How much Anthropic will pay EverWind to lease the facility has not been disclosed.

But Anthropic’s investor documents also warn that the company needs to increase sales to pay for its data centre leases and infrastructure. At the same time, the company says it needs to plan its data centre investments years in advance, without knowing whether its customers will be there for the long term.

“We May enter into these obligations based on revenue expectations that May not be realized,” said the company.

Investor documents show Anthropic’s revenue grew by 13 times to US$33.2 billion for the first nine months of the current fiscal year, but it reported a net loss of US$104 billion, including a charge of US$94 billion for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements.

Anthropic did not respond to questions about its Cape Breton lease. EverWind declined to disclose the terms.

“It’s a 20-year lease, structured with significant credit protections,” Laurel Munroe, EverWind’s vice-president of communications, said in an email. “EverWind is developing, owning and financing the data centre campus. This is a private investment on private land, and the risk sits with EverWind and our lenders, not Nova Scotians.”

York University researchers reported in June that 213 data centres were planned or under construction across Canada. They would have a total capacity to draw 22.2 gigawatts of power, more than 14 times Canada’s existing capacity.

Almost 80 per cent of those projects are planned for Alberta, where the Globe and Mail reported last month Anthropic is in talks to lease a planned 920-megawatt project northeast of Edmonton. The facility is slated for operation toward the end of 2027, around the same time the Cape Breton data centre is scheduled for completion.

AI firms such as Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI are expected to spend US$700 million on data centres this year alone. Blit, the economics professor, said the massive build-out is coming as AI algorithms and chips are becoming more efficient, driving down user costs. As the technology improves, he said many users May not need the newest and best AI models, instead opting for slightly older and cheaper technology.

Blit said new uses for AI technology will have to emerge to justify the unprecedented level of investment.

“You really have to ask the question whether one company, I don’t care how big or powerful it is, can sustain that much potential debt.… Is the demand for AI services going to grow at the rate that many people think, such that we’re going to need all that compute capacity?” he said.

Anthropic’s stock offering is the second massive artificial intelligence IPO in just a few months, after Elon Musk’s SpaceX, owner of the Grok AI agent, launched in June with a valuation of more than US$1.7 trillion.

Randy Goebel, co-founder of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute at the University of Alberta, said in an interview that the sector is likely building out more computing capacity than it actually needs.

He said the overhyped uses for AI technology have pushed company valuations to exorbitant levels. He says it was much the same during the dot-com bubble that popped in the early 2000s, taking many tech companies down with it.

“The confidence of investors fell apart,” he said. “And so lots of companies who were planning IPOs didn’t make it. And now the valuations for Anthropic, and the one anticipated from OpenAI, are orders of magnitude larger, at least. And that’s what seems out of whack.”

David Garrity, a U.S. tech consultant, finance expert and CEO of the cybersecurity company Fyeo, says the 800-pound gorilla in the sector is Nvidia, until recently the world’s most valuable company and still the global leader in AI chips.

Nvidia has lost almost 30 per cent of its value over the last month. The span saw the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang after multiple affairs were made public, including one with a company executive and another with a suspected Chinese spy.

Nvidia has invested billions in or lent billions to other AI companies, and other AI-related stocks such as Meta, CoreWeave and Google’s parent company Alphabet have also seen billions of dollars in value erased in the last month.

Garrity said interest rates are increasing and oil prices remain elevated, creating a significantly different investment outlook for the AI sector compared to just a few months ago. He also said markets historically tend to pull back in the weeks following U.S. midterm elections.

“While the wind was at SpaceX’s back (for its IPO), in this case for Anthropic, it’s basically heading right into the wind. And the wind is pretty fierce,” he said in an interview.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

The need for new revenues is among the risks highlighted in a prospectus for investors considering Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, which has become the biggest Wall Street debut of all time.

The company behind the Claude AI model said it is offering 980 million shares at US$83 each. Expected proceeds of US$81 billion put it ahead of the SpaceX, which raised about US$75 billion in June. Anthropic is now valued at about US$1.5 trillion.
Anthropic’s investor documents show it has committed to spend about US$901 billion on data centres by 2045, including US$70 billion by next September.

“Just to put it in perspective, US$900 billion is roughly Canada’s entire sovereign debt,” Joel Blit, economics professor at the University of Waterloo and co-founder of the Canadian AI Adoption Initiative, said in an interview.

Last month, Anthropic announced it had signed a 20-year lease for the first phase of EverWind Fuels’ proposed data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., which would be the Dario Amodei-led company’s first Canadian site.

stories.title: Avi Lewis sees Montreal byelections as a crucial part of rebuilding the NDP
stories.summary: Ottawa — The NDP faces daunting challenges in the Dec. 7 federal byelections as it tries to hold its last seat east of Winnipeg while flipping a neighbouring Montreal riding held by a former Liberal cabinet minister.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The NDP faces daunting challenges in the Dec. 7 federal byelections as it tries to hold its last seat east of Winnipeg while flipping a neighbouring Montreal riding held by a former Liberal cabinet minister.

NDP candidates Pierre Céré in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Nima Machouf in Laurier—St-Marie have been knocking on doors since the summer in anticipation of these byelections.

Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie was the last Quebec riding still in NDP hands after the 2011 “orange wave” that brought the party to official opposition status for the first time. Former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice held the riding for 15 years before resigning this summer to run successfully in Quebec’s provincial election for Québec solidaire.

The NDP held Laurier—St-Marie from 2011 until 2019, when Steven Guilbeault won the riding for the Liberals. Before 2011, the riding was held for about 21 years by former Bloc Québécois leader Gilles Duceppe.

“We could not be working harder,” NDP Leader Avi Lewis said Tuesday while standing alongside Machouf and Céré before a joint rally in Montreal.

That rally saw more than 300 NDP supporters and volunteers fill Ausgang Plaza, a concert and event venue in the Rosemont riding, to fire themselves up for the final weeks of the campaign.

Lewis said a win in either Montreal byelection would be “incredible” but he sees these contests — and the four others taking place across Canada on Dec. 7 — as a means to continue building up the Ndp’s support base for the next general election.

“These byelections are not going to change the math in Ottawa. They’re not going change the majority government into anything else and they’re not going change our party status,” he said.

“So for us as a party, we really are in a long-term rebuilding phase, and these byelections are incredibly helpful because they are a way to energize people, to refine our message, to find incredible candidates … and to really get the spirit at the base elevated again. And that’s what we’re seeing.”

The NDP currently holds just five seats in the House of Commons after Boulerice’s resignation and Nunavut MP Lori Idlout’s decision to join the Liberals in March.

Parties need 12 seats for recognized party status in the House of Commons. That recognition means increased visibility in question period, spots on standing committees and access to financial resources.

Céré said in French he is confident the NDP can hold Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie. He said Boulerice embodied the progressive values of the riding and he believes his former constituents still respond to those ideals.

Machouf is representing the NDP for the fourth time in Laurier—St-Marie. She finished a relatively close second to to Guilbeault in the 2021 election — within 10 points of the incumbent — but only took about 19 per cent of the vote in the 2025 election, when the NDP cratered.

Machouf said she’s seeing a different campaign play out in the riding now. Guilbeault was a prominent environmental activist before joining the Trudeau government; he was appointed environment minister after the 2021 election. He was shuffled to the Canadian Culture and Identity portfolio by Prime Minister Mark Carney before quitting cabinet after Carney signed an oil pipeline agreement with Alberta.

Machouf said voters in the riding used to tell her that they hoped Guilbeault “could change things from the inside.”

“Now people seem more free to be able to vote for what they want because they don’t have this faux espoir,” Machouf said, using the French term for “false hope.”

Philippe Fournier, the polling analyst behind election modelling website 338Canada, said these two Montreal ridings offer the NDP their best odds in Quebec.

His model predicts a tight contest between the NDP and Liberals in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and a Liberal win in Laurier—St-Marie.

He said Laurier—St-Marie has always been left-of-centre but boundary changes and gentrification have created more favourable conditions for the Liberals in the downtown Montreal riding.

“The only major issue that I can see that could that could block the Liberals would be the environment,” Fournier said.

“The environment often scores very high in the priorities in the polls, but it does nothing at the ballot box. It’s just that in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie, and also maybe a little bit in Laurier—St-Marie, it could make a difference. These are voters that are more environmentally wary than the average voter.”

NDP volunteers and supporters report renewed energy at the grassroots level.

Tony LaSalle has been the president of the Rosemont—La Petite—Patrie NDP riding association for about two years. He said he’s seen a warming trend in new memberships since the 2025 election campaign which saw the party record its worst ever federal result.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau cut into NDP support by taking the traditionally centrist Liberal party more to the left with an increased human rights and social focus. Last year’s election result was compounded by the NDP being tied to an unpopular government with through the supply and confidence agreement. The NDP exited that agreement in September 2024.

With Carney taking the Liberals back to the centre of the political spectrum, it has opened space for the NDP, particularly on policies such climate change.

LaSalle said many people who were Boulerice supporters in 2025 were less excited by then-NDP leader Jagmeet Singh. He said new people are coming to the party now because they believe in the ideas Lewis is putting forward.

“My first general assembly, it was like a good amount of people. But my last general assembly, that we had this year, we had about doubled the attendance that we had and Alexandre was not there,” LaSalle said.

“All those people, all those new members, they’re not there because they like the work of the NDP but because they want to keep a progressive voice, a left-leaning voice that represents Quebec in the House of Commons.”

People at Tuesday’s rally who spoke to The Canadian Press also said they’ve noticed new faces — younger faces — attending NDP events lately. They said these new supporters are drawn in by the party’s ideas on affordability, wealth inequality, artificial intelligence and the environment — and are turned off by the Liberals’ moves to accelerate resource projects and change labour laws.

Fournier said the byelections represent a test for the NDP. Maintaining their Montreal foothold and placing a strong second in Laurier—St-Marie would show there’s life in the party, he said — while anything less would be seen as failure.

“Perhaps we will see that the Liberal coalition that Mr. Carney is trying to build left and right, maybe it’s not working on the left,” Fournier said.

“(Dec. 7) is going to be a fun night for data nerds like myself.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Machouf said voters in the riding used to tell her that they hoped Guilbeault “could change things from the inside.”
“Now people seem more free to be able to vote for what they want because they don’t have this faux espoir,” Machouf said, using the French term for “false hope.”
Philippe Fournier, the polling analyst behind election modelling website 338Canada, said these two Montreal ridings offer the NDP their best odds in Quebec.
His model predicts a tight contest between the NDP and Liberals in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and a Liberal win in Laurier—St-Marie.
He said Laurier—St-Marie has always been left-of-centre but boundary changes and gentrification have created more favourable conditions for the Liberals in the downtown Montreal riding.
“The only major issue that I can see that could that could block the Liberals would be the environment,” Fournier said.

“The environment often scores very high in the priorities in the polls, but it does nothing at the ballot box. It’s just that in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie, and also maybe a little bit in Laurier—St-Marie, it could make a difference. These are voters that are more environmentally wary than the average voter.”
NDP volunteers and supporters report renewed energy at the grassroots level.

Tony LaSalle has been the president of the Rosemont—La Petite—Patrie NDP riding association for about two years. He said he’s seen a warming trend in new memberships since the 2025 election campaign which saw the party record its worst ever federal result.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau cut into NDP support by taking the traditionally centrist Liberal party more to the left with an increased human rights and social focus. Last year’s election result was compounded by the NDP being tied to an unpopular government with through the supply and confidence agreement. The NDP exited that agreement in September 2024.
With Carney taking the Liberals back to the centre of the political spectrum, it has opened space for the NDP, particularly on policies such climate change.

LaSalle said many people who were Boulerice supporters in 2025 were less excited by then-NDP leader Jagmeet Singh. He said new people are coming to the party now because they believe in the ideas Lewis is putting forward.

“My first general assembly, it was like a good amount of people. But my last general assembly, that we had this year, we had about doubled the attendance that we had and Alexandre was not there,” LaSalle said.

“All those people, all those new members, they’re not there because they like the work of the NDP but because they want to keep a progressive voice, a left-leaning voice that represents Quebec in the House of Commons.”

People at Tuesday’s rally who spoke to The Canadian Press also said they’ve noticed new faces — younger faces — attending NDP events lately. They said these new supporters are drawn in by the party’s ideas on affordability, wealth inequality, artificial intelligence and the environment — and are turned off by the Liberals’ moves to accelerate resource projects and change labour laws.

Fournier said the byelections represent a test for the NDP. Maintaining their Montreal foothold and placing a strong second in Laurier—St-Marie would show there’s life in the party, he said — while anything less would be seen as failure.
“Perhaps we will see that the Liberal coalition that Mr. Carney is trying to build left and right, maybe it’s not working on the left,” Fournier said.
“(Dec. 7) is going to be a fun night for data nerds like myself.”

stories.title: Could a weakened Howard Lutnick help Canada secure a U.S. trade deal?
stories.summary: A weakened Lutnick could give U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer more room to negotiate concessions, according to a former U.S. trade negotiator
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington — Between the Republicans’ U.S. midterm election results and the scandal involving Nvidia, Ottawa could see an unexpected opening in its trade dispute with Washington.

The American electorate delivered congressional control to the Democrats, who want to ease U.S. tariffs on Canada. Meanwhile, the Nvidia fallout has Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — a major proponent of Donald Trump’s tariffs, particularly those on autos, steel, and aluminum — facing increased pressure.

A weakened Lutnick could give U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer greater room to negotiate concessions, according to Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute and a former U.S. trade negotiator.

But a change in personnel would not necessarily change the policies blocking a deal.

Lutnick faces scrutiny over allegations that he resisted restrictions intended to prevent Nvidia’s advanced chips from reaching China, despite warnings involving the company’s CEO and an alleged Chinese spy. He also faces questions about potential conflicts of interest involving his family’s financial firm.

“Howard Lutnick has legally transferred his private business interests to his very young sons, but it has been reported that he has not been diligent in making chip companies accountable, which raises questions about how his family’s business has benefited from his public office,” said Andrew Hale, fellow at Advancing American Freedom in Washington.

“Naturally, Americans are concerned about this,” he added.

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News Sunday that he wants to question Lutnick.

“After Secretary Lutnick was made aware of these allegations of Chinese espionage and the relationships that Jensen Huang had, why did he not close that loophole? Why did he allow chip diversion and the smuggling to continue?” he asked.

Whether Lutnick will lose his job is unclear. Asked Monday whether he planned to fire the commerce secretary, Trump defended him.

“No, he’s done a very good job,” the president said.

Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said a Republican-controlled Senate could give Trump an incentive to nominate any replacement before January, when confirmation could become more difficult under Democratic control.

As commerce secretary, Lutnick oversees negotiations over the Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos that Ottawa wants eliminated or significantly reduced. That makes him important to the talks while he remains in office, Cutler said.

“I think a mistake would be to ignore Lutnick at this point, because he May be around,” she said.

Lutnick’s refusal to budge on tariffs was reportedly a major contributor to the collapse in Canada-U.S. talks in August.

“My sense is that Greer was close to a deal with Canada, and Lutnick, in the last days of the negotiation before it broke down, was fighting against the flexibility on steel, aluminum, and autos that Greer had offered Canada,” Cutler said.

But if Lutnick’s power does fade, she could see a path to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer taking a larger role, potentially helping Canada.

“My sense is it would open the door for Ustr Greer to have full reign on these negotiations, which could be a positive development, in my view, for Canada,” Cutler said.

But she and Manak also noted that Trump has been and will likely remain at the heart of trade decisions.

“His cabinet keeps saying that they basically do what the president asks them to do,” Manak said.

“One would imagine that this is coming directly from Trump, or that he signed off on it,” she added, noting that the president has likely approved of the hard approach on Canada.

Manak also cautioned that a diminished Lutnick could give other officials greater influence, and not necessarily make Washington more flexible.

“(Peter) Navarro has strong views on trade and on Canada, in particular, so perhaps he could also play a larger role,” she said. That “would basically mean no real change” in the approach toward Canada, she added.

There are many actors in this. There’s not just one person. It’s the combination of all those forces that sort of need to come together

Inu Manak Peterson Institute for International Economics

If Lutnick stays, he will face distractions beyond the trade talks. “Clearly, Lutnick is going to be distracted by the Nvidia developments at a minimum,” Cutler said.

Lutnick will probably face questions about the as-yet non-public investigations that led to the 232 tariffs and Nvidia matters.

“It’s likely that Lutnick is going to be potentially subject to some more transparency measures, to be called in front of Congress, and it’s going to take up a lot of his time,” said Manak.

That, Manak says, could lead to a change in heart in trade discussions.

“That, I think, is likely going to have some softening effect potentially on his approach to the tariffs, in addition to all the pressures that are sort of being faced, with this pushback against the tariffs on Canada in particular,” she said.

But changing negotiators or the U.S. approach to the U.S.-Canada talks would not remove the political obstacles to lowering the tariffs, Manak cautioned.

The bigger obstacle is the trade policy itself, she explained, because the sectoral tariffs are politically hard to remove.

“At the end of the day, the policies that have been put in place, these tariffs, they’re very sticky, so even if (Lutnick) were to go, there’s a question about whether or not somebody else would do much to reverse those,” Manak said.

The tariffs are sticky because of the national-security justification used to implement them. Manak says unwinding them could make Trump look weak. But industries and unions also benefit from the protections the tariffs offer, so they fight to keep them in place, which helps explain why some first-term Trump tariffs survived under Joe Biden.

“You lock in a lot of interests that actually are benefiting from these tariffs, and they don’t want them to go away,” she said.

Based in the U.S. capital region, Tracy Moran has covered Canada-U.S. relations for National Post since 2025. She previously reported on international news for DW, USA Today, Gzero Media and several online magazines. She holds a master’s degree in international affairs from George Washington University.

“My sense is it would open the door for Ustr Greer to have full reign on these negotiations, which could be a positive development, in my view, for Canada,” Cutler said.
But she and Manak also noted that Trump has been and will likely remain at the heart of trade decisions.
“His cabinet keeps saying that they basically do what the president asks them to do,” Manak said.
“One would imagine that this is coming directly from Trump, or that he signed off on it,” she added, noting that the president has likely approved of the hard approach on Canada.
Manak also cautioned that a diminished Lutnick could give other officials greater influence, and not necessarily make Washington more flexible.

“(Peter) Navarro has strong views on trade and on Canada, in particular, so perhaps he could also play a larger role,” she said. That “would basically mean no real change” in the approach toward Canada, she added.
There are many actors in this. There’s not just one person. It’s the combination of all those forces that sort of need to come together
Inu Manak Peterson Institute for International Economics
If Lutnick stays, he will face distractions beyond the trade talks. “Clearly, Lutnick is going to be distracted by the Nvidia developments at a minimum,” Cutler said.
Lutnick will probably face questions about the as-yet non-public investigations that led to the 232 tariffs and Nvidia matters.
“It’s likely that Lutnick is going to be potentially subject to some more transparency measures, to be called in front of Congress, and it’s going to take up a lot of his time,” said Manak.
That, Manak says, could lead to a change in heart in trade discussions.

“That, I think, is likely going to have some softening effect potentially on his approach to the tariffs, in addition to all the pressures that are sort of being faced, with this pushback against the tariffs on Canada in particular,” she said.
But changing negotiators or the U.S. approach to the U.S.-Canada talks would not remove the political obstacles to lowering the tariffs, Manak cautioned.
The bigger obstacle is the trade policy itself, she explained, because the sectoral tariffs are politically hard to remove.

“At the end of the day, the policies that have been put in place, these tariffs, they’re very sticky, so even if (Lutnick) were to go, there’s a question about whether or not somebody else would do much to reverse those,” Manak said.

The tariffs are sticky because of the national-security justification used to implement them. Manak says unwinding them could make Trump look weak. But industries and unions also benefit from the protections the tariffs offer, so they fight to keep them in place, which helps explain why some first-term Trump tariffs survived under Joe Biden.
“You lock in a lot of interests that actually are benefiting from these tariffs, and they don’t want them to go away,” she said.

Based in the U.S. capital region, Tracy Moran has covered Canada-U.S. relations for National Post since 2025. She previously reported on international news for DW, USA Today, Gzero Media and several online magazines. She holds a master’s degree in international affairs from George Washington University.

stories.title: Weapons investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 18, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after members of the London Police Service responded to a weapons-related call yesterday morning.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 18, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after members of the London Police Service responded to a weapons-related call yesterday morning.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at approximately 11:45 a.m., a man was travelling northbound on Lyle Street near King Street, when he heard a loud noise come from the hood of his vehicle.

The man looked toward a nearby residential building and observed an individual standing on a balcony holding what appeared to be a firearm.

Police were contacted and attended a residence in the 400-block of Lyle Street. Officers located the suspect male and recovered a replica firearm inside the residence.

Damage consistent with being struck by a pellet was also observed to the complainant’s vehicle.

The individual had reportedly discharged the weapon several additional times in the area.

There were no reported injuries.

The suspect male was arrested without incident.

As a result of the investigation, Thomas Bradley Watson, 57, of London, has been charged with:

Pointing a firearm; and

Mischief under $5,000.

The accused was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on February 18, 2027, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Anakana Schofield: I had visions of Moses walking on puddles in a MEC rain jacket
stories.summary: Climate change is coming for us, if autumn’s gales are any indication of things to come
stories.author: Anakana Schofield; Contributor
stories.content:
Living in British Columbia for the past years has felt like a non-stop recall audition for global warming . The rotation of forest fires, heat domes and atmospheric river systems confirm that the weather is not just coming for us — it’s here. Global warming has established a 24-hour test-driving centre out west.

November is the hardest month, because of the endless and draining rains, little light and an overwhelming damp feeling that can beset the brain. What’s a little rain I hear you chide; well rivers of rain will deplete the duck in the best of us.

During the early 2000s, in response to the annual Great Rains, I undertook a deep embrace of them and sought to find and discover every variation in them. I assessed each downpour for its distinct qualities. I would go out into it, walk, look up and examine it closely. I gave poetic names to the varieties of rain. On social media, I would issue “weather watchers to your stations” and “boil the kettle” alerts if there was a wind warning. I became infused with the spirit of rainy adventure. There were weeks, over the last couple of years, where there was so much rain, it felt as if it was raining inside my eyes!

Unfortunately, this has expired. I can no longer access any spirit of adventure or raise any interest in rain and this year; my enthusiasm is nil. Maybe there’s a point in life where you’ve simply lived so much rain, the damp breaches a levee inside your brain and you can only look at it defeated and soggy before you even open the door.

It is a melancholy dip to meet and greet the deluge of rain that is November in Vancouver. We are about to hit rainstorm number three in as many days and I believe there is more impending . As I write to you, the official updates oscillate between “heavy rain is expected” and “heavy rain is occurring” with 50 mm of rain locally in Vancouver promised, while some areas of BC could see over 300mm!

We have a yellow warning for rain, Vancouver Island has an orange warning for rain, and a yellow one for wind; there are high stream flow warnings for four areas of BC and a flood watch for the South Coast from the River Forecast Centre. This follows the weekend storm, which knocked out power to 135,000 and saw Zeballos, a village, ON Vancouver Island evacuated because of high landslide and flooding risk. The residents were allowed briefly to return, but then faced yet another evacuation announcement which was in place until last Friday. . One person was recently killed when a tree fell on two cars.

Last year, when a tributary of water hurtled past my feet everywhere I trod, I envisaged a pop-up system of covered walkways or hydraulic rising pavements. I had visions of Moses walking on top of puddles and floods in an MEC rain jacket.

Weather can be very confusing. Out the window, there might be a noticeable bluster, sure, but walk three blocks to the park and you discover giant trees are in a state of collapse. The volume of rain weakens the roots of the trees and a heavy blast of wind can soon have them turning their toes — er, roots — up to heaven.

A significant factor is that the volume of rain has increased. The words Atmospheric River entered our weather lexicon around 2019. The MIT researchers who coined the term explained “Atmospheric rivers are typically several thousand kilometres long and only a few hundred kilometres wide, and a single one can carry a greater flux of water than Earth’s largest river, the Amazon River.”

Now imagine that river in the sky coming to call on you overhead relentlessly for a week.

In 2019 the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society published the very necessary “Scale to Characterize the Strength and Impacts of Atmospheric Rivers.” It ranks atmospheric rivers from 1 to 5 and creates the categories “weak,” “moderate,” “strong,” “extreme” and “exceptional.”

And then, once the rain falls there’s the problem of where does it go? This is when the practical woman in me becomes exasperated because leaves block the drains, which causes floods and Vancouverites aren’t all willing to pause and liberate them.

There are 45,000 storm catch basins in the City of Vancouver (this swells to 120,000 in Toronto). The City of Vancouver has an Adopt a Catch Basin program, which currently has 33,000 available for adoption. Toronto doesn’t have a formal program but you can contribute by ensuring nothing is blocking the drains and ditches and following their online guidelines.

Tuesday night I morphed into an Atmospheric River Gladiator and liberated 6 storm drains using my ice scraper to oust the leaves, litter and muck blocking them. It was fantastically satisfying to watch the floodwater disappear and temporarily relieve the misery of pedestrians trying to cross that road around them to enter the hospital. As if nurses need wet feet after a 12-hour shift. I might even adopt those drains and become exclusive with them.

stories.title: Stolen vehicle recovered
stories.summary: London, ON (November 19, 2026) – A man was arrested after members of the London Police Service (LPS) recovered a stolen vehicle in the south end of the city earlier this week.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 19, 2026) – A man was arrested after members of the London Police Service (LPS) recovered a stolen vehicle in the south end of the city earlier this week.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at approximately 10:20 a.m., police were contacted in relation to a reported stolen pickup truck observed in the 800-block of Exeter Road.

Officers attended the area and learned the vehicle had left prior to their arrival.

A short time later, an officer observed the stolen vehicle travelling in the area and followed it to a parking lot in the 1300-block of Wellington Road.

The driver exited the vehicle and entered a nearby business. Officers entered the business and located the man, who was arrested without incident.

The stolen vehicle was recovered.

As a result of the investigation, Mark Storrie, 21, of Brighton, UK, has been charged with one count of possession of property obtained by crime exceeding $5,000.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on December 8, 2026, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Bradley Avenue extended with newly built road in southwest London
stories.summary: Improvements for drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians, along with upgrades to support the area's growthThe
stories.content:
The Bradley Avenue Extension project has added a new stretch of road between White Oak Road and Wharncliffe Road South, which is now open to traffic.

The newly built road fills a gap between two previously separate sections of Bradley Avenue, creating a continuous route between Wonderland Road South and the White Oaks area.

Bradley Avenue is expected to carry approximately 25,000 vehicles a day as southwest London continues to grow, with new homes and businesses being built in the area.

The existing stretch of Bradley Avenue between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard was also widened from two lanes to four lanes to provide continuity in the corridor.

The newly built road includes new sidewalks and cycling paths, giving people more options for getting around the area on foot or by bike.

New cycling paths were added alongside the existing sidewalks on Bradley Avenue between White Oak Road and Jalna Boulevard.

A new traffic signal was installed at Bradley Avenue and Wharncliffe Road South, making it easier and safer for people to turn onto and off Bradley Avenue and travel through the intersection.

The project included upgrades to underground water and sewer pipes to support existing and future homes and businesses in the area.

Work was also completed to improve how rainwater moves through the area. This included creating a new creek and wetland areas, along with improvements to existing drainage infrastructure and a stormwater management pond.

Together, these improvements help manage stormwater from the road and surrounding properties, support better water quality, and reduce the risk of flooding during heavy rainfall.

“Opening Bradley Avenue on schedule and before winter is an important achievement for the City and everyone involved. There was a lot happening beyond the road itself, and bringing all of that work together took coordination across the project. We’re excited to see people now using this new connection,” said Jennie Dann, Director of Construction and Infrastructure Services.

Construction began in June 2025, and all major road work was completed on time, with the new stretch of Bradley Avenue opening to traffic in November 2026.

Crews will return in spring 2027 to complete final asphalt paving on the new road, along with remaining finishing work and landscaping.

To learn more about construction projects across London, visit the Renew London map .

stories.title: Human trafficking
stories.summary: London, ON (November 19, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Human Trafficking Unit laid charges after a woman was assaulted and robbed following an investigation into an incident that reportedly took place late last month.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 19, 2026) –Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Human Trafficking Unit laid charges after a woman was assaulted and robbed following an investigation into an incident that reportedly took place late last month.

On October 19, 2026, police commenced an investigation into an incident that had occurred approximately one week earlier.

Through the investigation, investigators learned that a woman had arranged to meet a man at a London residence in Old East Village, after communicating with him online. The man attended the residence and provided money in exchange for sexual services.

Following the interaction, the man demanded the money back. When the woman refused, he attempted to take it from her and assaulted her before fleeing. She sustained minor injuries.

Through the investigation, members of the LPS Human Trafficking Unit identified a suspect.

As a result, ON Monday, November 16, 2026, Sarkes Khawaja, 22, of London, was arrested and charged with the following offences:

Robbery; and,

Obtain sexual services for consideration.

Investigators believe there May be additional victims and are releasing an image of the accused as part of the ongoing investigation. Anyone who May have had contact with him, or who has information relevant to this investigation, is encouraged to contact police.

The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court today, November 19, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Human trafficking is a serious offence that often involves the exploitation of a person through fear, control, or manipulation for financial gain. Warning signs May include someone being closely monitored or controlled, having limited access to identification or personal belongings, working excessively long hours, or appearing fearful, anxious, or submissive. Anyone who believes they May be a victim, or who has information about human trafficking, is encouraged to seek help and report it to police.

More information on recognizing the signs of human trafficking and available supports can be found on the London Police Service website: https://www.londonpolice.CA/crime-prevention/human-trafficking/

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: A legacy of care: Dr. Sonny Cejic honoured for excellence in family medicine
stories.summary: November 19, 2026
stories.content:
November 19, 2026

For nearly three decades Dr. Sonny Cejic has cared for generations of London-area patients and training residents to become compassionate and skilled family physicians. That commitment to comprehensive care and medical education has earned the Byron Family Medical Centre physician a Regional Family Physician of the Year Award from the Ontario College of Family Physicians (OCFP) .

The annual award recognizes six family physicians from across Ontario who provide exceptional care, contribute to the health and well-being of their communities, and dedicate themselves to educating future family doctors. Dr. Cejic’s career brings those qualities together through longstanding patient relationships, collaborative team-based care, and a deep commitment to learners.

Dr. Cejic’s career in family medicine at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has been shaped by patients, learners, colleagues, and the community. As Medical Director of Byron Family Medical Centre, he has helped connect comprehensive patient-centred care, medical education, and collaboration across LHSC and the Thames Valley Family Health Team, while keeping the patient–physician relationship at the centre of his work.

For Dr. Cejic, one of the greatest rewards of family medicine is the opportunity to support patients through many stages of life. He has watched young patients grow into adults and return years later with new questions, challenges, and milestones.

“It is a privilege to care for patients over time and to be part of their lives as they grow, change, and reach new milestones,” said Dr. Cejic. “You build relationships with families, and then you see children become adults and begin making decisions about their own health. That continuity is one of the most meaningful parts of family medicine.”

That same sense of continuity has also shaped his role as a teacher, where he helps the next generation of family physicians understand the lasting impact of patient-centred care.

As an Associate Professor at Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, Dr. Cejic regularly welcomes family medicine residents and medical students to Byron Family Medical Centre. He enjoys the opportunity to mentor learners as they build their clinical judgment, confidence, and approach to patient care.

“Seeing that transformation is very rewarding,” he said. “You see a resident start in the early stages, and you help guide them to the point where they are ready to graduate and succeed out there.”

When asked about the Regional Family Physician of the Year Award, Dr. Cejic is quick to share the recognition with the people around him. He credits physicians, nurses, family health team colleagues, and admin/reception staff with creating a collaborative environment that supports patients and learners alike

“I’m very honoured to receive this award and grateful to those who took the time to nominate me,” said Dr. Cejic. “While the award is a wonderful recognition, I see it as a reflection of the many colleagues, learners, and patients who have been such an important part of my career in family medicine. I’ve been fortunate to work with so many dedicated people, and I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to contribute to our profession and our community.”

Dr. Scott McKay currently serves as Department Head of Family Medicine at LHSC and spent time learning from Dr. Cejic as a resident more than 20 years ago. He credits Dr. Cejic’s teaching and mentorship as having shaped his entire career.

“Dr. Cejic’s dedication to his patients and learners, and his steadfast leadership within family medicine, have inspired generations of physicians, including myself,” said Dr. McKay. “On behalf of LHSC, I would like to offer our most sincere congratulations. This recognition is very well deserved.”

Dr. Cejic's work reflects the continuity, trust, and personal connection that define comprehensive primary care. As both a physician and educator, he has helped care for generations of patients while supporting medical students and residents as they develop the skills needed to serve their communities.

Above all, the Regional Family Physician of the Year Award honours the heart of Dr. Cejic’s legacy – the relationships he has built, mentorship he has provided, and his commitment to care that has touched countless lives across the community.

stories.title: Suspect sought after $120,000 in pool damage
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 19, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Patrol Operations Investigative Section (Pois) are asking for the public’s help to identify a suspect after a backyard pool was intentionally damaged earlier this year.

On July 24, 2026, at approximately 11:30 p.m., an unknown person attended the rear fence line of a residence in the area of Pinnacle Parkway and McGarrell Place and tossed yellow, orange and white rust-preventive paint into and around a swimming pool.

The homeowner discovered the damage and contacted police. Officers attended and collected evidence as part of the investigation.

The damage is estimated at approximately $120,000.

Members of the LPS Patrol Operations Investigative Section continue to investigate and are asking anyone who May have information about the incident or the person responsible to come forward.

Even seemingly minor details could assist investigators.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

Thursday, November 19, 2026

Dundas Street between Wellington Street and Waterloo Street will be closed to local traffic starting Monday, November 23 for private water service upgrades. The work is expected to be completed by Friday, November 27.

The bike lane and north sidewalk will also be closed during this work. Access to businesses will be maintained, and the south sidewalk will remain open.

Westbound traffic will detour across Waterloo Street to Queens Avenue and Wellington Street. Eastbound traffic will detour along Wellington Street to King Street and Waterloo Street.

Above: A map showing the road closure on Dundas St. with detours along Waterloo St., Queens Ave., Wellington St. and King St.

Drivers should follow signs and expect delays when travelling through the area.

For more information on construction impacts in London, view the Renew London map.

Thursday, November 19, 2026

Dundas Street between Wellington Street and Waterloo Street will be closed to local traffic starting Monday, November 23 for private water service upgrades. The work is expected to be completed by Friday, November 27.
The bike lane and north sidewalk will also be closed during this work. Access to businesses will be maintained, and the south sidewalk will remain open.
Westbound traffic will detour across Waterloo Street to Queens Avenue and Wellington Street. Eastbound traffic will detour along Wellington Street to King Street and Waterloo Street.
Above: A map showing the road closure on Dundas St. with detours along Waterloo St., Queens Ave., Wellington St. and King St.
Drivers should follow signs and expect delays when travelling through the area.

stories.title: Kpmg Canada says client documents accessed in cybersecurity breach
stories.summary: It's the latest in a string of cyberattacks targeting organizations in Canada, including those in the legal and financial sectors.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
KPMG Canada says some client tax documents were accessed in a cybersecurity breach.

The accounting firm did not provide details about the breach, including the scope or nature of the attack.

KPMG is reaching out to clients who were affected.

Spokesperson Sonja Cloutier-Bosworth says the company is confident that the accessed data is not available online or being misused for any purpose.

It’s the latest in a string of cyberattacks targeting organizations in Canada, including those in the legal and financial sectors.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said in an alert last month that multiple firms had been targeted by people impersonating internal IT support and directing employees to fake sign-in pages.

stories.title: Menopause experts raise concerns after Pfizer discontinues drug in Canada
stories.summary: Company will no longer supply Premarin cream and tablets used to treat menopause symptoms, citing commercial sustainability concerns
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup, Chris Hannay
stories.content:
Menopause specialists are concerned about how Canadian patients will be affected by Pfizer’s recent decision to stop supplying a vaginal cream and oral estrogen tablets in Canada, while continuing to offer them in the U.S.

Physicians say they fear patients will have to contend with the ramifications of Pfizer’s decision, made public last week, to discontinue Premarin cream and tablets in Canada, prescribed to those navigating menopause symptoms. Existing inventory is expected to last until next year.

Premarin was first developed and approved in Canada in 1941 and Pfizer manufactures the global supply of the active ingredient in Brandon, Man. It comes from the urine of pregnant mares in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Pfizer first notified Health Canada on Nov. 3 that it would stop supplying Premarin products, according to a federal drug-shortage database . The cream is being discontinued immediately and pills will be available while inventory lasts, potentially until next June, according to notices on the database.

Pfizer said Premarin products were “commercially unsustainable” in Canada.

The company “considered a range of factors, including manufacturing and supply costs, the pricing and reimbursement environment, and the ability to maintain sustainable supply over the longer term,” said Sophie Morin, a spokesperson for Pfizer Canada, in an e-mail.

The federal database shows the Premarin cream has been in shortage four times since the beginning of 2025.

In the U.S., demand has grown for menopause hormone therapy, including after the Food and Drug Administration initiated the removal of long-standing safety warnings on the treatments last November. Health Canada has not removed similar warnings on products here.

Demand for the products is also on the rise in Canada. In September, a report from Manulife Canada about its group benefits showed a 228-per-cent increase in hormone-replacement therapy claims over five years among women 45 to 54.

Canadian obstetrician-gynecologist Jen Gunter wrote Wednesday on her blog that Pfizer’s decision should concern all Canadians.

“This isn’t just about Premarin,” she wrote. “Every Canadian who cares about access to medications need to be engaged and speak up.”

In its cream form, Premarin allows for estrogen to be applied directly to vaginal tissue. It is used to treat atrophic vaginitis, including drying of the vaginal walls, as well as shrinkage of the skin of the vagina and vulva. It can also be used to address dyspareunia, which is pain or discomfort during intercourse.

While there are some alternatives available, Dr. Gunter wrote that Premarin May be better for some patients in terms of side effects and efficacy.

Also, physicians say stopping certain treatments can lead to a rebound of symptoms, such as hot flashes and vaginal irritation, and can set back patients in their menopause care.

A tube of Premarin cream in Canada typically retails for around $50 because of federal drug rules. By comparison, it retails for around $400 to $500 in the United States. Some patients can access the cream for a lower price if they have insurance coverage.

Rithvika Ramesh, a family physician in Toronto, said the discontinuation affects some of her patients.

It is the only vaginal estrogen cream covered under the Ontario Drug Benefit program, she said. The drug funding plan covers the cost of certain medications for eligible residents.

She said the vaginal cream has long been an important treatment option for patients experiencing genitourinary symptoms of menopause. Additionally, she said it is used to help prevent recurrent urinary tract infections.

Dr. Ramesh said for older adults in particular, preventing UTIs can be life-saving, noting that a seemingly uncomplicated infection can progress to kidney infection, hospitalization and, sometimes, sepsis.

Sepsis is when the body’s immune system reacts in an extreme way to an infection and it can cause organs to shut down and in some cases, lead to death.

“Access to effective vaginal estrogen is not simply a matter of quality of life but an important component of preventative health care,” Dr. Ramesh said.

Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said vaginal estrogen products identified by the Canadian Menopause Society, including a vaginal ring, tablet and inserts, are still covered on the provincial drug formulary.

The Canadian Pharmacists Association has developed a resource for health care providers to manage supply changes, she added.

Dr. Ramesh said those who rely on the product May face additional out-of-pocket costs and could have to transition to a product that doesn’t adequately align with their symptoms, preferences and needs.

Dr. Gunter also voiced concerns about how the discontinuation will affect patients and wants the federal government to get involved in the matter.

“The federal government oversees drug approvals and international trade policies,” Dr. Gunter wrote. “It is legitimate to ask our elected officials and members of the Senate to find out why this is happening.”

A spokesperson for federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel’s office said that Health Canada is assessing the effects of the discontinuation of Premarin on menopause hormone-therapy supply in Canada, and will act as needed to minimize the impact of shortages.

stories.title: Ontario medical regulator won’t investigate MP over Maid comments on mental illness
stories.summary: House of Commons Speaker defends members’ freedom of speech after a complaint was filed against Marcus Powlowski
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario said it is not investigating a federal MP, who is also a doctor, after a complaint was filed against him with the regulator for saying those who can’t access medical assistance in dying could use other means to end their lives.

The issue had drawn the attention of the House of Commons over concerns a probe and the potential repercussions for the Thunder Bay-Rainy River Liberal MP Marcus Powlowski would violate his right to speak freely in connection with his work in Parliament.

Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia called the risk of MPs feeling like they must censor themselves in the House of Commons “unacceptable.” He asked Parliament’s lawyers to send the Cpso a letter to remind them members’ freedom of speech is constitutionally protected.

The highly charged debate over Canada’s Maid regime continues in the House this week as the justice committee begins its study of a bill that would bar access to Maid for those whose only condition is mental illness.

In a statement to The Globe and Mail Wednesday, the Cpso said they were aware of the Speaker’s decision.

“I can confirm that Cpso is not currently investigating Dr. Marcus Powlowski in relation to this matter,” spokesperson Laura Zilke said by e-mail, adding the college would review any correspondence from the Speaker.

She declined to say why Cpso isn’t pursuing an investigation.

The complaint against Mr. Powlowski was filed earlier this fall. It followed the final report of the joint House of Commons and Senate committee studying the expansion of medical assistance in dying to those whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

Mr. Powlowski, who is also an emergency room physician, was a co-chair of the committee. It concluded in June that Maid should not be expanded, though it was not a unanimous recommendation.

Mr. Powlowski opposes the expansion of Maid. In a supplementary opinion laying out his rationale, he reflected on how, even if the government chose not to extend access, people can end their lives.

“Furthermore, there are painless options readily available. One example being illicit narcotics like fentanyl,” he wrote.

Claire Brosseau subsequently filed a complaint with the Cpso asking them to investigate whether Mr. Powlowski’s comments were “consistent with the professional conduct expected of an Ontario physician.”

In her complaint, a copy of which was obtained by The Globe, she wrote that Mr. Powlowski’s remarks validated lethal self-harm and, in turn, created “a profound sense of unsafety for vulnerable patients who rely on the medical profession to uphold suicide prevention standards.”

Ms. Brosseau, who has bipolar 1, a form of bipolar disorder, is currently suing the federal government over its refusal to allow her to access Maid. The case remains before the court.

In a statement to The Globe Wednesday, Ms. Brosseau said the Cpso process is not complete.

“I will be responding to its most recent correspondence by the deadline they have given me. Until that process is complete, I will not be commenting further,” she said in an e-mail.

Mr. Powlowski said he is pleased the college is not investigating. He said he agreed with the Speaker that he should not face repercussions for comments made as a parliamentarian.

“I don’t think that would be appropriate,” he said in an interview.

When asked if he had any comment with regard to Ms. Brosseau’s allegations, he said he didn’t think it was appropriate for him to be part of a public discourse about her specific situation.

Mr. Scarpaleggia told MPs about the Cpso letter in the House late Tuesday afternoon. His decision to weigh in was prompted by the Conservative MP for Kitchener South-Hespeler Matt Strauss. He is also a physician , and in October, asked the Speaker to examine whether the Cpso investigation would be a violation of parliamentary privilege.

The joint House of Commons and Senate committee was studying Maid for mental illness earlier this year because the current ban on it expires in March and the government had to decide what to do next.

This fall, the government tabled Bill C-41. The bill restricts access to Maid for those whose only condition is mental illness. At the same time, it proposes a system for advanced requests, allowing people with “capacity-limiting illnesses” such as Alzheimer’s the ability to ask for medical help to end their lives at a future date.

With a report from Kristy Kirkup
