Mr. Powlowski, who is also an emergency room physician, was a co-chair of the committee. It concluded in June that Maid should not be expanded, though it was not a unanimous recommendation.
Mr. Powlowski opposes the expansion of Maid. In a supplementary opinion laying out his rationale, he reflected on how, even if the government chose not to extend access, people can end their lives.
“Furthermore, there are painless options readily available. One example being illicit narcotics like fentanyl,” he wrote.

Claire Brosseau subsequently filed a complaint with the Cpso asking them to investigate whether Mr. Powlowski’s comments were “consistent with the professional conduct expected of an Ontario physician.”

In her complaint, a copy of which was obtained by The Globe, she wrote that Mr. Powlowski’s remarks validated lethal self-harm and, in turn, created “a profound sense of unsafety for vulnerable patients who rely on the medical profession to uphold suicide prevention standards.”
Ms. Brosseau, who has bipolar 1, a form of bipolar disorder, is currently suing the federal government over its refusal to allow her to access Maid. The case remains before the court.
In a statement to The Globe Wednesday, Ms. Brosseau said the Cpso process is not complete.
“I will be responding to its most recent correspondence by the deadline they have given me. Until that process is complete, I will not be commenting further,” she said in an e-mail.
Mr. Powlowski said he is pleased the college is not investigating. He said he agreed with the Speaker that he should not face repercussions for comments made as a parliamentarian.
“I don’t think that would be appropriate,” he said in an interview.
When asked if he had any comment with regard to Ms. Brosseau’s allegations, he said he didn’t think it was appropriate for him to be part of a public discourse about her specific situation.

Mr. Scarpaleggia told MPs about the Cpso letter in the House late Tuesday afternoon. His decision to weigh in was prompted by the Conservative MP for Kitchener South-Hespeler Matt Strauss. He is also a physician , and in October, asked the Speaker to examine whether the Cpso investigation would be a violation of parliamentary privilege.
The joint House of Commons and Senate committee was studying Maid for mental illness earlier this year because the current ban on it expires in March and the government had to decide what to do next.

This fall, the government tabled Bill C-41. The bill restricts access to Maid for those whose only condition is mental illness. At the same time, it proposes a system for advanced requests, allowing people with “capacity-limiting illnesses” such as Alzheimer’s the ability to ask for medical help to end their lives at a future date.

stories.title: Saskatoon proposes 5.45% property tax increase in next year’s budget
stories.summary: City administrators are recommending that the council cut next year's budget by $1.19 million from the amount previously approved.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatoon city administrators are proposing a 5.45 per cent property tax increase for 2027, marking a minor decrease from what councillors originally approved last year.

The 2027 budget was considered last year as part of the city’s multi-year budget process, where a 5.81 per cent property tax increase was given the green light for the year ahead.

City administration is recommending that council cut next year’s budget by $1.19 million from the amount previously approved.

The proposed adjustments are part of the city’s multi-year budgeting process, which would see councillors consider changes to both the operating and capital budgets. It allows the city to respond to economic changes or for councillors to bring forward other budget-related items for consideration, according to the city.

The city says it saw revenue increases from higher investment returns and property tax assessments, which offset higher diesel costs and lower revenue sharing from the province.

Administrators are also asking councillors to approve 39.5 additional full-time equivalent positions tied to the Link bus rapid transit rollout. This is not expected to add to the tax increase, as $4.3 million is being shifted from debt servicing to begin phasing in Link operations in January 2027, ahead of a full launch in 2029.

Saskatoon police still make up the largest spending item, at 22.5 per cent of the total budget.

However, police are not asking for any changes to their previously approved $167.8 million operating plan. In 2027, they will get an additional $9.73 million, or a 6.2 per cent increase, mostly due to 33 new positions and collective agreement costs, according to the city.

Meanwhile, fire is budgeted at $77.22 million, up 9.1 per cent from last year, due to inflationary costs of collective agreements, equipment maintenance and $610,400 for encampment response.

As for fee changes, administration is recommneding

Speaking to reporters following a business fireside chat Tuesday, Mayor Cynthia Block said the city is putting a lot of effort into presenting a budget that is as “affordable as possible” for residents, adding that keeping the tax rate artificially low will only increase property taxes in the future.

“That’s why we try to make sure that we’re paying for things as we go, whether that’s roads or sidewalks or underground infrastructure, to make sure that we are paying as we go and not putting this on future budgets or future generations,” said Block.

Last year, city councillors passed a budget with one of the highest property tax increases in over a decade, at 6.7 per cent , with police making up around a quarter of spending.

Councillors spent four days going through over 100 considerations to whittle that property tax number down.

Budget adjustment deliberations are slated to start on Tuesday.

stories.title: Calgary is proposing big spending to improve road quality but some councillors say it’s not enough
stories.summary: Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot told Global News he is looking at clawing back Calgary Transit's funding request to help find more money to improve city roads during budget talks.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Plugging potholes and rehabilitating bridges account for just some of the millions in road-related spending City of Calgary officials have proposed in the upcoming four-year budget, but some on council believe the funding doesn’t go far enough.

Over the next four years, city administration has proposed $420.2 million for road rehabilitation, $178.1 million for bridge upgrades, $44 million for “major road construction,” and $29.5 million earmarked for concrete rehabilitation.

The increased spending proposal comes after it was revealed earlier this year that 11 per cent of city infrastructure was in poor condition .

At the end of 2025, 38 per cent of city roadways were classified in good or better condition, below the national average of 61 per cent.

“City council is looking at investing in infrastructure and resurfacing,” said Troy McLeod, the city’s director of mobility. “When we’re able to resurface a roadway, we’re able to save costs from rebuilding, it’s seven to 10 times more expensive to rebuild the road than resurface.”

Calgary’s road network has grown to more than 17,000 lane-kilometres, giving Calgary one of the largest road networks among major Canadian cities.

So far this year, city crews have filled 35,641 potholes.

“Putting money into maintenance is critical,” said Matti Siemiatycki, director of the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute. “Road maintenance is something that’s highly visible to the public, it’s something that people complain about, it’s something that can damage a vehicle depending on how bad it is.”

According to budget documents, council’s approval of the road-related spending requests would “stabilize and, in some cases, reduce risk” related to road condition.

It noted pavement-condition inspections and lifecycle analysis would be used to prioritize resurfacing, rehabilitation and preventive maintenance.

However, Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said what’s proposed “does not deliver” on expectations to improve pavement quality across the city.

“I certainly expected to see a lot more invested into our road infrastructure,” he told Global News. “Insofar as what’s being proposed for a tax increase, I’m just not seeing enough of an investment into our pavement quality index and sidewalk replacement.”

Concerned over elevated costs to rebuild deteriorated roads rather than repave them, Chabot said he’d be looking to find funds from elsewhere, including budget requests from Calgary Transit, to reallocate towards road maintenance.

“It’s the capital implications of operational increases that I’m concerned about,” he said.

Calgary Transit has requested an additional $62 million in operating funding to implement its RouteAhead strategy, the service’s plan to increase transit service and frequency across the city.

As a result of implementing that strategy, budget documents show Calgary Transit would also require $300 million over the next four years in capital funds to buy new buses and invest in continued renewal of transit technology, facilities and fleet infrastructure.

Chabot suggested that increases in transit service should be “commensurate” with increases in ridership.

“Ridership is actually down, and yet we’re still looking at investing a whole bunch of more money to try and encourage more people to come in,” he said. “Cost recovery is so low on our transit system right now that we’re just throwing good money after bad.”

Alex Williams, with the advocacy group Calgary Transit Riders, said cutting the service’s budget request to invest in road repairs won’t fix the issue.

“It’s going to make transit less appealing, which then adds more people back onto the roads in their cars, which adds more wear and tear, more demand for more asphalt,” Williams told Global News. “Robbing Peter to pay Paul never served anyone except Paul, maybe.”

It’s expected to lead to a bumpy debate when budget talks begin on Nov. 23.

City officials have also proposed a $7 million increase to snow and ice control in the four-year budget, as Calgary emerges from a snowfall warning which was predicted to drop between 15 and 20 centimetres of snow on city streets.

“When compared with Edmonton, they’re currently at $73 million for their snow and ice control budget, and we’re currently just over $58 million,” McLeod told Global News.

“Ridership is actually down, and yet we’re still looking at investing a whole bunch of more money to try and encourage more people to come in,” he said. “Cost recovery is so low on our transit system right now that we’re just throwing good money after bad.”
Alex Williams, with the advocacy group Calgary Transit Riders, said cutting the service’s budget request to invest in road repairs won’t fix the issue.

“It’s going to make transit less appealing, which then adds more people back onto the roads in their cars, which adds more wear and tear, more demand for more asphalt,” Williams told Global News. “Robbing Peter to pay Paul never served anyone except Paul, maybe.”
It’s expected to lead to a bumpy debate when budget talks begin on Nov. 23.

City officials have also proposed a $7 million increase to snow and ice control in the four-year budget, as Calgary emerges from a snowfall warning which was predicted to drop between 15 and 20 centimetres of snow on city streets.
“When compared with Edmonton, they’re currently at $73 million for their snow and ice control budget, and we’re currently just over $58 million,” McLeod told Global News.

stories.title: Doug Ford says learning French ‘rougher than I thought’ after Montreal speech
stories.summary: The Premier’s inability to speak basic French has led to speculation about the viability of his political career beyond the Ontario legislature
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s ability – or lack thereof – to speak basic French was in the spotlight on Wednesday, raising questions about his federal political prospects and leading to some criticisms that he hasn’t worked hard enough to learn one of Canada’s official languages.

To some, however, Mr. Ford’s earnest attempt to speak French at a Metropolitan Montreal Chamber of Commerce event was an authentic moment that underscores his political appeal.

Mr. Ford was in Montreal this week, where he addressed a sold-out business crowd. Videos of his stilted stab at speaking a few sentences in French made the rounds on social media, with the mascot owl of language tool Duolingo even weighing in on the platform X with, “I definitely didn’t teach him this...”

As he struggled to get the words out Tuesday, Mr. Ford said, “Oh, I’m really messing this one up,” to laughter from the crowd.

French is the only official language in Quebec , and communicating in it is a must for federal politicians and certain big business leaders. The chief executive officer of Air Canada, for instance, retired from the job after facing backlash for delivering an English-only condolence message in March. Premiers of some other provinces, including Manitoba’s Wab Kinew , are fluent in both official federal languages.

New Brunswick, however, is Canada’s only officially bilingual province, according to the Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages for New Brunswick.

Mr. Ford has for years said he’s taking French lessons, although he’s rarely spoken more than a few words in public. Being bilingual is also crucial for any leader of a federal political party – leading to speculation about the viability of Mr. Ford’s political future beyond the Ontario legislature.

He has faced questions in recent years about whether he plans to jump to federal politics at some point. Mr. Ford has always stated that his focus is on the province.

In early 2025, he embraced the “Captain Canada” role, taking on the Trump administration over U.S. tariffs and sovereignty issues, declaring Canada will never be the 51st state. He also butted heads with federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre after the party failed to win the 2025 election.

On Wednesday, Mr. Ford brushed aside questions about whether he’s interested in pursuing federal politics.

“I’m focused on Ontario ... I love my job and moving the province forward,” he said. “Merci, thank you.”

Mr. Ford said learning the language has been difficult for him.

“It’s a little rougher than I thought. I was as nervous as anything, practicing four lines. But it was a very warm welcome in Quebec and Montreal specifically.”

After first being elected to provincial office in 2018, Mr. Ford said it’s important to communicate with French speakers and cited an affinity with Quebec. In 2019, he said he was working on his French and it would be “pretty easy” to pick up. The province has almost 750,000 Franco-Ontarians, according to L’Assemblée de la francophonie de l’Ontario, which calls itself the political voice of francophones in Ontario. The group did not provide a comment when asked Wednesday.

Mr. Ford has previously landed in hot water with the province’s French-speaking community. In 2018, the government folded the province’s independent watchdog on French-language services into the ombudsman’s office, leading to backlash. It also scrapped a plan for a French-language university in Toronto, a decision that was later reversed after the school received federal funding. The moves led to the departure of his party’s only francophone MPP.

Stéphanie Chouinard, a professor of political studies at Queen’s University who grew up in Labrador but considers herself Franco-Ontarian, called Mr. Ford’s speech a “clumsy attempt” at demonstrating his appreciation for the French culture.

“It also speaks to Doug Ford’s personality. He was trying to be personable, to demonstrate his understanding of place,” she said in an interview.

Still, she said it’s disappointing that he’s been promising to learn the language since 2018.

“If some rumours are true that Doug Ford has federal political ambitions, then it’s sort of a rite of passage that he needs to be able to at least communicate at a basic level in French,” she said.

“But at the same time, it was a very Doug Ford type of moment.”

Opposition parties at Queen’s Park were not amused.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said “it’s a little insulting” that Mr. Ford hasn’t learned the basics of a language spoken by hundreds of thousands of residents.

“I didn’t think it was particularly funny. It was kind of embarrassing to be honest,” she told reporters.

Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser said after eight years in office, Mr. Ford should be able to speak passable French.

“I heard somebody say yesterday that what he did to French was a hate crime,” he said. “It’s not something to laugh about.”

stories.title: Animal advocates call for stricter breeding licensing after 84 dogs seized during recent operations
stories.summary: More than 120 dogs have been seized during two major operations on P.E.I. this year, renewing calls for tougher provincial oversight of animal breeding.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown - More than 120 dogs have been seized during two major operations on P.E.I. this year, renewing calls for tougher provincial oversight of animal breeding.

The P.E.I. Humane Society is still caring for 84 dogs seized earlier this month, after another 43 were taken into custody in February. Neither case has been confirmed to involve breeders, and the latest investigation remains ongoing.

“It was really, really challenging to see that many animals coming in, in need (of medical care) all at one time,” said Ashley Travis, the Humane Society’s development and communications co-ordinator.

Advocates call for stricter measures

P.E.I. has standards of care for kennels, but no mandatory licensing system specifically for breeders.

Non-profit organization P.E.I. Cares, is behind a petition signed by nearly 2,000 people calling for licensing, routine inspections and record-keeping requirements, among other measures. It was presented to the provincial legislature Friday.

Karla Shalley, the organization’s president, said the Island’s Animal Welfare Act was fairly progressive when it came into force in 2017, but her group believes it remains inadequate.

“We see neglect and situations like this on a very small scale,” she said, adding that people contact the organization with concerns almost daily.

In a statement to CTV News, the Department of Agriculture said the existing law already requires breeders to meet national standards for animal health, housing and welfare. It said complaints are investigated and the province is always reviewing its legislation for possible improvements.

Elsewhere in Atlantic Canada, New Brunswick requires those breeding dogs for sale, to obtain a licence following an inspection.

In Nova Scotia , a veterinary health certificate is required when a cat or dog is sold.

“I think there’s room to talk to some other provinces about what they’re doing and how they’re strengthening their laws,” Travis said.

For now, the fate of the latest group of dogs remains uncertain as the legal process continues. The Humane Society is asking for donations to help cover their medical care and other ongoing needs.

stories.title: Cruise line scraps Halifax port call, extends Bermuda stay. Here’s why
stories.summary: Norwegian Cruise Line is setting sail in a different direction, scrapping nearly 20 stops in Halifax, N.S., next year to spend more time in Bermuda instead.
stories.author: Ethan Morneau
stories.content:
Norwegian Cruise Line is setting sail in a different direction, scrapping nearly 20 stops in Halifax, N.S., next year to spend more time in Bermuda instead. Its Breakaway ship typically travels from Boston to Halifax before heading south. But in an email to guests and travel partners, the cruise line says it has “enhanced” its itinerary — meaning some trips will opt for an “extended stay” in Royal Naval Dockyard, Bermuda.

The change, which will see the cruise line drop 17 stops in Halifax in 2027, comes “in response to guest feedback,” according to the email from Norwegian. The “original” itinerary saw the Breakaway dock in Halifax for less than a day, from 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Now, travellers will spend that day at sea before arriving in Bermuda a day early — giving them two nights on the tropical island.

The email to guests, which was shared in the Norwegian Breakaway 2026 and 2027 Boston to Bermuda Facebook group, included the “revised” itinerary. “By spending two nights on the island, you’ll have even more time to discover Bermuda at your own pace, enjoy its unique culture and natural beauty, and experience the destination both during the day and after sunset,” it reads.

Norwegian Cruise Line called the revision an “enhancement,” adding that “Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada will no longer be included in your itinerary.” ‘Very disappointed’ Online users gave mixed reactions to the change. In the Facebook group, one person commented that they were “excited for the original itinerary because we haven’t been to either Nova Scotia or Bermuda,” adding, “we are considering cancelling because of the change.”

“Us too!” another person said. “Very disappointed.” ‘It was really cold’ On the other hand, one person who previously travelled to Halifax said, “it felt like the area wasn’t super excited about having a cruise arrive. “Lots of neat looking shops and a brewery, but (they) were closed.” Another who did the cruise last year said they found Nova Scotia “lovely” but shared that their “main complaint was that it was really cold … heading north.”

Another commenter added, “It’s not (that) the people don’t like Nova Scotia. But you’re going on a cruise to Bermuda, people want to spend time in Bermuda…” But Norwegian Cruise Line isn’t saying goodbye to Halifax. A company spokesperson told CTV News on Wednesday that while the city is “no longer featured on specific voyages,” guests will still be able to visit the city on its Canada and New England itineraries throughout 2027 and 2028.

Halifax wraps up a ‘strong season’ At the start of the 2026 cruise ship season, Port Halifax anticipated 189 calls by 28 cruise lines, bringing approximately 363,000 guests. Officials described it as a “strong season” with “new itineraries and new homeports calling Halifax and the region.” A 2026 highlight for the port authority was Norwegian Cruise Line’s “increased presence in spring and summer with the addition of Bermuda itineraries that include a stop in Halifax.”

The outgoing season wrapped up on Nov. 5. Port Halifax also pointed to a 2023 study by the Cruise Lines International Association, which found that cruise generates nearly $200 million each year and close to 1,000 jobs in Nova Scotia, supporting businesses and attractions. An unexpected cruise ship visit came to Halifax in October, when The Oasis of the Seas departed New Jersey with thousands of passengers who paid to go to the Bahamas — only to have stormy weather divert them to Nova Scotia’s capital instead.

‘Halifax is a beautiful city’ Some travellers felt hopeful, while others lost their enthusiasm. “I am already from Canada, and I wanted to go to the Bahamas,” Toronto’s Nicholas Meli told CTV News last month. “I’m very disappointed.” Meanwhile, Walter MacDonnell of Hamilton, Ont., said: “I’m glad this happened because we are loving it here.

I was really impressed when I came here before.” “Halifax is a beautiful city,” added New Jersey’s Jim Matthews. Port Halifax lauds the city as a “world-class destination” that continues to see solid cruise growth year-over-year, remaining “the marquee cruise destination in Atlantic Canada with the ability to accommodate the world’s largest cruise ships.”

With files from CTV News’ Paul Hollingsworth, The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Norwegian Cruise Line is setting sail in a different direction, scrapping nearly 20 stops in Halifax, N.S., next year to spend more time in Bermuda instead. Its Breakaway ship typically travels from Boston to Halifax before heading south. But in an email to guests and travel partners, the cruise line says it has “enhanced” its itinerary — meaning some trips will opt for an “extended stay” in Royal Naval Dockyard, Bermuda.

The change, which will see the cruise line drop 17 stops in Halifax in 2027, comes “in response to guest feedback,” according to the email from Norwegian. The “original” itinerary saw the Breakaway dock in Halifax for less than a day, from 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Now, travellers will spend that day at sea before arriving in Bermuda a day early — giving them two nights on the tropical island.

The email to guests, which was shared in the Norwegian Breakaway 2026 and 2027 Boston to Bermuda Facebook group, included the “revised” itinerary. “By spending two nights on the island, you’ll have even more time to discover Bermuda at your own pace, enjoy its unique culture and natural beauty, and experience the destination both during the day and after sunset,” it reads.

Norwegian Cruise Line called the revision an “enhancement,” adding that “Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada will no longer be included in your itinerary.” ‘Very disappointed’ Online users gave mixed reactions to the change. In the Facebook group, one person commented that they were “excited for the original itinerary because we haven’t been to either Nova Scotia or Bermuda,” adding, “we are considering cancelling because of the change.”

“Us too!” another person said. “Very disappointed.” ‘It was really cold’ On the other hand, one person who previously travelled to Halifax said, “it felt like the area wasn’t super excited about having a cruise arrive. “Lots of neat looking shops and a brewery, but (they) were closed.” Another who did the cruise last year said they found Nova Scotia “lovely” but shared that their “main complaint was that it was really cold … heading north.”

Another commenter added, “It’s not (that) the people don’t like Nova Scotia. But you’re going on a cruise to Bermuda, people want to spend time in Bermuda…” But Norwegian Cruise Line isn’t saying goodbye to Halifax. A company spokesperson told CTV News on Wednesday that while the city is “no longer featured on specific voyages,” guests will still be able to visit the city on its Canada and New England itineraries throughout 2027 and 2028.

Halifax wraps up a ‘strong season’ At the start of the 2026 cruise ship season, Port Halifax anticipated 189 calls by 28 cruise lines, bringing approximately 363,000 guests. Officials described it as a “strong season” with “new itineraries and new homeports calling Halifax and the region.” A 2026 highlight for the port authority was Norwegian Cruise Line’s “increased presence in spring and summer with the addition of Bermuda itineraries that include a stop in Halifax.”

The outgoing season wrapped up on Nov. 5. Port Halifax also pointed to a 2023 study by the Cruise Lines International Association, which found that cruise generates nearly $200 million each year and close to 1,000 jobs in Nova Scotia, supporting businesses and attractions. An unexpected cruise ship visit came to Halifax in October, when The Oasis of the Seas departed New Jersey with thousands of passengers who paid to go to the Bahamas — only to have stormy weather divert them to Nova Scotia’s capital instead.

‘Halifax is a beautiful city’ Some travellers felt hopeful, while others lost their enthusiasm. “I am already from Canada, and I wanted to go to the Bahamas,” Toronto’s Nicholas Meli told CTV News last month. “I’m very disappointed.” Meanwhile, Walter MacDonnell of Hamilton, Ont., said: “I’m glad this happened because we are loving it here.

I was really impressed when I came here before.” “Halifax is a beautiful city,” added New Jersey’s Jim Matthews. Port Halifax lauds the city as a “world-class destination” that continues to see solid cruise growth year-over-year, remaining “the marquee cruise destination in Atlantic Canada with the ability to accommodate the world’s largest cruise ships.”
With files from CTV News’ Paul Hollingsworth, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London city council votes to create second deputy mayor position
stories.summary: Shortly after being sworn-in Tuesday, London's city council voted to create two deputy mayor positions: splitt...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
Shortly after being sworn-in Tuesday, London’s city council voted to create two deputy mayor positions: splitting the duties between Ward 2 Coun. Shawn Lewis and Ward 5 Coun. Corrine Rahman. Mayor Josh Morgan had pitched the idea earlier this month, as a way to split the focus on community driven jobs and the inter-government matters.

The vote marked council’s first meeting after its inaguration ceremony at RBC place in front of about 200 people.

During the night, Morgan introduced the new members of the 14 council to the job.

“You’re in for a pretty amazing experience,” he said. “It’s the hardest job you will ever have, but also the best job you will ever have.”

Morgan also addressed the trust that Londoners have in the 11 incumbent councillors.

“Eleven members of council have returned. That did not happen across Ontario,” he said. “Make no mistake, for those of us who are incumbents on the stage, Londoners have put a tremendous amount of trust in us.”

The new ward members included Ben Durham (ward 3), Tom Cull (ward 4), Johnathan Sher (ward 7) and Jason King (ward 14).

Steve Lehman (ward 8) and new face Tom Cull (ward 4) were selected for budget chair and vice budget chair.

Morgan also discussed the future of the city and plans that are in place, emphasizing the city must work to execute them.

stories.title: St. Thomas driver disputes Hyundai Canada engine warranty denial
stories.summary: A St. Thomas woman is raising concerns about Hyundai Canada’s handling of engine warranty claims, after her 2016 Hyundai Santa Fe XL suffered a catastrophic engine failure leaving her with a substantial repair bill and a battle for coverage.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
A St. Thomas woman is raising concerns about Hyundai Canada’s handling of engine warranty claims, after her 2016 Hyundai Santa Fe XL suffered a catastrophic engine failure leaving her with a substantial repair bill and a battle for coverage.

Kate Andrews believes her vehicle should be eligible for an engine replacement based on extended warranty provisions, similar to those available in the United States facing the same issue.

Andrews purchased the used 2016 Hyundai Santa Fe XL seven months prior to the incident, attracted by its low mileage and good service history.

“Even though it’s a ten year old vehicle, the kilometers were quite low. It had very good service history. So this was really a blind side for us,” she stated.

Her experience took an unexpected turn in May of this year while travelling near St. Thomas. She was about ten minutes south of St. Thomas, traveling along Fairview Road, approaching Fruit Ridge Line, when the vehicle simply came to a standstill.

“I had no warning at all. There was no engine lights, nothing telling me that something imminent was going to happen. The whole car started to vibrate. I could smell something,” Andrews recounted.

After the vehicle was towed to a London dealership, Andrews learned the engine would need to be replaced – an estimated $15,000 expense. That’s what she paid for the SUV.

The failed unit was identified as a 3.3-litre Lambda Two engine. It was during her research into the repair that Andrews discovered that similar engines with related problems had become eligible for extended warranty coverage.

However, a call to Hyundai Canada was met with a refusal. “It takes me to someone that can tell me ‘no’, basically, and they can’t escalate it for you,” Andrews expressed. “So they have now said my case is closed. There’s nothing else they can do for us.”

Andrews reports she has since connected with ten other Santa Fe XL owners across Canada who have experienced similar engine failures. Citing safety concerns, she is now escalating her case, having spoken with Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon and scheduled a meeting with Elgin-St. Thomas-London South MP Andrew Lawton for Friday. “It is such a safety concern, the way that Hyundai does not signal at all that this is going to happen,” she emphasized.

CTV London reached out to both Hyundai Canada and the Transportation Ministry for comment. Hyundai Canada had not responded by the time of publication.

Transport Canada, however, indicated that defect investigations are primarily driven by public complaints and aim to identify safety defects. As a result of such investigations, extended warranty coverage has been implemented by manufacturers. Specifically, Transport Canada launched defect investigation file no. 3280-08-78 to examine 3.3-litre engine failures in certain vehicles. The investigation identified various causes, including wear and tear and, in some cases, poor maintenance.

Consequently, both Hyundai and Kia issued extended warranty coverage for specific engine-related repairs.

Hyundai’s Campaign CO615 covers certain 2013-2019 Santa Fe XL vehicles equipped with the 3.3L engine that May experience abnormal engine noise or damage due to worn connecting rod bearings.

This campaign extends warranty coverage for eligible conditions to 15 years or 240,000 km from the original warranty start date, and is available to both original and subsequent owners. Eligibility is determined after an inspection of the vehicle’s engine and a review of maintenance records.

While Transport Canada confirms that an extended warranty has been put in place in Canada for such issues, Andrews maintains this information has not been passed on or applied to her situation by Hyundai Canada.

Transport Canada encourages vehicle owners who believe their vehicle May have a safety-related defect to report it to their Defect Complaints and Recalls Hotline at 1-800-333-0510 or submit a defect complaint form, as these reports are crucial for initiating and informing investigations.

stories.title: Drunk driving case falls apart because Mountie failed to disclose romantic relationship with key witness
stories.summary: 'The disclosure came from Crown counsel as a result of a chance encounter at a Canadian Tire store,' said the judge
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A woman who had already pleaded guilty in a drunk driving crash near Flin Flon, Man., that left another woman with life-altering injuries has escaped charges after a chance encounter at a Canadian Tire store revealed a Mountie failed to disclose he was involved in a romantic relationship with a nurse who was a key witness in the case.

Flin Flon RCMP charged Taylor Chodorowski after she was involved in a head-on collision on March 4, 2023, where both female drivers suffered serious injuries.

Chodorowski, who pleaded guilty in 2025, later applied to the Manitoba provincial court for a stay in the case, alleging abuse of process. That came after she learned about the relationship between RCMP Cpl. Jordan Tost — the investigator who applied to court for a production order to obtain her medical records from the Flin Flon Hospital — and Breanne Ballard, a nurse “whose observations formed part of the grounds” Tost relied on to obtain the production order.

Chodorowski “faced the enormous power of the state through a process in which material information was deliberately withheld at multiple stages,” Judge Victoria Cornick wrote in her Oct. 30 decision to grant the stay.

“The conduct here impaired the safeguards intended to balance investigative powers thereby contravening fundamental notions of justice and undermining the integrity of the judicial process. It therefore constitutes an abuse of process.

“The only remedy available in these particular circumstances is a stay of proceedings.”

Manitoba RCMP refused to say whether Tost has faced discipline for his role.

“Generally speaking, we are unable to provide details on internal HR matters,” RCMP spokesperson Michelle Lissel said Wednesday in an email.

Chodorowski’s defence argued that Tost “played a more active role in the investigation than was previously understood, including identifying Nurse Ballard and Nurse Sara Wilson as potential witnesses and directing that they be interviewed.”

The impact on this officer’s credibility cannot be overstated, and that will carry on into the future

RCMP Const. Christopher Chelmecki testified that Tost “suggested that the two nurses possessed relevant information and should be interviewed,” Cornick said. “Cpl. Tost denied having done so.”

Chodorowski argued that the “undisclosed relationship” between Tost and Ballard, “together with the alleged involvement of Cpl. Tost in identifying and directing witnesses whose information was later relied upon in the authorization process, created a conflict that should have been disclosed to both the authorizing justice and the court.”

Crown attorney Kameron Hutchinson argued that “while the relationship should have been disclosed, the evidence falls well short of establishing the deliberate deception or serious state misconduct required to support a finding of abuse of process.”

Tost’s application for a production order “was supported by ample grounds independent of any relationship between Cpl. Tost and Ms. Ballard,” Hutchinson told the court, noting “there was no intention to mislead the court, and that the integrity of the justice system has not been compromised.”

The judge sided with Chodorowski, who was permitted to withdraw her guilty plea this past January.

The “significance of the relationship” between the Mountie and the nurse “is that it supplied material context for assessing Nurse Ballard’s information,” said the judge. “It’s omission prevented that context from being considered during the application for the authorization and during the subsequent review of the authorization. The possibility that the production order might nevertheless have been issued did not relieve Cpl. Tost of his obligation to disclose it.”

Tost “knew that Nurse Ballard was his partner and that her information formed part of the grounds advanced in support of the production order. He had also identified her to Cst. Chelmecki as a possible witness,” Cornick said.

“This court does not accept his explanation that the relationship’s relevance did not occur to him. His initial response that he did not consider it relevant, followed by the statement that he did not consider it at all, does not provide a persuasive explanation when assessed against his experience, his acknowledged obligations, and his knowledge of Nurse Ballard’s role as a key witness in the investigation.”

Cornick was “satisfied on a balance of probabilities that Cpl. Tost deliberately withheld the relationship.”

Police officers “seeking judicial authorization owe a duty of candour to the authorizing justice,” said the judge.

Applications for a production order, known as an Information to Obtain (ITO), “must be full, fair, and frank and must not contain material misstatements or omissions,” Cornick said.

In Chodorowski’s case, “the abuse stems from the deliberate withholding of material information in a process that depends almost exclusively on candid presentation of information to function fairly,” said the judge.

Police seek production orders using an an ex parte, system, Cornick said. “That is to say, the target of the production order is rarely even aware that the application process is taking place let alone permitted to participate.”

When the production order was authorized in Chodorowski’s case, “the issuing justice lacked material context for Nurse Ballard’s information. Accuracy, truth, and completeness of the record are indispensable for an ex parte application system to work. An issuing justice cannot leave the four corners of the application to seek out additional information or confirmation,” said the judge.

Tost “never disclosed the omission of material information deliberately,” Cornick said.

“The disclosure came from Crown counsel as a result of a chance encounter at a Canadian Tire store. After this encounter Mr. Hutchinson learned about the relationship between Cpl. Tost and Nurse Ballard and took immediate steps to inform defence counsel.”

Hutchinson also didn’t oppose the withdrawal of Chodorowski’s guilty plea, said the judge.

“While Mr. Hutchinson’s swift and decisive actions are to be commended as they mitigated any further harm, they cannot excuse what the deliberate omission had already set in motion. The ex parte authorization process cannot rely on chance public encounters as safeguards against miscarriages of justice.”

The Crown figured out Tost and Ballard were in a romantic relationship after spotting them together in Canadian Tire, according to defence lawyers Matt Gould and Keenan Fonseca, who represented Chodorowski.

“The existence of the relationship between Nurse Ballard and Cpl. Tost is not the problem,” said the judge.

“The concern arises out of the deliberate withholding of the existence of the relationship by an experienced affiant and the consequences that flowed from that omission throughout the proceedings.”

The “most serious aspect of the misconduct,” she said, “is that judges were repeatedly asked to make decisions without information they were entitled to receive. Cpl. Tost was an experienced affiant. He knew that Nurse Ballard was both his partner and an important witness in the investigation. Yet the relationship was not disclosed during the authorization process or during the subsequent review. The omission therefore affected not only the initial authorization but also the judicial mechanisms designed to scrutinize that authorization. The proceedings advanced to the point of a guilty plea before the omission was discovered during a chance encounter at a retail store.”

Cornick was “mindful that there is a victim in this matter who suffered life-altering injuries as a result of alleged criminal conduct. Nobody deserves the adjudication of this matter on its merits more than her.”

But the judge found “that the resulting institutional prejudice would persist if the prosecution continued.”

Gould, one of Chodorowski’s lawyers, said in an email Wednesday that he hopes “this decision will prevent abuse of process from occurring in the future.”

“Regardless of whether or not disciplinary action is taken, there will be real consequences for (Tost) and the RCMP,” Gould said.

The “jeopardy” people face in cases like this “is astronomical,” Gould said, noting a conviction could result in years behind bars.

“We rely on the honesty and credibility of officers that participate in this process, and it is a major setback for the police and prosecutions when that trust is broken,” said Gould, a partner in the firm Brodsky Amy Gould Kinahan Mahoney.

He said he would be surprised if the Crown appeals the stay.

“This case is scary because it reveals how much power the police have and how much our system relies on the assumption that they are acting with integrity,” Gould said. “The fact that this abuse of process was exposed by happenstance is chilling, and it reveals how vulnerable everyone is to the authority we entrust to the police.”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

“The concern arises out of the deliberate withholding of the existence of the relationship by an experienced affiant and the consequences that flowed from that omission throughout the proceedings.”
Editor’s Picks

The “most serious aspect of the misconduct,” she said, “is that judges were repeatedly asked to make decisions without information they were entitled to receive. Cpl. Tost was an experienced affiant. He knew that Nurse Ballard was both his partner and an important witness in the investigation. Yet the relationship was not disclosed during the authorization process or during the subsequent review. The omission therefore affected not only the initial authorization but also the judicial mechanisms designed to scrutinize that authorization. The proceedings advanced to the point of a guilty plea before the omission was discovered during a chance encounter at a retail store.”

Cornick was “mindful that there is a victim in this matter who suffered life-altering injuries as a result of alleged criminal conduct. Nobody deserves the adjudication of this matter on its merits more than her.”
But the judge found “that the resulting institutional prejudice would persist if the prosecution continued.”
Gould, one of Chodorowski’s lawyers, said in an email Wednesday that he hopes “this decision will prevent abuse of process from occurring in the future.”
“Regardless of whether or not disciplinary action is taken, there will be real consequences for (Tost) and the RCMP,” Gould said.
The “jeopardy” people face in cases like this “is astronomical,” Gould said, noting a conviction could result in years behind bars.

“We rely on the honesty and credibility of officers that participate in this process, and it is a major setback for the police and prosecutions when that trust is broken,” said Gould, a partner in the firm Brodsky Amy Gould Kinahan Mahoney.
He said he would be surprised if the Crown appeals the stay.

“This case is scary because it reveals how much power the police have and how much our system relies on the assumption that they are acting with integrity,” Gould said. “The fact that this abuse of process was exposed by happenstance is chilling, and it reveals how vulnerable everyone is to the authority we entrust to the police.”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

stories.title: Police across region launch Festive Ride checks
stories.summary: Beginning Thursday, drivers will begin to encounter Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (Ride) checks on their travels.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Beginning Thursday, drivers will begin to encounter Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (Ride) checks on their travels.

Police services across the region are launching their annual Festive Ride campaigns.

“Police continue to encounter drivers who get behind the wheel after consuming alcohol or drugs,” said Lambton OPP Insp. Ross Stuart at a kickoff event in Point Edward Wednesday.

A group of representatives from area police and emergency services, as well as a spokesperson from Mothers Against Drunk Driving (Madd) gathered under the Bluewater Bridge for the event.

Erin Pollard, president of the Sarnia Lambton Chapter of Madd says impaired driving is a choice, and too often a tragic one.

“If you injure somebody in drinking and driving, you have to live with that. But there’s a whole family as well that has to live with either a loss or an injury from a choice that you made,” said Pollard.

In last year’s Festive Ride, OPP alone laid nearly 300 charges across Western Region.

“We are doing more Rides every year. We are stopping more vehicles every year. We continue to see impaired driving being one of the leading causes of death on the roadways,” said Insp. Stuart.

Also on hand at the kickoff, chiefs and supervisors from Anishinabek, Walpole Island, and Sarnia Police services.

“And I can’t describe how devastating the event can be. We witness it as professionals, trying to convince people that it just simply isn’t worth it,” said Sarnia Police Chief Mike Frederico.

“If you plan to drink alcohol or consume drugs, please plan ahead and arrange a safe ride home,” said Walpole Island Police Acting Staff Sgt. Rick Mathieson.

Penalties for impaired driving range from license suspension to vehicle impoundment, and a wide range of fines all the way to jail time or imprisonment, depending on the severity of the conviction.

The Festive Ride Campaign begins Thursday, and wraps up on New Year’s Day.

stories.title: Ex-banker who opened accounts, viewed PM’s data should get jail time: Crown
stories.summary: Ibrahim El-Hakim, who worked at a Royal Bank of Canada branch in downtown Ottawa, pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Crown says a former bank employee who admitted to opening fraudulent accounts and viewing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s personal information should be sentenced to two years behind bars.

Ibrahim El-Hakim, who worked at a Royal Bank of Canada branch in downtown Ottawa, pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft.

A sentencing hearing for El-Hakim, 24, took place in an Ontario court Wednesday.

The Ottawa-born man was not at the hearing. It’s the second consecutive court date he has missed.

Justice Norm Boxall told the court the Canada Border Services Agency notified the RCMP in late September that El-Hakim had left Montreal for Doha, Qatar, earlier in the month.

His baggage was checked through to Lebanon and no return flight was booked, Boxall said.

Police were unable to locate El-Hakim, the judge said.

“The only reasonable inference on the evidence or information before me in this case is that Mr. El-Hakim deliberately left Canada to thwart the sentencing process,” Boxall said.

The judge added the sentencing needs to be conducted in a timely manner.

“The administration of justice would be undermined if the sentencing was postponed to when he returns to Canada, if he ever does,” he said.

The RCMP began an investigation last year following a complaint from RBC.

An agreed statement of facts in the case says El-Hakim was recruited by someone he believed “to be associated with organized crime.”

The agreed statement says El-Hakim opened at least 43 fraudulent accounts at the bank between November 2023 and June 2025.

El-Hakim received at least $5,000 in compensation — $500 for each account, issued in the form of an e-transfer deposited into one of his accounts at other banks, the statement says.

On June 17, 2025, El-Hakim accessed the customer banking profiles of Carney, Justin Trudeau and another individual, the statement adds.

The Trudeau account he accessed “was determined not to belong to the former prime minister.”

While accessing these profiles, El-Hakim was observed consulting a smart watch, the statement says. On surveillance video, he was seen at one point taking a cellphone out of his pocket, using it and alternating his gaze between the phone and the computer screen of his bank workstation.

The Mounties have said the investigation did not lead them to believe there was any threat to Carney’s safety or to national security.

The Crown is seeking a sentence of 24 months in custody, followed by 24 months of probation with a variety of conditions.

Crown attorney Lindsay Little told the court Wednesday that El Hakim’s actions amounted to months of “sustained, dishonest conduct. This was not an isolated incident.”

Little highlighted the fact that El-Hakim queried Carney’s data and apparently tried to access Trudeau’s banking details.

“Public confidence is eroded by a case like this,” she said.

“Privacy is a right that applies to everyone, regardless of their status. Elected officials do not lose their financial privacy because they have chosen to dedicate their lives to politics or to the public sphere more generally.”

Ron Guertin, a lawyer who once represented El-Hakim, asked last month to be removed from the case because his client had left Ottawa.

Lawyer Paul Lewandowski has been appointed as amicus, or friend of the court, to assist with sentencing.

He said Wednesday in court that El-Hakim should receive a suspended sentence, meaning no jail time with a period of probation.

In the alternative, he said, a “short, sharp” jail term of 30 to 90 days would be appropriate.

Such a sentence would deter other bank employees from this kind of activity, given that “the spectre of a jail term is looming,” Lewandowski said.

Boxall said he plans to sentence El-Hakim next month.

stories.title: Ontario elementary teachers ‘overwhelmingly’ vote for strike, federation says
stories.summary: ‘Strong strike mandates’ show increasing challenges educators face in schools and workplaces, says Union’s president
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario says teachers and education workers have overwhelmingly voted in favour of central strike action.

The federation which represents both groups says 97 per cent of education workers, and 97 per cent of teachers and occasional teachers have voted to give their union strike mandates.

The union’s president says the “strong strike mandates” show the increasing challenges educators face in schools and workplaces across the province and underline “our members’ solidarity and support” for the union’s bargaining team.

David Mustin says the vote sends a strong message to the government and the Council of Ontario Directors of Education that the members of the federation are united and ready to take action if needed to bring meaningful improvements to their working conditions.

The union says it is looking to reach fair agreements at both negotiating tables to deliver improvements on its bargaining priorities that include smaller class sizes, fair compensation, and strengthening health and safety protections.

Mustin says the members overwhelmingly supported the strike mandates “because they are frustrated by years of chronic underfunding and deteriorating learning and working conditions.”

Bargaining at both negotiating tables for teachers as well as education workers is set to resume at the end of this month.

stories.title: Company built by Western students offers event medical services across Southern Ontario
stories.summary: Western students Ryan Lutz and Ethan Baxter founded Aventry Medical, offering event medical services across Southern Ontario.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Co-founders come together in all sorts of places.

Sometimes it’s a serendipitous meeting at a local coffee shop. Other times, it’s two friends or family members who have known, grown, and tussled with each other for years.

For Ryan Lutz and Ethan Baxter, it was being part of Western’s Student Emergency Response Team, or Sert, in 2024.

Lutz has a passion for entrepreneurship and was setting himself up for business school, while Baxter was pursuing a bachelor of medical science degree.

And as they spent the school year moving from one building to another with their signature red backpacks and light blue shirts, an idea was coming together.

Baxter had worked the summer at a very established event medical services company (and future competitor), taking care of attendees at concerts and sporting events across Ontario.

But he soon discovered a range of problems at his employer and other companies in the industry. For one, many of the hired medical staff weren’t properly trained and didn’t have the relevant experience.

Then there was the question of reliability.

“Event medical companies tend to cancel on their clients, like two days out, and then the clients are scrambling,” Baxter said.

After hearing directly from clients about the lack of reliability, professionalism, and disappointing quality of service, Lutz and Baxter saw a clear gap in the market.

A company that clients could depend on.

“With our shared medical experience and my interest in entrepreneurship, we saw an opportunity to build a company that could set a much higher standard for event medical care,” said Lutz.

And together, the pair launched Aventry Medical in the fall of 2025.

Today, Aventry Medical provides physician-directed event medical services across Southern Ontario, serving major concerts, festivals, races, sporting events, and corporate activations. Aventry operates under physician-developed protocols and the direction of its medical director, Dr. Frank Myslik, an emergency physician at London Health Sciences Centre and professor at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.

Members of the Aventry Medical team. (Submitted)

Together, Lutz and Baxter have built a team of over 40 medics and athletic trainers, all certified and ready to handle the complexities that arise on the job.

Not yet a year old, Aventry has already covered over 400 event days, with some events exceeding 10,000 attendees. Any given weekend, they could be supporting over a dozen events across Ontario.

Their promise on reliability and professionalism has yielded a growing base of repeat and recurring clients that have helped them secure contracts extending into 2027.

Revenue has not only allowed the team to grow and introduce additional training, but has also allowed Aventry to purchase their own Mobile Treatment Trailer, a UTV medical response vehicle, and two company automobiles, and build out an inventory of professional medical equipment, including defibrillators, emergency medications, oxygen, and other emergency response equipment.

However, Lutz and Baxter aren’t resting. The pair are continuing to hone how they operate, and how their medics and trainers can continue to give clients the best experience.

Having recently joined the Ivey HBA Program, Lutz is excited to see how his courses and discussions at Ivey will open more insights into how to run, manage and expand Aventry.

With Baxter in his final year at Western, the co-founders are excited for what the future holds for the company they started while being part of Sert.

Throughout that journey, the greatest lessons have come through the mistakes they made along the way, Lutz said. They were responsible for some of the company’s biggest improvements.

“When building a company, things will inevitably go wrong,” said Lutz.

“I have learned that there is little value in dwelling on what has already happened. Instead, I focus on understanding what went wrong, finding a solution and making sure we are better because of it. Entrepreneurship has taught me to focus on what I can control and always keep moving forward.”

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

Sometimes it’s a serendipitous meeting at a local coffee shop. Other times, it’s two friends or family members who have known, grown, and tussled with each other for years.
For Ryan Lutz and Ethan Baxter, it was being part of Western’s Student Emergency Response Team, or Sert, in 2024.
Lutz has a passion for entrepreneurship and was setting himself up for business school, while Baxter was pursuing a bachelor of medical science degree.
And as they spent the school year moving from one building to another with their signature red backpacks and light blue shirts, an idea was coming together.
Baxter had worked the summer at a very established event medical services company (and future competitor), taking care of attendees at concerts and sporting events across Ontario.

But he soon discovered a range of problems at his employer and other companies in the industry. For one, many of the hired medical staff weren’t properly trained and didn’t have the relevant experience.
Then there was the question of reliability.
“Event medical companies tend to cancel on their clients, like two days out, and then the clients are scrambling,” Baxter said.
After hearing directly from clients about the lack of reliability, professionalism, and disappointing quality of service, Lutz and Baxter saw a clear gap in the market.
A company that clients could depend on.
“With our shared medical experience and my interest in entrepreneurship, we saw an opportunity to build a company that could set a much higher standard for event medical care,” said Lutz.
And together, the pair launched Aventry Medical in the fall of 2025.
Scaling up to 40 staff, 400 days of events

Today, Aventry Medical provides physician-directed event medical services across Southern Ontario, serving major concerts, festivals, races, sporting events, and corporate activations. Aventry operates under physician-developed protocols and the direction of its medical director, Dr. Frank Myslik, an emergency physician at London Health Sciences Centre and professor at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.
Members of the Aventry Medical team. (Submitted)

Their promise on reliability and professionalism has yielded a growing base of repeat and recurring clients that have helped them secure contracts extending into 2027.

Revenue has not only allowed the team to grow and introduce additional training, but has also allowed Aventry to purchase their own Mobile Treatment Trailer, a UTV medical response vehicle, and two company automobiles, and build out an inventory of professional medical equipment, including defibrillators, emergency medications, oxygen, and other emergency response equipment.

stories.title: Ontario elementary teachers, education workers vote in favour of strike
stories.summary: Toronto - The Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario says teachers and education workers have overwhelmingly voted in favour of central strike action.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federation which represents both groups says 97 per cent of education workers, and 97 per cent of teachers and occasional teachers have voted to give their union strike mandates.

The union’s president says the “strong strike mandates” show the increasing challenges educators face in schools and workplaces across the province and underline “our members’ solidarity and support” for the union’s bargaining team.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

David Mustin says the vote sends a strong message to the government and the Council of Ontario Directors of Education that the members of the federation are united and ready to take action if needed to bring meaningful improvements to their working conditions.

The union says it is looking to reach fair agreements at both negotiating tables to deliver improvements on its bargaining priorities that include smaller class sizes, fair compensation, and strengthening health and safety protections.

Mustin says the members overwhelmingly supported the strike mandates “because they are frustrated by years of chronic underfunding and deteriorating learning and working conditions.”

Bargaining at both negotiating tables for teachers as well as education workers is set to resume at the end of this month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto mayor vows to tackle affordability, fiscal challenges in second term
stories.summary: Olivia Chow has pledged to build more affordable homes, crack down on bad-faith evictions and expand school nutrition programs
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
Olivia Chow laid out her vision for a second term as Toronto’s mayor, underlining her campaign promises to tackle affordability issues while also pointing to the city’s fiscal challenges.

Chow’s speech on Wednesday afternoon punctuated the usual fanfare and formalities of the first meeting of Toronto’s new council. She presided over a council with a boosted progressive bloc and without one of her chief rivals, Brad Bradford, whom she defeated in last month’s election.

Her speech alluded to pledges to build more affordable homes, crack down on bad-faith evictions, expand school nutrition programs and cap transit fares at 10 rides a week.

She connected her own upbringing to the city’s promise as a place where families could afford to “build a better life.” Toronto is a city, she said, where an immigrant child from Hong Kong raised by a hotel maid in a St. James Town apartment could rise through the political ranks and be twice elected mayor.

“I have never forgotten what Toronto gave my family. And I have spent my life trying to make sure other families have the same opportunities,” she said.

Chow also referred to the “enormous fiscal challenge” facing Toronto and other cities across Ontario. The city is facing an estimated $1.1-billion hole in the upcoming budget.

The remarks come after Premier Doug Ford earlier this month shot down the idea of renewing the so-called “new deal” he struck with Chow in the early days of her first term. That three-year deal saw Ontario provide $1.2-billion in operating dollars for transit and shelter costs, while taking on the long-term maintenance costs of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway.

Toronto cannot keep going back to Queen’s Park year after year asking for another agreement, “another Band-Aid solution,” Chow said.

“We need a structured financial solution that is fair, predictable and grows with the economy.”

A new speaker was elected by council for the first time in 16 years, after longtime rules enforcer Frances Nunziata was unseated last month, ending her more than four decades in city politics. Ausma Malik, a close ally of Chow and a deputy mayor during the last term, was elevated to the position.

Last month’s election set the table for a shakeup in Chow’s leadership team, with the retirement of housing chair Gord Perks and the defeat of transit chair Jamaal Myers. The mayor will have seven new councillors to consider for high-profile committee roles, including former Liberal MPs Nate Erskine-Smith and Shaun Chen. Those selections won’t be revealed until Thursday.

Affordable housing is at the top of Chow’s first agenda. When council reconvenes Thursday, she will look to advance a rental housing incentive program dating back to her first term.

The program offers financial breaks to purpose-built rental housing developers who dedicate at least 20 per cent of a project to affordable housing. Those affordable units are exempt from city property taxes and fees, ON top of a provincially mandated development charge exemption. For the other market-value rental units, the city offers a 15 per cent property-tax reduction and an indefinite deferral on remaining development charges.

The city has conditionally picked 19 projects for the latest funding round, representing 9,667 homes, including 2,059 affordable units. The city says those incentives add up to about $500 million, made possible by a $1.5-billion federal-provincial deal to offset a reduction in development charges citywide.

stories.title: LHSC names new board as hospital works toward end of provincial supervision
stories.summary: London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has appointed eight new volunteer board members and five community representatives, marking a significant step toward restoring local governance nearly two years after the province took control of the hospital.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has appointed eight new volunteer board members and five community representatives, marking a significant step toward restoring local governance nearly two years after the province took control of the hospital.

The renewed board will work alongside provincial Supervisor David Musyj until supervision ends, at which point it will assume full authority over the organization.

Ron Sapsford, a former Ontario deputy minister of health and long-term care and former CEO of the Ontario Medical Association, has been named board chair.

“It’s an important hospital, not only for London, but for southwestern Ontario. So I think it’s important to get the board back in operation. That to me is the crucial part,” Sapsford said.

The other board members are Scott Courtice, Cedric Gomes, Christi-Ann Poulette, Michael G. Power, David Smith, Melanie Stanley and Lori Van Opstal.

Five community members will also serve on board committees: Catherine Osborne, Leo Plue, Mike Tidy, Nick Vander Gulik and Lloy Wylie.

The appointments follow a recruitment process that attracted more than 90 applicants.

The move comes after a turbulent period for LHSC. In 2024, the province placed the hospital under supervision following serious concerns about governance, financial oversight and organizational leadership.

A provincial review identified significant governance failures, while subsequent investigations uncovered allegations of fraud involving former executives and contractors. The allegations have not been proven in court.

Musyj says the hospital has spent the past two years making structural changes to strengthen accountability and oversight.

Those changes include consolidating management positions, introducing 360-degree performance reviews, tightening spending controls, expanding internal audits and strengthening whistleblower protections.

The hospital has also refreshed its bylaws, policies and procedures and introduced additional oversight of budgeting, staffing decisions, quality indicators and patient safety.

“We’re in a good spot moving forward,” Musyj said, adding that the individuals involved in the alleged misconduct are no longer with the organization.

The renewed board will operate through four standing committees: finance and audit, quality and safety, human resources, and research.

Despite the appointments, Musyj says provincial supervision will not end immediately.

“You don’t want to do this again, right? So you don’t want to stay too long, but you don’t want to leave too early,” Musyj said.

Meanwhile, legal proceedings related to the alleged fraud remain ongoing. Musyj said the civil lawsuits are in the discovery phase, which involves exchanging documents and sworn evidence, as well as examinations for discovery.

He also confirmed the hospital is co-operating with a police investigation and responding to requests for information.

Musyj said further developments involving the civil proceedings are expected to be announced.

The renewed board’s first public meeting is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027. LHSC says meetings will be open to the public and livestreamed as part of its commitment to transparency and community engagement.

The hospital says the goal is to eventually return to local governance with stronger oversight and accountability measures in place.

Meanwhile, legal proceedings related to the alleged fraud remain ongoing. Musyj said the civil lawsuits are in the discovery phase, which involves exchanging documents and sworn evidence, as well as examinations for discovery.
He also confirmed the hospital is co-operating with a police investigation and responding to requests for information.
Musyj said further developments involving the civil proceedings are expected to be announced.

The renewed board’s first public meeting is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027. LHSC says meetings will be open to the public and livestreamed as part of its commitment to transparency and community engagement.
The hospital says the goal is to eventually return to local governance with stronger oversight and accountability measures in place.

stories.title: Lack of lawful access regime tied to ‘exponential growth’ of online child abuse material: police
stories.summary: They argued that police are feeling increasingly powerless to deal with online crimes with powers designed in the pre-Internet era
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
'If you have enough money, you’re going to find someone to do whatever you want.' — Dr. Ian MacArthur, a plastic surgeon

They argued that police are feeling increasingly powerless to deal with online crimes with powers designed in the pre-Internet era

Tom Stamatakis, president of the Ottawa-based Canadian Police Association. (Ashley Fraser / Postmedia)

November 18, 2026 at 5:53 p.m.

Ottawa — “Continuous kicking of the can” on lawful access reform like Bill C-22 has contributed to the “exponential growth” of online child abuse material, the head of a group of detectives focused on online child exploitation told senators.

On Wednesday, child protection agencies and law enforcement representatives made a passionate plea to senators on the national defence committee to quickly pass the Liberals’ controversial lawful access Bill C-22.

Every day that law enforcement don’t have access to a new lawful access regime fit for the digital age is another day where police struggle to tackle heinous online crime, particularly child sexual abuse material, they argued.

“To be blunt, our society is losing the effort to combat the exploitation of children over the internet,” said Andrew Ullock, chair of the Ontario Child Sexual Exploitation Investigators Association and a longtime detective with Peel Regional Police.

Ullock, as well as the heads of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Police Association and the National Police Federation, pleaded with senators to pass Bill C-22 as quickly as possible and dismissed calls for further tightening of the contested bill.

They argued that police are feeling increasingly powerless to deal with online crimes with powers designed in the pre-Internet era. They said that they are required to get court warrants to obtain the most basic information about online activity without knowing if a company even holds the data they seek.

“In practical terms, (Bill C-22) would help police avoid wasting valuable time by seeking judicial orders from the wrong service provider, obtain basic subscriber information based on reasonable suspicion, and address lengthy delays when critical evidence is held outside of Canada and at risk of disappearing,” said Tom Stamatakis, the president of the Canadian Police Association union.

Lawful access is one of the most intrusive powers afforded to police and intelligence agencies. Creating such a regime for the digital age in Canada has been the subject of fierce debate for decades.

Bill C-22 proposes a new lawful access regime which would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to intercept private communications or personal data as part of their investigations.

It creates new and faster legal tools for authorities to find out if a person is a client of a specific organization and then obtain some of their subscriber information with a warrant.

It also proposes new obligations to electronic service providers to organize and retain various types of client data in a way that makes it obtainable by law enforcement or Csis with a warrant.

That means that if passed, the bill would compel electronic service providers to store and make information like device locations or cameras available to police or Csis with the requisite warrant. That could be used to track a person’s live location in case they pose a threat to national security or are considered to be in danger, the government has said.

It also controversially allows the minister to issue a secret order compelling any electronic service provider to create such a capacity and retain users’ metadata for up to six months.

Some critics and privacy advocates told the committee that the metadata retention requirement is either too broad, too long, or both.

But police and child protection agencies dismissed those fears Wednesday, arguing that the bill shouldn’t only target specific metadata to be retained because police don’t know what information they will seek before an investigation is underway.

They also objected to suggestions the retention be reduced from six months to 30 days.

“If they only kept the metadata for 30 days, that would be useless to us,” Ullock added.

The bill has been applauded by police forces as a long-overdue fix to growing obstacles to investigations, but panned by civil liberties advocates and tech companies as an attack on privacy and encryption.

In an interview with National Post last week, a senior Meta executive said all options are on the table — including pulling uber-popular messaging app WhatsApp from Canada — if the government uses any proposed powers in its lawful access bill to undermine the company’s encryption.

But on Wednesday, many witnesses pooh-poohed Meta and other tech companies’ threats to leave the country over C-22.

“It’s a big bluff. I think everyone in this room knows that WhatsApp is not going to disappear from Canada if this legislation passed as is. It’s all a big gambit, that’s all it is,” said Lloyd Richardson, the director of technology at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01

stories.title: Ford admits his French needs work after shaky Montreal speech
stories.summary: Critics of the Ford government told reporters they didn’t find it funny that the premier of Canada’s largest province is unable to speak French, an official language.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
It’s all French to Premier Doug Ford, who is sheepishly hoping the public will excuse his shaky attempt to speak en français, after a video of him addressing a Montreal crowd went viral.

“It’s a little rougher than I thought,” Ford told reporters Tuesday.

“I was as nervous as anything, practising four lines, but it was a very warm welcome in Quebec,” he said.

The premier was in Montreal on Tuesday to promote stronger trade ties between the province and Quebec in the face of the trade war with the United States.

But it was his French during his address to the Chamber of Commerce of Metropolitan Montreal that drew the most attention.

“Oh, I’m really messing this one up,” Ford told the Chamber after stumbling through some French lines. Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Oh, I'm really messing this one up," Ford told the Chamber after stumbling through some French lines.

Critics of the Ford government told reporters they didn’t find it funny that the premier of Canada’s largest province is unable to speak French, an official language.

“It’s actually not something to laugh about,” said Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser.

Fraser, who also admitted that he too is not entirely fluent in French, said that at least he takes his weekly lessons seriously. ‘It’s important as a legislator to be able to do it,’ he said.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the “very significant” Francophone community in Ontario should expect their premier to know “basic phrases”.

“I wish he would practice a little more. I didn’t think it was particularly funny; I just thought it was kind of embarrassing,” she said.
