The Oaks reached the championship game with a dramatic 22-21 double-overtime win over Mother Teresa that featured a series of unusual plays unique to Canadian football.
“It was incredibly stressful from the start, but I’m honestly really happy that we came away with the win,” said Oaks linebacker Stefan Ivanisivec.
In the first overtime, the Spartans attempted to win on a rouge by punting the ball out of the end zone, but the Oaks returner was able to punt it back out to force a second extra session.
In the second overtime, the Oaks used the same strategy, but when the Spartans attempted to kick the ball back, it was blocked out of the back of the end zone by Kaden Kheav for the winning point.
“Momentum definitely played a part in the game, but we just tried to keep our heads up and keep going,” said Oaks wide receiver Mason Van Ness.
Now they face a significant challenge.
“They’re very big up front on the offensive line, so we’ve got to be able to match their physicality, and I think we’re able to come away with the win,” Ivanisivec said.
The Crusaders believe their size and experience in the trenches will be the difference over four quarters.
“We have a big offensive line,” said Crusaders linebacker Marley Asuncion.
Sims said the excitement surrounding Oakridge is real, but the Crusaders are focused on what they do best.
That means blocking out outside noise and relying on their depth in pursuit of another title.
“That’s why we came back, and I know a lot of Grade 12-plus students right now are looking for that three-peat,” said Sims.
“We want to see our Grade 11s moving up into senior football thrive. We want to see them start their senior football careers with a win.”
The Oaks last won the city championship in 1977, defeating Clarke Road 18-15. Their most recent appearance in the final came in 1980, when they lost 16-14 to Lucas.
Kickoff is scheduled for 8 p.m. Friday at 1Password Park in St. Thomas, Ont.
The South Lions won the Tvra AA championship last week with a 30-10 victory over Parkside.
Mustangs prepare for huskies in Saturday’s Mitchell Bowl
The Atlantic University Sport conference has not won a national semifinal since the Saint Mary’s Huskies defeated Laval 24-2 in the 2007 Uteck Bowl.
Those same Huskies will try to end that streak Saturday at Alumni Stadium in London, Ont., when they face the Yates Cup champion Western Mustangs.
“Our motto is to fear no one but respect everyone, so we’re going to stay true to that this week,” said Mustangs quarterback Ben Casselman.
The Mustangs have spent the week studying film on an opponent they have never faced.
One player who can offer some insight is Halifax native Rory Litt, who transferred to Western from Acadia University this season.
“I’ve played them probably six or seven times at this point,” said Litt, who will face his hometown school.
“I think they bring a couple of new formations that we’re not used to seeing, but if we follow our rules and do everything the way we’re supposed to and the way we’re taught, we’re going to be OK.”
Litt said he knows several players on the Huskies roster.
“My friends would be dying for the opportunity to still be playing this time of year,” he said.
“I’m super excited and I know all the boys here are super excited to be here, but it’s a testament to our hard work this season and that’s why we’re here.”

“All those ouchies, you kind of forget them because you’d rather be playing sore than not playing at all and have your season be done. We are a seven-day-a-week operation, so the last day our players weren’t in this facility was way back on Aug. 31.”
The forecast calls for unseasonably warm conditions for a mid-November football game, although the matchup will be played earlier than Western’s typical home start time.
“It’s a noon kickoff and I know we’re used to 1 p.m. kickoffs,” said Faulds.
London Knights goaltender Arvin Jaswal is hoping to help his club return to the win column.
The Knights have dropped four straight games and fallen from second place in the Western Conference standings to a tie for sixth.
“There’s always a hump in the road and that’s just kind of where we are right now,” said Jaswal, who was acquired from the Barrie Colts on Oct. 25.
“We’re doing everything we can to turn it around, and I have full confidence that we will.”
Jaswal, who was recovering from a lower-body injury when he was acquired, has appeared in one game for the Knights.
He stopped 23 of 27 shots in a 5-4 shootout loss to the Soo Greyhounds.
“The first week was a little tough because the guys were on the road and I was still coming back from my injury, so I didn’t end up going on the road, which sucked,” said Jaswal.
“It was good to have that road trip last weekend and really bond with the guys in the hotel and on the bus.”
The Pickering, Ont., native posted an 18-3-3 record, a 2.45 goals-against average and a .924 save percentage in 24 games with Barrie last season.
The Knights paid a significant price for that experience, sending four draft picks to the Colts to acquire the netminder.
Jaswal was already familiar with London, having visited the city several times while his sister attended Western University.
He has adjusted quickly to life with the Knights, having previously played minor hockey with Cody Wood and spring hockey with Jaxon Cover. He has also trained alongside Cooper McAslan.

The Knights traded Aleksei Medvedev, who went 3-0 with a 1.65 goals-against average after being dealt to Peterborough, as part of the move to bring Jaswal to London to share goaltending duties with Brian Cooke.
“They brought me here to win games,” said Jaswal.
“I’m going to do my best.”

November 18, 2026 at 12:51 p.m.

Ottawa — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson was pressed by reporters on Wednesday about his government’s record on fulfilling its campaign promise to double the pace of housing construction, which he said ultimately is out of his government’s hands.

“The Government of Canada cannot force Canadians to build housing,” said Robertson, ON his way into a caucus meeting. “So, we are focused on building as much housing as we possibly can.”

The Liberal government ran on campaign promise in the 2025 federal election to double Canada’s current rate of residential construction over the next decade to reach 500,000 homes per year. This promise was made in the interest of helping young Canadians buy their first homes, but the Liberals also acknowledged that it would require the public and private sector to get it done.

Despite that promise, the Parliamentary Budget Office has pointed out that housing starts have not kept pace with the federal government’s target to double supply by 2035.

In 2021, housing starts in Canada totaled 271,198 according to Statistics Canada. In 2025, housing starts slid to 259,028. The drop in single-detached housing starts is even more stark, falling from 82,116 in 2021 to 52,274 in 2025.

A report published on Tuesday by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc), showed the six-month trend in housing starts declined 1.7 per cent in October to 246,231 units.

In a report published in September, the Cmhc projects Canada still faces a long-term housing supply gap of 187,000 to 238,000 homes per year over the next decade.

Minister of Housing and Infrastructure Gregor Robertson speaks to journalists before attending the Liberal party caucus meeting on Parliament Hill Nov. 18, 2026. Hyungcheol Park/Postmedia

Robertson said his government is doing “everything” it can to reinvigorate the Vancouver and Toronto housing markets.

“Those are our biggest markets that are struggling right now,” he said, pointing to the GST/HST rebate on new homes in Ontario and cuts in development charges in British Columbia. “We have to continue focusing on where we intervene, working with provinces and cities to get them building as much as possible.”

The housing minister also pointed to the federal government’s efforts to build more non-market housing through its new housing agency, Build Canada Homes.

“You look at the moves that we’re making; they’re unprecedented,” he said. “The scale of interventions, both on market and non-market side, we will continue to do that.”

The federal budget made a promise to “end homelessness” within a decade and the new investments will bring the total capitalization of Build Canada Homes to $45 billion, which includes the initial $13 billion the housing agency was allocated in Budget 2025. The federal government said this will put the crown corporation on track to build 200,000 homes in the next 10 years, which equates to 20,000 affordable units per year.

During question period on Tuesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the prime minister’s spending on housing is not leading to more houses being built.

“The prime minister is simultaneously blowing the budget on his failed housing expenditures, while delivering fewer homes built,” said Poilievre. “Just today, we learned that homebuilding is down three per cent year-over-year, not doubled as he promised.”

Jordan Gowling joined National Post's parliamentary bureau in 2026 after two years as Financial Post's economics reporter on Parliament Hill. She previously worked as a producer at CTV News in Ottawa.

stories.title: Minister says discussions with Meta 'confidential' following reports of possible deal
stories.summary: Ottawa - Culture Minister Marc Miller says he won’t talk about any discussions the government has had with Meta about restoring news content to the company's platforms in Canada.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Culture Minister Marc Miller said Wednesday he won’t talk about any discussions the government has had with Meta about restoring news content to the company’s platforms in Canada.

A day after Politico reported the company and the government were close to a deal before trade talks with the United States collapsed in August, Miller told reporters the discussions with Meta are confidential.

“Meta could always put news back online. They are the ones who removed it,” he said in French.

Meta blocked news from its platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, after the Online News Act became law in 2023. The bill requires Meta and Google to compensate news publishers for the use of their content.

Citing an unnamed official, Politico said Meta put forward a proposal that would see it stop blocking news content in Canada, pursue commercial deals with publishers and fund two positions at the Canadian Journalism Collective.

In exchange, it would obtain an exemption from the law. Google already has an exemption, which it received after agreeing to pay $100 million to Canadian news outlets.

Politico reported the proposal was part of the wider U.S.-Canada trade negotiations. Ottawa shut down those talks in August after accusing the White House of demanding last-minute changes that threatened Canada’s sovereignty.

Meta declined to comment on the Politico report Wednesday.

Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the publishers’ group News Media Canada, said in an email Meta should only be exempt from the Online News Act if the company provides “fair compensation to Canadian news businesses just as Google has. They should not get our content for free.”

“Canada should not return to the dark days prior to the Online News Act when Google and Meta were picking the winners and losers” in Canadian media, he added.

In a brief interview, Deegan said before the Online News Act became law, Google and Meta were signing content licensing agreements with large news publishers but with not smaller independent publishers.

“You don’t want to have a situation where they’re only doing deals with the few, and then frankly potentially have outside influence with some of those publishers. Whereas if they’re doing deals with everyone, then everyone is under the same terms. And that’s really our concern if there’s any weakening of the Online News Act,” he said.

Kevin Desjardins, president and CEO of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, said in an email a “deal is never a deal until it’s done, and how ‘close’ it was is in the eye of the beholder.”

He said the door has always been open to “Meta receiving an exemption from the Online News Act, as Google already has, provided that they offer something of true value to compensate news publishers for the various ways they make use of their content, including in their AI products.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Politico reported the proposal was part of the wider U.S.-Canada trade negotiations. Ottawa shut down those talks in August after accusing the White House of demanding last-minute changes that threatened Canada’s sovereignty.
Meta declined to comment on the Politico report Wednesday.

Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the publishers’ group News Media Canada, said in an email Meta should only be exempt from the Online News Act if the company provides “fair compensation to Canadian news businesses just as Google has. They should not get our content for free.”
“Canada should not return to the dark days prior to the Online News Act when Google and Meta were picking the winners and losers” in Canadian media, he added.

In a brief interview, Deegan said before the Online News Act became law, Google and Meta were signing content licensing agreements with large news publishers but with not smaller independent publishers.

“You don’t want to have a situation where they’re only doing deals with the few, and then frankly potentially have outside influence with some of those publishers. Whereas if they’re doing deals with everyone, then everyone is under the same terms. And that’s really our concern if there’s any weakening of the Online News Act,” he said.
Kevin Desjardins, president and CEO of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, said in an email a “deal is never a deal until it’s done, and how ‘close’ it was is in the eye of the beholder.”

He said the door has always been open to “Meta receiving an exemption from the Online News Act, as Google already has, provided that they offer something of true value to compensate news publishers for the various ways they make use of their content, including in their AI products.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa to supply Ukraine with ammunition, winter clothing, food
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is funding more military aid for Ukraine, including ammunition, winter clothing and food.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
National Defence Minister David McGuinty announced in Brussels Tuesday that Canada will donate another $45 million to the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that works to deliver extended-range ammunition and critical air-defence equipment to Ukraine.

Canada is also donating up to 1.6 million rounds of surplus Canadian Armed Forces ammunition, about 250,000 meal packs and $30 million worth of winter clothing and equipment.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

McGuinty says Canada will also provide $80 million for advanced sensor systems to help Ukraine defend itself against missile and drone attacks.

The minister says the donations will help strengthen Ukraine’s air-defence capabilities, sustain its military operations and support personnel deployed in difficult field conditions.

The government says that since February 2022, Canada has committed more than $8.5 billion in military assistance to Ukraine as part of almost $25.5 billion in total aid.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto police charge 21 people in crimes connected to the towing industry
stories.summary: Police launched probe and gathered evidence of alleged conspiracy to commit murder, firearms trafficking, auto theft, arson, fraud and other criminal offences
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Twenty-one people are facing dozens of charges in a police investigation into alleged murder plots and other crimes connected to a towing company that was contracted by Toronto police.

Det.-Sgt. Steve Matthews said Toronto police launched the investigation, dubbed Project Swords, in September 2025 and gathered evidence of alleged conspiracy to commit murder, firearms trafficking, auto theft, arson, fraud and other criminal offences.

“Over the course of approximately 14 months, investigators gathered evidence relating to a range of serious crimes,” he said in a news conference on Wednesday.

“What emerged was more than a dispute connected to the towing services.”

He said officers executed 13 search warrants on Nov. 12 across the Greater Toronto Area.

Matthews said officers arrested 21 people and laid 112 criminal charges including charges related to planned murders.

“One of the most significant outcomes of this investigation was the disruption of an alleged conspiracy to murder two individuals connected to the towing industry,” he said.

“As a part of the conspiracy, individuals involved in organizing and planning the murders had arranged for the surveillance of the intended victims. Because of our work, we intervened before that plan could be carried out.”

Matthews said a 43-year-old Whitby, Ont., resident allegedly directed a plan to carry out two murders and he was the “de facto leader” of Williams Towing, which was one of four towing companies contracted to work with police in the city.

“Following the execution of search warrants on Nov. 12, the Toronto Police Service immediately terminated its contractual relationship with Williams Towing,” he said.

“We allege that although ownership and assets were registered to other individuals (the accused) exercised control over aspects of those operations.”

He said charges were also laid in relation to firearms trafficking, organized auto theft operation, arson investigations, stock fraud offences, and breach of trust allegations involving a correctional employee.

“There was a correctional employee at the Toronto East Detention Center that was looking to assist (the accused 43-year-old Whitby, Ont., resident) while he was in custody,” he said.

“Officers got wind of what was happening and prevented him from interfering in any way and contacted our partners at correctional services.”

Matthews said charges were also laid in relation to fraudulent physiotherapy clinics.

“Through the towing, the operators (of the tows) would have connections to the owners of the vehicle,” he said.

“They would figure out whether they had insurance plans and then essentially milk the plans through the clinics.”

Investigators say they seized multiple firearms, ammunition and drugs during Project Swords.

Chief Supt. Joe Matthews said the Greater Toronto Area has seen a sharp escalation in crimes linked to the towing industry since early 2023 and police have been working to address this rise in criminal activities.

He said 62 shooting and firearm incidents were linked to tow truck disputes in 2024, accounting for nearly 13 per cent of all such incidents in Toronto.

Joe Matthews said there were 18 incidents in 2025, representing seven per cent, and there have been five so far this year, accounting for approximately two per cent.

“There are multiple factors that can explain fluctuations in gun violence numbers, and this is one of them … good police work,” he said.

“By targeting organized crime groups in these investigations, we have had a direct impact on reducing gun violence in our city.”

Toronto police had said they made 20 arrests and laid 111 charges in June 2025 in another investigation into the towing industry dubbed Project Yankee.

“Last year we announced the results of Project Yankee, targeting one faction in particular, and today we are announcing the results of Project Swords targeting another faction,” Joe Matthews said.

“These are lengthy, complex investigations, and they require collaboration with other law enforcement agencies.”

stories.title: Porter pilots cast ballots on strike mandate ahead of first-ever contract
stories.summary: Porter Airlines pilots hit the picket line at their home base in Toronto on Wednesday, kicking off a strike mandate vote ahead of their first-ever contract.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
Porter Airlines pilots hit the picket line at their home base in Toronto on Wednesday, kicking off a strike mandate vote ahead of their first-ever contract.

The Air Line Pilots Association said roughly 200 of the carrier’s 900-odd aviators were on the ground at Billy Bishop airport near the city’s downtown alongside workers from more than a dozen other North American airlines.

The sticking points after months of negotiations remain wages, scheduling and quality of life, with the union asking for gains on par with peers in the sector, said Brian Smith, who chairs the union’s Porter contingent.

“Porter pilots are prepared to take decisive action if that’s what’s required to secure a fair agreement,” he said in a release.

“We’re not asking for anything extraordinary. We’re asking for a contract that respects the work we do and the responsibility we carry, and to share in Porter’s continued success and growth.”

Porter declined to discuss specifics related to the talks.

“We value our pilots and recognize the important role they play. Discussions are progressing and Porter remains committed to reaching an agreement that supports our pilots and reinforces our positive working relationship over the last 20 years,” said spokesperson Robyn van Teunenbroek in an email.

Two months of federal conciliation is slated to end on Sunday, followed by a 21-day cooling-off period if no deal is reached, with a strike or lockout possible as early as Dec. 14.

A majority of yes votes would authorize union leadership to launch a job action starting that day.

Porter has struggled amid the soaring price of jet fuel caused by the Iran war, securing a $125-million bailout loan from Ottawa over the summer after big expenditures to fund a rapid expansion in recent years.
paragraphs: Porter Airlines pilots hit the picket line at their home base in Toronto on Wednesday, kicking off a strike mandate vote ahead of their first-ever contract.

The Air Line Pilots Association said roughly 200 of the carrier’s 900-odd aviators were on the ground at Billy Bishop airport near the city’s downtown alongside workers from more than a dozen other North American airlines.

The sticking points after months of negotiations remain wages, scheduling and quality of life, with the union asking for gains on par with peers in the sector, said Brian Smith, who chairs the union’s Porter contingent.
“Porter pilots are prepared to take decisive action if that’s what’s required to secure a fair agreement,” he said in a release.
“We’re not asking for anything extraordinary. We’re asking for a contract that respects the work we do and the responsibility we carry, and to share in Porter’s continued success and growth.”
Porter declined to discuss specifics related to the talks.

“We value our pilots and recognize the important role they play. Discussions are progressing and Porter remains committed to reaching an agreement that supports our pilots and reinforces our positive working relationship over the last 20 years,” said spokesperson Robyn van Teunenbroek in an email.
Two months of federal conciliation is slated to end on Sunday, followed by a 21-day cooling-off period if no deal is reached, with a strike or lockout possible as early as Dec. 14.
A majority of yes votes would authorize union leadership to launch a job action starting that day.

Porter has struggled amid the soaring price of jet fuel caused by the Iran war, securing a $125-million bailout loan from Ottawa over the summer after big expenditures to fund a rapid expansion in recent years.

November 18, 2026 at 12:30 p.m.

A First Nations group in the United States has added its voice to those opposing the U.S. president’s decision to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

In a resolution first passed by the National Congress of American Indians at the group’s October conference, the group notes that “Lake Ontario is one example of the enduring Indigenous relationships with geographic features that this resolution seeks to protect, having been known to and used by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee peoples since time immemorial.”

It adds: “In the Seneca language, Lake Ontario is known as Sga:nyodai:yoh, meaning ‘beautiful lake,’ reflecting the Seneca people’s enduring cultural and linguistic relationship with this body of water.”

The resolution, “Protecting Indigenous Geographic Names and Tribal Cultural Heritage in Federal Geographic Naming Actions,” says the Ncai opposes the unilateral federal renaming “and calls upon the President of the United States to rescind the August 27, 2026 Executive Order and restore ‘Lake Ontario’ as the name used by the United States Government.”

Established in 1944, the Ncai describes itself as the oldest and largest national organization of American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments. The resolution was signed by Ncai president Mark Macarro.

Last month, the Assembly of First Nations in Canada released a statement saying it stood with the Ncai, and calling on governments on both sides of the border “to respect First Peoples’ cultures, languages and histories in the face of aggressive moves by the Trump administration to attempt to rename Lake Ontario.”

“Lake Ontario is and always will be Lake Ontario,” said AFN National Chief Woodhouse Nepinak, adding: “The name is important because the core issue is recognizing and respecting the languages, cultures and histories of the First Peoples of this land. We predate the border and stand in solidarity with our brothers and sisters to the south and will not allow any government to try to erase our rights, our cultures and contributions.”

The name Lake Ontario appears on European maps as far back at the 1600s, but is much older than that.

The Museum of Indigenous People notes: “The name is commonly connected to the Wendat, also known as the Huron-Wyandot, word Ontarí:io (or Ontare). It has been translated as ‘great lake’ or ‘beautiful lake.’ Other explanations connect it with related Iroquoian words such as kanadario or skanadario, translated as ‘sparkling water’ or ‘beautiful water.'”[](https://www.CBC.CA/news/Canada/ottawa/kingston-mayor-calls-trump-lake-america-renaming-ridiculous-9.7323747)

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: LHSC appoints renewed board as governance overhaul continues
stories.summary: London Health Sciences Centre unveiled its renewed board of directors Wednesday, a key step in the hospital’s governance overhaul as it prepares for the eventual end of provincial supervision.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) unveiled its renewed board of directors Wednesday, a key step in the hospital’s governance overhaul as it prepares for the eventual end of provincial supervision.

The new volunteer board will work alongside LHSC Supervisor David Musyj until supervision concludes, at which point it will assume full authority for the organization.

The appointments follow a two-year renewal effort focused on strengthening governance, accountability, oversight and organizational performance.

LHSC announced eight volunteer board members and five volunteer community members who will serve on board committees. The appointments followed a recruitment process that attracted more than 90 applicants from across the community.

“The appointment of the renewed Board represents an important milestone in that journey,” Musyj said.

The board’s creation marks what hospital leaders describe as the next stage of LHSC’s renewal plan, which began after the province placed the organization under supervision in 2024.

According to Musyj, the hospital has spent the past two years implementing structural changes aimed at improving accountability and oversight.

Those changes include consolidating management positions, introducing 360-degree performance reviews for managers, strengthening spending controls, expanding internal auditing and providing additional mechanisms for whistleblower reporting. Hospital leaders have also established new oversight processes for budgeting, staffing decisions, quality indicators, and patient safety performance.

The renewed board will operate through four standing committees: finance and audit, quality and safety, human resources, and research.

A dedicated human resources committee will oversee matters related to LHSC’s workforce, which represents roughly 70 per cent of the organization’s operating costs.

Musyj said measures have been built into bylaws, policies and governance structures to ensure reforms continue beyond his tenure.

“The goal is simple: fewer layers, clearer responsibilities, stronger oversight and real accountability that outlasts any one leader,” he said.

The renewed board is chaired by Ron Sapsford , a former Ontario deputy minister of health and long-term care and former CEO of the Ontario Medical Association.

Other board members include Scott Courtice, Cedric Gomes, Christi-Ann Poulette, Michael G. Power, David Smith, Melanie Stanley and Lori Van Opstal.

Five community members will serve on board committees: Catherine Osborne, Leo Plue, Mike Tidy, Nick Vander Gulik and Lloy Wylie.

The board’s first public-facing meeting is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027. LHSC said public meetings will be open to community members and livestreamed as part of its commitment to transparency and public engagement.

stories.title: Norwegian cruise line drops 17 stops in Halifax, citing guest feedback
stories.summary: Halifax - A Norwegian cruise line has dropped 17 stops in Halifax next year in favour of more time in Bermuda, saying the cancellations were in response to guest feedback.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - A Norwegian cruise line has dropped 17 stops in Halifax next year in favour of more time in Bermuda, saying the cancellations were in response to guest feedback.

Some trips on the cruise ship Norwegian Breakaway, which had stopped in both Halifax and Bermuda during the 2026 spring and summer season, will skip Nova Scotia and spend an extra night at the Royal Naval Dockyard in Bermuda next spring and summer.

stories.title: Toronto look-alike contest saw everything but the real Nathan Fielder
stories.summary: The doppelgangers referenced the multi-hyphenate’s diverse career, from his stint as the host of Comedy Central’s Nathan For You to his role as creator and star of The Rehearsal
stories.author: Photography by David Pike
stories.content:
West-end Torontonians: your eyes did not deceive you. Why would they? On Tuesday night, Bloor Street was indeed awash with Nathan Fielders as the Paradise Theatre held a look-alike contest to crown the person who most closely resembled the feted director of hit documentary You Can See Everything . There were 26 entrants of diverse gender in the contest, whose host was dressed as – of course – Elizabeth Holmes.

The various Fielders in attendance weren’t just dressed as director Nathan, but also referenced the Canadian multi-hyphenate’s long and singularly diverse career, from his stint as the host of Comedy Central’s Nathan For You to the creator and star of The Rehearsal . The sold-out event, which took place ahead of a screening of an episode of Fielder’s series The Curse , featured five elimination rounds, and the winner was ultimately crowned by audience applause. His possible competitive edge? Remaining deadpan throughout.

Editor’s note: This article has been updated to clarify that the contest took place ahead of a screening of an episode of 'The Curse.'

stories.title: Toronto police charge 21 people in crimes connected to towing industry
stories.summary: Twenty-one people are facing dozens of charges after a Toronto police investigation into organized crime and violence connected to the towing industry.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Twenty-one people are facing dozens of charges in a police investigation into alleged murder plots and other crimes connected to a towing company that was contracted by Toronto police.

Det.-Sgt. Steve Matthews said Toronto police launched the investigation, dubbed Project Swords, in September 2025 and gathered evidence of alleged conspiracy to commit murder, firearms trafficking, auto theft, arson, fraud and other criminal offences.

“Over the course of approximately 14 months, investigators gathered evidence relating to a range of serious crimes,” he said in a press conference on Wednesday.

“What emerged was more than a dispute connected to the towing services.”

He said officers executed 13 search warrants on Nov. 12 across the Greater Toronto Area.

Matthews said officers arrested 21 people and laid 112 criminal charges including charges related to planned murders.

“One of the most significant outcomes of this investigation was the disruption of an alleged conspiracy to murder two individuals connected to the towing industry,” he said.

“As a part of the conspiracy, individuals involved in organizing and planning the murders had arranged for the surveillance of the intended victims. Because of our work, we intervened before that plan could be carried out.”

Matthews said a 43-year-old Whitby, Ont., resident allegedly directed a plan to carry out two murders and he was the “de facto leader” of Williams Towing, which was one of four towing companies contracted to work with police in the city.

“Following the execution of search warrants on Nov. 12, the Toronto Police Service immediately terminated its contractual relationship with Williams Towing,” he said.

“We allege that although ownership and assets were registered to other individuals (the accused) exercised control over aspects of those operations.”

He said charges were also laid in relation to firearms trafficking, organized auto theft operation, arson investigations, stock fraud offences, and breach of trust allegations involving a correctional employee.

stories.title: If children ran city hall: Parks, housing top wish list
stories.summary: According to the report, parks and recreation was the most commonly identified theme, appearing 177 times in responses.
stories.content:
As London’s newly elected city council takes office, a new report from the London Children’s Museum suggests the city’s youngest residents are paying close attention to issues ranging from parks and recreation to housing affordability.

The report, My Voice Counts , compiled 2,504 responses from children collected during the 2026 municipal election through classroom programs, museum activities and online participation.

Children were asked what matters most in their community, what changes they would like to see and what questions they would ask candidates seeking to lead the city.

According to the report, parks and recreation was the most commonly identified theme, appearing 177 times in responses. Children called for more playgrounds, sports facilities, accessible recreation opportunities and safe public spaces.

Housing and homelessness ranked second, with 165 mentions. Children called for more affordable housing, additional shelters and greater support for people experiencing homelessness.

Other frequently cited themes included environment, nature and animals (138 mentions), affordability and economic concerns (134 mentions), and transportation and infrastructure (127 mentions).

The report said children expressed concerns about protecting green spaces, reducing pollution, lowering the cost of housing and food, improving road safety and addressing traffic and construction issues.

Beyond those topics, children also raised questions about community safety, health care, education and municipal leadership.

One notable finding was the limited focus on technology. Screens and technology were mentioned in only four of the 1,044 written responses.

“Children are paying attention to what’s happening. They see challenges facing our community, and they experience the impact of decisions made around them,” said Kate Ledgley, executive director of the London Children’s Museum.

“When we take the time to listen, children have so much to tell us about the places they live, learn, and play. Their perspectives can help us better understand our city and the people it serves.”

The museum released the report as London’s new council was sworn in, saying the findings offer insight into the priorities and concerns of children living in the city.

stories.title: Demand for Canadian ETFs soars, boosting access to financial wealth
stories.summary: Market eclipses ​global growth over past decade
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
Canada’s adoption of exchange-traded funds is accelerating faster than the global rate as strong equity market performance and growth in the domestic discount brokerage industry increase demand for low-cost, diversified investments.

The Canadian ⁠ETF market ​expanded at a 26 per cent compound annual growth rate over the past decade versus 21.5 per cent globally, according to TD Securities. Data from Canada’s Securities and Investment Management Association (Sima), a trade association for the investment industry, shows a sharp increase in the sales pace this year.

Net sales of Canadian ETFs rose 81 per cent to $156-billion in ​the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period in ‌2025, according to the Sima data, far outstripping growth in the much larger mutual fund category. An ETF holds a basket of securities and trades like a stock, unlike a mutual fund that investors buy or sell directly from the fund company.

Increased use of ETFs, which tend to charge lower fees than mutual funds, could help more Canadians accumulate financial wealth, reducing their dependency ‌on housing equity ​for retirement savings. But like other ‌market investments, they carry risk at a time of market volatility as well as uncertainty around the future of ​Canada’s U.S. trade agreement and AI.

ETFs could facilitate greater exposure to ⁠international stocks and bonds. Domestic stocks account for 50 per cent of Canadians’ equity portfolios, roughly 15 times ⁠Canada’s weight in the global equity market, a Vanguard research note showed.

Equity markets globally are on track to advance for a ​fourth straight year, including gains for Canada’s main stock index, the S&P/TSX Composite. The TSX has climbed 9 per cent since the start of 2026 after adding 28 per cent in 2025, outperforming the S&P 500 both years.

“Those gains lift the value of existing investments and can encourage investors to put additional money into markets,” said Ian Bragg, Sima’s vice-president of research and statistics.

“Online investing has expanded access,” Bragg ⁠said. “ETFs fit naturally into brokerage accounts, where investors can buy a diversified fund much as they would an individual stock. And there has been tremendous growth overall in this channel.”

The ratio of Canadian financial assets to non-financial assets has climbed to the highest level since 2000, at 124 per cent, second-quarter household data from Statistics Canada showed.

Retail investors increasingly trade commission-free on mobile applications operated by Canadian banks’ discount brokerages or by independent brokerages, such as Wealthsimple, ⁠a fast-growing fintech company.

“There’s the rise of social media and so-called finfluencers on ​YouTube and Instagram and TikTok and so on,” said Daniel Straus, managing director of ETFs and financial products research at ⁠National Bank of Canada Capital Markets (Nbccm). “We definitely see that when an ETF or investment vehicle goes viral on these platforms, volumes that seem to be coming ‌from self-directed channels very much increase.”

Trends this year include increased demand for ETFs that hold multiple asset categories and those ​that target international stocks, Nbccm’s research shows. That demand includes leveraged ETFs that use financial derivatives to amplify returns, increasing potential losses in a downturn.

“It seems to be that Canadian investors are still feeling very bullish. They want market exposure, they want the AI trade, they even want single stocks with leverage. And ​so leverage is a way to make your money go further, but of course it’s quite risky,” Straus said.

stories.title: Housing minister won’t reaffirm Liberal pledge to double home construction
stories.summary: Ottawa — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn't reaffirm the Liberal government's long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters today.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Housing Minister Gregor Robertson wouldn’t reaffirm the Liberal government’s long-standing goal of doubling the pace of home building when pressed by reporters on Wednesday.

The Liberals campaigned during the 2025 election on a pledge to double the annual pace of housing starts to roughly 500,000 over a decade.

But that promise was absent from the federal budget tabled on Nov. 5. The Liberal government instead set new goals in Budget 2026 to triple the pace of non-market housing construction over the next decade and to end homelessness.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan noted the missing reference to doubling home construction in a series of reports analyzing the budget published Tuesday.

“While Budget 2026 announces new measures for homelessness and housing affordability, it is not on track to double housing starts per Budget 2025, with year-to-date housing starts 4 per cent lower in 2026 than 2025,” one of Ryan’s report read.

The Canadian Press asked Robertson’s office last week whether the Liberals were sticking to the target. A spokesperson for his office pointed to a statement sent to The Canadian Press six months earlier reaffirming the pledge.

Reporters asked Robertson as he was heading into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday if the government is sticking to the pledge it campaigned on a year and a half ago.

“We’re just focused on supply overall for the time being. Affordable supply first and foremost,” he said in response.

Robertson said the goal of doubling housing starts was based on the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp.’s estimates of the supply gap, or the number of homes the country needed to add to restore affordability to 2019 levels.

Hitting that annual pace requires the private sector to build at scale, he said, adding the government is “doing everything” it can to stabilize markets like Toronto and Vancouver that are struggling to get shovels in the ground.

The minister said the government has made “unprecedented” interventions to stimulate construction, including moves to axe the GST on many newly built units and other federal incentives to get municipalities to lower costly development charges.

But “the Government of Canada cannot force Canadians to build housing,” he said.

“Right now we’re doing everything that we can in a very challenging time for our economy,” Robertson said.

“We have to continue focusing on where we intervene, working with provinces and cities to get them building as much as possible and looking at the affordable side. That’s where the role of government is, to make sure there’s affordable housing getting built.”

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built — but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

Conservative housing critic Scott Aitchison accused the Liberals of quietly dropping their homebuilding target and moving the goalposts.

“Their big promises have become another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not make homes affordable again,” he said in a media statement on Tuesday.

In its fall housing supply report, the Cmhc wrote that the country is entering a “new phase” where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The Cmhc’s “business-as-usual” forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the Cmhc said.

Experts point out that many of the levers to increase housing supply are outside the government’s direct control, such as Bank of Canada interest rates and the cost of building materials.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, told The Canadian Press last week that he never liked the goal of doubling housing starts because it could be “excessive” and lacks a nuanced approach to the mix of homes Canada must build.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ex-Alberta premier Jason Kenney says Quebec Conservatives could take power
stories.summary: Nicolet - Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney believes the Quebec Conservative Party could one day take power in the province.
stories.author: Frédéric Lacroix-Couture The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nicolet - Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney believes the Quebec Conservative Party could one day take power in the province.

Kenney praised the momentum and leadership of Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime as he joined a caucus meeting with the party’s newly-elected legislature members.

The Quebec Conservatives finished third in the provincial election with 19 seats, behind the minority Parti Québécois government and the official Opposition Quebec Liberals.

Duhaime told reporters in Nicolet, Que. on Tuesday that he and Kenney are longtime friends.

He said the former Alberta leader can offer insight to the Quebec Conservative members, the vast majority of whom are newcomers.

Duhaime noted that Kenney spent years in opposition in the House of Commons before rising to power, which is what the Quebec Conservatives aspire to do.

Kenney served on the opposition benches in the House of Commons before becoming a minister under Stephen Harper’s Conservative government, and later led Alberta from 2019 to 2022.

On Tuesday, Kenney told reporters that he believes Duhaime’s party could form government, possibly as soon as the next election.

Duhaime’s party failed to win a seat in the 2022 Quebec election and subsequent byelections before it broke through in the Oct. 5 election.

“It’s clear given the momentum,” Kenney said in French. “And I believe that what Éric has demonstrated is leadership in speaking for everyday people about their everyday concerns — the cost of living, taxes.”

“I’m not from Quebec, but I believe there’s enormous potential for his team to potentially become the government,” he said, adding he hoped it would happen “next time.”

Kenney’s advice to the new Conservative legislature members is to stay focused on people’s day-to-day concerns and to remain disciplined. He urged them “not to be ideological,” but rather pragmatic.

The presence of the former leader of Alberta’s United Conservative Party shows that the Quebec Conservatives can count on allies elsewhere in Canada, Duhaime said.

“The message we’re sending to our members of the national assembly is that, yes, we are the first wave of Conservative members of the national assembly to be elected in nearly a century,” Duhaime told reporters.

“But we’re also part of a large, pan-Canadian family, and we have allies who support Quebec’s autonomy and the centre-right elsewhere. That’s an advantage that we’re the only party to have.”

On Thursday, the final day of the pre-session caucus, Senator Josée Verner — a former Conservative minister under Stephen Harper’s government — was also expected to offer advice to the newly elected members.

The parliamentary session in Quebec City is set to begin on December 1.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario to increase fines against drivers who create excessive noise
stories.summary: Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says the province will soon table legislation to increase fines for drivers who are revving their engines or installing illegal mufflers.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario is set to make it tougher on drivers who wheel around with excessive noise.

Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says the province will soon table legislation to increase fines for drivers who are revving their engines or installing illegal mufflers.

He says the minimum fine will increase from $60 to $200 while the maximum fine remains at $1,000.

Peel Police Deputy Chief Marc Andrews says they have been conducting targeted enforcement on noise violators for years, but they wanted more teeth in the law to dissuade lawbreakers.

The force has handed out more than 5,000 noise violation tickets as part of Project Noisemaker, which began in 2020.

Police already have the authority and detection tools to enforce current excessive noise laws in the Highway Traffic Act, but Andrews says the increased fines will have an effect that should help quieten communities.

stories.title: Air cadet leader paralyzed from the waist down after restaurant attack
stories.summary: Capt. Kenneth Kunkel was allegedly attacked in Hamilton, Ont. earlier this month
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A cadet leader who underwent spinal surgery after a violent attack says he is currently paralyzed from the waist down and will require months of physical rehabilitation.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel provided an update on his situation last week in a statement shared online by a Hamilton member of Parliament.

Kunkel says he is in continual pain and his doctors cannot give him a prognosis at this time, but he remains “hopeful and positive.”

He thanked those who have reached out to express support or donated to an online fundraiser set up for his family.

Police have said the Nov. 1 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.

They said two youths approached young air cadets who were selling poppies in front of a restaurant on Barton Street East and blew an air horn “directly into their ears.”

Investigators said a man who was supervising the cadets followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them, leading to a struggle.

They allege a woman jumped in to help the youths and assaulted the air cadet leader, who fell to the ground. One of the boys allegedly hit the man multiple times.

A 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman were charged with aggravated assault in the incident.

In his statement, Kunkel said he wanted to clarify some details of what happened that day.

He said he confronted a youth in the restaurant about assaulting one of the cadets and told him they needed to go to the front and call police. The youth “immediately tried to run away,” Kunkel said, adding he grabbed the youth’s backpack and started walking toward the front of the restaurant while asking staff to call police.

The youth started punching him, he said, and a woman intervened on the youth’s behalf. Kunkel said he told her the boy had assaulted a cadet and they needed to speak with police.

While his attention was on the woman, the boy grabbed the lanyard holding Kunkel’s car key and ripped it off his neck, he said. When Kunkel reached to grab it back, the woman “blindsided” him, slamming him into a concrete pillar, he said.

“My legs buckled beneath me and I collapsed,” he said. “While I was lying on the ground helpless, the young male proceeded to violently punch me directly in the face numerous times.”

Kunkel was taken to hospital and underwent surgery that night, he said.

A GoFundMe page set up on behalf of Kunkel and his family said he is the commanding officer of 826 Gryphon Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, and has been with the cadets for 20 years.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this article incorrectly reported that the attack occurred Nov. 8. This version has been corrected.

stories.title: Loblaw now allows users to buy groceries via Meta’s Muse AI
stories.summary: Meta said its new agentic AI 'can remember brand preferences and information like food allergies, making next week’s planning even easier.'
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Loblaw is now allowing users to let Meta’s Muse AI buy their groceries for them, a move that comes as big banks in Canada and other countries, along with companies like Amazon, are restricting agentic AI tools over security concerns.

“With participating Loblaw banners, Canadian shoppers can now ask Muse to help with meal planning, build their basket and check-out, all in Muse,” Meta said in a statement.

Meta said its new agentic AI “can remember brand preferences and information like food allergies, making next week’s planning even easier.”

Loblaw said in a statement that the collaboration will give shoppers “more choice, better access to the products they need and greater convenience in how they shop.”

Meta launched Muse, its personal AI agent, in September and within weeks, the AI agent billed as a kind of a personal butler jumped to the top spot on Apple’s App Store.

“The experience is designed to help Canadians discover what they need, shop with greater ease, and get more of their everyday needs taken care of through agentic AI,” Loblaw said.

Muse is what some experts refer to as agentic AI tools, meaning they have agency to act on their own.

With an AI chatbot like ChatGPT or Grok, you would have to enter a prompt to get a response. But an agentic AI tool can autonomously take action on your behalf.

The suite of actions that Meta is promising is sweeping.

It can take on tasks like selling your car on an online marketplace, filling out forms or negotiate on your behalf if you want to buy a coffee table on Facebook Marketplace.

But to make bookings or cancel subscriptions, you would have to hand over your credit card details to these AI agents and also grant them access to your email account.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada warns Canadians to “limit the personal information that you share about yourself” with AI tools.

The privacy commissioner recommends not even using your real name or disclosing any personal details about other people while using AI tools, because “the information may be collected and stored” and may be used to either train the AI system or disclose your private information to others.

Muse is already raising red flags with other tech firms. In September, Amazon said it would block Muse from making purchases on its platform because the AI agent violates Amazon’s conditions of use.

However, Meta put out a statement after the release of Muse detailing their privacy guardrails.

“We designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage — the harness runs in its own isolated cell, it doesn’t see real credentials, and every interaction with the outside world runs through a Sentinel which the agent can’t override,” the company said.

Your data will be stored in a “virtual machine” or a isolated Linux box.

“Your dedicated VM is the system of record for everything you put in Muse. Muse sends limited data out of the VM when necessary for inference and telemetry as described below,” it added.

Users will also be able to grant AI different kinds of access to their email, depending on whether they want to grant read access or write access.

Meta said they treat users’ money “especially carefully” since making purchases is the most popular use case for Muse so far.

“If you shop on a website where your payment credentials are already on file, we’ve built detection that you’re on a checkout page into the browser and prompt for a human in the loop approval with the exact details of the purchase every time,” Meta said.

“For sites where you haven’t shopped before, Muse contains a wallet where payment credentials can be stored compliantly,” it added.

stories.title: N.S. woman’s face and neck seriously injured by police dog: police oversight agency
stories.summary: A woman in Nova Scotia is recovering from serious injuries to her face and neck caused by a police dog.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A woman in Nova Scotia is recovering from serious injuries to her face and neck caused by a police dog.

Nova Scotia’s police oversight agency says the woman was believed to be in a vehicle that failed to stop for Cape Breton Regional Police outside Sydney on November 12th.

The Serious Incident Response Team says that after officers found the vehicle abandoned, the police dog tracked down one of the suspects and a struggle ensued.

The woman, identified as an adult female passenger, was taken to hospital to be treated for serious injuries.

The independent agency issued a statement Tuesday saying its account of what happened was based on preliminary information.

The police watchdog says it started its investigation immediately after receiving a referral from Cape Breton Regional Police on Nov. 13.

stories.title: Fanshawe horticulture students launch their annual holiday poinsettia sale
stories.summary: Fanshawe's educational poinsettia sale has made its annual comeback roughly six weeks before Christmas, this y...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Fanshawe’s educational poinsettia sale has made its annual comeback roughly six weeks before Christmas, this year with three different variations.

Horticulture students are now out on Fanshawe campus with 500 plants for sale, similar to the amount that sold out in three weeks last year.

“It’s almost Christmas time here and everyone’s getting excited,” said horticulture student Ethan Darminio, while looking around the greenhouse at the tables full of poinsettias. “There’s Christmas Joy Red, and that’s the name of it. It’s more of a festive type of plant.”

The two other variations students are selling this year include white and marble.

Spriet Family Greenhouse at Fanshawe College (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

“We’ve got a great crop. Potentially our best crop ever,” said Jeff Hicks the professor behind the poinsettia sale.

Students learn about the tradition of poinsettia-selling, starting with the Ecke family who immigrated to Southern California from Germany in the early 1900s.

“It now symbolizes Christmas for many people,” said Hicks. “The ‘euphorbia pulcherrima’ species has been revolutionary for our industry — to have something to sell at Christmas,” he said, referring to the scientific name for pointsettias.

While the horticulture program is mainly about learning to grow and manage plants, the poinsettia sales provide insight into business they May enter after graduation.

“The main objective is to give students real life learning instead of sitting in the classroom and talking about it,” said Hicks. “Horticulture is very much a handmade craft or profession. You’re either working on your business or in your business. To get real life experience is way better than learning about it.”

Students working the tables this week echoed Hicks’ perspective.

paragraphs: Fanshawe’s educational poinsettia sale has made its annual comeback roughly six weeks before Christmas, this year with three different variations.
Horticulture students are now out on Fanshawe campus with 500 plants for sale, similar to the amount that sold out in three weeks last year.

“It’s almost Christmas time here and everyone’s getting excited,” said horticulture student Ethan Darminio, while looking around the greenhouse at the tables full of poinsettias. “There’s Christmas Joy Red, and that’s the name of it. It’s more of a festive type of plant.”
The two other variations students are selling this year include white and marble.
Spriet Family Greenhouse at Fanshawe College (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)
“We’ve got a great crop. Potentially our best crop ever,” said Jeff Hicks the professor behind the poinsettia sale.
Students learn about the tradition of poinsettia-selling, starting with the Ecke family who immigrated to Southern California from Germany in the early 1900s.

“It now symbolizes Christmas for many people,” said Hicks. “The ‘euphorbia pulcherrima’ species has been revolutionary for our industry — to have something to sell at Christmas,” he said, referring to the scientific name for pointsettias.
While the horticulture program is mainly about learning to grow and manage plants, the poinsettia sales provide insight into business they May enter after graduation.

“The main objective is to give students real life learning instead of sitting in the classroom and talking about it,” said Hicks. “Horticulture is very much a handmade craft or profession. stories.title: Ontario to increase fines for drivers who create excessive noise
stories.summary: Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says minimum fine will increase from $60 to $200 while the maximum fine remains at $1,000
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario is set to make it tougher on drivers who wheel around with excessive noise.

Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says the province will soon table legislation to increase fines for drivers who are revving their engines or installing illegal mufflers.

He says the minimum fine will increase from $60 to $200 while the maximum fine remains at $1,000.

Peel Police Deputy Chief Marc Andrews says they have been conducting targeted enforcement on noise violators for years, but they wanted more teeth in the law to dissuade lawbreakers.

The force has handed out more than 5,000 noise violation tickets as part of Project Noisemaker, which began in 2020.

Police already have the authority and detection tools to enforce current excessive noise laws in the Highway Traffic Act, but Andrews says the increased fines will have an effect that should help quieten communities.

stories.title: Cbsa seizes 81 kg of cocaine in lettuce truck crossing from U.S. into B.C.
stories.summary: Officers intercepted a commercial truck arriving from the U.S. on Oct. 23 after noting concerns with its paperwork, the agency said in a news release,
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The Canadian Border Services Agency seized 81 kilograms of suspected cocaine coming from the United States at a border crossing into British Columbia last month, the agency said.

The seizure comes amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and accusations from the U.S. administration that Canada has not done enough to prevent fentanyl trafficking into the U.S.

Officers intercepted a commercial truck arriving from the U.S. on Oct. 23 after noting concerns with its paperwork, the agency said in a news release on Tuesday.

During a search of the truck, officers seized two duffel bags containing 65 packages of suspected cocaine on top of boxes of romaine lettuce.

The driver was arrested and the truck was taken for further examination, the Cbsa said.

The driver and the cocaine were then transferred into the custody of the RCMP.

“This seizure demonstrates the Cbsa’s ongoing commitment to combatting organized crime. We know criminals will try to use any means to get dangerous substances into Canada, and our officers are skilled at catching them. Working with our partners in the RCMP, we are bringing those responsible to justice,” Nina Patel, regional director general of the Cbsa Pacific Region, said in a news release.

The investigation is ongoing.

The Norwegian energy company says the attack is not a virus and cannot spread, and it doesn’t seem to have affected employees, partners or suppliers.

stories.title: London police seek second suspect in hotel assault investigation
stories.summary: Two men are facing multiple charges after police said a woman was assaulted, threatened with weapons and held against her will at a south London hotel.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two men are facing multiple charges after police said a woman was assaulted, threatened with weapons and held against her will at a south London hotel.

Police said a woman went to a hotel room around 1 a.m. on Nov. 14 after a man requested sexual services in exchange for money. Investigators allege that once she arrived, she was assaulted and forcibly confined by two suspects, who threatened her with what police said were a firearm and a knife and prevented her from leaving.

Around 2 a.m., the London Police Service received a call requesting a welfare check on the woman.

Officers attended the hotel and located the victim and one suspect inside a hotel room. Police said the suspect fled but was arrested a short distance away.

Investigators reviewed security footage that allegedly showed the suspect throwing a bag underneath a vehicle while fleeing. Police recovered the bag and found an imitation firearm inside.

Police said the investigation determined the two suspects were attempting to exploit the woman in the sex trade for financial gain.

The case was later reassigned to the London Police Service’s human trafficking unit, which identified a second suspect.

Chad Kuzler, 45, of St. Thomas, and David H. Janssens, 57, of Thamesford, have each been charged with:

Forcible confinement;

Assault with a weapon;

Possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000;

Obtaining sexual services for consideration; and

Kuzler is also charged with pointing a firearm.

Police said Kuzler remains in custody and was scheduled to reappear in a London court on Wednesday.

Janssens remains wanted and has been charged by warrant, police said.

The victim suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Investigators believe there May be additional victims and have released photographs of both accused as the investigation continues.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Canadian women’s flag football team to hold camp
stories.summary: It's back to work for Rachel Lessard and the Canadian women's flag football team.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Ottawa – It’s back to work for Rachel Lessard and the Canadian women’s flag football team.

The defending world champions will hold a nine-day national camp that begins Saturday in Chula Vista, Calif. Twenty-four players will participate, including 10 from the 12-person squad that won gold at last year’s world championship in Germany.

Defensive backs Samantha Hopkins and Laurence Caron will both miss the camp due to injury.

The world championship victory qualified Canada for the 2028 Los Angeles Games, where flag football will make its Olympic debut. This camp will be the first for the national team in its preparation for the inaugural Grand Slam of Flag Tournament on Feb. 9-10, which takes place during Super Bowl LXI week in Los Angeles.

“Coming off a world championship win, there’s a lot of excitement around bringing this group back together and getting back to work,” Lessard said. “This first camp is an important opportunity for us to build on what we accomplished in Duesseldorf, continue developing as a team and start putting the pieces in place for LA28.”

Among the national team veterans invited to attend are quarterback Sara Parker, receiver/team captain Caroline Moquin-Joubert and defensive back Sabrina Gervais.

Eighteen participants will be selected for a camp in Chula Vista from Jan. 31-Feb. 7. From there, the 12-player Grand Slam roster will be chosen.

Also, Football Canada will host an open ID camp in January. Players from outside the national team will get the chance to compete for Canada’s 2027-28 team selection cycle.

The Canadian men’s squad, which has also qualified for the L.A. Games, will continue training for the next phase of team selection in early 2027. But head coach Paul LaPolice will oversee a camp involving 20 CFL players in California from Nov. 29-Dec. 6.

Among the players invited is Montreal Alouettes receiver Tyson Philpot — the league’s top Canadian this season and the outstanding Canadian in Sunday’s Grey Cup game. Philpot led the CFL in catches (124), yards (1,809) and was tied with teammate Tyler Snead for most TDs (13).

Philpot set single-season records for receptions and yards by a Canadian.

Cornerback Tyrell Ford of the Grey Cup-champion Edmonton Elks was also invited. But the CFL’s interceptions leader (seven) suffered a leg injury early in Sunday’s game and returned to watch his club’s 37-30 win over Montreal on crutches.

The camp is designed to educate pro players on the rules and nuances of flag football. Both the CFL and NFL will allow their players to participate in the L.A. Games.

The Canadian men’s team qualified for Los Angeles by finishing third in last year’s world championship.

Ford and Philpot both have twin brothers in the CFL — quarterback Tre Ford of the Hamilton Tiger-Cats and receiver Jalen Philpot of the Calgary Stampeders. All four were invited to the flag football camp.

The eight other defensive backs selected alongside Tyrell Ford were Alonzo Addae (Ottawa), Cristophe Beaulieu (B.C.), Malcolm Bell (Hamilton), Tevaughn Campbell (Saskatchewan), Jackson Findlay (B.C.), Adrian Greene (Calgary), Ashton Miller-Melancon (Calgary) and Stavros Katsantonis (Hamilton).

Joining the Philpots at receiver are: Nic Demski (Winnipeg); Samuel Emilus (Saskatchewan); Justin McInnis (B.C.); Kevin Mital (Toronto); Kian Schaffer-Baker (Saskatchewan); and Keelan White (Ottawa).

Nathan Rourke of the B.C. Lions and Taylor Elgersma of the Winnipeg Blue Bombers were the other quarterbacks selected.

Canadian-born NFL players will attend a separate camp in early spring 2027, while additional players will have an opportunity to be considered by Football Canada for selection to next year’s open camps.

“With flag football making its Olympic debut in 2028, we have an opportunity to showcase the depth of talent across the country and bring together athletes from different pathways within the game,” LaPolice said. “The sport has grown tremendously across Canada, and these camps are another step in building on that momentum and strengthening the foundation of our men’s program.”

The final men’s and women’s Olympic rosters will be announced ahead of the 2028 Games.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Carney says he hopes to sign trade arrangement deal with Taiwan soon
stories.summary: Shenzhen - Prime Minister Mark Carney says a trade arrangement with Taiwan finalized more than a year ago might be signed soon.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Shenzhen - Prime Minister Mark Carney says a trade arrangement with Taiwan finalized more than a year ago might be signed soon.

“There’s been good progress on the economic co-operation agreement and we’re hopeful that that will be signed soon,” Carney told a Wednesday news conference in Shenzhen, China.

Documents the government tabled in Parliament in September say Ottawa and Taipei finalized a trade co-operation framework agreement in March 2025 and the federal government consulted the provinces on it two months later.

The agreement has been translated into French and Chinese and is “being considered for signature,” according to the documents.

Taiwan’s delegation to Ottawa wrote in June that negotiations on the deal ended more than a year prior and the “the legal review” was “largely complete.”

When asked why the deal has been left unsigned for a year, Carney said he’s “hopeful” it “will be signed soon.” His office did not explain why the deal has not been signed.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Carney wrote that Canada has strong ties with Taiwan and cited the government’s long-standing “One China” policy, which officially recognizes the government in Beijing as the sole government of China.

“Diligent work toward the Canada-Taiwan Trade Cooperation Framework Arrangement continues,” the spokesperson said. “Recognizing the importance of Canada’s unofficial relations with Taiwan, we aim to bring consideration of the arrangement to a conclusion in the near term.”

Noting that Taiwan is part of Canada’s Indo-Pacific strategy, the House of Commons foreign affairs committee recommended last month that the government sign the agreement.

Back in April, senior Canadian diplomat Weldon Epp told MPs that the government is “considering the timing and the nature of moving forward.”

Epp told MPs the framework is not a treaty that would need to be tabled in Parliament. The document includes processes for more specific agreements that could address green technologies, artificial intelligence and supply chains.

The Bloc Québécois this week accused Carney of slow-walking the deal with Taiwan to avoid upsetting China, which claims control over the self-governing island.

Conservative foreign affairs critic Eric Duncan told the House of Commons last month the Liberals have “refused to sign, simply bowing to Beijing’s intimidation.”

Vina Nadjibulla, CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said it seems the deal keeps getting delayed and Ottawa is not offering an explanation.

“Timing could be connected to stabilization of relations with Beijing and negotiations on tariff deals,” she wrote in an emailed response.

“Holding up a deal with Taiwan in order not to upset Beijing is a mistake. Canada should be able to pursue both objectives, a stable and constructive relationship with Beijing and deeper economic ties with Taiwan,” Nadjibulla wrote, adding that countries such as Australia have done so.

Carney is wrapping up a lengthy Asia trip this week after attending summits in the Philippines, Cambodia and China. A major focus of the trip has been the pursuit of trade or investment deals, including investment protection pacts.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Calgary to explore new rules for data centres but temporary pause will go to public hearing
stories.summary: The move comes as a rezoning application is under review at city hall that would make way for a large-scale data centre in northeast Calgary.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Calgary city council has taken steps to develop new regulations for large-scale data centres in the city, but a proposed temporary pause to restrict new projects will require a public hearing in the spring.

On Tuesday, city council voted in favour of a motion from Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness, co-signed by Couns. Raj Dhaliwal, Andrew Yule, John Pantazopoulos and Mayor Jeromy Farkas, to create more oversight over data centre projects in Calgary.

“You don’t know how council is going to vote when there is no consistent policy,” Wyness told reporters. “You’re letting politics lead the decision when there is no set of rules for an applicant to fall back on.”

The motion directs city administration to create a new zoning district that defines data centres, and takes into consideration the varying scales of data centre proposals by March.

City administration has also been directed to study “the risks, implications and opportunities of data centres,” including environmental and economic impacts as well as potential effects on regional water servicing and municipal water infrastructure.

That report, which is expected to be complete by the end of 2027, would also take into account environmental, jurisdictional, legal and legislative considerations.

“This is an acute issue for us. We know that about 80 per cent of Canada’s data centre development is poised to occur here in the province of Alberta,” Farkas said. “Given the constraints that we have around electricity and around water, we need to have our eyes wide open.”

Although that portion of the motion passed unanimously, another piece that leads the way to a potential temporary pause on new data centre proposals was approved 13-2 with Couns. Myke Atkinson and Landon Johnston voting against.

According to Wyness, Calgary can issue a moratorium under the Municipal Government Act but there is a gap in the city’s land-use bylaw that requires a change to impose one while new regulations are created.

That proposed amendment is expected to go to a public hearing in March, which would give Calgarians the opportunity to weigh in on a temporary pause.

The move comes months after Rocky View County put a temporary freeze on data centre projects to establish regulations for future proposed projects.

The motion noted other municipalities like Oakville, Ont., Mississauga, Ont., Cumberland, N.S. and Saskatoon, Sask. have done the same.

However, Atkinson said he’s concerned changing the bylaw to allow for a temporary moratorium could have broader impacts.

“It will give council the authority on new kinds of land-uses that are unknown, not just A.I. data centres… we can just turn it off and say ‘no, we’re not going to listen to that,” he told Global News. “We need to be able to hear it, vet it, make decisions on it. Council needs to own that responsibility.”

It comes as a rezoning application is under review at city hall that would make way for a large-scale data centre on an undeveloped parcel of land east of 52 Street NE and north of the community of Redstone.

According to city administration, a number of studies have been requested before a decision is made on the application.

In a statement, the Canadian Coalition for Digital Infrastructure (Ccdi) said data centres bring significant investment, jobs and economic growth, and noted Calgary is “already home to many facilities” that have been in operation for years.

The organization said its members are “committed to ensuring this infrastructure is built responsibly and sustainably.”

“Many of Calgary’s data centres are cooled using technology much like any typical commercial or light industrial building, using minimal potable water,” Ccdi said in a statement. “We believe a pause, moratorium or substantial changes to the existing framework would send the wrong signal, putting that investment and the benefits it delivers at risk.”

When asked about the message a temporary pause could send to businesses looking to invest, Farkas said council wants to ensure businesses are operating on a “level playing field.”

“Calgary needs to be open for business,” Farkas said. “But we’re not open to being taken advantage of.”

However, Atkinson said he’s concerned changing the bylaw to allow for a temporary moratorium could have broader impacts.
