stories.title: Canada wants to get close to tariff-free trade in Cusma talks: Charette
stories.summary: President Donald Trump said in July that the U.S. would not renew the Cusma deal in its current form, forcing it to be reviewed annually.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Canada’s chief trade negotiator with the U.S. said the current goal of the review of Cusma is to get “as close as we can to tariff-free trade.”

Janice Charette made the comments during a parliamentary committee hearing on Tuesday when asked if the federal government’s plan was to return to trade with the U.S. without tariffs.

“We’d very much like to get back to that position, but I think we have to prepare ourselves for a world that, like other countries, that’s not an arrangement that we are able to arrive at with the United States,” she told MPs at the standing committee of international trade. “As we pursue negotiations with the United States to reduce the sectoral tariffs, which have a number of different forms associated with them, our objective is then to try to get us back as close as we can to tariff-free trade.”

The trade agreement has shielded both Canada and Mexico from many of Trump’s tariffs, though both countries have still faced a number of sectoral duties including on steel and automobiles.

In her comments, Charette noted tariff-free trade has been the premise for Cusma and what made it so successful.

The U.S. stance on tariffs though has shifted after Trump was re-elected in 2024, something she said has been clear at the table.

“We have another partner on the other side of the table and they have shown to date an unwillingness to enter into any arrangement in which there is full, tariff-free trade,” Charette said.

She added she has suggested getting the lowest rate of tariffs “on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access” for Canadian workers and businesses.

Cusma, also known as the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, was struck by the three countries in 2019 as a replacement for the North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta).

But in July, Washington said it won’t renew the deal in its current form. That means the trade deal must be reviewed annually, adding to the volatility and economic uncertainty facing businesses.

— with files from Global News’ Uday Rana

stories.title: Manning-led report says Western Canada can unite, gain power within Confederation
stories.summary: Calgary - A report examining the future of Western Canada suggests provinces should seek more sovereignty and provincial control rather than consider leaving Canada.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - A report examining the future of Western Canada suggests provinces should seek more sovereignty and provincial control rather than consider leaving Canada.

The report stems from a two-day video conference in mid-September with the Alberta and the West Assembly group. The conference came a month before Albertans voted in a provincewide referendum to keep the province in Canada and avoid holding a second, binding vote on separation.

Dozens of delegates looked at how to address the divide between Ottawa and Western Canada. The report says there were tens of thousands of online views of the sessions.

Preston Manning, a conservative elder statesman leading the report, said it makes two important points.

One is “unite the West and leave the rest.” The other is that there can be sovereign provinces within Confederation.

“I actually think one of the biggest problems the current federal government’s got is in this whole area of federal-provincial relations,” Manning said Tuesday in Calgary.

“You’ve got Newfoundland, you’ve got Quebec, you got the Western provinces that are alarmed by federal intrusions in areas of provincial responsibility.”

Manning, founder of the Reform Party and former federal Opposition leader, chaired the assembly with former Liberal B.C. premier Gordon Campbell.

The report’s recommendations broadly push for more provincial sovereignty across the four westernmost provinces, particularly in Alberta, and suggest ways provinces can better communicate their demands to Ottawa and the roles each government has in agreements.

It says a large part of that is all working toward the same goal line as a team in a united West.

It also suggests using Quebec as a yardstick to see how willing the federal government is to bend to provincial pushback.

“I think there’s lot that could be imitated with respect to Quebec’s pushing for sovereignty within the federation, but not going so far as the (Parti Québécois) government is now to advocate secession,” Manning told reporters.

The report says it took Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum question on separation into account. Separatist leaders argued the province was better on its own than having to work with federal leadership.

In one reference, the report suggests Alberta use the 1991 Canada-Quebec Immigration Accord as a template for its own, similar agreement.

There were nine other questions on immigration and the Constitution in the Alberta referendum, and the majority of voters said Alberta should take more control over immigration.

The report encourages a jurisdictional audit to examine federal and provincial authority and where they overlap, as well as consider how Charter and Indigenous rights play into federal and provincial agreements.

It also encourages provinces, especially in the West, to pick up on Alberta’s steps toward sovereignty.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said the province is doing well to address what she called the nine bad laws imposed by the federal government, largely on energy-related rules.

Manning said he plans to ask members of Parliament and the legislatures in B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to respond to the report’s recommendations.

British Columbia’s recently elected majority Conservative government is more likely to be on the same page as their conservative counterparts in Alberta and Saskatchewan, Manning added.

“I think it strengthens the possibility for this, ‘unite the West and leave the rest.’”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: P.E.I. nurses rally for new contract as spending on private agency staff climbs
stories.summary: Prince Edward Island nurses took their contract fight outside the legislature Tuesday, calling on the province to invest in its public health-care workforce and reduce spending on private staffing agencies.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – Prince Edward Island nurses took their contract fight outside the legislature Tuesday, calling on the province to invest in its public health-care workforce and reduce spending on private staffing agencies.

More than 1,600 registered nurses, registered psychiatric nurses and nurse practitioners have been without a collective agreement for more than a year and a half. Their rally comes as the cost of relying on temporary agency workers climbs. According to the P.E.I. Nurses’ Union, Health P.E.I. spent approximately $44 million on agency staff in 2025–26.

“What it means for our members is the focus is purely on filling the gaps and not the causes of why those vacancies are there,” said union President Kim Sears. “The focus needs to be on retention. Recruitment alone isn’t going to help when you can’t retain the nurses.”

Sears said she’s also hearing that spending could approach $60 million in the current fiscal year, though that projection has not been confirmed.

The union wants the health authority to prioritize working conditions for permanent staff, pointing to what it describes as unsafe staffing ratios, inadequate recognition of specialized nursing roles and compensation that falls behind other provinces.

Wages could push nurses to leave P.E.I.

P.E.I. general-duty registered nurses have the lowest base hourly wages in Atlantic Canada, according to a November comparison by the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions.

For nurse practitioner Laurie Thomas, the concern is that pay hasn’t kept pace with growing responsibilities.

“Our role and responsibility in the system has grown exponentially, and our wages haven’t,” she said.

Thomas, who has worked as a nurse practitioner on the Island since 2013, worries more of her colleagues could leave Health P.E.I. for opportunities elsewhere if a new agreement doesn’t reflect the work they do.

P.E.I. ’s fall fiscal update forecasts the province’s health authority will run $74.3 million over its 2026–27 operating budget, with agency staffing listed as one of several pressures, but not the sole cause.

According to reporting by The Guardian , Health P.E.I. spent more than $27 million on private agency staff between Jan. 1 and July 10, 2026. The figures were detailed in a freedom of information request received by the Charlottetown newspaper.

Region-wide ban on travel nurses

Health Minister Cory Deagle said the Island is working to reduce its reliance on nurses supplied by private agencies, adding taxpayers can’t afford the cost. But for now, several facilities can’t operate without them, and they also allow permanent nurses to take vacations.

“The reality is we’d have to close beds if we reduce those staff,” he said. “Our system can’t handle that overnight.”

He added that it will take time for staffing reductions to show up in spending figures.

Deagle also plans to meet with counterparts in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, ideally before year’s end, to advocate for a region-wide ban on travel nurses.

“Our goal should always be zero. Will it get there? My hope is yes,” he said.

The pressure on pay extends beyond the Island. Statistics Canada found that registered nursing employees aged 25 to 54 earned 1.4 per cent less per hour in 2025 than before the pandemic, once inflation is factored in.

Meanwhile, hours purchased from private staffing agencies by Canadian hospitals more than doubled between 2019–20 and 2023–24, according to the Canadian Institute for Health Information .

The nurses’ union says it walked away from negotiations in September after 32 days of bargaining, citing a lack of meaningful counterproposals from Health P.E.I.

“We felt we were being stonewalled at the bargaining table and had no choice but to walk,” Sears said.

She added that it was the first time in 24 years the union had taken that step.

“We did not take this lightly.”

The two sides are scheduled to meet with a conciliation officer on Dec. 21 and 22, in an effort to resolve the outstanding issues and reach a new agreement.

stories.title: Western Mustangs maintain their status as a top program in the Ontario University Football league
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs have long established their legacy of being one of the top programs in Canadian universit...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
The Western Mustangs have long established their legacy of being one of the top programs in Canadian university football. Their Yates Cup championship last weekend over the Queen’s Gaels cemented that reputation. Again.

With the Ontario title secured, Western is now preparing for the Mitchell Bowl, where they’ll face Halifax’s Saint Mary’s Huskies, from of the Atlantic University Sport (AUS) on Nov. 21. And the Huskies are doing the same.

“Western is an extremely strong team,” said Saint Mary’s Huskies head coach Steve Sumarah. “It’s going to be a very challenging endeavor.”

Saint Mary’s is undefeated in the AUS regular season this year, and the Mustangs have had a strong run, with only two losses in the Ontario division.

A major factor behind the Mustang’s success this year has been the team’s chemistry, said starting quarterback Ben Casselman.

Western Mustangs Field. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

“We’re a young team, but also deep at a lot of positions,” he said. “We’ve been in the stadium together for almost three months straight.

“All of those things lead to a lot of trust in the locker room.”

Western head coach Michael Faulds said the team has continued to improve throughout the season, despite a few setbacks.

“We had a couple of hiccups in the regular season, but I can honestly say we truly have improved each and every week,” he said. “That’s built on … our body work and our process.”

The Mustangs latest victory over the Gaels did not come without its share of late-game drama.

Western came out strong in the second and third quarter, building a commanding 29-3 lead heading into the fourth quarter. The Gaels didn’t give up and started to mount a comeback, scoring 24 points in the final quarter. Despite the late push from Queen’s, the Mustangs held on to secure a 36-27 victory and captured their 36th Yates Cup championship title in program history.

Faulds mentions how their first-week bye played a factor in their success.”That allowed us to have new people in new places, and really be the best they could be at those positions”

The Western Mustangs host the Saint Mary’s Huskies on Nov. 21 at Western Alumni Stadium.

stories.title: 7 bird flu cases across Prairies linked to Saskatchewan poultry show
stories.summary: Seven cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza have been detected in the Prairie provinces after an exposure at a Saskatchewan poultry show earlier this month.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
An exposure to highly pathogenic avian influenza (Hpai) at a Saskatchewan poultry show has resulted in cases across the Prairie provinces, according to the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia).

Seven cases spanning Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have been linked so far to a Nov. 8 gathering in Moose Jaw, Sask. The show associated with the American Poultry Association drew farmers from all three provinces to the city, and anyone who brought, bought or sold farmed birds at the event is being told to take precautions.

The confirmed cases were said to have occurred at non-commercial farms, meaning the flocks had fewer than 1,000 birds that were used for local sales in limited quantity or breeding, the Cfia said.

“Participants who brought poultry to the event and/or, those who purchased or sold poultry at the event are considered a high risk contact due to potential exposure and are being placed under Cfia quarantine,” the agency said in an emailed statement to Global News.

The agency added that it is working with organizers to identify people who have been affected by the avian flu exposure and ensure they are abiding by the Cfia’s post-contamination guidelines.

Those regulations include the requirement to monitor and test flocks, if the farms are indicated to do so by the food inspection agency, it said. The statement noted that people who attended without birds, but have them at home, should also monitor their flocks.

Global News reached out to the American Poultry Association for comment. None was received prior to publication.

Hpai, also known as bird flu, is considered highly contagious. The virus mainly infects domesticated birds, but can be spread by wild birds, including geese and other waterfowls.

If a case of highly pathogenic avian flu is confirmed in a farmed bird, it must be reported to the Cfia so the agency can quarantine the area to limit Hpai exposures, the agency said. It abides by a stamping out policy, meaning the flock will be culled.

Symptoms of avian flu in birds include lethargy, respiratory issues and swollen eyes, wattles and combs, according to the Cfia’s statement. Hpai can be transmitted two to 14 days after exposure and is spread when an infected bird makes contact with others or indirectly, through contaminated clothing or footwear.

The Cfia is asking flock owners with sick birds to contact its sick-bird call-line at 403-338-5225.

stories.title: Ontario English public high-school teachers vote in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: All five of province’s major K-12 education unions have been without a contract since August
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
Ontario’s English public high-school teachers delivered an overwhelming strike mandate on Tuesday, just days before their union is set to return to the bargaining table.

Teacher and occasional teacher members of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation (Osstf) voted 96 per cent in favour of the move, if needed, as did 92 per cent of education workers. The union represents roughly 60,000 employees.

The results make it clear that educators “cannot continue to do more with less,” Osstf president Martha Hradowy said at Queen’s Park on Tuesday.

All five of Ontario’s major K-12 education unions – the Osstf, the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association, the Association des enseignantes et des enseignants franco-ontariens and Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions – have been without a contract since the end of August.

Bargaining has been stalled because of a dispute over which issues should be addressed centrally with the government and which should be handled at the local level with school boards.

But with the Ontario Labour Relations Board expected to make its ruling on the matter before the end of the week, the Osstf has negotiations with the province scheduled for Friday.

Parents need not worry about any strike action happening before the holidays, Ms. Hradowy said.

“I will say to parents, I don’t want them to worry yet. We’re still early on in the process and I’m committed to getting to the table to reach a fair collective agreement.”

Education Minister Paul Calandra said the Osstf’s strong strike mandate vote is a message for both the union and the province.

“It is their members saying to the union as much to us, ‘Get to the table and negotiate a fair deal,’ ” he said. “We have many months of negotiating ahead of us, and there is absolutely no reason why we can’t come to a deal that puts student achievement at the heart of everything that we do.”

On Monday, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association said its members voted 98 per cent in favour of authorizing strike action, if needed.

The three remaining unions are finalizing their strike mandate votes this week.

The strike mandate votes stem from the many problems in Ontario schools, interim Liberal Leader John Fraser said. “Classes, our schools, they’re not safe places to work or learn because class sizes are too big. Special education has been starved. The mental-health crisis has stopped being addressed, and the vote that you see is a reflection of exactly that.”

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the Osstf vote is a repudiation of Mr. Calandra. “It’s saying very clearly is that this minister has failed, and it is a strong sign of support, I would say, for education worker unions in their fight with this government.”

The Osstf has three priorities when it comes to negotiating a new collective agreement, Ms. Hradowy said: “investments in public education, supports for students and restoring respect to teachers and education workers in this province.”
paragraphs: Ontario’s English public high-school teachers delivered an overwhelming strike mandate on Tuesday, just days before their union is set to return to the bargaining table.

Teacher and occasional teacher members of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation (Osstf) voted 96 per cent in favour of the move, if needed, as did 92 per cent of education workers. The union represents roughly 60,000 employees.
The results make it clear that educators “cannot continue to do more with less,” Osstf president Martha Hradowy said at Queen’s Park on Tuesday.

All five of Ontario’s major K-12 education unions – the Osstf, the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association, the Association des enseignantes et des enseignants franco-ontariens and Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions – have been without a contract since the end of August.
Bargaining has been stalled because of a dispute over which issues should be addressed centrally with the government and which should be handled at the local level with school boards.
But with the Ontario Labour Relations Board expected to make its ruling on the matter before the end of the week, the Osstf has negotiations with the province scheduled for Friday.
Parents need not worry about any strike action happening before the holidays, Ms. Hradowy said.
“I will say to parents, I don’t want them to worry yet. We’re still early on in the process and I’m committed to getting to the table to reach a fair collective agreement.”
Education Minister Paul Calandra said the Osstf’s strong strike mandate vote is a message for both the union and the province.

“It is their members saying to the union as much to us, ‘Get to the table and negotiate a fair deal,’ ” he said. “We have many months of negotiating ahead of us, and there is absolutely no reason why we can’t come to a deal that puts student achievement at the heart of everything that we do.”
On Monday, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association said its members voted 98 per cent in favour of authorizing strike action, if needed.
The three remaining unions are finalizing their strike mandate votes this week.

The strike mandate votes stem from the many problems in Ontario schools, interim Liberal Leader John Fraser said. “Classes, our schools, they’re not safe places to work or learn because class sizes are too big. Special education has been starved. The mental-health crisis has stopped being addressed, and the vote that you see is a reflection of exactly that.”

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the Osstf vote is a repudiation of Mr. Calandra. “It’s saying very clearly is that this minister has failed, and it is a strong sign of support, I would say, for education worker unions in their fight with this government.”

The Osstf has three priorities when it comes to negotiating a new collective agreement, Ms. Hradowy said: “investments in public education, supports for students and restoring respect to teachers and education workers in this province.”

stories.title: LeBlanc fields questions about trade negotiations with Trump administration
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc faced questions at a committee hearing in Ottawa today about Prime Minister Mark Carney's version of the events leading to the collapse of trade talks with the Trump administration.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc maintained Tuesday that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s version of the events leading up to the collapse of U.S. trade talks was accurate as he was questioned by members of Parliament in Ottawa.

“The prime minister accurately described the conversations we had in those last days in Washington,” LeBlanc told MPs on the standing committee on international trade.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war rapidly escalated after trade talks broke down in August, as Ottawa and Washington accused each other of pushing eleventh-hour changes.

Carney said at the time that Trump’s team wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries, endanger Canada’s protections for language and culture, and maintain hefty tariffs on some automobiles.

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in response that the prime minister’s description of the trade talks “goes far beyond anything we’ve discussed.”

Conservative MP Jacob Mantle questioned LeBlanc about the competing narratives. “Who is telling the truth?” he asked.

“I think the prime minister was absolutely correct to say on that last day were introduced elements that would have restricted Canada’s ability to enter into free trade agreements with other countries,” LeBlanc said.

“Certain sectors were identified by the Americans. At the end of the day it was a balance … where the prime minister concluded that that is in the sovereign interest of Canada.”

Mantle pointed to sections of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma, that already bar partner countries from entering into trade agreements with non-market economies. LeBlanc replied that Mantle was assuming those conversations were about non-market economies.

Tuesday’s hearing provided no real insights into the trade talks or the current state of negotiations.

LeBlanc told the committee that he and Greer agreed not to publicly discuss details. The minister said he remains in contact with Greer and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

A bilateral deal that benefits Canada and the United States is still possible, LeBlanc told the hearing.

The Trump administration softened its public stance toward Canada after Democrats swept this month’s midterm elections — a result that was a clear rebuke of the president’s policies, including his sweeping tariff agenda.

Democrats have indicated that ending the trade war with Canada will be a top priority when they take the majority in Congress in January. Some experts say it May be challenging for Democrats to achieve the supermajority they would need to override the president’s veto.

Observers also have said Democrats likely will only tackle one of Trump’s tariff tools — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — while leaving in place other duties still hammering parts of the Canadian economy.

Trump used Section 338 to hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent levies. Weeks later, using the same Depression-era statute, he banned imports of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.

Democrats are expected to be much less likely to take down Trump’s separate sectoral tariffs or his 10 per cent duty linked to claims of forced labour in supply chains.

Democrats have a broad protectionist streak of their own and many of their newly elected members of Congress are not opposed to using tariffs to protect domestic industries.

At Tuesday’s hearing, Conservative MP Shuvaloy Majumdar asked Canada’s chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, if Ottawa’s goal is still to achieve tariff-free trade.

Charette said the United States is changing its trade with every country and all of Trump’s deals have included some level of tariffs. Canada has to prepare for a world where a tariff-free arrangement May not be possible, she said.

The objective is to “get to the lowest rate of tariff on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers,” Charette added.

“That is the premise for the Cusma agreement. That is what has made us so successful, so prosperous as three countries in North America, and we’d like to try and get as close back to that as possible,” she said.

“But we do have another partner on the other side of the table and they have shown to date an unwillingness to enter into any arrangement in which there is full tariff-free trade.”

Charette and LeBlanc also fielded questions about how Canada is reaching out to Mexican colleagues as Ottawa and Mexico City continue to advocate for a renewal of the continental trade pact.

The Trump administration in July chose not to renew Cusma. The decision triggered a rolling annual review for up to a decade, at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

Carney met earlier Tuesday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on the sidelines of an economic summit in China.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

stories.title: Rabid bat in Quebec care home leaves authorities searching for answers
stories.summary: Contact occurred at Chsld Élisabeth-Lafrance in Sorel-Tracy on Nov. 8 with 16 residents now receiving preventive treatment
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Quebec government says it’s working with a long-term care facility to solve its bat problem after a resident came into contact with an animal infected with rabies earlier this month.

A spokesperson for the Environment Department says specialists will meet with the facility and an exterminator on Wednesday to make a plan to stop bats from getting inside.

Health authorities say the resident who came into contact with the bat is receiving treatment.

The contact occurred on Nov. 8 at Chsld Élisabeth-Lafrance in Sorel-Tracy and 15 other residents are receiving preventive treatment.

A spokesperson for Santé Québec Montérégie-Est says it has been granted permission to exterminate the bats, which are protected by provincial and federal laws.

But the environment department says it had a plan to capture the bats alive and transfer them to a local sanctuary.

“This winter, thermal cameras will allow the colony’s entry points to be located, in order to plan an efficient intervention,” a spokesperson wrote. “The bats can then be captured alive and transferred to the Granby zoo refuge.”

The environment department says it generally recommends sealing off entrances and installing netting as the best short-term way to stop bats from getting inside a building.

The department also notes that less than one per cent of the province’s bats carry rabies, and the presence of one infected animal doesn’t mean the rest of the colony are carriers.

A spokesman Santé Québec Montérégie-Est said Monday that the long-term care facility has had issues with bats dating back to 2017, but this is the first one to test positive for rabies.

Pierre-Yves Séguin told The Canadian Press that the facility has tried to manage the problem through non-lethal means, such as sealing off entry points.

“We’ve captured and then relocated other bats. But now, with this new incident, we’ve reached a point where we need to take further action,” said Séguin.

Rabies is fatal once symptoms begin, but treatment can prevent the disease from developing in a person who has been exposed. Séguin said the resident who had contact with the bat is doing well.

The department also notes that less than one per cent of the province’s bats carry rabies, and the presence of one infected animal doesn’t mean the rest of the colony are carriers.
A spokesman Santé Québec Montérégie-Est said Monday that the long-term care facility has had issues with bats dating back to 2017, but this is the first one to test positive for rabies.
Pierre-Yves Séguin told The Canadian Press that the facility has tried to manage the problem through non-lethal means, such as sealing off entry points.
“We’ve captured and then relocated other bats. But now, with this new incident, we’ve reached a point where we need to take further action,” said Séguin.
Rabies is fatal once symptoms begin, but treatment can prevent the disease from developing in a person who has been exposed. Séguin said the resident who had contact with the bat is doing well.

stories.title: After parking the RV, this B.C. couple looks for a home
stories.summary: With a third child on the way, they wanted a larger home with plenty of outdoor space to play
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
When COVID-19 hit in March 2020, Tyler and Rebecca Nestman had just given birth to their son, Lucas, and were living in a rented basement apartment in Squamish, B.C. Once Tyler’s paternity leave ended, he returned to his job as a track foreman for CN Rail, which required travel across Western Canada. So the couple bought a fifth-wheel RV to join Tyler, 35, on the road. “People thought we were crazy for being able to live in that trailer with a newborn, but we made it work,” Rebecca, 30, says.

By June 2020, Tyler switched jobs and joined a friend’s equipment rental business, managing outside sales and rentals – a role that no longer required extensive travel. The family parked their RV at Tyler’s parents’ home in Gibsons, B.C., about 90 minutes north of Vancouver, to contemplate their next move.

They decided Rebecca would continue being a stay-at-home mom. The Nestmans considered buying an apartment in Gibsons but were discouraged after being outbid on a unit they liked. Then Tyler’s parents came up with an idea: they’d build a carriage house on their property and rent it to Tyler and Rebecca at below market rates. It took a year for the carriage home to be built, during which the young family moved into Tyler’s parents’ house and the couple found out they were pregnant again. In February 2022, they moved into the new two-bedroom, 900-square-foot carriage home and Rebecca gave birth to their second son, Logan, shortly after.

The two boys comfortably shared the second bedroom in the carriage home and the family enjoyed their proximity to Tyler’s parents. “They were right there to help with the kids,” Tyler says. Then, in February 2026, Tyler and Rebecca found out they were pregnant again and would welcome another baby to the family that December. They briefly considered expanding the carriage house but discovered that the cost – nearly $300,000 to extend it by 40 feet – was disproportionately high. That shifted them to think about buying again.

Thanks to help from both their parents: Tyler’s offering below-market rent and Rebecca’s giving a cash gift toward their down payment, the couple had a budget of $800,000. With that, they hoped to buy a detached home in Gibsons with at least three bedrooms, two bathrooms and lots of outdoor space. “We wanted the room for them to play,” Tyler explains. “We would take that over having a bigger kitchen or a bigger living room.” They planned to stay in Gibsons, close to Tyler’s parents (Rebecca’s parents are on Vancouver Island), with Lucas’s school (he is now 6 and Logan is 4) and the firehall nearby. “I’m part of the volunteer fire department here, so it needed to be close to the firehall for us to be able to respond,” Tyler explains.

In May, the Nestmans connected with Sutton Group realtor Cody Robinson – who is also a volunteer firefighter alongside Tyler – to guide their search. “Spring and early summer were unseasonably slow this year in our market,” Robinson explains. “There was a lot of uncertainty in the world at that time. Interest rates were tough for first-time and entry-level buyers to get into the market.”

The circumstances did pose an opportunity for buyers like the Nestmans to negotiate. “Take the listing price with a grain of salt,” he says. “There are conversations to be had with sellers right now, so don’t be afraid to start that conversation at a number that you’re comfortable with.”

Here were the family’s top three options:

The couple were initially drawn to this home in Gibsons because of the location. It was within walking distance to the firehall, schools and amenities like restaurants and a community centre. They liked having an additional bedroom they could grow into, and there was also a wood-burning stove inside. Outside, there was a large detached garage behind the home, which could be turned into a secondary suite, and a wraparound deck. However, most of the yard space was gravel, with just a small patch of grass underneath a tree, which wouldn’t be ideal for the kids to play. They also found the layout, with a sliding door as their main entrance, a bit unusual. The home, spanning 1,328 square feet on one level, was listed for $739,900.

Their realtor was actually the listing agent on this 1,678-square-foot property in Gibsons and encouraged the Nestmans to view it. The home was recently renovated inside with new flooring, and fresh paint inside and out. It had three bedrooms with a bonus room that could be used as a fourth bedroom or a rec room, which could function as an indoor play space for the kids. It sat on a generous quarter-acre lot with a large backyard, but the outdoor space was overgrown and would need some landscaping work before it was fit for their kids to play in. They also hesitated on the home’s septic system and its location on a higher-traffic street. This property was listed for $699,000, which was comfortably under their top budget.

This 2,200-square-foot home was actually split into two self-contained units that had previously been rented out to tenants: a one-bedroom, one-bathroom basement suite and a three-bedroom, one-bathroom main house on two levels. While the lot size was smaller than the previous home, it had a fenced-in wraparound yard with ample space for play. There was also a bonus room in the basement, separate from the rental suite, that the family could use as a rec room. However, there was only one bathroom in the upper unit which would soon need to be shared by five people. The upper level of the home had carpeting, which they worried would be an issue for their asthmatic son. The carpeting in the basement suite was also quite worn. This home was listed at the top of their budget, at $798,000.

The Nestmans were actually the first people to view this home, thanks to a lead from a realtor on Tyler’s recreational baseball team. Given the slower housing market in Gibsons at the time, the couple initially offered $720,000 and, after some back-and-forth negotiations with the seller, settled on a final price of $750,000. “It was a surreal moment,” Tyler says of finalizing their purchase. “I didn’t think we would own a house. It was exciting.”

They had the keys to their new place by July 2026 and spent a few weeks replacing all the flooring in the home, including the worn-out carpeting upstairs and in the basement, with laminate flooring before moving in at the end of July. While they considered taking over the whole home, they decided to rent out the basement suite instead. “The income of that rental is supporting our mortgage,” Tyler explains. “Potentially, when Rebecca goes back to work, maybe we can take over and use the whole house or use it as an in-law suite for our relatives or family members.”

Meanwhile, they’re making it work with one bathroom for the family. As their kids get older, they might consider adding a powder room to their home and have already earmarked a space in their laundry room, off the kitchen, to do it. Their two older sons will continue to share a bedroom while their new baby will have its own room.

The kids have taken a liking to their new home, thanks in part to an above-ground pool that their parents bought and set up in the yard for summer. In between, they’re playing knee-hockey in the basement rec room, riding their dirt bikes and exploring nearby walking trails as a family. They’re only two blocks away from Tyler’s parents, who they still visit often. “Their support is huge because they’re in our community,” he says. His parents have since rented out their carriage home to tenants.

Tyler and Rebecca are excited to be settled into a new, larger home before they become a family of five – something that couldn’t have happened without help from their parents. “I know a lot of people out there don’t have that opportunity to have family support in purchasing a home,” Rebecca explains. “We’re just grateful that they were able to help out.”

stories.title: 3 exemptions added to new Alberta driver’s licence rules amid renewal headaches
stories.summary: Exemptions will be considered for long-established Albertans with historical document issues, those with 'exceptional hardships' and people waiting on the federal government.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
The Alberta government is changing the new requirements for driver’s licence and identification card renewals after numerous complaints arose when the updated rules came into effect earlier this year .

In July, the province rolled out new three-in-one driver’s licences and ID cards that include citizenship markers and residents’ health numbers — replacing Alberta’s long-reviled paper health cards.

But the new cards came with new rules: residents have to produce documentation such as a birth certificate, current/non-expired passport, citizenship certificate or NEXUS card to confirm citizenship.

However ,some people who have undergone a name change, in particular married women, started being turned away at the registry because the names on their documents didn’t match.

Global News has received many complaints over the past four months from residents frustrated with being unable to renew driver’s licences they’d held their entire adult life.

Many women were told to return with their original marriage licence — and for some Albertans, the document was not easily found, forcing them to spend money on a new copy .

Now, the province is adding three exemptions to the process, starting Nov. 19 for driver’s licence renewals, followed by ID cards on Dec. 7.

Service Alberta said the changes will help existing licence and ID card holders, including those whose credentials expired within the past six months, who cannot obtain the documents required for renewal due to circumstances beyond their control.

The exemption streams are as follows:

Long-established residents with historical document issues : For eligible Albertans who face significant difficulty obtaining older citizenship, birth or related records. Applicants will be assessed against established criteria and will provide supporting evidence where it can reasonably be obtained.

Federal processing delays : For eligible Albertans who cannot provide an acceptable document because they are waiting for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada or another responsible authority to issue or replace it. Applicants will need to provide evidence that they have applied for the required document.

Exceptional hardship: For rare circumstances not addressed by the other two streams, which could include the need for a licence to maintain employment, documents destroyed in a fire or flood, barriers associated with remote access or vulnerable individuals who cannot access historical records.

Service Alberta said all exemptions will require the applicant to obtain a signed declaration.

Eligible Albertans may be able to renew their driver’s licence for up to five years unless another requirement, such as a medical condition or licence class, limits the renewal period.

Albertans using an exemption can still renew their driver’s licence or ID card without a Canadian citizenship marker, the province said on Tuesday, adding the citizenship marker will only be included if acceptable documentation verifying citizenship is provided.

The province announced the three-in-one licence in the fall of 2025, saying it would make it more convenient for Albertans to access health care as they wouldn’t have to carry multiple documents.

While some provinces have offered enhanced identification in the past , Alberta is the first Canadian jurisdiction to add citizenship and also the only jurisdiction in Canada to make the change mandatory.

Since the plan was announced last year, conversation has stirred around whether the inclusion of the citizenship marker — or lack thereof — could lead to discrimination.

The new Alberta licence features the province’s new branding, including an oil pumpjack replacing the icon of a dinosaur fossil, and the words “Alberta Strong and Free” on the back, along with 54 unique security features.

While the enhanced cards will come at no additional charge, anyone renewing their licence will have to pay the regular renewal fee, even if their old licence is still valid for a few more years.

The rollout of the new health care cards will cost $17 million over the next six years before all existing Alberta identification cards expire and are eventually replaced.

With files by The Canadian Press and Erik Bay, Skylar Peters and Craig Momney, Global News

stories.title: Mississauga data centre moratorium challenged by U.S. real estate giant, Toronto firm
stories.summary: Mississauga's data centre moratorium is facing a pair of challenges from a U.S. real estate giant and a Toronto asset manager.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mississauga’s data centre moratorium is set to face a legal challenge, as a U.S. real estate giant and a Toronto asset manager move to overturn the pause at the Ontario Land Tribunal.

The appeals by Prologis and Toronto-based Montcrest could test the power of municipalities to invoke temporary bans on data centres as they figure out how to regulate a wave of projects driven by the artificial intelligence boom.

“The fight is not done,” said Martin Reid, a city councillor who championed the moratorium, in a video posted to social media Tuesday.

“We can never put development before planning.”

Passed in September, Mississauga’s one-year interim control bylaw blocks new data centres with energy demands above 10 megawatts, roughly enough electricity for 10,000 homes. Mississauga is one of at least six Ontario municipalities to enact a similar pause in recent months, and the largest of that group.

Officials have framed the pause, which can be extended for a second year, as a necessary window to study grid strain, noise and land-use impacts before drafting rules around the projects. The city did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

The move froze a proposed 40-megawatt data centre project backed by Prologis in the city’s Meadowvale business park along Highway 401. In a statement, the company said the moratorium was “poorly conceived, without justification for its restrictions or consideration of the consequences for businesses seeking to invest in Mississauga.”

“This broad restriction is creating uncertainty and delaying investment,” read the statement.

While the discussion around Mississauga’s data centre moratorium has frequently referred to the Prologis project, there has until now been little mention of Montcrest.

Montcrest’s notice of appeal cites the moratorium’s impact on the “potential future use” of its land known as the Tahoe Centre, near Dixon Road and Eglinton Avenue south of Toronto Pearson Airport. The company did not respond to questions about whether the project was intended to be a data centre or whether it had active applications to hook up to Ontario’s energy grid.

In a statement, a company spokesperson said it had appealed the moratorium to ensure “clear guidelines for future building in the community.” The spokesperson said the company was committed to working “within the regulatory regime” for “any potential data centre development proposals we advance.”

While Ontario has long hosted data centres handling cloud storage, financial transactions or websites, the AI boom has led to a surge in proposed projects with far more intensive energy demands, some exceeding 100 megawatts.

Premier Doug Ford has been critical of the local restrictions, framing data centres as a promising investment. But several municipal leaders have said they have been left with little guidance or enforceable standards. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, who will preside over the first council meeting of her new term Wednesday after her re-election last month, campaigned on a promise to bring in a moratorium on AI data centres.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec government says it's looking at options after rabid bat enters care home
stories.summary: Montreal - The Quebec government says it’s working with a long-term care facility to solve its bat problem after a resident came into contact with an animal infected with rabies earlier this month.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Quebec government says it’s working with a long-term care facility to solve its bat problem after a resident came into contact with an animal infected with rabies earlier this month.

A spokesperson for the Environment Department says specialists will meet with the facility and an exterminator on Wednesday to make a plan to stop bats from getting inside.
paragraphs: Montreal - The Quebec government says it’s working with a long-term care facility to solve its bat problem after a resident came into contact with an animal infected with rabies earlier this month.

stories.title: Left-wing Québec solidaire accuses rivals of trying to 'cancel' party
stories.summary: Quebec's left-wing party is accusing its rivals of trying to shut it out by denying it official parliamentary status in the provincial legislature.
stories.author: Vicky Fragasso-Marquis and Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Québec solidaire house leader Alexandre Leduc says the governing Parti Québécois, Liberals and Conservatives appear to have formed a coalition to “cancel” his party following a second round of negotiations.

But Liberal André Fortin says negotiations are progressing well, and the parties plan to meet again on Friday.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Québec solidaire won nine seats and 12.42 per cent of the vote in last month’s provincial election, falling short of the 12 seats or 20 per cent of the vote required to be automatically recognized as a party in the legislature.

That status would give the party access to research funding and more speaking time in the legislature.

Québec solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal points to previous exceptions, including the Parti Québécois, which secured official recognition with just three seats in 2022.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, which lost all its seats in last month’s election, is backing Québec solidaire’s request for recognition.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Fundraising begins for homelessness ‘Connection Centre’ in Goderich
stories.summary: In Huron County, over 150 people currently don’t have a place to call home. To try and get those folks housed, the United Way of Perth-Huron is opening a new Connection Centre in Goderich.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
In Huron County, over 150 people currently don’t have a place to call home. To try and get those folks housed, the United Way of Perth-Huron is opening a new Connection Centre in Goderich.

“We think it’s really important to make sure that we continue to build a system that responds rapidly to people who are experiencing homelessness. So, we know in every community, and Goderich of course, is one of the places where there are far too many people experiencing homelessness, we have to find a way to better connect with them immediately,” said Ryan Erb, executive director of the United Way of Perth-Huron.

Connection Centres aren’t homeless shelters. There are no overnight beds, but there are showers, food, clothing, companionship, and place to connect to social services, including housing options.

“Ultimately, what we’re trying to do is to rapidly rehouse people, because if they’re housed quickly, it means that we can help them faster. If someone experiences homelessness for more than six months, it’s harder to help them to get out of the situation. And so we want to do it faster. This is the entry point for the system,” said Erb.

The United Way will open Goderich’s Connection Centre inside the new headquarters of the Canadian Mental Health Association (Cmha), who are moving from downtown Goderich to a building near Goderich’s fire hall on McEwan Street.

“Being downtown and having, you know, our folks there, sometimes causes disturbances. So, it’s nice to be able to have a space that’s ours, and we can design the way we know it needs to be, and gives people a really safe place to be,” said Catherine Hardman, executive director of the Cmha Huron-Perth Addiction and Mental Health Services.

Two years ago, there were 104 unhoused residents in Huron County. That number was at 151 this August and has hovered around 150 since early 2025. More than ¾ of those folks have been unhoused for more than six months.

“We have a challenge, every month we house, you know, let’s just say about 10 people in the County of Huron. The problem is there’s usually 11 who become unhoused. So, we’re slowly losing. But, with a better system that’s more responsive, we can turn the corner over time,” said Erb.

Hardman and Erb are launching a $906,000 fundraising campaign to get the new Cmha Huron-Perth headquarters and United Way Connection Centre in Goderich off the ground.

“So somebody might come in and say, “Look, actually, I’m not experiencing homelessness yet, but I might be. I’ve just got an eviction notice.’ So what do we do about that? We bring all the staff from all the different organizations to the Connection Centre, and it’s one hub to help people who are in that situation,” said Erb.

“Since the pandemic, mental health and addiction issues have risen significantly in all communities. Homelessness has risen significantly in our communities. And so this is a really nice partnership and a really nice way to be able to provide those services for people who, you know, don’t have service or don’t maybe attach themselves to services in the same way that kind of traditional people would do. We can really build services that are meant for them, and that really fit them,” said Hardman.

Erb and Hardman expect the new Cmha headquarters and United Way Connection Centre to be open by the fall of 2027.

“A Connection Centre is the front door to meet people in their urgent need, to provide food and clothing and warmth on a cold day. All those things are critically important for the Connection Centre, but most important is to build a relationship, and to get them on the path to finding housing,” said Erb.

There are currently four other Connection Centres for Huron-Perth’s unhoused, located in Stratford, Listowel, Wingham, and Exeter.

stories.title: Expert insight: Why Canada has a moral imperative to address homelessness
stories.summary: Western University professor Nicole Fice argues homelessness in Canada does not stem from individual choices, but by those made as a society.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced a plan in the 2026 federal budget aimed at eliminating homelessness in the next decade. A statement about the plan says homelessness “strikes at the heart of Canadian values of fairness, solidarity, and human dignity.”

What are these values and how exactly are they impacted by homelessness? The announcement does not clearly answer these questions. As a researcher in public health ethics, I want to fill the gaps by drawing on empirical and philosophical research to explain why, exactly, the urgent need to address homelessness is matter of ethics.

Dignity refers to a kind of inherent worth that all people hold equally by virtue of being human. It serves as the foundation for human rights, which provide people with entitlements and establish obligations for others (including governments) to treat people in ways that respect their rights.

Violations of those human rights, which include a guarantee to adequate housing, are one way people experience a loss of dignity when homeless. Some policy responses to homeless encampments have also violated rights guaranteed under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and therefore peoples’ dignity.

Homelessness violates dignity in other ways. A lack of shelter, housing and a home – understood as a place of belonging – leads people to experience shame and ostracism.

Homelessness excludes people from meaningful participation in social life. That leaves them on the margins of society, with little to no resources or options, reduced social status and a lack of freedomand authority over their lives since much of what they do, even just to survive, is criminalized.

In these ways, homelessness reduces people to being less-than, unworthy, and unequal.

This brings us to fairness and related questions about what a just society looks like.

In one view, a just society involves how people stand in terms of equality with one another rather than in hierarchic relations. The failure of the state to adequately respond to homelessness is a profound injustice because it demonstrates a lack of equal concern for some of the most vulnerable members of society. And, as some argue, this is precisely what’s at play in terms of homelessness.

Another famous view comes from American philosopher John Rawls. For him, justice as fairness is concerned with the distribution of benefits and burdens in society, according to two principles.

The first principle states that everyone has an equal claim to basic liberties. The relevant part of the second principle, called the difference principle, holds that any social and economic inequalities in a just society should give the greatest benefit to the least advantaged members of society.

Although this view tolerates some inequality, homelessness remains incompatible with its principles of justice.

Rawls didn’t name housing as one of the benefits to be distributed under these principles. Some scholars have argued that it must be one of the social goods we should be concerned about distributing fairly, through, say, social housing models.

The fact that homelessness exists to the degree it does in a wealthy country like Canada does in fact suggest a lack of fairness in a broader distributive sense. Some people are left without shelter altogether, some have subpar shelter while others have plenty.

But the causes of homelessness are complex and multi-faceted. The problem has been made worse by a lack of affordable housing, higher unemployment and overall higher costs of living associated with rising inflation.

In research on the causes, experts and advocates agree that it’s not caused by the choices people make, but the choices we make as a society.

Such social choices have ripple effects, as people who experience homelessness face risks to their health and well-being. Homelessness disproportionately affects some populations, which can lead to vicious cycles of poor health, higher risk of infectious disease and premature death. Homelessness therefore leads to inequities in health.

Homelessness is an affront to human dignity, and it’s unfair. The concept of solidarity speaks to the need for society generally to address injustices as a collective. Failing to do so results in the social and moral abandonment of people experiencing homelessness as they are left to suffer the injustices of homelessness alone.

While these arguments make a compelling ethical case for ending homelessness, the real work lies in translating justification into action. In addition to monitoring and evaluating the practical outcomes of the promised federal funds, Canadians should not lose sight of the ethical values underpinning them and the overarching goal of ending homelessness.

We need to ensure our policies not only reflect our ethical values, but also produce outcomes that actively support them. We must consider whether the policies and programs implemented align with our ethical values, and whether their outcomes are effective in promoting them as well.

Nicole Fice, Assistant Professor, School of Health Studies, Western University

Homelessness disproportionately affects some populations, which can lead to vicious cycles of poor health, higher risk of infectious disease and premature death. Homelessness therefore leads to inequities in health.

Homelessness is an affront to human dignity, and it’s unfair. The concept of solidarity speaks to the need for society generally to address injustices as a collective. Failing to do so results in the social and moral abandonment of people experiencing homelessness as they are left to suffer the injustices of homelessness alone.

While these arguments make a compelling ethical case for ending homelessness, the real work lies in translating justification into action. In addition to monitoring and evaluating the practical outcomes of the promised federal funds, Canadians should not lose sight of the ethical values underpinning them and the overarching goal of ending homelessness.

We need to ensure our policies not only reflect our ethical values, but also produce outcomes that actively support them. We must consider whether the policies and programs implemented align with our ethical values, and whether their outcomes are effective in promoting them as well.
Nicole Fice, Assistant Professor, School of Health Studies, Western University

stories.title: Norwegian Cruise Line drops Halifax from select 2027 sailings, but port expects strong season
stories.summary: The changes affect select Norwegian Breakaway's seven-day Bermuda round-trip sailings from Boston, and will see passengers extending their stay in Bermuda instead.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Norwegian Cruise Line has decided to change its spring and summer schedule next year and will be skipping Halifax across 17 sailings “in response to guest feedback.”

The changes affect select Norwegian Breakaway’s seven-day Bermuda round-trip sailings from Boston between May and August 2027.

In an email, which was shared in multiple public Facebook groups for Norwegian Breakaway 2026 and 2027 passengers, the cruise line writes, “In response to guest feedback, we’ve enhanced your itinerary to allow for an extended stay in Royal Naval Dockyard, Bermuda.”

“By spending two nights on the island, you’ll have even more time to discover Bermuda at your own pace, enjoy its unique culture and natural beauty, and experience the destination both during the day and after sunset.”

After departing Boston on Sunday, the ship was originally scheduled to stop in Halifax from 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Tuesday, but will now head straight to Bermuda instead.

Global News has not received the email, but has reached out to Norwegian Cruise Line for comment about the posts. Global has not received a reply.

In response to the change, the Port of Halifax says it works closely with cruise lines as they plan their itineraries and stresses that Halifax is a “highly regarded cruise destination.”

“Cruise itineraries evolve for many reasons, and in this case Norwegian Cruise Line has adjusted spring and summer 2027 sailings by the Breakaway to provide guests with a longer stay in Bermuda,” wrote spokesperson Lori MacLean in an email.

“We were pleased to have Halifax included on Norwegian’s itinerary this year, welcoming thousands of guests and giving them an opportunity to experience Nova Scotia, perhaps for the first time. We hope these visits inspire future travel, with Halifax selected as one of the world’s top destinations by National Geographic for 2027.”

She confirms the Norwegian Breakaway will still stop in Halifax next fall as part of the Canada-New England itinerary. As well, other Norwegian ships will make calls during the season.

For 2027, the Port of Halifax is anticipating 173 ships between April and November.

It’s estimated that the cruise ship sector generates nearly $200 million annually and supports about 1,000 jobs in Nova Scotia, according to a study by the Cruise Lines International Association.

Lorn Sheehan, a business professor at Dalhousie University and tourism expert, says ports of call have a “huge economic impact” for the province and city.

“They have a direct economic impact just in passenger port fees, which for 17 sailings of almost 4,000 passengers per sailing, at $15 a head, you’re talking close to a million dollars in port fees alone,” he said.

“And if you think about beyond that, when you have passengers coming out into the community, spending money in our restaurants, in our various attractions and tours that are departing from the Halifax waterfront. And add all of that up, that’s probably another $8 million that’s being lost with this decision.”

At the same time, he says the cruise industry — and travel industry in general — is constantly adapting and changes to itineraries aren’t unheard of.

“Cruise lines are making decisions all the time as to what ports of call to include or drop. And this is really based on a number of factors, not the least of which is what demands the passengers are making (and) what trends are occurring,” he said.

He says some passengers May be looking for “fun in the sun,” while others are looking for more variety in their ports of call and experiences.

Ultimately, Sheehan says while the decision is disappointing for the local tourism industry, the overall picture for Halifax has been positive over the past decade, despite interruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

“We win some, we lose some here in Halifax,” he said.

“This is a case of where we’re losing one, I guess, to the Norwegian Cruise Line. But we will win other ones where we’ll have new cruise lines that have decided to put Halifax on the list of port call for a particular cruise that they’re doing … I certainly hope and expect that we will be gaining other cruise ships in their itinerary that weren’t there in previous years.”

stories.title: What could more Chinese steel and aluminum mean for Canadians?
stories.summary: After a meeting between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Ottawa said it would grant greater market access to more steel and aluminum items from China.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada and China are looking to expand trade relations, with Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Xi Jinping announcing relaxation of trade restrictions after a bilateral meeting on Tuesday.

Among the concessions was Canada’s decision to grant greater access to Chinese steel and aluminum products in the Canadian market.

In Tuesday’s meeting, China agreed to remove a 25 per cent tariff on Canadian exports of frozen pork cuts, along with frozen cold-water shrimp, Greenland halibut, some mollusks and sea cucumber.

Carney’s spokesperson said this represents approximately $400 million in Canadian exports annually.

In exchange, Ottawa said it would expand what is called remissions coverage to 32 more steel and aluminum items from China.

That includes 23 steel items and nine aluminum goods for which the supply in Canada is either insufficient or unavailable.

They agreed to open market access for Canadian fava beans, chickpeas and lentils to China, and would work toward an agreement on pet food and wild aquatic products by the end of the year.

Canada has had “fairly severe restrictions on Chinese steel imports,” said McMaster University economist Colin Mang.

These restrictions have tightened since 2024, when the Canadian Steel Producers Association and the Aluminum Association of Canada warned of “dumping” of cheap Chinese products.

“The national government in China gives the industry cheap loans, cheap energy in order to subsidize production. And that’s always been the big concern,” Mang said.

Chinese steel products can have “artificially low” prices because of the supports provided by Beijing, said Blair Dickerson, president and CEO of the Canadian Steel Producers Association.

“ Canadian steel producers want to compete on a level playing field. We’ll compete with the best as long as it’s fairly priced,” she said.

The current deal, however, includes a “very technical” and “niche” set of products like construction rebar wire made out of stainless steel, she said.

“This is a really specific and a narrow amount of volume that we’re talking about,” Dickerson said.

The biggest beneficiary could be Canada’s construction sector, Mang said, since the deal involves allowing access to Chinese goods that Canada doesn’t make itself.

“One of the biggest things is long beams. Canada stopped making long beams in the early 1990s, shortly after the (North American) free trade agreement,” he said.

Canada’s biggest source of foreign steel by far is the United States, which accounts to 36.2 per cent of its steel imports, followed by South Korea (9.9 per cent) and China (5.9 per cent), according to the U.S International Trade Administration.

Most of Canada’s steel imports from China include long products, such as rebar and beams, followed by pipes, tubes and stainless-steel products.

While Canada is a major aluminum producer, with Quebec alone accounting for 60 per cent of North America’s supply, Canada still relies on imports for certain finished goods.

The beer industry’s supply chain and market are largely domestic — with Canadian grain being used to make beer for Canadian consumers — but it needs U.S. aluminum processing industry for packaging.

According to Beer Canada, around 80 per cent of Canada’s beer is packaged in aluminum cans, mostly made in the U.S.

“The United States and China, because there’s such large consumer markets, they have a scale advantage in manufacturing some consumer goods, like aluminum cans,” Mag said.

A deepening trade relationship between Ottawa and Beijing could make Chinese-made cans more competitive against American-made ones, Mang said.

“If you’re eliminating tariffs on Chinese made aluminum products, that makes them more competitive against American aluminum products,” he said.

This is part of Carney’s diversification strategy, Mang said, as Canada’s steel and aluminum industry still faces a 25 per cent tariff from U.S. President Donald Trump.

–with files from Canadian Press

stories.title: Owen Sound homicide victim identified, suspect charged with second-degree murder
stories.summary: Owen Sound police continue to investigate a homicide that left a 36 year old dead, and a 30 year old charged with second-degree murder
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Owen Sound police have provided an update to a homicide investigation from last week .

Police say officers attended an apartment vestibule around 2:45 a.m. Nov. 13 in the 700 block of 2 nd Avenue East, in response to a violent altercation.

The victim, 36-year-old Nebojsa Malinovic, of Owen Sound, was transported to hospital where he was pronounced dead.

Sheldon Cutting, 30, of Owen Sound, has been charged with second-degree murder.

Cutting was arrested without incident by Owen Sound Police Service officers in the area of 7 th Street East and 9 th Avenue East later that day.

He remains in custody and is next scheduled to appear in court by video later this month.

The accused and the victim were known to each other, according to police.

The investigation remains ongoing and anyone with information is encouraged to contact Owen Sound police.

stories.title: Mistrial declared in trial of former Saskatoon massage therapist
stories.summary: The courtroom filed with gasps and tears after hearing the declaration of a mistrial completely halting the jury trial for former massage therapist, 70, Kenneth Braun.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
A Saskatoon King’s Bench courtroom filled with gasps and tears Tuesday, as Justice Daryl Labach declared a mistrial in the sexual assault trial of former massage therapist Kenneth Braun.

Defence counsel applied for a mistrial over crown counsel overstepping in the questioning of Braun and potentially put forward inadmissible evidence in front of the jury.

Braun is still facing three charges of sexual assault and one count of sexual exploitation of a minor. How those charges will be dealt with following Labach’s decision is yet to be determined.

Part of the submission included putting forward the option to remove the jury, shifting to a judge alone trial. Crown prosecutor Lana Morelli declined the option and offered to instead give a direction to the jury to not take into consideration the evidence raised.

“It had started with the jury and should end with the jury,” said Morelli.

“We believe it took an extraordinary amount of courage for all of these complainants to come forward, to testify, and to give their stories of what happened. We support the justice system, which include these complainants that have waited several years if not longer to say their stories.”

Morelli also pointed to the difficulties of arguing this case in a singular trial with multiple proceedings and multiple complainants.

“The fact that we are where we are is not a result of forethought, it is not a result that the Crown was trying to put forward inadmissible evidence, it was simply an error,” said Morelli.

Morelli says how the trial will move forward will depend on whether or not the defence will elect for a jury trial, and what the Crown can do with the evidence already brought forward.

Defence lawyer Pfefferle was also remorseful for what this might mean for the victims of the case possibly having to testify again. He also addressed the complexity of the case.

“This was a big issue about perception and so for that reason it was a complicated response that the accused had to give in order to toe the line and as a result of that that’s really what put us in this in this situation. So, it’s an unfortunate result but one that we believed in and as I say for that reason, we’re glad that we’re granted it,” said Pfefferle.

Pfefferle also said there is a good chance the charges May be dropped completely.

“ We have a court system that is absolutely bursting at the seams with judges sitting on holidays, over weekends,” said Pfefferle. “ With the burden on the court system, one of the real concerns here is can we get to a trial fast enough to be reasonable and deal with the constitutional principle that an accused has a right to a trial within a reasonable period of time .”

Morelli disagrees, saying there are other options still available. Morelli says how the trial will move forward will depend on whether or not the defence will elect for a jury trial and what the Crown can do with the evidence has already been brought forward.

The case will go before pre-trial proceedings in the next few weeks.

stories.title: Nova Scotia hosting three virtual information sessions on AI data centres this week
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government is hosting virtual information sessions this week to answer questions about AI data centres.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government is hosting virtual information sessions this week to answer questions about AI data centres.

The government made the announcement Tuesday morning, saying the first of three sessions would take place at 7 p.m. that same evening.

The sessions will be livestreamed on YouTube and Facebook.

A proposed $10-billion AI data centre in southern Cape Breton has been met with opposition from many residents and sparked protests across the province earlier this month.

Premier Tim Houston says the sessions will provide an opportunity for Nova Scotians to ask questions, and for experts to address misinformation about AI data centres.

Also on Tuesday, the government confirmed that it was randomly calling Nova Scotians to ask if they would like to pose a question during the live session.

The two other sessions have been scheduled for Wednesday night and Thursday afternoon.

stories.title: Cadet captain paralyzed from waist down after Hamilton attack
stories.summary: Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A cadet leader who underwent spinal surgery after a violent attack says he is currently paralyzed from the waist down and will require months of physical rehabilitation.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel provided an update on his situation last week in a statement shared online by a Hamilton member of Parliament.

Kunkel says he is in continual pain and his doctors cannot give him a prognosis at this time, but he remains “hopeful and positive.”

He thanked those who have reached out to express support or donated to an online fundraiser set up for his family.

Police have said the Nov. 8 attack stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies.

They said two youths approached young air cadets who were selling poppies in front of a restaurant on Barton Street East and blew an air horn “directly into their ears.”

Investigators said a man who was supervising the cadets followed the youths into the restaurant to confront them, leading to a struggle.

They allege a woman jumped in to help the youths and assaulted the air cadet leader, who fell to the ground. One of the boys allegedly hit the man multiple times.

A 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman were charged with aggravated assault in the incident.

In his statement, Kunkel said he wanted to clarify some details of what happened that day.

He said he confronted a youth in the restaurant about assaulting one of the cadets and told him they needed to go to the front and call police. The youth “immediately tried to run away,” Kunkel said, adding he grabbed the youth’s backpack and started walking toward the front of the restaurant while asking staff to call police.

The youth started punching him, he said, and a woman intervened on the youth’s behalf. Kunkel said he told her the boy had assaulted a cadet and they needed to speak with police.

While his attention was on the woman, the boy grabbed the lanyard holding Kunkel’s car key and ripped it off his neck, he said. When Kunkel reached to grab it back, the woman “blindsided” him, slamming him into a concrete pillar, he said.

“My legs buckled beneath me and I collapsed,” he said. “While I was lying on the ground helpless, the young male proceeded to violently punch me directly in the face numerous times.”

Kunkel was taken to hospital and underwent surgery that night, he said.

A GoFundMe page set up on behalf of Kunkel and his family said he is the commanding officer of 826 Gryphon Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets, and has been with the cadets for 20 years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.
