stories.title: Twenty years, 12 Zodiac records: Toronto punk band finishes one of music’s most-ambitious projects
stories.summary: The band that pushes punk boundaries shares the ups and down of a musical journey that took two decades to come full circle
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Perhaps the most enduring trait of the Toronto punk band Fucked Up, guitarist Mike Haliechuk says, is that whenever its members are faced with the question Are you really going to do this? – be it literally or rhetorically – the answer is always yes.

This is, after all, a band that has both expanded and pushed past the boundaries of punk music; has a history of semi-secret companion albums to major releases ; performed in concert for 12 hours straight ; has written and recorded an album in 24 hours while being live-streamed ; and has had members collaborate with multiple opera companies.

In 2006, its members accidentally began a project that would become their most ambitious, convoluted, genre-bending work. At some point in making a nine-minute-long single that year, drummer Jonah Falco recalls, a band member heard a radio announcer say that no one would ever make a song as good as the Stooges’ I Wanna Be Your Dog. In turn, the band decided to try and one-up it. Soon, too, one of them realized it was the Lunar New Year, and that they’d stepped into the Year of the Dog. It simply made sense to title the track Year of the Dog .

Haliechuk likes to turn limitations into structure. The band has long been placed in the box of hardcore punk – a genre it excels at, yet whose parameters it routinely circumvents. There are 12 signs in the Chinese Zodiac, which offered the band 11 more opportunities to try something new. The prospect of a standalone series, however rigidly themed, offered the band a specific kind of creative freedom.

On Nov. 13, almost exactly 20 years after Year of the Dog ’s release, Fucked Up released Year of the Rooster (Tankcrimes/FU Records) – the twelfth and final entry in its Zodiac series and a much different creature than Dog . Anchored in recent years by the relentless ambition of Haliechuk and Falco, the series has grown into a suite of ever-more-complicated, omni-genre rock operas stitched together as a massive work of immersive fiction.

Rooster is a double-LP concept album and the third part, along with Year of the Goat and Year of the Monkey , of a three-record epic called Grass Can Move Stones . It is both the apotheosis of the band’s quarter-century-long career and a commentary on it, following the life-changing journey of a goat and a monkey (voiced by guest Tuka Mohammed and frontman Damian Abraham, respectively) and featuring an extraordinary list of vocal collaborators from across punk, rock and underground music’s history, from Sonic Youth’s Thurston Moore and Black Flag co-founder Keith Morris to the Weather Station’s Tamara Lindeman and the National’s Matt Berninger.

The breadth of Zodiac is unique in popular music, if you’re inclined to slot punk into that categorization. It’s more than eight hours long with a maze of recurring characters and motifs. It fits more neatly into the world of actual operas than rock operas, yet runs nearly double the length of Richard Wagner’s Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg or Philip Glass and Robert Wilson’s Einstein on the Beach .

Though the snarling-but-charming, wrestler-embodying vocalist Abraham is the on-stage face of the band, the Zodiac series in particular has been Haliechuk’s primary creative outlet for the past 10 years. “The enduring thought I had while I was making these last three is that nothing like this has ever been done before,” he says.

The band has been active for about 25 years; its current and most consistent members are Haliechuk, Falco, Abraham, bassist Sandy Miranda and guitarist Josh Zucker. They won the Polaris Music Prize for 2008’s The Chemistry of Common Life , then spent the 2010s often skirting the more abrasive strictures of hardcore punk for brighter sounds – though Abraham’s harsh vocals been a consistent throughline. The 2011 concept album David Comes to Life won them fans across indie rock; 2014’s Glass Boys included a cameo by Gord Downie; 2018’s Dose Your Dreams embraced both groovy and industrial sounds.

It did not take long for the Zodiac project’s release schedule to fall out of step with the actual Zodiac calendar; if anything, the releases instead map the trajectory of the band’s growth. Year of the Dog , from 2006, is a lo-fi dirge with the contours of hardcore punk; 2007’s Year of the Pig , bearing segments that sounded like Pink Floyd, “made people sort of take our dalliances with experimentation kind of seriously,” Falco says; 2012’s Year of the Tiger sounds bright, sharp, almost ecstatic. In 2017’s Year of the Snake , the band took cues from ambient and noise music in segments stitched together with more traditional punk elements.

There are two distinct eras to the Zodiac series. They mirror the band’s own trajectory. Until about 2016, the band worked non-stop, focusing on Zodiac releases in between their more traditional albums and relentless tours. Then the band slowed down. Falco moved to London that year, and began working with Haliechuk in intense bursts on trips back to Toronto, shifting the band’s writing process from the practice room to the studio.

In 2015, he and Falco had worked with Toronto’s Tapestry Opera to develop a mini-opera with a libretto co-written with David James Brock, whom they befriended. A few years later, Haliechuk asked Brock to work on a concept-album story in the form of a screenplay. It followed a mythical horse named Perceval seeking a return to its home among the stars.

Year of the Horse , released in 2021, became the ninth entry in the series. Haliechuk savoured the writing process, taking years to flesh it out. To match the sprawling story, he and Falco also spend years working with their go-to recording engineer, Alex Gamble. They met regularly in recording studios to work out motifs, song segments and transitions, sometimes on a riff-by-riff basis.

Gamble is a prog-rock fan, and was enamoured to discover that his favourite band, Rush, was rehearsing for its unexpected reunion tour down the hall at Toronto’s Union Sound during later Zodiac sessions. Rush’s 1976 song suite 2112 was a masterwork of prog storytelling in spite of the limitations of analog recording technology. Fucked Up was trying something much more ambitious.

“Their presence in the studio was a reminder for me: You can keep going ,” Gamble says. With digital technology, “you’ve actually got it easy, and you have no excuse. So use whatever ingenuity you have; try things you haven’t tried before.”

This meant, as the band decided to double down on the rock opera of Horse with the final trilogy of Grass Can Move Stones , they embraced full maximalism, with dozens of characters and sonic tributes to the band’s own back catalogue. One side of the Year of the Monkey double LP includes 505 individual audio tracks.

The Zodiac series was recorded with vinyl as its listening medium, and Grass Can Move Stones moves across six vinyl sides. It’s loosely based on the 16th-century Chinese novel Journey to the West , believed to be authored by Wu Cheng’en, itself based on a Buddhist monk’s journey to find sacred texts in India. After 20 years developing a project based on one aspect of Chinese mythology, Haliechuk says framing the final pieces around Journey to the West was a way to more directly acknowledge the country’s mythological influence on his work.

Each Zodiac character and many others reappear as they prepare to take on the series’ antagonist, Jade Monkey, voiced by hardcore-punk torchbearer John Brannon of Negative Approach.

“I was conscious of wanting these last three records to be a commentary about the band, as well and about the trajectory of our career,” Haliechuk says. It’s a story about growth, of struggle, and about disagreements, but also victories – including that the band had reached a place in punk history where collaborating with the likes of Brannon and Morris was possible. “The records are about these mythological creatures, and we were able to fill them with mythological creatures from our own lives.”

They’ve also extended a hand to others in their community to be a part of their own history. “Their ambition and unwavering creative vision is not only unparalleled in the world of punk and hardcore – it’s downright intense,” says Graeme MacKinnon, vocalist of the Edmonton band Home Front, who plays the role of Young Prince Grin. Jennifer Castle, who makes appearances on 2007’s Pig and 2025’s Goat , is in admiration of how the band saw its vision through, no matter how much work it was: “They gave it the time it needed to come to completion. It takes time, and that is what 20 years teaches you.”

“There’s never been a a project in music that has had this scope, this much continuity, this much follow through,” Haliechuk says. “I just hope people will look back on it and be like, It’s crazy that somebody was able to do something like that . Because it is.”

stories.title: ‘Women are not punchlines’: London establishment removes controversial marquee sign
stories.summary: A London establishment has removed a marquee sign reading ‘Giddy up **uts’ after the wording sparked outrage from community members, a local advocate, and the father of a young woman killed in an intimate partner violence case.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London establishment has removed a marquee sign reading ‘Giddy up **uts’ after the wording sparked outrage from community members, a local advocate, and the father of a young woman killed in an intimate partner violence case.

The sign was posted outside Cowboys Ranch Saturday, prompting criticism over its language and the timing of the message, which appeared during November’s Shine the Light campaign, an annual initiative raising awareness about gender-based violence.

Brett Broadfoot, whose 17-year-old daughter Breanna was killed in a case of intimate partner violence, says he was distraught when he drove past the establishment Tuesday morning and saw the sign.

“I was just beside myself, to be quite honest with you. I could not and still cannot believe that somebody would put something of this up,” Broadfoot said.

“It just honestly boggles my mind, especially when we’re thinking about protecting survivors and victims in our communities. The month that we’re in is Shine the Light, which makes it even more disrespectful and unimaginable.”

Jennifer Dunn of the London Abused Women’s Centre says she received photographs of the sign Tuesday morning and was deeply upset by the messaging.

Women are not jokes,” Dunn said. She says the wording contributes to a culture in which women are routinely objectified and sexualized.

“I think it’s important to note that we live in a culture where misogyny is real and women are constantly objectified, sexualized, and this contributes to that, especially at a well-known establishment like that,” she said.

Dunn says the community has a responsibility to speak out against messages that objectify women and girls.

She adds the sign was particularly upsetting during Shine the Light month, when the focus is on supporting survivors and reminding women and girls, they should not carry shame or blame for what has happened to them.

London Mayor Josh Morgan also condemned the sign after being notified about it Tuesday morning. Morgan says he immediately contacted the city’s bylaw department to report the signage.

“This is a pretty clear one where common sense would tell you this is not a slogan that you should be putting up on a public building,” Morgan said.

“It’s inappropriate, it’s degrading.”

Just before noon Tuesday, the sign was removed from the establishment.

In a statement provided by an employee, the business said staff decided to incorporate the phrase into its signage after noticing it was trending online.

The employee said the intention was to be lighthearted and fit the venue’s ‘playful atmosphere’, not to offend or disrespect anyone.

“In hindsight, it is recognized that the wording was inappropriate and could understandably be offensive,” the statement read.

“We apologize to anyone who was offended. It was a poor judgment call, and certainly not a reflection of any intention to disrespect our community.”

The employee also confirmed the sign would be taken down once staff arrived at the establishment. It was subsequently removed shortly before noon Tuesday.

For Dunn, the incident is a reminder of the importance of challenging language that objectifies women, while Broadfoot says the message was particularly difficult to see during a month dedicated to raising awareness about violence against women.

stories.title: Response in helping victims of Lapu-Lapu attack ‘insufficient’: Filipino BC group
stories.summary: Vancouver — The group that organized the Lapu Lapu Day festival where 11 people were killed in a vehicle ramming wants British Columbia's auditor general to investigate the provincial government's management, funding and readiness for the tragedy, saying it was "insufficient."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Vancouver — The group that organized the Lapu Lapu Day festival where 11 people were killed in a vehicle-ramming attack wants British Columbia’s auditor general to investigate the province’s response to the tragedy, saying it was “insufficient.”

Kristina Corpin-Moser, executive director of Filipino BC, said the group was still providing benefits and counselling supports to survivors and she didn’t know of any other community group that’s been so heavily relied on to lead in such a crisis.

“Early action from a community organization does not mean the B.C. government could abandon its responsibility to manage and co-ordinate its own full-scale crisis response,” she told a news conference on Tuesday.

Filipino BC has asked the auditor to look at which part of the government was responsible for reacting, and how the system failed 100 or so victims of the attack in getting counselling, medical and income assistance.

The purpose is to understand whether public systems worked as intended and what changes would fill gaps in future emergency response, Corpin-Moser said.

A statement from the auditor general’s office said it had received the request from the group, but it doesn’t comment on the details of potential or ongoing audits.

Adam Kai-Ji Low pleaded not guilty this month to 11 counts of second-degree murder and 31 counts of attempted murder for allegedly driving an SUV through a crowd at the event. His B.C. Supreme Court trial is expected to start next spring.

Corpin-Moser said there was a large difference between the tens of millions of dollars in funding that followed the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, which left eight victims dead in the small community last February, and support supplied to the victims and the families of the Lapu Lapu Day attack in April 2025.

“I think now we’ve seen through the response in Tumbler Ridge, but also other mass casualty events that have occurred globally, that the response has been insufficient,” she said of the vehicle-ramming attack.

“We also feel that there are just some questions around which ministries are responsible and if they’ve met their responsibilities to the public and to victims and survivors.”

The group’s early requests for help from the Canadian Red Cross were denied by the province, which claimed the attack didn’t qualify for support because it was not a natural disaster, Corpin-Moser said.

She said there was a substantial difference in the response in Tumbler Ridge, including the deployment of the Red Cross and victim services, along with federal funding.

While the tragedies are distinct, Corpin-Moser said there are enough parallels to show the response to the Lapu Lapu attack wasn’t good enough.

Filipino BC received about $550,000 from the province. Corpin-Moser said the money was used to support the group’s staff, programs and the opening of its resilience centre, as well as direct payments to victims and survivors.

“I will say, though, that if community-based supports over five years is $40 million in the case of Tumbler Ridge, then $500,000 as a response seems wholly inadequate.”

She said Filipino BC made more than a dozen requests for funding and wrote numerous proposals at the behest of various ministries and members of the legislature in an effort to secure greater support.

“We even asked the provincial government just to meet with victims and survivors to hear what their experiences (have been) as we’re navigating these systems.

“And we rarely received a response,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘United we stand’: Doug Ford shares economic vision for Ontario-Quebec alliance in Montreal
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the best way forward for Canada’s two largest economies, against the backdrop of a trade war with the United States, is to work together. Speaking at the Chamber of Commerce of Metropolitan Montreal on Tuesday, Ford said a partnership between Quebec and Ontario is more important than ever. “Together, we’re […]
stories.author: Lola Kalder
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the best way forward for Canada’s two largest economies, against the backdrop of a trade war with the United States, is to work together.

Speaking at the Chamber of Commerce of Metropolitan Montreal on Tuesday, Ford said a partnership between Quebec and Ontario is more important than ever.

“Together, we’re an absolute powerhouse,” he said.

“Quebec and Ontario make up 61 per cent of Canada’s population and 58 per cent of our economy, with a combined GDP of more than $1.8 trillion. Our two provinces would be bringing the 17th largest economy in the entire world.”

Ford spoke to a crowd of about 1,000 people, with notable guests including former Quebec premier Jean Charest and Quebec Economic Development Minister Stéphane Paquet.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon could not attend as he is currently out of the country. The two premiers did meet earlier this month in Toronto.

“Quebec and Ontario, their economy is not only interlinked but they can also do a lot of things to help one another because as a matter of fact we are neighbours,” said political analyst Daniel Tran. “So a lot of businesses can also go and explore in Ontario and vice versa at the same time.”

A repeated target of Ford’s in his speech was U.S. President Donald Trump. The Ontario premier says Canada can no longer rely on the U.S. as it once did, making cooperation between provinces more important than ever.

“There’s two great things that President Trump did: he woke us up and he’s united us as a country like we’ve never been united before,” Ford said.

“United we stand, united we fall. We have to do things differently than we have in the past.”

Ford said Donald Trump’s administration has “taken aim” at Canadian workers and businesses, and he called for an end to internal trade barriers.

CityNews spoke to some Montrealers about Ford’s message.

“We are so much stronger as a country, as people, when we collaborate and it’s time we do it,” said Audrey Robichaud.

“We have some tariffs with the U.S. and everything, so I think to build a strong relationship with all the provinces would be good,” said Derek Roy.

“We should build a relationship with everybody in Canada,” added Sonia Perron. “Ontario is a great province. It’s our neighbour, so yes, it’s a good idea.”

But building that partnership could come with political challenges.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, who was also in attendance, says with the PQ government’s push for Quebec independence, questions remain about how that political divide could affect efforts to strengthen interprovincial trade and remove internal trade barriers.

“Premier Ford has been always a true federalist, a true and proud Canadian,” Milliard said. “And so obviously they’re going to encounter some obstacles and we’ll follow that along the way.”

“The priority from the different premiers to also lower the amount of red tape that you have to favour inter-provincial trade, especially in this context with the trade war,” added Tran. “It’s really important to be all hands on deck and really help businesses.”

stories.title: Liberals limit debate on assisted dying bill as Conservatives call for changes
stories.summary: Ottawa — As Opposition MPs call for more study, the Liberal government has limited debate on its proposed changes to Canada's medical assistance in dying law.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government’s bill proposing changes to Canada’s medical assistance in dying law will be studied by the House of Commons justice and human rights committee after it passed second reading Tuesday.

Members of Parliament voted 225 to 89 to send the bill to committee. Several Opposition MPs voted for the bill to move to committee, despite some raising concerns about the legislation.

The Liberal government on Monday limited debate on Bill C-41, which was introduced in the House of Commons on Oct. 27. Members of Parliament adopted a motion by Justice Minister Sean Fraser to limit debate at second reading to one more day, despite calls from the Opposition for more time to study the bill.

Debates at second reading took place on Oct. 30, Nov. 4 and Nov. 16.

The bill would amend the Criminal Code to allow people to make advance requests to access Maid. It also would prevent a scheduled expansion of Maid access to those suffering solely from a mental illness.

The bill needs to pass the House of Commons and the Senate before March 17 — the date on which the current law would extend Maid access to people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

Conservatives say they support the proposal to bar Maid access for those suffering solely from a mental illness. The party also urged the government to split the bill to give parliamentarians more time to study advance requests.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called on the government Tuesday to stop the expansion of Maid for mental illness and “prevent dangerous new experiments that could take the lives of vulnerable people who don’t want to die.”

“Instead of looking for more ways to end life, we should be looking for ways to help people live their fullest lives,” Poilievre said in a social media post.

Conservative MP Tamara Jansen said Monday it’s “absolutely shameful” that the government is shutting down debate on a bill that deals with life and death. She accused the Liberals of denying MPs the information they need to do their jobs.

“The Liberals had all summer, and now it has been nearly three weeks since Bill C-41 was introduced. We still have not seen the government’s own analysis of how this bill could affect Canadians’ charter rights, and yet they are already shutting down debate,” Jansen said Monday.

“Surely, if there was ever a bill that deserves careful scrutiny, this is it.”

Bloc Québécois MP Martin Champoux said in French that it’s disturbing to see the government “muzzle” the House of Commons and silence those who are “genuinely interested in having their say” on a “delicate and divisive” matter.

“I am at a loss for words to describe how I feel about the government employing this manoeuvre, especially on such a sensitive topic,” said Champoux.

“I understand that the government wants to move forward quickly, and I understand that it wants to avoid the possibility of ideological filibustering by the Conservatives, but a public conversation is called for. I think that the government is wrong to impose time allocation on this debate.”

Fraser said in reply that MPs have had “ample opportunity” for debate in Parliament and through a joint study by various parliamentary committees. He said that debate will continue during the committee study of the bill.

Fraser also said Parliament still faces a deadline of March 17 to get the bill passed. On that date, a temporary exclusion expires which currently prevents individuals from accessing Maid if their sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

“It is also not lost on me that we are dealing with a set of circumstances in which if we do not adopt this law expeditiously, we are going to come up against a mandated timeline that exists in the Criminal Code with another issue for which there is a greater consensus,” said Fraser.

The government has repeatedly pushed back the date when mental illness could become a qualifying factor for an assisted death, and asked a special parliamentary committee to study the issue. The committee concluded in June that people suffering solely from a mental illness should be excluded indefinitely from accessing Maid.

Under Canada’s current laws, a medically assisted death is available to individuals who are at least 18 years old, have a serious and incurable physical illness, disease or disability, and are in an advanced or irreversible state of decline. They also must be able to make a voluntary request and give informed consent for the procedure, including at the time it is administered.

An advance request would allow a person who suffers from a degenerative condition, such as dementia or ALS, to ask that an assisted death be carried out once they no longer have the capacity to consent.

The government said in a press release the decision to request Maid must be “voluntary, free from external pressure, and remain protected by rigorous safeguards.”

Bill C-41 would amend the Criminal Code to allow people to make advance requests for Maid. It would be up to provincial governments to decide whether to fulfil those requests through their own health systems, and to enact legislation.

Fraser told reporters last month he wasn’t certain how many provinces would do so. Quebec is the only province that already has an advance request regime in place. Alberta has passed legislation to bar the use of advance requests.

Fraser told reporters that while he’s somewhat concerned about the prospect of a patchwork of different rules across the country, he would be “more concerned about extending access without the safeguards in place, including the safeguards that must be legislated by provincial governments.”

The safeguards for advance requests included in the federal bill include a requirement that two independent medical or nurse practitioners agree the person meets the criteria.

The legislation also says the procedure will not be administered “if the person demonstrates, by words, sounds or gestures, refusal or resistance to have the substance administered to them.”

It says if the person demonstrates such refusal or resistance, “medical assistance in dying can no longer be provided to them on the basis of that request.”

Fraser said last month he wants to see the bill pass through the House of Commons before the parliamentary sitting ends in December.

Fraser said this would give “ample time for the Senate, where I know there are individuals who have unique perspectives on this issue, to raise their concern, to participate in debate, but ultimately pass this law before we face the potential consequence of the lapsing of the existing timeline.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

— With files from Anja Karadeglija

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada makes progress toward measles-free designation as U.S., Mexico status revoked
stories.summary: Toronto - International health officials say Canada has achieved an important milestone toward regaining its status as a measles-free country, as the United States loses its designation.

stories.content:
Toronto - As the United States loses its status as a measles-free country, international health officials say more cases south of the border will only make it harder for Canada to regain its status.

The Pan American Health Organization declared at a news conference Tuesday that the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia have lost their status after uninterrupted spread of the measles virus for 12 months or more.

Canada lost its status last November, which Paho called a “major setback” for the region, now marked by a “further deterioration” that reflects persistent concentrated vaccination gaps.

The U.S. has lost its measles-free status. The highly contagious virus has spread at the highest rate in over 30 years, mainly among the unvaccinated. (Nov. 17, 2026)

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world and can spread rampantly from one person to as many as 18 susceptible people. It often starts with common symptoms like a fever or cough before the telltale rash appears days later.

“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf. It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day,” Paho director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said.

Paho, the World Health Organization’s office for countries in North and South America, is responsible for granting and revoking measles-free status.

However, Barbosa said there is also some good news in the region. No new cases have been reported in the country in the last 60 days, he said.

“Canada has interrupted the transmission associated with the outbreak that resulted in the loss of its elimination status last year,” Barbosa said.

The Public Health Agency of Canada declared last month that a two-year measles outbreak that infected more than 6,400 people was officially over.

To get its elimination status back, Canada will need at least 12 months of no transmission.

Dr. Dawn Bowdish, a professor of medicine at McMaster University in Hamilton, said Canada’s progress is encouraging, “but we have to be on guard because we’re not out of the woods until we get those vaccination rates up above 95 per cent again.”

Measles requires 95 per cent vaccination coverage to obtain herd immunity. Data suggests vaccination rates for kids have fallen to about 80 per cent, depending on the area, Bowdish said.

“Reasonably, what we can expect is that there will be more cases entering the country. So either (from) Mexico, the U.S., or other parts of the world where measles circulates, and the concern is that with low vaccination rates, we May see these periodic outbreaks again, especially among vulnerable children,” Bowdish said.

The United States had held its measles elimination status since 2000.

Infectious disease experts have attributed the return of measles to declining vaccination rates, misinformation-fuelled vaccine hesitancy and distrust of authority, as well as disruptions to routine immunizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.title: National Congress of American Indians calls on Trump to reverse Lake Ontario change
stories.summary: The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The organization, which represents American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments in the United States, says the order demonstrates disrespect for Indigenous geographic names and Indigenous cultural, spiritual and historical relationships with lands and waters.

A resolution rejecting the name change, passed at the organization’s October assembly, was introduced by the Seneca Nation of Indians, a community based in Western New York.

Trump directed all arms of the federal government to start calling the body of water Lake America in August, to the dismay of Haudenosaunee communities on both sides of the border whose languages are the source of the name “Ontario.”

Lake Ontario is known in Seneca as “sga:nyodai:yoh,” meaning “beautiful lake,” and in Wendat as “ontari:io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The resolution says unilateral efforts to rename geography risk erasing Indigenous history and calls on the U.S. federal government to suspend its use of the term “Lake America.”

“The National Congress of American Indians opposes the removal, replacement, or erasure of Indigenous names of lakes, rivers, mountains, and other geographic features and calls upon federal, state, and local governments, geographic naming authorities, and public and private entities to preserve and respect those names in consultation with affected Tribal Nations,” it says.

“Lake Ontario is one example of the enduring Indigenous relationships with geographic features that this resolution seeks to protect, having been known to and used by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee peoples since time immemorial for travel, trade, diplomacy, subsistence, and cultural practices, and bearing a commonly used name derived from Indigenous linguistic roots.”

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard told The Canadian Press his nation was “shocked” to hear about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario. He called it an attempt to eradicate their history in the region.

The Wendat occupied parts of the St. Lawrence Valley up to the Great Lakes and the area was rich with both pre- and post-contact trade routes.

The name Lake Ontario predates the founding of both Canada and the United States.

Trump’s move was ridiculed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat. He posted a video of himself at a McDonalds restaurant, signing a fast food napkin to decree that Lake Michigan would now be called “Lake Wisconsin.”

“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the lake remains Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”

stories.title: This organization is calling on Donald Trump to reverse Lake Ontario name change
stories.summary: The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The organization, which represents American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments in the United States, says the order demonstrates disrespect for Indigenous geographic names and Indigenous cultural, spiritual and historical relationships with lands and waters.

A resolution rejecting the name change, passed at the organization’s October assembly, was introduced by the Seneca Nation of Indians, a community based in Western New York.

Trump directed all arms of the federal government to start calling the body of water Lake America in August, to the dismay of Haudenosaunee communities on both sides of the border whose languages are the source of the name “Ontario.”

Lake Ontario is known in Seneca as “sga:nyodai:yoh,” meaning “beautiful lake,” and in Wendat as “ontari:io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The resolution says unilateral efforts to rename geography risk erasing Indigenous history and calls on the U.S. federal government to suspend its use of the term “Lake America.”

“The National Congress of American Indians opposes the removal, replacement, or erasure of Indigenous names of lakes, rivers, mountains, and other geographic features and calls upon federal, state, and local governments, geographic naming authorities, and public and private entities to preserve and respect those names in consultation with affected Tribal Nations,” it says.

“Lake Ontario is one example of the enduring Indigenous relationships with geographic features that this resolution seeks to protect, having been known to and used by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee peoples since time immemorial for travel, trade, diplomacy, subsistence, and cultural practices, and bearing a commonly used name derived from Indigenous linguistic roots.”

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard told The Canadian Press his nation was “shocked” to hear about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario. He called it an attempt to eradicate their history in the region.

The Wendat occupied parts of the St. Lawrence Valley up to the Great Lakes and the area was rich with both pre- and post-contact trade routes.

The name Lake Ontario predates the founding of both Canada and the United States.

Trump’s move was ridiculed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat. He posted a video of himself at a McDonalds restaurant, signing a fast food napkin to decree that Lake Michigan would now be called “Lake Wisconsin.”

“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the lake remains Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the lake remains Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”

stories.title: Toronto sees another stretch of warm weather with temperatures in mid-teens
stories.summary: Environment Canada is forecasting clear and sunny weather and temperatures hitting 13 degrees on Tuesday. The average high for Nov. 17 historically has been 7.8 degrees.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted November 17, 2026 12:54 pm

Toronto and the surrounding areas are getting another stretch of unusually warm weather in the middle of fall.

Environment Canada is forecasting clear and sunny weather and temperatures hitting 13 degrees on Tuesday in Toronto.

The agency says temperatures will hit a high of 14 degrees on Wednesday, 13 degrees on Thursday and 14 degrees on Friday.

The average high for Toronto on Nov. 17 historically has been 7.8 degrees.

The Weather Network says current warm and dry conditions are forecast to dominate across Ontario over the next several days.

The network says mild air is being pulled form the south due to an upper-level troughing pattern over the Western half of North America, triggering the development of a strong ridge over the east.

It says temperatures will likely reach the mid-teens across southwestern Ontario into next weekend.

The network says it can’t rule out temperatures approaching the 20-degree mark over the next 10 days in some areas of the region.

stories.title: Ontario secondary teachers vote 96% in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: The vote by teachers represented by the Ontario Secondary School Teachers' Federation comes before central bargaining has fully started, with negotiations beginning next week.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
A second public high school union now has a strong strike mandate, raising the risk that the Ford government could be facing widespread teacher walkouts across the province if contract negotiations are not ironed out.

The Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation (Osstf) announced Tuesday that the public high school teachers it represents have voted 96 per cent in favour of giving their union a strike mandate if necessary.

Those results come one day after Ontario Catholic teachers voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate, with 98 per cent voting yes.

“(Teachers) working in publicly funded high schools are sending a clear message to this minister that they cannot continue to do more with less,” said Osstf president Martha Hradowy.

Osstf’s education worker members also voted 92 per cent in favour of a strike mandate. The vote comes before central bargaining has fully started, with negotiations beginning next week.

“Our members have given us a clear mandate that they want investments in public education. They want supports for their students, and quite frankly, they want respect restored to the teaching and education profession. And that’s what we’re going to get to the table,” she told reporters Tuesday.

1:47 Ontario Catholic teachers deliver strong strike mandate

A strike mandate does not mean a strike will happen, with additional legal steps required before one could take place.

Hradowy said teachers have been pushed to the brink in their profession due to the Ford government under-funding education.

She said teachers across the province have been concerned about ballooning class sizes, less support for students and less respect for educators as the system is buckling due to staff shortages.

“Ontario parents are having to keep their children at home because there isn’t enough support for their child in classrooms, and that is not unique,” she said.

Cuts to staffing for educational assistance, speech language pathologists, professional supports and social workers, she said, have left teachers responsible for dealing with complex student needs without assistance and vulnerable to workplace violence.

“We should not be going to the bargaining table, just asking for the basics in public education,” Hradowy said.

Ontario teachers have been left with no contract since August. Bargaining has been delayed as the government and major education unions were at an impasse on what issues should be negotiated centrally and what should be left to local unions and boards.

Osstf and the other education unions have said they encouraged the government to begin negotiations early in the spring, but they were ignored.

Education Minister Paul Calandra said the recent union votes are not unusual to the bargaining process and it’s an indication that members are urging the unions and the government to negotiate a fair agreement.

“These numbers aren’t surprising or shocking to me. I mean, you go back over 30 years, the numbers remain consistent no matter who’s in office,” he said.

He said it’s the unions who took their disputes to the Ontario Labour Relations Board, while the government has been “open” for negotiations.

The government can’t “give them anything that they want,” he said. “I have to balance taxpayers.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Calandra is wrong to view the strike mandate vote results as an indication of support for his ministry.

“It’s saying very clearly that this minister has failed,” she said. “All you have to do is listen to a parent, a student, any education worker right now and they will tell you firsthand that this is unsustainable.”

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ford government moves to shield itself from lawsuits related to Osap fraud probe
stories.summary: Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s minister of colleges and universities sidestepped questions in the legislature Tuesday about the government looking to grant itself legal immunity.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Facing mounting pressure over a growing private career college loan scandal, the Ford government is moving to shield itself from lawsuits tied to its decision to freeze student funding over fraud allegations.

The province has introduced an indemnity clause, folded into Bill 148, to modify existing career college legislation.

If passed, the new legislation will completely eliminate the right to sue the Ontario government including its ministers and other officials, for financial damages, negligence or other civil claims stemming from any specific regulations the Ford government passes.

“We’re holding these institutions accountable,” said Nolan Quinn, the colleges and universities minister, in the legislature Tuesday. “These are very serious criminal allegations and that is why we had to put a (Ontario Student Assistance Program) pause because one dollar going out towards fraudulent use is one dollar too many,” he said.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles fired back, stating that Quinn “didn’t do his job.”

“Now they’re trying to pass legislation to protect themselves from lawsuits. And it’s retroactive, so shame on you,” she said.

“To all of the students and the families that are watching this today, let me tell you this government cares more about protecting themselves in court over a mess that they made, than they do about your future,” she said.

2:02 Online petitions ask Ontario to restore Osap for private college students

The Ford government is currently cracking down on private career colleges over alleged student loan fraud. In October, the government implemented a sweeping student loan freeze across all 242 private career colleges as it said it was investigating “serious concerns” raised by the federal government, advocacy groups and internal audits and inspections.

The province has said it’s examining allegations of third parties completing student coursework within minutes, thousands of Osap applications submitted from the same IP addresses and students who could not identify their school, program or courses.

The government has also introduced legislation that will cap Osap growth at private career colleges, limit Osap funding to in-person and hybrid programs at those institutions and require them to have a physical location, and prohibit them from operating unrelated businesses on campus.

But the blanket Osap freeze that remains in place has meant many students are now struggling to pay for rent, food and childcare costs. Many report having to drop out of their programs.

The indemnity clause would specifically bar anyone from suing the province for financial damages resulting from fraud investigations, school registration revocations or any decisions on the student Training Completion Assurance Fund, which is a provincial program that protects students enrolled in registered private career colleges if their institution closes unexpectedly.

Several career colleges have said they are now in a financial freefall and are having to lay off staff for the first time due to the Osap freeze.

Interim Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser called the proposed indemnity legislation “window dressing.”

“This government is always doing something to protect itself rather than protect Ontarians. They’re covering their asses,” he told reporters Tuesday.

“If you can take money away from people that you’ve committed to, like they did with all these students, all these moms and dads, then you can do what they’re doing in that bill with the same powers that you have,” he said.

“They just need to come clean.”

In a statement to Global News, Quinn’s office said “through our legislation, we are strengthening accountability to ensure anyone who intends to abuse our Osap system for personal gain is held to the full extent of the law.”

“With this legislation, our government would better protect Osap from misuse, enforce stronger penalties against wrongdoers, and stop bad actors in their tracks. We will pursue all avenues to return fraudulently used funding to the taxpayers,” said Bianca Giacoboni, Quinn’s press secretary.

stories.title: N.B. commits $200K to support relatives caring for children unable to live with parents
stories.summary: The program, which is in partnership with the New Brunswick Adoption Foundation, help kinship caregivers create more stability and permanency for children and youth.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The New Brunswick government is committing $200,000 for a three-year pilot project that supports relatives and caregivers who step forward when children can’t live with their parents.

The program, which is in partnership with the New Brunswick Adoption Foundation , helps kinship caregivers provide greater stability and permanency for children and youth.

“Kinship caregivers provide stability, family connections and a sense of belonging when children and youth cannot remain with their parents,” the province said in a Tuesday release.

“The new program will help caregivers navigate the challenges of their role and get support from others with similar experiences.”

The pilot, which runs until Oct. 31, 2029, will provide monthly support groups, webinars and resources to discuss subjects such as trauma and complex needs.

“We have spent years building a network of support for families across New Brunswick, grounded in lived experience and strengthened through peer connections, support groups, education, resources and opportunities to build community,” said Suzanne Kingston, executive director of the New Brunswick Adoption Foundation, in the release.

“Kinship caregivers were already finding their way to us before this pilot began. This pilot allows us to build on those existing foundations, with dedicated staff and programming that recognize and respond to the unique experiences and needs of kinship families.”

stories.title: Gaming should be ‘top priority’ for new digital safety regulator, advocacy group says
stories.summary: Ottawa — Advocacy group Children First Canada said Tuesday the Liberal government’s proposed digital safety bill should eventually cover gaming platforms.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A children’s advocacy group said Tuesday it wants the government’s proposed digital safety bill to eventually cover gaming platforms.

Children First Canada founder Sara Austin said young people face grave harms on platforms like Roblox and Minecraft and argued the digital safety bill’s planned new regulator should address gaming platforms.

“There are provisions in the bill that would allow the digital commissioner to make sure that these are addressed as soon as the bill is passed, and to be making sure that this is a top priority,” Austin said.

‘This is an area in particular where young people are highly vulnerable.”

Children First Canada held a press conference on Parliament Hill Tuesday as the House heritage committee prepared to begin its study of the bill.

Bill C-34 imposes a duty to act responsibly on the companies behind social media platforms and AI chatbots. It also would force social media platforms to block access for kids under 16, though platforms will be able to obtain an exemption if they put sufficient safeguards in place.

Culture Minister Marc Miller told The Canadian Press last month there is growing concern about the social media-like aspects of online gaming.

“The compliance of those platforms is of concern to me. So that is an area where I think probably the committee will lean into,” Miller said.

Miller was asked whether the government would be open to bringing gaming under the legislation’s scope.

“ I wouldn’t say entirely,” he replied. “But I think to the extent that there are features of gaming … I think they have to be very vigilant in the way they are interacting with children and allowing adults and particularly predators to interact with kids.”

He said there are “some awful things happening in certain platforms that we need to make sure that they’re compliant with the regime.”

The House of Commons heritage committee heard from a number of witnesses Tuesday, including the Canadian Constitution Foundation, Kids Help Phone and advocate Carol Todd.

Todd’s daughter Amanda died by suicide after being targeted for online sextortion more than a decade ago.

In her opening statement, Todd praised the bill for not putting the burden on children or parents, but instead placing “responsibility where it belongs — on the companies creating and profiting from these products.”

“Families, advocates, and survivors have waited a long time for protections that reflect the realities of today’s digital world,” Todd said.

“Children’s safety must come before corporate profits and platforms must be held accountable. Stronger and safer design features must be put in place so that there are better protections in place that will save lives.”

Robyn Young, whose daughter Jorja died by suicide in April, took part in the Children First Canada press conference virtually.

Young said her daughter was a victim of online exploitation on multiple social media platforms, and found herself involved in online communities focusing on self-harm and eating disorders “where members encouraged these behaviours.”

“As a mother who’s had to bury my child, my question to you members of Parliament is, how many more children have to die before you pass Bill C-34?” she said.

Young said she is not looking for a ban on social media.

“Let’s face it, children will always find a way. What I’m asking for is that these platforms be held accountable for their content and the addictive algorithms,” Young said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Buyer pauses search to sell own home, then lands condo at lower price
stories.summary: MIMICO
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
30 Shore Breeze Dr., No. 2418, Toronto

Asking price: $799,000 (September 2026)

Previous asking prices: $819,900 (April 2026); $859,900 (March 2026); $879,900 (February 2026); $899,900 (July 2025)*under previous agent

Selling price: $791,800 (October 2026)

Previous selling prices: $950,000 (March 2022); $817,00 (October 2020); $431,392 (June 2020)

Taxes: $3,665 (2025)

Days on the market: 30

Property days on market: 361

Buyers’ agent: Nutan Brown, Royal LePage Terrequity Realty

Agent Nutan Brown guided her client through several two-bedroom and two-bathroom condos around the Etobicoke waterfront and Bloor West Village this spring. Her client paused their search to sell their home, and once accomplished, resumed shopping with a clear-cut budget in the fall. This corner unit looked better than the first time they saw it at Eau du Soleil, across from Humber Bay Park, especially since its price had been reset below $800,000.

“[The buyer] had a very saleable home, but you just don’t know what you’ll get and how it’ll play out,” said the buyer’s agent Nutan Brown.

“This was one of the units on our mind, but we could not proceed at the time. When we returned to it, the price had changed, and it was still available.”

The buyer was ultimately won over by the property’s unobstructed views through floor-to-ceiling windows and a 300-square-foot wraparound balcony. They negotiated a purchase before Thanksgiving at a price $158,200 below what the owner paid at the height of the market in 2022.

“It’s a corner unit with south and west exposures, lots of windows and three walkouts to the balcony,” Ms. Brown said.

“The wow factor was that it has a panoramic, waterfront view of the lake.”

This roughly six-year-old unit has nine-foot ceilings, new hardwood flooring and sliding balcony doors in the bedrooms and living room.

There are two full bathrooms, and a kitchen with quartz countertops and stainless-steel appliances.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $750 cover heating and concierge. Residents also have access to a car wash bay, fitness centre and saltwater pool.

“The amenities were amazing in this building,” said Ms. Brown.

“The amenities of the neighbourhood, like restaurants, shops and services, have grown leaps and bounds.

“Everything is available within walking distance.”

stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:

stories.title: Price cuts on King West condo finally draw in buyer
stories.summary: Fashion district
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
478 King St. W., No. 606, Toronto

Asking price: $799,000 (August 2026)

Previous asking prices: $849,900 (July 2026); $879,900 (June 2026); $899,900 (March 2026); $949,900 (January 2026)

Selling price: $740,000 (October 2026)

Previous selling prices: $580,000 (October 2014); $461,333 (August 2012)

Taxes: $4,562 (2025)

Days on the market: 41

Property days on market: 247

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

This two-bedroom unit has 920 square feet of living space, which made it larger than most models up for sale this January at Victory, a 14-year-old building on King Street West near Spadina Avenue. Its long-time owner was in no rush to sell and hoped the extra space would justify their asking price of $949,900.

“At the time, we hadn’t seen any two-bedroom units this size selling in the building, and the majority of the turnover had been smaller, one-bedroom suites,” said agent Christopher Bibby.

“We thought we’d go out and test the market.”

To stand out amid the glut of condos for sale nearby, the price tag was gradually trimmed back $20,000 to $50,000 every month or two. When the asking price sank under $800,000, a past visitor purchased the unit for $740,000.

“As we made reductions, the frequency of showings picked up,” Mr. Bibby said.

“The pricing in that pocket has suffered, from Blue Jays Way to Spadina, especially one- and two-bedroom units.”

The unit has a kitchen with an island, and a living room with access to a south-facing balcony.

There are two full bathrooms and laundry machines, as well as a storage area converted from an original den.

The unit has two storage lockers and tandem parking for two cars. Heating and water are covered by monthly fees of $863, along with concierge services and use of recreational amenities.

“This would have appeal to buyers or couples,” Mr. Bibby said. “Having a second bedroom is perfect for a home office, nursery or guest room.

“Overlooking King Street was a little more picturesque, and from the balcony there’s a sliver to see the CN Tower off in the distance.”

stories.title: Are Gen Z Canadians the new snowbirds? New data reveals U.S. travel plans
stories.summary: Political tensions have kept many Canadians from travelling to the U.S. during the winter, but as months go by some May be returning.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
It’s almost snowbird season and a new survey shows a growing number of Gen Z say they plan to head to the U.S. this winter, while the traditional baby boomer snowbirds are still holding back.

The Travel Health Insurance Association of Canada’s Winter Smart Traveller Survey found 52 per cent of Gen Z Canadians, those generally born between 1997 and 2012, plan to visit the U.S. this winter. It’s an increase from 44 per cent last year.

By comparison just eight per cent of baby boomers, those born from 1946 to 1964, say they plan to do the same. The small number is a decrease from 10 per cent last year, but a big drop from the 31 per cent seen in 2024 before the U.S. trade war and threats by the U.S. administration to Canada’s sovereignty.

“I think we can take a look at it and think about the ease of access and also cost,” said Will McAleer, spokesperson for the Thia. “The easier it is to get someplace, typically the cheaper it’s going to be. So for the younger groups, hey, maybe it’s getting in a car and doing a road trip.”

By comparison, he said boomers are choosing further distances like Europe, Mexico or the Caribbean because they can afford air travel and May be able to spend much longer than a single week away.

The survey showed of Canadians going away this winter, about half of Gen Z travellers plan to take a week-long trip, while only six per cent of boomers plan a similar length. Yet 27 per cent of boomers who do plan a winter trip say they are planning one that lasts more than a week but less than a month.

Travel to the U.S. has shown a slight rebound in recent months after seeing consistent declines after President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025.

Data from Statistics Canada showed Canadians took 1.9 million trips to the U.S. by automobile and air in October 2026, up three per cent from the same time last year. Road trips were up by 2.2 per cent from the same period, while air travel rose by 5.6 per cent.

It was the seventh consecutive month of increasing travel to the U.S., but road travel was still down 29 per cent compared to 2024 and air travel down by 19 per cent.

Even with an increase, political tensions are still on Canadians’ minds.

The Thia survey showed 37 per cent said those tensions remain a top barrier for travelling outside their home province, followed by financial concerns and rising airfare.

Of the 1,527 Canadians surveyed, 65 per cent said they were unlikely to travel to the U.S. during winter this year compared to the 72 per cent who said the same last year.

“Whether it’s the news of large manufacturing losses, particularly heading south, and the government has been quite active on those files, that’s obviously a large concern,” McAveer said.

“I think you throw in the fact that there are initiatives south of the border that are focusing on immigration and anti-immigration, not feeling like you want to get mixed up in that can be a part of the decision-making process for Canadians this winter.”

A common place for snowbirds, Florida, recently saw voters approve a major cut in property taxes for permanent residents but Canadians who own property could be stuck with the bill. They could also see the assessed value on their property increase up to five per cent a year.

The U.S. May still be a choice destination for Canadians who are deciding to travel, having reclaimed the top spot for primary winter destinations at 15 per cent. Travel within Canada sits at 14 per cent, with the Caribbean at 10 per cent.

content_blocks.text: The Travel Health Insurance Association of Canada’s Winter Smart Traveller Survey found 52 per cent of Gen Z Canadians, those generally born between 1997 and 2012, plan to visit the U.S. this winter. It’s an increase from 44 per cent last year.

By comparison just eight per cent of baby boomers, those born from 1946 to 1964, say they plan to do the same. The small number is a decrease from 10 per cent last year, but a big drop from the 31 per cent seen in 2024 before the U.S. trade war and threats by the U.S. administration to Canada’s sovereignty.

“I think we can take a look at it and think about the ease of access and also cost,” said Will McAleer, spokesperson for the Thia. “The easier it is to get someplace, typically the cheaper it’s going to be. So for the younger groups, hey, maybe it’s getting in a car and doing a road trip.”
By comparison, he said boomers are choosing further distances like Europe, Mexico or the Caribbean because they can afford air travel and May be able to spend much longer than a single week away.

The survey showed of Canadians going away this winter, about half of Gen Z travellers plan to take a week-long trip, while only six per cent of boomers plan a similar length. Yet 27 per cent of boomers who do plan a winter trip say they are planning one that lasts more than a week but less than a month.
Travel to the U.S. has shown a slight rebound in recent months after seeing consistent declines after President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Tourism industry still positive despite U.S. warning to travellers'

content_blocks.text: Data from Statistics Canada showed Canadians took 1.9 million trips to the U.S. by automobile and air in October 2026, up three per cent from the same time last year. Road trips were up by 2.2 per cent from the same period, while air travel rose by 5.6 per cent.
It was the seventh consecutive month of increasing travel to the U.S., but road travel was still down 29 per cent compared to 2024 and air travel down by 19 per cent.
Even with an increase, political tensions are still on Canadians’ minds.
The Thia survey showed 37 per cent said those tensions remain a top barrier for travelling outside their home province, followed by financial concerns and rising airfare.
Of the 1,527 Canadians surveyed, 65 per cent said they were unlikely to travel to the U.S. during winter this year compared to the 72 per cent who said the same last year.
“Whether it’s the news of large manufacturing losses, particularly heading south, and the government has been quite active on those files, that’s obviously a large concern,” McAveer said.

“I think you throw in the fact that there are initiatives south of the border that are focusing on immigration and anti-immigration, not feeling like you want to get mixed up in that can be a part of the decision-making process for Canadians this winter.”

A common place for snowbirds, Florida, recently saw voters approve a major cut in property taxes for permanent residents but Canadians who own property could be stuck with the bill. They could also see the assessed value on their property increase up to five per cent a year.

The U.S. May still be a choice destination for Canadians who are deciding to travel, having reclaimed the top spot for primary winter destinations at 15 per cent. Travel within Canada sits at 14 per cent, with the Caribbean at 10 per cent.

stories.title: Ontario secondary teachers vote 96 per cent in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario public high school teachers have voted 96 per cent in favour of giving their union a strike mandate.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The vote by teachers represented by the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation comes before central bargaining has fully started, with negotiations beginning next week.

Teachers across the province have been without a contract since August, but the start of substantive bargaining has been delayed as the government and major education unions could not agree on what issues should be negotiated centrally, and which should be left to local unions and boards.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Osstf president Martha Hradowy says in a statement that its members have sent the government a message that they are united and are prepared to stand together for better working conditions.

A strike mandate does not mean a strike will happen, with additional legal steps required before one could take place.

Osstf’s education worker members voted 92 per cent in favour of a strike mandate.

The results come a day after English Catholic teachers voted 98 per cent in favour of a strike mandate. All of the major education unions have strike votes this month.

Education Minister Paul Calandra said after the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association vote results were made public Monday that he looks at the high number as teachers telling their union and government to get to the table and come to a fair agreement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: TTC ‘unwavering’ in creating safe workplace amid report of conduct probe into CEO
stories.summary: While the transit agency hasn’t directly confirmed a probe into Mandeep Lali, the TTC told Global News any allegations of misconduct are taken seriously.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The TTC says it’s “unwavering” in creating a safe workplace amid a report of a conduct investigation into its CEO.

While the transit agency hasn’t directly confirmed a probe into Mandeep Lali, the TTC told Global News any allegations of misconduct are taken seriously.

Toronto Today reported Nov. 13 that Lali, a former New York City transit executive, is being investigated by the TTC board of directors for his alleged treatment of subordinates.

Lali became TTC CEO in July 2025, replacing Rick Leary, who resigned over misconduct allegations that he denied.

“The TTC and its CEO are unwavering in their commitment to a safe, respectful and inclusive workplace, where all employees are valued, supported and treated with dignity. Our people are our greatest strength and central to everything we do. Any allegations that run contrary to that are taken seriously,” the agency told Global News.

“The CEO is directly accountable to the Board and there are strict policies and procedures governing the conduct of the CEO. The TTC and the CEO cannot comment on confidential personnel matters, especially those that May fall under the exclusive purview of the Board.”

ATU Local 113, the union representing TTC workers, told Global News it expects a thorough, fair and impartial investigation.

The TTC introduced a policy in January 2025 to address complaints about a CEO’s conduct following the allegations against Leary. That policy allows for an independent external probe.

“We hope that due process will be followed. The union has no further comments on the complaints while this investigation is ongoing,” the union said in a statement.

“We urge the TTC Board to act swiftly and to show transparency and accountability throughout this process.”

stories.title: Canada following Ukraine’s Starshield difficulties ‘very closely’: defence minister
stories.summary: Repeated restrictions on Ukraine's use of the Starshield system, run by Elon Musk's SpaceX company, have hampered its ability to intercept Russian attacks.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Ukraine’s struggles with the Starshield military satellite network show why Canada is pursuing its own sovereign low-Earth orbit satellite network, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Tuesday.

On his way into Nato headquarters in Brussels, where the Ukraine Defence Contact Group was meeting Tuesday, McGuinty said the federal government is following the issue “very closely.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said in recent days that repeated restrictions on his country’s use of the Starshield military satellite communications system, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, have undermined its ability to intercept Russian attacks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stressed on Tuesday that the US has the capacity to assist Ukraine in striking Russia's missile launchers and eliminating the threat. Instead, he said, the opposite is happening, and "unfortunately, the speed limit on Starshield in the temporarily occupied territories still remains in place." (Nov. 17, 2026)

Restrictions on Ukraine’s use of the satellite service have throttled the speeds at which its drones can operate to intercept incoming attacks.

The Liberal government has pledged billions of dollars to support a host of sovereign space capabilities — including money to build up Telesat’s low-Earth orbit Lightspeed network for future military communications.

When asked by reporters if Canada will bring up Ukraine’s access to Starshield with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, McGuinty said he expects Prime Minister Mark Carney will follow through.

“It’s an issue that we’re following very closely. You can imagine, of course, ON a continental basis with Norad, with integrated air-and-missile defence systems between Canada and the United States, this is something that we are following,” McGuinty said.

“It’s also one of the reasons why Canada is building its own domestic sovereign capabilities in this area. It’s something that I’m sure the prime minister will touch upon with the president in due course.”

A spokesperson for McGuinty clarified later on Tuesday that the minister was referring to President Zelenskyy, not Trump.

Zelenskyy has questioned whether the problems with Starshield are actually technical in nature and has said SpaceX appears to have imposed the restrictions. Moscow has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power grids.

Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte told reporters Tuesday that the “relevant parties are working very hard to make sure that as soon as possible things are back to normal” with Ukraine’s access to the satellite system.

Rutte said Tuesday’s discussions are about ensuring Ukraine has what it needs to get through the winter and stand strong in peace negotiations with Russia.

McGuinty told reporters in Brussels that, based on the reports he’s read, Russia’s negotiating position is “predictable” and unserious.

“I don’t think that that’s good-faith negotiation, but I’m not at the negotiating table,” McGuinty said.

Media reports have suggested Russia is demanding control of the Donbas region and a ban on Ukraine joining the Nato alliance in exchange for ending the war.

Russia’s terms reportedly would also have the defensive alliance withdraw to its 1997 borders by removing Nato troops from its easternmost European member countries.

Canada is currently leading a multinational brigade in Latvia, where it has some 2,000 troops stationed.

The Pentagon has urged Western supporters of Ukraine to focus their military aid on equipment for front-line combat, rather than support for Ukraine’s deep strikes into Russia.

U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby said deep strikes have “not been effective in driving an end to the war.”

The defence ministers of the United Kingdom and Germany pushed back against the suggestion that Ukraine should not strike deep into Russian territory — indicating a wide gulf between American and European views on how to end the war.

German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said criticizing strikes against strategic military targets in Russia is “quite a stupid thing.” He said the focus should be instead on Russia’s “terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heating infrastructure in Ukraine.”

Tuesday’s meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, an alliance of more than 50 countries, was called by the U.K. and Germany.

A meeting of some three dozen countries that support Ukraine, known as the coalition of the willing, is set for Berlin on Thursday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press
