stories.title: Ottawa’s spending up $331.6 billion under Carney, budget watchdog says
stories.summary: Ottawa — The parliamentary budget officer is questioning the federal government's vow to spend less and invest more.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal budget watchdog wants parliamentarians to look beyond the size of the deficit when scrutinizing the Liberal government’s spending plans.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan released a series of reports on Tuesday analyzing the federal budget tabled Nov. 5, and the broader shift in public finances under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“The government promised to spend less to invest more. This budget spends more, invests more and borrows more,” Ryan said in a media statement on Tuesday.

The PBO projects the cost of federal measures is $331.6 billion higher in the three spending plans tabled so far under Carney.

The PBO also said the Liberal government’s overall fiscal situation is a bit rosier than the forecast in Ottawa’s last spending update in April.

Improved revenues from better-than-expected economic results and a tailwind of tax dollars from higher global oil prices have improved the government’s bottom line since the spring.

But Ryan said Ottawa has used up 96 per cent of that new fiscal room through fresh spending commitments, instead of meaningfully reducing the deficit.

“Confident countries invest,” Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told the Senate’s national finance committee on Tuesday, when questioned about the decision to spend rather than pay down debt.

“We’re one of the very few countries in the G7 who can afford to do that, which is investing in the growth, but at the same time supporting Canadians at the time of need … with affordability measures.”

The PBO report projects that total borrowing outlined in Budget 2026 is expected to reach $765 billion over five years — $476 billion more than the cumulative deficit of $289 billion.

Total borrowing includes loans to Crown corporations and the purchase of assets — much of that debt does not appear directly on Ottawa’s balance sheets. Capital investments like military equipment are considered assets and show up in the deficit over time as they depreciate, even though they’re paid for upfront.

The government will have to find that $765 billion whether it adds to the deficit or not — and the PBO notes that the recent Bank of Canada interest rate hike is set to increase borrowing costs for Canadians and governments alike.

Public debt costs now account for the fastest-growing line item on a year-over-year basis in the federal budget, Ryan noted during an appearance at the House of Commons’ finance committee on Tuesday. Those costs are expected to grow larger than the cost of federal health transfers to provinces in the years to come.

The PBO report confirms what the Conservatives and other critics have been saying about the Liberals’ handling of the public purse, Conservative finance critic Michael Chong argued Tuesday.

“That the government is not on a fiscally sustainable track, that the debt is growing at ever-increasing rates, and that the interest on the national debt is now consuming much more than the federal government spends on public health care,” the MP told reporters.

The PBO also noted that loans, advances and investments for Crown corporations are presented as a single line item in the budget, making it difficult to determine what sort of risks the government is taking on.

John Fragos, Champagne’s spokesperson, said instances in the budget of the government borrowing beyond its means are focused solely on generating future growth and setting the stage for greater investments in Canada.

The fact that Canada’s economy is still growing despite a trade dispute with the United States, and while foreign direct investment is rising, shows markets and the global investment community are backing Canada’s approach, he argued.

Ryan told MPs on the committee Tuesday that taking on debt to pay for spending today means paying the bill in the future.

Some of those borrowing costs are paid back through interest on loaned money or returns on investments. But loans can go bad and projects might flounder, so those returns are not guaranteed.

“Investments now in things like military equipment, infrastructure, pipelines, and so on, have these very real costs that will need to be paid back — hopefully from successful projects and greater prosperity,” Ryan told MPs at the committee on Tuesday. “But if not, they still need to be paid back.”

Liberal MP Ryan Turnbull asked the budget officer during her testimony how Canada’s fiscal position stacks up against its peers in the G7.

“It’s quite favourable, keeping in mind that the other six G7 countries are in increasingly difficult fiscal situations,” Ryan responded.

Fragos also pointed to the government’s fiscal anchors — a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio and a pledge to balance the operating budget — as proof of prudent financial management.

The debt-to-GDP ratio — a fiscal anchor for past Liberal governments — is also on a lower trajectory in Budget 2026.

While the government laid out a path to balance the operating budget a year ahead of schedule in the budget, the PBO warned Tuesday its margin for success is narrow.

The PBO acknowledged that Budget 2026 does move the needle toward Carney’s capital agenda, but Ryan continues to raise concerns about how the government defines capital versus operating spending.

That definition matters a lot when determining whether the government is meeting its pledge to balance the operating budget, so that all future borrowing goes toward productive capital investments.

In Tuesday’s report, Ryan argued that if the government used more internationally accepted definitions for capital and operating spending, Ottawa would fail to balance its operating budget over the forecast horizon.

“Whether the anchor is met depends on how capital is defined,” the report said.

Ottawa’s efforts to restrain program spending are limited to less than half of its expenses, the report said, since major transfers to persons and provinces are excluded from cost-cutting exercises.

The PBO noted that the government’s efforts to reduce the head count in the public service were close to its target at 332,000 employees as of August 2026.

But the office also pointed out that staff at Crown corporations are not reflected in the budget and these organizations are often the ones tasked with executing the government’s capital agenda.

“A broader measure that includes Crown corporations could show a different trend,” the PBO report said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hart Hub is making a difference. London needs more: advocate
stories.summary: The biggest problem with the new provincially-funded homelessness and addiction treatment initative, is that i...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
The biggest problem with the new provincially-funded homelessness and addiction treatment initative, is that it can’t help everyone who needs it, says the head of a London outreach program.

That’s because the Homelessness and Addiction Recovery Treatment (Hart) Hub is making a difference, aid Chris Moss, exective director of London Cares, which works with Londoners experiencing homelessness and addiction. Based at the Salvation Army’s Centre Centre of Hope downtown, Hart Hub has re-housed 20 people since the beginning of the program in late October and many people within the community hope the program will be expanded.

“We definitely need more. When we think about needs, we have about 2300 people on our streets, many of which need help,” said Moss. “And unfortunately, we need more than what the one hub has.”

With the success of the program, Moss hopes that more funding can be given to these treatment programs such as the Hart hub.

The program is among many approaches the city and organizations are taking to try to help those in need of housing and support. In recent years, the city of London has also opened some “highly-supportive housing” spaces, and last winter it opened a micro-modular shelter complex on Cheese Factory Road.

“The province did come to the table for Hart Hubs,” said Moss. “I’m hoping it’s something they consider is to increase more treatment, but we haven’t heard any word yet.”

stories.title: Nova Scotia must strengthen environmental assessments for wind projects: auditor
stories.summary: Nova Scotia's auditor general says the province's Environment Department must strengthen its environmental assessment process for onshore wind energy development.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
Nova Scotia’s auditor general says the province’s Environment Department must strengthen its environmental assessment process for onshore wind energy development.

That’s the key finding of Kim Adair’s latest audit, which offers 13 recommendations to improve the environmental assessment process and compliance monitoring after a project is approved.

She says it’s important to ensure environmental oversight is effective, given that Nova Scotia is relying on onshore wind energy to reach its renewable energy targets by 2030.

Adair’s report says Nova Scotia’s environmental assessment process is generally consistent with other provinces, but her office found weaknesses in how the department oversees projects.

stories.title: Carney, Sheinbaum discuss future of Canada-Mexico trade on sidelines of Apec summit
stories.summary: Both countries are navigating a tumultuous relationship with Washington as they make progress on deepening their trade ties
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney met Tuesday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on the sidelines of an economic summit in China, as both leaders navigate tumultuous and unpredictable trade talks with the United States.

The meeting was an opportunity for the two leaders to commiserate over stalled negotiations and the future of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement.

However, the two leaders kept the focus on Canadian-Mexican relations in public remarks during their meeting Tuesday in Shenzhen, China, ON the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit.

“We see many opportunities for further co-operation with each other and working together with partners around the world – including the United States,” Carney said.

Sheinbaum said in Spanish that the meeting was a chance to discuss continental trade and a possible agreement between the three countries, but the important thing for her was the “extraordinary relationship” between Canada and Mexico.

Carney visited Mexico in September 2025 where both governments agreed to an action plan for deeper ties.

He said Tuesday that 120 initiatives from that plan have been accomplished, with trade up 18 per cent compared with a year prior.

The Prime Minister called that “an indication both of the strength of the relationship and the scale of the opportunity between Mexico and Canada.”

While Canada and Mexico have had differing approaches to U.S. President Donald Trump ’s massive tariff agenda – the outcome has been similar.

Mexico and Canada continue to be slammed by Trump’s tariffs , with threats of new duties looming, and both countries had trade talks sidelined by the interference of a close Trump ally and administration official.

Reports said U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick created an impasse in Mexican trade talks last month while he was also blamed for the eleventh-hour breakdown in negotiations with Canada in August.

Ottawa and Mexico City had been negotiating with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who stated that his goal is to have interim limited agreements by the end of the year. But reports said Lutnick intervened in both sets of trade talks and was unwilling to budge over Trump’s sector-specific tariffs on things like automobiles.

Canada and Mexico are also looking to find a pathway to renew the trilateral trade pact, known as Cusma, bringing predictability and tariff relief back to their economies.

The Trump administration in July chose not to renew Cusma. The decision triggered a rolling annual review for up to a decade, at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

Cusma was negotiated to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during the first Trump administration. But Trump returned to the White House emboldened, armed with a wide array of tariff tools and surrounded by advisers willing to support all his trade impulses.

That has caused challenges for both Canada and Mexico.

Typically, it would be clear which American officials that Canada and Mexico are negotiating with, said Andrea Van Vugt, who was a foreign-policy adviser to former prime minister Stephen Harper.

“It’s become clear in the last six months it’s not just Ambassador Greer. It’s also Secretary Lutnick and then it is the president’s office and then it is the president,” the chief operating officer of Wellington Advocacy told a panel discussion for the Washington International Trade Association on Monday.

“That is a really hard dynamic to negotiate in and it makes it very hard to understand how to bring a negotiation to conclusion.”

She said the goal of Canadian negotiators will be to preserve as much of the trilateral trade pact as possible while also lifting tariffs, adding it’s not clear how much of that is possible.

Trump escalated the trade war, hitting an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banning the import of others after talks broke down this summer. Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs.

Mexico has not retaliated to Trump’s tariffs with its own round of levies. Kenneth Smith Ramos, the former Mexican chief negotiator during the first Trump administration, told a panel discussion that Sheinbaum’s initial goal was to find a way to get tariffs dropped before Cusma negotiations started.

Mexico worked with Trump administration on human and drug trafficking, as well as to resolve other bilateral issues. No matter what was offered, Mexico did not see duties decrease nor was it given an indication that it would get preferential tariff treatment through the continental trade agreement, Ramos said.

“We are sort of spinning our wheels in the U.S.-Mexico discussion because it’s a little bit of a game of chicken,” said Ramos, a partner at Mexico City-based Agon.

Antonio Ortiz-Mena, the former minister for economic affairs at Mexico’s embassy in the United States, said it is positive that many goods compliant with Cusma are not being hit with levies but added that tariff threats are always changing.

Ortiz-Mena noted how Mexico is under investigation for new duties related to overcapacity.

“There’s a question, I think a legitimate question, ON the Mexican side of what else do we need to do?” Ortiz-Mena said at the panel. “Is this a moving goal post? What else does the U.S. want?”

stories.title: Annual pace of Canadian housing starts falls 2% from a month earlier
stories.summary: October figure signals reduced momentum for housing construction, Cmhc economist says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. says the annual pace of housing starts in October edged down 2 per cent compared with September.

The housing agency says the seasonally adjusted annual rate of housing starts came in at 244,558 units in October compared with 250,072 in September.

The result came as actual monthly housing starts in communities with a population of 10,000 or more rose 6 per cent year-over-year to 21,059 in October, compared with 19,806 in October 2025.

The annual rate of rural starts was estimated at 13,675 units for October.

The six-month moving average of the seasonally adjusted annual rate was down 1.7 per cent in October at 246,231.

Kevin Hughes, deputy chief economist at Cmhc, says the results for October signal reduced momentum for housing construction, with the national trend decreasing, driven by declines in Ontario, British Columbia, and the Atlantic provinces.

stories.title: My work shift was cancelled but no one told me. Should I still get paid?
stories.summary: If the school failed to communicate the PA day to you, there would be a legal obligation to pay you for the day of work, expert says
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
Interested in more careers-related content? Check out our new weekly Work Life newsletter . Sent every Monday afternoon.

I recently started as a support worker at a small private school. The position is five days a week during school hours but there was a PA day and no one told me about it. I only found out when I showed up at the school and the kids weren’t there and they said I could go home. I’m obviously not getting paid for that day but it seems unfair that no one told me I didn’t have to be at work, especially when I could have picked up a shift at my second job. Is this allowed? Should the school owe me any money for showing up when no one gave me notice that there was no work that day?

Ryan Edmonds , managing lawyer and Thulasi Kandiah , associate lawyer, Ryan Edmonds Workplace Counsel , Toronto

You have every reason to be frustrated. Schools generally know their PA days well in advance and making sure employees know when they are expected to work should not be difficult.

There are two issues here: whether the school was required to give you notice of the PA day and whether it owes you any money.

In Ontario, the Employment Standards Act does not require employers to provide advance notice of a cancelled shift. Your employment agreement May provide otherwise, but by default, the school’s failure to notify you is not necessarily unlawful.

However, Ontario has what is commonly referred to as the “three-hour rule.” If you regularly work more than three hours a day, are required to report for work and are available to work but are sent home early, your employer generally must pay you for at least three hours at your regular rate.

If you were expected to work that day and had never been told otherwise, you should be entitled to three hours’ pay, even though you performed no work.

There is, however, an important caveat to the “three-hour rule”. If it had been previously communicated to you that you would not work on PA days, for example, and this is stated in your employment agreement or referenced in a school calendar, then the “three-hour rule” May not apply, even if nobody reminded you. This is because the “three-hour rule” is meant to compensate for the inconvenience of being sent home after being required to report to work.

As for your second job, while the lost opportunity to earn additional income is understandably frustrating, the school is unlikely to be responsible for wages you might have earned elsewhere.

Potential legal entitlements aside, this is really a matter of basic workplace courtesy and communication. If the school is unwilling to provide you with three hours of pay, then you should at least be given a clear schedule of upcoming PA days and school closures.

Muneeza Sheikh , founding partner, Muneeza Sheikh Employment and Human Rights , Toronto

Given that you work full-time at five days a week, it is entirely reasonable to assume that you would be informed by the school if there was a day that you would not have work. The school has an obligation to keep you informed of PA days, so you can, as you say, make plans to take the day off or work at another job. It is my view that if the school failed to communicate the PA day to you, there would be a legal obligation to pay you for the day of work.

With that being said, I am wondering what steps the school took to communicate the PA day to staff. Was it something that was discussed, posted or circulated and perhaps you just missed it? Were you provided with a list of scheduled PA days at the time of hire? If they did none of the above, I think it is entirely reasonable for you to be asked to be paid for that day. If you missed the chance to work elsewhere through no fault of your own, it is something that the school should be responsible for unless they can prove they did nothing wrong.

If after speaking to the school, they can demonstrate that you ought to have known about the PA day, they would owe you nothing. If they refuse to pay you despite being responsible for the lack of communication, you can certainly retain a lawyer to demand payment on your behalf or perhaps take the case before your local ministry of labour. In my practice, where similar issues have arisen, I have seen employees who make the choice to forego the issue and put the employer on warning that nothing like this can happen again, although it is your right to demand payment.

stories.title: A Canadian teen was blackmailed after sending nude images. How AP found his scammer in Nigeria
stories.summary: Lagos, Nigeria (AP) — The teenage boy felt his heart drop. His mind went blank.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Erika Kinetz, The Associated Press,

Posted November 17, 2026 8:35 am.

Last Updated November 17, 2026 9:14 am.

LAGOS, Nigeria (AP) — The teenage boy felt his heart drop. His mind went blank.

He’d sent the nude photo the girl wanted, and now she was demanding money. She threatened to post the picture to his family, friends and boss and effectively destroy his life.

“My mind couldn’t think anymore,” he told The Associated Press. “It couldn’t even comprehend the situation I was in.”

He no longer believed there was a buxom brunette with a sweet smile on the other side of his phone. But he never imagined that one day he’d find out who was.

The teen was trapped in a scam that increasingly targets young men: Sextortion. The FBI has warned of a surge in financially motivated sextortion of minors – threatening to expose people’s private images unless they send money. This year is on track to be the worst ever.

By August, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) had received more than 40,000 reports of financial sextortion , against a total of 50,000 for all of last year. The impact can be lethal: Dozens of young people have taken their own lives after being sextorted.

Most sextortion crimes are never solved. But the AP and FRONTLINE met the teen’s scammer in Lagos: A soft-spoken Nigerian student named Ayomide.

“Scamming is not good,” said Ayomide, who in his early 20s is not much older than his victim. “I do feel bad. But as a man, you have to make money.”

Ayomide shared chat histories of some of his successful scams, including with his victim in Canada. The AP does not publish the names of underage victims, and reached out to the teen after he turned 18. He spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss traumatic events he had not even discussed with his family.

Ayomide told him that if he didn’t want his photo posted, he’d have to pay. Panicked, the teen said he sent $500.

“Are we done now?” he remembers asking. “Let’s go our separate ways.”

The response is seared on his brain: “Not just yet. This isn’t that simple.”

‘There’s no shame in being a Yahoo Boy’

Ayomide is part of a thriving subculture in Nigeria, in which scamming has been normalized — fueled, some say, by the legacy of colonialism. Yahoo Boys — as online scammers are known locally — are helping drive a global surge in sextortion by exploiting Western social media and payment infrastructure to blackmail their victims, the AP and FRONTLINE found. Even as sextortion rates reach record highs, steps some major social media platforms have taken to increase privacy have only made teens more vulnerable, data shows.

“These perpetrators are becoming more and more aggressive,” said Charles Smith, the FBI’s law enforcement attaché in Abuja. “It can happen to any of our children, any child with access to a computer or online.”

The share of U.S. middle and high school students who say they have been victims of sextortion has tripled in the last decade, to nearly 15%, according to researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire and Florida Atlantic University. They also found that sextorted teens are nine times more likely to attempt suicide. More than 60 teens under 18 years old from around the world have killed themselves after being financially sextorted since the end of 2021, according to Paul Raffile, a cybersecurity analyst.

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

Like other Yahoo Boys the AP and FRONTLINE met, Ayomide said he learned how to use his phone to blackmail foreigners from his friends. All the scammers spoke on condition that their full names not be published because of their illegal work.

Some aspiring scammers in Nigeria join so-called Hustle Kingdoms — groups of young men who live and work together under the guidance of an experienced scammer who takes a cut of earnings. Universities have also become training grounds for scammers.

Sextortion has proven so profitable it is drawing the attention of organized criminal groups in West Africa and Southeast Asia, according to Interpol and the nonprofit International Justice Mission, which traced reports of child sextortion to scam compounds in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

“There’s no shame in being a Yahoo Boy,” said Adedeji Oyenuga, a professor of criminology at Lagos State University. “There is pride.”

For many in Nigeria, scamming is just another hustle in a country where more than 90% of workers don’t have stable, formal jobs. Hit songs celebrate Yahoo Boys and videos on social media show scamming rich Westerners as a way to quick, flashy wealth.

But Ayomide seems out of place in the nightclubs that rise from dark, dirt streets on the outskirts of Lagos, where young men spray crisp paper money at the throbbing, beautiful crowd to prove how much they have to waste.

He described himself as a “soft boy” and said he was apprenticing at a barbershop while pursuing a degree in computer science. He said he’d rather cut hair than scam, but the math was not working in his favor.

His parents sell clothes in a local market, he said. It was up to him to squeeze 110,000 naira ($82) for school fees and 250,000 naira ($186) for his annual rent from an economy where 70% of people lived on less than $4.20 a day last year, according to the World Bank.

Some Nigerian parents see cybercrime as an appealing career opportunity for their kids, according to Oyenuga and others. Parents have pushed their sons into Hustle Kingdoms and arranged for their daughters to marry Yahoo Boys, he said.

Oyenuga got a call late one night from a student’s father, who asked the professor to help his son become a Yahoo Boy, he said. Oyenuga tried — and failed — to steer the engineering student toward foreign exchange trading instead.

“For the parents it’s poverty,” he said. “They just want their children to be successful.”

For Yahoo Boys themselves, scamming is often a temporary stage, a way to earn enough to get a foothold in the legitimate economy.

Ayomide said he hadn’t told his mother about his work because he knows she’d disapprove. He vowed to stop scamming within a year and figured he’d eventually earn enough as a barber to stay afloat. His dream, he said, is to be an engineer and work on planes out at the airport.

“Everything in Nigeria is all about money,” Ayomide said. “But I pray everything works out.”

Sextortionists use American tech to blackmail kids

Ayomide’s method was simple: impersonate a beautiful woman, follow hundreds of foreign men and boys on TikTok and chat up the ones who followed him back: What’s your name? Are you alone today? Do you want to have fun? Then he’d move the conversation to a private messaging app.

For every 50 people Ayomide follows on TikTok, he said, around 10 follow him back, and five of those are willing to chat.

Once he hooks someone, Ayomide said, he has them buy Apple or Steam gift cards, which he cashes out in local currency using CardBrother, a gift card resale app that markets to Nigerian users.

Steam said that it was phasing out physical gift cards this year, in part as a response to abuse by scammers.

Apple said it educates users about risks of gift card scams, including a warning on its gift card landing page. Apple said it removed CardBrother from its app store this year after finding it was connected to another account engaged in fraudulent activity.

The app was still available on Google Play, where it had gotten more than 1 million downloads. CardBrother’s developer did not respond to emailed requests for comment.

Google said it runs 10,000 safety checks on every app and scans 350 billion apps a day. Google removed the CardBrother app after AP flagged its fictitious US address and a dead phone number.

Ayomide also exploited PayPal, paying money mules he found on WhatsApp to use their accounts.

The AP provided PayPal with three accounts Ayomide used to extort his victims. PayPal said the accounts had been restricted shortly after they were created. The company said it is committed to providing a safe platform and invests in systems to disrupt suspicious activity. Meta said it has systems in place to detect malicious behavior on WhatsApp and bans millions of accounts each year.

One of Ayomide’s most successful characters was Ava, an attentive young woman with an extraordinary body.

The Canadian teen said he was 15 when Ava followed him on TikTok.

Just exchanging messages seemed harmless. And it was easy to avoid TikTok’s ban on direct messaging for under-16 accounts by inventing a birthday when he signed up.

Ava asked the teen to move their conversation to an encrypted messaging app called Zangi.

He said he called Ava but never managed to get through for one reason or another. Sometimes she tried him back, but when he picked up, all he heard was a woman saying “hello … hello … hello.”

Later, he would realize that he shouldn’t have followed Ava to Zangi and that the voice was likely a recording.

Ava told him it was hard for a girl to trust people online. Could he send a copy of his driver’s license?

Yes, he could.

Ayomide now had a weapon in his hands: A copy of the teen’s learner’s permit, with his address and date of birth.

Ayomide copied a naked photo he’d found online and sent it to the teen, telling him it was Ava.

“Of course, in my 15-year-old mind, I wanted more,” he told AP.

Then Ava asked for one in return. One evening, he sent it.

“Wow, that was nice,” Ayomide replied.

Ayomide was following a highly scripted – and ruthlessly efficient – playbook. Child safety advocates say apps with direct messaging are where children are most often targeted by sextortionists, who quickly move them to encrypted platforms.

Changes companies have made to increase privacy are making kids more vulnerable

Design changes some social media platforms have made to increase privacy are making teens more vulnerable, data shows. After TikTok expanded direct messaging and allowed users to exchange images last year, user reports of financial sextortion on the platform skyrocketed, data from Canada’s Cybertip.ca hotline shared with the AP shows.

TikTok U.S. said it reminds users to share images only with people they trust, and in keeping with U.S. industry norms it doesn’t require proof of age to create an account. The company added that because messaging is not end-to-end encrypted, the platform is less attractive to bad actors.

The spread of end-to-end encryption, which allows only the sender and receiver to access messages, has raised alarm among child advocates. Under U.S. law, when companies become aware of child sexual abuse, including sextortion, they must report those incidents to NCMEC.

But platforms cannot report what they don’t see.

NCMEC said the expansion of end-to-end encryption made it more difficult to detect potential abuse and contributed to a 19% drop in overall reports in 2024.

“It creates a Wild, Wild West,” said Lauren Coffren, executive director of NCMEC’s Exploited Children Division. “I can imagine what we don’t know and it’s terrifying.”

Meta, the world’s largest social media company, completed its rollout of end-to-end encryption by default on Facebook Messenger in 2024. The company, which files more reports to NCMEC than any other, said it was aware of child safety concerns and only put in the default encryption after it had developed new safety features.

“We work aggressively to fight sextortion, disrupting networks of scammers and supporting law enforcement in prosecuting them,” Meta said in an email. “These determined criminals do everything they can to avoid detection.”

The legacy of slavery, corruption and ritual sacrifice power scammers in Nigeria

The demands started a week after they’d exchanged explicit photos, the Canadian teen recalled. After the first payment, Ayomide kept pressing for more.

“That’s all they need is one photo,” he told AP.

Alone and afraid, he found himself crying at night. He couldn’t see a way out.

“If I told somebody about it, I’d have to suffer the consequences of the embarrassment and my whole identity being ruined for life,” he said. “But at the same time, it felt like if I didn’t comply with this person’s orders, that was going to happen anyway.”

As Ayomide pummeled him for more money, the teen sank deeper into isolation. He said he was afraid to report the crime because he didn’t want his family to find out.

“I had no hope in my existence,” he said. “This guy was telling me no one is here for you, you got nobody. He would call me his slave.”

The legacy of slavery is part of the reason scammers thrive in Nigeria today, according to the Rev. Lateef OgoOluwa Bakre, a pastor who has spent two decades ministering to Yahoo Boys.

“A lot of us believe that the colonial masters cheated on us,” he said. “They molested our parents, our forefathers were treated very badly and they were extorted. So these guys feel it is our turn.”

Yahoo Boys sometimes turn to local spiritual leaders for rituals they believe will help them make more money – a practice known as Yahoo Plus.

Scammers seeking occult power have brought money to places like Owode Egba, a village northeast of Lagos. Among those who have prospered is Akeem Olajide, an Ifa diviner, or babalawo.

Two shrines sit in front of his low concrete home, heaped with the bones, feathers and grease of past sacrifices. When Yahoo Boys come to him seeking wealth, he does his best to help.

“I also want to make money,” he explained. “Whatever I have, I would use it to help the person succeed, and when the person becomes successful, they will come back and reward me.”

The day before, a Yahoo Boy who’d come for help with an uncooperative “client” gave him 20,000 naira ($15) as thanks, he said. He gestured to his motorbike — a gift from another Yahoo Boy who prospered from his services, he said.

Olajide lifted the lid off a chipped white enamel pot in the dim room where he works. Inside, pieces of a dove floated in thick black liquid — an offering to curry favor with the forces of wealth and prosperity for a client, Olajide said.

The liquid in the pot was alive with maggots. A good sign: The more maggots, the more money.

Nigerian authorities have decried the spread of Yahoo Plus. And Nigerian law enforcement has cooperated with the FBI to crack down on transnational scams, including a high-profile operation launched in 2023 that led to the arrest of 22 suspected sextortionists – around half allegedly involved in cases that led to a suicide.

“Rest assured, Nigeria is no longer going to be a safe haven for fraudsters or criminal activities,” Olanipekun Olukoyede, the Chairman of Nigeria’s Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), said in a rare interview with AP/FRONTLINE. He has called Yahoo Boys a “national shame.”

Despite stepped-up law enforcement, many Yahoo Boys continue to work with impunity.

Godspower and Junior, two other scammers, told AP and FRONTLINE they’d had run-ins with police. Both said they paid a bribe and were released.

EFCC officials acknowledged that corruption is a problem in Nigeria, as elsewhere, but said perpetrators are punished.

“Look, even among my staff, I won’t sit down here and tell you everybody’s a saint,” Olukoyede said. “But as much as we get them, we expose them and we sanction them. We do what we need to do.”

Bakre, the pastor, has taken a different approach to fighting scams. With his Zion of Love ministry, he started a free school down the road from the babalawo to divert kids from a life of crime.

The school sits near a house with two luxury cars parked outside – wealth that came from scams, the pastor said.

“People are celebrated for what they have,” he said. “It’s no more about the source of what they’ve gotten.”

Ayomide mocked up a fake news video using the teen’s photo.

The teen kept blocking Ayomide online, but Ayomide would pop right back up.

“Not even a minute later a random email or number will message you saying, ’Why did you block me? Don’t block this number. You’re only making this situation a whole lot worse,’” he explained.

He cut Ayomide off on Zangi. Ayomide found him on WhatsApp.

“Hello (wave emoji) How are you doing today?”Ayomide wrote on WhatsApp on Sept. 13, 2024.

He sent screenshots as proof of the PayPal transfer.

LAGOS, Nigeria (AP) — The teenage boy felt his heart drop. His mind went blank.
He’d sent the nude photo the girl wanted, and now she was demanding money. She threatened to post the picture to his family, friends and boss and effectively destroy his life.
“My mind couldn’t think anymore,” he told The Associated Press. “It couldn’t even comprehend the situation I was in.”
He no longer believed there was a buxom brunette with a sweet smile on the other side of his phone. But he never imagined that one day he’d find out who was.

The teen was trapped in a scam that increasingly targets young men: Sextortion. The FBI has warned of a surge in financially motivated sextortion of minors – threatening to expose people’s private images unless they send money. This year is on track to be the worst ever.

By August, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) had received more than 40,000 reports of financial sextortion , against a total of 50,000 for all of last year. The impact can be lethal: Dozens of young people have taken their own lives after being sextorted.
Most sextortion crimes are never solved. But the AP and FRONTLINE met the teen’s scammer in Lagos: A soft-spoken Nigerian student named Ayomide.
“Scamming is not good,” said Ayomide, who in his early 20s is not much older than his victim. “I do feel bad. But as a man, you have to make money.”

Ayomide shared chat histories of some of his successful scams, including with his victim in Canada. The AP does not publish the names of underage victims, and reached out to the teen after he turned 18. He spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss traumatic events he had not even discussed with his family.
Ayomide told him that if he didn’t want his photo posted, he’d have to pay. Panicked, the teen said he sent $500.
“Are we done now?” he remembers asking. “Let’s go our separate ways.”
The response is seared on his brain: “Not just yet. This isn’t that simple.”
‘There’s no shame in being a Yahoo Boy’

Ayomide is part of a thriving subculture in Nigeria, in which scamming has been normalized — fueled, some say, by the legacy of colonialism. Yahoo Boys — as online scammers are known locally — are helping drive a global surge in sextortion by exploiting Western social media and payment infrastructure to blackmail their victims, the AP and FRONTLINE found. Even as sextortion rates reach record highs, steps some major social media platforms have taken to increase privacy have only made teens more vulnerable, data shows.

“These perpetrators are becoming more and more aggressive,” said Charles Smith, the FBI’s law enforcement attaché in Abuja. “It can happen to any of our children, any child with access to a computer or online.”

The share of U.S. middle and high school students who say they have been victims of sextortion has tripled in the last decade, to nearly 15%, according to researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire and Florida Atlantic University. They also found that sextorted teens are nine times more likely to attempt suicide. More than 60 teens under 18 years old from around the world have killed themselves after being financially sextorted since the end of 2021, according to Paul Raffile, a cybersecurity analyst.
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

Like other Yahoo Boys the AP and FRONTLINE met, Ayomide said he learned how to use his phone to blackmail foreigners from his friends. All the scammers spoke on condition that their full names not be published because of their illegal work.

Some aspiring scammers in Nigeria join so-called Hustle Kingdoms — groups of young men who live and work together under the guidance of an experienced scammer who takes a cut of earnings. Universities have also become training grounds for scammers.

Sextortion has proven so profitable it is drawing the attention of organized criminal groups in West Africa and Southeast Asia, according to Interpol and the nonprofit International Justice Mission, which traced reports of child sextortion to scam compounds in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.
“There’s no shame in being a Yahoo Boy,” said Adedeji Oyenuga, a professor of criminology at Lagos State University. “There is pride.”

For many in Nigeria, scamming is just another hustle in a country where more than 90% of workers don’t have stable, formal jobs. Hit songs celebrate Yahoo Boys and videos on social media show scamming rich Westerners as a way to quick, flashy wealth.

But Ayomide seems out of place in the nightclubs that rise from dark, dirt streets on the outskirts of Lagos, where young men spray crisp paper money at the throbbing, beautiful crowd to prove how much they have to waste.

He described himself as a “soft boy” and said he was apprenticing at a barbershop while pursuing a degree in computer science. He said he’d rather cut hair than scam, but the math was not working in his favor.

His parents sell clothes in a local market, he said. It was up to him to squeeze 110,000 naira ($82) for school fees and 250,000 naira ($186) for his annual rent from an economy where 70% of people lived on less than $4.20 a day last year, according to the World Bank.

Some Nigerian parents see cybercrime as an appealing career opportunity for their kids, according to Oyenuga and others. Parents have pushed their sons into Hustle Kingdoms and arranged for their daughters to marry Yahoo Boys, he said.

Oyenuga got a call late one night from a student’s father, who asked the professor to help his son become a Yahoo Boy, he said. Oyenuga tried — and failed — to steer the engineering student toward foreign exchange trading instead.
“For the parents it’s poverty,” he said. “They just want their children to be successful.”
For Yahoo Boys themselves, scamming is often a temporary stage, a way to earn enough to get a foothold in the legitimate economy.

Ayomide said he hadn’t told his mother about his work because he knows she’d disapprove. He vowed to stop scamming within a year and figured he’d eventually earn enough as a barber to stay afloat. His dream, he said, is to be an engineer and work on planes out at the airport.
“Everything in Nigeria is all about money,” Ayomide said. “But I pray everything works out.”

Ayomide’s method was simple: impersonate a beautiful woman, follow hundreds of foreign men and boys on TikTok and chat up the ones who followed him back: What’s your name? Are you alone today? Do you want to have fun? Then he’d move the conversation to a private messaging app.
For every 50 people Ayomide follows on TikTok, he said, around 10 follow him back, and five of those are willing to chat.
Once he hooks someone, Ayomide said, he has them buy Apple or Steam gift cards, which he cashes out in local currency using CardBrother, a gift card resale app that markets to Nigerian users.
Steam said that it was phasing out physical gift cards this year, in part as a response to abuse by scammers.

Apple said it educates users about risks of gift card scams, including a warning on its gift card landing page. Apple said it removed CardBrother from its app store this year after finding it was connected to another account engaged in fraudulent activity.
The app was still available on Google Play, where it had gotten more than 1 million downloads. CardBrother’s developer did not respond to emailed requests for comment.
Google said it runs 10,000 safety checks on every app and scans 350 billion apps a day. Google removed the CardBrother app after AP flagged its fictitious US address and a dead phone number.
Ayomide also exploited PayPal, paying money mules he found on WhatsApp to use their accounts.

The AP provided PayPal with three accounts Ayomide used to extort his victims. PayPal said the accounts had been restricted shortly after they were created. The company said it is committed to providing a safe platform and invests in systems to disrupt suspicious activity. Meta said it has systems in place to detect malicious behavior on WhatsApp and bans millions of accounts each year.

The Canadian teen said he was 15 when Ava followed him on TikTok.
Just exchanging messages seemed harmless. And it was easy to avoid TikTok’s ban on direct messaging for under-16 accounts by inventing a birthday when he signed up.
Ava asked the teen to move their conversation to an encrypted messaging app called Zangi.
He said he called Ava but never managed to get through for one reason or another. Sometimes she tried him back, but when he picked up, all he heard was a woman saying “hello … hello … hello.”
Later, he would realize that he shouldn’t have followed Ava to Zangi and that the voice was likely a recording.
Ava told him it was hard for a girl to trust people online. Could he send a copy of his driver’s license?
Yes, he could.
Ayomide now had a weapon in his hands: A copy of the teen’s learner’s permit, with his address and date of birth.

“Of course, in my 15-year-old mind, I wanted more,” he told AP.

“Wow, that was nice,” Ayomide replied.

Design changes some social media platforms have made to increase privacy are making teens more vulnerable, data shows. After TikTok expanded direct messaging and allowed users to exchange images last year, user reports of financial sextortion on the platform skyrocketed, data from Canada’s Cybertip.ca hotline shared with the AP shows.

TikTok U.S. said it reminds users to share images only with people they trust, and in keeping with U.S. industry norms it doesn’t require proof of age to create an account. The company added that because messaging is not end-to-end encrypted, the platform is less attractive to bad actors.

But platforms cannot report what they don’t see.
NCMEC said the expansion of end-to-end encryption made it more difficult to detect potential abuse and contributed to a 19% drop in overall reports in 2024.
“It creates a Wild, Wild West,” said Lauren Coffren, executive director of NCMEC’s Exploited Children Division. “I can imagine what we don’t know and it’s terrifying.”

Meta, the world’s largest social media company, completed its rollout of end-to-end encryption by default on Facebook Messenger in 2024. The company, which files more reports to NCMEC than any other, said it was aware of child safety concerns and only put in the default encryption after it had developed new safety features.

“We work aggressively to fight sextortion, disrupting networks of scammers and supporting law enforcement in prosecuting them,” Meta said in an email. “These determined criminals do everything they can to avoid detection.”

As Ayomide pummeled him for more money, the teen sank deeper into isolation. He said he was afraid to report the crime because he didn’t want his family to find out.
“I had no hope in my existence,” he said. “This guy was telling me no one is here for you, you got nobody. He would call me his slave.”

“A lot of us believe that the colonial masters cheated on us,” he said. “They molested our parents, our forefathers were treated very badly and they were extorted. So these guys feel it is our turn.”
Yahoo Boys sometimes turn to local spiritual leaders for rituals they believe will help them make more money – a practice known as Yahoo Plus.
Scammers seeking occult power have brought money to places like Owode Egba, a village northeast of Lagos. Among those who have prospered is Akeem Olajide, an Ifa diviner, or babalawo.
Two shrines sit in front of his low concrete home, heaped with the bones, feathers and grease of past sacrifices. When Yahoo Boys come to him seeking wealth, he does his best to help.

The liquid in the pot was alive with maggots. A good sign: The more maggots, the more money.

Despite stepped-up law enforcement, many Yahoo Boys continue to work with impunity.

EFCC officials acknowledged that corruption is a problem in Nigeria, as elsewhere, but said perpetrators are punished.
“Look, even among my staff, I won’t sit down here and tell you everybody’s a saint,” Olukoyede said. “But as much as we get them, we expose them and we sanction them. We do what we need to do.”

content_blocks.text: Ayomide is part of a thriving subculture in Nigeria, in which scamming has been normalized — fueled, some say, by the legacy of colonialism. Carney said that Canada plans to increase its overall trade with China by 50 per cent by 2030

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney (C) arrives at the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summiton November 16, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. (Pool / Getty Images)

November 17, 2026 at 8:35 a.m.

Ottawa — The Canadian and Chinese governments continued their rapprochement Tuesday, with China agreeing to provide tariff relief on roughly $400-million of Canadian pork, fish and seafood while Canada opened the door to more Chinese steel and aluminium.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office made the announcement Tuesday morning after he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China.

“Exchanges between our two countries have increased significantly and we have greater capability and stability,” Carney told Xi during opening remarks to the meeting, adding that Canada plans to increase its overall trade with China by 50 per cent by 2030.

According to the federal government, China agreed to extend until 2028 an agreement that provided tariff relief on imports of Canadian frozen pork cuts as well as certain fish and seafood products such as frozen cold-water shrimp and prawns, molluscs and Greenland halibut. The deal — first signed when Carney visited China in January — was set to expire at the end of the year.

In exchange, Canada agreed to extend and expand its tariff remission program on certain Chinese steel and aluminium products until 2028. The Canadian release says that new Chinese products covered by the remissions are “items for which Canadian supply is insufficient or unavailable.”

The remission program allows importers to get a refund of the 25 per cent surtax imposed on Chinese steel and aluminium since 2024.

The extension and slight expansion of tariff relief between both countries appears to be a small step towards further rapprochement between both countries after years of frosty relations. Efforts to boost trade between both countries began in earnest after a key bilateral meeting between Carney and Xi in Beijing in January.

Canadian exports to China have surged just over 40 per cent since then, hitting $4.4 billion in September from $3.1 in January, according to Statistics Canada.

Ahead of the meeting, a key advisor to American President Donald Trump and frequent critic of Canada warned that a closer relationship between Carney and Xi could be seen as a step away from the U.S.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive — as it is already doing,” Peter Navarro wrote on X on Monday.

In a readout of the meeting, Carney’s office said he and Xi explored ways to deepen cooperation in “clean and conventional energy industries, including oil and gas, low-carbon technologies, and electric vehicles,” but did not provide further detail.

The prime minister has frequently signaled that he’s interested in having Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers set up assembly lines in Canada. Ahead of the bilateral with Xi, he said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade talks with the U.S. fail and American automakers continue reshoring their production South of the border.

But the Chinese companies would have to set up significant manufacturing operations and use Canadian labour, materials and critical minerals rather than simply send “kits” from China and assemble the cars in Canada.

During the meeting, Carney promised to send another “major” trade delegation to China in 2027 and announced Air Canada would launch new flights from Vancouver to Guangzhou by mid-2027.

“We both recognize that the enduring ties between the Canadian and Chinese people provide an exceptionally strong foundation for practical, respectful collaboration,” Carney told Xi at the onset of the meeting.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01 cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Toronto’s Promise Robotics raises $40-million to automate more homebuilding
stories.summary: Startup has already landed Mattamy Homes and D.R. Horton as early customers and set up factories in Calgary and outside Edmonton
stories.author: Murad Hemmadi
stories.content:
Promise Robotics Inc., a Toronto-based artificial intelligence startup, has raised $40-million in fresh financing to scale up an automated approach to homebuilding that’s attracting interest from major residential developers.

Founded in September 2020, the company is applying AI to the construction sector, where productivity growth has long been slow and skilled workers are in short supply .

“We don’t have enough industrial capacity in construction to build all the homes we need,” said Ramtin Attar, Promise’s chief executive and co-founder, in an interview.

The company has developed software that breaks up dwelling designs into pieces that robots can produce in a factory. It then ships the parts to developers’ residential projects and hires construction crews to stand them up as finished houses.

Promise has set up factories in Calgary and just outside Edmonton. And it has plans for a new facility in Phoenix, the start of a big push into the U.S.

The company has built about 200 homes to date, and it is currently working to scale its production to 700 homes a year. It has contracts to supply more than 2,500 to clients. Half of that volume is through a deal the company landed last month with D.R. Horton, an Arlington, Tex.-based company that is the largest homebuilder in the U.S.

Promise has also signed up the Alberta division of Mattamy Homes, one of Canada’s largest residential developers.

“There’s a lot more pressure on home builders – on their margins, ON their ability to build more consistently,” said Mr. Attar.

Promise first developed an AI system that controls off-the-shelf industrial machines to produce the frame, roof, floors and other major components for any house design. Each cell consists of two robots that share a worktable; together, they can produce a home in eight hours, Mr. Attar said. The company can also add Hvac systems and plumbing, and it has plans to expand into electrical wiring.

It distinguishes its approach from modular houses, which are also produced in factories, but are purpose-designed for mass manufacturing. By contrast, Promise follows clients’ existing designs.

The company now follows the house out the factory gate. For some projects, it uses its own construction crews, after realizing that challenges with labour scheduling were lengthening building timelines. “All the components were arriving at the site and then sitting there for a week for a crew to come,” said Mr. Attar.

White Star Capital, a London-based venture firm with Canadian operations, led Promise’s Series B round, which closed in the second quarter. Returning backers in the financing included the Public Sector Pension Investment Board; Radical Ventures, a prominent AI investor based in Toronto; and Horizons Ventures, a Hong Kong investment firm backed by billionaire Li Ka-shing.

“Home construction is a massive industry that needs a new way to keep up with demand,” Sanjay Zimmermann, a Toronto-based general partner at White Star, said in a statement.

Promise will spend its new capital on technology research and development, and expanding its 85-person work force to more than 100 staff. paragraphs: Promise Robotics Inc., a Toronto-based artificial intelligence startup, has raised $40-million in fresh financing to scale up an automated approach to homebuilding that’s attracting interest from major residential developers.
Founded in September 2020, the company is applying AI to the construction sector, where productivity growth has long been slow and skilled workers are in short supply .
“We don’t have enough industrial capacity in construction to build all the homes we need,” said Ramtin Attar, Promise’s chief executive and co-founder, in an interview.

The company has developed software that breaks up dwelling designs into pieces that robots can produce in a factory. It then ships the parts to developers’ residential projects and hires construction crews to stand them up as finished houses.
Promise has set up factories in Calgary and just outside Edmonton. And it has plans for a new facility in Phoenix, the start of a big push into the U.S.

The company has built about 200 homes to date, and it is currently working to scale its production to 700 homes a year. It has contracts to supply more than 2,500 to clients. Half of that volume is through a deal the company landed last month with D.R. Horton, an Arlington, Tex.-based company that is the largest homebuilder in the U.S.
Promise has also signed up the Alberta division of Mattamy Homes, one of Canada’s largest residential developers.
“There’s a lot more pressure on home builders – on their margins, ON their ability to build more consistently,” said Mr. Attar.

Promise first developed an AI system that controls off-the-shelf industrial machines to produce the frame, roof, floors and other major components for any house design. Each cell consists of two robots that share a worktable; together, they can produce a home in eight hours, Mr. Attar said. The company can also add Hvac systems and plumbing, and it has plans to expand into electrical wiring.
It distinguishes its approach from modular houses, which are also produced in factories, but are purpose-designed for mass manufacturing. By contrast, Promise follows clients’ existing designs.

The company now follows the house out the factory gate. For some projects, it uses its own construction crews, after realizing that challenges with labour scheduling were lengthening building timelines. “All the components were arriving at the site and then sitting there for a week for a crew to come,” said Mr. Attar.

stories.title: For its newest home collection, Hermès gets crafty
stories.summary: Hermès’ latest collection for the home paints a vibrant picture of a design team infatuated with material, craft and colour
stories.author: Andrew Sardone
stories.content:
A caravan of chauffeured cars quietly crawls through a warren of narrow streets in downtown Toronto. They arrive at a private laneway and deposit their passengers, who make their way down a cobblestone path to the motor court of a red brick Georgian estate perched on the edge of the Don Valley. Through the front door, glasses of champagne are being passed out to the curious crowd, who schmooze and snoop from room to handsome room, taking in the latest furniture and housewares from Hermès.

For a few days in the early fall, this private home has been reimagined by the Parisian house as Maison 24, a showcase that demonstrates how living with Hermès can extend well beyond a walk-in closet lined with Birkin and Kelly bags. Its latest decor releases are the standouts of the night.

In the wood-panelled dining room, a box with a top in marquetry squares of moody-hued leather sits on a sideboard surrounded by silver goblets. The den is lined with stacks of folded blankets including cashmere throws with bands of equestrian webbing that add texture and graphic interest to their edges. On one shelf, a cylindrical basket called Confetti in pink calfskin is cut-out like a game of Connect 4, revealing an array of vibrant dots.

Taking in the scene are customers, a gaggle of Toronto starchitects and Charlotte Macaux Perelman and Alexis Fabry, the artistic directors of the house’s Home Universe. Since 2014, when CEO Axel Dumas and artistic director Pierre-Alexis Dumas paired up the creative duo to oversee Hermès’ home products as well as Saint-Louis crystal and Puiforcat tableware, the architect (Macaux Perelman) and the photography curator (Fabry) have elevated its profile in the design world. Seeing their contemporary, tailored and often colourful aesthetic styled in a space that grandly represents the coziness of a historic Canadian home reinforces the versatility of Hermès’s work, especially when you consider the much more spare environment in Milan where the newest objects were unveiled earlier in the year.

During the week of the annual Salone del Mobile furniture fair each spring, design and fashion brands compete for exhibition space in the northern Italian city. Securing exclusive use of the most recently unearthed hidden courtyard, pedigreed villa or abandoned military hospital is essential for increasing buzz and visitor attendance. But Hermès, in its slow-and-steady style, has been returning to the same space since 2021. La Pelota, a former sports court in the Brera district, is reinvented every year as a frame for the new collection. In 2022, furniture vignettes were staged within four glowing structures that resembled the forms of water towers. In 2024, a dark space focused visitors’ attention downwards to a patchwork of wood, stone, slate and terracotta flooring meant to conjure a feeling of being grounded.

The 2026 installation, From Object to Space, was a landscape of white plaster cubes inlayed with slivers of beechwood that emphasized a rawness of material. Hand-written labels in graphite pencil identified showpiece debuts including the Stadium d’Hermès dining table by Brits Edward Barber and Jay Osgerby, its curved Carrara Venato top edged in a circle of Verde Alpi marble. Hammered metal, the elemental focus of the year, was incorporated as a centrepiece dish with edges wrapped in blue and purple leather laces, and a tubular vase nestled in tiers of sharply chopped horsehair. Overall, the message was harmony between style and substance.

“I believe that we’re very much attached to materiality,” said Macaux Perelman through a translator at the exhibition preview. “We give a lot of attention to the reality of craftsmanship, the fact that things are done by hand, that they’re all unique.” While the palladium-finish metal could feel cold, Macaux Perelman said its hammered texture gives it a warmth and duality by connecting it to the manual work involved in its creation. “The material used is important because it’s at the very heart of the product.”

Macaux Perelman and Fabry describe their role at Hermès as editors, overseeing teams who specialize in different product categories, establishing guidelines and helping designers and artisans course-correct through the creative process. “This is a small team, but it works hard,” Fabry said. “There are some things that are negotiable. The things that are not negotiable are creativity and the freedom of expression and quality.”

A very specific eye for colour is also essential. Hermès’s most iconic hues are the rich orange of its shop boxes and the gold skins used in its leather goods. The tones incorporated into its design pieces evoke a similar earthiness. “They’re not something fossilized, something that remains unchanged,” Fabry said of the house’s preferred spectrum. “Some years, we’ve changed the palette of colours more definitely than in other years. This year, perhaps, the change was more sudden. We opted more for muted colours.”

Hermès’s back catalogue includes furniture pieces by Jean-Michel Frank (a saddle-stitched leather Club armchair), Barber & Osgerby (the porcelain Halo table lamp) and Noé Duchaufour-Lawrance (who highlighted leather and cane in the frame of his Sellier sofa). Though these pieces were conceptualized across decades, what they have in common is a contemporariness in the moment they’re introduced, as well as years later.

“We don’t really think of our objects inside a Hermès boutique or in the home of someone. We ask ourselves instead, ‘is this object going to be passed on to the next generation,’” Macaux Perelman said. “Is this going to survive its era?”

As the Maison 24 house installation in Toronto illustrated, the design team wants their pieces to transcend space as much as time. “Each person is going to mix our objects through a kind of porosity with the environment where the object stays,” Fabry said. Pieces are meant to reflect, he noted, “the life of the person who’s bought the object, the trips, the travels this person does, and the evolution of a person’s taste.”

The Globe and Mail Style Magazine travelled as a guest of Hermès, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

stories.title: Trillium College students disappointed at selective return to classes
stories.summary: Students at one career college are decrying its approach to the Osap pause, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.

Lorraine Eaton, who is in the law and security program at Trillium College, was supposed to graduate in January and had a security guard job lined up. Now, because she was relying completely on Osap loans and can’t pay tuition out of pocket, she has been told she can’t attend class.

“I am frustrated to all hell,” she said.

“I’ve actually had a couple of my classmates tell me they’re in class right now and … (our teacher) has this list of how many people can go into the class and there’s a lot of people not on that list anymore.”

Trillium College, with five campuses around the province, announced last month that it was suspending classes due to uncertainty created by the provincial government’s Osap pause. For many career colleges, Osap-funded tuition makes up a sizable portion of their revenue, and many say they are struggling, having to lay off staff or even consider closing.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced in early October that Osap would not flow for students at private post-secondary institutions during a government-commissioned audit of the sector that Quinn says has uncovered serious and widespread concerns.

He has not offered a timeline for resumption of Osap for career college students other than saying it would be in the new year, and low-interest, third-party bank loans Quinn said he was trying to arrange have not yet materialized.

Now, nearly a month after Trillium paused its classes, they are starting to resume, but only for some students.

Certain cohorts started returning last week, but some students told the school they couldn’t afford a payment plan without their Osap loan.

“Those students will remain on temporary academic pause and will not return with their cohort unless an eligible funding source or approved payment arrangement is confirmed,” Trillium wrote in a note to students.

Students on a payment plan have to pay weekly in advance of the following week’s classes and if a payment is missed, the student’s attendance May be “temporarily paused,” the school wrote.

A spokesperson said in a statement that Trillium is focused on resuming instruction “wherever this can be done responsibly and on helping as many students as possible complete their education.”

“Students and cohorts that are not included in the initial phases of the return will remain on temporary academic pause,” Jennifer Miles wrote.

“They have not been automatically withdrawn from Trillium College. The pause will continue while the college and affected students await an accessible government funding solution or establish another viable arrangement that supports the responsible completion of their programs.”

Jennifer Koster is in Trillium’s law clerk program and was supposed to graduate in February.

She said she could not pay the full amount Trillium had proposed for a payment plan and offered lesser instalments, but the school did not accept that so she remains on academic pause while some classmates have returned.

“I just want somebody to help,” she said. “There’s a lot of students just like me that are stuck in the same position, and we’re not getting what was promised. … It’s us taking responsibility for a mess that we didn’t create.”

Marina Whitehead, a student in Trillium’s community developmental service worker program, is in her program’s placement right now, so she is not attending classes.

But she does still owe the school nearly $6,000 from earlier in the term that Osap was supposed to cover, and she worries she won’t be able to graduate as planned in February if Osap doesn’t come through. Whitehead’s placement involves working 40 hours a week unpaid.

“We’re working for free,” she said. “Where would you like me to pull that much money out of?”

stories.title: Mohawk teacher, 73, earns McGill’s first PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization
stories.summary: Mary Onwá:ri Tekahawákhwen McDonald has taught the Mohawk language to thousands of students over the past decades, from elementary school all the way to university level.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie
stories.content:
By her own estimate, Mary Onwá:ri Tekahawákhwen McDonald has taught the Mohawk language to thousands of students over the past decades, from elementary school all the way to university level.

But when someone suggested she might pursue a PhD, the idea of returning to class in her 70s was a daunting prospect.

“(I said) ‘no, why would I want to do that?'” the now-73-year-old says with a laugh. ” … How do I compete with 20-year-olds? Can I really do this?”

Today, the Mohawk educator, linguist and elder can add the title of “doctor” to her list of accomplishments. Earlier this year, she became the first person to graduate from McGill University with a PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization.

McDonald said she was eventually convinced to apply to the program out of a desire to write down the knowledge she’s accumulated over 45 years of teaching and studying language.

McDonald, who is from the Akwesasne community that straddles Quebec, Ontario and New York, is a native Mohawk speaker who only learned to speak English in second grade.

She went on to study Iroquoian linguistics, with a concentration in Mohawk, in university in Albany, N.Y., and later got a teaching certification in Ontario.

Over the years, she said, she became interested in studying how native speakers learn the language as children.

“Kinship words” used to describe close relatives come first, she said, followed by the words used to describe other people close to them. Pronouns, commands, and nouns follow, as children learn increasingly complex sentences.

She said she learned that this knowledge can help to teach second-language students, too. “If you follow this pattern, you’re coming very close to duplicating a natural learning pattern,” she said.

McDonald summed up part of her research in her dissertation, entitled “Kanien’kéha Through the Eyes of a First-Language Speaker.”

And along the way, she also became a peer mentor to some of those twenty-something-aged students who she was once intimidated to join.

She recently invited reporters to meet some of her young peers, who were gathering to discuss their research. She chatted with a young man in Mohawk, and gave advice to another student who was presenting to the group. McDonald jokingly refers to the group as fellow “super-nerds.”

Jessica Coon, the program director for the ad hoc graduate program in Indigenous language revitalization, was one of McDonald’s supervisors. Coon said McDonald’s contribution to the program is “hard to overstate.”

“As a thesis supervisor, I think we always get to learn something from our students, but this has never been more true than in the case of working with Mary because she just knows so much about the language,” she said in an interview.

She said the program was created in part to accommodate students whose interest in language revitalization spans different disciplines — such as linguistics and education, in McDonald’s case.

“We really want the program to be broad enough to accommodate students approaching language revitalization of their languages from a variety of different perspectives and to have the flexibility built in to do that across different disciplines,” she said.

She says another student graduated with McDonald at the Master’s level, and there are four more students who started this fall, including two more PhD candidates. McDonald “is the first, but she won’t be the last,” she said.

While McDonald now describes herself as “retired,” she is clearly keeping busy. She travels back to McGill every two weeks, where she serves as an elder in residence and meets with the research group.

She also still works with more advanced Mohawk language-learners, pushing them to expand the bounds of their abilities and express themselves with not only accuracy, but “pizzazz.”

She said she plans to keep building on her thesis, and writing down the concepts she has spent a lifetime studying.

“I’ll do this till the day I pass because it’s a lot of fun,” she said.
