stories.title: Flying out of Kelowna is about to get more expensive as airport fees increase
stories.summary: Travellers flying out of Kelowna International Airport will soon be paying more for parking and airport improvement fees.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Travellers flying out of Kelowna International Airport will soon be paying more for parking and airport improvement fees.

On Monday, Kelowna City Council unanimously approved a new fee structure that will see several airport charges increase, including short-term and long-term parking rates.

The changes take effect Dec. 1.

The hourly rate for short-term parking will move to a flat $3 per hour, replacing the current rate of $2.25 for the first hour and $3.50 for each additional hour.

But the daily maximum for short-term parking will increase significantly, climbing from $27 to $50.

Airport officials say the higher daily rate is intended, in part, to discourage travelers from using the short-term lot for extended stays.

Weekly parking in the long-term lot will also become more expensive, increasing from $88 to $100.

“I fly out twice a year and in between, so it’s not a good thing at all, ” said Penticton resident Rona Schwager.

Parking isn’t the only thing going up. The Airport Improvement Fee (AIF), paid by every departing passenger, will gradually increase from the current $31 to $39 over the next five years, an increase of approximately 26 per cent.

The first increase from $31 to $33 takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Kelowna International Airport’s CEO said the revenue is needed to help fund $423 million in planned capital investment projects over the coming years at the country’s 9th busiest airport.

“When you look at our growth rate of our airport, we’ve been amongst the busiest airports in the country,” said Sam Samaddar. “With that passenger growth, we, you know, we need different infrastructure investments to support that growth.”

Some of the major investments include terminal expansions, runway resurfacing and a new roundabout for easier airport access.

Samaddar said that a review of airport fees found the new rates are comparable to other similarly-sized airports.

“The airport improvement fee that I understand,” said Kelowna resident Colin Chatfield, who was concerned about rising parking costs. “Parking fees are already quite high.”

There is some good news for travelers who drive to the airport.

A new seven-storey parkade is nearing completion and will add more than 1,000 stalls to the parking inventory.

stories.title: Carney meets with President Xi in Shenzhen, China ahead of Apec summit
stories.summary: It's the second in-person meeting the two have held in China this year. The meeting took place in the high-tech hub in the Pearl River Delta megacity region in southeast China.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting in the metropolis of Shenzhen as Carney seeks to expand trade with China on everything from agriculture and energy to financial services and automobiles.

The meeting took place mid-morning on Tuesday in the high-tech hub in the Pearl River Delta megacity region in southeast China, where Xi will host the Apec leaders summit on Wednesday and Thursday.

It’s the second in-person meeting the two have held in China this year. In January, Carney travelled to Beijing for a meeting with Xi, marking the first official discussion between a Canadian prime minister and Chinese president in more than eight years.

Carney says there are “clear guardrails” about what is on the table with China and that discussions around the auto sector are also dependent on ongoing trade talks with the United States.

Canada’s turn to China is in part because of its pivot away from the United States, which under President Donald Trump has imposed wide-ranging tariffs and even threatened to annex Canada through economic coercion.

Carney has reinvigorated Canada’s economic relationship with China as part of his bid to expand Canada’s trade away from an overreliance on the United States.

Since that January meeting, Canada’s exports to China have surged 40 per cent as both countries agreed to drop various tariffs including on electric vehicles and some agricultural products.

Oil, canola and peas are among the products that have seen big jumps in exports to China.

Ahead of the trip, Carney said Canada could do more with China in terms of agriculture, clean and conventional energy, and financial services.

Carney is in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or Apec. Earlier on this trip, he was in the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, Cambodia for the Francophonie summit, and Ireland for a European Political Community meeting.

Carney said he expected to speak with Xi about “the evolution of the international system, China’s role in that and Canadian priorities.”

An overarching topic will be Chinese investments into Canada’s auto sector. Both countries agreed earlier this year to allow a limited amount of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada.

Carney has said he wants Chinese carmakers to set up shop, but only if they provide decent jobs, saying he is wary of plants where workers assemble cars using components mostly made in China. Canada has already said no to that as an option for the shuttered Stellantis plant in Brampton, Ont.

Carney said trade talks with Washington will shape how Canada approaches Chinese investment, and that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail.

Those comments prompted blowback from Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S,” Navarro posted on X on Monday. “This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive — as it is already doing.”

Navarro went on to say Vancouver is not British Columbia, it’s “PRC” or People’s Republic of China.

The relationship between Canada and China had soured during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, largely over accusations from Canada about foreign interference from China.

Before leaving Canada, Carney said he would raise foreign interference with Xi, prompting a Chinese government spokesperson to deny any such activities take place.

stories.title: Alert Ready will test national emergency alarm on Wednesday
stories.summary: Torontonians can expect to receive alerts over the phone, television and radio at 12:55 p.m. on Nov. 18.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
On Wednesday, Alert Ready will be testing Canada’s national emergency alert system. Torontonians can expect to receive alerts over the phone, television and radio at 12:55 p.m. on Nov. 18.

Alert Ready is used to notify Canadians of emergencies such as Amber Alerts, environmental hazards, national security threats, major fires, natural disasters and other threats to public safety.

stories.title: Peloza pitches changing how London’s committee chairs and vice-chairs chosen
stories.summary: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza wants to change how the chairs and vice-chairs of three standing committees at city hall are chosen, in a move that acknowledges Strong-Mayor Powers, but would give individual councillors a voice in the process.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Elizabeth Peloza wants to change how the chairs and vice-chairs of three standing committees at city hall are chosen, in a move that acknowledges Strong-Mayor Powers, but would give individual councillors a voice in the process.

Among the Strong-Mayor Powers given to Mayor Josh Morgan by the provincial government last term, was the legislative authority to appoint the chairs and vice-chairs of city hall’s standing committees.

However, Peloza’s motion recommends each standing committee be asked to nominate its own choices for the roles for appointment by Morgan.

“The mayor does have, and has used, his Strong-Mayor Powers to appoint the chairs of these committees. My motion would allow for a vote by all committee members to make the selection of chair and vice chair themselves,” she told CTV News.

Her motion would be restricted to three standing committees at city hall, the Infrastructure and Corporate Services Committee (Icsc), the Planning and Environment Committee (PEC), and the Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee.

Peloza believes giving each committee member a say in the decision would strengthen the sense of collaboration following last month’s election, “I believe this will help set the tone as the next four years for this council.”

Current policies require the deputy mayor to chair the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc), and the budget chair to lead the Budget Committee and Audit Committee.

Mayor Josh Morgan has responded to Peloza’s motion in a letter.

“I firmly believe it is important that Council and committee members have the opportunity to confirm their support for those serving in these roles,” he wrote prior to listing three councillors for consideration as standing committee chairs.

- Infrastructure and Corporate Services: Coun. Shawn Lewis

- Planning and Environment Committee: Coun. Skylar Franke

- Community and Protective Services Committee: Coun. Hadleigh McAlister

Morgan explained, “I am asking Sppc to consider and ratify these nominations before I formally exercise my appointment authority.”

He added, “I believe this motion allows chairs to know they have the support of their colleagues, and recognizes the importance of experience, stability and continuity as we begin a new term of Council.”

Peloza acknowledges the mayor has final authority, but believes her proposal is more collaborative.

“Recognizing Strong Mayor Powers are something he inherently has at any moment, [and] can use them or revoke any chair or vice chair, even if we decide to go this way,” she explained. “But it’s the spirit of collaboration I’m trying to get to.”

A council committee will consider Peloza’s motion, and the mayor’s letter, at a meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 17.

Morgan explained, “I am asking Sppc to consider and ratify these nominations before I formally exercise my appointment authority.”

He added, “I believe this motion allows chairs to know they have the support of their colleagues, and recognizes the importance of experience, stability and continuity as we begin a new term of Council.”
Peloza acknowledges the mayor has final authority, but believes her proposal is more collaborative.

“Recognizing Strong Mayor Powers are something he inherently has at any moment, [and] can use them or revoke any chair or vice chair, even if we decide to go this way,” she explained. “But it’s the spirit of collaboration I’m trying to get to.”
A council committee will consider Peloza’s motion, and the mayor’s letter, at a meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 17.

stories.title: Two senior Poilievre staffers decamp to BC Conservatives
stories.summary: Both say decision to join provincial team reflected desire to return home, have not lost confidence in Conservative Leader
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Two senior members of federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre ’s office are joining B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s team as the provincial Tories prepare take over the reins of government and Mr. Poilievre’s party struggles to gain momentum in opposition.

Mr. Poilievre’s director of communications, Micah Green, and his director of media relations, Sam Lilly, announced Monday they have taken positions with Mr. Doerkson’s government.

Both men have roots in British Columbia and said their decision to join the provincial Conservative team reflected a desire to return home. Mr. Green and his wife, Hayley Quipp – who also works Mr. Poilievre – are expecting their first child in the spring. The pair met knocking on doors for the federal party. Ms. Quipp is also leaving her job.

Both Mr. Lilly and Mr. Green said they have not lost confidence in Mr. Poilievre.

“Pierre has my full support. I believe he can win the next election, and I believe he would be an outstanding prime minister. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together,” Mr. Green said in a statement.

“This decision is about becoming a father, returning to my home province, and accepting an exceptional career opportunity.”

Staff switching between federal and provincial political parties isn’t uncommon, especially after an election.

But the exodus from Mr. Poilievre’s office also reflects the federal political landscape. Prime Minister Mark Carney now has a majority government, and the next chance for Mr. Poilievre to try for a victory with the electorate is likely three years away.

In a memo to caucus and staff sent late Monday announcing the staff changes, Mr. Poilievre’s chief of staff, Steve Outhouse, noted the pull of B.C. for federal staffers who hail from the province as he thanked the departing staff.

“Last month’s election of a Conservative government in British Columbia was exciting for the conservative movement,” he wrote in the memo, a copy of which was obtained by The Globe and Mail.

In addition to Mr. Green, Ms. Quipp and Mr. Lilly, Mr. Poilievre’s senior policy adviser Andrew Evans also announced his departure Monday for a role in the private sector.

Aaron Wudrick, Mr. Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff, told colleagues earlier this month that he’s leaving the office. Mr. Poilievre’s director of photography, John Lehmann, also departed this month.

The staff departures are on top of the loss of nine Conservative MPs since the 2025 election.

One MP stepped down so Mr. Poilievre could run in a by-election after losing his seat in the general election. Then, four crossed the floor to the Liberals, one quit and accepted a Senate appointment, one recently announced he’ll resign later this year, and two have already stepped down.

By-elections for the latter two seats – Yorkton–Melville in Saskatchewan and Brantford–Brant South in Ontario – are taking place next month.

The Saskatchewan seat is a Conservative stronghold, but the Ontario riding is expected to be a tougher fight for Mr. Poilievre’s party.

He appointed a candidate for the riding, but a long-time Conservative Party volunteer is running as independent, raising the potential for a vote split on the right.

Nationally, polls suggest the Poilievre Conservatives lag around 10 percentage points behind Mr. Carney’s Liberals.

Six Liberals have also resigned since the 2025 election, including former cabinet ministers Chrystia Freeland, Steven Guilbeault, Jonathan Wilkinson and Bill Blair. The latter two were given diplomatic appointments.

Mr. Poilievre’s staff are joining a team of seasoned operatives in British Columbia as the Doerksen government prepares to be sworn in on Friday.

The premier-designate’s chief of staff is Dimitri Pantazopoulos, a fixture in conservative politics for decades, and Angelo Isidorou is Mr. Doerkson’s principal secretary.

Mr. Isidorou served as executive director of the BC Conservative Party before resigning under the leadership of former party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Ms. Findlay stepped down just ahead of Premier David Eby’s decision to call an election. Mr. Doerkson became interim leader and beat Mr. Eby’s New Democrats. The BC Conservatives’ campaign director was Katy Merrifield, who had previously served as Mr. Poilievre’s director of communications.

She was replaced by Mr. Green after she had left Mr. Poilievre’s staff.

stories.title: ERs report overcrowding as flu cases continue to rapidly rise
stories.summary: Alberta, British Columbia and Yukon have the highest levels of flu activity, with Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and Quebec close behind
stories.author: Alanna Smith, Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Influenza season is well under way across Canada, but experts warn that the worst is yet to come as case counts barrel upward.

Don Vinh, an infectious-disease specialist at Montreal’s McGill University Health Centre, said the flu has “its own agenda” and there’s no telling when cases will peak. He said hospitals across the country will remain under intense strain from the flu for at least several weeks, if not months.

“We don’t know exactly when we’re going to hit our peak or how long we’ll be at that peak before things quiet down,” Dr. Vinh said. “This is the unknown that can cripple already fragile health care systems.”

The flu virus has hit Canada hard and fast with cases rapidly rising since the season officially started in early October, forcing some provinces to adjust vaccination plans. Nearly 14 per cent of flu tests came back positive in the week ending Nov. 7, according to the latest update from the Public Health Agency of Canada.

Since Aug. 30, according to Phac, roughly 16,500 flu cases have been detected in Canada, the majority being Influenza A, which matches this season’s vaccine. Alberta, British Columbia and Yukon have the highest levels of flu activity, with Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and Quebec close behind.

Data on previous viral periods show that the 2023-24 and 2025-26 flu seasons began in late November, with peaks in early January. The 2024-25 season didn’t officially begin until mid-December and peaked in late February, underscoring how early this season is.

Emergency departments already overflowing with patients are now being packed further with flu cases. In Montreal, for example, hospital emergency wards were running at 150 per cent of their stretcher capacity on Monday, according to Quebec’s Index Santé website.

On Monday afternoon, Montreal hospitals had an intake of 654 patients requiring stretchers, but only had 435 functional gurneys. This left 219 people to wait on hallway stretchers. Non-urgent patients on stretchers had to wait an average of more than 18 hours at Montreal General Hospital and more than 39 hours at Lakeshore General.

Health authority Santé Québec issued a statement last Thursday acknowledging the impact of respiratory infectious diseases and urging sick people to consider other options in lieu of visiting emergency departments, such as calling medical hotlines.

Emergency physician Raghu Venugopal, who works at three Toronto hospitals, said Ontario’s situation is also dire. He said about 20 per cent of patients he has seen in recent weeks, both young and old, are presenting with influenza-like illnesses. Meanwhile, EDs in the region are seeing record-breaking numbers and what he called “insane” wait times.

“It is a train rolling to the cliff and the whole thing comes crashing down as usual between, say, Christmas and school starting again for the kids,” Dr. Venugopal said. “That period is going to be, I think at least in Toronto, where I’m most confident, extremely messy.”

Patients will have to wait even longer for care, he added, and some will leave without being seen, putting them at greater risk of harm. “Our cardinal sin remains, we just don’t have beds,” Dr. Venugopal said.

Ontario’s flu activity is still considered low in comparison with other provinces, reaching a 7.7-per-cent positivity for the week ending Nov. 7, according to provincial data. In neighbouring Quebec, the province’s public health institute reported a 12.2-per-cent flu rate for the same week.

Roughly one year earlier, Quebec’s flu rate was 3.6 per cent.

Quebec is the only Canadian province to end universal flu vaccine coverage this season. Only certain vulnerable Quebeckers – including people 65 and over, patients with certain chronic conditions, pregnant women and nursing home residents – can still get vaccinated at no charge.

Lower vaccination rates across Canada have contributed to viral spread, Dr. Vinh said. Making matters worse, vaccine campaigns launched a “little too late” this season, he said, as flu cases popped up earlier than expected.

Even when the vaccine became available in Montreal, appointments were booked up quickly, Dr. Vinh said, leaving some more vulnerable people at increased risk while they waited for their shot. Others aren’t getting vaccinated because they believe it isn’t effective, he added.

Dr. Vinh stressed that reports from Canada and the United States indicate this year’s vaccine is between a 95-per-cent and 100-per-cent match for the circulating strains. Even a mismatch – like last year’s vaccine – still protects against serious complications and hospitalization.

“If you have a time machine, I’d say go back a few weeks and get it,” Dr. Vinh said. “But if you don’t have a time machine, now would be the second-best time.”

stories.title: Witness testifies that accused was angry with the victim moments before being set ablaze
stories.summary: When he testified, Robert Beasley told a London, Ont. courtroom that he had a close relationship with both 29-year-old Jonathan Graham and the accused in this case, 36-year-old Bradley Joudrey.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
When he testified, Robert Beasley told a London, Ont. courtroom that he had a close relationship with both 29-year-old Jonathan Graham and the accused in this case, 36-year-old Bradley Joudrey.

He said he was with them both on July 12, 2022, when they got into an altercation at an after hours hangout in east London, saying, “Jon and Brad got into a fight. I think it had something to do with a girl ... Jon punched Brad.”

He continued, “Brad takes it and is pissed off ... he had been drinking.”

Beasley said he ended up leaving and so did the accused.

When they met up later, he said Joudrey was on the phone with Graham’s brother saying, “That fer’s going to get it, that fer’s going to die.”

Beasley said when they got to Joudrey’s shared apartment on Hilton Avenue, he saw the accused doing something, “I went outside, I remember it smelled like gasoline at the side of the house.”

The Crown’s theory is that Graham and Joudrey met at a convenience store parking lot at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street minutes after the altercation.

The victim was doused with gasoline and set on fire. He died in hospital from thermal injuries.

Joudrey sped away and crash his vehicle along Royal Crescent.

Officers found his identification inside the silver Dodge Journey.

Within minutes, Joudrey was arrested and he has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder.

Earlier in the day, Tabetha Passmore testified that she rented her basement to Joudrey at the time.

She said the accused woke her up in the middle of that July night, “All he (Joudrey) was yelling was, ‘I crashed the car.’”

The trial, which is now into its second week, resumes on Tuesday.

stories.title: Recreation funding, ice rental fee increases criticized in Calgary’s proposed budget
stories.summary: The City of Calgary's upcoming four-year budget proposal includes potential increases to ice time fees for youth sports like hockey, figure skating and ringette.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
How much Calgary is planning to spend on sports and recreation, as well as some rising costs, has the upcoming four-year budget proposal drawing the ire of some minor sports organizations.

The criticism comes ahead of budget deliberations, which are set to begin with a public hearing on Nov. 23, after the spending plan was made public last week.

According to the city, the budget proposal includes $284 million to fund projects though the GamePLAN strategy including including the Forest Lawn recreation facility replacement, Kingsland and Belmont athletic parks and a reaffirmed commitment to the city’s portion of the Foothills Fieldhouse.

Another $66 million is earmarked to maintain arenas, aquatic centres and the Calgary Soccer Centre. However, the Calgary Minor Soccer Association (Cmsa) believes the budget misses the mark when it comes to addressing facility shortages across the city.

“We’re extremely disappointed not to see any funding for indoor facilities, in particular the Rocky Ridge Fieldhouse and design funding for the Southland Fieldhouse,” Cmsa executive director Carlo Bruneau told Global News.

The Rocky Ridge Fieldhouse is listed as one of 17 prioritized projects in the first wave of GamePLAN, the city’s investment strategy for recreation and sports facilities.

According to Bruneau, the city had already committed funding for preliminary design work for the project, and its construction costs are estimated to be just over $70 million.

“For Cmsa alone, it would allow 3,000 more kids to play soccer, it would allow us to have over 200 more soccer teams and over 1,500 more games per year,” he said.

“That impact for us is transformational, and really at the end of the day it’s a small investment for the city in the grand scheme of things.”

However, Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said there’s limited room for additional investment in the budget proposal due to a lengthy list of projects and spending set to cost $21 billion over the next four years, for things like water infrastructure, roads, and transit.

“We are so leveraged out when it comes to our commitments that we can’t possibly take on any more,” he told reporters Monday.

“I know everyone wants us to do more, but the problem is we’ve already committed ourselves to too much.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I know everyone wants us to do more, but the problem is we've already committed ourselves to too much."

Chabot was part of the previous council that approved the GamePLAN strategy, including a funding commitment of up to $250 million annually for recreation infrastructure entitled “Making Waves.”

The representative from Ward 10, who instead voted for a lower funding stream of up to $150 million annually, said the commitment was “too far reaching.”

Ward 3 Coun. Andrew Yule, meanwhile, agreed the proposed spending in the budget falls short to address the capacity issues at local sports and recreation facilities.

“We’re not making waves with this budget,” Yule said. “Phase 1 of GamePLAN is barely scraping the surface of what we need for recreation in Calgary.”

The price to play could also increase under the proposed budget, with a number of fee increases scheduled over the four-year plan.

According to the proposal, rental fees for athletic fields and artificial turf field are set to rise nearly 10 per cent over the next four years.

Ice rentals are also set to increase with minor prime time slots proposed to jump from $230.30 to $270.83 in 2027, and minor non-prime time slots could rise from $82.30 to $133.33 next year.

Kevin Kobelka, executive director of Hockey Calgary, told Global News the proposed fee increases came as a shock, with no warning or engagement with city officials prior to the budget’s release.

Kobelka said city rates for ice times are typically lower than private facilities, but the move could have a significant impact on the organization, as well as for figure skating and ringette.

“Sixty-five to 70 per cent of the cost of youth hockey is ice costs, so we’ll have to pass this on,” he said. “We’re a non-profit organization — if there’s going to be a 17 per cent price increase on ice, then that’s going to have to go to the end user.”

When asked about the proposed increases, Chabot said the hikes that could impact youth sports “is not the direction to go.”

“When it comes to promoting active lifestyles, especially to our youth, those are the people we should not be targeting insofar as increasing their fees,” he said.

“Surely we can recover those costs from other user groups.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Surely we can recover those costs from other user groups."

stories.title: New bone-density scanner at Parkwood Institute expected to reduce wait times for osteoporosis patients
stories.summary: A new bone-density scanner at Parkwood Institute is expected to reduce wait times for patients at risk of osteoporosis while opening the door to new research.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A new bone-density scanner at Parkwood Institute is expected to reduce wait times for patients at risk of osteoporosis while opening the door to new research.

The second DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) machine at St. Joseph’s Health Care London is expected to double the organization’s scanning capacity, helping patients receive a diagnosis and treatment sooner.

For Londoner Jan Saddy, regular bone-density scans have been an important part of monitoring her health.

“I was diagnosed with osteopenia, which is how it all starts. And then, as I would get an annual bone mineral density test and progressed, and now I have osteoporosis,” Saddy said.

Osteopenia is a condition in which bone density is lower than normal, while osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more susceptible to fractures.

The new scanner at Parkwood Institute will work alongside the existing machine at St. Joseph’s Hospital. The two machines are cross-calibrated, allowing specialists to compare results regardless of where a patient receives their scan.

“This machine at Parkwood is cross calibrated with the one at St. Joseph’s Hospital, which means we’ve basically doubled our capacity to be able to scan patients,” said Dr. Jenny Thain, a geriatrician at St. Joseph’s.

DXA technology uses low-dose X-rays to measure bone density and assess a person’s risk of fractures. Thain says osteoporosis is a common but often undetected condition because it does not typically cause symptoms until someone experiences a fracture.

“Osteoporosis is an incredibly common condition. So one in three women and one in five men will suffer a fracture at some point in their lifetime,” Thain said. “People often don’t know that they have it until they’ve either suffered what we call a fragility fracture, or if they have a bone-density scan.”

The new scanning suite is also designed to improve access for patients with significant mobility challenges, including those recovering from strokes or spinal cord injuries. It includes a body-lift system to help accommodate patients who May have difficulty transferring onto the scanning equipment.

Beyond patient care, the technology is expected to support research into fracture risks among populations that are often underrepresented in clinical studies.

Dr. Jamie Fleet, a physiatrist and researcher, says having the scanner at Parkwood will allow researchers to expand their work with patients who have complex mobility needs.

“Through having the Dexa here at Parkwood, we’re going to be able to do more research studies on these underserved populations that aren’t normally included in research studies,” Fleet said.

The scanner was acquired as both a clinical and research tool through the Gray Centre for Mobility and Activity, with support from a gift made by philanthropists William and Lynne Gray through the St. Joseph’s Health Care Foundation.

Appointments for a bone-density scan require a referral from a primary-care provider.

The new scanner at Parkwood Institute will work alongside the existing machine at St. Joseph’s Hospital. The two machines are cross-calibrated, allowing specialists to compare results regardless of where a patient receives their scan.

“This machine at Parkwood is cross calibrated with the one at St. Joseph’s Hospital, which means we’ve basically doubled our capacity to be able to scan patients,” said Dr. Jenny Thain, a geriatrician at St. Joseph’s.

DXA technology uses low-dose X-rays to measure bone density and assess a person’s risk of fractures. Thain says osteoporosis is a common but often undetected condition because it does not typically cause symptoms until someone experiences a fracture.

content_blocks.caption: New DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) machine at Parkwood Institute in London, Ont. on Nov. 16, 2026. (Reta Ismail/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: “Osteoporosis is an incredibly common condition. So one in three women and one in five men will suffer a fracture at some point in their lifetime,” Thain said. “People often don’t know that they have it until they’ve either suffered what we call a fragility fracture, or if they have a bone-density scan.”

The new scanning suite is also designed to improve access for patients with significant mobility challenges, including those recovering from strokes or spinal cord injuries. It includes a body-lift system to help accommodate patients who May have difficulty transferring onto the scanning equipment.
Beyond patient care, the technology is expected to support research into fracture risks among populations that are often underrepresented in clinical studies.
Dr. Jamie Fleet, a physiatrist and researcher, says having the scanner at Parkwood will allow researchers to expand their work with patients who have complex mobility needs.
“Through having the Dexa here at Parkwood, we’re going to be able to do more research studies on these underserved populations that aren’t normally included in research studies,” Fleet said.

The scanner was acquired as both a clinical and research tool through the Gray Centre for Mobility and Activity, with support from a gift made by philanthropists William and Lynne Gray through the St. Joseph’s Health Care Foundation.
Appointments for a bone-density scan require a referral from a primary-care provider.

stories.title: Several staffers leaving Poilievre's office weeks after B.C. election
stories.summary: Ottawa - Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is losing five more staff members, including his deputy chief of staff and two of his senior communications aides.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Five staff members are leaving the office of Opposition Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, including his deputy chief of staff and two of his senior communications aides.

Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff, Aaron Wudrick, confirmed he told his colleagues last week he had accepted an opportunity in the private sector and will be leaving his position on Nov. 27.

“I want to thank all of you for your co-operation and hard work in our shared mission to make Pierre Poilievre our next prime minister leading a Conservative government, and remain fully confident that this goal remains achievable in the next election,” he said in an email to the Conservative caucus and Poilievre’s office.

“I will miss life on Parliament Hill and working with all of you, but am looking forward to a new challenge that will allow me to spend more time with my family.”

Wudrick is leaving after nearly three years in the role.

Media relations director Sam Lilly is departing after spending six years working in the Opposition leader’s office, including since Poilievre became leader in 2022. Lilly said he is moving to British Columbia to join the new provincial Conservative government that is being sworn in later this week.

“My roots are in British Columbia. It’s where I grew up, graduated high school, joined the military and formed some of my fondest family memories,” said Lilly. “After a wonderful career that has taken me across our great country, it is time to come home and be a part of the team that will build British Columbia’s brightest days ahead.

“Pierre has made a difference to this country, he continues to have my support and I know that our team will continue the work of ensuring he is the next prime minister of Canada.”

Poilievre’s office also confirmed CBC and CTV reports that communications director Micah Green is also joining the B.C. government, and that executive assistant Hayley Quipp and senior policy adviser Andrew Evans are also both leaving.

These departures signal a significant shakeup in Poilievre’s inner circle and come after the departures of longtime chief of staff Ian Todd in May, and former communications director Katy Merrifield, who left to return to B.C. in April.

Merrifield was the campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives in the recent provincial election, which saw that party oust the NDP from government, after former premier David Eby called a snap election.

The latest departures also come just a few weeks before voters head to the polls in six federal byelections in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan.

Wudrick joined Poilievre’s team as a policy adviser in 2024, and moved into the deputy chief of staff role in May when Todd announced his retirement. When he started, the Conservatives were well ahead of the Liberals in the polls and appeared poised to win a large majority government in the next federal election.

That lead evaporated in a matter of weeks in the winter of 2025, after former prime minister Justin Trudeau announced his departure and Mark Carney joined the race to replace him. Carney won that contest and led the Liberals to a minority government in April 2025, the fourth consecutive election loss for the Conservatives.

A year later, Carney turned his minority into a majority, luring one NDP and four Conservative MPs to join his caucus. The Liberals also turned a fifth Conservative seat red earlier this year, winning a byelection in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, after Quebec MP Richard Martel resigned to take an appointment to the Senate.

The federal Conservatives have continued to drag in the polls well behind Carney and the Liberals, who have built a significant lead as he shepherds Canada’s response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation.

Evans joined the Opposition leader’s office around the same time as Wudrick, while Quipp has been Poilievre’s executive assistant since June 2023. Green has been part of Poilievre’s communication team since 2022, and was promoted to director in April, when Merrifield departed.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario’s safer supply changes paused due to legal challenge
stories.summary: Sweeping changes to the safer supply prescription regime were set to come into effect on Monday
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario says it was served with the legal action on Friday, which includes a motion for an injunction to prevent the regulator from enforcing the new safer supply rules.

The changes were set to come into effect on Monday, but the college says it’s pausing enforcement to allow time to respond to the injunction.

The college approved sweeping changes to the safer supply prescription regime last month that would require doctors to prescribe safer supply drugs only in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.

Safer supply drugs are medications given to people at high risk of overdose as an alternative to illicit opioids while opioid agonist therapy uses medications such as Suboxone and methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The new rules would also require patients to take their safer supply medications in front of health-care professionals, rather than take them home – a change that has raised accessibility concerns especially for patients in rural Ontario and those who work regular hours.

The medical regulator has said the changes were approved in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids prescribed as safer supply drugs making their way to the streets.

The chair of the regulator’s board, Dr. Patrick Safieh, has said police forces in Ontario are noticing patients’ safer supply drugs being diverted to the black market.

stories.title: How 3D printed puppets from Western are helping baby raptors in distress
stories.summary: Young birds of prey found to be in distress are unable to feed themselves.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Young birds of prey found to be in distress are unable to feed themselves.

However, handfeeding them yourself May not be the best solution either.

“They see you as Mom,” explained Brian Salt, founder of the Strathroy area Salthaven Rehabilitation and Education Centre .

“That’s a fail, as far as we’re concerned because you can’t release them like that because they relate to people more than they relate to their own kind,” he further explained.

The solution May lie in realistic 3D printed hand-puppets. The Western University Faculty of Engineering has produced four new feeding puppets to help caregivers at Salthaven feed young raptors, reducing the birds’ contact with people.

“The arm goes right up in the sleeve, and then we use these forceps that go into the back there, and we can put food in there, and then we can feed the babies,” said Salt, while demonstrating how the puppets work.

“This is far outside the realm of what mechanical engineers typically think they’re going to do in their career,” said Ryan Willing, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at Western.

Willing says the design came from Joel Sierra, a visiting undergrad student from Peru.

“He started the process by finding actual photographs of the birds that Brian wanted heads for. And he found some software that you could use to actually turn those images into 3D models,” Willing explained.

A local artist then pained the heads and canvas sleeves to match each species.

According to Salthaven, baby raptors often fall out of trees and out of their nests in the springtime, often caused by a windstorm, or other extraneous events. They’ll have little chance of survival if they’re not scooped up and brought somewhere to be nursed and fed.

Salt says they’re looking forward to trying out the puppets next year when any number of baby birds in distress find their way to the rehab centre.

“If anybody out there finds baby raptors in the spring, they can feel comfortable that we can handle the baby raptors without imprinting them and be able to release them into their natural environment again so they can take care of themselves,” Salt said.

Salt says if you find a bird, you can contact Salthaven to make arrangements for it to be brought in for feeding and rehab.

stories.title: Canada is heading for a record corn crop. So why could prices rise?
stories.summary: Farmers and grain buyers on Prince Edward Island are facing both a late and expensive harvest, even as Canada heads for record corn production.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Belfast, P.E.I. – Farmers and grain buyers on Prince Edward Island are facing both a late and expensive harvest, even as Canada heads for record corn production.

Rain in late summer and early fall delayed maturity, pushing harvesting back by weeks. While the moisture helped plants grow after last year’s drought, grey skies and soggy fields have made the work more challenging.

“Everybody’s trying to get the job done before weather prohibits them (from) getting their crop in,” said Robert MacDonald, chair of the Atlantic Grains Council.

MacDonald said corn sold to feed mills must have a moisture level no higher than 15.5 per cent. Normally harvested at around 25 to 28 per cent, some of this year’s grain is coming in at more than 32 per cent, requiring considerably more time to dry.

Charges have nearly doubled, from about $40 per tonne last year, to $75 to $80 this year, according to MacDonald.

‘An expensive corn harvest’

High propane and electricity prices are adding to the bill for buyers like Mary van den Broek-Grant. She co-owns and manages Cardigan Feed Services, which purchases and sells grain, cleans seed and supplies agricultural products.

“This is going to be an expensive corn harvest. And the price of corn will be expensive this year,” van den Broek-Grant said.

For her business, higher prices mean keeping more cash on hand. Her customers, including livestock producers raising cattle and hogs, will also feel the pressure. There’s only so much they can get for their animals in the marketplace, making it harder to turn a profit when feed prices rise.

There’s also a shortage of drying infrastructure. Van den Broek-Grant estimates there are about 20 dryers across P.E.I., some owned by farmers, while grain is also sent off-Island.

“There’s not nearly enough drying capacity on P.E.I. for this,” she said.

She’s concerned that if grain elevators in Nova Scotia stop operating next year, Island producers could be in “big trouble.”

Shorter, darker days bring safety concerns too, with farmers working from early morning until late at night. Safety is one of van den Broek-Grant’s biggest concerns.

MacDonald said climate change May be working in farmers’ favour this time, with recent Decembers bringing little to no snow.

“If we keep weather like this, the corn will get harvested,” he said.

Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada is forecasting a record 16.6 million tonnes of corn nationally this year, up 11 per cent from 2025.

Its benchmark cash price is also projected to rise from $233 a tonne in 2025-26 to $255 in 2026-27, largely reflecting expectations for higher U.S. corn prices.

stories.title: Edmonton Elks want ‘City of Champions’ signs to return
stories.summary: The Edmonton Elks are champions again, and they want their city to show it.
stories.author: John Korobanik
stories.content:
The Edmonton Elks are champions again, and they want their city to show it.

Basking in the glory of Sunday’s Grey Cup victory — Edmonton’s first since 2015 — members of the Elks, from management to players, continued calling for a return of the City of Champions signs that once welcomed people to Alberta’s capital.

“The City of Champions is back,” proclaimed linebacker Nick Anderson, sustaining the call quarterback Cody Fajardo made after the Elks’ 37-30 win over the Montreal Alouettes in the CFL championship game.

Elks general manager Ed Hervey wondered why the signs were ever taken down as the team had arrived back at Commonwealth Stadium on Monday afternoon.

“See, here’s the reality for me. I always believe once you’re a champion, you’re always a champion,” he said.

“If you look at the Grey Cup and you look on there… Edmonton, those champions are still there … obviously the Oilers won their championships. I didn’t know it was the city of most recent champions. That’s not what the sign ever said, right?

“So, with that being said … put it back and let it be,” he said, pointing to the 15 Grey Cup championships the city now has, to go along with the five Stanley Cup wins by the Oilers.

The city first put up the signs in 1988 to honour championship victories by the then-named Eskimos, the Oilers, the Edmonton Grads basketball team, university championships and the city’s response to a devastating tornado in 1987.

The six signs marking the entrances to the city were removed in the spring of 2015.

Overnight, someone posted a temporary “City of Champions” sign on the southern entrance to the city on Monday, but mayor Andrew Knack told reporters the signs are still in the archives.

Head coach Mark Kilam, clutching the Grey Cup like he was never letting it go, said the Elks have taken one step towards bringing back the signs.

“There’s one more team that’s going to handle their business, and I know they will,” he said of the Oilers, who last won the Stanley Cup in 1990.

While it May take more than just one national championship to see the signs resurrected, Hervey said the Elks have the players and the program to be long-term Grey Cup contenders.

“Average age of this roster, we’re the youngest in the CFL,” Hervey said.

A mixture of youth and veterans, combined with the type of players on the roster now and in the future, and maintaining continuity will lead to continued success, Hervey said.

“We talked about continuity at the start of the year and continuing to build that,” he said. “And our goal is to do that. And as long as we have buy-in and there are people who see Edmonton as a destination we believe that we can be a force in this league for quite some time.”

Kilam said that while he would like to just enjoy the victory for a few more days, “you know we’re gonna continue to build. You know we’re just getting started here.”

Kilam said winning one championship is difficult to do, and it was a lot of hard work by a lot of people in the organization.

“And that’s why it’s so special, because this is representative of so many people on so many levels of this organization, putting in the time and buying into what we’re trying to do and what (president) Chris (Morris) is saying, what Ed is saying, you know, and representing the Thompson family. So that’s really what this is representative of.”

stories.title: Officers won't be charged after man suffers broken collarbone during arrest: SIU
stories.summary: Ontario’s police watchdog says it found no reasonable grounds to criminally charge Waterloo regional police officers in relation to a man’s broken collarbone during his arrest over the summer.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s police watchdog says it found no reasonable grounds to criminally charge Waterloo regional police officers in relation to a man’s broken collarbone during his arrest over the summer.

The Special Investigations Unit says officers observed a man committing an alleged traffic violation while riding a bike in the area of Duke Street West and Victoria Street North in Kitchener on July 24.

stories.title: Ford holds off on new cash for Stellantis plant, contradicting minister
stories.summary: Doug Ford's minister responsible for the tariffs response said the province is willing to offer Stellantis additional financial support to stay in Brampton.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford is tamping down suggestions that Ontario taxpayers might offer Stellantis even more funding to keep the Brampton auto assembly plant running, contradicting his own economic development minister, who said provincial funds are on the table.

Days after a face-to-face meeting with the auto maker, federal government and Unifor, Ford addressed the issue for the first time, ON Monday, and said the province is willing to entertain options that would keep the plant in operation.

“If they’re making sure that they’re going to employ three, four thousand people, then we’d sit down and have a discussion with them,” Ford told Global News. “We want to make sure that Stellantis hires back the people that they let go. Simple as that.”

In order to scuttle the sale, Ford’s minister responsible for the tariffs response said the province and federal governments are willing to offer the company additional financial support to stay in Brampton.

“We need Stellantis to keep the plant open, keep it warm and keep it ready for a new model,” Vic Fedeli told the Ontario legislature.

“Our plan is to meet with Stellantis’ global CEO in the coming weeks, where we will bring our message to him directly. We have the supports in place; we announced them weeks ago—$2.5 billion. Those supports are in place to keep these companies exactly where they are today.”

That $2.5 billion fund – a billion of which comes from Ontario taxpayers – offers automotive companies capital investments to prepare factories for “connected and electrified vehicles.”

While Fedeli didn’t say how much could be available to Stellantis, Ford suggested he’s not willing to put up any cash for now.

“I’m not confirming we’re going to offer money. The federal government will be sitting at the table with Stellantis like they have been the whole time,” Ford said.

The premier pointed out that while the province offered Stellantis $132 million in 2022 to help the automaker retool its facilities, the company received “absolutely nothing” from the province.

The company has received $55 million from provincial taxpayers to upgrade the Windsor plant, the government said.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles accused the government of allowing the situation to worsen.

“I don’t see any sense of urgency here,” Stiles said in the legislature. “The Premier loves a camera when he gets to pat himself on the back, but when it comes to standing up for workers, he is missing in action every single time.”

“Three thousand good union jobs are at stake here. At least 30,000 spin-off jobs all gone because this premier was asleep at the wheel.”

“I’m not confirming we’re going to offer money. The federal government will be sitting at the table with Stellantis like they have been the whole time,” Ford said.
The premier pointed out that while the province offered Stellantis $132 million in 2022 to help the automaker retool its facilities, the company received “absolutely nothing” from the province.
The company has received $55 million from provincial taxpayers to upgrade the Windsor plant, the government said.
NDP Leader Marit Stiles accused the government of allowing the situation to worsen.

“I don’t see any sense of urgency here,” Stiles said in the legislature. “The Premier loves a camera when he gets to pat himself on the back, but when it comes to standing up for workers, he is missing in action every single time.”
“Three thousand good union jobs are at stake here. At least 30,000 spin-off jobs all gone because this premier was asleep at the wheel.”

stories.title: Four more staff leave Pierre Poilievre's office, with two joining B.C. Conservatives
stories.summary: Departures comes at a tense moment for Pierre Poilievre, with much-watched byelection looming.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — At least four more staffers in Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s office are heading for the door, marking the largest exit from his staffing ranks since losing last year’s election.

Two of those leaving are Poilievre’s director of communications Micah Green along with Green’s wife Hayley Quipp, who also works in Poilievre’s office as his executive assistant and scheduler. Sam Lilly, Poilievre’s director of media relations, who has worked in that office under various leaders since 2021, is also departing.

Green and Lilly, who are both originally from British Columbia, will be moving to work for the newly elected B.C. Conservative government , led by incoming premier Lorne Doerkson. It comes as those inside Poilievre’s office are bracing for more potential departures to B.C., mainly among junior staff. In an email to the party’s caucus on Monday, the same day the current spate of exits were finalized, Steve Outhouse, his chief of staff and the party’s next campaign manager, pointed to that win to account for the departures.

“Last month’s election of a Conservative government in British Columbia was exciting for the conservative movement. As the BC Conservatives get ready to take the helm of the province, they are building a team, and that is obviously of particular interest to Conservatives across the country who hail from British Columbia, who are keen to bring about change in their home province,” he wrote in the email, obtained by the Star.

Outhouse also confirmed the exit of Poilievre’s senior policy adviser, Andrew Evans, who was leaving to work elsewhere in the private sector.

“More information about new team members will follow in due course,” he wrote.

The departures come after Aaron Wudrick, Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff who first entered his office as a policy director more than two years ago, announced earlier this month that he would be leaving to take a private-sector job.

In a statement at the time, Wudrick told MPs and fellow colleagues that “it had been an honour and a privilege to serve” Poilievre. He added that he was “fully confident” that the goal of making Poilievre Canada’s next prime minister “remains fully achievable in the next election.”

The spate of departures comes at a tense moment for Poilievre, as Conservatives watch to see whether he will be able to hold onto an Ontario seat the party has held for the past 18 years in an upcoming byelection on Dec. 7.

That race in Brantford-Brant South is expected to be a fight for the Conservatives, who have won it comfortably for years. Outhouse has been on the ground for that race, along with a flurry of Conservative MPs who have been out door-knocking.

With some on Poilievre’s team looking to work within B.C.‘s new Conservative government — a chance that came up earlier than expected, thanks to the snap election called by former NDP premier David Eby — McKenzie Kibler, who joined Poilievre’s office after last year’s election, left as his issues management director earlier this summer to return to working for Alberta’s United Conservative Party government.

Poilievre’s office has struggled to retain staff since last year’s election, with the first several months spent looking to replace those who left, including his former director of communications, Ben Woodfinden.

Katy Merrifield, who held that job until earlier this year, left and went on to steer the B.C. Conservatives to victory along with former members of Poilievre’s staff and leadership team, including Woodfinden and Anthony Koch.

Earlier this year Poilievre also saw the resignation of his longtime chief of staff Ian Todd, who had been in that job since shortly after Poilievre won the leadership in 2022.

Questions have swirled for months about Poilievre’s leadership within caucus and the wider party as successive public opinion polls show the Conservatives trailing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals. Poilievre has lost a total of eight MPs since the last election, four through defections to the Liberals, three to resignations and one who was appointed to the Senate.

Liberals' 'lawful access' bill vulnerable to constitutional challenge: professor

stories.title: Liberals’ ‘lawful access’ bill vulnerable to constitutional challenge: professor
stories.summary: Ottawa — A law professor says a Liberal government bill that would make it easier for police and spies to navigate the online world could be found unconstitutional due to a provision on retaining metadata.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A law professor says a Liberal government bill that would make it easier for police and spies to navigate the online world could be found unconstitutional due to a provision on retaining metadata.

The “lawful access” bill would require service providers to keep metadata — digital traces of a communication, but not the email or text itself — for up to six months.

The government agreed to shorten the period, which was originally up to one year, after expressions of concern.

On Monday, University of Ottawa law professor Michael Geist told a Senate committee studying the bill the provision remains “constitutionally vulnerable with little evidence of its necessity.”

Geist said metadata May not include the content of a message, but it tells a story: who we contact, when, where and from what device.

The government says the bill will ensure law enforcement has the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians in a manner consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Opponents argue the legislation unnecessarily expands the powers of police and intelligence agencies, endangering the privacy of Canadians, flouting the Charter and placing unreasonable demands on companies.

Geist said police seeking access to metadata can use existing Criminal Code provisions allowing targeted preservation and production orders tied to a specific investigation with judicial oversight.

He said the bill’s metadata regime should be removed. Failing that, requiring metadata retention for up to 30 days would address the concerns about meeting immediate investigative needs prior to obtaining a preservation order, Geist said.

Tamir Israel, director of the privacy, surveillance and technology program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, also called on Monday for removal of the data retention regime, or at least limiting it to apply only to data already under the control of telecommunication providers.

The bill would require electronic service providers to develop and maintain the technical capabilities necessary to enable police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to effectively obtain communications and information for investigations.

Critics of the legislation say it could allow the government to force companies to break encryption by inserting backdoors into their products.

Israel told the senators the bill “effectively grants the government a blank cheque to impose its evolving surveillance objectives onto electronic service providers in secret.”

Earlier this month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the Senate committee the bill “is not about weakening privacy protections. It is not about surveillance. It is not about creating backdoors to Canadians’ private communications.”

In addition to the shorter metadata retention period, a House of Commons committee adopted a safeguard clarifying that electronic service providers would not be required to comply with an order if it would introduce a systemic vulnerability in their services or prevent them from fixing one.

Robyn Greene, director of privacy and public policy at Meta Platforms, the company behind Facebook, told the senators Monday the company provides end-to-end encrypted services to help Canadians protect their most sensitive information.

“It is not technically feasible to give law enforcement backdoor access to encrypted data without introducing a vulnerability that malicious actors will exploit,” Greene said.

“Simply stated, forcing service providers like Meta to break, weaken, circumvent or undermine encryption would significantly harm Canadians’ privacy, cybersecurity, economic and national security.”

Greene said the government’s well-intentioned amendments do not achieve their goal.

“We also remain concerned the technical order authorities could force providers to install government or third-party spyware onto our systems.”

In addition, Greene said, the metadata retention obligations “treat all Canadians as potential criminal suspects.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Longtime Maritime broadcaster Todd Veinotte dies at 57
stories.summary: Long-time Maritime media personality and former Global News reporter, Todd Veinotte, has died at the age of 57.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Long-time Maritime media personality and former Global News reporter, Todd Veinotte , died Monday at the age of 57, following a battle with Parkinson’s disease.

His wife, Kelly Gillis Arsenault Veinotte, confirmed his passing in a social media post .

“Todd and I found each other later in life, and from the beginning, there was something so special about us,” she wrote in a tribute to her late husband.

“We May not have had decades together, but the love, laughter, adventures and memories we packed into our time together could have filled a lifetime.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We May not have had decades together, but the love, laughter, adventures and memories we packed into our time together could have filled a lifetime."

Veinotte was a veteran journalist and broadcaster with more than 30 years of experience in television, radio, and podcasting.

He joined Global News in 2018 as a videojournalist and was based in Saint John, N.B.

Veinotte was a familiar voice to Maritimers as the host of The Todd Veinotte Show. He later hosted a twice-weekly podcast.

In recent years, he spoke about his Parkinson’s diagnosis and adjusting to the “new reality.”

Parkinson’s is a disorder of the central nervous system that mainly affects one’s motor functions. The condition causes gradual damage to parts of a person’s brain, resulting in numerous symptoms, including tremors, slow movement, and stiff and inflexible muscles.

More than 120,000 people in Canada live with Parkinson’s, according to Parkinson Canada.

While there is currently no cure, medications can help manage symptoms and treatments such as physiotherapy, speech therapy and exercise can play a vital role in improving quality of life, according to the organization.

Arsenault Veinotte said Parkinson’s disease is cruel and it slowly took so much from a man who had so much life left to live.

But, she added she was incredibly grateful for the time they had, saying it was a privilege to be his wife.

“Parkinson’s never took away the man I fell in love with,” she wrote in her post. “His humour, his intelligence, his love of music, his stubbornness, and that wonderful ability to make me laugh when I least expected it.

“I don’t want our story to be remembered for how it ended. I want it to be remembered for how beautifully we lived it.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I don't want our story to be remembered for how it ended. I want it to be remembered for how beautifully we lived it."

Funeral details for Veinotte have not yet been released.

With a file from Katie Scott, Global News

stories.title: Proposed Saint John data centre could generate tax windfall, critics unconvinced
stories.summary: The study on the proposed Spruce Lake data centre was commissioned by Beacon Data Centers, the company behind the proposal alongside U.S.-based VoltaGrid.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
A proposed data centre in Saint John, N.B. could bring in tens of millions of dollars in property taxes annually, but while the potential windfall has the city’s mayor encouraged, it’s also begging the question of how realistic those projections are.

And there are concerns about what the city would have to give up in return if the controversial project goes ahead.

The study on the proposed Spruce Lake data centre was commissioned by Beacon Data Centers, the company behind the proposal alongside U.S.-based VoltaGrid.

The report estimates Saint John would receive $25 million annually in taxes and the province would receive $18 million each year.

“I was shocked to hear the number,” said Mayor Donna Reardon.

“And that’s just for the building, that’s without machinery and equipment, which is not taxable in the province of New Brunswick currently.”

Similar to some other jurisdictions, Reardon wants the province to consider taxing equipment at new industrial sites, while also letting cities keep all heavy-industry tax revenue.

She says the money could repair aging pipes and roads, improve transit and parks and potentially even lower taxes for citizens.

Consultant David Campbell, who prepared the report, estimates a $1 billion taxable value for the nearly $6 billion project.

For the property tax assessment, he counted land, buildings and power infrastructure.

“There could be a variance by a few million dollars either way. It could end up being considerably higher or it could be slightly lower,” said Campbell, president of Jupia Consultants Inc.

“If somebody were to look at other data centres across the country they would see similar amounts.”

Service New Brunswick, which officially assesses properties, tells Global News it considers land, building size, construction, age, condition, replacement costs and market values in its assessments.

Its methodology depends on the property, available evidence and information from the owner.

The mayor says property taxes are vital for a city.

“Every municipality in New Brunswick can only generate money through property tax,” she said.

But a group of citizens opposed to the data centre project says the environment and health implications attached to the project are too high a price to pay.

“Our community stance is that no dollar value can compensate for what our community is actually losing,” said Chris Watson, a member of Save Lorneville.

Watson questions the results of noise and air-quality testing for the development, which would use both NB Power and on-site natural gas generation.

The study also forecasts 210 permanent jobs, and up to 2,900 construction jobs at the peak of the project.

In an email to Global News, Beacon Data Centers says the projected benefits depend on regulatory approvals and construction and adds that the final property assessment and tax bill will be determined by authorities.

stories.title: Guilty pleas entered in fatal beating of London man
stories.summary: Four people appeared in court Monday, charged in the death of a man from an incident in July 2024.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson, Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Four people appeared in court Monday, charged in the death of a man from an incident in July 2024.

In an agreed statement of facts, the court heard that 48-year-old Darko Lukic was beaten to death when confronted over a drug overdose at an apartment on Base Line Road.

The court also heard that Lukic had severe head trauma and a severe brain bleed caused by blunt force trauma after being beaten with a bat.

A victim impact statement from the victim’s family read, in part, “It (Lukic’s death) altered the lives of everyone who were close to him. We fear we May never fully recover from what happened.”

Dauntae Johnson and Joseph Mark Mercer Veneau were initially charged with first-degree murder, but pleaded guilty to manslaughter.

Both the Crown and the defence agreed on a five-year sentence for Johnson.

Mercer Veneau also pleaded guilty to assault with a weapon. His sentence is still to be determined on April 1, 2027.

Kerry Ann Bailey and Jamile-Lynn Bailey were charged with accessory after the fact to murder, and those charges were withdrawn.

stories.title: Western student entrepreneur builds promising tech startup to support founders
stories.summary: Western student entrepreneur Vinesh Nathan founded Formbase, a platform to help companies keep corporate records and be ready for fundraising
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
“If your ambition isn’t scaring you, it’s not big enough.”

Western student entrepreneur Vinesh Nathan lives by these words. Over the last year, the fifth-year software engineering student founded Formbase, an online platform that helps businesses automate the administrative and regulatory work of running a company.

“I want Canadian founders to be able to easily run their business, focus on their product and customers, and leave the housekeeping to us,” he said.

Rather than looking for a job after graduation this spring, Nathan plans to devote his full-time efforts to growing his company.

Vinesh Nathan

“If not now, then when am I ever going to do this? It’s the best time to be a student taking business risks,” he said. “We have access to some of the greatest tools at Western, nearly for free, and so much opportunity.”

Nathan will be able to build momentum before he graduates, with his recent acceptance into the Western Accelerator, a 13-week program run by the Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship. The Accelerator offers funding, mentorship, workspaces and resources for scaling up a business. He starts in January, joining other Western students, alumni, faculty and staff who have founded high-potential ventures. Nathan says two startups, and even one long-established company, have already signed on as Formbase customers.

“I’m not building this to stay small. In five years, I want thousands of Canadian companies running on Formbase, and a team of 30 to 50 people behind it,” he said.

The ambition that turned Nathan into a Western student entrepreneur was first forged at home. He grew up in a family where “convertible notes” and “fully diluted shares” were part of ordinary talk around the dinner table. Both his parents and his grandfather ran businesses in India. Their conversations about strategy, financing and business development influenced him early.

Western student entrepreneur Vinesh Nathan credits his parents (L to R) Venkat Nathan and Aarti Venkat, for nurturing his interest in business from an early age. (Submitted)

“For my entire childhood, I watched my parents build an amazing software services company, and I saw the struggle and the sacrifice that goes on behind the scenes,” he said.

Nathan developed his own company when he saw the needs of other founders who struggled to keep up with corporate compliance obligations while juggling product development, customers, employees and fundraising. As companies raise money and issue shares or stock options, keeping track of who owns what – and managing the growing volume of corporate records – becomes increasingly complex. Formbase simplifies the process and even manages the documentation founders need when seeking investment. He says the stakes go well beyond administrative inconvenience.

“I’ve talked to founders who lost deals because of messy data rooms, and that’s millions of dollars,” he said. “Making sure all your compliance and documents are clean, on record and fundraise-ready can save your company.”

Nathan says spreadsheets aren’t built for this kind of record-keeping, and U.S. software may not suit Canadian corporations. With Canadian tech founders leaving the country in growing numbers, he hopes Formbase will help more companies stay and grow in Canada. He plans to be one of them.

Formbase isn’t Nathan’s only business venture. In his first year, he tutored his fellow Saugeen-Maitland residents in calculus. As more students approached him for help, he and his roommate, Sneh Patel, began matching students with peers interested in tutoring for extra income.

Western students (L to R) Vinesh Nathan and Sneh Patel, went from roommates to business partners, founding TutorMatch. (Submitted)

Demand grew so quickly that the pair built an online platform called TutorMatch to line up qualified tutors with students, and manage the payments. Nathan says the platform led to more than 600 tutoring sessions, with another 400 likely by the end of the year, though the co-founders have no plans for expansion.

“We’ve scaled to about 14 universities and we’re keeping it that way for now. It pays both our rents,” he said.

That experience actually sparked his main venture. The difficulties of incorporating TutorMatch and running its compliance requirements motivated Nathan to build Formbase. He developed his business and his entrepreneurial mindset by taking advantage of opportunities both within and beyond Western.

He took a year off his studies to complete an eight-month co-op placement, supported by Student Experience, at a fintech startup company in New York. Last year, he spent two months in an incubator program affiliated with Toronto Metropolitan University. While in Toronto, he also connected with staff from Morrissette Entrepreneurship and later pitched his idea to its advisory board. He also attended the speaker series events among Morrissette’s offerings for founders or students exploring business ideas.

“The Morrissette team was very supportive in connecting me with founders who could use my product, even before I’d been accepted into the Accelerator,” he said.

Those connections are particularly valuable as Nathan works to overcome one of his biggest challenges – earning respect as a 22-year-old founder pitching his product to leaders who have spent decades building their companies.

“It’s been a challenge to convince larger companies to rate my product on its merit, instead of my age, but I’m building their trust by showing them what it’s capable of,” he said.

For Nathan, the confidence to embrace risk comes from knowing he has done everything possible to make his business succeed. Now, with a working product, paying customers and resources at Morrissette, he’s eager to find out just how far that ambition can take him.

“I’m ready to take the big swing, trust the process and do the work.”
