stories.title: Former ambassadors caution tariffs May stay but say Canada-U.S. trade deal possible
stories.summary: Ottawa - A former United States Ambassador to Canada says he's optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump's tariffs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A former United States Ambassador to Canada said he’s optimistic a bilateral deal between the two nations is looming but cautioned Canadians not to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to reign in President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

“I am saddened by where the relationship stands today but I really do remain optimistic about its future,” said David Cohen, who served as ambassador under former president Joe Biden.

“The ties between our countries run deep and I believe we have the foundation to rebuild trust, strengthen our partnership and move forward together.”

Appearing by video at the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development in Ottawa Monday, Cohen said the U.S. midterm elections were a historic rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies.

But he’s worried about “unrealistic optimism” from Canadians after Democrats said ending Trump’s trade war with Canada will be a top priority when they become a Congressional majority in January.

Cohen said it will be very challenging for Democrats to convince enough Republicans to defy Trump over his signature economic policy in order to achieve the supermajority they need to bypass the president’s veto powers.

Other observers have said Democrats will likely only tackle one of Trump’s tariff tools — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — while leaving in place other duties still hammering parts of the Canadian economy.

The Canada-U.S. relationship has been shaken by Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation but tensions rapidly escalated after negotiations between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August.

Trump used Section 338 to hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent levies and weeks later, using the same Depression-era statute, banned imports of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products. The president also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Cohen said Carney was right to walk away from trade talks. While the prime minister has faced criticism domestically for not providing details of the possible deal, Cohen said strategically it is better to negotiate behind closed doors.

“I think Canada has conducted itself extraordinarily well under a very intense and, I think, unfair set of pressures that have been created by U.S. trade policy by the current administration,” Cohen said. “I think Prime Minister Carney has played the hand that Canada has extraordinarily well.”

Cohen said he is hopeful a bilateral agreement can be agreed by years end or in January.

Last month, Trump said he expects a trade deal with Canada soon. United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said he wants to deliver “arrangements” for Canada and Mexico to the president by the year’s end.

The Canada-U.S. relationship is durable but it May require a future U.S administration to apologize for Trump’s rhetoric, Cohen added.

Even if a temporary agreement emerges, negotiations over the future of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade will continue into next year.

The Trump administration in July chose not to renew the trilateral trade pact, known as Cusma. That triggered a rolling annual review for up to a decade, at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

David MacNaughton was the Canadian ambassador to Washington during the first Trump presidency and had a front-row seat when Cusma was negotiated to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement.

The former ambassador told the committee that current negotiations are different because “the fact of the matter is (Trump) had advisers who were sane and were trying to build a relationship that was good for both sides.” Now the president is surrounded by people who will agree with whatever Trump wants, MacNaughton said.

The former ambassador said Greer, who played a role in Cusma negotiations, is professional but ultimately the decisions come out of the White House.

MacNaughton said Canada should look to make a deal and find a tariff off-ramp but the bilateral relationship has ultimately changed. He said Canada must diversify trade and boost domestic productivity.

“Let’s diversify our trade but also let’s find a way to get some kind of a long-term agreement with the United States back in place,” he said. “And thirdly, let us work on becoming more productive as a country because this does give us a chance.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

stories.title: Warm, sunny stretch ahead for southern Ontario
stories.summary: Monday’s cloudy conditions were the result of a temperature inversion trapping moisture from the Great Lakes near the surface.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
After a grey start to the week, southern Ontario residents can look forward to several days of sunshine and above-seasonal temperatures, according to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Atchison said Monday’s cloudy conditions were the result of a temperature inversion trapping moisture from the Great Lakes near the surface.

“It’s feeling very November-like today with overcast conditions and an inversion setting up, which is trapping some Great Lakes moisture at the surface and keeping us cloudy,” Atchison said.

She noted temperatures were expected to rise a few more degrees through the afternoon as drier air gradually moves into the region, helping to break up the cloud cover.

The improvement is tied to a large area of high pressure that is expected to settle over the eastern seaboard and remain in place for much of the week.

“Nothing’s really going to be moving. A blocking pattern is developing, and we’re on the good side of the block,” said Atchison. “Western Canada will have a big trough, but eastern areas of the country will be soaking up beautiful sunny days and warming temperatures.”

A southerly wind is forecast to develop Tuesday, helping push temperatures above seasonal norms.

“We have a beautiful week setting up in southern Ontario with back-to-back days of sunshine,” Atchison said.

Overnight lows are expected to fall to between 0 C and 1 C Monday night, with slightly milder temperatures along the Lake Erie shoreline.

The forecast calls for full sunshine Tuesday through Thursday, with daytime highs ranging from 11 C to 13 C.

“Some gorgeous weather is on the way, and that looks to hold into the weekend,” Atchison said.

stories.title: What is Roshel, the company buying a Stellantis auto plant in Ontario?
stories.summary: Company says it wants to increase its capacity as Canada builds out its defence sector
stories.author: Daniel Johnson
stories.content:
Defence contractor Roshel is slated to take over the Brampton, Ont., assembly plant that has been idle for years after buying it from automaker Stellantis Stla-N .

While questions and criticism swirl about the sale and what will happen to jobs at the facility, Roshel says it wants to increase its capacity as Canada builds out its defence sector.

The Brampton-based company is a large manufacturer of smart armoured vehicles for both commercial and government organizations. Its trucks are used by military, law enforcement and security customers to protect occupants.

Roshel’s customers include government agencies such as Canada’s Department of National Defence, Nasa and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, along with law enforcement agencies such as the Peel Regional Police and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Its security customers include The Brink’s Co. and GardaWorld Security.

Roshel is a privately held company founded by its CEO Roman Shimonov in 2016.

The sale of the plant has drawn the ire of the union representing Stellantis workers and government officials, but some defence industry experts say they are not surprised as to who is buying the facility considering Canada’s new-found appetite for building out its military and defence capabilities.

“As the sector expands, defence companies will need to invest in new facilities, expand existing ones, or repurpose industrial properties as they become available. This is a good example of that broader trend,” said Peter Graham, a national sector leader of aerospace and defence at Kpmg Canada, in a statement Thursday.

Canada and its Nato allies agreed in June 2025 to substantially hike their defence spending target to 5 per cent of annual GDP by 2035. The latest federal budget says Canada will reach 4 per cent by 2030. As defence spending rises, domestic companies like Roshel could benefit from military procurements.

Shimonov has said it’s looking to capitalize on these new opportunities.

“With the demand that is growing all around the world, we need more space, we need more capacity. And we also need the ability to create an infrastructure to address future need for companies that are willing to invest in Canada,” Shimonov said this week in an interview.

In February, the government outlined a new $6.6-billion defence strategy aimed at helping small- and medium-sized Canadian businesses break into the defence industry and reorient spending decisions to prioritize equipment made in Canada, instead of relying on foreign military contractors such as American firms. The document claims it will create 125,000 jobs over a decade.

“(Roshel) is buying (the plant) basically because defence spending in Canada is scheduled to go through a significant increase and what they’re trying to do is get some more capacity for defence manufacturing,” Jerry McGinn, the director of the Center for the Industrial Base, said in an interview.

In recent years, Roshel has been increasing its presence in the defence industry.

In October, it completed an acquisition of French armoured vehicle producer Centigon. In June, it signed a memorandum of understanding with Daimler to jointly develop and produce armoured military vehicles for Nato and allied customers.

In April, it signed a deal with Algoma Steel Group Inc. on a joint venture called Roshel Algoma Defence, which will produce ballistic steel for military vehicles as well as other industries. The partnership includes metal fabrication, forming, welding, and machining in Canada.

And in August of 2025, it partnered with Swedish steel company Swebor in a deal that allowed it to use Swebor’s intellectual property to produce ballistic steel in Canada. Ballistic steel is a special type of relatively lightweight, hardened steel that protects against blasts or bullets.

The company has previously faced criticism for its ties to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

U.S. government procurement records from November 2025 laid out plans for a rush order worth the equivalent of about C$10 million for 20 Senator Stang emergency response tactical vehicles made by Roshel. The purchase quickly drew criticism from arms control advocates and politicians in Canada due to the law enforcement agency’s alleged record of human rights abuses.

The company’s vehicles have also been sent overseas.

In 2023, then Defence Minister Anita Anand announced that Canada was sending an additional 200 armoured vehicles to Ukraine, which were purchased from Roshel at a cost of $90 million.

Stellantis announced the sale of its Brampton facility and associated equipment to Roshel for an undisclosed amount last Monday. The companies said they expect the transaction to close by the end of this year, however, it is subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.

Shimonov said that the Brampton plant wouldn’t be limited strictly to defence.

“We want to continue looking for opportunities within automotive, not necessarily in defence, to create a brighter future, but it will be dependent on many other things that we are not certain of. We need certainty before committing to anything,” he said.

Shimonov added that the exact work being done at the facility will be dictated by the contracts it is able to secure.

With the facility changing ownership and possibly pivoting to defence, McGinn said other changes will likely be necessary.

“The processes might be similar but I just think the controls and the facility access, those kind of things will be a little different because they’re going be different regulations governing those for defence items versus automotive parts and the like,” he said.

stories.title: $110M long-term care home breaks ground in Seaforth
stories.summary: Ontario Minister of Long-Term Care Natalia Kusendova-Bashta said the project will help seniors remain close to their families while creating stable, well-paying jobs in a rural community.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A groundbreaking ceremony was held in Seaforth for a new $110-million long-term care home.

Ontario Minister of Long-Term Care Natalia Kusendova-Bashta said the project will help seniors remain close to their families while creating stable, well-paying jobs in a rural community.

The province is providing 85 per cent of the capital funding for the 256-bed facility, representing approximately $94 million in government support. The five-acre site was donated by the Seaforth Hospital Trust and Seaforth Development Trust.

“We know we have an older home that’s in transition, and we don’t know the final details of when or what’s going to happen with it,” said outgoing Huron East Mayor Bernie MacLellan. “We certainly didn’t want those residents to be moved out of the community. We didn’t want the employment to be moved out of the community.”

The home will be built and operated by Omni Quality Living, which operates 29 seniors’ facilities in Ontario and New Brunswick. The company is also constructing long-term care homes in Peterborough and Brighton.

“We definitely have the need, but now we have a government that supports this and is investing in the right places,” said Omni Quality Living president and CEO Raheem Hirji. “We’re building across the province, and we’re happy to be part of that initiative.”

The facility, which will be located near Seaforth Community Hospital, is expected to welcome its first residents in early 2029.

Kusendova-Bashta said long-term care projects help reduce pressure elsewhere in the health-care system, including hospitals that care for alternate level-of-care patients.

Hirji said Seaforth was selected because of both staffing opportunities and demand for long-term care beds in the region.

MacLellan said he hopes some of the facility’s future employees will choose to settle in the community.

“We’ve got building lots that are ready to go. We’ve got contractors that are already building neighbourhoods,” he said. “We’ve got spots for people to come and live here if they want to work here.”

stories.title: One hospitalized after fire at Montreal apartment building
stories.summary: The fire began around 3:30 p.m. in Montreal's Pierrefonds-Roxboro borough, ON Riviera Street at the corner of Riverdale Boulevard.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
One person was taken to a hospital after a fire broke out in Montreal on Sunday afternoon.

The fire began around 3:30 p.m. in the Pierrefonds-Roxboro borough, ON Riviera Street at the corner of Riverdale Boulevard.

About 150 firefighters responded to the blaze at the three-storey building, which contains 73 apartments.

Firefighters got control of the blaze at around 10:45 p.m., and ten people were taken in by the Red Cross.

Fire investigators are at the scene to determine the cause of the fire, which remains unknown.

The condition of the person taken to hospital was not immediately available.

stories.title: No complaint received by ombudsman after children allegedly confined in locker
stories.summary: Quebec's ombudsman's office says it won't be able to investigate or issue recommendations until a parent or student files a complaint.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron
stories.content:
Quebec’s student ombudsman says it has not received any complaints regarding allegations that elementary school students were confined in a locker at a school in the Laurentians, north of Montreal.

The ombudsman’s office says it won’t be able to investigate or issue recommendations until a parent or student files a complaint.

The Cogeco media network reported last week that at least three children between five and seven years old were isolated and sometimes locked in a lightly padded metal locker in order to get them to calm down.

They also said four employees, including a teacher and the school principal, were suspended following the allegations.

The media report said the alleged confinement occurred at a primary school operated by the Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles, but did not name the school.

Local police, youth protection services and the education minister have all announced investigations.

stories.title: B.C. tribunal orders WestJet to pay, but only 50 per cent passengers' alcohol tab
stories.summary: Vancouver - A British Columbia tribunal has ordered WestJet to compensate two passengers over a cancelled flight that caused an overnight delay, although it cut the couple's alcohol expense claim in half.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A British Columbia tribunal has ordered WestJet to compensate two passengers over a cancelled flight that caused an overnight delay, although it cut the couple’s alcohol expense claim in half.

The B.C. Civil Resolution Tribunal decision dated Nov. 13 says Kevin and Susan Myles claimed $2,000 under air passenger protection regulations, along with delay-related meal expenses during their trip from Cancun, Mexico, to Kamloops, B.C., in 2024.

stories.title: Ontario’s medical regulator pauses safer supply drug changes after legal challenge
stories.summary: Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario says it was served Friday with the legal action, which includes a motion for an injunction to prevent the regulator from enforcing the new safer supply rules.

The changes were set to come into effect on Monday, but the college says it’s pausing enforcement to allow time to respond to the injunction.

The college approved sweeping changes to the safer supply prescription regime last month that would require doctors to prescribe safer supply drugs only in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.

Safer supply drugs are medications given to people at high risk of overdose as an alternative to illicit opioids while opioid agonist therapy uses medications such as Suboxone and methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The new rules would also require patients to take their safer supply medications in front of health-care professionals, rather than take them home — a change that has raised accessibility concerns especially for patients in rural Ontario and those who work regular hours.

The medical regulator has said the changes were approved in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids prescribed as safer supply drugs making their way to the streets.

The chair of the regulator’s board, Dr. Patrick Safieh, has said police forces in Ontario are noticing patients’ safer supply drugs being diverted to the black market.

The medical regulator has said the changes were approved in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids prescribed as safer supply drugs making their way to the streets.
The chair of the regulator’s board, Dr. Patrick Safieh, has said police forces in Ontario are noticing patients’ safer supply drugs being diverted to the black market.

stories.title: Grey Cup festivities didn’t push Calgary’s water use beyond restriction threshold
stories.summary: City of Calgary officials say a surge in CFL fans in Calgary for the Grey Cup didn't overburden the water system, despite ongoing water restrictions.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Officials say a surge in CFL fans in Calgary for the Grey Cup didn’t overburden the Calgary water system, despite ongoing water restrictions.

They say water use reached 490 million litres on Sunday, when the city and visitors watched the championship football game and closed out several days of celebrations.

Calgary is about halfway through three weeks of water restrictions, with a 500-million-litre per day usage threshold, as it repairs a water main that supplies treated water to more than half its residents.

The city’s goal with the restrictions is to ensure it doesn’t strain its water plant or risk running low on water to fight fires.

Mayor Jeromy Farkas says the city has stayed below its typical water use, despite welcoming about 35,000 visitors for the Grey Cup.

“The fact that we’re below where we were two years ago, despite the fact that we’re putting on the Grey Cup … that is an astonishing achievement,” Farkas said Monday.

— More to come…

stories.title: ‘I can shoot you dead’: Video captures confrontation outside Chinese Consulate in Toronto
stories.summary: A video showing an alleged assault against two Falun Gong demonstrators outside China’s consulate in Toronto has prompted renewed calls for Prime Minister Mark Carney to confront Beijing over alleged transnational repression in Canada.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Toronto - Human rights advocates say a video obtained by CTV News is a flagrant example of transnational repression by China. The video shows a man tearing down Falun Gong banners set up outside the Chinese consulate in Toronto and threatening to “shoot dead” a female demonstrator and kicking another woman who was videotaping the incident.

Activists are calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to raise the issue of China’s human rights abuses when he meets with President Xi Jinping on Tuesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.

“It’s important that Prime Minister Carney raise this issue and put an immediate stop to this blatant transnational repression happening in Canada,” says Joel Chipkar, the spokesperson for the Falun Dafa Association of Canada.

“This is creating fear and insecurity for Canadians here who escaped (China’s) tyrannical regime and came here for a better life.”

The two women are part of a rotating group of volunteers who stand outside the consulate each day to draw attention to China’s persecution of Falun Gong practitioners.

Falun gong is a spiritual movement which has gained a mass following of millions in China and around the world.

According to human rights group, Safeguard Defenders, China has labelled Falun Gong one of “five poisons” including democrats, Taiwan, Tibet and Xinjiang that are considered threats to stability of the regime .

Chipkar told CTV News that one demonstrator was a Canadian citizen and that the other woman was a refugee who fled to Canada in 2024. Both women have families who have been imprisoned in China because of their religious beliefs.

“They feel the Chinese Communist Party has too much influence in Canada. We have people in our community who have been assaulted. They have been followed home, and their family members have been threatened in China.”

‘This is Chinese territory’

The Toronto incident that occurred on Sept. 22 is one of dozens of examples cited in a new Safeguard Defenders report, which alleges that Beijing has created a massive network of overseas associations, that Chinese Communist Party (CCP) agents are using to monitor and control its diaspora. The report claims that there are at least 18 illegal police stations in Canada.

The four-minute video reveals a confrontation on Toronto’s George Street in front of the Consulate-General of the People’s Republic of China.

It involves an altercation between two demonstrators and a man wearing a black jacket with the flag of China sewn on it.

Angered by the message on the protest banners, which drew attention to China’s repression of the Falun Gong, the man begins tearing apart the signs. The female demonstrator urges her friend to call the police, while the man tells someone off camera to start recording video as well.

A copy of the video has been sent to the Toronto Police Service. CTV News has independently verified the accuracy of the English subtitles on the video.

“These are illegal,” the man says, referring to the banners. “This is the entry to the embassy. This is Chinese territory – do you know that? You have violated China’s anti-secession law. I can shoot you dead.” He continues, pointing his finger at her: “I will make you fall to your death. Believe it or not. I will shoot you to death believe it or not.”

Later on in the video, the woman tries to grab him from behind to stop him from tearing down more signs. That’s when the man shoves her back, nearly knocking her glasses off. Then the man walks toward the woman recording the video and kicks her.

Chipkar helped the women report the incident to police. Witnesses were able to record the licence plate of the Uber vehicle the man got into. Chipkar says investigators were able to identify the man.

They found out through the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) that he had returned to China.

“Police did tell us that if he returned, he would be detained at the border, charged for the assault, threats and mischief to property.”

Chipkar says that police are not releasing the perpetrator’s name.

It’s not clear if the suspect was a Chinese police officer or a diplomat.

Toronto police has confirmed to CTV News that there is an open investigation into the incident. A spokesperson said the Toronto Police Service is unable to provide more information until the lead investigator returns from leave.

CTV News has contacted the Chinese Embassy for comment but has yet to receive a response.

New Chinese law could lead to more transnational repression

Margaret McCuaig-Johnston, an advisory board member of the China Strategic Risks Institute, calls the incident “disturbing.”

She says the foreign affairs minister needs to summon the ambassador and “read him the riot act to ensure this doesn’t happen in Canada again and that there will be major consequences.”

She says the individual should be barred from returning to Canada.

McCuaig-Johnston is also concerned that China’s new “ethnic unity law” will lead to more cases of transnational repression in Canada and across the globe.

The new Chinese law , which came into effect July 1, grants China extraterritorial powers to act against organizations and people that it feels threaten the aims of the CCP.

The law, along with an expansion of the global network to monitor the diaspora, can be used to silence the voices of people advocating for minority rights such as those of the Falun Gong, Uyghurs or Tibetans.

Democracy activists from Hong Kong, or Taiwanese Canadians who are against unifying with China, can also be targeted.

“China thinks their law extends anywhere, including the streets of Canada,” says McCuaig-Johnston.

Other than the Toronto incident, McCuaig-Johnston says there are other cases of human rights abuses that Carney should raise with Xi. She points out that Uyghur Canadian activist Huseyin Celil has been imprisoned in China for 20 years.

There’s also Jimmy Lai, a Hong Kong media mogul who supported the democracy movement. He’s serving a 20-year jail sentence for collusion and sedition. The 78-year-old has family in Canada.

Before leaving for Asia, Carney said he would raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada with Xi.

The prime minister also said that the partnership between the two countries “is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we’re involved.”

Former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig, who was detained for more than 1,000 days by China, says the prime minister needs to be pressed on what those guardrails are.

“The government needs to explain more to Canadians what the guardrails are, what they’re for, and how effective they’ve been, and what Ottawa is doing to strengthen them,” said Kovrig during an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV’s Question Period.

Kovrig, who now runs his own geopolitical risk advisory firm, says Carney should make it a “top priority” to bring up the findings of the Safeguard Defenders report, which claims that China May be operating at least 18 illegal police stations to control the diaspora in Canada.

“That is a violation of Canadian sovereignty, and it’s a threat to the rights of Canadian citizens. And so, I think that is a top priority, frankly, to raise with President Xi, and convey to him very clearly that that kind of thing is not acceptable, and that Canada will investigate it, and we will follow processes to ensure that Canadians are secure.”

stories.title: Ontario Catholic teachers vote strongly in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: The union representing Catholic teachers says educators are dealing with chronic classroom underfunding by the Ford government.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Teachers in Ontario’s English-speaking Catholic schools have delivered an overwhelming strike mandate, with 98 per cent voting in favour of approving a strike action if necessary, announced the union representing the educators Monday.

“Catholic teachers have spoken with one, clear, united voice,” said René Jansen in de Wal, the president of the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association (Oecta), the union that represents more than 45,000 teachers across the province.

The vote took place on Nov. 12 and 13.

Oecta is one of five major education unions in the province that have already held or are completing province-wide strike mandate votes this month, following the expiration of collective agreements at the end of August.

Negotiations have stalled out as the Ontario Labour Relations Board decides on a dispute between the teachers’ unions and the government on which issues should be bargained centrally, and what should be left to local unions and school boards.

“With an overwhelming 98 per cent strike mandate, we are sending an unmistakable message to the government,” he said in a statement. “The time for meaningful action at the bargaining table is now.”

Catholic teachers are contending with the “consequences of this government’s chronic underfunding of our schools,” he said, which include overcrowded classrooms, staff shortages, increased violence and scarce resources.

“Catholic teachers have been raising these concerns for years, yet the government continues to ignore the realities facing our schools,” he said. “Our members have made it clear that enough is enough.”

Education Minister Paul Calandra’s office previously told Global News that the unions scheduling strike votes while talks are paused is “premature and detrimental to students.”

Unions took their disputes to the Ontario Labour Relations Board, which is the cause of the delays, Calandra’s office said in September.

Four other unions, the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, the Ontario School Board Council of Unions and Aefo, the French-language teachers union are all currently holding strike mandate votes.

stories.title: Countries willing to pay more for stable energy supply from Canada, Hogan says
stories.summary: Ottawa - Calgary MP Corey Hogan says countries are willing to sign on to longer-term energy supply deals with Canada, even if it costs them a bit more.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Countries are willing to pay more to sign long-term energy supply deals with Canada because it can offer both security and stability, Calgary MP Corey Hogan said at an energy conference Monday.

Hogan, the parliamentary secretary to the minister of energy, was the keynote speaker at an energy security conference in Ottawa hosted by the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

He said countries are still reeling from global energy disruptions earlier this year, after U.S. military action prompted Iran to limit, and at times halt, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the most important global energy supply routes.

About one-fifth of world supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas used to flow through that strait, and its disruption has led to soaring gas prices and shortages in some parts of the world.

Hogan joked that the Georgia Strait — between Vancouver Island and mainland B.C. and a key shipping route out of Canada — isn’t likely to be shut down.

“Right now everybody is talking about diversification of supply and the durability of supply chains, and they look at Canada and they say ‘there’s a country that is a reliable trader. That is a country that is not known to use trade as a lever over people. It’s in a safe part of the world,’” Hogan told the room.

“We are a natural partner in that sense, and frankly, they’ll even pay a little bit more for it sometimes because that supply assurance is something that’s increasingly important.”

Hogan said the case is an easy one for Canada to make right now, but noted it won’t always be so easy.

“I’m a cynical guy, and I think that it doesn’t take as much time as you hope for people to forget the lessons that they learned. And that will only take us so far,” Hogan said.

And Canada is seeking longer-term deals with other countries, at least one country feels the willingness to pay more for reliable supply isn’t a long-term play.

Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Patnaik also spoke at the conference later in the day. In an interview with The Canadian Press, he said charging a premium for energy right now is opportunistic for Canada given the global supply chain disruptions. But it isn’t something his country is willing to entertain long-term.

“In the long run, this will be very difficult. Right now, they’re paying the premium. But they will not pay the premium forever,” Parnaik said.

“If you want to sell your oil and gas, you have to be competitive. With so many facilities coming up around the world, if you don’t supply at the same time — unless there is a crisis — why would they buy from you?”

One of the issues, Parnaik said, is Canadian energy is inherently more expensive because of the country’s limited capacity to export.

“I’m buying Canadian crude and gas from the U.S., from the Gulf Coast. You don’t have the facility, the ability to provide it to me at cost,” he said.

“So cost is very important, and it’s going to remain important. No global business pays a premium on things they can get somewhere else for a cheaper price. Why are they paying a premium now? Because there’s a crisis.”

Canada is aiming to produce 100 million tonnes per year of liquefied natural gas by 2040, which S&P Global Energy says would make Canada the third-largest supplier globally.

The S&P report forecasted global LNG demand to rise by 176 million tonnes by 2050. But it also said there are more than 600 million tonnes of projects under development.

The bulk of those projects comes from the United States, accounting for 220 million tonnes of added supply. Another 80 million comes from Russia, 29 million from Argentina, 24 million from Mozambique, and 23 million from Qatar.

Current project proposals in Canada account for 36 million tonnes of added LNG supply.

“Canada has to move now to get projects into the queue to take market share from those it’s competing with,” said Kevin Birn, one of the report’s authors and the vice-president and chief Canadian energy analyst at S&P Global Energy.

“Canada can do this. It has an advantage resource in terms of greenhouse gas intensity as well. But it has to move at pace if it wants to capture that.

“It’s not a question whether this demand will be met. Yes, it will. It’s a question of who will bring it to market and who will service it. Our track record isn’t great.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026

— With files from Lauren Krugel in Calgary

November 16, 2026 at 11:59 a.m.

Toronto Police provided updates Monday on two high-profile crimes in the city, having made three arrests in connection with a home invasion last month in the Bridle Path neighbourhood, and one in connection with the Nov. 10 murder of 18-year-old Brandon Blake. However, suspects in both cases, including one 17-year-old accused of two murders, remain at large.

In the Bridle Path case, which took place in the early hours of Oct. 29, police announced the arrest of Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto.

He was arrested Saturday in Ottawa, coincidentally in the Bridle Path Drive area of that city. He has been charged with 14 counts, including break and enter, four counts of aggravated assault, four counts of robbery, and three of discharging a firearm with intent to wound, endanger life or prevent arrest.

Two weeks ago, Police Chief Myron Demkiw bristled at the suggestion that they had somehow lost the suspect, after it was revealed that Richards was briefly admitted to hospital on the night of the crime, but then released.

“I actually take umbrage with the way you frame that question,” Demkiw said at the time. “We are following the evidence as it becomes available. Had there been evidence to allow us to do something different, that’s what would have happened. We are following the evidence as expeditiously as we can, and the investigation continues to unfold.”

Asked Monday by a reporter if Richards was “still behind bars,” Inspector Kristy Smith of the Hold Up Squad replied: “I’m very happy to say yes, he is.”

Smith said two other individuals had been charged for allegedly knowingly harbouring Richards to help him evade arrest.

Gesley Fenelus, 27, and Melanie Riddell, 28, both of Ottawa, have been arrested and charged with accessory after the fact. They are due in court in February.

Two other suspects remain at large in connection with the home invasion. They are considered armed and dangerous. Police have also released an image of a dark grey Honda CR-V that was seen fleeing the area that night. It has a spare tire mounted on the front driver’s side.

Police released this image of a dark grey Honda CR-V that was seen fleeing an Oct. 29 home invasion. Handout / TPS

Anyone with information about the suspects or the vehicle is asked to contact the Hold Up Squad at 416-808-7350 or 33 Division at 416-808-3300.

In the homicide case, police have arrested and charged one person and identified an additional suspect.

On Saturday, officers arrested a 16-year-old male of Vaughan, Ont., who cannot be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act (Ycja). He has been charged with first-degree murder.

Last week, police named Joseph Kunene, 19, of Toronto, as a suspect in Blake’s murder. He is described as six feet tall, 175 lbs., with black hair and brown eyes, and a distinctive tattoo on his right hand. An image has been released.

On Monday, police said they had obtained judicial authorization to identify an additional 17-year-old suspect, even though he is a young person under the Ycja. The authorization will expire at noon on Thursday.

That suspect, described as having a thin build, with his hair in two braids on either side of his head, is wanted for first-degree murder in the Blake case.

However, he is also wanted on a Canada-wide warrant for second-degree murder in connection with the homicide of 18-year-old Malik Abass that occurred on Nov. 7, 2026.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: TC Energy plans to grow Alberta pipeline network to serve oilsands, power plants
stories.summary: Calgary - TC Energy Corp. is looking to seize on booming natural gas demand in Alberta, announcing plans Monday to expand its pipeline network that criss-crosses much of the province.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - TC Energy Corp. is looking to seize on booming natural gas demand in Alberta, announcing plans Monday to expand its pipeline network that criss-crosses much of the province.

The Calgary-based company is proposing a roughly 370-kilometre, west-to-east pipeline called Alberta Growth Connector. The 48-inch diameter pipeline would add an initial billion cubic feet per day of new capacity, serving the oilsands region in the province’s northeast.

stories.title: Teen wanted in 2 deaths, including Barrie man killed in Toronto shooting
stories.summary: A 17-year-old teenager is wanted in connection to two killings in Toronto, including the shooting death of a Barrie man, police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 17-year-old is wanted in connection with two killings in Toronto, including the shooting death of a Barrie man.

Toronto police Det.-Sgt. Sandra Arruda said Monday the teen is among three suspects sought in connection with Brandon Blake’s death.

The 18-year-old was shot and killed on Nov. 10 in Etobicoke .

Police said officers received a call at 12:56 a.m. for the sound of gunshots near Martin Grove Road and Finch Avenue West. The shooting happened at a residential complex on Pittsboro Drive, which is near the Elmbank Community Centre at 10 Rampart Rd.

Officers found Blake near the community centre. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Blake ran from the residential complex when the shooting unfolded. Several evidence markers were visible at the scene when Global News attended.

It’s not clear why Blake was in the area overnight.

Three suspects are wanted. One suspect – a 16-year-old from Vaughan – was arrested Saturday and was charged with first-degree murder.

Toronto resident Joseph Kunene, 19, is wanted for first-degree murder. He is described as six feet tall, weighing 175 pounds and as having black hair, brown eyes and a distinctive tattoo on his right hand.

Normally, the Youth Criminal Justice Act prevents media from reporting the identity of a youth accused of a crime. In this case, police obtained judicial authorization, which expires Nov. 19, to identify the third suspect – 17-year-old Toronto resident Cameron Marlor. He is wanted for first-degree murder.

He is also wanted for second-degree murder related to the Nov. 7 death of 18-year-old Malik Abass .

Marlor is described as having a thin build, with his hair in two braids on either side of his head. At the time of Blake’s death, police say he was wearing all black clothing with the hood up, and a face mask covering most of his face.

Police released photos of Kunene and Marlor. They are considered armed and dangerous.

“The violence involved in these crimes demonstrates a serious, flagrant disregard for human life,” Arruda said.

“We are actively searching for these individuals and we will continue to do so until they are located.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

content_blocks.text: Blake ran from the residential complex when the shooting unfolded. Several evidence markers were visible at the scene when Global News attended.
It’s not clear why Blake was in the area overnight.
Three suspects are wanted. One suspect – a 16-year-old from Vaughan – was arrested Saturday and was charged with first-degree murder.

Toronto resident Joseph Kunene, 19, is wanted for first-degree murder. He is described as six feet tall, weighing 175 pounds and as having black hair, brown eyes and a distinctive tattoo on his right hand.

Normally, the Youth Criminal Justice Act prevents media from reporting the identity of a youth accused of a crime. In this case, police obtained judicial authorization, which expires Nov. 19, to identify the third suspect – 17-year-old Toronto resident Cameron Marlor. He is wanted for first-degree murder.
He is also wanted for second-degree murder related to the Nov. 7 death of 18-year-old Malik Abass .

“The violence involved in these crimes demonstrates a serious, flagrant disregard for human life,” Arruda said.

stories.title: Infant among 3 dead in Burlington townhouse fire
stories.summary: Officials confirmed Monday that an adult male, a 12-year-old child and a one-year-old baby have died. An adult female and one other child remain in critical condition.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Two children, including a baby, and one adult have died from their injuries following a house fire in Burlington on Saturday.

It’s an incident that officials are calling a “tragic event,” as two other members from the same family remain in critical condition.

“We had a family of five … I’m very saddened to announce we’ve had some passing, ” said Ontario Fire Marshal Jon Pegg at a news conference Monday.

Emergency services were contacted around 6:45 a.m. Saturday, Halton Regional Police said, to respond to reports of a fire within a residential unit at a townhouse complex located at 1300 Maple Crossing Blvd.

They said at the time that that three children and two adults, one male and one female, were taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. One child is at least five years old and another is 12, police said. The third has been identified as a one-year-old baby.

Pegg confirmed Monday that the man, the 12-year-old and the infant have died. The woman and the other child remain in critical condition.

“Our continued thoughts and prayers are with those family members,” said Pegg.

He said the “scene portion” of the investigation has wrapped up, but forensic testing will be conducted next to determine the cause of the fire. Until those results are released to the public, Pegg said officials want to focus on safety messaging.

“We are heading into what historically across Ontario is our most dangerous time of year. As we get into the colder months … we see the highest increase in fire fatalities,” he said.

The public needs to ensure they test their smoke alarms, and to do so monthly, and to create a “home escape plan,” said Pegg.

“It’s the only thing that will save your family’s life,” he said.

“As a fire marshal, (fire) can literally happen to any of us, including myself, my family. My kids know exactly what to do in the event of an alarm going off, and I beg, I ask that everybody practice that with their family,” he said, adding there should be two ways out of each room and alternatives need to be discussed in advance.

Firefighters rushed into an “inferno” Saturday trying to rescue the family and risked their lives to do so, he said.

Burlington fire crews were able to extinguish flames quickly and remove the victims from their homes, he said. The fire did not spread to any neighbouring homes.

stories.title: AI making it harder to spot fake retailers ahead of holidays, RBC poll says
stories.summary: For more than eight out of 10 (84 per cent) of Canadians, AI has made fake ads harder to spot, according to the Royal Bank of Canada’s 2026 Holiday Shopping Scams Poll.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canadians are turning to artificial intelligence this holiday shopping season , but they’re also concerned that AI could make it easier for them to get targeted by scammers and fake retailers, new polling shows.

For more than eight out of 10 (84 per cent) of Canadians, AI has made fake ads harder to spot, according to the Royal Bank of Canada’s 2026 Holiday Shopping Scams Poll.

A similar number said spotting fake online retailers (82 per cent) and fake celebrity and influencer endorsements (77 per cent) was harder because of AI tools.

Only half of the respondents (50 per cent) said they were confident that they could spot an AI-generated shopping scam, with 73 per cent concerned about AI recommending a fake retailer, product or deal.

“Fake websites, social media ads and marketplace posts, as well as AI-generated content are becoming more convincing, making it harder to know what’s real,” said Amit Sahdu, vice president of credit and fraud management at RBC.

“If a deal or an unfamiliar retailer pops up in your feed, don’t click through. Look up the retailer yourself, check the website and URL carefully,” Sadhu said, adding that Canadians should be especially careful when buying from secondhand marketplaces to verify the seller before transferring any money.

Fake ads are especially rampant on social media platforms, the RBC report said. More than half of respondents (54 per cent) said they regularly see posts from fake retailers or brands on social media and a quarter (25 per cent) said they have spotted ads that seemed legitimate at first but later turned out to be scams.

Data privacy remains the top concern for most, with nearly seven in 10 (68 per cent) said they were worried about scammers collecting their personal or financial information.

Half of the respondents (50 per cent) said they were worried about paying for something that never arrives, while a similar number (47 per cent) saying they were worried they would not realize they’d been scammed until it’s too late.

The RBC data comes as another poll suggests Canadians are turning to artificial intelligence this holiday season.

AI is projected to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spend globally, up 13 per cent since 2025, a report from Salesforce said, adding that 16 per cent of Canadians will turn to AI as the first stop in their shopping journey.

However, more than half (53 per cent) said they would not let an AI agent make a purchase for them.

stories.title: Final paving to bring overnight closures on Fanshawe Park Road
stories.summary: The final stage of a major road rehabilitation project on Fanshawe Park Road is set to begin this week, bringing overnight road closures between North Centre Road and Adelaide Street North.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The final stage of a major road rehabilitation project on Fanshawe Park Road is set to begin this week, bringing overnight road closures between North Centre Road and Adelaide Street North.

The City of London says final paving work will begin Monday at 7 p.m. and require the roadway to be closed in both directions overnight while crews complete asphalt paving.

The work is expected to take four nights, with a fifth night available if needed, weather permitting. Crews will work nightly from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., starting at Adelaide Street North and moving west toward North Centre Road, completing roughly one section each night.

Drivers are being asked to follow posted detours using Adelaide Street North, Windermere Road or Sunningdale Road, and Richmond Street.

Residents in the Stoneybrook neighbourhood south of Fanshawe Park Road will face limited access from Adelaide Street during paving operations. Daleview Crescent residents will continue to have access from Adelaide Street, while other residents are being directed to use the west leg of Hastings Drive on the first night of work. As paving progresses westward, the east leg of Stoneybrook Crescent will also serve as a neighbourhood entrance.

Special constables will be on site to direct traffic and help maintain access for residents.

The city says sidewalks are expected to remain open for most of the project, although temporary closures and signed pedestrian detours May be required. Businesses in the area will remain open, with access maintained wherever possible.

London Transit Commission buses will also be detoured around the construction zone during the overnight work.

Once paving is complete, crews will move on to road markings and finishing work, including boulevard restoration, sidewalk installation where required and electrical work. That phase is expected to begin the week of Nov. 23 and take two to three weeks, with some temporary lane and sidewalk restrictions remaining in place.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Jamal Francique hears from Peel region constable
stories.summary: An inquest into the death of a Black man who was shot by police in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago is hearing from a constable who arrived at the scene after the shooting.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A police constable told a coroner’s inquest Monday he was concerned about the risk of an ambush as he approached a car that had crashed into a pillar after it was hit by police gunfire during a botched arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago.

It was dark at the time and the car’s windows were heavily tinted, making it difficult to see inside, Peel regional police Const. Marc Charlebois, then a member of the force’s tactical unit, told the inquest into the death of Jamal Francique.

The tactical unit had been dispatched around 7:46 p.m. on Jan. 7, 2020, and arrived at the townhouse complex about 20 minutes later, he said.

As he came up toward the back of the car, carrying a ballistic shield more than a metre long and a metal bar designed for breaking or prying into windows, the officer said he and a colleague called out some commands, but there was no answer.

Charlebois, who is the first witness in the inquest, said he managed to see the lone person in the car after breaking the rear passenger window.

“I can just see the back of his right side, the right side of his head. … I can hear the male struggling for breath,” he said.

Charlebois saw blood, he said, but didn’t yet realize Francique had a gunshot wound. There was no sign of movement, he said.

“Was it clear to you at that point … that he was dying?” inquest counsel Roger Shallow asked the constable.

“I knew that there was a traumatic incident that required some intervention,” Charlebois answered.

After breaking the rear driver’s side window, the officer noticed “a lot of blood” from a wound around Francique’s left ear and knew it was a “medical emergency,” he said.

Discarding his shield and bar, Charlebois opened the driver’s door and crouched down, he testified. He moved to take off what he thought was Francique’s seatbelt but turned out to be a satchel, he said.

The bag had a “considerable weight,” which led the officer to believe there was a gun inside, he said, adding he alerted the others as a precaution. Charlebois handed off the satchel to his sergeant but did not look inside, he said.

He and another officer got Francique out of the car and away from the rubble and debris that surrounded it, he said. Once Francique was in an ambulance, Charlebois checked the satchel and found a gun, he said.

Francique died in hospital days later.

The inquest previously heard police had been investigating Francique, a 28-year-old Black man, for days in the leadup to the shooting. It was dark at the time and the car’s windows were heavily tinted, making it difficult to see inside, Peel regional police Const. Marc Charlebois, then a member of the force’s tactical unit, told the inquest into the death of Jamal Francique.
The tactical unit had been dispatched around 7:46 p.m. on Jan. 7, 2020, and arrived at the townhouse complex about 20 minutes later, he said.

As he came up toward the back of the car, carrying a ballistic shield more than a metre long and a metal bar designed for breaking or prying into windows, the officer said he and a colleague called out some commands, but there was no answer.

Charlebois saw blood, he said, but didn’t yet realize Francique had a gunshot wound. There was no sign of movement, he said.

stories.title: 3 arrests made, 2 suspects outstanding in Bridle Path home invasion
stories.summary: Toronto police say three people are facing charges, and two suspects remain outstanding in connection to a home invasion in the city’s Bridle Path neighbourhood.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police say three people are facing charges, and two suspects remain outstanding in connection to a home invasion in the city’s Bridle Path neighbourhood.

Insp. Kristy Smith told reporters Monday the arrests were made in Ottawa over the weekend – almost three weeks after the break-in that sent four members of the same family to hospital .

Two people have been charged with accessory after the fact, Smith said.

“When you know someone who is wanted for a crime and you help them to avoid and hide from the police, you can be charged with a criminal offence. This is true in this home invasion case,” Smith said.

Police were first called to a home on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:45 a.m. on Oct. 29.

Three masked men in their 20s allegedly forced their way into the home and eventually confronted the family inside, police said. The men were armed with handguns. One suspect had a hammer.

Daijohn Richards , 23, was identified as a suspect and was arrested in Ottawa.

Police said Richards took himself to the hospital following the home invasion for treatment of a gunshot wound to his right shoulder. He was not arrested at the time.

He has been charged with break and enter, disguise with intent, four counts of aggravated assault, four counts of robbery, three counts of discharge firearm with intent to wound, endanger life or prevent arrest and possession of a firearm or ammunition contrary to a prohibition order.

Two suspects remain outstanding. They are to be considered armed and dangerous. Their identities weren’t released by police.

The dark-coloured SUV seen fleeing the area before police arrived has been identified as a grey Honda CR-V with a spare tire mounted on the front driver’s side. Police released an image of the suspect vehicle to help generate leads.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Toronto Police arrest one suspect in Bridle Path home invasion case
stories.summary: Search continues for two other suspects, authorities say
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Toronto Police say they have arrested a fugitive suspect in last month’s “horrific” home invasion that injured a family of four in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood.

In a press conference on Monday, Inspector Kristy Smith said Daijohn Richards, 24, was arrested in Ottawa over the weekend.

She said police had also arrested two other people in Ottawa suspected of being accessories after the fact for allegedly helping hide the fugitive from authorities. Both of those suspects are in their late 20s, police say.

Toronto Police had previously identified Mr. Richards as one of the three suspects connected to the Bridle Path invasion.

Early morning on Oct. 29, masked assailants had shot three members of the family and attacked all four with a hammer, according to police and a statement from the family.

Police had said Mr. Richards was inadvertently shot by another attacker during the home invasion. Authorities interacted with him in hospital immediately after the attack while he was seeking treatment, but said they were unable to arrest him at the time for lack of evidence.

Two suspects in the home invasion remain at large, and police said they are considered armed and dangerous.

Insp. Smith told reporters that police have security video of the attack, recorded inside the home of 75-year-old David Morton, his 64-year-old wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, and their two adult daughters, Cristina and Maggie Zohil-Morton.

“It’s horrific, I can say that about it,” she said. She declined to provide further details.

The existence of such evidence, she said, could potentially help prosecutors advocate for a strong sentence because videos showcase “the gravity of the level of violence” and how “violent these actors are when preying in your own home.”

On Monday, the family at the centre of the Bridle Path attack released an unsigned statement asking the public to “continue to have faith in our police services.”

“We are thankful to share that all of our members have been discharged from the hospital,” the family’s statement reads. However, they also decried the dozens of home invasions that have occurred in Toronto this year.

“How many more families must experience something like this before meaningful change happens?” the statement reads. “Enough is enough.”

Newly filed court records show Mr. Richards May live about 20 kilometres west of the Bridle Path. His listed address is a high-rise apartment near the intersection of Jane Street and Lawrence Avenue.

Colm Cobb Howes, a representative of the Ontario Ministry of the Attorney-General, previously told The Globe and Mail “there is no publicly accessible information available” to release about Mr. Richards’s past.

However, criminal justice records obtained by The Globe from Thunder Bay court show he was charged in that city five years ago with dealing fentanyl and cocaine.

Such charges can result in stiff sentences in Northwestern Ontario, where judges have condemned out-of-town drug dealers for targeting the region’s vulnerable populations.

But in this case, Mr. Richards, who was 18 at the time, pleaded guilty within weeks of his arrest to the lesser charge of possessing cocaine.

Instead of a jail or prison sentence, a prosecutor and a defence lawyer filed a joint submission saying that he could be given a suspended sentence, followed by 12 months probation.

During that 2021 sentence hearing, defence lawyer Richard Garrett said Mr. Richards was a Toronto resident with a Grade 10 education, living in “precarious financial circumstances” with no job, assets or income.

The court ordered that Mr. Richards stay out of Thunder Bay after Crown attorney Ronald Poirier argued the city was being “invaded” by drug traffickers from Southern Ontario.

In the Bridle Path case, charge sheets now filed in the Ontario Court of Justice allege Mr. Richards committed 14 criminal offences in total – including allegations that he broke into the home on Hyde Park Circle while hiding his face “by means of a balaclava.”

The charges, which have not been proven in court, say that he committed aggravated assaults against each of the four family members with the intent to “wound, maim, disfigure, or endanger life.”

He further stands accused of using a handgun to rob the family and shoot Mr. Morton and his two daughters.

Toronto lawyer Salma Azzam is listed on Mr. Richards’s charge sheets. Reached by phone on Monday, she would not confirm whether she is representing him and declined comment.

Police say Mr. Richards made an appearance on Sunday in a Toronto court. He is now barred from communicating with the victims or the two people arrested for allegedly sheltering him.

Insp. Smith told reporters that police are investigating whether Mr. Richards May have participated in other Toronto home invasions. Police say this type of crime is increasing in Canada’s largest city, even as homicides and shootings are steeply declining.

She said Toronto Police will continue to make “visible and covert deployments” in some neighbourhoods to deter similar attacks.

One day before Mr. Richard’s arrest in Ottawa on Saturday, several senior police leaders spoke about the case at a Toronto Police Services Board meeting.

“Any arrest or detention must be supported by evidence and lawful grounds,” Deputy Chief Frank Barredo said. “I know the public wants to know if we did surveillance ... We cannot discuss specific investigative techniques or disclose sensitive details while the investigation remains active.”

Deputy Chief Barredo said there have been more than 100 home invasions in Toronto in 2026, and that police know these crimes have “profoundly” affected people’s sense of safety.

Police Chief Myron Demkiw said at Friday’s board meeting that he has signed a letter supporting an initiative by Ontario Premier Doug Ford that urges federal MPs to toughen the Criminal Code.

“There’s one proposal in particular that would create a standalone offence for violent home invasions with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment,” Chief Demkiw said.

“These are important reforms,” he said. “In the case of home invasions, it would send a clear message that this kind of violence is unacceptable.”

With a report from Willow Fiddler in Thunder Bay

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story misstated the age of the suspect arrested owing to incorrect details from a Toronto Police news release. This version has been corrected.

Police say Mr. Richards made an appearance on Sunday in a Toronto court. He is now barred from communicating with the victims or the two people arrested for allegedly sheltering him.

Insp. Smith told reporters that police are investigating whether Mr. Richards May have participated in other Toronto home invasions. Police say this type of crime is increasing in Canada’s largest city, even as homicides and shootings are steeply declining.
She said Toronto Police will continue to make “visible and covert deployments” in some neighbourhoods to deter similar attacks.
One day before Mr. Richard’s arrest in Ottawa on Saturday, several senior police leaders spoke about the case at a Toronto Police Services Board meeting.

“Any arrest or detention must be supported by evidence and lawful grounds,” Deputy Chief Frank Barredo said. “I know the public wants to know if we did surveillance ... We cannot discuss specific investigative techniques or disclose sensitive details while the investigation remains active.”
Deputy Chief Barredo said there have been more than 100 home invasions in Toronto in 2026, and that police know these crimes have “profoundly” affected people’s sense of safety.
Police Chief Myron Demkiw said at Friday’s board meeting that he has signed a letter supporting an initiative by Ontario Premier Doug Ford that urges federal MPs to toughen the Criminal Code.
“There’s one proposal in particular that would create a standalone offence for violent home invasions with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment,” Chief Demkiw said.
“These are important reforms,” he said. “In the case of home invasions, it would send a clear message that this kind of violence is unacceptable.”

stories.title: Do you remember these drinks? Share your stories
stories.summary: Which of these limited-edition or cult-favourite drinks do you remember?
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Before pumpkin spice everything and endless energy drink flavours, Canadians had some truly strange beverages on store shelves.

Now we’re wondering: which of these limited-edition or cult-favourite drinks do you remember, and are there any other bizarre beverages from the past you’d like to see make a comeback?

Share your stories by emailing Lauren.stallone@bellmedia.CA

Crystal Pepsi: The clear cola that made a splash in the 1990s. It looked like water but tasted like Pepsi, leaving many Canadians both curious and confused.

Orbitz: Part drink, part science experiment. This colourful beverage featured floating edible gel balls suspended throughout the bottle, making it one of the most unusual drinks ever sold in Canada.

Bawls: Known for its distinctive blue bottle and high caffeine content, Bawls developed a loyal following among gamers and late-night study sessions.

Jones Soda Turkey & Gravy: Perhaps the strangest of them all. Jones Soda released a Thanksgiving-themed turkey and gravy-flavoured pop that became famous for daring drinkers to give it a try.

stories.title: Canada recorded 36K consumer insolvencies for 3rd straight quarter
stories.summary: In July, August and September, 36,797 Canadians filed for insolvencies, according to the Canadian Association of Insolvency and Restructuring Professionals (Cairp).
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
So far, the first three quarters of 2026 have seen the highest volume of consumer insolvencies in Canada since 2009, new data shows.

Consumer insolvencies — a measure that indicates how many Canadians filed for relief under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act — reached record highs in the first three quarters of 2026, according to data from the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy.

In July, August and September, 36,797 Canadians filed for insolvencies, according to the Canadian Association of Insolvency and Restructuring Professionals (Cairp).

This is the highest volume of Canadians filing for insolvencies since the first three quarters of 2009, Cairp said, when the Canadian economy was reeling from the aftershocks of the Great Recession of 2008.

However, the rate of insolvencies was at 1.1 per 1,000 Canadian adults in the third quarter, still lower than the 1.5 per 1,000 in the third quarter of 2009.

The lower rate is because of high population growth, but a “persistently high” volume of fillings show that Canadians are struggling to keep up with debt, said Wesley Cowan, licensed insolvency trustee and Cairp vice chair.

Between September 2025 and September 2026, consumer insolvencies increased by five per cent compared to the 12-month period between September 2024 and September 2025.

In September alone, 12,836 Canadians filed for insolvency, up 9.2 per cent from August and 1.3 per cent compared to September 2025.

Atlantic Canada accounted for the largest increases in annual increases in insolvency filings compared to September 2025. Filings rose 15.9 per cent to 175 filings in Prince Edward Island, 5.4 per cent to 649 in Newfoundland and Labrador, and five per cent to 1,125 in Nova Scotia.

In the third quarter, 1,133 Canadian businesses filed for insolvencies. While this was a drop of 11.6 per cent compared to the second quarter (April, May and June), it was up 2.3 per cent compared to the third quarter of 2025.

The accommodation and food services sector saw the largest increase in insolvency fillings, up 35 per cent to 182 fillings, followed by transportation and warehousing with a 15 per cent increase to 96 filings.

Accommodation and food services (16.4 per cent) accounted for the largest share of business insolvencies in Canada, followed by the construction sector (14.9 per cent).

Bank of Canada’s Tiff Macklem won’t seek a 2nd term as governor

Canada’s inflation was steady at 3.1 per cent in October, StatCan says

stories.title: Toronto police arrest suspect in Bridle Path home invasion investigation
stories.summary: Toronto police say one man has been arrested in last month's violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto police have arrested one suspect in last month’s violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood.

Police say 24-year-old Daijohn Richards was arrested in Ottawa over this past weekend following a weekslong investigation after the violent attack that left a family of four injured in the early hours of Oct. 29.

The family was attacked after masked intruders allegedly forced their way into the home through the rear door, armed with guns and a hammer. A 75-year-old man, identified as CEO of Mac Group David Morton, and his two adult daughters were shot. Morton and his wife were both hit with a hammer.

Toronto police announce the arrest of one suspect in last month’s violent Bridle Path home invasion. Daijohn Richards, 24, was arrested in Ottawa while two outstanding suspects remain at large. (Nov. 16, 2026)

Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith told a news conference Monday that a 27-year-old man and a 28-year-old woman were also arrested for harbouring Richards for the last three weeks and have been charged with accessory for helping him evade arrest.

“They were all together at the time a warrant was executed for his arrest,” Smith said.

Richards has been charged with several offences, including four counts of aggravated assault, and remains in police custody.

In a statement released Monday afternoon, the Morton family said all four members of the family have been discharged from the hospital and they were all healing, “both physically and emotionally.”

“We are a strong, close-knit family, and together, we will get through this,” the statement said.

It said the family was thankful for the arrests that have been made but “remain hopeful that further progress will follow as the investigation continues.”

“As our family continues to recover, we respectfully ask that our privacy be respected and that law enforcement be given the space to carry out their work without interference,” it said.

Richards is the same suspect who police say was treated for a gunshot wound and released from a west-end hospital before investigators had the evidence to arrest him. Smith previously said that Richards had interactions with police in the hospital before his release.

Investigators have said they believed he was accidentally shot in his right shoulder by one of the two other alleged intruders. Those two suspects are still wanted by police and are considered armed and dangerous.

Police say the three suspects demanded valuables before getting into an “altercation” with people inside the home. Smith confirmed Monday no valuables were taken from the home.

While Richards has not been officially connected to the 107 other home invasions in Toronto and across the GTA this year, Smith said she “wouldn’t put it past that realm of possibility” that he was involved in other incidents.

“I believe these criminals have the ability to conduct any type of crime that is profitable to them,” she said.

Police have also identified the suspects’ vehicle as a grey Honda CR-V with a front spare tire on the driver’s side.

The vehicle linked Richards as a suspect in the hospital to the home invasion after a “substantial amount” of neighbourhood canvassing, Smith said. It’s unclear if it is a stolen vehicle.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

Note to readers: This is a corrected story. A previous version stated the suspect was 23 years old based on information shared by Toronto police. In fact, the suspect is 24 years old.

stories.title: Bank of Canada’s Tiff Macklem won’t seek a 2nd term as governor
stories.summary: Tiff Macklem took on the role of Bank of Canada governor in June 2020 at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic and is expected to serve until June 2027.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Tiff Macklem , the governor of the Bank of Canada , says he will not be seeking a second term, setting up a search for the next person to lead the country’s central bank into the next decade.

The bank announced Macklem’s decision in a news release on Monday morning, saying he would not return when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said in a statement. “My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

Macklem took on the role June 3, 2020 in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic, though he had been at the central bank since 1984.

Prior to his appointment, he was senior deputy governor while also serving as dean of the Rotman School of Management in Toronto. He was previously expected to take on the top job in 2013, but was passed over for Stephen Poloz.

When Macklem took on the role, the central bank had already slashed its target overnight interest rate to 0.25 per cent and started an unprecedented bond-purchasing program to fund federal fiscal stimulus.

He cautioned against negative interest rates , calling them too disruptive for an already disrupted financial system, adding he was comfortable with 0.25 per cent being as low as the bank would go.

Macklem, 65, has since seen the bank through the pandemic and multiple interest rate hikes as that period tapered off in an effort to tame inflatoin, followed by several cuts.

A search committee has been set up by the Bank of Canada’s board of directors to start a recruitment process to select the next governor. The process is expected to be completed by spring 2027.

The new governor would be appointed to start their term beginning June 3, 2027, once approved by Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne and the federal cabinet.
