stories.title: New project aims to bring forgotten Canadian history to life for younger generations
stories.summary: The Cihe's Canada 160 Project will tell the stories of 160 Canadians who helped shape the nation
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
With the 160th anniversary of Canada’s Confederation approaching on July 1, 2027, a group whose mission is to promote historical literacy through research, education and public engagement is launching a new initiative to enshrine Canada’s nation builders and hopefully spur younger generations to learn more about their country.

The Canadian Institute for Historical Education’s Canada 160 Project, set to launch on Canada Day next year, will be a collection of 160 people’s stories in the form of a short film. The viewer will be introduced to the subject’s significance to Canadian history, “followed by an in-depth study and links to allow further research.”

The thinking is that “people remember what they participate in.”

Don Cranston, chair of the Cihe’s board of directors, said the project is designed in part to reach younger Canadians who May not be drawn to traditional presentations of history.

“We’re trying to capture the imagination or the interest of younger Canadians,” he told National Post, noting the organization started developing the digital initiative after its History Matters social media campaign piled up more than five million views and 15,000 followers across major platforms.

The response, he said, demonstrated considerable interest in Canadian history, particularly when presented in accessible formats.

Cranston said U.S. President Donald Trump and his rhetoric surrounding Canada and the repeated jibes about it becoming the 51st state since being re-elected have only led to further navel-gazing.

“A lot of Canadians, including young Canadians, have been asking the question: Who are we? Why are we different? How did our country come into being the way that it did? And that’s a good thing.”

While there are a lot of obvious Canadians to venerate — think civil rights activist Viola Desmond, father of Medicare Tommy Douglas and national hero Terry Fox — Cranston said Cihe’s mission is to shed a brighter and longer-lasting light on the stories of historic people forgotten, sidelined and sometimes denigrated.

The Cihe itself was founded about three and a half years ago in response to familiar figures from Canadian history becoming the target of activists’ campaigns to take down statues erected in their honour and to remove their name from public buildings and street signs.

Canada’s first prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, was one such target, and the Cihe counts the return of his statues to Queen’s Park in Toronto and the Prime Ministers Walk display in Baden, Ont., as victories.

A statue of Canada’s first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald at Queen’s Park in Toronto. Ernest Doroszuk / Ernest Doroszuk/Toronto Sun/Postmedia

“We realized about a year and a half ago that that reactionary fight will continue, but the way Canada got to the way it did is that Canadians, especially young Canadians, do not know or appreciate their history, and so now it’s become more of an educational and research-based organization,” explained Cranston.

A lifelong enthusiast who believes “history is a unifier,” Cranston said he cringes when he hears people say Canadian history is “boring.”

Among the fascinating stories he hopes Canadians will discover through the project is the 1849 burning of the Parliament buildings in Montreal by angry Tories protesting legislation that provided compensation for property losses suffered during the rebellions of 1837 and 1838.

Cranston said that piece of history would include the saga of “the picture of Queen Victoria that’s in the Parliament buildings in Ottawa, being dutifully cut out with a knife and rolled up, and the person basically just jumped out of the building in time to save that painting and avoid being burned to death.”

Another might be the tale of Jeff Nicklin, a Winnipeg Blue Bombers football player who appeared in five Grey Cups before joining the Canadian Army during the Second World War. He then became a commanding officer of Canada’s first parachute battalion and participated in the D-Day airborne operation in Normandy, France, before being killed later in the war.

Winnipegger Lt.-Col. Jeff Nicklin was the commanding officer of the 1st Canadian Parachute Battalion in Germany during World War II. Handout / SunMedia

Cranston described encountering Nicklin’s grave while attending a Liberation commemoration in the Netherlands last year.

“After reading about Nicklin all these years, I just look to my right, and… there’s Nicklin’s tomb right and burial plot right there, one of these larger-than-life Canadians that no one’s ever heard of.”

Of particular importance to Cranston is that the project features a myriad of Canadian stories, not just those from the largest urban centres, and Cihe is liaising with “friend organizations” in other parts of the country to ferret out those important locals.

Each builder’s story will be presented in a two- to three-minute video vignette detailing “what challenges they faced, their actions, and how they impacted the history of our nation,” as cited in sources like the Dictionary of Canadian Biography and reviewed by a research and academic advisory committee made up of history professors from across Canada.

Cihe said it will use “AI reconstruction” in instances where archival footage of a person doesn’t exist, but Cranston said they’re being very careful about using AI-generated video of long-dead historical figures.

For example, a preliminary reconstruction of Second World War Victoria Cross recipient Filip Konowal, a Ukrainian immigrant who served in the Canadian Army, revealed historical inaccuracies involving his uniform, weaponry and battlefield conditions.

Cranston said the experience reinforced the need for careful review and fact-checking.

A small cross bears the picture of Cpl. Filip Konowal, the only Ukrainian- Canadian to be awarded the Victoria Cross. Mike Hensen / The London Free Press/Postmedia

The videos will be clearly identified as AI, with disclaimers explaining that dialogue attributed to a historical figure is “an interpretation or representation” and not a direct recording of their words.

“We don’t want to be accused of trying to dupe people,” insisted Cranston, who figures most people will know the difference.

After the video, the viewer can dig into a study and its cited sources to learn more about how the builder’s “life and actions, both beneficial and detrimental,” contributed to Canada’s development.

Aligning with the launch date, the first people to be featured will be the fathers of the Confederation — the 34 delegates representing British North American colonies at one or more of the conferences that led to the creation of the Dominion of Canada in 1867.

“Viewers will be able to follow how colonies with very diverse interests negotiated an accord that created a single country,” Cihe explained.

The Cihe also hopes the project can become a resource for schools, museums, libraries and other educational entities, rather than a one-time anniversary celebration. Cranston sees it one day becoming part of school curricula.

Cihe is also developing an $8 million fundraising campaign to establish an endowment that will support its long-term work, and is inviting individuals, families, foundations, corporations, and public partners to contribute.

A related ongoing Cihe initiative, called Telling Canada’s Stories, meanwhile, is providing opportunities to highlight historical figures with particular significance to individual communities, including people whose contributions May be well known locally, but largely unknown elsewhere in the rest of Canada.

“The goal is not to celebrate famous people,” the Cihe writes on its website, where users can submit a short video or provide a short essay about a person they think should be better known.

“The goal is to discover and share the stories of 160 Canadians who helped shape our country in celebration of Canada’s 160th Anniversary.”

Some examples are Joe Shuster, the Jewish Toronto-born creator of Superman, and Sir Joseph-Adolphe Chapleau, a former Macdonald cabinet minister known as the golden voice of Quebec politics.

A lifelong enthusiast who believes “history is a unifier,” Cranston said he cringes when he hears people say Canadian history is “boring.”

Among the fascinating stories he hopes Canadians will discover through the project is the 1849 burning of the Parliament buildings in Montreal by angry Tories protesting legislation that provided compensation for property losses suffered during the rebellions of 1837 and 1838.

Cranston said that piece of history would include the saga of “the picture of Queen Victoria that’s in the Parliament buildings in Ottawa, being dutifully cut out with a knife and rolled up, and the person basically just jumped out of the building in time to save that painting and avoid being burned to death.”

Another might be the tale of Jeff Nicklin, a Winnipeg Blue Bombers football player who appeared in five Grey Cups before joining the Canadian Army during the Second World War. He then became a commanding officer of Canada’s first parachute battalion and participated in the D-Day airborne operation in Normandy, France, before being killed later in the war.
Winnipegger Lt.-Col. Jeff Nicklin was the commanding officer of the 1st Canadian Parachute Battalion in Germany during World War II. Handout / SunMedia
Cranston described encountering Nicklin’s grave while attending a Liberation commemoration in the Netherlands last year.

“After reading about Nicklin all these years, I just look to my right, and… there’s Nicklin’s tomb right and burial plot right there, one of these larger-than-life Canadians that no one’s ever heard of.”

Of particular importance to Cranston is that the project features a myriad of Canadian stories, not just those from the largest urban centres, and Cihe is liaising with “friend organizations” in other parts of the country to ferret out those important locals.

Each builder’s story will be presented in a two- to three-minute video vignette detailing “what challenges they faced, their actions, and how they impacted the history of our nation,” as cited in sources like the Dictionary of Canadian Biography and reviewed by a research and academic advisory committee made up of history professors from across Canada.

Cihe said it will use “AI reconstruction” in instances where archival footage of a person doesn’t exist, but Cranston said they’re being very careful about using AI-generated video of long-dead historical figures.

For example, a preliminary reconstruction of Second World War Victoria Cross recipient Filip Konowal, a Ukrainian immigrant who served in the Canadian Army, revealed historical inaccuracies involving his uniform, weaponry and battlefield conditions.
Cranston said the experience reinforced the need for careful review and fact-checking.
A small cross bears the picture of Cpl. Filip Konowal, the only Ukrainian- Canadian to be awarded the Victoria Cross. Mike Hensen / The London Free Press/Postmedia

The videos will be clearly identified as AI, with disclaimers explaining that dialogue attributed to a historical figure is “an interpretation or representation” and not a direct recording of their words.
“We don’t want to be accused of trying to dupe people,” insisted Cranston, who figures most people will know the difference.
After the video, the viewer can dig into a study and its cited sources to learn more about how the builder’s “life and actions, both beneficial and detrimental,” contributed to Canada’s development.

Aligning with the launch date, the first people to be featured will be the fathers of the Confederation — the 34 delegates representing British North American colonies at one or more of the conferences that led to the creation of the Dominion of Canada in 1867.
“Viewers will be able to follow how colonies with very diverse interests negotiated an accord that created a single country,” Cihe explained.

The Cihe also hopes the project can become a resource for schools, museums, libraries and other educational entities, rather than a one-time anniversary celebration. Cranston sees it one day becoming part of school curricula.

Cihe is also developing an $8 million fundraising campaign to establish an endowment that will support its long-term work, and is inviting individuals, families, foundations, corporations, and public partners to contribute.

A related ongoing Cihe initiative, called Telling Canada’s Stories, meanwhile, is providing opportunities to highlight historical figures with particular significance to individual communities, including people whose contributions May be well known locally, but largely unknown elsewhere in the rest of Canada.
“The goal is not to celebrate famous people,” the Cihe writes on its website, where users can submit a short video or provide a short essay about a person they think should be better known.
“The goal is to discover and share the stories of 160 Canadians who helped shape our country in celebration of Canada’s 160th Anniversary.”
Some examples are Joe Shuster, the Jewish Toronto-born creator of Superman, and Sir Joseph-Adolphe Chapleau, a former Macdonald cabinet minister known as the golden voice of Quebec politics.

stories.title: Canada’s Alert Ready emergency system will test notifications on Wednesday
stories.summary: The emergency alerts are used by governments to inform the public of emergencies including tornadoes, floods, wildfires and Amber Alerts
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Canadians’ phones, TVs and radios are set to sound off on Wednesday as the country’s national emergency alert system performs its second test of the year.

The Alert Ready tone will broadcast on Nov. 18 in all provinces and territories through TV, radio, and any mobile device connected to an LTE or 5G network.

Wednesday’s test is designed to “test” the functionality of the system and build the public’s awareness of emergency alerts. They issue a tone, accompanied with a message.

British Columbia at 1:55 p.m.

Alberta at 1:55 p.m.

Saskatchewan at 1:55 p.m.

Manitoba at 1:55 p.m.

Ontario at 12:55 p.m.

Quebec at 1:55 p.m.

New Brunswick at 10:55 a.m.

Nova Scotia at 1:55 p.m.

Prince Edward Island at 12:55 p.m.

Newfoundland and Labrador at 9:55 a.m.

Northwest Territories at 1:55 p.m.

Yukon at 1:55 p.m.

Nunavut at 1:55 p.m.

The emergency alerts are used by governments to inform the public of emergencies including tornadoes, floods, wildfires and Amber Alerts

People cannot opt out of receiving a test alert or the Alert Ready system as a whole.

The tests typically take place in May and November.

stories.title: Canada to test its emergency alert system Wednesday
stories.summary: Canadians will see their phones buzzing this Wednesday as the country takes part in a nation-wide testing of its public alerting system.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canadians will see their phones buzzing this Wednesday as the country takes part in a nation-wide testing of its public alerting system.

A message will be sent to all compatible wireless devices connected to an LTE or 5G network, including cell phones and smartwatches, beginning at 9:55 AM NST in Newfoundland and Labrador.

The Alert Ready test will also be broadcast on television and radio.

“This public test helps ensure the system continues to function effectively and helps Canadians recognize alert signals in the event of a real emergency,” officials wrote in a press release.

“The test message will simulate an emergency alert and will begin with the Canadian Alert Attention Signal,” officials added. “It will clearly indicate that it is a test and that no action is required.”

The Alert Ready system is used to raise public awareness during real emergencies such as tornadoes, floods, wildfires and Amber Alerts.

There is no option to opt out of the test or actual emergency alerts.

So far in 2026, the system has sent over 1,215 emergency alerts across Canada.

stories.title: Meet some of the young cowboys taking over the future of bull and bronc riding
stories.summary: Toronto - Dozens of cowboys and cowgirls from across Canada donned their hats, brushed their denim and slid on their boots to participate in this year’s Royal Rodeo at the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Dozens of cowboys and cowgirls from across Canada donned their hats, brushed their denim and slid on their boots to participate in this year’s Royal Rodeo at the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair.

A striking number of this year’s contestants inside Toronto’s Exhibition Place looked fresh out of school, eager and bright-eyed to tackle some of the toughest sports in the country.

Hundreds of cheering rodeo fans packed the arena on Sunday to watch the athletes tackle barrel racing, pole bending, lurching horses and bucking bulls.

Bull rider Austin Lightfoot talks about his love of the sport and how he got his start at the age of 16. The sport involves trying to stay on the back of a 900-kilogram bull, who thrashes the entire time for eight seconds. (Nov. 16, 2026)

Austin Lightfoot, 19, has been riding bulls since he was 16 years old.

The sport involves climbing onto the back of a 900-kilogram bull, who thrashes and bucks the entire time. The contestant needs to try and stay mounted for eight seconds while holding on with one hand, known as “covering” the bull.

“My first year, I was bucked off every single bull,” he said with a smile. “Then in my second year, I ended up covering almost every junior bull I got on.”

For Lightfoot, it’s a proud, thrilling experience to be a part of. Like many of the other contestants, he wore a dark-coloured head helmet as he held onto the bull, his flashy orange chaps flying with him.

“It’s a rhythm you learn with the bulls,” he said. “I like to stay calm and cool and just be ready for any moment.”

In bronc riding, similar to bull riding but with horses, Austin Martin stood next to a dark brown stallion. Occasionally, the horse kicked its stall and a violent clanking echoed through the already-loud stadium.

Martin, unfazed, continued stretching next to the horse, sometimes jumping high up in the air before moving his legs around.

The 17-year-old managed to stay on the bucking animal beyond eight seconds. It’s a routine the teenager is familiar with after being involved in the sport since he was roughly 12 years old.

“If you have a good ride, you feel like you’re 10-feet-tall and bulletproof,” he said. “If you have a bad ride, then it’s not fun. It hurts.”

Around him, rodeo crews stretched and practised runs.

One bullfighter, in bright clothing with paint on his face, whose job is to distract the bull if a rider falls off, practised jumping and swerving out of the animal’s way before bravely heading out into the arena.

“Usually, when I’m about to get on my horse, I say, ‘I’m gonna spur the horse every jump … and I am the best in the world,’” said Martin.

“If you tell yourself you’re the best, it’s a lot more likely you’re going to be the best.”

Ben Hoogers, 20, managed to stay on the longest on a violently thrashing bull on Sunday, despite only getting two hours of sleep the night before.

When asked about any training strategies he has, Hoogers said it’s just about getting back on every time the bull inevitably throws you off.

“It just works out better when you don’t think,” Hoogers said of what he does to prepare before the competition. He always takes a moment or two to listen to his favourite artists, such as Metallica, before competing.

While most cowboys were focused on stretching, checking on the stallions and putting their gear on, one athlete knelt down with his cowboy hat over his face as he appeared to be praying.

After a few minutes, the cowboy stood up and mounted the large horse next to him. He practised placing his hand over his head for a few minutes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Your business’s next owner May already be on the payroll
stories.summary: Canada introduced employee ownership trust (EOT) rules in 2024, giving business owners another way to transfer their companies
stories.author: Sarita Harbour
stories.content:
Aaron Schroeder’s climate consulting firm, Brightspot Climate, was growing. He knew his employees were driving the company’s success; he started wondering how they could share in the wealth they were creating.

One evening in 2022, the Vancouver-based founder wrote his employees a letter. He didn’t yet know how it would work, but he pledged to move the company toward employee ownership. He made the promise to the entire staff, not just senior employees.

“I want our company to change the way that we accumulate wealth and how we share it,” Mr. Schroeder recalls telling them.

The idea had roots in Mr. Schroeder’s upbringing on a Saskatchewan dairy farm, where he saw how hard work built value. Brightspot already paid bonuses linked to project profitability, but he wanted employees to have something more lasting.

On April 1, 2025, Brightspot transferred ownership to an employee ownership trust (EOT). Its 40 or so employees became beneficiaries of a trust holding the company’s shares, without having to buy in themselves.

In his 40s, Mr. Schroeder wasn’t planning to retire yet. But as Brightspot grew, he began thinking about succession, wanting to ensure the company would continue to thrive after he moved on. He explored selling the company upon receiving inquiries from large consulting firms and private-equity investors, many based in the United States, but feared an outside sale would change Brightspot’s culture.

“I very quickly decided that that’s not the route I wanted to take,” he says.

Canada introduced EOT rules in 2024, giving business owners another way to transfer their companies. Under the structure, a trust buys the company for employees’ benefit. The purchase is generally financed over time from the company’s earnings. In June 2026, Ottawa made permanent a capital gains exemption of up to $10-million for qualifying sales to employee ownership trusts and worker co-operatives.

The change comes amid a wave of business succession. A January 2026 study by the Business Development Bank of Canada found that 61 per cent of small and medium-sized businesses are led by owners aged 50 or older, and nearly one in five expect to exit within five years.

Jon Shell, vice-chair of the non-profit Employee Ownership Canada, says business owners often care deeply about what happens to their companies after a sale. “The vast majority of them are deeply committed to the communities in which they operate, deeply committed to their employees,” he says.

But EOTs aren’t right for every business. Businesses need dependable cash flow to finance the purchase and the structure involves additional administration . Mr. Shell says limited awareness among business owners and advisers is another obstacle.

At Brightspot, the day-to-day engineering work didn’t change much under the EOT structure, but the firm’s governance did. As founder and CEO, Mr. Schroeder was previously the company’s sole director. He now reports to a board of directors. Mr. Schroeder shared the company financials prior to the transition with employees who helped shape the ownership structure. “We started very early trying to build financial literacy in the company,” he says.

Deepika Mahadevan, a senior manager in Brightspot’s Toronto office, helped develop the formula for distributing employee dividends and was elected to an employee representative group. At a staff retreat, she recalls, employees were encouraged to question the proposed change. Her technical work has not changed, but she sees the company’s future differently.

“I’m not just helping build someone else’s business. I’m helping build our business,” she says. “I think one of the things that makes employee ownership exciting is that the business success is also connected to our own financial success.”

In Calgary, Peter Jeune is pursuing a similar transfer for The Camera Store, an independent photography retailer he co-founded with Anabela Ferreira in 1996. Ms. Ferreira’s brother Julian joined them in 1999. Today the business has about 35 employees including the founders, with deep ties to the photography community.

“We’ve always said, we don’t sell boxes,” he says, describing the store’s active presence among local camera clubs, photography schools and community events.

Mr. Jeune worried an outside buyer might cut wages or benefits and change the store’s character. The company belongs to a living-wage network, and employees stay an average of eight years, he says. With no children interested in taking over, an EOT offered another path forward.

“It gets personal if you build something for 30 years and build a very specific culture,” he says.

As of early November 2026, Mr. Jeune says the EOT transaction had not yet closed, though it’s very close. Mr. Jeune plans to stay on after the deal to facilitate the transition. Employees have welcomed the idea of becoming an EOT, he says, but he acknowledges it will take time for them to see financial benefits while the sale is being paid off.

At Brightspot, Mr. Schroeder has noticed staff paying closer attention to project profitability and bringing forward ideas for new services. It’s too early to know how much employee ownership will change the company’s long-term fortunes, but he sees an immediate shift in how people approach the business.

“I think we’ve created 40 entrepreneurs here all of a sudden,” he says.

stories.title: Russia calls for ‘consequences’ on Canada after World Juniors hockey ban
stories.summary: Russia's Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov is calling on the International Olympic Committee to impose “consequences” which would affect Canada hosting future sports events.
stories.author: James Ellingworth
stories.content:
Russia is demanding the ice hockey world junior championships are moved out of Canada after the International Ice Hockey Federation ruled its team out of the tournament .

Russian officials are appealing to the International Olympic Committee to intervene on their behalf against the Iihf, with Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov calling for “consequences” which would affect Canada hosting future sports events.

With just over a month until teams arrive in Edmonton and Red Deer for the Dec. 26-Jan. 5 World Juniors, the Iihf confirmed Sunday that Russia was out of the tournament, after the Canadian government said it would not allow Russian participation.

“The only legitimate decision would be to move the tournament out of Canada to a country which is prepared to ensure the participation of all eligible national teams including Russia,” Degtyaryov, who also heads the Russian Olympic Committee, posted on social media late Sunday.

“We are convinced that the actions of the Iihf, Hockey Canada and the Canadian government should receive the very toughest assessment from the IOC, international sports organizations, and bring about consequences for their status and the right to host international competitions.”

The Russian hockey federation said the Iihf decision was made “solely due to political reasons, in violation of a binding and effective ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport,” and indicated it wanted compensation.

The IOC did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday after the Russian demands.

Canada’s block on Russia followed a ruling from the Court of Arbitration for Sport which overturned an Iihf ban on Russian national teams which had been in place since shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

The CAS ruling has prompted a backlash in hockey. Seven European nations at the 16-team men’s world championships have said they will not play against Russia in the tournament in May, and Germany is weighing up whether it can continue as host.

The Iihf is also facing pressure from sponsors who don’t want their brands associated with the Russian team.

Besides Canada, governments in Finland, Sweden and Norway have all either tightened their border controls to bar entry to Russian athletes, or have said they are planning to do so.

The new ‘Bachelor’ will be NFL quarterback Sam Hartman

stories.title: Western Mustangs claim 2026 Yates Cup
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs win 2026 Yates Cup against rival Queen's University. They return home for the Mitchell Bowl on Nov. 21.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
For the 36th time in program history, the Western Mustangs are Yates Cup Champions.

A 36-27 win over Queen’s on Nov. 14 in Kingston, Ont., clinched the OUA Championship for the Mustangs.

Two major highlights came from game MVP Thomson Silcox, with a pick-six, and a 77-yard punt return by Brenna Keba.

“Just a huge credit to our defence, Coach Paul Gleason, Coach Craig Butler, really putting our guys in a good position. You can see we got pressure on their quarterback and didn’t make it easy for them in the first half,” said head coach Michael Faulds.

“Offensively, we did pretty well in the first half, mainly the one explosive play by Emmett Charles, which everyone’s getting used to. Coming out in the third quarter, we knew we wanted to take the wind and show our dominance. You’ve got the big touchdown there by Emmett, followed by Keba’s big return touchdown, and that opened the floodgates.”

The Mustangs now progress to the 2026 U SPORTS Mitchell Bowl, which will be played at Western Alumni Stadium on Nov. 21 at 12 p.m. The Mustangs will take on St. Mary’s University, the Atlantic University Sport football champions, to determine which team makes it the Vanier Cup.

The Mustangs win over Queen’s marks the fifth Yates Cup for Coach Faulds, two as a player and now three in his OUA coaching career. It is his first title as a Mustangs coach.

“It feels incredible. I told our guys, I’ve been to many Yates Cups as a player and as a coach. Although we’re going to play a bigger game next week and we hope to play a bigger game in two weeks, Yates Cup Day is my favourite day of the year,” said Faulds.

“There’s something special knowing you’re fighting for a trophy that is older than any other football trophy in the world. The OUA has 11 football teams; tt’s a gruelling conference, and our pathway to the Yates Cup meant we were playing three teams – Laurier, Windsor and Queen’s – for the 2nd time. Our guys showed so much resiliency, and you can see that. For a young team that just played their 11th game in a row, each and every week we truly are getting better.”

The Mustangs found an early downfield play while the game was still scoreless, breaking an 80-yard gain in the second quarter. The offence finished with 228 passing yards and 144 rushing yards, with Ben Casselman completing 17 of 23 passes for 228 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Emmett Charles was tied directly to the passing production with five catches for 106 yards and two touchdowns, while Ethan Dolby added 106 rushing yards on 12 carries.

The Mustangs also shaped the game through returns and defensive plays as Queen’s piled up 539 total yards and 28 first downs. Western intercepted two passes for 112 return yards, including a touchdown, and Thomson Silcox finished with both interceptions. Brennan Keba added a punt-return touchdown as part of a 160-yard punt-return day. In the fourth quarter, the Mustangs added a goal-line stand, denying Queen’s a touchdown from close range as part of a defensive effort that also included three sacks.

The Mustangs were held scoreless in the first quarter, while Queen’s took the only points on Tyler Mullan’s 36-yard field goal at 9:04. Western’s best field position came after Keba’s 14-yard punt return, and Casselman completions to Nik Shewchuk and Charles helped move the ball to the Queen’s 46 before Oliver Griffiths punted. Conner Franzisi and Nawaz Oyewale combined on a late sack, and the Mustangs finished the quarter trailing 3-0.

A safety started Western’s 12-point second quarter before Casselman connected with Charles for an 80-yard touchdown and Mateo Pasquini added the extra point. Pasquini later made a 42-yard field goal, and Silcox intercepted Alex Vreeken to halt a Queen’s possession.

stories.title: Telus conducting ‘thorough review’ of $31B takeover offer from Quebecor
stories.summary: Quebecor has sent an unsolicited offer to acquire Telus in a merger deal valued at approximately $31 billion, which represents an enhanced proposal from June.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Québecor said Monday it has sent an unsolicited offer to acquire Telus in a merger deal valued at approximately $31 billion, which represents an enhanced proposal from June.

Telus confirmed it received the offer from Québecor on Monday, and is conducting a “thorough review,” but there remain concerns about regulatory approvals potentially delaying such a merger.

“With the support of our advisors, the Special Committee is conducting a thorough review of Québecor’s proposal to determine the course of action that will be in the best interests of TELUS and its stakeholders,” said John Manley, Chair of the TELUS board of directors in a press release.

Telus revealed in its press release that Monday’s proposal represents an enhanced offer from a private offer Québecor made in June. Manley highlighted that the potential merger still carries significant risk, which was a concern with the initial proposal.

“To date, this review has surfaced a number of significant risks associated with Québecor’s proposal, including the fact that more than four months after its initial proposal, Québecor has yet to explain how what it is proposing could be approved under the current telecom regulatory framework in Canada and that a regulatory review of such a transaction would be a long and costly process for our shareholders,” said Manley.

Telus says it will consider other strategic alternatives to Québecor’s offer to maximize value.

Québecor said in its own press release Monday that the two companies decided to make the merger discussions public given what’s at stake.

“Québecor continues to favour constructive dialogue with the TELUS Board of Directors and respects the review it is conducting. However, Québecor believes it is in the public interest to make its proposal known at this time,” said Québecor in its release.

“The telecommunications sector is undergoing profound change, and the proposed combination has implications beyond the purely financial realm: it directly affects consumers, business customers, employees, communities and the shareholders of both companies.”

– more to come.

stories.title: London police release images of suspect sought in stabbing investigation
stories.summary: Police said the suspect fled north on an e-bike before officers arrived. A search of the area was conducted, but the suspect was not located.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police have released images of a suspect they hope the public can help identify following a stabbing earlier this month.

The stabbing occurred on Nov. 7 at about 9 p.m. in the area of Dundas and Elizabeth streets.

Officers responded to reports of a stabbing and located a male victim suffering from serious, but non-life-threatening injuries. The victim was transported to hospital by paramedics.

Police said the suspect fled north on an e-bike before officers arrived. A search of the area was conducted, but the suspect was not located.

Investigators describe the suspect as a white man, approximately 5-foot-8 and between 25 and 40 years old. He was wearing a black jacket, black jogging pants with a white logo on the left pant leg, and white-and-blue running shoes.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area at the time, knows the identity of the suspect, or has dashcam, residential or business surveillance video from the area of Dundas and Elizabeth streets between 8:40 p.m. and 9:10 p.m. on Nov. 7 to contact police.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Canadian inflation expected to have ticked up to 3.2% in October
stories.summary: Economists say elevated energy prices remain a key driver, as Statscan is set to release data Monday
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s inflation rate held steady in October as higher prices for gas, groceries and clothes were partly offset by cheaper cellphone plans and slower rent price growth, Statistics Canada said Monday.

The annual rate of inflation was steady at 3.1 per cent last month, slightly below economists’ expectations of 3.2 per cent.

The inflation reading raises questions about whether the Bank of Canada will need to raise interest rates again in December, said Benjamin Reitzes, Bmo’s managing director of Canadian rates and macro strategist.

“There’s nothing in these numbers at the moment that really screams rate hike for the Bank of Canada,” he said. “They’ve been particularly hawkish over the past few weeks and they raised rates in October and signalled that more could be necessary.”

The central bank raised its key rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent on Oct. 28, its first hike in more than three years, amid concerns that elevated energy costs could fuel broader inflation.

It aims to keep inflation at 2 per cent, the midpoint of its target range of 1 per cent to 3 per cent.

Mr. Reitzes said October’s inflation numbers “don’t necessarily signal that they need to do something immediately, but again, that doesn’t mean they won’t. There’s no clearcut case here either way.”

Gasoline continued to be a key driver of headline inflation, rising 30.9 per cent year-over-year in October compared with 27.8 per cent the month before amid continued conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Higher energy costs could eventually push up prices elsewhere, said Royal Bank of Canada economist Abbey Xu.

“The longer energy prices remain elevated, the more cost pressures will filter through to consumer prices with a lag,” she said in a client note.

“The path of energy prices also remains highly uncertain despite the decline in gasoline prices so far in November.”

Statscan said gasoline prices rose at a faster annual pace last month partly because prices fell sharply in October 2025, making the year-over-year increase appear larger.

On a monthly basis, however, gasoline prices fell 2.5 per cent in October.

Excluding energy, annual inflation eased to 2 per cent in October from 2.1 per cent in September.

“Underlying price pressures stayed comparatively contained,” Ms. Xu said, noting that the Consumer Price Index excluding both food and energy slowed to 1.8 per cent.

Rbc’s diffusion index, which measures how widespread inflation is across the economy, continued to show that “unusually strong price growth has been concentrated in a relatively narrow share of the consumer basket,” she said.

Meanwhile, Canadians once again faced higher prices at grocery stores.

Statscan said the cost of food purchased from stores accelerated to 2 per cent year-over-year in October after four consecutive months of slower price growth.

Fresh vegetable prices rose 1.4 per cent year-over-year in October after falling 2.9 per cent in September while condiments, spices and vinegars were up 2.6 per cent.

Compared with October 2020, the agency said grocery prices have climbed 31.9 per cent.

Even as inflation slows, Canadians are still feeling the effects of years of rising prices, Mr. Reitzes said.

“The reality is inflation is only prices going higher; prices don’t come back down in general,” he said.

“What we need to happen is a lengthy period of relatively low inflation and some good wage growth and that’ll make everyday Canadians feel much better.”

Meanwhile, prices for clothing were up 1.8 per cent in October, driven by a 2.2-per-cent year-over-year increase in women’s clothing and a 1.4-per-cent increase in men’s clothing.

Clothing prices were up 3.4 per cent month-over-month in October, the largest monthly increase since September 2019.

Statscan said the price increases coincided with higher shipping costs.

In Ontario, prices for natural gas rose 3 per cent year-over-year in October after declining 18.7 per cent in September.

Prices for cellphone plans fell 6.2 per cent year-over-year in October, after rising 0.8 per cent in September.

Statscan said the decline was largely due to comparisons with a year ago, when companies had raised prices.

Slower rent price growth also helped ease inflation, particularly in British Columbia, while rents in Ontario rose 1.1 per cent year-over-year in October.

stories.title: Milton, Ont. to swear in first new mayor in 46 years as Gord Krantz leaves office
stories.summary: George Minakakis and eight regional and town councillors will take their oaths of office at the council’s inaugural meeting Monday night.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The town of Milton is set to swear-in a new mayor for the first time since 1980.

George Minakakis and eight regional and town councillors will take their oaths of office at the council’s inaugural meeting Monday night.

Minakakis takes the reins from Canada’s longest-serving mayor, Gordon Krantz, who held Milton’s top job for 46 years before being defeated in October’s municipal election.

First elected to the town’s council in 1965, Krantz helped steward Milton’s transformation from agricultural community to rapidly growing suburb, negotiating the “Big Pipe” project that brought the town fresh drinking water from Lake Ontario in 2000 and sparked a population boom.

During Krantz’s tenure as mayor, Milton’s population more than tripled and the town was Canada’s fastest-growing municipality for a 10-year stretch.

The 89-year-old told The Canadian Press in an interview before October’s election that he was running again for mayor because he still felt he had more to do.

But ultimately, voters rewarded Minakakis, who ran on a platform of strengthening Milton’s economy and attracting more businesses to the bedroom community to spur local job growth.

The former business executive had served as a Milton town councillor for a year after winning a 2025 byelection.

Krantz told The Canadian Press in October that pragmatism guided his long political career.

“Separating out your wants from your needs for your community is important,” he said of the “delicate” balancing act of expanding services while keeping taxes low as Milton grew.

“As I will often say, there really is no free lunch. You pay me now or you pay me later,” he said.

Krantz said he correctly predicted that Milton would one day be home to highrise buildings when he was a town councillor back in 1965, an idea “way out in left field” at the time.

His next prediction for Milton’s future? Urbanization and a move away from cars.

“You’re going to find places like Oakville, Burlington, Milton, and the region of Halton, York and Durham be part of one great metropolis 100 years from now. Urbanization is here to stay in this part of the world,” he said.

stories.title: Woodstock woman dies after being struck by SUV; police seek video footage
stories.summary: Woodstock police are continuing to investigate a fatal collision that occurred Saturday at about 5:17 p.m. near Dundas Street and Marlboro Street.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A Woodstock woman has died after being struck by a vehicle over the weekend.

Woodstock police are continuing to investigate a fatal collision that occurred Saturday at about 5:17 p.m. near Dundas Street and Marlboro Street.

Police said a 64-year-old Woodstock woman, who was a pedestrian, was taken to hospital, where she was later pronounced dead.

Investigators said the collision involved a grey 2011 Lexus RX 450h. The driver remained at the scene and is cooperating with the investigation.

Members of the Woodstock Police Service, including an accident reconstruction officer and an identification officer, attended the scene and are assisting with the investigation.

Police have released a reference photo of a grey 2011 Lexus RX 450h to help members of the public review any potential video footage related to the collision. The image provided by police is not of the actual vehicle involved.

Police said this includes dash cam, doorbell camera, residential or business surveillance footage, or any other video that May have captured the area or the vehicle.

stories.title: N.S. football player dies suddenly while attending U.S. boarding school
stories.summary: A talented young football player from Halifax, Nova Scotia, who was set to play in the Ncaa next year has died while attending a boarding school in the United States.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A talented young football player from Halifax, Nova Scotia, who was set to play in the Ncaa next year has died while attending a boarding school in the United States.

Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School in Georgia says Marcellus Young Casario died after being transported to hospital Friday morning due to a sudden medical emergency.

The six-foot-six, 225-pound defensive lineman had recently committed to play football for the University of Georgia Bulldogs.

The school says in a Facebook post Casario was expected to graduate from the boarding school in December before enrolling at the university in January.

Rabun Gap-Nacoochee says Casario’s love of football began at a young age and was inspired by his father and grandfather.

Casario’s coach, Derek White, also says in the Facebook post that Casario was everything a coach wants in a player.

“He was known for his relentless dedication, and his journey as a student-athlete was marked by hard work and a true brotherhood with his teammates,” White said.

stories.title: A new flight path for First Nations health care
stories.summary: Ottawa should hand over responsibility for medical transport services
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
For First Nations in remote northern Ontario and Manitoba, getting to a medical appointment often means getting on an airplane to travel hundreds of kilometres. It can be a life or death situation, and is an integral part of health care, not a perk from Ottawa.

Those services, provided under the federal government’s Non-Insured Health Benefits (Nihb) program for First Nations, are also a money-eating logistical nightmare vulnerable to unpredictable variables that can leave patients stranded.

The Nihb program was the only chance Miranda Mamakwa had to get the aftercare she needed following her open-heart surgery in May. She died in September after missing four scheduled appointments because staff at the federal office in rural Sioux Lookout didn’t book her travel, according to her family’s lawyer. The Mamakwa family has since asked the Ontario Provincial Police to launch a probe for criminal negligence.

In Canada, health care is the constitutional responsibility of the provinces and territories, who have jurisdictional expertise over its service and delivery. Except when it comes to Indigenous people, the federal government is responsible for providing health care.

A federal health transfer policy established nearly four decades ago is supposed to hand off some control to Indigenous-led groups. The Health Transfer Policy for Indigenous people was established under the National Health and Welfare and the Treasury Board of Canada in 1989. Meant as a pathway to shift control from the federal health branch to Indigenous-led administration, it gives First Nations who opt-in local control over community-based health services and delivery.

However, the Nihb program isn’t eligible for such transfers currently.

No one is more familiar with the gaps in the system than the First Nations who’ve had to navigate bureaucracy without falling through those cracks. Dropping the reins and handing over responsibility of medical transportation, one of the benefits offered under the Nihb program, to First Nations is necessary for ensuring full access to health care.

The Nihb program is but one example of Ottawa’s archaic and paternalistic approach to fulfilling its obligations to Indigenous people.

Ms. Mamakwa’s death wasn’t an isolated incident. There are thousands of other patients like her from the north relying on Ottawa’s Nihb program experiencing similar failures.

The disconnect between Ottawa and the north plays out on the ground in bureaucracy-heavy scenarios typical of what Ms. Mamakwa faced.

For Northern Ontario, that looks like a single office in rural Sioux Lookout where federal bureaucrats are responsible for co-ordinating medical transportation for thousands of patients in dozens of remote communities accessing health care not available at a local nursing station.

Local health care workers in respective communities help facilitate the process to ensure patients get to their appointments, however it is a system designed to fail, too often leaving those patients in limbo.

The line of accountability when an appointment is missed because of no travel arrangements is even less clear.

Almost a quarter-million people in Ontario are eligible for Nihb, according to Indigenous Services Canada’s 2024-2025 report. About half, or roughly 129,000 people, claimed pharmaceutical coverage in that year.

There are no data for how many people utilized medical transportation in Ontario but the costs of scheduled flights, air ambulance, meals, and lodging totalled $185.5-million, more than doubling from fiscal 2020-21. For Manitoba, it was $304.2-million, nearly double from 2020-21.

Previous attempts to hand over control of medical transportation foundered on fiscal inflexibility. If a First Nation didn’t accurately predict how many people would require transportation and exceeded its budget, they would have curtail that service. Ottawa needs to use a more flexible budgeting approach.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he’s willing to recast Ottawa’s relationship with First Nations. Easing the federal government’s bureaucratic grip on health care would be a demonstration of the seriousness of his intent.

stories.title: Video captures confrontation outside Chinese Consulate in Toronto
stories.summary: A video showing an alleged assault against two Falun Gong demonstrators outside China’s consulate in Toronto has prompted renewed calls for Prime Minister Mark Carney to confront Beijing over alleged transnational repression in Canada.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Toronto - Human rights advocates say a video obtained by CTV News is a flagrant example of transnational repression by China. The video shows a man tearing down Falun Gong banners set up outside the Chinese consulate in Toronto and threatening to “shoot dead” a female demonstrator and kicking another woman who was videotaping the incident.

Activists are calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to raise the issue of China’s human rights abuses when he meets with President Xi Jinping later this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.

“It’s important that Prime Minister Carney raise this issue and put an immediate stop to this blatant transnational repression happening in Canada,” says Joel Chipkar, the spokesperson for the Falun Dafa Association of Canada.

“This is creating fear and insecurity for Canadians here who escaped (China’s) tyrannical regime and came here for a better life.”

The two women are part of a rotating group of volunteers who stand outside the consulate each day to draw attention to China’s persecution of Falun Gong practitioners.

Falun Gong is a spiritual movement which began in the 1990s. The Chinese government labelled the spiritual movement a “heretical cult” as justification for cracking down on its millions of followers.

Chipkar told CTV News that one demonstrator was a Canadian citizen and that the other woman was a refugee who fled to Canada in 2024. Both women have families who have been imprisoned in China because of their religious beliefs.

“They feel the Chinese Communist Party has too much influence in Canada. We have people in our community who have been assaulted. They have been followed home, and their family members have been threatened in China.”

‘This is Chinese territory’

The Toronto incident that occurred on Sept. 22 is one of dozens of examples cited in a new Safeguard Defenders report, which alleges that Beijing has created a massive network of overseas associations, that Chinese Communist Party (CCP) agents are using to monitor and control its diaspora. The report claims that there are at least 18 illegal police stations in Canada.

The four-minute video reveals a confrontation on Toronto’s George Street in front of the Consulate-General of the People’s Republic of China.

It involves an altercation between two demonstrators and a man wearing a black jacket with the flag of China sewn on it.

Angered by the message on the protest banners, which drew attention to China’s repression of the Falun Gong, the man begins tearing apart the signs. The female demonstrator urges her friend to call the police, while the man tells someone off camera to start recording video as well.

A copy of the video has been sent to the Toronto Police Service. CTV News has independently verified the accuracy of the English subtitles on the video.

“These are illegal,” the man says, referring to the banners. “This is the entry to the embassy. This is Chinese territory – do you know that? You have violated China’s anti-secession law. I can shoot you dead.” He continues, pointing his finger at her: “I will make you fall to your death. Believe it or not. I will shoot you to death believe it or not.”

Later on in the video, the woman tries to grab him from behind to stop him from tearing down more signs. That’s when the man shoves her back, nearly knocking her glasses off. Then the man walks toward the woman recording the video and kicks her.

Chipkar helped the women report the incident to police. Witnesses were able to record the licence plate of the Uber vehicle the man got into. Chipkar says investigators were able to identify the man.

They found out through the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) that he had returned to China.

“Police did tell us that if he returned, he would be detained at the border, charged for the assault, threats and mischief to property.”

Chipkar says that police are not releasing the perpetrator’s name.

It’s not clear if the suspect was a Chinese police officer or a diplomat.

Toronto police has confirmed to CTV News that there is an open investigation into the incident. A spokesperson said the Toronto Police Service is unable to provide more information until the lead investigator returns from leave.

CTV News has contacted the Chinese Embassy for comment but has yet to receive a response.

New Chinese law could lead to more transnational repression

Margaret McCuaig-Johnston, an advisory board member of the China Strategic Risks Institute, calls the incident “disturbing.”

She says the foreign affairs minister needs to summon the ambassador and “read him the riot act to ensure this doesn’t happen in Canada again and that there will be major consequences.”

She says the individual should be barred from returning to Canada.

McCuaig-Johnston is also concerned that China’s new “ethnic unity law” will lead to more cases of transnational repression in Canada and across the globe.

The new Chinese law , which came into effect July 1, grants China extraterritorial powers to act against organizations and people that it feels threaten the aims of the CCP.

The law, along with an expansion of the global network to monitor the diaspora, can be used to silence the voices of people advocating for minority rights such as those of the Falun Gong, Uyghurs or Tibetans.

Democracy activists from Hong Kong, or Taiwanese Canadians who are against unifying with China, can also be targeted.

“China thinks their law extends anywhere, including the streets of Canada,” says McCuaig-Johnston.

Other than the Toronto incident, McCuaig-Johnston says there are other cases of human rights abuses that Carney should raise with Xi. She points out that Uyghur Canadian activist Huseyin Celil has been imprisoned in China for 20 years.

There’s also Jimmy Lai, a Hong Kong media mogul who supported the democracy movement. He’s serving a 20-year jail sentence for collusion and sedition. The 78-year-old has family in Canada.

Before leaving for Asia, Carney said he would raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada with Xi.

The prime minister also said that the partnership between the two countries “is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we’re involved.”

Former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig, who was detained for more than 1,000 days by China, says the prime minister needs to be pressed on what those guardrails are.

“The government needs to explain more to Canadians what the guardrails are, what they’re for, and how effective they’ve been, and what Ottawa is doing to strengthen them,” said Kovrig during an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV’s Question Period.

Kovrig, who now runs his own geopolitical risk advisory firm, says Carney should make it a “top priority” to bring up the findings of the Safeguard Defenders report, which claims that China May be operating at least 18 illegal police stations to control the diaspora in Canada.

“That is a violation of Canadian sovereignty, and it’s a threat to the rights of Canadian citizens. And so, I think that is a top priority, frankly, to raise with President Xi, and convey to him very clearly that that kind of thing is not acceptable, and that Canada will investigate it, and we will follow processes to ensure that Canadians are secure.”

stories.title: Meta could pull WhatsApp from Canada if bill requires undermining encryption
stories.summary: Meta argues the bill still allows the government to issue a secret order requiring companies to build a 'backdoor' into encrypted services
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Meta says all options are on the table — including pulling uber-popular messaging WhatsApp from Canada — if the government uses proposed powers in its lawful access bill to undermine the company’s encryption.

“We’re not going to break or weaken encryption, specifically vis-a-vis services like WhatsApp,” Rachel Curran, Meta’s head of public policy for Canada, told National Post Friday.

Lawful access is one of the most intrusive powers afforded to police and intelligence agencies. Creating such a regime for the digital age in Canada has been the subject of fierce debate for decades.

Bill C-22 proposes a new lawful access regime which would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to intercept private communications or personal data as part of their investigations.

It has been applauded by police forces as a long-overdue fix to growing obstacles to investigations, but panned by civil liberties advocates as an attack on privacy and encryption.

In an interview ahead of her testimony Monday, the Meta executive said that amendments made by MPs to C-22 in the spring were a step in the right direction, but did not go far enough.

She argued that the bill still allows the government to issue a secret order requiring companies like Meta to build a “backdoor” into encrypted services like WhatsApp. That, in turn, would automatically create a potentially vulnerability in the data protection that could be exploited by bad actors to steal any worldwide user’s data, she said.

In the spring, the government amended Bill C-22 to state that electronic service providers would not be required to comply with the legislation if it created a “systemic vulnerability” that brings a “credible risk” of unauthorized access to data.

The government has fiercely rejected any claim that the legislation mandates the creation of any “backdoor” in encrypted services. The bill states that authorities could request encrypted data from companies, but not require them to decrypt it for them.

The change was meant to address a chorus of fears that the obligations in the bill for “core service providers” to collect and retain specific user data for it to be available to authorities with a warrant would effectively force them to create vulnerabilities in their systems.

But, Curran argued, the government also quietly added a “loophole” to the clause that allows for the creation of a systemic vulnerability if it’s to obtain information related to someone who is the target of a police of Csis warrant.

“So you build a backdoor for one targeted investigation, you basically compromise the entire system for everyone,” Curran argued, adding that Meta would never accept to do so for encrypted services like WhatsApp.

Asked if that meant that Meta would consider pulling the app from the Canadian market, Curran said all options are on the table.

An earlier version of the bill set the retention period to 12 months, but was reduced after critics complained of the privacy risks linked to storing so much potentially sensitive user data for so long.

The proposed six-month retention period would impose costly data retention obligations on companies like Meta and force them to essentially create a “surveillance database.”

Instead, Curran argued that the government should formalize a scheme where federal authorities can ask companies like Meta to retain certain data on specific users while they conduct their investigations and seek a warrant for the information.

“Besides being, we think, problematic from a legal perspective, it treats all Canadians as potential criminals,” Curran said. “Those databases… will inevitably become a target for bad actors as well.”

He also argued that the current iteration of the legislation struck the right balance between privacy rights and helping police and intelligence agencies do their work.

“We’re not going to break or weaken encryption, specifically vis-a-vis services like WhatsApp,” Rachel Curran, Meta’s head of public policy for Canada, told National Post Friday.
Lawful access is one of the most intrusive powers afforded to police and intelligence agencies. Creating such a regime for the digital age in Canada has been the subject of fierce debate for decades.
Bill C-22 proposes a new lawful access regime which would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to intercept private communications or personal data as part of their investigations.
It has been applauded by police forces as a long-overdue fix to growing obstacles to investigations, but panned by civil liberties advocates as an attack on privacy and encryption.

She argued that the bill still allows the government to issue a secret order requiring companies like Meta to build a “backdoor” into encrypted services like WhatsApp. That, in turn, would automatically create a potentially vulnerability in the data protection that could be exploited by bad actors to steal any worldwide user’s data, she said.

stories.title: Secrecy in case of former top RCMP official curtailed defence, appeal asserts
stories.summary: Cameron Ortis’s case at Ontario Court of Appeal is set for February
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
Cameron Ortis, who was convicted of violating Canada’s secrecy laws while working as a top RCMP intelligence director, insists he didn’t get a fair trial, according to a legal filing ahead of a highly anticipated appeal at Ontario’s top court.

Mr. Ortis’s lawyers argue that his ability to mount a full defence was badly hampered because of the secrecy that has enveloped the case.

Mr. Ortis doesn’t deny having intentionally communicated special operational information – the reason the RCMP arrested him in 2019 and the basis of his conviction after a jury trial in 2023 – but he asserts that he wasn’t able to properly explain his actions.

He had been accused of trying to pass along highly sensitive police dossiers to transnational gangs. The work of his team at the RCMP included gathering secret information on such groups. At trial, Mr. Ortis said he worked with a counterpart at a foreign agency and had tried to lure suspected criminals into using an encrypted e-mail service where authorities could tap their communications.

The 54-year-old former director general of the RCMP’s National Intelligence Coordination Centre had been sentenced in early 2024 to 14 years, minus time served, for a total of 7½ years. The Parole Board of Canada in February granted day parole, saying that Mr. Ortis posed a low risk to reoffend.

In a legal filing at the Ontario Court of Appeal, Mr. Ortis’s lawyers argue his “position at trial was severely curtailed” by pretrial secrecy rulings. The jury trial was at the Ontario Superior Court but related decisions were made in Federal Court, as the federal government successfully won orders there that included a prohibition on Mr. Ortis testifying to classified information in his defence.

“The jury was left with an incomplete picture because of these evidential handcuffs,” lawyers Matthew Gourlay, Jon Doody and Matthew Kay state.

The details behind this argument, however, are secret, submitted to the appeal court in a confidential filing.

The appeal at Ontario’s top court had been scheduled to start on Monday but because the case wasn’t ready to proceed, it is now booked for February. Like the jury trial in the fall of 2023, the appeal will be heard partly in secret.

Based on the new schedule, the public portion of the appeal will take place on Feb. 8 and 9 in Toronto. The secret portion is set for a secure facility known colloquially as the bunker at the Federal Court in Ottawa on Feb. 11 and 12.

Such secrecy is unusual in the Canadian justice system, in which the principle of open courts is foundational, yet it has been a defining theme of Mr. Ortis’s case.

This secrecy, and its alleged undermining of Mr. Ortis’s ability to mount a full defence against the charges, is one pillar of his appeal. Before the jury trial began, several other charges were dropped because the court decided various restrictions meant Mr. Ortis wouldn’t be able to fully defend himself on those accusations.

Mr. Ortis in his appeal also argues the trial judge incorrectly interpreted the Security of Information Act, under which he was found guilty in November 2023 of four counts of unauthorized communication of special operational information – the first time such charges were tested at trial under provisions that date back to 2001.

His appeal filing states that Mr. Ortis, in his former role as an RCMP intelligence director, had been praised at trial by numerous witnesses and that his bosses held him in high regard.

“His commitment to Canada’s national security was evident from their testimony,” the legal filing says. “The Crown put forward no tangible motive for his actions and even the trial judge could not understand why [Mr. Ortis] did what he did.”

The federal government is also appealing the case, arguing that Mr. Ortis’s sentence was far too lenient. The Crown in its legal filing says he betrayed his country and put Canada’s entire security apparatus at risk.

The Public Prosecution Service of Canada argues the judge should have levied a much longer sentence, near or at the maximum. At sentencing, the Crown called for 28 years’ imprisonment, which is more than the minimum jail time for first-degree murder.

In February 2024, when the Prosecution Service announced its planned appeal, it cited “the seriousness of the offence and the moral blameworthiness of the offender.”

The Crown says Mr. Ortis, in his job near the top of the RCMP, was privy to the highest levels of classified information and had a “profound responsibility” to keep that information, and his country, safe.

“Instead,” argue Crown counsel Lisa Mathews, Jennifer Conroy and Judy Kliewer in their appeal filing, “he engaged in conduct that breached his duty to safeguard that information, and he put lives – and Canada’s entire security apparatus – at risk.”

The federal government further argues that Mr. Ortis’s actions “harmed Canada’s international reputation for safeguarding intelligence [and] thwarted ongoing domestic and international criminal organization investigations.”

Later in the legal filing, the Crown states: “His conduct betrayed the Canadians he was meant to serve.”

In the February report from the Parole Board that granted day parole, it states that Mr. Ortis at the start of his sentence maintained that he believed he had the authority to share the information he did, the kinds of decisions his job required a half-dozen times each year, and he had to occasionally walk a fine line in such choices.

But the Parole Board then states Mr. Ortis has since acknowledged and understood he did not have the authority to share the information and should have consulted others.

“You have expressed regret for your actions,” the Parole Board states, “and are aware of the negative impact your actions have had on others.”

stories.title: Margaret Atwood among thousands raising alarm over U.S. company’s plan for radio tower on Pelee Island
stories.summary: Residents say they were caught unaware of the township’s council approval of the tower last year
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Thousands of birding advocates have sent messages asking the federal government to intervene in a U.S. company’s plan to build an enormous radio tower on Pelee Island in southwestern Ontario.

The picturesque Lake Erie isle, which covers about 40 square kilometres, is home to Canada’s southernmost community.

Conservation groups and residents are raising concerns that the planned 182-metre tower, along with the cables needed to support it, would become a deadly obstacle for the hundreds of thousands of birds that traverse the island during annual spring and fall migrations each year.

The tower is slated to be built next year on township land leased by DRW Holdings, LLC, a private trading company based in Chicago. It is intended to facilitate the rapid transmission of stock trading data to the east coast of the United States via microwaves.

It was approved by the island’s township council last year, but many property owners say they only become aware of the full scope of the project this summer.

That includes Canadian literary icon Margaret Atwood, who has resided on the island part-time for decades. Together with her late husband Graeme Gibson, she helped to establish the Pelee Island Bird Observatory , which tracks avian activity through one of North America’s busiest bird flyways.

Because of the island’s geographic position at the confluence of two major migration corridors, it and nearby Point Pelee National Park are internationally renowned for birdwatching. In September, the observatory opened a new $3.5-million research facility , funded by Ms. Atwood and others.

On Thursday, Ms. Atwood posted a message on her Substack alerting followers to the potential implications of the tower for migrating bird species, many of which move at night when they are more likely to be affected by a tower’s flashing lights and susceptible to collisions with unseen cables.

“If you wanted to kill a lot of birds with a huge, deadly tower—a LOT of birds—you couldn’t have planned it better,” Ms. Atwood wrote.

Ms. Atwood also invited people to fill out a digital letter that will be sent to Canada’s Minister of Environment, Julie Dabrusin, and the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada, the federal organization that has the jurisdiction to decide whether a project requires an environmental assessment before it can proceed. Another recipient is Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, which has yet to grant DRW a licence to broadcast from the planned tower.

The period for public comment on the project expires on Monday.

Matthew Gibson, one of Graeme Gibson’s sons, who sits on the bird observatory’s board and is spearheading its public awareness campaign, said that as of Sunday evening, the effort has generated upwards of 26,000 letters calling for a federal assessment of the tower.

That includes a letter from the township’s property-owners’ association, which notes the degree to which the island’s economy and real estate values depend on nature-based tourism.

The letter also notes that an impact study commissioned by the company does not assess bird collisions.

In statements to media, DRW has said it is committed to mitigating the impact of the tower on birds.

Despite the council’s approval of the tower last year, many residents did not know of it until a council meeting in July when a second tower by a different proponent was voted down. Social media groups about the topic reveal some public confusion, including the mistaken impression that the tower will be used to improve cellphone service on the island.

Individually, some residents have expressed frustration over a lack of transparency about the DRW tower, and the fact that no public meeting was called to provide information about the project.

“It’s preposterous and it’s appalling all at the same time,” said Ron Tiessen, who has lived on Pelee Island for 47 years.

Mr. Tiessen added that the tower would be a “visual blemish,” obvious from any location on the island, in addition to its environmental impacts.

The details of the township’s agreement struck with DRW, including the amount that the municipality will receive for leasing the property for the tower, have not been made public.

In an e-mail to The Globe and Mail, Cathy Miller, who just completed her four-year term as mayor of the township, said the council had met its obligations according to federal rules and Ontario’s Municipal Act.

In August, in an e-mail exchange with the bird observatory’s board chair, Deborah Egan, obtained by The Globe, Ms. Miller wrote that the lease would raise significant revenue for township infrastructure, which she said would have been irresponsible for her to ignore.

Ms. Miller also helped to set up a meeting between DRW and representatives of the bird observatory, but the discussion did not shed much more light on the details of the project, said Mr. Gibson.

The conservation organization Birds Canada also sent a representative to that meeting to participate in the discussion with DRW.

In a statement, David Browne, senior vice-president for conservation and policy at the organization, said “Birds Canada is very concerned that the tower will not be designed to eliminate impacts on birds and will become an ongoing source of mortality.”

Ms. Egan said that the bird observatory’s board is now pursuing a freedom of information request to learn the details of the township’s arrangement with DRW.

Dave DeLellis, the incoming mayor, who was also on the council when it approved the tower, said he was not able to respond to questions about the matter but that it would be a “top priority” for the new council after it is sworn in on Tuesday.
