The alarming portrait of the province’s child welfare system is included in the long-awaited report, released Monday as the provincial government announced new legislation and regulatory changes it says will strengthen the sector.

But while the changes tighten financial oversight and impose new safety measures, experts and critics say they do not address the underlying issues that are sending kids with complex health needs to the doorsteps of children’s aid.

“We have a child welfare system that is ill-equipped to deal with the demands presenting themselves,” said Kiaras Gharabaghi, professor at Toronto Metropolitan University’s school of child and youth care, after reviewing the audit’s findings.

“Ontario governments continue to respond to these issues with a mixture of indignation that it costs money to ensure the well-being of children and an absurd confidence that tinkering with technical aspects of the system is somehow going to produce transformative change,” Gharabaghi said. “It will not.”

When asked Monday why the legislation does not address long-standing systemic issues, Michael Parsa, minister of children, community and social services, pointed to the government’s “record funding” in the sector — some $2 billion — even as the number of children and youth in care has decreased by 20 per cent. He said placement decisions are made by societies, not the government.
“We have an expectation to make sure that those placements are safe, so every child and youth in the province is supported, protected, and their outcomes improved,” he said.

Alexa Gilmour, NDP critic for children, community and social services and MPP for Parkdale—High Park, said on Monday that she is “livid” the legislation meant to address the audit findings are “tucked in” to an omnibus bill, along with health-care issues, long-term-care home requirements and sweeping new changes to Osap .
“There is nothing that really tackles the seriousness of (the issues) these families are facing,” Gilmour said, adding that children who are in crisis now cannot wait months for change.
Alexa Gilmour, NDP critic for children, community and social services and MPP for Parkdale—High Park, said children who are in crisis now cannot wait months for change.

The release of the report, which examined 37 non-Indigenous societies, comes in the wake of Star reporting that revealed the findings have been in the government’s hands for almost a year — despite repeated promises from the province it would make the results public.
The delay drew sharp criticism from advocates and critics who say the child welfare system has continued to deteriorate in the two years since the premier announced the audit.

Despite raising the alarm since 2020, child welfare agencies are still struggling to find appropriate treatment and housing for kids with complex mental health and other developmental needs. The lack of options has forced agencies to rely on unlicensed settings, including budget motels, and other emergency placements.
The Star recently reported on a teen boy in southwestern Ontario who lived in his family’s shed for months while under the watch of children’s aid.
Previous Star reporting has shown these emergency placements are driving up agency costs and harming vulnerable children and youth.

The audit found the same. Spending across the child welfare sector is heavily concentrated in high-cost, reactive protection ($437 million) and care ($642 million), while prevention and early intervention accounts for only $53 million — under four per cent — of spending.
Three quarters of all placement spending went to outside purchased resources, or OPRs, which can include private foster or group care providers that children’s aid societies purchase services from.
The increasing reliance on OPRs stems from a provincewide decline in foster families and the increasing complexity of needs among children in care, the audit said.

The number of serious safety incidents for kids in care nearly doubled over the five years reviewed by auditors, with incidents of exploitation such as sex trafficking increasing by 33 per cent and assaults up 18 per cent. Most of these incidents occurred in OPRs, the audit noted.
Ford ordered the third-party audit of the sector in October 2024, alleging he’d heard “nightmare stories” of agencies misusing taxpayer dollars instead of properly funding care.

At the time, union leaders representing thousands of child protection workers called the audit a “smokescreen” and stated the government needed to adequately fund the social services system to ensure children got the help they need.

The audit was conducted by an outside contractor and looked at the quality of child protection services and examined operational costs, including executive compensation and staffing. The review did not include Indigenous child and family well-being agencies.

While the Kpmg audit did not make formal recommendations, noting that it wasn’t in the scope of its contract with the provincial government, it offered “considerations” for future policy and decision-making. Among them, auditors warned that sector-wide structural changes May be needed to address high-cost placements that are out of agencies’ control.

Parsa said the proposed legislation includes new oversight for social workers that would see their licenses suspended or revoked if they are found to have committed sexual misconduct involving a client. That ban would remain in place for a minimum of 10 years.

stories.title: Canada exploring ‘other options’ with Europe, Asia to grow auto sector: Carney
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the auto sector remains part of trade talks with the U.S., but Canada is also looking at "other options" in Europe and Asia.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says the auto sector remains part of trade talks with the U.S., but Canada is also looking at “other options” in Europe and Asia.

Carney made the remarks while taking questions from reporters at the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

The prime minister says Ottawa wants Canadian auto workers to have the best opportunities possible in an integrated North American market.

He says that market has become less integrated as Washington has threatened hefty tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Canadian autos by January.

“It’s an ongoing discussion that we’re having with the U.S. administration, myself with the president,” Carney told reporters.

“It’s part of the trade negotiations, as you know, depending (on) where that settles, there’ll be other options — European options, Asian options.”

Carney has said Canada would not ink a U.S. trade deal that failed to support a viable Canadian auto sector.

Amid trade tensions, Carney signed a deal with China earlier this year to import up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent.

Carney is expected to meet this week with President Xi Jinping, where more discussions around the two nations’ trading relationships are likely.

By Ryan Baynton Nov 15, 2026 | 10:03 PM

Around lunch Thursday many people reported that Microsoft’s Outlook, alongside other services were not working. The network stayed down for nearly a full day, the longest shutdown in Microsoft history.

Microsoft has not come out with what happened but said it was not a cyber attack.

“It’s like removing a lane from a highway, the remaining servers had to handle all the traffic,” said London technology analyst Carmi Levy, when describing why the servers went down in quick succession and why some people may still have been receiving emails.

The mass network failure had many businesses in a panic, as they were not able to work without the networks provided from Microsoft.

Many companies have been advised to re-evaluate their emergency plans not just for when they are facing internal problems, but also when the client they use goes down.

stories.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
stories.summary: Phnom Penh, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Phnom Penh, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney says auto sector remains part of trade talks with U.S. but that Canada is looking at ‘other options’ in Europe and Asia. Carney was taking questions from reporters at the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. (Nov. 16, 2026)

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction” on behalf of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets.

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro lashed out on social media Monday in response to Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

“The federal government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars,” Ford said on social media on Monday.

Trump’s tariffs have battered Canada’s auto industry, potentially unraveling decades of cross-border integration. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the company moved its plans for Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto reported from Toronto.

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction” on behalf of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets.
“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
White House trade adviser Peter Navarro lashed out on social media Monday in response to Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers.
“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.
“The federal government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars,” Ford said on social media on Monday.

Trump’s tariffs have battered Canada’s auto industry, potentially unraveling decades of cross-border integration. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the company moved its plans for Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.
Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto reported from Toronto.

stories.title: Death of fifth soldier highlights vulnerable state of CFB Wainwright fire victims
stories.summary: Severely burnt soldiers have suffered devastating trauma to their faces, heads and torsos, according to sources
stories.author: Mercedes Stephenson, Alanna Smith, Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
The death of a fifth soldier from injuries sustained in last month’s massive fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright has underlined the vulnerable condition of the more seriously hurt victims of the Oct. 17 blaze.

Three sources with direct knowledge of some of the military personnel who remain in hospital described a number of soldiers’ injuries as profound, severe and life-altering. The sources described cases of devastating facial, head and neck trauma from the burns, as well as severe damage to hands, arms and upper torsos.

For some, the sources said, the injuries to the upper-body area were so significant the victims could not be easily identified after being pulled from the grass fire that erupted near the CAF base in central Alberta during a training exercise, or later in hospital.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to discuss the soldiers’ conditions publicly.

The latest fatality, Private William Douglas Dal Bianco of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died Friday, nearly four weeks after he was hospitalized. He was receiving medical care in Ontario, the Department of National Defence said in a statement Saturday.

Of the 38 remaining injured soldiers, 24 are still in hospital, the statement said. Four members of the battalion – Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark – were pronounced dead in the immediate aftermath of the fire.

In an e-mail response to The Globe, the department said it cannot provide more information on the hospitalized soldiers because “patient status falls within the clinical purview of provincial health authorities and attending clinicians.”

The department has refused to answer broad questions about how many soldiers remain in critical condition or remain intubated, citing privacy.

Acute Care Alberta said 21 of the military victims remain hospitalized in that province, with nine of them in critical condition as of Nov. 10.

Patients who suffer severe burns can die from complications weeks or months after the original injury, because they are in such a medically vulnerable state, Alan Rogers, a surgeon at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre, said in an interview.

“This is a recognized feature of severe burn injury. Surviving the first few days is an important milestone, but it does not necessarily mean that the danger has passed,” Dr. Rogers said. “This is particularly relevant when burns involve more than half the body’s surface, although burn depth, age, smoke inhalation and underlying health also influence the outlook.”

Part of Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, the Ross Tilley facility is Canada’s highest-volume adult burn unit, and it is among the hospital departments that have dispatched specialists to help treat the victims of the Wainwright fire.

Many of the soldiers injured at CFB Wainwright sustained extreme burns that will require multiple surgeries and extensive rehabilitation. Those with skin so scorched that it cannot heal on its own have required skin grafts, a surgical procedure where donated skin or a patch of healthy skin from another part of the patient’s body is removed and transplanted to the area needing repair.

In the first few hours and days after a serious burn, the immediate priorities involve maintaining the patient’s blood circulation and breathing, Dr. Rogers said. Following that initial phase, he said the threat becomes complications, such as infections, sepsis, blood clots, organ failure and lung issues.

“One reason for the prolonged vulnerability is that the skin is a vital protective organ,” he said. “Extensive, deep burns remove a large part of that barrier, and restoring durable wound coverage can require multiple operations. At the same time, a major burn profoundly disrupts the immune system.”

For those reasons, Dr. Rogers said, a patient can improve for a period of time, but then deteriorate rapidly should a complication develop.

“There is no particular day or week after which every patient is safely out of danger,” he said. “Many people survive very extensive burns, but achieving that recovery can require weeks or months of co-ordinated surgery, intensive care, specialist nursing, nutritional support and rehabilitation.”

The CFB Wainwright incident is one of Canada’s worst peacetime training tragedies on home soil, with dozens more affected than the Slesse Range disaster in 1988 that killed six military engineer trainees and seriously injured three others during a demolition exercise at CFB Chilliwack.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a statement posted to social media on Saturday, said Canadians are holding all those who are grieving in the wake of last month’s tragedy in their hearts.

“Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada. With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours,” he said. “That is service. Now, we serve them.”

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, offered her condolences to Pte. Dal Bianco’s family, friends and those who served alongside him.

“We will honour his dedicated service and continue to stand with all those affected by this tragedy along the difficult road ahead. My thoughts are also with our injured members and their families, and I am deeply grateful to everyone involved in providing care and support during this time of tremendous sadness,” Gen. Carignan said in a statement.

Canadian Forces Provost Marshal Vanessa Hanrahan, who heads the military police, has said that the fire had started on CFB Wainwright’s automatic grenade launcher range and was monitored continuously throughout the day. “A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity and rate of speed which led to these tragic events,” Brigadier-General Hanrahan said.

Military police have launched an investigation into the circumstances of the fire. The CAF has promised a separate investigation by its board of inquiry. Alberta’s chief medical examiner is also investigating.

stories.title: Canada plans up to 200,000 extra permanent residence spaces. Here’s who could benefit
stories.summary: A new federal immigration plan aims to accelerate permanent residence applications for thousands of Hong Kong and Ukrainian nationals already living in Canada, offering hope to people who have spent years waiting for decisions.
stories.author: Kamil Karamali
stories.content:
After more than two years of waiting for a decision on his permanent residence application, Felix Tong was considering leaving the life he had built in Toronto and returning to Hong Kong.

Then Ottawa announced plans to speed up applications under its Hong Kong pathways, giving him renewed hope of staying.

“I think it’s a big surprise for all Hong Kongers. We are so happy for that,” Tong told CTV News Sunday. “If they were not going to process our application this year, then I think maybe I need to go back to Hong Kong.”

His hopes have now been lifted by a broader federal plan to create up to 200,000 additional permanent residence spaces in 2027 for people already living in Canada.

Announced alongside the immigration levels plan earlier this month, the measure covers two groups: up to 100,000 workers and eligible family members, and up to 100,000 people in what Ottawa calls a humanitarian group.

Within that humanitarian group, the government aims to finish processing applications by the end of next year – that would result in up to 32,000 people becoming permanent residents through the Hong Kong pathways and up to 18,800 through the Ukrainian pathway.

Both pathways have stopped accepting applications, with the Hong Kong programs closing in August of this year, and the Ukrainian applications window closing two years ago.

Ottawa immigration lawyer Warren Creates said the measure could help people who have spent years waiting to learn whether they can settle permanently.

“We’re going to finalize what has been started years ago, and we will eliminate the uncertainty for this group of people that have been waiting all too long,” Creates said.

The humanitarian cohort also includes up to 12,600 people already found eligible for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds – and up to 45,000 spouses, common-law partners and dependent children of Canadian citizens or permanent residents who are living in Canada.

The other group provides up to 100,000 spaces for workers already living in communities outside Quebec and their eligible family members, with provinces and territories helping identify workers needed in their communities.

These roughly 200,000 additional permanent residence spaces sit outside Ottawa’s regular target of 380,000 admissions for 2027.

“So the math says 580,000 people are going to be landed as immigrants in 2027. But the politics say only 380,000 are planned arrivals,” said Vancouver-based immigration lawyer and policy analyst Richard Kurland to CTV news via Zoom on Sunday.

In a social media post this month, Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner said “Mark Carney just announced the highest level of permanent immigration in Canadian history, and tried to hide it.”

https://t.co/WK77aFZ7Jb — Michelle Rempel Garner (@MichelleRempel) November 6, 2026

https://t.co/WK77aFZ7Jb

“This is on top of hundreds of thousands of new temporary immigrants that Mark Carney also approved,” she added.

Ottawa says the additional spaces will help it honour earlier humanitarian commitments, reunite families and clear applications from people who have already established lives in Canada. Its explanation for including the Hong Kong and Ukrainian pathways centres on completing work under programs it had already created.

Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said the measure would help Canada “deliver faster on our promises to people from Hong Kong and Ukraine.”

The Hong Kong permanent residence pathways opened in 2021 for eligible people in Canada with Canadian education or work experience. At the time, Ottawa cited concerns about China’s national security law and deteriorating human rights in Hong Kong.

The Ukrainian pathway opened in 2023 as part of Canada’s response to Russia’s invasion. It allowed eligible Ukrainian nationals already in Canada to seek permanent residence based on qualifying family ties to Canadian citizens or permanent residents.

The latest announcement follows a shift toward lower immigration targets that began in 2024. That October, the federal government reduced its planned permanent resident admissions for 2025 from 500,000 to 395,000, saying the cuts would ease pressure on housing, infrastructure and social services.

Under the current plan, Ottawa’s regular permanent resident target is 380,000 annually from 2027 through 2029, separate from the additional measures.

For temporary residents, the plan sets annual targets of 220,000 new worker arrivals and 150,000 new international student arrivals over those same years.

With files from CTV News’ James Kim

stories.title: Snowbirds take final Tutor jet flight over Grey Cup: ‘It’s been an honour’
stories.summary: 'Thank you for sharing this historic moment with us,' Snowbird 1 pilot Major Maciej Hatta said as the troupe soared the sunset skies over Calgary's McMahon Stadium.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
After months of nostalgic farewell appearances at events across the country, the Canadian Forces Snowbirds have retired their iconic but aging jets.

The Snowbirds soared the sunset skies over Calgary on Sunday evening for their final public flight in the aircraft flown since the team’s inception.

The military aerobatics squadron made a flypast McMahon Stadium , where the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes are battling Sunday evening for football championship trophy.

“The Snowbirds’ longstanding friendship with the Canadian Football League and fans comes full circle, as we perform for you one last time before retiring our venerable CT-114 Tutor aircraft. Thank you for sharing this historic moment with us,” Hatta said.

The legendary team has previously performed at three past Grey Cups — the 101st, 106th and 109th.

Hatta repeated his message in French before concluding with an expression of gratitude for the decades of love the squadron has received.

“Thank you Canada, for 55 years of support. It’s been an honour serving our great nation.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Thank you Canada, for 55 years of support. It's been an honour serving our great nation."

The flight marked an end of an era for the aging CT-114 Tutor jets, which were used by the Canadian Forces as “basic pilot-training aircraft” between 1963 and 2000.

The Snowbirds, officially known as 431 Air Demonstration Squadron based out of Moose Jaw, Sask., have been performing with the Tutor aircraft since 1971.

The final flight had previously been scheduled to take place in Sacramento, Calif., where the Snowbirds performed at the California Capital Airshow on Oct. 10 and 11.

But then in September, the Grey Cup appearance was solidified — allowing the Canadian icons to say farewell at home.

Now, the Snowbird team will start a hiatus that could last until 2030.

The jets are being retired ahead of transitioning to new CT-157 Siskin II turboprop planes .

The federal government announced this past spring it would replace the roughly 60-year-old Tutor jets, which have encountered various problems with upgrades meant to extend their lifespans out to 2030.

Costs, timelines and the growing scarcity of replacement parts threw a wrench into plans to keep them in the air longer.

Acquiring the Siskin II, also known as the Pilatus PC-21, is part of the Royal Canadian Air Force’s plan to modernize its fleets and overhaul its training.

The air force said the the modern aircraft are well suited both to aerial acrobatics and to preparing pilots for the more advanced aircraft the air force is bringing online.

The CF Snowbirds, 431 Air Demonstration Squadron, are based about 72 kilometres west of Regina at 15 Wing Moose Jaw and comprised of Canadian Armed Forces members and National Defence Public Service employees.

Representing the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Snowbirds team includes pilots, technicians (aviation, avionics, aircraft structure, supply), mobile support operators, resource management support clerks, an engineering officer, a logistics officer and a public affairs officer.

With files from Prisha Dev and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada beats Sweden 3-0 to reach final at women’s worlds
stories.summary: Sarah Fillier continued her goal-scoring streak as Canada advanced to the world women's hockey championship gold-medal game with a 3-0 win over Sweden on Sunday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sarah Fillier continued her goal-scoring streak as Canada advanced to the world women’s hockey championship gold-medal game with a 3-0 win over Sweden on Sunday.

Fillier has scored in four straight games after missing Canada’s first two contests in Denmark with an injury sustained in a tournament warm-up game against the United States.

After struggling to a 3-2 win over Czechia in Friday’s quarterfinals, Canada was in control for the entire game against the Swedes.

Sarah Wozniewicz and Emma Maltais also scored for Canada, while Ann-Renée Desbiens made 13 saves for the shutout.

Sweden goaltender Ebba Svensson Traff allowed three goals on 30 shots.

Canada will face the defending champion U.S. on Monday in a rematch of last year’s gold-medal game, while Sweden will play Finland for bronze.

Canada and the United States have met in 23 of 24 finals since the tournament’s debut in 1990. Canada has won 13 of those matchups, though the U.S. has taken gold at 10 of the last 14 championships.

The U.S. is also coming off a 2-1 overtime win over Canada at the 2026 Winter Olympics.

Sweden’s Mira Jungaker, left, is challenged by Canada’s Rosalie Tremblay during the semifinal match between Canada and Sweden at the Women’s Ice Hockey World Championship in Herning, Denmark, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Petr David Josek)

Canada dominated the first period on Sunday, outshooting Sweden 12-5, but couldn’t beat Svensson Traff. The Canadians were coming off an uncomfortable one-goal quarterfinal win over Czechia despite outshooting their opponent 41-16, and appeared destined for another close game.

The Canadians were finally rewarded for controlling the puck when Fillier opened the scoring on a power play at 7:15 of the second period. Fillier received a pass from Jessie Eldridge, stepped in from the left wing and fired a shot past Svensson Traff.

Wozniewicz gave Canada some breathing room at 12:57 of the second when she took a pass at the Swedish blue line and scored on a breakaway.

Maltais put the game away with her fourth goal of the tournament on another Canadian breakaway at 8:08 of the third period.

stories.title: Telus pulls out of two planned Vancouver AI data centres
stories.summary: Lack of local support caused company to reconsider the projects with Westbank, source says
stories.author: Irene Galea, Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
Telus Corp. T-T is ending its participation in two planned artificial intelligence data centres in Vancouver, the company said Sunday, after heavy local opposition and recent shifts in its AI investment strategy.

Telus said in May that it would co-develop two data centres with Vancouver-headquartered real estate developer Westbank Corp., citing growing demand among Canadian businesses and government for computing power.

With Telus no longer taking part, Westbank has said that it will continue developing the data centres with a new, yet-unannounced partner.

The two companies had planned to build one new data centre in Vancouver’s downtown core and convert an existing office building outside the city centre for AI use. Telus had also signed a memorandum of understanding with the federal government to support its data-centre initiatives, though the terms of the agreement have not been finalized.

Telus had said it would equip the two data centres with some 63,000 computer chips from Nvidia Corp. Nvda-Q over time and draw up to 163 megawatts of electricity. The converted facility in Vancouver’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood was expected to open at the end of 2026, while the new build downtown was to come online in 2029.

However, Telus “has decided not to proceed” with those projects, said spokesperson Richard Gilhooley in an e-mail Sunday. Telus did not provide an explanation for the decision.

A source familiar with the matter said a lack of local support had caused Telus to reconsider. The level of opposition in Vancouver would have made it challenging to proceed, though the company remains open to opportunities at these sites in the future, the source said.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source because they are not authorized to talk publicly about the matter.

During the summer, hundreds of people gathered for protests in the city, calling for the projects to be cancelled because of concerns about environmental, community and housing impacts.

One of the two Vancouver locations remains subject to rezoning. Meanwhile, a motion from a city councillor, due to be considered in November, could impose stricter requirements on data-centre owners, including independent environmental assessments and possible fees.

Mr. Gilhooley said the company would continue expanding its facility in Kamloops, B.C., and is evaluating new partnerships and locations to expand its sovereign compute capabilities.

“These new sites will scale our capacity to meet the growing demand we are seeing at our existing facilities, which leverage clean, renewable energy and industry-leading power efficiency,” he said.

Telus’s data-centre push was one of the last initiatives taken under Darren Entwistle, who retired as chief executive officer in June after 26 years at the company. In May, he and federal AI Minister Evan Solomon announced the data-centre expansion and said Telus and Ottawa had signed a memorandum of understanding to develop the projects.

The federal government touted Telus as a key part of its efforts to make the country less reliant on U.S. cloud-computing providers.

A spokesperson for Mr. Solomon’s office referred questions about the project to Telus and said the MOU is a framework for exploring more compute capacity. The spokesperson added that the government remains focused on building domestic computing infrastructure for Canadian companies, researchers and the public sector.

Mr. Entwistle’s plan for some of the company’s data-centre projects entailed purchasing the specialized and costly chips required for compute, a strategy that some analysts said came with heavy costs and the added risk that the chips could become outdated and need replacing.

Since then, new chief executive officer Victor Dodig has altered the company’s course, moving to sell off assets that had been acquired in previous years and cutting the dividend. AI data centres have become more central to the Telus plan under Mr. Dodig, but with a shift toward leveraging the company’s existing fibre networks.

Telus could help other data-centre developers by providing connectivity through its fibre network and is assessing a new initiative in data-centre shells with secured power, he told analysts during the company’s latest quarterly earnings call. A data-centre shell is the outer building without the interior compute components.

Westbank did not respond to The Globe’s request for comment Sunday. It previously confirmed Telus’s departure to the Daily Hive and said it was proceeding with a new partnership.

AI data centres have been a major source of turbulence for stock markets in recent months, driven by unease over high debt levels associated with the AI buildout and concerns that a Democratic midterm sweep in the U.S. could stall data-centre construction.

Last week, Nvidia suffered a massive sell-off when co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations of two affairs with employees and another with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.

In the latest federal budget, the government said it is targeting 500 megawatts of new processing capacity domestically and will use backstop and offtake agreements to stimulate demand. That means the government could commit to buying capacity at these facilities or underwrite debt to fund them.

Some government and industry officials contend that Canada is an ideal place to situate data centres, in part owing to its cool climate and renewable energy capacity.

So far, major data-centre announcements have come from U.S. tech companies. Meta Platforms Inc. is constructing a $13-billion data-centre campus in Alberta, while Anthropic will lease space in one to be built in Nova Scotia. Anthropic is also in talks to lease space at another facility in Alberta, The Globe has reported.

To address public concerns about data centres, the federal government in September launched a voluntary framework around development. Signatories, which include Telus and BCE Inc. BCE-T , pledged to be transparent about the impacts of their projects, not shift electricity costs on to Canadians and create benefits for communities.

stories.title: Canadians aren’t sold on the budget or a trade deal with Trump: Ipsos
stories.summary: A new Ipsos poll for Global News found Canadians believe the federal budget will have a greater impact than the U.S. midterms, but most remain indifferent toward the budget.
stories.author: Pooja Misra
stories.content:
Canadians May see the federal budget as more consequential than the recent U.S. midterm elections, but when it comes to what the government is offering, most aren’t giving it a thumbs up or a thumbs down.

Instead, they’re giving the budget a collective shrug.

A new Ipsos poll conducted for Global News found that 44 per cent of Canadians believe the federal budget will have a greater impact on the country than the U.S. midterms, compared with 24 per cent who believe the elections will have the bigger impact. Another 33 per cent said they didn’t know enough to say.

But despite its importance, 62 per cent described the budget as neither good nor bad, while just 17 per cent viewed it positively and 21 per cent gave it a negative assessment.

“Well, at this point, it looks like it’s just kind of, as the kids say, a meh, you know?” Darrell Bricker, chairman of Ipsos Canada, told Global News.

“I don’t really see what the effect is going to be. Maybe I’m going to wait and see, but at the moment, it’s basically a shrug.”

Only 14 per cent of Canadians believe the budget will personally help them financially compared with 21 per cent who expect it to hurt them. Another 65 per cent believe it will neither help nor hurt.

Bricker said Canadians have yet to see how the budget could meaningfully change their lives, describing it as a “non-event for most Canadians.”

While Canadians remain largely indifferent toward the federal budget, the U.S. midterm elections appear to have sparked some optimism about trade relations with their southern neighbour.

A separate Ipsos poll found 49 per cent of respondents are more optimistic about reaching a trade deal that’s good for Canada.

Still, 53 per cent believe Canada should wait until Donald Trump leaves office before making a new deal, while 55 per cent of Canadians say they can never trust Americans the same way again.

“Canadians have been shaken by what’s happened in the United States and are unlikely to come back easily to think that the United States is a reliable partner,” Bricker said.

Bricker said Trump’s unpredictable approach has left Canadians questioning whether a trade deal with the U.S. would hold up.

“He could wake up one day thinking the one thing and be going to bed at night thinking something completely different,” said Bricker.

Only 39 per cent of Canadians believe Prime Minister Mark Carney will succeed in negotiating a new trade deal with Trump, while 64 per cent expect trade and economic disputes between the two countries to continue for several years.

stories.title: Alouettes and Elks battle it out in 113th Grey Cup in Calgary
stories.summary: The final game of the 2026 CFL season is here and it features the East Division Champions — the Montreal Alouettes — and the West Division Champions — the Edmonton Elks. The Alouettes enter the Grey Cup with a record of 14-4 and having defeated the Winnipeg Blue Bombers 33-23 in the East Final. Meanwhile […]

By News Staff

Posted November 15, 2026 5:13 pm.

The final game of the 2026 CFL season is here and it features the East Division Champions — the Montreal Alouettes — and the West Division Champions — the Edmonton Elks.

The Alouettes enter the Grey Cup with a record of 14-4 and having defeated the Winnipeg Blue Bombers 33-23 in the East Final.

Meanwhile the Elks enter with a record of 13-5 and having defeated the BC Lions 28-16 in the West Final.

Both teams enter the game with a chance to repeat history. For the Elks, the last time they hosted the West Final, they would go on to win the Grey Cup. For the Alouettes, the last time they went undefeated at home, they went on to win the Grey Cup. One of those feats has a chance to be repeated.

The game marks the 12th meeting between Edmonton and Montreal in the Grey Cup, and the second time, they have met in Calgary. Edmonton leads the all-time series 8-3, including taking the 63rd Grey Cup in Calgary in 1975 by a score of 9-8. The last time they met was in the 93rd Grey Cup at BC Place Stadium in 2005, when Edmonton won 38-35 in overtime.

Sunday’s game also marked one of the earliest Grey Cup games, happening in mid-November, after the CFL bumped up the season schedule. Additionally the weather in Calgary was warmer than normal too.

CityNews will have coverage of the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary.

Prior to kickoff, the Snowbirds were honoured as they conducted the pregame flyover, in what would end up being their final flight.

Sunday’s game also marks an historic end to Canadian football as we know it.

In 2024, the Canadian Football League announced that it would be making a number of changes, including to the field size.

A hand full of the changes were implemented during the 2026 season, including a partial 35 running play clock.

The CFL in 2027 will be a big change and only time will tell how well the die hard fans will take the changes.

stories.title: Russia won’t be able to compete in World Juniors, Iihf says
stories.summary: Russia's hockey federation is calling the decision by the Iihf is "unlawful" and plans to appeal the decision to the International Olympic Committee.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Russia won’t be permitted to play in next month’s World Junior Championship in Alberta, the International Ice Hockey Federation announced on Sunday.

The Iihf cited Canada’s restrictions as its rationale not to allow Russia to participate.

“The Iihf confirms that due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian Government, the Russian U20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship,” a statement posted on the Iihf’s website said.

Sunday’s decision comes days after the Prime Minister’s Office reiterated Ottawa’s stance saying, “athletes from Russia and Belarus will not be able to compete for their countries in Canada so long as the unjustified war against Ukraine continues.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney made similar comments last week, as several European countries warned they would not play against Russia if they were slated to face off at the World Juniors.

The Iihf announced that after exploring other alternatives, Canada will remain the tournament host from Dec. 26 to Jan. 5, 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer, Alta.

Russia was banned from participation in various sports tournaments by multiple international federations after its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The groups included the Iihf and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

But last month, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on Oct. 30 that the Iihf must allow Russia to compete in its sanctioned events, including the World Juniors.

Norway’s own hockey federation last Sunday said the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the men’s under-20 tournament at Norway’s expense.

The Iihf has not formally announced the change, and its website still lists Norway among the 10 teams in the tournament.

Following comments by Canada, Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak threatened to seek compensation from Canada and push for relocation or cancellation of the tournament if Russia was barred from competing.

In response to the Iihf’s decision Sunday, the Russian hockey federation said it expressed its “strong protest” against a decision it calls “unlawful” and “unacceptable.”

The federation went on to say the decision was in violation of the CAS decision and that it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee.

It also said it would pursue all available legal avenues to ensure the CAS ruling is enforced and Russia can compete.

— with files from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Flame of Hope still burns at Banting House on World Diabetes Day
stories.summary: For 45 years, Shari Stevens has been waiting for a cure for her Type 1 diabetes.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
For 45 years, Shari Stevens has been waiting for a cure for her Type 1 diabetes.

“The Flame (of Hope) is still burning which means we are still waiting for a cure,” said Stevens while taking in the World Diabetes Day (WDD) festivities at Banting House Museum in London, Ont.

“I look forward to the day that I can literally see the light go out on that flame because that will mean we have a cure.”

Stevens was one of hundreds of diabetics and their families who came to the “birthplace of insulin” for the event which is celebrated annually on Nov. 14th, the birthday of Sir Frederick Banting.

It’s a worldwide awareness campaign focusing on early diagnosis, risk reduction, access to quality care, and reducing stigma.

“We have people from British Columbia in the west, Massachusetts in the east, Kansas in the south, and the Sault in the north,” said Grant Maltman, curator of Banting House.

Stevens and her friend Nan Borchardt are the visitors who came 1,400 km from Kansas to London.

“My diabetic journey has been an adventure,” said Borchardt, a recently retired diabetes educator.

“I’m 66 now and I was diagnosed 60-and-a-half years ago.”

On her first trip to Banting House, Borchardt was taking in the sights and visiting the place where Dr. Banting woke up at two o’clock in the morning on Oct. 31, 1920 with the idea that led to the discovery of insulin.

“It was meaningful to me to see what changes have made seeing the old pump, seeing the old equipment,” said Borchardt.

“Sherry and I poked through most of those and say, ’I bought that one and I used this one.’ We recognized everything and even talk about the huge blood glucose meters we had and the fact that we had all seen that U40 insulin is what we both started out with.”

Since first being diagnosed 60 years ago, Borchardt reflected on the advancements in technology.

“My mom and dad had to boil my own insulin syringes in the morning before they gave me my insulin shot,’ she joked.

“We had nothing like disposable syringes, so it’s just the little things like that have made our lives much easier.” Borchardt has been able to live comfortably and even enjoys long-distance cycling.

She hopes to eventually see a cure, even if it isn’t during her lifetime.

“It sounds cliche, but we’re closer (to a cure) than we’ve ever been before,” said Maltman.

“Diabetes Canada, we have over 80 projects from coast to coast. We invested over $180 million in the last 50 years to find a cure, for research, to limit complications and address the stigma that’s caused by diabetes.”

Ahead of WDD, Ontario Deputy Premier and Minister of Health, Sylvia Jones announced an expansion to insulin pump therapy funding through the province’s Assistive Devices Program (ADP). These changes are intended to allow nearly 4,000 Ontarians with Type 1 diabetes to access funding for insulin pumps and supplies up to a year sooner.

“Diabetes Canada has been working tirelessly as advocates for Canadians living with diabetes, and we’re starting to see the results from the government and understanding that we need to help these people live better, healthier lives,” said Maltman.

As part of the WDD celebrations, dozens of bricks were unveiled recognizing the diaversary of many diabetics. A diaversary is the annual anniversary of the day a person was diagnosed with diabetes.

While Borchardt was making her first trip to Banting House to see her new brick, Stevens was visiting for the second time.

“I married a wonderful Canadian, and as we went along, I told him that Banting basically saved all of our lives,” said Stevens.

“Four years ago, I made my first kind of pilgrimage up to Banting House and it was very moving. I don’t think I had a dry eye through the entire experience. It’s just so neat because as we visited with other people, despite how old or young you are, it turned into what pump are you wearing? I’m wearing this. It’s just a natural draw we have with each other.”

stories.title: Canoe trio arrives in Vancouver, marking end of 8,000-kilometre cross-Canada journey
stories.summary: Vancouver - It's a welcome party more than 200 days in the making as three canoeists complete their final landing in Vancouver after an 8,000-kilometre cross-country journey.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
It was an emotional welcome for a trio of canoeists as they made their final landing in Vancouver on Sunday afternoon, completing an 8,000-kilometre cross-country journey.

Despite a recent spate of stormy weather, Nolan Aziz, Will Vyse and Georges Kirijian landed near the Jericho Sailing Centre under sunny skies where they were greeted by family with hugs and tears, and supporters breaking into an impromptu rendition of O Canada.

The three 24-year-olds believe their journey from Tadoussec, Que., to Vancouver is the longest single-season canoe trip ever recorded, at more than 200 days.

A trio of canoeists landed at Jericho Beach in Vancouver on Sunday, marking the end of a more than 200-day and 8,000-kilometre journey across Canada to raise money for charity. (Nov. 15, 2026)

The trio previously finished a 60-day trip in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and decided to see if they could push that further and travel across the country in support of Truth North Aid, a charity that helps northern and remote Indigenous communities.

The friends paddled long distances every day and camped almost every night on Crown land, provincial parks, or once on a farm, with the owner’s approval.

When travel by water wasn’t possible, they portaged over land, sometimes using a cart to pull the canoe, and other times carrying it on their backs.

Vyse said the coast-to-coast journey revealed the generosity and hospitality of the Canadians who greeted them at different stages of their trip.

“I think our biggest takeaway is that there’s a lot of really beautiful people out there, really kind people,” he said on the shore of Jericho Beach on Sunday.

Highlights of the trip included the icy waters of the Saguenay fjord in Quebec, the beautiful rocks and clear water of Lake Superior, and the Fond du Lac river in Saskatchewan with its sandstone shores and easy current.

“Athabasca sand dunes (in Western Canada) was something like we’d never seen before. It’s just like sand as far as you can see,” Aziz said.

The trip brought beautiful views, but challenges too.

Vyse said cold weather was a particular obstacle in Quebec, and a late thaw threw a wrench in the group’s timeline.

“We had to portage for like 3 weeks straight because the lakes just weren’t thawing,” he said, referring to the practice of carrying their canoe over land.

The group faced another tough portage in B.C. in order to avoid the unnavigable currents of Hells Gate and the roaring Fraser River.

Their longest portages reached between 50 and 80 kilometres, Vyse said.

In B.C., the group also climbed over a hydroelectric dam to get to the Peace River as they paddled through the Rockies.

Despite recent B.C. storms, Vyse said the group had good luck with the weather on the last leg of their journey.

“We’ve sort of been travelling in a little hole of sunlight with the clouds around us, just kind of perfectly escaping the rain,” he said.

Kirijian said the group faced their challenges with the awareness that they were sharing just one canoe, and that if something went wrong help wouldn’t come. That meant they made the decision to portage at certain stages of the journey instead of facing potentially unsafe rapids.

The tired trio said their first priorities back on land is a shower and a nap.

They thanked their supporters and said supporting True North Aid is one way of giving back to the northern communities who treated them with kindness, regardless of cultural or language barriers.

“We all have this really cool shared national identity as Canadians and it’s a really beautiful thing,” Aziz said.

paragraphs: It was an emotional welcome for a trio of canoeists as they made their final landing in Vancouver on Sunday afternoon, completing an 8,000-kilometre cross-country journey.

Despite a recent spate of stormy weather, Nolan Aziz, Will Vyse and Georges Kirijian landed near the Jericho Sailing Centre under sunny skies where they were greeted by family with hugs and tears, and supporters breaking into an impromptu rendition of O Canada.
The three 24-year-olds believe their journey from Tadoussec, Que., to Vancouver is the longest single-season canoe trip ever recorded, at more than 200 days.
A trio of canoeists landed at Jericho Beach in Vancouver on Sunday, marking the end of a more than 200-day and 8,000-kilometre journey across Canada to raise money for charity. (Nov. 15, 2026)

The trio previously finished a 60-day trip in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and decided to see if they could push that further and travel across the country in support of Truth North Aid, a charity that helps northern and remote Indigenous communities.
The friends paddled long distances every day and camped almost every night on Crown land, provincial parks, or once on a farm, with the owner’s approval.
When travel by water wasn’t possible, they portaged over land, sometimes using a cart to pull the canoe, and other times carrying it on their backs.
Vyse said the coast-to-coast journey revealed the generosity and hospitality of the Canadians who greeted them at different stages of their trip.
“I think our biggest takeaway is that there’s a lot of really beautiful people out there, really kind people,” he said on the shore of Jericho Beach on Sunday.

Highlights of the trip included the icy waters of the Saguenay fjord in Quebec, the beautiful rocks and clear water of Lake Superior, and the Fond du Lac river in Saskatchewan with its sandstone shores and easy current.
“Athabasca sand dunes (in Western Canada) was something like we’d never seen before. It’s just like sand as far as you can see,” Aziz said.
The trip brought beautiful views, but challenges too.
Vyse said cold weather was a particular obstacle in Quebec, and a late thaw threw a wrench in the group’s timeline.
“We had to portage for like 3 weeks straight because the lakes just weren’t thawing,” he said, referring to the practice of carrying their canoe over land.
The group faced another tough portage in B.C. in order to avoid the unnavigable currents of Hells Gate and the roaring Fraser River.
Their longest portages reached between 50 and 80 kilometres, Vyse said.
In B.C., the group also climbed over a hydroelectric dam to get to the Peace River as they paddled through the Rockies.
Despite recent B.C. storms, Vyse said the group had good luck with the weather on the last leg of their journey.
“We’ve sort of been travelling in a little hole of sunlight with the clouds around us, just kind of perfectly escaping the rain,” he said.

Kirijian said the group faced their challenges with the awareness that they were sharing just one canoe, and that if something went wrong help wouldn’t come. That meant they made the decision to portage at certain stages of the journey instead of facing potentially unsafe rapids.
The tired trio said their first priorities back on land is a shower and a nap.
They thanked their supporters and said supporting True North Aid is one way of giving back to the northern communities who treated them with kindness, regardless of cultural or language barriers.
“We all have this really cool shared national identity as Canadians and it’s a really beautiful thing,” Aziz said.
-With files from Ashley Joannou

stories.title: Flight ground stop in Canada, like the Faa's on Friday, unlikely: aviation expert
stories.summary: An aviation management expert says Canada is less likely than the United States to ground flights nationwide as that country did on Friday afternoon, calling the Canadian system a model its southern neighbours should look to.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — An aviation management expert says Canada is less likely than the United States to ground flights nationwide as that country did on Friday afternoon, calling the Canadian system a model its southern neighbours should look to.

John Gradek says the Canadian system is more robust and modernized than the one the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration operates with.

The FAA had issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday, citing communications issues affecting the nearly two dozen air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports across the country.

Airports across Canada suspended flights to and from the United States, and Air Canada said late Friday that it was cancelling the rest of those flights for the rest of the day.

The U.S. order was lifted late Friday and flights resumed, but airlines warned it could take days before things are back to normal.

Gradek says the American FAA is underfunded and operating with outdated equipment, with NAV Canada saying redundancies are built into the system to ensure operations can continue safely.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 15, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Former MP Mike Morrice elected Green Party leader
stories.summary: Outgoing leader Elizabeth May said in her own video Morrice has worked very hard for his community, and that his election is "a dream come true."
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Green Party of Canada has elected former MP Mike Morrice to lead the party — the sole candidate running in the leadership race.

Morrice served as the MP for Kitchener Centre from 2021 to 2025, but lost his seat to Conservative MP Kelly DeRidder in the last federal election by fewer than 400 votes.

Nira Dookeran withdrew from the Green leadership race in September for “personal and family reasons,” but the party’s constitution still requires a vote, even when only one leadership candidate remains.

Morrice said in a video posted on social media on Saturday night that there is a renewed energy in the party to make life more affordable for Canadians while taking on what he called “the oil and gas giants.”

“Tonight is the start of all of that, and I’m so excited for it,” he said.

Outgoing leader Elizabeth May said in her own video Morrice has worked very hard for his community, and that his election is “a dream come true.”

“Thank goodness the party is in good shape,” May said. “I pass the torch to you fully confident that there’s a great team, that we don’t have any debt, that we have supporters from coast to coast to coast.”

May is the sole Green MP in the House of Commons.

In an interview with The Canadian Press earlier in the fall, Morrice said he hopes to win back his seat, but that he doesn’t plan to run in any of the six pending byelections.

“The plan is to win back Kitchener Centre at the first opportunity, recognizing how important it is to have the leader of the party in the House of Commons,” Morrice said in the interview.

“And for my community, how much more of a platform I hope to give folks in Kitchener Centre to hopefully be back in the House of Commons as leader of the party.”

Morrice takes over the Greens as the federal government claws back many of the emissions-reduction measures implemented by former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

In a video in June, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trudeau government’s plan was too expensive and divisive and “not sustainable over the long term,” while acknowledging Canada’s emissions will rise under his plan.

“I’m making clear that, as leader, I think we need to be really focused on how life has gotten more expensive for most people in this country, but it’s as a result of this continued wealth transfer we’re seeing from regular folks to the billionaire class,” Morrice said earlier in the fall.

— With files from Nick Murray

stories.title: Grey County residents name 23 snowplows ahead of winter
stories.summary: Grey County residents have chosen names for all 23 of the county’s snowplows ahead of the 2026-27 winter season.
stories.content:
Grey County residents have chosen names for all 23 of the county’s snowplows ahead of the 2026-27 winter season.

More than 650 suggestions were submitted through the county’s Connect Grey online engagement platform, followed by two weeks of public voting.

Some of the winning names include Blizzard Wizard, Blizzard of Oz, Darth Blader and Fast and Flurrious.

The winning names will be added to the plows for the upcoming winter season.

“We were having a lot of fun watching the votes come in, and we’re looking forward to seeing these names out on County roads this winter,” said Rob Hatten, the county’s communications manager.

Grey County Transportation Services maintains 835 kilometres of two-lane roads across nine municipalities, with crews working around the clock during winter weather.

Last winter, operators cleared an average of 460 centimetres of snow accumulation and applied a combined 36,000 tonnes of pre-treated salt and winter sand.

Hatten is reminding motorists to be patient and give snowplows plenty of room, noting there is always a person behind the wheel.

The Name the Plow contest was the first project on Connect Grey, which launched Oct. 9. Residents submitted suggestions until Oct. 22 and voted on their favourites until Nov. 6.

The full list of winning names is available online .

stories.title: It’s getting harder to live with my full grown autistic son
stories.summary: A routine trip to Starbucks left me in the darkness for days
stories.author: Payton Kennedy
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

Me and my son tend to do the same things every weekend. If he had it his way, we would do the same things every day. Sameness equals predictability which a lot of the time, suits my nervous system just fine. Arm in arm we walk toward our local Starbucks... In the summer heat, our dog Gracie pants along behind us on her leash. I settle them at a table on the patio and go to get our drinks, like I do every time. Greyson wants a peach-green tea lemonade and chocolate-chunk cookie. I’ll have a coffee. My 20-year-old son has my phone to look at pictures, and I’ll be gone three minutes, tops.

As I am about to pay, I hear one of the staff say, “he’s tipping over the planters.” I know immediately the “he” is my son. I leap toward the front door, out into a crowd of people and the sound of my son’s voice, loud and ragged. A little boy stands off to the side crying, his parents crouching down talking softly to him. Customers who were previously sitting outside enjoying their iced lattes are now standing with various stages of concern on their faces. My son is like a wild animal, kicking out at anyone trying to get close, screeching and pounding on the glass window beside the table.

“Greyson, stop!” I yell, hoping to snap him out of his fury. But I know he’s already gone. I learn that he’s hit the little boy who approached our fluffy dog. He’s turned over tables and planters and hurled insults, slurs and spit towards everyone around him. The staff have called the police. I don’t know this until I do the same. We’ve been here before and I’m not going to be able to de-escalate him without intervention.

The police arrive quickly and collect the version of events from the staff and bystanders. They come to me and I explain.

“He’s autistic. We come here all the time, this hasn’t happened before. I don’t know how to calm him down. I don’t know if he will calm down.”

“I’m so sorry” I say to the parents, and the little boy. They get it, he is autistic, too.

The police officers have formed a circle around Greyson. I am holding my breath, silently praying that he will snap out of his rage. When he starts to utter threats, they stand him up, move his hands behind his back and put cuffs on him. When I think about that moment now, I remember Greyson’s face and the look of incredulousness, like he couldn’t believe they were cuffing him. He’s never looked so neurotypical. They lead him to a police cruiser and put him in the back seat. I am talking but have no idea what I’m saying. The tinted windows of the cruiser don’t allow me to see whether my son is freaking out, crying or calm.

One of the officers drives me home and before I know it, I’m sitting on the couch, calling my partner, John. My breath is shallow and shaky, my head suddenly pounding.

Greyson is not with me. Greyson is not with his dad. Greyson is somewhere. . . with strangers.

The police explained that they would take him to the hospital and an hour later, a doctor calls and asks me the questions they all ask. They are simply following a protocol. He’s given a larger dose of his usual medication; the doctor will call back soon and let us know when he can be picked up. Time stretches and then snaps back when the call comes in.

This is the moment when everything could have changed for Greyson and for me. I am told (or reminded) months later, if this happens again, if the police come and they take him, the only way to get my son the services he truly needs – a funded residential spot – is to refuse to bring him back into my home. Years ago, I remember hearing a story on the news : a mother drops her autistic 19-year-old son off at the local Ministry of Children’s office and leaves him there. She can’t do it any more. She has no help and her only chance to get him the support he needs, is to abandon him: her grown son whom she has cared for every day of his life, now bigger than her, aggressive and unmanageable.

We get to the hospital and see that Greyson has charmed the staff, chatting amiably with the two officers that are hanging around. He gives the security guard a thumbs up as we leave. We depart with nothing more than a recommendation to follow up with our family doctor. I take him home, fix him a snack and he passes out almost immediately. I feel the heaviness and the exhaustion roll in. It wraps itself around me and I let it pull me down underneath the surface of my life. I will be there in the darkness for days.

Payton Kennedy lives in Ottawa

Me and my son tend to do the same things every weekend. If he had it his way, we would do the same things every day. Sameness equals predictability which a lot of the time, suits my nervous system just fine. Arm in arm we walk toward our local Starbucks... In the summer heat, our dog Gracie pants along behind us on her leash. I settle them at a table on the patio and go to get our drinks, like I do every time. Greyson wants a peach-green tea lemonade and chocolate-chunk cookie. I’ll have a coffee. My 20-year-old son has my phone to look at pictures, and I’ll be gone three minutes, tops.

I leap toward the front door, out into a crowd of people and the sound of my son’s voice, loud and ragged. A little boy stands off to the side crying, his parents crouching down talking softly to him. Customers who were previously sitting outside enjoying their iced lattes are now standing with various stages of concern on their faces. stories.title: ‘It was too late’: Squamish Valley boating tragedy survivor recounts incident
stories.summary: One of the survivors says the boat was pushed sideways by a large branch and was pulled into a log that crossed the opening of the creek, causing it to overturn.
stories.author: Sean Previl, Jordan Armstrong
stories.content:
A survivor of a boating incident in the Squamish Valley earlier this week that killed three people says it’s been a “challenging” ordeal.

The incident happened on Thursday, with Squamish RCMP confirming a day later that eight people were on board the boat. Five were rescued.

At approximately 1:52 p.m., police say they were called about a boat incident in the area north of Vancouver. Due to elevated water levels and challenging weather conditions, search and rescue and any recovery efforts were extremely difficult and unsafe. Search and recovery operations resumed Friday.

Spencer Seabrooke told Global News he and the other seven people were on board a fan boat trying to help others caught up in the flooding hitting B.C. this past week.

“It is very challenging, everybody has lost friends and family on the boat,” Seabrooke said in an interview.

He said the boat was in a “shallow area” that is off the main river when the incident occurred.

According to Seabrooke, the boat was pushed sideways by a large branch and was pulled into a log that crossed the opening of the creek.

“We hit it sideways and the right side of the boat popped up and the left side went under and it grabbed and turned the boat over and sucked it down underneath,” he said.

All eight people on board were thrown off the boat, with Seabrooke saying he was briefly sucked under the log but was able to pop back up on the other side. He fought to get to shore and, once out of the water, ran down the path watching the others struggle.

At one point, he lost sight of most of those in the water but eventually saw the boat operator and screamed that he was coming. The operator told him to go back upriver where people needed help.

B.C.’s Sea-to-Sky region has been hit hard by the recent series of storms.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Village of Pemberton issued an evacuation order for properties on Airport Road, which includes the community’s airport, wastewater treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course due to flooding and “high-risk river levels.”

On Wednesday night, an evacuation alert was issued for the Electoral Area C portion of the valley and the village.

The province’s River Forecast Centre put the Sea-to-Sky corridor and Pemberton Valley under a flood warning on Thursday, but that was downgraded on Friday morning.

While conditions were difficult in parts of the province, Seabrooke said they were on flat water with no white caps, in a boat made to go over debris.

“The only thing that’s making this much more difficult is people piping up with their opinions about why we were out there and what we were doing and what our intentions were,” Seabrooke said.

He added that people have been putting out false information about how long the group was out in the area and what they were doing, saying people have “dug their nose into the business.”

“It was simply an accident that happened so quick,” he said. “Nobody was drunk, nobody was driving erratically, speed was not a factor. We simply had this split second of pushing off from the shore, getting hit with a branch and by the time we tried to pull away from the hazard, it was too late.”

— with files from Global News’ Amy Judd

stories.title: Iihf confirms Russia will not compete at world juniors in Canada
stories.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed that Russia will not compete at the 2027 world junior hockey championship in Alberta due to restrictions imposed by the Canadian government. More to come
stories.author: John Marchesan; The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The International Ice Hockey Federation confirms in a statement that Russia will not have a team at the world junior hockey championship next month in Alberta, citing government restrictions in Canada.

The Iihf says Russia will not be able to play at the tournament starting Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer, despite a mandate for the country’s reinstatement from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, following restrictions put in place by the federal government.

The organization says Canada will remain as host despite going against the Cas’s ruling.

Russia and Belarus have been banned from competing in international hockey tournaments since 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The CAS mandated Russia’s immediate reinstatement in an Oct. 30 ruling. The ruling would be in effect for the world junior championship and would affect four other tournaments, including the women’s world championship set for November 2027 in Quebec City.

The federal government pushed back quickly, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying Nov. 3 at a meeting of Commonwealth countries in Antigua that Russians and Belarusians would be barred from competing in Alberta regardless of the Cas’s decision.

“While Russia and Belorussia (sic) are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney said.

“So if you’re asking specifically about the world juniors, the Russians will not be there.”

The Cas’s decision was met with immediate pushback. Finland’s hockey federation said Nov. 2 that its national teams would not play Russia in international tournaments as long as the war in Ukraine continued. Sweden, Czechia and Latvia were among the other countries to follow Finland’s lead over the next few days.

The ice hockey federation of Sweden, the defending world junior champion, said: “The Swedish line was and is crystal clear — Sweden will not play ice hockey matches against Russia in the situation we are in right now.”

The court later defended its decision, saying the Iihf failed to provide sufficient evidence to justify continuing its ban on Russian teams, noting the ruling was based strictly on legal arguments and evidence presented.

But Ottawa maintained its stance, clarifying later that even Russian players with valid visas to compete in Canada would be barred from the world juniors.

The impasse left the tournament in limbo, with Norway’s federation saying it would be bumped from the competition in favour of a Russian team, a decision that was never confirmed publicly by the Iihf.

Meanwhile, hockey officials in Russia vowed to respond. Russian ambassador to Canada Oleg Stepanov criticized Ottawa’s decision, accusing the government of bringing politics into sports.

Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak threatened to seek compensation from Canada and push for relocation or cancellation of the Alberta world juniors if Russia was barred from competing.

He also asked the Iihf ethics council to investigate and punish national federations organizing boycotts of games against Russia.
