That’s likely to happen when more countries impose import controls on seafood tainted with illegalities or unsustainable practices. “That’s when investors will begin to see material — not just reputational — risk, and companies will have to adjust.”
paragraphs: Much of the fish meal and fish oil that support farmed salmon and imported seafood consumed in Canada come from global supply chains linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food insecurity in poorer countries.

In November 2024, the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance gathered in Ottawa to unveil what it called its first national sustainability report for salmon farming. The industry’s message was blunt: Wild fisheries had reached their limits, and farmed salmon was the responsible way forward. “Farm-raised salmon have a key role in helping to feed Canada and the world as capture fisheries reach their limits,” the group said. Its president, Timothy Kennedy, was even more sweeping: “Our goal is to be nothing less than the most sustainable animal protein product in the world.”

This ocean-sustainability argument for fish farming — “grow more, so we can catch less” — is one of the reasons that the $313-billion (U.S.) global aquaculture industry is currently the fastest-growing food sector, and why half of the seafood eaten around the world is now farm-raised rather than caught at sea.

There’s a problem, though, one which is not limited to Canada. “The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular types of farmed seafood in the U.S. and elsewhere — salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained. Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fish meal and fish oil, ingredients made by cooking and pulverizing wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

An extensive five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, DC, uncovered a variety of the hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories. The investigation found that these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In Gambia and Mauritania , the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fish meal factories for export. In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labour on ships, farms, and in factories. In other countries, including India and Peru , this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labour strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish.

The Outlaw Ocean Project mapped roughly the entire global fish meal industry, including more than 1,400 fish meal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fish meal ships at sea.

The investigation revealed that the fish meal industry also contributes to geopolitical tensions. For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity. In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal , after a fisherman was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fish meal boat. Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara , a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various UN resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illegal catch into fish meal in Western Saharan plants, then exporting it with Moroccan labels to farms globally. A violent clash over trucks, many of them carrying this fish and fish meal out of Western Sahara, led to the collapse of a 29-year ceasefire between the countries in 2020.

The unsustainability of this feed protein is a global challenge. Unlike growing bivalves, like oysters, clams, and mussels, which do not typically require external feed, the toughest challenge to raising carnivorous seafood, such as salmon and shrimp, is feeding them. Canada prohibits boats targeting fish for the sole purpose of making fish meal or fish oil. Therefore, the fish meal produced in Canada is typically made by processing offcuts, or inedible parts of fish that would otherwise be thrown away, which is widely viewed as a more sustainable way to produce feed protein than using whole fish suitable for human consumption.

Canada has more than 200 fish farms, most of them depending on fish meal or fish oil that, when made domestically, comes primarily from Pacific anchoveta, chub mackerel, herring, haddock, pollock, sardines, and frigate tuna. However, much of the fish meal Canadian fish farms use — roughly 55,000 tons in 2024 — is sourced from abroad, tying Canadian consumers to these hidden and overseas social costs. Canada also imports more than $4 billion of seafood annually, of which a third is primarily farmed salmon and shrimp that rely heavily on fish meal and fish oil, making the country further complicit.

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fish meal production in at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by ocean-focused civil-society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets. For example, less than 30 per cent of the fleet had publicly available location information, and less than 25 per cent had a unique vessel identification number, or ship licence plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fish meal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the ships in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish, often indiscriminately sweeping in large volumes of bycatch and nontarget species. At least 165 of the ships in the global fish meal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Pauly. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fish meal and fish oil. However, as aquaculture overall grows, so too does the demand for fish meal. Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from the IFFO , the international fish meal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system.” She added that “sustainability frameworks won’t work if they ignore real-world economics,” and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat.”

Researchers have explored alternative protein sources — seaweed, cassava waste, black soldier-fly larvae, even single-cell proteins derived from fungi or bacteria — but none are yet affordable at scale. For now, the pattern persists: Wild fish are caught and rendered into feed, while the costs of this production are left elsewhere.
In 2025, there were at least seven fish meal and fish oil plants in Canada : four on the Atlantic Coast, two on the Pacific coast, and one on Hudson Bay. Two of the Atlantic plants export fish oil.

These facilities are not without problems. Between 2021 and 2024, at least two Canadian fish meal plants were reportedly tied to pollution or unsustainable fishing practices, according to Bait to Plate , an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries. In one case, local news coverage described a plant’s stench as “rancid, fishy, bloody, sour, and chemical.” Another plant reportedly processed fish species that Fisheries and Oceans Canada described as being in the “critical zone,” a designation for heavily depleted stocks.

The far greater burden of food insecurity, collapsed fish stocks, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fish meal or fishmeal-fed seafood Canada imports. For example, over a third of shrimp consumed in Canada comes from India, where the investigation found explosions, fires, and worker asphyxiations at factories producing fish meal that supplies the country’s shrimp farms. In 2020, at one Indian factory called United Marine Products, government inspectors discovered that plant operators had dumped wastewater into hidden bore holes, likely contaminating groundwater and making nearby villagers and livestock sick. The plant owner denied wrongdoing.

As recently as 2022, United Marine Products supplied fish meal to Skretting Canada, which produces feed for many of Canada’s fish farms. At another factory called Bismi Aquatic Products in 2021, a migrant worker died while he cleaned a wastewater tank and passed out from the fumes. Major shrimp brands like IFC and AZ Gems, which source much of their shrimp from India, are sold across Canada at major supermarket chains like Metro Canada , Fortinos (owned by Loblaw Companies Limited), and Costco Canada. In a written response to The Outlaw Ocean Project, Bismi Aquatic Products stated that the worker who died was not following safety protocols and added that the incident “left an indelible mark” with “lessons learned ensuring better operating safety guidelines.” The company also said that it provided financial compensation to the deceased worker’s family.

Skretting has zero tolerance for breaches of its policies that clearly state business partners abide by all applicable laws and regulations governing their business activities, said the company’s sustainability and communications director, Jorge Diaz, and it has opened an investigation to verify the information found in this reporting. For its part, Metro requires all suppliers “ to respect working conditions across the supply chain as outlined in our Supplier Code of conduct for responsible procurement (SCoC),” said company spokesperson Stephanie Bonk. IFC, AZ Gems, and Loblaws did not respond to requests for comment.

As the production of seafood has grown more globalized, its supply chains have stretched longer, and it has become tougher for consumers to know whether it was harvested sustainably or legally. Most grocers who sell the seafood are in the dark as well because tracking is difficult and costly. Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said this is partly because grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. The other reason may be plausible deniability, he added. “Companies can escape blame or the need to fix problems if they’re unaware of them.”

The investigation revealed a surprising diversity of hidden costs in the global feed industry. In Senegal , fish meal production accelerated overfishing, eroding traditional fishing grounds and helping to drive thousands of young men to attempt deadly and desperate sea voyages to Europe. In Russia , fish meal workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country or were stuck on ships far from shore. “People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fish meal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.

In Chile , several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks, demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fish meal.

In 2025, Canada imported more than $710 million worth of seafood from China, which is rapidly expanding its aquaculture industry and now raising more than four times the amount of fish that it catches. One of the fastest-growing regions in this boom is China’s mountainous and desert inland west, particularly Tibet and Xinjiang, known for intense political repression.

The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, much of which is exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States and Canada. The United States bans all goods produced “wholly or in part” by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region on the presumption that they were made with state-sponsored forced labour. Canada’s laws do not cite China specifically but prohibit imports tied to forced labour of any kind.

In one case, local news coverage described a plant’s stench as “rancid, fishy, bloody, sour, and chemical.” Another plant reportedly processed fish species that Fisheries and Oceans Canada described as being in the “critical zone,” a designation for heavily depleted stocks.

content_blocks.text: The far greater burden of food insecurity, collapsed fish stocks, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fish meal or fishmeal-fed seafood Canada imports. For example, over a third of shrimp consumed in Canada comes from India, where the investigation found explosions, fires, and worker asphyxiations at factories producing fish meal that supplies the country’s shrimp farms. In 2020, at one Indian factory called United Marine Products, government inspectors discovered that plant operators had dumped wastewater into hidden bore holes, likely contaminating groundwater and making nearby villagers and livestock sick. The plant owner denied wrongdoing.

content_blocks.text: As recently as 2022, United Marine Products supplied fish meal to Skretting Canada, which produces feed for many of Canada’s fish farms. At another factory called Bismi Aquatic Products in 2021, a migrant worker died while he cleaned a wastewater tank and passed out from the fumes. Major shrimp brands like IFC and AZ Gems, which source much of their shrimp from India, are sold across Canada at major supermarket chains like Metro Canada , Fortinos (owned by Loblaw Companies Limited), and Costco Canada. Most grocers who sell the seafood are in the dark as well because tracking is difficult and costly. Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said this is partly because grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. Critics say these programs serve more as a sustainability smokescreen while giving downstream customers a way to avoid having to look deeper into their supply chains.

content_blocks.text: The programs generally focus on environmental crimes, mostly overlooking labour abuses on ships. Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at the strategic litigation non-profit group Corporate Accountability Lab, said that on land — at processing plants or on farms — certification programs rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the reassurances given by managers at the factories. Instead, the programs frequently alert companies before inspectors show up, which gives them a chance to clean up the scene so there are no violations. At sea, these programs also often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors directly visit and check conditions offshore on vessels, where crimes are most common.

content_blocks.text: Partly bolstered by these certification programs, seafood companies routinely make marketing claims about the ethics and sustainability of their seafood. Often, these claims fail to reckon with crimes or social concerns further up their supply chains, including on the ships or plants that produce the feed for the fish farms. This disconnect is creating growing legal risk for seafood companies and grocers. Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies across five U.S. jurisdictions.

stories.title: Is it legal to mount a phone on the windshield?
stories.summary: In British Columbia, a mounted phone can’t block your view of the road – practically, that means it shouldn’t be on your windshield at all, experts said
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
I see people driving around with phones mounted on the windshield that look like they might block the view of the road. Is that legal? I even saw a guy talking to his mounted phone in what looked like a video call. I got a ticket a few years ago for just having my phone sitting in my centre console so it seems surprising that people can have phones mounted and visible. – Sarah, Vancouver

In British Columbia, a mounted phone can’t block your view of the road – practically, that means it shouldn’t be on your windshield at all, experts said.

“Realistically, if you’re going to stick it on the windshield, it is going to obstruct your view in some fashion,” said Kyla Lee, a Vancouver-based criminal defence lawyer. “So they’re not supposed to be mounted there – but, of course, I see people with [phones mounted on their windshields] all the time.”

In B.C., there’s not a law that specifically addresses distracted driving. Instead, the law covers electronic devices , including cellphones.

Generally, that law doesn’t specify where your phone can or can’t be mounted, just that it can’t obstruct your view or interfere with your car’s controls, Lee said.

“The wording is broad, so it allows for leeway,” she said.

Lee said she’s never had anyone ask her to fight a ticket for having a phone mounted on a windshield. But proving that a mounted phone obstructed the driver’s view could be tough because what a driver can see depends on their height and how seats are adjusted, she said.

RCMP Sergeant Michael McLaughlin, a spokesman for B.C. Highway Patrol, pointed to a separate B.C. law against driving with an obstructed view and said it bans driving with a cellphone mounted on the windshield.

While the rules vary by province, most, including Alberta , Ontario and Quebec , ban anything that can block your view.

Sean Shapiro, a traffic safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop, said it’s generally up to an officer to decide if your mounted phone is a problem.

“If [it’s] in the driver’s view and blocks their vision in any way, [you could be charged],” he said. “I use a cupholder mount.“

The rules vary by province , but most ban holding or touching a hand-held electronic device while driving – even when you’re stopped at a red light.

In B.C., ”you’re only allowed one touch for the purposes of ending, accepting, or declining a [hands-free] call,” Lee said. “So if you were to touch it to shuffle to a different song or to accept a change to your GPS directions, that would be using it even if it was mounted.”

Also, whether it’s mounted or not, you generally can’t physically “interact with the features of the device,” Lee said, or watch anything other than GPS directions on the screen.

That means no TikTok, YouTube or Zoom calls. You also can’t scroll through contacts or playlists, or read texts or anything else off the screen.

In most provinces, including B.C. and Ontario , you can generally only look at a GPS map on your phone or tap it to answer or end a call if it’s securely mounted – and not, for instance, if it’s sitting loose in a cupholder, open centre console or on the seat.

In B.C., there were cases of police charging drivers just for having phones loose in the cupholders or in the centre console – even when they weren’t touching or looking at them. But courts there have ruled that just having a phone sitting in your cupholder or otherwise loose in your vehicle isn’t illegal if you’re not using it, Lee said.

That includes a 2021 B.C. Supreme Court ruling that a driver didn’t break the law just because his phone was playing a podcast through the car’s audio system while loose in the cupholder – because he wasn’t holding it, touching it or watching the screen.

“Just sitting there [isn’t an] offence,” Lee said, adding that the message isn’t out to all police officers. “Every once in a while we get clients who’ve been ticketed for it, and usually it’s a pretty easy win in court.”

But BCHP’s McLaughlin said you could get a ticket – which comes with a $368 fine and four demerits – if your screen is lit.

That’s why it’s a good idea to keep your phone out of sight, for instance, in a bag or the glove compartment, Lee said.

“You can’t touch it, [so] you won’t fall prey to the temptation of your phone just sitting there,” she said. “But also, if the police can’t see a phone, they can’t charge you.”

We couldn’t find any province that specifically bans keeping your phone loose in the vehicle.

“You’re perfectly entitled to keep your phone [in the cupholder],” Shapiro said. “However, if it rings, you generally can’t reach down and start interacting with it.”

Screen time?

In B.C., the electronic device law has been in place since 2010 and doesn’t specifically ban using your phone – and apps on it – through your car’s infotainment system.

“You can be playing [around] on your Apple CarPlay on the [infotainment] screen, and that’s perfectly legal because it’s part of the vehicle, even though it’s just as distracting,” Lee said. “The law is out of step with technology these days.”

But if fiddling with your infotainment screen causes you to make a dangerous move on the road or get into a crash, you could face charges including careless driving , McLaughlin said.

Distracted driving is a serious problem on B.C. roads and “may be getting worse,” he said.

In B.C. last year, police issued more than 27,000 tickets for using an electronic device while driving.

And in a month-long campaign against driving while using devices this year, BCHP issued 1,587 tickets and warnings – more than twice as many as last year’s campaign.

“[Using cellphones] is still by far the biggest issue,” McLaughlin said. ”Infotainment screens, eating while driving and distractions with other vehicle occupants are also concerning.”

stories.title: Toronto-born artist Lotus L. Kang wins $100,000 2026 Sobey Art Award
stories.summary: A Toronto-born artist known for combining photography, sculpture and installation work has received one of Canada's most prestigious contemporary art honours.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A Toronto-born artist known for combining photography, sculpture and installation work has received one of Canada’s most prestigious contemporary art honours.

Lotus L. Kang was named the winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony at the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa, receiving the $100,000 grand prize.

The jury praised Kang’s decade-long commitment to her craft and the growing international recognition of her work, which often incorporates photographic film, found objects and everyday materials.

Five other shortlisted artists, Melaw Nakehk’o, Samuel Roy-Bois, Audie Murray, Caroline Monnet and Shane Perley-Dutcher, will each receive $25,000. Another 24 longlisted artists will receive $10,000 apiece, bringing the award’s total value to $465,000.

Now in its 23rd year, the award recognizes Canadian contemporary artists at pivotal stages in their careers.

Works by all six finalists are on display at the National Gallery until Jan. 3, 2027.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published November 15th, 2026.

David Augustine, The Canadian Press

stories.title: A dementia diagnosis is devastating. What happens when you're only 48?
stories.summary: Toronto - Mark Breslaw sat in his car at a four-way stop just minutes from home, but suddenly didn't know which way to turn.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Mark Breslaw sat in his car at a four-way stop just minutes from home, but suddenly didn’t know which way to turn.

“It was like I blinked and I opened my eyes and I didn’t know where I was. I had no recollection of how I got to this particular position and the worst feeling was I didn’t know what to do and there’s people lining up behind me,” recalled the 50-year-old former human resources executive.

“I just thought the safest thing is just to go straight, which wasn’t actually what I was supposed to (do),” said Breslaw, who had been driving the same route from work to his home in Surrey, B.C., for 18 years.

“I didn’t get far before I went, ‘OK, there’s the elementary school. I know I’m close ... and then I was back.”

Although he was scared, Breslaw didn’t tell his wife what had happened when he got home that day three years ago, because he didn’t want to alarm her. He also didn’t connect the memory lapse to some problems that he — normally a very high performer in a fast-paced job — had been having at work.

Sometimes he would forget the names of people he worked with every day. Other times he couldn’t remember what floor he was taking the elevator to. Usually an excellent planner, he was finding tasks like scheduling his week took far longer than they used to. Once he missed three back-to-back meetings.

“None of this was constant and so, you know, it would happen and you’d be like ‘that was weird.’ But then it would happen again, maybe a week later, two weeks later,” Breslaw said.

He was worried, but chalked it up to stress, lack of sleep and a busy life balancing work with raising a young son. He also has two grown children who live on their own.

But when he found himself lost at that four-way stop two more times, he made an appointment to see his family doctor in January 2024.

What he thought would be a quick discussion turned into a long process that resulted in a diagnosis neither he nor his doctor expected: young-onset Alzheimer’s disease.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common type of dementia, which is the umbrella term for a group of diseases that damage brain cells. Although it most often affects older adults, dementia is not a normal part of aging.

An estimated 772,000 people live with dementia in Canada and could grow to a million by 2030, the Alzheimer Society of Canada says.

Dementia is defined as “young-onset” when it is diagnosed in someone under 65 years old. It’s relatively rare — a 2024 report by the society estimates there were about 28,000 people living with young-onset dementia in Canada in 2020. It projects that number will reach more than 40,000 by 2050.

“Gathering accurate statistics on young onset dementia in Canada is ... complicated by the fact that currently there is no national system for tracking all cases of dementia more broadly, let alone for people who develop dementia under the age of 65,” the report says.

A dementia diagnosis is devastating for anyone, but younger people face specific issues and services often don’t meet their needs, said Cathy Barrick, CEO of the Alzheimer Society of Ontario.

“These are people who are often in the prime of their life. They’re still working. They may have children still at home. They may have children in university,” she said.

“The very first service that is the biggest challenge is actually (getting) a diagnosis. So, I mean, diagnosis is challenging for dementia at any age, but even more so at a younger age because it is so not assumed that that is the problem.”

That was Breslaw’s experience during visits with both his family doctor and a neurologist.

“You’re too young to have dementia, essentially, was the message,” he said.

He went through a series of tests and scans looking for brain tumours, evidence of stroke, depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder — anything that could explain his symptoms.

Even when he scored lower than expected for his age on a cognitive test, his neurologist still didn’t think dementia was likely.

Finally, about a year after he first went to his doctor, a cerebrospinal fluid test revealed the amyloid beta protein that is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease.

Breslaw was 48 years old.

Immediately, Breslaw had to give up his driver’s licence because he now had spatial impairment. He also had to leave the career he loved, because his doctor explained the work would quickly become too complex to manage as his disease progressed.

He and his wife pushed through their shock and grief to take control of anything they could, from seeing a financial planner to picking out a cemetery plot.

People with Alzheimer’s disease can live for 10 years or more and have a good quality of life with the right supports, said Saskia Sivananthan, CEO and co-founder of the Brainwell Institute, a dementia think-tank.

Although there is no cure, there are a few medications approved by Health Canada that can help manage symptoms or slow the rate of progression — but each individual case is different and patients need to discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor.

The disease is ultimately fatal as it progresses through different parts of the brain and eventually affects control over breathing, swallowing and other bodily functions, said Sivananthan, who is a neuroscientist.

Developing dementia while they are still young often forces patients and their families to figure out how to deal with the unexpected loss of income, she said.

Breslaw’s wife, now 46, has a senior job she loves at a local hospital foundation. He said he wants her to continue working full-time rather than taking time off to be his caregiver — not only because of the financial need, but because she has an identity that extends beyond his illness.

They worry about what they’ll have to spend as Breslaw needs more and more care, as they want to make sure their eight-year-old son has money for post-secondary education in the future.

“These are the things that we have to think about. You get diagnosed at 48, you immediately go into all the what-if scenarios,” he said.

LONG-TERM CARE VS HOME CARE

Breslaw’s family also figures prominently into where he wants to receive round-the-clock care when he needs it.

“I hear ... people who are younger want to stay at home longer and I believe that to be very true for many people. It’s not true for me because I have an eight-year-old son,” he said.

“I don’t want it to look like a hospital and kind of see dad in that sort of very vulnerable way.”

Breslaw would rather move into a long-term care home to spare his family.

“I’m going to be largely surrounded by people who are, you know, two and a half decades older than me, if not older than that.”

His ideal living situation would be a transition house that could keep younger people who can no longer function on their own safely, but also allow them to have a better quality of life than in long-term care.

That’s an area where young-onset dementia support is definitely lacking, Sivananthan said.

“Most long-term care or assisted living places are not really set up for him. They are set up for older adults.”

Almost two years after his diagnosis, Breslaw can still walk his son to school and stay home while his wife is at work.

But he can no longer use the stove or microwave after doing so “almost led to a very catastrophic fire in our house.”

He was warming up some food for what he thought was 30 seconds but was actually 30 minutes and then walked away to fold laundry.

Breslaw forgot about the microwave altogether until the kitchen was full of smoke.

He knows as his Alzheimer’s disease progresses, he may need to go to a day program. They are available in many communities, but mostly designed for older people in their 70s, 80s and 90s, Breslaw said.

Barrick, of the Alzheimer’s Society, said someone with young-onset dementia may actually find that experience confusing if they are in later stages of the disease.

“He may be like, ‘why am I here with all these old people? Like, this is weird, I should be at work. Where is my wife?’” she said.

“As his brain changes, he may not be able to put those pieces together. And so it can actually create some behaviours that get exhibited in programs like that, because they can become quite distressed.”

Breslaw, who volunteers for the Alzheimer Society of British Columbia and Yukon, is part of a “small and mighty group” of people with young-onset dementia that advocates for more resources, such as transition houses, age-appropriate day programs and guidance on how to talk to children about what lies ahead.

The federal government recently announced it planned to amend the Criminal Code to allow people with dementia to make advance requests for medically assisted dying (MAID) before they lose their mental capacity to do so.

Those requests would lay out specific conditions when they would reach the point of intolerable suffering and want MAID to be administered, such as deterioration to the point where they don’t recognize their family.

But it’s up to the provinces to decide if their health-care systems will honour advance requests.

B.C. has not announced a position yet.

Breslaw doesn’t know whether or not he would make an advance request if it’s allowed, but said knowing it’s an option would give him peace of mind.

“It literally is something that keeps me up at night and it would be a weight lifted off my family just to have the choice,” he said.

The federal government recently announced it planned to amend the Criminal Code to allow people with dementia to make advance requests for medically assisted dying (MAID) before they lose their mental capacity to do so.

Those requests would lay out specific conditions when they would reach the point of intolerable suffering and want MAID to be administered, such as deterioration to the point where they don’t recognize their family.
But it’s up to the provinces to decide if their health-care systems will honour advance requests.
B.C. has not announced a position yet.
Breslaw doesn’t know whether or not he would make an advance request if it’s allowed, but said knowing it’s an option would give him peace of mind.
“It literally is something that keeps me up at night and it would be a weight lifted off my family just to have the choice,” he said.

stories.title: Amid climate pessimism, a surprise: Global emissions are down for 2026
stories.summary: A new report finds the drop is driven more by the Iran crisis than by a durable change.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved
stories.content:
Despite widespread sentiment that the world is failing in its effort to limit the most pernicious effects of global warming, with deadly climate-fuelled natural disasters like wildfires , heat waves and flash floods proliferating, a surprising study has found fossil fuel emissions are actually falling.

As delegates from around the world met in Turkey this week for the annual climate talks known as COP, the carbon emissions caused by burning fossil fuels unexpectedly dropped in 2026, according to projections published in Nature .

The authors, researchers at the Cicero Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway, said the slight reduction of 0.4 per cent (the equivalent of 22 per cent of Canada’s national emissions) was more due to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz than a real, durable transition away from them.

The cost of fuel has soared after the U.S.-Iran conflict choked off the strait to shipping earlier this year. In Canada, diesel hit a peak national average of more than $2.70 a litre in September.

“The only times in history when emissions have gone down is when there is a global crisis — and this is just another one,” said Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Cicero and one of the report’s authors. “Instead of hoping that we’ll have more and more crises to get emissions down, which is of course a ridiculous idea, we actually need to turn this around.”

The last two times global emissions dropped — in 2008, after the financial crisis and 2020, after the COVID-19 pandemic — carbon emissions quickly rebounded and continued to grow.

The UN has warned that the global goal set in Paris a decade ago, to keep global warming to 1.5 degrees, is effectively impossible to meet . The federal government’s climate report found that Canada has already warmed 2 degrees and can expect one more by 2040. While these results mean climate disasters are now inevitable, they also underline the importance of limiting future warming by cutting fossil fuel use as quickly as possible, experts say.

Fortunately, there are quiet signs that beyond the oil shock, there are economic forces accelerating the adoption of clean energy and electrification, which have been causing emissions growth to slow down.

“Under that global number, there are lots and lots of things that add up. And lots of those have turned. They are on the way down,” Andrew said.

Every EV and heat pump sold around the world reduces demand for fossil fuels, and every solar panel, battery and wind turbine installed creates the clean energy to power those electric technologies. And while adoption and deployment of these non-emitting alternatives is currently insufficient to start bringing down global emissions on their own, they’re growing at a phenomenal rate.

Ships anchored near the Strait of Hormuz. Middle East oil exports have rebounded significantly since the early days of the crisis.

For the past several years, China’s production of renewable power and clean technology were greater than the rest of the world combined , allowing it to slow down and stop the rise in its national emissions (which are by far the largest of any country in the world). This year, with the domestic economy stalling, Chinese clean tech is being exported, flooding markets around the world, which are in turn seeing dramatic effects on their own emissions.

In 2026, Chinese clean tech exports grew at a rapid pace, increasing by 61 per cent for EVs, 45 per cent for wind turbines, 39 per cent for batteries and 22 per cent for solar panels. According to an analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, these exports allowed the world to avoid emitting 450 megatonnes of carbon — the equivalent of Brazil’s national emissions — this year alone.

Unlike fossil fuels, which are burned once and then need to be extracted again, clean tech continues to operate, emissions-free, for 20 years or more. Over the course of the lifetime of these pieces of equipment, they will replace enough fossil fuels to prevent the emission of 8.4 gigatonnes of carbon — the same as the U.S. and India combined emit in a year, Crea found. The solar panels and wind turbines alone will generate the same amount of power as 100 coal plants.

“China is the world’s largest manufacturer of clean energy technologies … It can enable other countries to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels,” said Qi Qin, a China policy analyst at Crea.

Of course, it’s not just solar panels and wind turbines, Chinese EVs are also selling rapidly in countries around the world, and every kilometre driven without burning gas provides immediate climate benefits. According to Mobility Global, which tracks auto sales, electric and hybrid vehicles are increasing their market share worldwide.

Cars that run on gasoline made up less than half of global passenger vehicle sales for the first time in 2026, down from 73 per cent five years ago. While American policies hostile to EVs have slowed sales in North America, the transition to electric driving is accelerating nearly everywhere else, with 49 of the 56 countries tracked by clean energy think tank Ember setting EV sales records this year .

People walk past a showroom for Chinese EV maker BYD in Seoul, South Korea.

Many of these leading indicators are tracked closely on the international level, but granular information on the trends that contribute to Canada’s emissions have, until recently, been harder to come by. This week, however, the Canadian Climate Institute published its Climate Progress Tracker that provides up-to-date data on 40 indicators of the country’s transition to a carbon-free economy.

Ontario’s Home Renovation Savings Program requires homeowners to choose between $10,000 and the ability to sell power back to the grid.

While researchers, policymakers and the public used to have to wait almost two years to get official government emissions numbers, now the climate tracker updates a myriad of statistics ranging from electricity generation to carbon pricing on a monthly basis with a three-month lag.

“The transition to cleaner energy is multi-faceted and to see it, you need to put a lot of indicators together,” said Ross Linden-Fraser, Acting Director of Cci’s 440 Megatonnes data project. ”We’ve organized the data into these signals that reflect our understanding of the most important things that need to happen to bring our emissions down and build a cleaner economy.”

Canada’s picture is decidedly mixed, he said, with individual indicators performing well, “but if you zoom out to the overall context, we’re not moving fast enough.”

Renewable energy generation, for example, has grown by 40 per cent since 2020, but its share of overall generation is actually dropping as drought reduced hydro production and nuclear refurbishments led to increased reliance on gas plants .

While the Hormuz crisis is the largest factor in 2026’s global emission drop, crises don’t always produce lasting change, says Cicero’s Andrew. A lot of industries and consumers will attempt to soften the blow of increased prices by reducing their use of fossil fuels, but the cost of buying new equipment to permanently switch to electricity is a big deterrent to lasting change.

Historically, oil shocks have started long-term trends that far outlasted the crisis — toward smaller, more economical cars after the 70s oil embargo, for example. Researchers at Cicero say fuel-switching could be enough to reduce emissions growth, but is not yet sufficient to “lock in a peak and decline.”

Increasing emissions from AI data centres are also a big question mark over the next decade. Already responsible for approximately 0.5 per cent of the world’s emissions, the UN has projected they could nearly double in size by 2030 — though the emissions produced would vary depending on whether they’re powered by fossil fuels or renewables.

One market intelligence firm projects that the current crisis in the Persian Gulf could push countries to electrify in order to bolster energy sovereignty, lowering their emissions along the way.

“Energy security and decarbonization do not always pull in opposite directions,” said Wood Mackenzie in a statement accompanying their Energy Transition Outlook this week. “As countries seek to reduce dependence on imported fuels, greater electrification, renewables, nuclear, storage and domestic infrastructure can strengthen energy security while lowering emissions as a by-product.”

Correction — Nov. 16, 2026

This article has been updated. The slight 0.4 reduction that researchers with the Cicero Center for International Climate Research found in carbon emissions worldwide, is equivalent to 22 per cent of Canada’s national emissions — not the equivalent of Canada and Saudi Arabia’s total national emissions combined, as stated incorrectly in a previous version of this article.

While these results mean climate disasters are now inevitable, they also underline the importance of limiting future warming by cutting fossil fuel use as quickly as possible, experts say.

Fortunately, there are quiet signs that beyond the oil shock, there are economic forces accelerating the adoption of clean energy and electrification, which have been causing emissions growth to slow down.
“Under that global number, there are lots and lots of things that add up. And lots of those have turned. They are on the way down,” Andrew said.

Every EV and heat pump sold around the world reduces demand for fossil fuels, and every solar panel, battery and wind turbine installed creates the clean energy to power those electric technologies. And while adoption and deployment of these non-emitting alternatives is currently insufficient to start bringing down global emissions on their own, they’re growing at a phenomenal rate.
Ships anchored near the Strait of Hormuz. Middle East oil exports have rebounded significantly since the early days of the crisis.

For the past several years, China’s production of renewable power and clean technology were greater than the rest of the world combined , allowing it to slow down and stop the rise in its national emissions (which are by far the largest of any country in the world). This year, with the domestic economy stalling, Chinese clean tech is being exported, flooding markets around the world, which are in turn seeing dramatic effects on their own emissions.

In 2026, Chinese clean tech exports grew at a rapid pace, increasing by 61 per cent for EVs, 45 per cent for wind turbines, 39 per cent for batteries and 22 per cent for solar panels. According to an analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, these exports allowed the world to avoid emitting 450 megatonnes of carbon — the equivalent of Brazil’s national emissions — this year alone.

Unlike fossil fuels, which are burned once and then need to be extracted again, clean tech continues to operate, emissions-free, for 20 years or more. Over the course of the lifetime of these pieces of equipment, they will replace enough fossil fuels to prevent the emission of 8.4 gigatonnes of carbon — the same as the U.S. and India combined emit in a year, Crea found. The solar panels and wind turbines alone will generate the same amount of power as 100 coal plants.
“China is the world’s largest manufacturer of clean energy technologies … It can enable other countries to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels,” said Qi Qin, a China policy analyst at Crea.

Of course, it’s not just solar panels and wind turbines, Chinese EVs are also selling rapidly in countries around the world, and every kilometre driven without burning gas provides immediate climate benefits. According to Mobility Global, which tracks auto sales, electric and hybrid vehicles are increasing their market share worldwide.

Cars that run on gasoline made up less than half of global passenger vehicle sales for the first time in 2026, down from 73 per cent five years ago. While American policies hostile to EVs have slowed sales in North America, the transition to electric driving is accelerating nearly everywhere else, with 49 of the 56 countries tracked by clean energy think tank Ember setting EV sales records this year .
People walk past a showroom for Chinese EV maker BYD in Seoul, South Korea.

Many of these leading indicators are tracked closely on the international level, but granular information on the trends that contribute to Canada’s emissions have, until recently, been harder to come by. This week, however, the Canadian Climate Institute published its Climate Progress Tracker that provides up-to-date data on 40 indicators of the country’s transition to a carbon-free economy.
Ontario’s Home Renovation Savings Program requires homeowners to choose between $10,000 and the ability to sell power back to the grid.

While researchers, policymakers and the public used to have to wait almost two years to get official government emissions numbers, now the climate tracker updates a myriad of statistics ranging from electricity generation to carbon pricing on a monthly basis with a three-month lag.

“The transition to cleaner energy is multi-faceted and to see it, you need to put a lot of indicators together,” said Ross Linden-Fraser, Acting Director of Cci’s 440 Megatonnes data project. ”We’ve organized the data into these signals that reflect our understanding of the most important things that need to happen to bring our emissions down and build a cleaner economy.”
Canada’s picture is decidedly mixed, he said, with individual indicators performing well, “but if you zoom out to the overall context, we’re not moving fast enough.”

Renewable energy generation, for example, has grown by 40 per cent since 2020, but its share of overall generation is actually dropping as drought reduced hydro production and nuclear refurbishments led to increased reliance on gas plants .

While the Hormuz crisis is the largest factor in 2026’s global emission drop, crises don’t always produce lasting change, says Cicero’s Andrew. A lot of industries and consumers will attempt to soften the blow of increased prices by reducing their use of fossil fuels, but the cost of buying new equipment to permanently switch to electricity is a big deterrent to lasting change.

Historically, oil shocks have started long-term trends that far outlasted the crisis — toward smaller, more economical cars after the 70s oil embargo, for example. Researchers at Cicero say fuel-switching could be enough to reduce emissions growth, but is not yet sufficient to “lock in a peak and decline.”

Increasing emissions from AI data centres are also a big question mark over the next decade. Already responsible for approximately 0.5 per cent of the world’s emissions, the UN has projected they could nearly double in size by 2030 — though the emissions produced would vary depending on whether they’re powered by fossil fuels or renewables.
One market intelligence firm projects that the current crisis in the Persian Gulf could push countries to electrify in order to bolster energy sovereignty, lowering their emissions along the way.

“Energy security and decarbonization do not always pull in opposite directions,” said Wood Mackenzie in a statement accompanying their Energy Transition Outlook this week. “As countries seek to reduce dependence on imported fuels, greater electrification, renewables, nuclear, storage and domestic infrastructure can strengthen energy security while lowering emissions as a by-product.”

stories.title: Mark Carney defuses tensions with Quebec premier before facing Xi, Putin and Trump at Apec
stories.summary: The prime minister described his conversation with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon as 'fun,' constructive and respectful.
stories.author: Tonda MacCharles
stories.content:
Phnom Penh, Cambodia—Prime Minister Mark Carney says the level of Chinese investment he’ll allow in Canada’s auto sector depends on the outcome of U.S. trade talks and whether any deal protects a North American auto supply chain.

Ahead of his meetings in China , where he will sit down with Asia-Pacific summit host President Xi Jinping, Carney told reporters that Canada is working on options other than the U.S., and is open to more Chinese investment as long as it meets certain conditions, including the use of critical minerals from Canada, labour standards for Canadian workers and the exclusion of knock-down or ready-to-assemble kits. He said there must be a “strong value-add” in what is manufactured in Canada, not just the addition of final or finished components.

“There have to be real factories, real processes with supply chains that increase with time in Canada.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney says auto sector remains part of trade talks with U.S. but that Canada is looking at ‘other options’ in Europe and Asia. Carney was taking questions from reporters at the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. (Nov. 16, 2026)

However, Carney suggested his first option is to retain the fully integrated North American automotive industry.

“We have the best autoworkers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market. That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions. It’s an ongoing discussion that we’re having with U.S. administration — myself with the president. And it depends; that’s the first issue.”

“It’s not leverage, but, you know, action: reaction. It depends what — great autoworkers, important market, real assets in Canada — if they’re not fully utilized in a North American context that provides other opportunities, Canada’s gonna move forward either way.”

If international summits are all about showing up for valuable face time with other leaders, this year’s Francophonie and Asia-Pacific summits show the upsides, and the potential downsides, for the prime minister.

On the sidelines, the prime minister appeared to score a significant win when he met with the newly elected premier of Quebec.

The separatist Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon emerged Sunday from his first face-to-face meeting with Carney declaring that, despite their public sparring in recent weeks, he was delighted with a conversation he described as “fun,” constructive and respectful.

Quebec reporters asked Carney if it was a new “bromance,” and Carney laughed, replying “bromance? Why not?” before soon saying, “Non. I have a wife.”

Plamondon had enthused over the meeting, mentioning six times that he and Carney exchanged phone numbers, calling it “a good sign,” and toned down some of his sharpest rhetoric against Ottawa. This is from a premier who has antagonized Carney since taking office in early October.

Plamondon was unapologetic about his demands for a greater say in Canada-U.S. trade negotiations and more power to set temporary immigration levels, saying not all of his disputes with Carney could be resolved in an initial meeting that ran past its allotted half-hour and lasted 47 minutes.

But he claimed victories, saying Carney agreed to provide more transparency and to consult with Quebec in the Canada-U.S. trade talks .

“What we agreed upon is that we needed immediate and enhanced communication among our staff and between each other.”

However, Carney made clear Monday morning before leaving Cambodia that it is the federal government that will negotiate trade treaties.

Plamondon touted as victories the fact that Carney supported his proposed 2027 francophone business leaders’ summit in Quebec, and agreed Quebec will decide how homelessness and housing funding will be spent. Plamondon said he “regretted nothing” about his advocacy for Quebec’s interests.

Yet from the perspective of the prime minister, those were easy concessions.

So, what seemed like a charm offensive from the get-go appears to have worked.

In the same way Carney has deflated tensions with other ornery or Ottawa-skeptical premiers, whether over energy in Alberta, environmental policy in British Columbia or auto-sector jobs in Ontario, he appears to have deflated Quebec-Ottawa tensions, at least for now.

And it was clear which of the two was more at ease when Carney and he shook hands and smiled for the cameras before their meeting. They joked about who was in shape and who was the better goalie when each played hockey at Oxford University, but their body language signalled this was the start of an uneasy friendship.

Carney was looser, more relaxed and complimentary toward the Quebec leader. Plamondon stood in an awkward, legs-akimbo posture throughout the photo opportunity. Earlier, cameras also captured images of a more serious exchange between the duo.

Carney speaks at an event at Francotech in Phnom Penh Sunday.

Plamondon had skipped the Canada-EU summit in Montreal , calling Carney’s invitation, which did not include a prominent speaking role, tantamount to making him a “waiter” at the table. He declared Quebec would negotiate trade terms directly with U.S. lawmakers. Most importantly, Plamondon has vowed to hold another referendum on Quebec sovereignty once U.S. President Donald Trump is out of the White House.

On Sunday, Plamondon dodged questions about whether he raised his sovereigntist project at the francophone summit.

Next stop Monday on Carney’s whirlwind Asia tour is the Asia-Pacific summit in China, where there will be more dragons from a political perspective.

Xi will welcome Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump alongside the other leaders of the 21-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

Carney said on Monday that Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva told him he had encouraged Xi, Trump and Putin to meet in order to try to find a way forward to resolve the war in Ukraine. But Carney has already made clear he will not be equally welcoming to Putin. “Out of respect for the host,” Carney said in Manila that he will stand onstage with Putin for the Apec leaders’ so-called family photo.

But he emphasized Canada’s repudiation of Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Carney will meet separately with Xi to advance the Canada-China relationship reset that began in January after a deep freeze triggered by the Meng Wanzhou affair, trade reprisals and the nearly three-year detention of the Two Michaels.

And although he said he would welcome a trilateral meeting on the sidelines with Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, he isn’t holding his breath, given the “current trajectory” of trade talks between them with the U.S.

Even before Carney set foot on Chinese soil, Canada’s Conservatives dismissed his approach to trade and international relations, which he describes as “values-based realism” — tailoring relations to areas where Canada can find common ground even amid disagreements.

“From China to Qatar, Turkey and the UAE, Prime Minister Carney has made the deliberate choice to build not only deeper trading relationships but also ‘strategic partnerships’ with nations that, in many cases, do not share our fundamental values and freedoms,” said Conservative international trade critic Stephanie Kusie.

“It’s not leverage, but, you know, action: reaction. It depends what — great autoworkers, important market, real assets in Canada — if they’re not fully utilized in a North American context that provides other opportunities, Canada’s gonna move forward either way.”

If international summits are all about showing up for valuable face time with other leaders, this year’s Francophonie and Asia-Pacific summits show the upsides, and the potential downsides, for the prime minister.
On the sidelines, the prime minister appeared to score a significant win when he met with the newly elected premier of Quebec.

The separatist Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon emerged Sunday from his first face-to-face meeting with Carney declaring that, despite their public sparring in recent weeks, he was delighted with a conversation he described as “fun,” constructive and respectful.
Quebec reporters asked Carney if it was a new “bromance,” and Carney laughed, replying “bromance? Why not?” before soon saying, “Non. I have a wife.”

Plamondon had enthused over the meeting, mentioning six times that he and Carney exchanged phone numbers, calling it “a good sign,” and toned down some of his sharpest rhetoric against Ottawa. This is from a premier who has antagonized Carney since taking office in early October.

Plamondon was unapologetic about his demands for a greater say in Canada-U.S. trade negotiations and more power to set temporary immigration levels, saying not all of his disputes with Carney could be resolved in an initial meeting that ran past its allotted half-hour and lasted 47 minutes.
But he claimed victories, saying Carney agreed to provide more transparency and to consult with Quebec in the Canada-U.S. trade talks .
“What we agreed upon is that we needed immediate and enhanced communication among our staff and between each other.”
However, Carney made clear Monday morning before leaving Cambodia that it is the federal government that will negotiate trade treaties.

Plamondon touted as victories the fact that Carney supported his proposed 2027 francophone business leaders’ summit in Quebec, and agreed Quebec will decide how homelessness and housing funding will be spent. Plamondon said he “regretted nothing” about his advocacy for Quebec’s interests.
Yet from the perspective of the prime minister, those were easy concessions.
So, what seemed like a charm offensive from the get-go appears to have worked.

In the same way Carney has deflated tensions with other ornery or Ottawa-skeptical premiers, whether over energy in Alberta, environmental policy in British Columbia or auto-sector jobs in Ontario, he appears to have deflated Quebec-Ottawa tensions, at least for now.

And it was clear which of the two was more at ease when Carney and he shook hands and smiled for the cameras before their meeting. They joked about who was in shape and who was the better goalie when each played hockey at Oxford University, but their body language signalled this was the start of an uneasy friendship.

Carney was looser, more relaxed and complimentary toward the Quebec leader. Plamondon stood in an awkward, legs-akimbo posture throughout the photo opportunity. Earlier, cameras also captured images of a more serious exchange between the duo.
Carney speaks at an event at Francotech in Phnom Penh Sunday.

Plamondon had skipped the Canada-EU summit in Montreal , calling Carney’s invitation, which did not include a prominent speaking role, tantamount to making him a “waiter” at the table. He declared Quebec would negotiate trade terms directly with U.S. lawmakers. Most importantly, Plamondon has vowed to hold another referendum on Quebec sovereignty once U.S. President Donald Trump is out of the White House.
On Sunday, Plamondon dodged questions about whether he raised his sovereigntist project at the francophone summit.
Next stop Monday on Carney’s whirlwind Asia tour is the Asia-Pacific summit in China, where there will be more dragons from a political perspective.
Xi will welcome Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump alongside the other leaders of the 21-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

Carney said on Monday that Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva told him he had encouraged Xi, Trump and Putin to meet in order to try to find a way forward to resolve the war in Ukraine. But Carney has already made clear he will not be equally welcoming to Putin. “Out of respect for the host,” Carney said in Manila that he will stand onstage with Putin for the Apec leaders’ so-called family photo.
But he emphasized Canada’s repudiation of Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Carney will meet separately with Xi to advance the Canada-China relationship reset that began in January after a deep freeze triggered by the Meng Wanzhou affair, trade reprisals and the nearly three-year detention of the Two Michaels.

And although he said he would welcome a trilateral meeting on the sidelines with Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, he isn’t holding his breath, given the “current trajectory” of trade talks between them with the U.S.

Even before Carney set foot on Chinese soil, Canada’s Conservatives dismissed his approach to trade and international relations, which he describes as “values-based realism” — tailoring relations to areas where Canada can find common ground even amid disagreements.

“From China to Qatar, Turkey and the UAE, Prime Minister Carney has made the deliberate choice to build not only deeper trading relationships but also ‘strategic partnerships’ with nations that, in many cases, do not share our fundamental values and freedoms,” said Conservative international trade critic Stephanie Kusie.

stories.title: Carney to cap off Asean summit with focus on trade deals, ahead of Francophonie
stories.summary: Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney is wrapping up a brief visit to the Philippines and heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney has wrapped up a brief visit to the Philippines and is heading to Cambodia, as the government pushes for more trade access in the region.

On his one-night visit to Manila, Carney attended a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, announced the conclusion of free-trade negotiations with the Philippines and unveiled funding for protecting tropical rainforests.

“What Canada presents is certainty to the world,” Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu told reporters in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

Carney was among foreign leaders including U.S. President Donald Trump who were invited to the summit by the Philippine chair, who is holding the rotating presidency of Asean, a bloc of 11 countries.

Ottawa is continuing talks for a trade deal with Asean, which Sidhu said would give Canada access to smaller countries, while Canada also has deeper agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines.

“You can get more into the weeds. You can upgrade later on, when you’re dealing with (one deal that is) bilateral, as opposed to an agreement with 11 partners,” he said in Manila on Sunday, which was late Saturday in Canada.

“It’s the fastest growing region in the world, 700 million consumers, an economy valued at $6 trillion.”

Sidhu also expressed confidence for Canadian pork producers, as the Philippines moves toward restricting pork imports from a wide array of countries, including Canada.

“They’ve got a global safeguards investigation ... for 60 days. Canada is not the culprit, and you’ll find out once the investigation is done,” he said.

Carney also met meet with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on the sidelines of the summit, where he announced $540 million for an initiative to protect rainforests, as part of a project co-led by Brazil and Norway.

The money is part of a $6 billion fund promised by Ottawa this spring in support for international climate finance. It is meant to attract public and private investment for preserving biodiversity and supporting communities that rely on these ecosystems.

Through an interpreter, Lula described the money as investments that will yield a profit and not “donations, money for free.”

Carney suggested he would have further talks with Brazil, which is part of the Mercosur trade bloc with whom Canada is negotiating a trade deal. Lula’s office has previously said Carney would visit the country.

“By May, we will also have an opportunity to discuss our economic co-operation, our largest training partner in Latin America by far, (with) $15 billion dollars in trade,” Carney said.

Carney is now en route to Cambodia for a summit of the Francophonie, including a side event on technology trade in Phnom Penh.

While there, Carney will meet with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who is pushing for more autonomy in Quebec’s international relations, though Sidhu says Ottawa is working constructively with the province.

“Quebec has many of their own trade officers in our embassies around the world, and we’ll continue working collaboratively,” Sidhu said, noting that Quebec’s aerospace sector has recently achieved large sales in Asia.

Later this week, Carney will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in China, months after Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to have a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles sold in Canada.

Sidhu also said Chinese automaker Chery is among those seeking Transport Canada certification to sell lower-cost vehicles into Canada. He said some Chinese manufacturers will likely clear that process by the end of the year.

He said he is also hopeful Chinese companies will create automotive jobs for Canadians.

“There is an interest from Chinese manufacturers to utilize our workforce in Canada, but before you invest billions of dollars you need to understand the market,” he said.

“Every time I sit down with them I look at what they’re doing in Europe and I ask them how they can replicate that in Canada with Canadian supply chains, with Canadian workers.”

The minister said Canada is still navigating trade issues with China, despite some recent progress on extending access to beef, canola meal, crab and peas.

“We’re still continuing to engage on pork, ON pet food and others. We’re not relenting,” he said.

Sidhu also said Canada is working with Beijing to have more opportunities for Canadian small and medium businesses to sell consumer goods to China on online platforms like Alibaba.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Latest travel disruption could cost Canadian airlines millions, expert says
stories.summary: Carriers are expected to take until Tuesday to resume normal operations after the U.S. ordered a nationwide ground stop
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Canadian airlines could face millions of dollars in costs and days before operations return to normal after the United States halted all flights on Friday night when its air traffic control system went down.

The carriers are expected to take until Tuesday to resume normal operations after cancelling 720 flights on Friday, when the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all civilian flights.

Traffic resumed on Friday night but at least 260 Canadian flights are cancelled on Saturday and Sunday, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. This includes flights from the U.S., Mexico and the Caribbean.

Airlines are now grappling with the challenge of getting fresh crews to destinations where their planes were grounded and pilots and flight attendants burned through their available flight duty hours on the ground, said John Gradek, an aviation lecturer at McGill University. This can lead to crew shortages elsewhere in the network.

“The knock-on effect can be significant,” he said.

The U.S. ground stop brings expenses that include the costs of moving fresh crews and planes around to help stranded customers, in addition to hotel and food claims made by passengers whose journeys were delayed during rebooking.

Airlines are rebooking customers on the next available flight or offering refunds. Given the backlog, the next available flight might not be until the next day or later, which could leave the airline open to claims for hotel and meal expenses under Canada’s Air Passenger Protection Regulations, Mr. Gradek said. The initial delay or cancellation is outside the control of the airlines and therefore not covered.

Canadian airlines have responded to reduced demand for travel to the U.S. under President Donald Trump by trimming cross-border schedules beginning last year. This lessened the impact of the outage. However, flights to and from Mexico and the Caribbean were also affected, given they must pass through U.S. airspace and use U.S. air traffic control.

It is impossible to place a price tag on the impact of the ground stoppage, but Canada’s airlines could face millions of dollars in new costs. “It’s significant,” Mr. Gradek said.

The toll of the stoppage comes as airlines are grappling with soaring jet fuel prices caused by the U.S. war on Iran.

Christophe Hennebelle, a spokesman for Air Canada, said the U.S. ground stoppage affected 23,000 customers on Friday. It is hard to say when normal operations will resume, he said, or how quickly stranded passengers can resume their trips.

“It’s really case by case,” he said by phone.

“We are rebooking people, so we will contact people directly, and of course they’ve got the option either to accept the rebooking that we’re proposing or get a refund if they don’t want to travel any more,” Mr. Hennebelle said.

Almost a third of Friday’s 26,200 flights departing in the U.S. were cancelled, Cirium said. On Saturday, more than 4,100 flights are cancelled. This includes flights operated by Canadian airlines.

In a statement, Porter Airlines said it will likely take the weekend for normal scheduling to resume. For customers with flexibility, the airline is waiving fees for rebooking a different flight or selecting a nearby airport.

WestJet Airlines said on Saturday it is preparing for a return to normal operations over the next 48 hours.

stories.title: What Canadians should know about their air passenger rights amid U.S. travel chaos
stories.summary: As Canadian airlines and airports continue to deal with the aftershocks of the Friday grounding of U.S. air traffic, some travellers are facing cancellations and delays to their plans.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
As Canadian airlines and airports continue to deal with the aftershocks of the Friday grounding of U.S. air traffic, some travellers are facing cancellations and delays to their plans.

Under Canada’s Air Passenger Protection Regulations, passengers have the right to be rebooked if their flight is cancelled or subject to a lengthy delay.

Airlines must rebook travellers on the next available flight operated by them or a partner airline that departs within 48 hours of the passenger’s original departure time.

Some Canadian airports and airlines spent Saturday issuing travel notices and catching up on a backlog left behind by a freeze on U.S. air traffic. (Nov. 14, 2026)

Gabor Lukacs, an air passenger rights advocate, says for international travel, like to and from the U.S., if airlines can’t find a flight within that 48-hour period, they are required to rebook passengers on a competing airline.

When disruptions are within an airline’s control, passengers are guaranteed more protections and can claim compensation, but Lukacs says that isn’t the case here.

The nationwide grounding of U.S. air traffic is an “extraordinary circumstance” that is out of the airline’s control, Lukacs says.

Air Canada says it cancelled about 250 flights, affecting some 27,000 passengers after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued the ground stop order on Friday, halting all U.S. flights for more than four hours.

Meanwhile, Porter Airlines and WestJet say it will likely take the whole weekend for flights to return to normal schedules.

Lukacs notes that travellers flying between Canada and the U.S. are protected under both countries’ air passenger regulations, but Canada’s protections are stronger.

For Canadians stuck in the U.S. who May have had to book hotels and cover the cost of additional meals because of travel delays, Lukacs says airlines are not required to pay travellers back.

“In Europe, passengers would still be getting meals and accommodation,” Lukacs says, even for disruptions outside the airline’s control. “In Canada, that’s not an obligation.”

Lukacs says if Canadians feel airlines have not met their obligations under the law, they should document their communications with the airline and take them to small claims court.

The U.S. government says the ground stop order was issued on Friday after new technology was added to the nation’s air traffic control system, overloading antiquated equipment and causing intermittent communications and radar gaps.

The matter is under investigation.

stories.title: Canadian travellers face delays, cancellations as airlines recover from U.S. ground stop
stories.summary: More than 100 flights were cancelled Saturday, leaving some travellers stranded
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Kate Helmore
stories.content:
Canadian air travellers continued to face disruptions Saturday as more than 100 flights were cancelled and airlines scrambled to deal with the fallout from Friday’s U.S. nationwide ground stop that brought air travel to a grinding halt.

While Canadian air traffic systems continued to operate normally, the grounding of all flights departing from the U.S., which lasted about five hours, triggered a major knock-on effect in Canada and around the world.

Air Canada said Saturday it was adding extra flights to help stranded travellers get to their destinations, and several other airlines including WestJet and Porter said they were offering flight changes free of charge.

Spokesperson Yasmine Mehdi said Air Canada cancelled roughly 250 flights on Friday, affecting about 27,000 passengers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” Ms. Mehdi wrote in an e-mail statement.

In Toronto, 143 U.S.-bound flights were cancelled on Friday, a spokesperson for Pearson International Airport said. Another 63 were cancelled on Saturday.

Dozens of flights were also cancelled on Saturday in Montreal, Ottawa, Vancouver and Calgary.

The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said on Saturday.

Some Canadians stranded away from home said they were anxious to resume their journeys after spending hours stuck in airports or onboard parked planes.

John Jacques had just walked up to his gate in Brisbane, Australia when news of the ground stoppage broke. The Toronto resident was returning home on a flight connecting through Dallas, Texas.

“When you’re on the opposite side of the world it’s just about the last thing you would expect,” he told The Globe and Mail.

His flight to Dallas still boarded but had to await takeoff clearance on the tarmac. Including the journey time, Mr. Jacques spent 16 hours inside the plane. He arrived in Dallas in time to make a connection to Toronto, which was also delayed. For the time being, he is making the most of being off a plane.

“I’m quite happy to just be out of that and stretching my legs before the second hop,” he said.

“I’m used to the long hauls from Brizzy to Toronto but today is really feeling long,” he said, adding that the total journey is now stretching more than 24 hours.

But Mr. Jacques feels he got lucky compared to other passengers on his flight. He has a seat on the plane back home to Toronto. Others had to scramble to find other options, he said.

Maggie Sepulveda is a long-haul truck driver who drove from Dallas to Ontario this week. She had hoped to fly home to Dallas on Friday but said she’s still stuck in Toronto Pearson airport.

Her flight has changed three times. She had to pay to stay in an airport hotel last night and is late for her next job. On top of that, her phone is acting up and she’s had to sit in the airport Starbucks to get wireless internet.

In total, the delay has cost her more than $250 in accommodation and food, and she’s not expecting to be reimbursed. It’s the last thing she needs right now. Life is already expensive enough, she said. But she’s keeping things in perspective.

“I’m hopeful that I’ll be able to get out tonight, and I’m thankful that I’m safe,” she said. “Everything happens for a reason.”

South of the border, meanwhile, officials are still searching for answers around what caused the longest nationwide flight shutdown since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday that FAA contractor L3Harris’ installation of at least one new router at a remote facility triggered the disruption.

Mr. Duffy said that the router being replaced started “flooding” other routers in the country’s air traffic control system, disrupting communication lines to airplanes and scrambling radar feeds.

But it’s unclear whether the problems were the result of “incompetence” or a faulty router, Mr. Duffy said.
