stories.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global disruption
stories.summary: Microsoft products are fully operational after a massive outage that left some users unable to access emails for more than 24 hours, the company said Saturday morning.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Microsoft products are fully operational after a massive outage that left some users unable to access emails and other services for more than 24 hours, the company said Saturday morning.

“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” Microsoft said in a post on social media.

The outage was first reported on Thursday and affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services for users across the globe. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The outage, which Microsoft said was caused by a network strain due to servers suddenly being unavailable, affected governments, hospitals and businesses across the globe.

AI Minister Evan Solomon said the Government of Canada was also impacted.

“Ensuring government digital services are secure, reliable and resilient is a priority and we continually assess our systems and dependencies with that objective in mind,” he said in a statement Friday.

Brett Caraway, associate professor of media economics at the University of Toronto, said there is a lot of convenience that comes out of having a centralized system, “but it also exposes you to a great deal of risk.”

The Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal (Chum), as well as Montreal’s Jewish General Hospital and Unity Health in Toronto, both said they experienced outages on Thursday, but by Friday services had been restored.

A spokesperson for Chum said that “there May be an additional delay in processing some appointment requests.”

Officials in the U.K, Australia, India, the Philippines and Japan also said they experienced disruptions.

Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.

Microsoft apologized for the disruption on Friday and said the outage had nothing to do with AI agents or a cyberattack.

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” the company said.

It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.

The company said it was monitoring progress Friday before it officially declared the outage over on Saturday morning.

The disruption is yet another example of what can happen when so many communications and technology platforms rely on one company , experts said.

“The fact that Canada basically closed for business because one U.S. company had a glitch on some servers shows how dependent we are, how vulnerable we are,” says Joshua Pearce, who holds the Thompson Chair of Innovation at Western University.

While it’s difficult to know exactly how many people were impacted, Microsoft said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

– With files from Global News’ Uday Rana and Ariel Rabinovitch and The Associated Press

stories.title: Former environment minister says Canada’s commitment to climate targets ‘factually untrue’
stories.summary: Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is being accused of lying by two of her predecessors for saying Canada is still committed to its Paris targets.
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is being accused of lying by two of her predecessors for saying Canada is still committed to its Paris targets.

Dabrusin is in Antalya, Turkey for COP31, the annual United Nations climate conference.

In an interview with The Canadian Press before the trip, Dabrusin said Canada is “absolutely committed” to its Paris Accord climate commitments. It’s a line the government has maintained despite every report and study over the past 18 months saying Canada is unlikely to meet those Paris targets.

Former environment minister Catherine McKenna said the claim that Canada is still committed to its targets is “factually untrue.”

“Canada now has zero chance of meeting its 2030 Paris commitment and has no path to meet net zero by 2050 (and this is before any new oilsands or LNG),” McKenna, who is also attending COP31, posted on X.

Speaking to The Canadian Press from COP31 on Friday, former environment minister Steven Guilbeault said Dabrusin’s claim to conference delegates that Canada is still committed to its Paris targets “defies reason.”

“I think in general you should tell the truth, and I think as a politician we — I guess I’m no longer a politician — but I always felt that I needed to be genuine with Canadians,” Guilbeault said, pointing to the government’s modelling and reports from the Canadian Climate Institute.

“(Dabrusin) knows that, and she’s seen those analyses. For her to claim that Canada is still committed to meeting the Paris targets, it’s disingenuous and it should have no place in politics.”

Under Prime Minister Stephen Harper, Ottawa promised to bring Canada’s emissions to 30 per cent below 2005 levels.

In 2021, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government increased that target to between 40 and 45 per cent and set a goal of hitting net-zero by 2050.

According to the latest government figures, as of 2024, Canada had only achieved a 10.3 per cent reduction from 2005 levels, with total emissions down 78 million tonnes in 21 years — making it the worst-performing country in the G7. The Canadian Climate Institute’s modelling suggests Canada will not achieve net-zero by 2050.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in June that Canada’s emissions were likely to rise over the next few years, suggesting Canada has abandoned its 2030 commitments — even if his government hasn’t formally admitted it.

Jerry DeMarco, Canada’s environment commissioner, reported last month that the government’s latest projections indicate Canada will only achieve a emissions reduction of 28 per cent by 2030, taking into account the rollbacks in federal climate policy over the past 18 months.

DeMarco’s report cited the cancellation of the consumer carbon price, the two billion trees program, the oil and gas emissions cap, the electric vehicle mandate and the low-carbon fuel procurement program.

The report also cited the decision to weaken the industrial carbon price.

Carney said in June the climate policies introduced under the Trudeau government were too expensive and divisive.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, Dabrusin’s office doubled-down on Canada’s targets.

“Our government stands by the Paris Agreement and is committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, using a pragmatic and durable approach,” press secretary Amy Falkner wrote.

“We have a strong plan fit for this moment, recognizing that we cannot achieve our climate goals when we are divided. Our focus is on results by building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, making significant investments in the low-carbon economy, and working in co-operation with provinces and territories.”

She pointed to the government’s efforts to build out its grid, and the $50 billion commitment in last month’s federal budget — of which $38 billion was tax credit measures.

“Our government is moving with urgency to fight climate change, while working together to build the energy security, industrial capacity, and strategic autonomy that will define this century for Canada,” Falknew said.

— With files from Mia Rabson

stories.title: One person arrested, other suspects at large after overnight home invasion in Mt. Brydges
stories.summary: One person is in custody, and others remain at large after a home invasion in Mt. Brydges, Ont. west of London.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
One person is in custody, and others remain at large after a home invasion in Mt. Brydges, Ont. west of London.

Around 3:55 a.m., officers from the Middlesex County OPP, and officers from Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service (Scps) responded to reports of a break and enter involving possibly armed individuals in the area of Edinburgh Road, Adelaide Road, Parkhouse Drive and Ferne Drive.

“We had a police officer that was on scene within one minute,” said Staff Sgt. Jason Cartwright of the Scps.

“The officer, when she arrived, actually was confronted by one of the suspects who was exiting the residence (on Parkhouse Drive) at that time. She got into a short-foot pursuit with the suspect, at which time the suspect did get away. She returned to the residence and called for more assistance and continued the investigation.”

While the person on foot did get away, an officer who was in the area was able to locate what was believed to be a suspect vehicle.

“He attempted to stop that vehicle, but the vehicle did not stop for police,” said Cartwright.

Police say they don’t have much information on the two outstanding suspects other than they are still searching for two black males between the age of 20 and 30 who were wearing dark clothing.

Hours after the home invasion, police tape surrounded a home on Parkhouse Drive, where a couple was home at the time of the break in.

A contractor was rebuilding the front door which was kicked in and Scps officers along with K9 were searching the area near the residence.

CTV News spoke with a couple of neighbours along Parkhouse Drive who wished to remain anonymous. They said the incident is “very unnerving” and one even went as far as to track down OPP officers and ask them to come double-check the area around her home and under her porch.

Another neighbour told CTV News he plans to upgrade from a doorbell camera to a full security system.

“This is unnerving for sure,” said Cartwright.

“This is a a serious incident that occurred. There will be police presence in Mt Brydges today in the area. We are potentially looking for one or more suspects still. If there’s anything suspicious in the area, call 911 or our emergency line and we will certainly have somebody come out and see them.”

Police say despite early reports, there is no evidence that the suspects had a firearm.

stories.title: CFB Wainwright incident Highlights reserve pay disparities: former bureaucrat
stories.summary: A former director general for the Canadian military’s reserves and cadets says the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright casts a spotlight on disparities in pay and benefits for reservists.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A former director general for the Canadian military’s reserves and cadets says the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright casts a spotlight on disparities in pay and benefits for reservists.

John Milne, a retired major-general, told The Canadian Press reservists on short-term contracts get less compensation than the regular force members they train with. He said the recent training accident at CFB Wainwright shows those short-term reservists face the same risks as their regular force colleagues.

Four soldiers died and 39 others — including several reservists — were injured when a fire suddenly overtook a training area at CFB Wainwright last month.

Military pay is not a straightforward matter and is calculated based on a range of factors.

Unlike regular force members, reservists usually study or work at full-time civilian jobs while they serve under one of a number of different service classes for the military. Those service classes affect how their benefits are determined.

Milne — who has written academic papers on military pay structure — said the formula the federal government uses to calculate daily reservist pay has amounted to an earnings penalty of roughly 32 per cent for part-time reservists compared to the regular force.

He said it’s a “matter of equity” and the daily rate for reservists should be made the same as what regular force members get. He also said the policy governing their benefits should be rewritten to be more fair.

“As the government grows and increases its military commitments and has intentions of using reservists in more dangerous and more complex environments, then it’s a matter of equity that the daily rate for the reservists should actually be the same as the daily rate for the regular,” he said.

Reservists injured in training also normally receive lower-tier compensation and benefits during their recovery, Milne said. He added he believes the military has reclassified the Wainwright reservists’ contracts from short to long-term service classes to improve their access to benefits.

The Department of National Defence did not respond to questions about the reclassification of injured reserve members’ contracts by deadline.

Official information about the Wainwright tragedy has been limited. Three separate investigations are taking place.

Milne sent a submission to the House of Commons national defence committee in the hopes that Parliament would take up the matter. In it, he writes that there is “no justification” for the earnings penalty, which affects other benefits such as disability payment amounts.

He also wrote directly to Defence Minister David McGuinty. A response letter he received from the minister’s office said the military’s pay structure is complex and involves “specific military considerations” different from civilian pay, and denied that Milne had identified pay inequities.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a military pay hike last year, which included a 13 per cent boost for some reserve force ranks. It did not address how pay is structured.

The Canadian Armed Forces Ombud has flagged for years systemic financial inequities and administrative delays with reservist pay as major problems the government must fix, but has reported little progress.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Jensen Huang’s downfall, Ottawa’s fight with Stellantis and Stelco recalls laid-off Hamilton workers: Must-read business and investing stories for the week of Nov. 14
stories.summary: Plus, Canada’s instant payments network launches after years of delays
stories.author: Abigale Subdhan
stories.content:
Getting caught up on a week that got away? Here’s your weekly digest of The Globe’s most essential business and investing stories, with insights and analysis on the biggest headlines, stock tips, personal finance strategies and more.

Markets are bracing as Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of AI giant Nvidia. Reuters senior correspondent Danilo Masoni has more on the potential impact on global markets and the AI trade. Chief fina…

After a week of bombshell reports, plunging stocks and mounting pressure, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday in a massive downfall that clouds the future of the chipmaker and its role in the artificial intelligence boom. He also stepped down from its board of directors, with both exits effective immediately. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will lead the company on an interim basis, Nvidia said on Thursday.

The tech leader had faced growing calls to step down from Nvidia Corp. – the company he founded in 1993 and transformed into the world’s predominant supplier of computer chips to power AI development – after reports of two extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The company’s board had opened an independent investigation into whether Mr. Huang was the target of a foreign espionage operation after he disclosed an extramarital affair.

Mr. Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia and with the AI industry as a whole. His resignation creates uncertainty not only about Nvidia, but about the pace of AI infrastructure spending, which is expected to reach US$7.6-trillion within the next five years, according to an April report from Goldman Sachs.

In a potential end to the face-off between Cleveland-Cliffs and Ottawa, Stelco Inc. said on Friday that it is recalling 175 laid-off steel workers effective Dec 1. The steel maker cited sufficient demand from customers for its steel for the decision.

The restart of operations will take several weeks and all impacted employees will be compensated retroactively for any pay missed while off the job, the company said in a statement.

Stelco announced on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., because of its inability to make money in its galvanized-steel business.

Stelco said in its Friday statement that its customers have vowed to support the restart of its Hamilton operations, and it criticized the government for not doing enough to reduce what it characterizes as a “continued flood” of cheap foreign steel into the market.

Earlier this week, auto maker Stellantis NV said it has finalized the sale of its idled factory in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel Inc. for an undisclosed amount.

Stellantis closed the plant, which employed more than 3,000 people, for retooling in 2023, and moved planned production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois last year, after the U.S. imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars. The deal is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory requirements, the companies said in a joint statement.

Ottawa is not pleased. Prime Minister Mark Carney called the sale “completely outrageous,” vowing to protect workers and ensure that previous government subsidies to Stellantis are returned.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has given Stellantis NV 30 days to reverse the sale of its auto plant in Brampton, Ont. Failure to do so, Eric Atkins reports , could see the federal government take Stellantis to court to recoup the money Ottawa advanced the company to refit the factory.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Ottawa is prepared to sue Stellantis to return the 'hundreds of millions' of dollars the automaker received as part of a federal funding agreement…

Payments Canada has launched its real-time rail national payment system after years of delays, which enables the instant transfer of money and speeds up payments for businesses and consumers. The country’s payments infrastructure has become a priority piece of Ottawa’s bid to bolster sovereignty.

Through the RTR, payments will send almost instantly, 24 hours a day and 365 days a year, and will include data that makes it easier to track the flow of funds. The clearing and settlement process – a traditionally time-consuming behind-the-scenes process that is invisible to most consumers and businesses – will happen almost instantly.

This means that companies could pay their workers immediately after a task is completed, retailers and restaurants could receive funds in real time once a customer has paid them and landlords would receive rent payments instantly with a confirmation of funds.

Canada is the last G7 country to launch a real-time rail system. Many of Canada’s global peers already have instant payments systems, including the United States, Britain, India and Brazil.

Shares of GFL Environmental Inc. fell this week after the board said it was formally shutting down a review of unsolicited bids to take the company private. The country’s largest trash collector turned down a US$22-billion buyout offer from Wall Street private equity funds after the waste-disposal giant’s board decided their offer was inadequate.

News that deal talks are off led Gfl’s share price to fall on Tuesday by US$3.47 or 7.6 per cent to close at US$42.41 on the New York Stock Exchange.

The company did leave the door ajar for potential suitors. Dino Chiesa, the GFL board’s lead independent director, said: “We remain open to considering any proposal that is in the best interests of shareholders.”

GFL was founded in Vaughan, Ont., in 2007 by entrepreneur and current chief executive officer Patrick Dovigi, who built a company known for its bright green garbage trucks through a series of takeovers. It is now headquartered in Miami.

content_blocks.text: Payments Canada has launched its real-time rail national payment system after years of delays, which enables the instant transfer of money and speeds up payments for businesses and consumers. The country’s payments infrastructure has become a priority piece of Ottawa’s bid to bolster sovereignty.
content_blocks.html: Payments Canada has launched its real-time rail national payment system after years of delays, which enables the instant transfer of money and speeds up payments for businesses and consumers. The country’s payments infrastructure has become a priority piece of Ottawa’s bid to bolster sovereignty.

content_blocks.text: Through the RTR, payments will send almost instantly, 24 hours a day and 365 days a year, and will include data that makes it easier to track the flow of funds. The clearing and settlement process – a traditionally time-consuming behind-the-scenes process that is invisible to most consumers and businesses – will happen almost instantly.

content_blocks.html: GFL Environmental turns down buyout offer from Wall Street private equity funds

First Nations are often at the centre of the country’s most important debates, but we know little about where Indigenous Canadians stand on public policy. National Post aims to change that. This is the first annual Postmedia/Leger poll of First Nations, with a groundbreaking snapshot of public opinion in disparate communities with disparate attitudes.

Canada’s First Nations are divided over whether land acknowledgements are useful in achieving reconciliation, with more than 40 per cent saying such pronouncements have “lost their meaning,” according to an exclusive poll.

In a new Postmedia-Leger survey of 503 Indigenous people, 41 per cent of respondents said land acknowledgements have become overused, while 47 per cent said they remain an important way to help First Nations mend relations with non-Indigenous people. The remaining 12 per cent said they were not sure either way.

Land acknowledgements, or the formal recognition of an Indigenous peoples’ connection to specific lands, have become routine at government press conferences, corporate events, music recitals and any number of other public gatherings in recent years.

They became increasingly common during former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s time in government, seen by some as a way to raise awareness about Indigenous claims to their traditional territories. For others, including some First Nations, they’ve become rote declarations that fail to properly contemplate the full meaning behind the statement.

The Postmedia-Leger poll, which relied solely on First Nations respondents, offers a rare insight into Indigenous perspectives on the land acknowledgement issue.

Andrew Enns, executive vice-president of Leger’s central Canada operations, said he was somewhat surprised by the number of Indigenous respondents who seem to have cooled on land acknowledgements.

“With 41 per cent saying they’ve become overused and lost their meaning, that’s a fairly significant percentage of the Indigenous population that have a question with respect to: ‘Do these really mean much now?’”

Leger conducted the online survey of Indigenous Canadians between Oct. 8 and 16, with respondents spread more or less equally across the provinces. Respondents were split roughly evenly between male and female, and across age ranges from 18 to older than 75.

The poll asked whether “land acknowledgements have become overused to the point that they have lost their meaning,” or whether they “still carry important meaning and help move truth and reconciliation forward with non-Indigenous Canadians.”

The results found that among Indigenous people aged 18 to 44, feelings of acknowledgements being overused were higher, at 46 per cent, compared with 35 per cent for those aged 45 and older. Those in Alberta were also more likely to believe they are overused, at 48 per cent, compared with those in Quebec (30 per cent).

“It’s kind of interesting that there is a bit of a generational divide on this, where younger Indigenous people are more apt to say the acknowledgements have lost their meaning.”

Overall, 54 per cent of respondents said a “moderate amount of progress” has been made on the issue of Canada’s reconciliation with First Nations. That compares with 17 per cent saying there had been a “great deal” of progress and 22 per cent saying a “small amount” had been achieved. The remaining respondents said they did not know.

stories.title: Owen Sound man charged with second-degree murder
stories.summary: A 36-year-old man has died following a violent incident in Owen Sound early Friday morning.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A 36-year-old man has died following a violent incident in Owen Sound early Friday morning.

Owen Sound police say emergency responders were called to the 700 block of 2nd Avenue East during the early morning hours of Nov. 13.

The man was taken to Brightshores hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Police say an investigation led to the arrest of a 30-year-old Owen Sound man, who has been charged with second-degree murder.

The accused is scheduled to appear in bail court Saturday, Nov. 14.

Police say there is no ongoing threat to public safety. The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Grey Cup game bids farewell for now to iconic Snowbirds aerial team
stories.summary: The national anthem is set to ring through McMahon Stadium on Sunday and herald across the sky nine Snowbirds jets, in a fitting show retiring the planes of Canada’s military aerial ambassadors. The CFL’s Grey Cup championship game will be the last time the Snowbirds fly in their CT-114 Tutor jets for a scheduled public […]
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
By Dayne Patterson, The Canadian Press

Posted November 14, 2026 8:24 am.

The national anthem is set to ring through McMahon Stadium on Sunday and herald across the sky nine Snowbirds jets, in a fitting show retiring the planes of Canada’s military aerial ambassadors.

The CFL’s Grey Cup championship game will be the last time the Snowbirds fly in their CT-114 Tutor jets for a scheduled public spectacle.

Capt. Marc-André Plante, who flies as Snowbird 8 on the team, says it’s the perfect sendoff.

“It is Canada’s demonstration team. It’s Canada’s football league. It’s like all these things just kind of make sense, when you look at it where we just celebrate Canada as a whole,” he said in an interview.

The Snowbirds, based out of the 15 Wing Air Force base at Moose Jaw, Sask., have never flown anything but the Tutors.

They have performed roughly 2,700 times for more than 140 million people across North America in more than a half-century of service.

At the end of the year, the Tutors are to be retired and will eventually be replaced by the CT-157 Siskin II. The team is expected to be temporarily grounded until the early 2030s.

But on Sunday, the team will soar.

The jets are to set off from the Calgary International Airport and zoom over the stadium as close to their minimum flight height of about 150 metres from the tallest point that they’re flying over, creating a memorable chorus of ooohs and ahhhs.

As celebrated Canadian musician Sarah McLachlan finishes her final note of O Canada, the jets are to roar over the stadium one last time.

Plante and his squadron will then return to the airport, tuck the planes into a hangar and bus to the stadium to watch the rest of the game.

The team will later head home to Saskatchewan on Monday.

“Of course, as we’re flying back to Moose Jaw, if we have sufficient gas, we’ll probably do a little flyover of our hometown as we are coming in.

“But as far as an invited assembly of persons, (the Grey Cup) would be our last.”

End of a chapter in military history

The official retirement plan, and the future of the planes, is outside of the crew’s control, Plante added.

He said the federal government’s announcement in May hasn’t changed his last few months flying with the squad.

If anything, the team has tried to fly over as many towns and cities as gas and time allowed, he said.

Flying with the Snowbirds has been the highest honour so far in his military career, said Plante.

“Being able to inspire hundreds, thousands of Canadians across Canada to pursue their own forms of excellence — whatever that May be, whether or not it’s joining the military or doing anything else that’s contributing to Canada — I think is an amazing thing to do.”

Skeptical about snowbirds return

For Snowbirds enthusiast William Gilson, the flyover will be historic and memorable.

“This flight over the Grey Cup on Sunday is really going to be, I feel, the end of a very important part of my life and an important chapter in Canadian military history.”

It’s a shame the team will be grounded for the next several years, he said.

“So I want to be there.”

Gilson, from Calgary, is a full-time teacher and a military aviation photographer. He estimates he has taken about 10,000 to 15,000 photos of the Snowbirds and expects to add another few hundred to his photo library Sunday.

He said he’s skeptical that Snowbirds will return after being grounded. Petitions have also been circulating to keep the Snowbirds in the sky, including one brought to the House of Commons with more than 2,000 signatures.

Gilson’s love of aviation was born out of his family’s military background and the high-flying stunts of the Snowbirds.

He was 11 when he saw them perform at the airport in Abbotsford, B.C., in 1972. He went to shows every year after, until just recently.

“They’re not overly powerful but demonstrate the true thing to be Canadian: calm, cool, collected, thinking with a smart head.”

Gilson said his camera is going to be perched Sunday on a toboggan hill just southwest of the stadium when the red-and-white birds fly overhead.

He expects to be joined by several hundred other aviation enthusiasts — and maybe some of his family.

His daughter recently called him and asked when he started to become interested in airplanes. His three-year-old granddaughter has said she loves them too.

“It’s just in my blood and it’s in the family’s blood, I guess.”

stories.title: Manitoba NDP gathers at annual convention as it prepares for 2027 election
stories.summary: Winnipeg - Manitoba NDP members are meeting in Winnipeg this weekend at the party's annual convention as it prepares for next year's general election.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis is set to speak this morning, and Premier Wab Kinew scheduled to give a speech at a gala fundraiser in the evening.

Kinew said Friday that his party has $3.5 million in campaign funding and is well positioned well for the upcoming vote.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

He said the party has enough candidates on its slate to expand its majority.

The election is scheduled for Oct. 5, 2027 but could happen sooner.

Kinew didn’t provide specifics on when he May call an election, but he said delivering a balanced budget in the spring is the last major piece of unfinished business before he does so.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Can Canada defend the Arctic? How military exercises in the Far North went off the rails
stories.summary: For Canadians seeking reassurance that the military can assert sovereignty over our Arctic, recent exercises near Resolute Bay were cold comfort
stories.author: Hyungcheol Park; Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Grey skies, near-constant wind and a snow-dusted, barren landscape stretching down to sandy beaches border the freezing waters of the Arctic Ocean. They provided the backdrop for soldiers getting a taste of what it’s like to operate in Canada’s High Arctic.

The land around Resolute Bay in Nunavut features a radar station, several crashed aircraft from decades past, still in pristine condition, and at least one whale skeleton.

But for Canadians seeking reassurance that the military can assert sovereignty over our Arctic, September’s exercises near Resolute Bay were cold comfort.

The plan was to use Chinook helicopters to fly soldiers to Little Cornwallis Island for a series of war games dubbed Operation Nanook-Nunakput, which aimed to integrate the Canadian Armed Forces’ maritime, land and air capabilities to enhance Arctic surveillance, mobility and operational readiness.

Reservists from 31 Brigade that are part of the Land Task Force exercise close quarter combat at the staging area of the Operation Nanook-Nunakput, Canadian Armed Forces’ annual Arctic operation at Resolute Bay, Nunavut on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo BY Hyungcheol Park/Postmedia) Arctic Final Edit Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Unfortunately, technical difficulties with the military’s fleet of medium-to-heavy-lift helicopters meant the choppers didn’t show up. That meant using navy and coast guard ships to ferry soldiers to the island about 100 kilometres northwest of where the exercise was based just outside Resolute Bay.

“That operation was successful, but we did experience several delays, mostly due to ice floes,” Lt.-Col. Christopher van den Berg told reporters, including Postmedia photographer Hyungcheol Park, who joined the junket to see how Canada’s military could assert itself in the Arctic.

“They had to break their way through, which caused a few hours’ delay. Ultimately, though, we were able to move the force successfully.”

The problem was that journalists who flew 800 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle to document the Canadian military in action didn’t get to see it because there just wasn’t enough room for them on the boats, according to van den Berg, who led troops during the operation involving about 350 Armed Forces personnel.

“I can’t have a media package going on the operation affecting my ability to meet my operational objective,” he told reporters, in video captured by Park. “For every one of you, one soldier cannot be on the boat.”

A barge ferries soldiers from the beach to Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray, the Royal Canadian Navy’s sixth Arctic and Offshore Patrol Vessel. The ship carried supplies and troops to the Little Cornwallis Island for the Caf’s annual Arctic mission. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Optics aside, the logistics kerfuffle is an apt demonstration of how the Arctic can mess with pretty much anyone, even when conditions are relatively mild. While soldiers did see some snow during the September exercises, it got quite muddy when it melted, and they also experienced fog and milder weather.

“One of the challenges of operating up here … is you just don’t have as many options to solve your problems as you do down south,” van den Berg said.

The plan had been to use ships as well as Chinooks to transport soldiers to the island, he said.

How Arctic climate presents challenges for the military

Journalists embedded with the military for Operation Nanook-Nunakput also didn’t get to see much of the hamlet of Resolute Bay, known as Qausuittuq, or “place with no dawn,” in Inuktitut. But they did get a quick drive-through of the community, which swung past the RCMP detachment and the post office.

The Canadian Forces is now investigating how the media junket that was supposed to promote the military’s mission in the Arctic went off the rails with allegations journalists were physically jostled by military police while others were allegedly called “f–king rats” by some soldiers. The friction between soldiers and journalists was first reported by independent journalist Christy Somos on her substack.

Park, who was on the junket, left early and didn’t witness that behaviour.

Here are some of the images he captured during his time in the Arctic.

Soldiers stayed in tents equipped with small heaters and slept on cots near the Resolute Bay airport for the duration of the exercise. Constant wind was their companion on some nights. They mainly ate packaged military rations during the exercise, but were fed fresh food once every three days, which differed each time and included meat, vegetables and fruits, along with a vegetarian option. Military rations also had vegetarian options.

Tents are pitched at the staging area at the Martin Bergmann Complex ground in Resolute Bay, Nunavut, ON Sept. 2. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Members of the land task force gather for a briefing at the staging area on Cornwallis Island in Nunavut on Sept. 2, as they prepare to participate in Operation Nanook-Nunakput. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Maj. Tiago Carvalho, left, and Sgt. Jessica Sutherland from CFB Edmonton’s 1 Field Ambulance prepare the mobile dental clinic at the Martin Bergmann Complex in Resolute Bay, Nunavut, ON Sept. 3. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Soldiers eat lunch with their C7 rifles next to them inside the dining hall at the staging area on Sept. 4. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Master Cpl. Anniraniq Michael from 1 Canadian Rangers Patrol Group, out of frame at right, uses a traditional ulu knife to prepare narwhal, caribou, and Arctic char for the soldiers to try in the dining hall at the staging area on Sept. 4. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

A soldier holds his cup of coffee, a Bible and his C7 rifle as he attends Sunday mass inside the moral and welfare tent at the staging area on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

A C-130 Hercules aircraft takes off from the Resolute Bay Airport after delivering equipment for the mission on Sept. 5. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Tents form a grid in the staging area on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

While journalists didn’t get the opportunity to witness the main event on Little Cornwallis Island, they did capture images of soldiers before they set out on their main mission. Soldiers in green uniforms tended to stick out against the Arctic terrain, while the sandy-coloured version offered more camouflage.

Members of the land task force conduct an up tent, down tent exercise to test the equipment on Sept. 5. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

A soldier attempts to dig a shovel into the frozen and muddy ground on Sept. 5. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Soldiers camp out on a field outside the staging area on Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Cpl. Matt Catton, left, a signaller from Ottawa’s 33 Signal Regiment, and Capt. Gregory Outram Kuzma from 48th Highlanders of Canada wait to be transported to a ship that will take them to Little Cornwallis Island on Sept. 8. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Soldiers in full gear ruck around the staging area on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Cpl. Pancham, a reservist from 31 Brigade, takes part in a section attack exercise on Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Reservists from 31 Brigade take up positions during a section attack exercise on Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Snow obscures a line of soldiers on exercise, with a red-clad ranger watching out for polar bears, ON Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

A Fat Truck, one of the Caf’s amphibious vehicles, splashes through a small ravine around Crystal City on Cornwallis Island on Sept. 4. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

The military used naval and coast guard ships to move soldiers from a staging area next to the airport, almost seven kilometres from the hamlet, to Little Cornwallis Island, about 100 kilometres northwest of Resolute Bay. While the exercise did employ a Hercules aircraft and a coast guard helicopter, the military was unable to get any of its Chinook helicopters up to the area, as planned, to take soldiers to Little Cornwallis Island.

A helicopter airlifts supplies to Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray, the Royal Canadian Navy’s sixth Arctic and offshore patrol vessel, ON Sept. 8. The ship transported supplies and troops to Little Cornwallis Island. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Soldiers on an inflatable boat conduct reconnaissance on Sept. 6 with Ccgs Henry Larsen, a medium icebreaker, visible in the background. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Troops jump to shore in Resolute Bay as they return from a reconnaissance mission to Little Cornwallis Island on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

A barge from Ccgs Henry Larsen arrives at the beach on Sept. 8 to transport troops and supplies to the ship, and then on to Little Cornwallis Island. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Soldiers wait on the beach to be taken to either Ccgs Henry Larsen, left, or Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray on Sept. 8. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Soldiers load supplies onto a barge to be transported to one of the ships in the bay on Sept. 8. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Ccgs Henry Larsen, anchored at Resolute Bay on Sept. 8, provided support to troops for Operation Nanook-Nunakput. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

There are about 5,000 Canadian rangers, reservists who live and work in remote, isolated and coastal regions of the country. They are widely known as the eyes and ears of Canada’s military in the Far North, looking out for the arrival of strange ships and aircraft. During Operation Nanook-Nunakput, the rangers were on polar bear patrol around the camp to guard against the apex predators considered the largest carnivorous land mammals on Earth.

A ranger from 1 Canadian Rangers Patrol Group keeps a lookout for polar bears on Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Cpl. Pearl-Ann Kriterdluk, left, and Sgt. Naomi Allinaq from 1st Canadian Rangers Patrol Group provide predator patrol on Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

A ranger and a member of the Military Police examine a map during a battle update brief on Sept. 5 at the Land Task Force Headquarters at the staging area. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

The remote radar station at Resolute Bay, Nunavut, ON Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Colourful buildings under a dusting of snow mark the hamlet that is home to area residents on Resolute Bay. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

The weathered structure housing Resolute Bay’s Canada Post office, shown on Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Resolute Bay’s RCMP detachment works out of a portable. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

The problem was that journalists who flew 800 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle to document the Canadian military in action didn’t get to see it because there just wasn’t enough room for them on the boats, according to van den Berg, who led troops during the operation involving about 350 Armed Forces personnel.

“I can’t have a media package going on the operation affecting my ability to meet my operational objective,” he told reporters, in video captured by Park. “For every one of you, one soldier cannot be on the boat.”

A barge ferries soldiers from the beach to Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray, the Royal Canadian Navy’s sixth Arctic and Offshore Patrol Vessel. The ship carried supplies and troops to the Little Cornwallis Island for the Caf’s annual Arctic mission. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Optics aside, the logistics kerfuffle is an apt demonstration of how the Arctic can mess with pretty much anyone, even when conditions are relatively mild. While soldiers did see some snow during the September exercises, it got quite muddy when it melted, and they also experienced fog and milder weather.
“One of the challenges of operating up here … is you just don’t have as many options to solve your problems as you do down south,” van den Berg said.
The plan had been to use ships as well as Chinooks to transport soldiers to the island, he said.
How Arctic climate presents challenges for the military

Canada’s Arctic: 3 Surprising Ways to Cash in on the North

Journalists embedded with the military for Operation Nanook-Nunakput also didn’t get to see much of the hamlet of Resolute Bay, known as Qausuittuq, or “place with no dawn,” in Inuktitut. But they did get a quick drive-through of the community, which swung past the RCMP detachment and the post office.

The Canadian Forces is now investigating how the media junket that was supposed to promote the military’s mission in the Arctic went off the rails with allegations journalists were physically jostled by military police while others were allegedly called “f–king rats” by some soldiers. The friction between soldiers and journalists was first reported by independent journalist Christy Somos on her substack.
Park, who was on the junket, left early and didn’t witness that behaviour.
Here are some of the images he captured during his time in the Arctic.
Staging Area

Soldiers stayed in tents equipped with small heaters and slept on cots near the Resolute Bay airport for the duration of the exercise. Constant wind was their companion on some nights. They mainly ate packaged military rations during the exercise, but were fed fresh food once every three days, which differed each time and included meat, vegetables and fruits, along with a vegetarian option. Military rations also had vegetarian options.
Tents are pitched at the staging area at the Martin Bergmann Complex ground in Resolute Bay, Nunavut, ON Sept. 2. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Members of the land task force gather for a briefing at the staging area on Cornwallis Island in Nunavut on Sept. 2, as they prepare to participate in Operation Nanook-Nunakput. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Maj. Tiago Carvalho, left, and Sgt. Jessica Sutherland from CFB Edmonton’s 1 Field Ambulance prepare the mobile dental clinic at the Martin Bergmann Complex in Resolute Bay, Nunavut, ON Sept. 3. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Soldiers eat lunch with their C7 rifles next to them inside the dining hall at the staging area on Sept. 4. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Master Cpl. Anniraniq Michael from 1 Canadian Rangers Patrol Group, out of frame at right, uses a traditional ulu knife to prepare narwhal, caribou, and Arctic char for the soldiers to try in the dining hall at the staging area on Sept. 4. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
A soldier holds his cup of coffee, a Bible and his C7 rifle as he attends Sunday mass inside the moral and welfare tent at the staging area on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
A C-130 Hercules aircraft takes off from the Resolute Bay Airport after delivering equipment for the mission on Sept. 5. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Tents form a grid in the staging area on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Land Training

While journalists didn’t get the opportunity to witness the main event on Little Cornwallis Island, they did capture images of soldiers before they set out on their main mission. Soldiers in green uniforms tended to stick out against the Arctic terrain, while the sandy-coloured version offered more camouflage.
Members of the land task force conduct an up tent, down tent exercise to test the equipment on Sept. 5. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
A soldier attempts to dig a shovel into the frozen and muddy ground on Sept. 5. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Soldiers camp out on a field outside the staging area on Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

Cpl. Matt Catton, left, a signaller from Ottawa’s 33 Signal Regiment, and Capt. Gregory Outram Kuzma from 48th Highlanders of Canada wait to be transported to a ship that will take them to Little Cornwallis Island on Sept. 8. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Soldiers in full gear ruck around the staging area on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Cpl. Pancham, a reservist from 31 Brigade, takes part in a section attack exercise on Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Reservists from 31 Brigade take up positions during a section attack exercise on Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Snow obscures a line of soldiers on exercise, with a red-clad ranger watching out for polar bears, ON Sept. 9. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
A Fat Truck, one of the Caf’s amphibious vehicles, splashes through a small ravine around Crystal City on Cornwallis Island on Sept. 4. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Sea Training

The military used naval and coast guard ships to move soldiers from a staging area next to the airport, almost seven kilometres from the hamlet, to Little Cornwallis Island, about 100 kilometres northwest of Resolute Bay. While the exercise did employ a Hercules aircraft and a coast guard helicopter, the military was unable to get any of its Chinook helicopters up to the area, as planned, to take soldiers to Little Cornwallis Island.

A helicopter airlifts supplies to Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray, the Royal Canadian Navy’s sixth Arctic and offshore patrol vessel, ON Sept. 8. The ship transported supplies and troops to Little Cornwallis Island. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Soldiers on an inflatable boat conduct reconnaissance on Sept. 6 with Ccgs Henry Larsen, a medium icebreaker, visible in the background. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Troops jump to shore in Resolute Bay as they return from a reconnaissance mission to Little Cornwallis Island on Sept. 6. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
A barge from Ccgs Henry Larsen arrives at the beach on Sept. 8 to transport troops and supplies to the ship, and then on to Little Cornwallis Island. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Soldiers wait on the beach to be taken to either Ccgs Henry Larsen, left, or Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray on Sept. 8. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Soldiers load supplies onto a barge to be transported to one of the ships in the bay on Sept. 8. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Ccgs Henry Larsen, anchored at Resolute Bay on Sept. 8, provided support to troops for Operation Nanook-Nunakput. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Canadian Rangers

There are about 5,000 Canadian rangers, reservists who live and work in remote, isolated and coastal regions of the country. They are widely known as the eyes and ears of Canada’s military in the Far North, looking out for the arrival of strange ships and aircraft. During Operation Nanook-Nunakput, the rangers were on polar bear patrol around the camp to guard against the apex predators considered the largest carnivorous land mammals on Earth.
A ranger from 1 Canadian Rangers Patrol Group keeps a lookout for polar bears on Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Cpl. Pearl-Ann Kriterdluk, left, and Sgt. Naomi Allinaq from 1st Canadian Rangers Patrol Group provide predator patrol on Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
A ranger and a member of the Military Police examine a map during a battle update brief on Sept. 5 at the Land Task Force Headquarters at the staging area. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
The remote radar station at Resolute Bay, Nunavut, ON Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Colourful buildings under a dusting of snow mark the hamlet that is home to area residents on Resolute Bay. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
The weathered structure housing Resolute Bay’s Canada Post office, shown on Sept. 7. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News
Resolute Bay’s RCMP detachment works out of a portable. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia News

stories.title: A reading test that doesn’t actually require reading
stories.summary: The widespread use of assistive technology is undoubtedly inflating Ontario’s already weak Eqao scores
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
The Eqao tests are Ontario’s main tool for measuring student literacy. There is, however, one problem with that literacy test: students don’t need to be able to read to take it.

All students – even those without learning disabilities – can use a text-to-speech tool built into the e-assessment system to play audio versions of text, questions and multiple-choice answers. They can achieve scores showing they meet or exceed provincial standards, without being able to read.

This widespread misuse of assistive technology, which is intended to help students with disabilities, is undoubtedly inflating Eqao scores. The practice needs to end so Ontarians can get a true picture of children’s literacy.

Ontario’s Education Quality and Accountability Office was created in 1996 to boost accountability in public education and improve outcomes for reading, writing and math. Its standardized Grade 3 and Grade 6 reading and writing tests don’t count toward students’ individual grades, but are instead meant to measure literacy in the province.

The Eqao says the numbers of students using the text-to-speech tool aren’t available this year. When asked it if had captured that data, it didn’t directly respond, but said it is “currently conducting research to further validate how students use the built-in text reader.”

The agency did say that 6.3 per cent of students used third-party text-to-speech software such as the Read&Write for Google Chrome extension or similar tools for reading, writing and math assessments. This allows students to listen to audio versions of text and have their speech transcribed. Access is limited to students with a special needs accommodation on their individual education plan, but other students can still use the built-in tools.

A 2021 report from International Dyslexia Association Ontario sounded the alarm about the widespread use of assistive technology and other accommodations on the Grade 3 and 6 Eqao reading assessments. In 2019, when the test was still primarily written on paper, 18 per cent of students used accommodations to listen to a digital version of text passages and dictate their answers, the report says. Many students had a teacher or volunteer read the questions to them, with the adults writing down the students’ verbal responses.

Alicia Smith, executive director of Dyslexia Canada, believes the number of students using assistive tech on the tests is likely even higher now, given any student can use it.

Disability advocates say assistive tech has an important place in the classroom, and can provide crucial support to kids with physical and learning disabilities. It can allow older children with reading difficulties to keep up in subjects like science or history, for example. But it shouldn’t be used for younger children learning to read – or to measure literacy.

The technology can be used to mask other issues and give a false impression that students and educators are doing well, says Todd Cunningham, an associate professor at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education. Teachers shouldn’t use technology to help young children struggling to read, and instead, should focus on teaching fundamental reading skills like decoding words, he says.

The use of assistive technology is surely lifting Eqao scores, which are weak nonetheless. In the latest tests , 25 per cent of Grade 3 students and 14 per cent of Grade 6 students at English-language school boards fell below the provincial standard for reading.

In a statement to The Globe and Mail, the Eqao defended its approach. It says that while decoding words is an integral part of reading, comprehension depends on things such as vocabulary, sentence structure, background knowledge and the ability to connect ideas, which are measured in Eqao assessments.

These skills are indeed part of comprehension, but if students are unable to decode words unassisted, they shouldn’t be counted as meeting the provincial reading standard. The Eqao should end the practice of allowing students to use assistive technology on tests that measure reading and writing unless those children have physical disabilities, such as motor function issues.

Real improvements have been made in teaching reading in Ontario in recent years, but there’s a long way to go. The Eqao needs to fulfill its purpose of providing accountability and clean up its tests so Ontarians have a true measure of children’s ability to read.

stories.title: Former environment ministers accuse Dabrusin of lying about meeting climate targets
stories.summary: Ottawa - Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is being accused of lying by two of her predecessors for saying Canada is still committed to its Paris targets.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin is being accused of lying by two of her predecessors for saying Canada is still committed to its Paris targets.

Dabrusin is in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual United Nations climate conference.

In an interview with The Canadian Press before the trip, Dabrusin said Canada is “absolutely committed” to its Paris Accord climate commitments. It’s a line the government has maintained despite every report and study over the past 18 months saying Canada is unlikely to meet those Paris targets.

Former environment minister Catherine McKenna said the claim that Canada is still committed to its targets is “factually untrue.”

“Canada now has zero chance of meeting its 2030 Paris commitment and has no path to meet net zero by 2050 (and this is before any new oilsands or LNG),” McKenna, who is also attending COP31, posted on X.

Speaking to The Canadian Press from COP31 on Friday, former environment minister Steven Guilbeault said Dabrusin’s claim to conference delegates that Canada is still committed to its Paris targets “defies reason.”

“I think in general you should tell the truth, and I think as a politician we — I guess I’m no longer a politician — but I always felt that I needed to be genuine with Canadians,” Guilbeault said, pointing to the government’s modelling and reports from the Canadian Climate Institute.

”(Dabrusin) knows that, and she’s seen those analyses. For her to claim that Canada is still committed to meeting the Paris targets, it’s disingenuous and it should have no place in politics.”

Under Prime Minister Stephen Harper, Ottawa promised to bring Canada’s emissions to 30 per cent below 2005 levels.

In 2021, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government increased that target to between 40 and 45 per cent and set a goal of hitting net-zero by 2050.

According to the latest government figures, as of 2024, Canada had only achieved a 10.3 per cent reduction from 2005 levels, with total emissions down 78 million tonnes in 21 years — making it the worst-performing country in the G7. The Canadian Climate Institute’s modelling suggests Canada will not achieve net-zero by 2050.

Despite the criticism from her predecessors and environmental groups at home, Dabrusin said at a news conference on Saturday in Turkey that other countries have praised Canada for its climate direction.

“What I have heard here at COP has been actually a lot of excitement about Canada’s leadership,” Dabrusin said. “We are absolutely leaders. And I’m not only hearing that, frankly, from other countries, but also from civil society.”

She touted Canada’s work on reducing methane emissions and boosting funding to help developing countries reduce their emissions.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in June that Canada’s emissions were likely to rise over the next few years, suggesting Canada has abandoned its 2030 commitments — even if his government hasn’t formally admitted it.

Jerry DeMarco, Canada’s environment commissioner, reported last month that the government’s latest projections indicate Canada will only achieve a emissions reduction of 28 per cent by 2030, taking into account the rollbacks in federal climate policy over the past 18 months.

DeMarco’s report cited the cancellation of the consumer carbon price, the two billion trees program, the oil and gas emissions cap, the electric vehicle mandate and the low-carbon fuel procurement program. The report also cited the decision to weaken the industrial carbon price.

Carney said in June the climate policies introduced under the Trudeau government were too expensive and divisive.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, Dabrusin’s office doubled-down on Canada’s targets.

“Our government stands by the Paris Agreement and is committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, using a pragmatic and durable approach,” press secretary Amy Falkner wrote.

“We have a strong plan fit for this moment, recognizing that we cannot achieve our climate goals when we are divided. Our focus is on results by building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, making significant investments in the low-carbon economy, and working in co-operation with provinces and territories.”

She pointed to the government’s efforts to build out its grid, and the $50 billion commitment in last month’s federal budget — of which $38 billion was tax credit measures.

“Our government is moving with urgency to fight climate change, while working together to build the energy security, industrial capacity, and strategic autonomy that will define this century for Canada,” Falknew said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026

— With files from Mia Rabson in Ottawa and Kathryn Mannie in Toronto

stories.title: Democrats want to kill some of Trump's tariffs — but that might not end the trade war
stories.summary: Washington - Scott Colom never lost faith. After a week of ballot counting, the Democrat on Wednesday officially won a Mississippi Senate seat, making him the first Black person elected to statewide office since the Reconstruction era.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington - Scott Colom never lost faith. After a week of ballot counting, the Democrat on Wednesday officially won a Mississippi Senate seat, making him the first Black person elected to statewide office since the Reconstruction era.

“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom told supporters at his victory party. “I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”

The historic flip in the deep-red state spread was just the crest of a blue wave that swept across the United States in the midterm elections, as Americans voted to reject President Donald Trump and one of his most controversial policies: tariffs.

While the outcome gives the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress a clear mandate to rein in the president’s destructive tariff agenda, it’s unlikely to alleviate trade tensions with Canada on its own.

Trump returned to the White House on a promise of bringing down the cost of living. The cornerstone of his economic policy was the notion that sweeping tariffs on trading partners would secure more favourable terms of trade and bring manufacturing back to the United States.

Marc Trussler, director of data science for the University of Pennsylvania’s program on opinion research and election studies, said exit polling shows that affordability was the main factor driving Americans’ midterm votes.

“They don’t need to be macroeconomists to understand or to see that the tariffs aren’t helping in bringing the costs down,” said Trussler, who is Canadian.

Trump’s trade war with Canada dominated campaign advertising in critical border states like Michigan and Maine. Trussler said exit polls showed less than 10 per cent of people in Maine thought tariffs helped their local economy.

Canada is one of Mississippi’s top trading partners. Trade tensions with Canada were not an explicit factor in the state campaign, but the president’s disruptive tariff policies were definitely on the ballot.

Colom, who was widely praised for his creative campaign ads, attacked Trump’s trade war in multiple videos. In one viral ad — which referenced the hit movie “Sinners” — Colom said Trump’s tariffs are hurting farmers.

This anti-tariff message helped Democrats win seats in other historically Republican states like Texas, South Carolina and Iowa.

The “big tent” the Republicans assembled from Trump’s 2024 victory was ripped apart in the midterms. Polling showed major shifts away from Republicans among Hispanic Americans and young voters, especially young men.

“I think regardless of how your state trades with the outside world or Canada in particular, you’re going to look at these tariffs and see an economic policy that’s not delivering for you,” Trussler said.

While the Trump administration has continued to defend the duties since the election, its rhetoric toward Canada has softened. The trade war escalated rapidly after trade talks blew up in August.

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Cnbc on Thursday that Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney speak “with some regularity.”

”(Canadians) would love to go back to how things used to be, where there’s just unfettered free trade between our two countries. We want to have a deal that makes sense for them and for us,” Greer said. “Part of it means protecting our supply chains and getting them here, but also making accommodation when possible.”

Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, the ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, said that when Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will prioritize lifting Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

But it’s likely Democrats will only tackle one of Trump’s tariff tools while leaving in place other duties still hammering parts of the Canadian economy.

Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent levies after negotiations between Ottawa and Washington broke down. Weeks later, using the same Depression-era statute, Trump banned imports of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.

Trump’s unprecedented use of Section 338 — never previously used for tariffs — has alarmed many American businesspeople. A lawsuit challenging the duties argues they are beyond the president’s powers.

Democrats will be looking for a quick win to show Americans that they’re taking their cost-of-living concerns seriously. Overturning the Section 338 tariffs could do that for them.

But it might not be easy, even with a congressional majority. Democrats will have to convince enough Republicans to defy Trump over his signature economic policy in order to achieve the supermajority they need to bypass the president’s veto powers.

If the bipartisan push is successful, it would kill the Smoot-Hawley-era tariff provision.

Democrats are much less likely to take down Trump’s separate sectoral tariffs on Canada slamming industries like steel, aluminum, automobiles and cabinetry, or the president’s 10 per cent duty linked to claims of forced labour in supply chains.

Democrats have a broad protectionist streak of their own and many of their newly elected members of Congress are not opposed to using tariffs to protect domestic industries.

Former president Joe Biden kept in place tariffs introduced during the first Trump administration and expanded others.

Kamala Harris, the former vice president who ran against Trump, was among the Democrats who voted against the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: How a CTV News investigation connected bag tag cases around the world
stories.summary: The last people Megan Maurer expected to come to her aid in her drug smuggling trial were the police who arrested her. Especially since the suitcase packed full of cannabis literally had her name on it.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Avery Haines
stories.content:
What happens when a simple trip turns into a nightmare? Part four of W5’s five-part investigation on CTVNews.CA follows travellers who say they went from passenger to prisoner, caught in a scheme that crossed borders and changed lives forever.

The last people Megan Maurer expected to come to her aid in her drug smuggling trial were the police who arrested her. Especially since the suitcase packed full of cannabis literally had her name on it.

But federal officers testified that organized criminals have successfully infiltrated Toronto’s Pearson International Airport, leaving the judge at her Brampton, Ont. trial little choice but to find Maurer not guilty.

Meanwhile, ON the other side of the world, in New Zealand, another Canadian with a similar case was found guilty and sentenced to almost 10 years in prison.

How the scheme works

W5 first exposed the scheme in the documentary Trafficked: The Airport Conspiracy last May, revealing how Canadians were being wrongly accused in countries around the world.

Here’s how tag-swapping works: a corrupt airport employee takes the tag off luggage belonging to an unsuspecting passenger and attaches it to a suitcase filled with drugs. An accomplice is waiting to pick up the drug bag at its destination. But if the suitcase is intercepted, the innocent passenger is left trying to explain why their name is on a bag of drugs.

W5 has now identified more than two dozen cases, almost exclusively originating at Pearson Airport.

‘Multiple such incidents’

Two years ago, 30-year-old Canadian Megan Maurer was travelling from Calgary to Dusseldorf, Germany, with her first layover at Pearson International Airport.

That’s where a customs officer found two suitcases stuffed with dozens of vacuum-sealed packages of cannabis — 24.5 kilograms in all, worth up to $170,000.

On the handles: tags with Maurer’s name on them.

It didn’t look good.

At trial, Crown lawyers argued that Maurer being a drug smuggler was “the only reasonable inference” based on the evidence.

But around the time the trial began in early April, Maurer’s lawyer, Jessica Zita, told W5 that she saw CTV News’ early coverage of bag tag switching .

She remembered thinking, “I have to seize on this opportunity. This is timely.”

So when the Crown called to the stand two RCMP officers and a Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) agent involved in Maurer’s arrest, she asked them about it.

Law enforcement isn’t usually eager to give defendants an easy out, Zita said.

All three officers “acknowledged that tag switching occurs at Pearson Airport, describing it as a known and ongoing issue and ‘trend,’” Justice Robert Tomovski of the Brampton Court of Justice wrote in his not-guilty ruling.

If you have any information regarding tag switching or corruption at Canadian airports, please reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA.

The two RCMP officers went further, saying they had personally investigated “multiple such incidents” at Pearson, the judge wrote.

The Crown’s key witnesses had just given Zita a reasonable explanation for why her client’s name was on those drug bags.

“As a lawyer, I’m like, ‘This is great,’” Zita said.

“But I’m also thinking … ‘Wow, this must be a very serious issue. This must be more than a trend. This must be an ongoing problem, if not maybe a crisis, that Pearson is facing,’” she said.

In delivering the not-guilty verdict, the judge referenced the testimony about tag switching at Pearson, which gave him “reasonable doubt.”

Before this case, defence lawyers didn’t have much to show a judge or jury that tag-switching is a trend, Zita said.

Now, she said, there’s a new “tool in their toolbox.”

“And I think that — I wouldn’t go so far to say precedent — but it does make the argument more palatable and more available for use,” she said.

On the other side of the world, one imprisoned Canadian is banking on it.

Across the globe, the opposite outcome

Two months after Maurer was arrested in late 2024, Tawheed-Ul Moyeen — who goes by Tommy — was also picked up on drug smuggling charges after flying from his home in Toronto to Auckland, New Zealand.

Moyeen checked a red suitcase at Pearson, but it didn’t meet him in Auckland.

Authorities did. And they said they had his blue suitcase right there.

“I’m like, ‘That’s not my bag,’” he said in a phone interview from prison with W5. “My bag is red. That’s a blue bag.”

Inside that blue bag was 23 kilograms of 80 per cent pure methamphetamine. And, like Maurer, his tag was on the handle.

But there’s a twist to Moyeen’s case: while he didn’t touch the blue meth suitcase, someone else did.

A ‘fascinating’ case that a judge found ‘difficult to assess’

Vancouver man Le Tan Pham checked an identical blue suitcase onto that flight. It was filled with just six white towels. But when he got to the carousel in Auckland, he collected the drug bag with Moyeen’s name on it.

Moyeen and Pham both had layovers in Dubai on their way to Auckland. It’s unclear whether the tag swap happened in Dubai or Toronto.

Both Canadians were arrested. No evidence was presented at trial that the two men knew each other or communicated with each other.

In the trial last year, the judge wrote that Pham’s guilt was obvious, going so far as to mock his attempts at deception.

“It is sometimes said that the world of large-scale drug importations is littered with ‘bad actors’ — meaning people with disruptive or malevolent intent. You were a bad actor in a more literal sense — in that your acting was bad,” he wrote in his ruling.

Pham claimed he checked a suitcase with only towels because he didn’t trust hotel towels — an explanation that “clearly did not wash with the jury,” the judge added.

Pham’s job was clear, the judge ruled: he was the “catcher,” tasked with picking up the drugs and getting them out of the airport.

Moyeen’s role, however, he found “difficult to assess.”

Part 1: Pearson luggage tag switch leaves Toronto man facing 15 years in Albania

Part 2: Who’s responsible? Pearson tag-switching victims sue across the system

Part 3: Federal government moves to overhaul airport security after CTV News investigation

Moyeen’s only direct connection to the drug bag was his tag. The Crown never proved he touched it, or had any contact with Pham.

Still, several facts worked against him.

Both Moyeen and Pham booked their trips just days before their travel dates, which is a red flag to authorities.

Despite sitting over 30 rows apart, Moyeen left the plane directly after Pham.

At the Auckland airport, Moyeen sent encrypted texts to someone saying “pulled me aside” and “don’t message me.”

Those texts, which were later deleted, were “central to the jury’s verdict,” the judge wrote.

Moyeen told W5 the messages were taken out of context. If the jury had seen the entire conversation with his friend, they wouldn’t have thought it was so suspicious, he said.

The judge wrote that Moyeen’s texts could reflect the fact that he was senior to Pham, “or at least … engaged in some sort of supervisory capacity.”

In the end, the Crown argued Moyeen’s role was making his tag “available” to the drug bag, sowing “confusion” and creating “plausible deniability.”

The whole scheme was “not entirely typical” and “frankly … quite fascinating,” the judge wrote.

A jury found them both guilty. Pham was sentenced to 10 years, while Moyeen got nine years and seven months. He has been behind bars for almost two years so far.

While the judge said the importation must have been an “inside job,” referring to at least one crooked airport worker, there was no explicit mention of tag switching in Moyeen’s trial.

Moyeen’s hoping to change that in his appeal, which he said will heavily feature W5’s journalism.

“Everything happening in the documentary and the research is what’s being used to give strength to my appeal,” he said.

“I don’t know how long this will take, how long it will take for me to get a date,” he said. “I hope it’s really soon. I hope I can be home for Christmas.”

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Sunday at 10 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave following the Grey Cup.

stories.title: Why these university students are spending hundreds of hours rebuilding a brutal war battle in miniature
stories.summary: A group of university students are dedicating hundreds of hours of their time to put a significant piece of Second World War history into perspective.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Saskatoon – A group of university students are dedicating hundreds of hours of their time to put a significant piece of Second World War history into perspective.

Linaya Taylor is one of the students helping construct a miniature model of the Battle of Ortona inside the Saskatoon Museum of Military Artifacts.

“It is (a battle) that a lot of people do not actually know about, so that is why we are making a model,” she said.

The lesser-known Battle of Ortona was vicious. Canadians fought against Germans in hand-to-hand combat during Christmas 1943.

More than 500 Canadians were killed as they helped liberate the Italian city from the Germans.

For Taylor, the details are the most important part of telling any war story.

“I like seeing individual people’s stories. It makes it really real for me,” she said.

The model will include two buildings – a bank and apartment – built from wood, with individual rooms inside that depict Canadian and German combat with plastic, hand-painted figurines. Tanks and troops will fill the replicated streets just as they did in real life.

Taylor, 20, spent hours researching the battle, the buildings, and the soldiers who sacrificed their lives.

“I found a picture of a man who was being lifted onto a stretcher and taken away,” she explained, pointing to the part of the model where it happened. “He was an actual person who needed help.”

Kevin Hicks, British war veteran and museum project manager, has been working with young volunteers like Taylor for the last five years.

He said the younger generation has helped turn the museum into a place filled with stories rather than just artifacts.

“It is humanizing history,” he told CTV News.

“It is just wonderful because the students see it and they are enjoying it.”

Hicks, who served in the Cold War for the Royal Military Police, had a friend who fought in the Battle of Ortona.

He wanted to honour the sacrifices those soldiers made in a meaningful way.

“They fought incredibly hard and I thought, come on, they deserve more of a mention than just a tiny, little model,” he said.

Hicks, 71, expanded one of the museum walls to make room for the new model and constructed the replica buildings out of wood.

He said it was important to include mouse holes in the building walls, which were key in the real-life battle.

The Canadians used the famous war tactic to move through buildings while being shielded from outside attacks.

“They dug a hole in a room, threw a load of hand grenades and machine gunned through the hole and then followed through to fight the Germans literally face-to-face,” Hicks explained.

The Ortona model is one of many that fills the museum, located in the basement of the Nutana Legion.

Last year, students completed a replica of Juno Beach made of 3-D printed houses. The entire exhibit took over 1,800 hours to finish.

Several other exhibits are works in progress.

Evelyne Clark, 20, recently started volunteering at the museum. She’s constructing a model of the Vimy Ridge tunnels using Styrofoam.

She believes models can help the younger generation better understand history.

“Having a visual representation of something rather than just hearing about it or listening about it through a textbook, can make you a lot more interested in it,” she said.

“You can make connection that you cannot always make on paper.”

The group hopes to complete the Ortona and Vimy Ridge exhibits in the new year.
