He said the younger generation has helped turn the museum into a place filled with stories rather than just artifacts.
“It is humanizing history,” he told CTV News.
“It is just wonderful because the students see it and they are enjoying it.”
Hicks, who served in the Cold War for the Royal Military Police, had a friend who fought in the Battle of Ortona.
He wanted to honour the sacrifices those soldiers made in a meaningful way.
“They fought incredibly hard and I thought, come on, they deserve more of a mention than just a tiny, little model,” he said.
Hicks, 71, expanded one of the museum walls to make room for the new model and constructed the replica buildings out of wood.
He said it was important to include mouse holes in the building walls, which were key in the real-life battle.
The Canadians used the famous war tactic to move through buildings while being shielded from outside attacks.

The group hopes to complete the Ortona and Vimy Ridge exhibits in the new year.

stories.title: Should I stay or should I go? My experience of Canada’s housing crisis
stories.summary: Unaffordability in some of our cities forces people like me, who dream of owning a house, to leave their communities and the places they’ve always called home
stories.author: Catherine Owen
stories.content:
Catherine Owen is the author of 17 collections of poetry and prose. Her latest book is Sixteen Homes: A Memoir .

As a born-and-raised Vancouverite now living in Edmonton, some days I gaze at my beautiful 1905 home, my five-months-of-the-year flourishing garden and feel ashamed that I had to leave my place of birth to own it. Is owning a house, no matter where or how, not an unqualified success? Shouldn’t I be continuously rejoicing that I, an underpaid Gen-X writer, scraped the means together to squat on that golden property ladder?

Raised in a duplex in Burnaby, B.C., I became aware when I was a teenager that buying a house would likely never be a reality for me in my home province. Throughout the 1990s, prices kept surging, and even though I co-purchased a condo in 2014 (lost in 2016 after a split), I was dissatisfied that it wasn’t an actual house, with a yard, a fence, and that fabled stability I had been taught to yearn for.

Furthermore, as a writer who has toured 13 times across Canada and stayed in a range of welcoming homes, I kept feeling that ache, not to own property as an investment, but to be a land holder, to steward a place in the world I could also offer up to others as host. By 2018, shocked at the annual increase in rent for my aging apartment in New Westminster (but oh, that Fraser River view!), I gathered up my savings from working in the film industry, combined with a small pension my deceased partner had left me, and began my online quest for a house.

The first place I looked was Edmonton. I had lived there before. From 2006 to 2009, I rented a house in Mill Woods while my partner worked as a boilermaker. I had survived the winters, even as a non-driver. I still had artsy friends there from that time. Back then, there were plenty of jobs, food was cheaper, I was younger. But I didn’t consider any of that in 2018. I just knew this is where I would return to buy a heritage home in the oldest and most affordable neighbourhood. It was a place where, after a parental loan towards the down payment, I was truly able to afford the monthly mortgage.

I am, of course, not the first to travel this path, nor the last. A 2025 report on interprovincial migration from the Business Council of British Columbia noted up to 70,000 people relocated from B.C. to other provinces the previous year, leading co-author Jairo Yunis to conclude: “If people believe they can build a better life elsewhere in Alberta or Ontario, then that points to deeper problems at home.”

Deeper problems at home? Why yes. As reported by CityNews Vancouver: “In 1994, the average home in Vancouver cost approximately eight times the median after-tax household income. In 2024, it costs approximately 14 times the median after-tax household income.” Scarcity of land, offshore purchasing power, incredible natural scenery? Just a few reasons why housing prices have been relentlessly climbing in the Lower Mainland, making the purchase of even a condo, never mind a house, prohibitive to most people.

And home prices aren’t even the whole picture. There is also the price of living in the province – food, clothing, gas, and other essentials. As Mathieu Laberge, chief economist at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc), put it, “The cost of that basket of goods – deemed essential for a ‘modest, basic standard of living’ – is highest in British Columbia, with Alberta ranking second.” But while moving from B.C. to Alberta makes sense when it comes to the money you save, it does also bring up the question of what might be lost.

We are an itinerant nation. Mobility is at our core. We migrate from province to province in search of more things, better situations, a greater guarantee, however delusional, of personal progress. But what does this do to our sense of connection, our ties to a place and its history? Are we more bonded to our country as we pick up and move for a better job or a cheaper house or, in the process, do we see our attachment to the land as discardable too?

There has been little research on the psychological, emotional and even environmental costs of being a migratory nation. Some people are able to relocate blithely with only low-impact regrets; for others, being separated from family or the land they were raised on, while feeling they had no choice but to move for what we are sold as a “better life,” can lead to long-term angst.

In her book, No Place Like Home: The Missing Key to Our Housing Crisis, Jessica Barrett acknowledges that “home is an unwieldy concept,” holding different connotations for everyone. Having initially moved in the opposite direction to me, from Edmonton to Vancouver, which she calls “patient zero for the housing crisis,” she notes that, although she eventually left the city for a more viable place to live in Calgary, she had discounted, among other elements, how much Vancouver’s “physical beauty” had contributed to her “mental health.” And she addresses the distinction between feelings of “empowered choice” in relocating to more affordable provinces and being “forced out” by appallingly high housing costs.

It should be said that no comparison is being made to those forced to become refugees due to war and deprivation, but still, being unable to afford to live in the place you call home to the point that you will accept either horrendous living conditions (overcrowded suites full of mould, cockroaches, and non-working appliances, say, or an apartment with an abusive landlord) or you must move to another place without a sense of community, history or environmental bond, remains a form of being “cast out.” As Ms. Barrett further emphasizes, “The choice to continually move is freedom. Being forced to do so is an act of violence.”

Was I forced to move to Edmonton and buy a house? One answer: No. I chose to move because I knew I would never be able to afford a house in Vancouver. Another answer: Yes. I was forced to move because I knew I would never be able to afford a house in Vancouver. Another angle: Did I need a house? Is living in a house a human right? Adequate shelter is a human right, but again, adequate is open to interpretation. I grew up in a house. So, despite having moved 15 times before I bought my own home, I was determined that I would eventually end up, in middle age, with a house, and a garden, to call my “own.”

But what are the unseen costs of making this possibly tortuous choice?

Perhaps it is only now, eight years after I decided to leave Vancouver “forever” to buy a house in Edmonton, that I am starting to wonder. Back in Burnaby, my parents are aging. And although my grown daughter recently relocated to Edmonton, for some of the same reasons of Vancouver’s unaffordability, my adult son remains there in a decaying single-room occupancy building but is unwilling to leave. Then there are days (despite the gorgeousness of the North Saskatchewan River) that I yearn for the ocean, forests and mountains so painfully I can barely breathe. Sometimes I even think about becoming old or dying in this land, ON the Prairies versus the coast. Do I want that to be my end?

But I bought a home. As a poet! And I console myself, despite what I’ve lost, with the thought that I’ve fulfilled one of my deepest wishes. And with the ochre and cornflower blue hues that my current partner painted on the walls. And with the sunflowers that fill my Prairie garden on the edge of another brief autumn.

content_blocks.text: Perhaps it is only now, eight years after I decided to leave Vancouver “forever” to buy a house in Edmonton, that I am starting to wonder. Back in Burnaby, my parents are aging. And although my grown daughter recently relocated to Edmonton, for some of the same reasons of Vancouver’s unaffordability, my adult son remains there in a decaying single-room occupancy building but is unwilling to leave. Then there are days (despite the gorgeousness of the North Saskatchewan River) that I yearn for the ocean, forests and mountains so painfully I can barely breathe. Sometimes I even think about becoming old or dying in this land, ON the Prairies versus the coast. Do I want that to be my end?

stories.title: British Columbia once showed how people recover from addiction and can do it again
stories.summary: As the B.C. Conservatives take over, they can learn from the research that exists
stories.author: Julian M. Somers
stories.content:
Julian M. Somers is a clinical psychologist and distinguished professor in the Faculty of Health Sciences at Simon Fraser University. He is completing a book, Mass Addiction , from which this piece has been adapted.

In 1955, a small Vancouver clinic called the Narcotic Addiction Foundation became the first program in North America to use methadone in treating addiction. Its clinicians didn’t regard the drug as the treatment. They called it a transitional aid, and they measured success based on steady work, friends who didn’t use drugs, less crime, and a responsible place in family life.

British Columbia has since become known for a very different approach. On Oct. 24, voters elected a government that has promised to move from “safe supply” to prevention, treatment and recovery. Whatever one makes of the politics, the new government won’t need to start from scratch. Some of the best Canadian evidence on how people recover from severe addiction was produced here over the past 20 years.

So, what have we learned in B.C.?

Specialized courts work. Vancouver’s Drug Treatment Court significantly reduced reoffending compared to traditional court in the Downtown Eastside neighbourhood, even though more than half its participants were rated at severe risk. At the Downtown Community Court, the highest-need offenders assigned a case management team had significantly fewer reconvictions than matched offenders in regular court.

Housing works too, including for people who had been written off as “hardest to house.” In a randomized trial involving nearly 300 homeless Vancouverites with addiction and serious mental illness, the participants who were offered housing with intensive support were stably housed about three-quarters of the time over two years.

Those left to existing services were stably housed about a quarter of the time and the accommodations they received were rated as objectively poor quality. By contrast, people given apartments in ordinary buildings around the city had roughly 70 per cent fewer criminal sentences and about half as many medical emergencies. One participant summed up their experience: “Life’s gone from chaotic to meaningful.”

Medication helps when people can take it consistently. Among British Columbians with criminal records, periods when methadone was dispensed were associated with about a third less crime, fewer deaths and fewer hospital admissions. But many patients received it less than half the time it was prescribed.

Importantly, housing on its own didn’t reduce daily substance use. A healthy home is necessary for recovery, but not sufficient. Recovery depends on what people build afterward including relationships, purpose, work and a valued place in a community. The Narcotic Addiction Foundation understood this 70 years ago.

Ignoring this evidence is expensive. Among 14,000 people sentenced in provincial court in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside, we identified the few hundred who used the most health, justice and welfare services. Over five years, each cost the public between $168,000 and $247,000, with no evidence of improvement. Nearly all had a diagnosed mental disorder, and more than 80 per cent had an addiction alongside another mental illness.

We already know how to help people overcome addictions. It’s the standard of care we give physicians, airline pilots and others in safety-sensitive jobs and consists of intensive psychosocial support, close monitoring and a clear expectation of recovery. When B.C. began offering recovery-oriented care to its own public servants, the share who returned to work within a year doubled.

Why should people living in poverty be offered less?

For B.C.’s new government I’d recommend a few overarching priorities. Measure recovery and restore the cross-ministry evaluation that operated from 2002 to 2021.

Wind down “safe supply” carefully, offering everyone who receives it a supported transition to methadone or buprenorphine. Expand drug treatment courts and case management. Make dispersed housing with intensive support the default for people with the highest needs. And intervene earlier, particularly with young people leaving government care, whose records show warning signs years in advance of crises.

The new government also intends to expand involuntary care, which can be improved by first answering two questions. Did we take reasonable steps to prevent the need to intervene? And do we have good reason to expect the person will be grateful afterward, with housing and support in place when they leave care? If the answers are no, then involuntary care is likely to be one more turn of a costly revolving door.

B.C. has spent a decade as the world’s most visible experiment in one approach to addiction. It now has the chance to show what recovery-oriented policy can do, and to measure the results honestly. The evidence has been here all along, some of it since 1955.

November 14, 2026 at 6:00 a.m.

Washington — American leaders have been criticizing Canada for falling short on defence commitments for decades — a critique that has only intensified in recent years to include “free riding” and “delinquency.”

The recent release of Canada’s first national security strategy in over 22 years comes amid demands that Ottawa contribute more to allied defence as well as worsening security threats, military capability gaps, and concerns about relying too much on the United States. “The Plan for a Stronger Canada” pledges a greater contribution to allied defence and strategic autonomy for Canada.

“To protect Canada’s sovereignty, strengthen our strategic autonomy, and meet our Norad and Nato targets, the Canadian government is changing how we invest in defence,” Ottawa said in announcing the plan. The document calls for a “cooperative, clear-eyed relationship with the United States” and “a robust domestic industrial base.”

While Prime Minister Mark Carney’s defence agenda could strengthen Canadian defence capabilities, it could also test U.S. tolerance for non-American equipment, expanded domestic production and greater Canadian freedom of action. So is the Trump administration likely to applaud this as welcome burden-sharing — or see it as problematic?

Mark Cancian, a senior adviser in defence and security at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said he had not seen a U.S. government response to the strategy, but he predicted Washington would welcome much of it. Ottawa’s push for greater independence, however, could prove politically sensitive.

“(President Donald) Trump prefers acquiescence or acceptance rather than defiance,” he said. “I think that will be an irritant.”

If we went for a non-U.S. combat aircraft, that would create significant … tension

Cancian predicts Washington will appreciate the strategy’s call to hit five per cent of GDP defence spending by 2035. He also noted Carney’s increase to two per cent over the past year, calling it a “pretty substantial increase from where it was before.” Canada’s commitment to Norad and pledges to stop illegal guns, drugs and human smuggling will also be seen favourably, he believes, as will the fact that the strategy avoids discussion of China, particularly as a counterweight to the U.S.

“I think that’s very wise,” he said. “That’s a red line … for the administration.”

The seven references to “strategic autonomy,” however, could be a problem.

“We all know what that means or at least what the implication is,” Cancian said, explaining that it’s seen as “pulling away from the United States and being less dependent on the United States.”

Justin Massie, a politics professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal and co-director of The Network for Strategic Analysis, says it’s less about strategic autonomy and more about Canada “hedging its bets” — adding new partners and creating more opportunities without abandoning the American relationship.

The real question will come down to how strategic autonomy is defined in practice, according to Philippe Lagassé, a professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Affairs at Carleton University, who added that the strategy is really just a framework that needs fleshing out.

“I don’t think either in this government’s mind or really in any Nato ally’s mind that it’s (defined as) entirely separate from the United States,” he said.

“It’s more (about) having confidence that you can operate absent the United States and in a worst-case scenario, even in the face of American opposition,” he added, referring to the freedom to make and move on decisions Washington might not support.

Canada’s strategy also refers to Europe as a “like-minded” partner with whom Canada will “significantly deepen our connections and cooperate on strategic capabilities to reinforce our collective strength and resilience.” Discussions about getting closer to Europe, Cancian said, could be another irritant for the U.S.

But Andrea Charron, director of the Centre for Defence and Security Studies and professor at the University of Manitoba, argues that stronger Nordic partnerships can strengthen continental defence by improving coordination between Norad and Nato across the Arctic.

“We are anchored in North America and with the United States, but because of that seam we need to also create new partnerships that include the Nordic countries,” she said.

“The U.S. is doing the same,” she added. “Everybody recognizes this is a problem and that we have to take advantage of the fact that we have this alliance of 32 states.”

Buying European raises a different set of questions. Massie and Lagassé say an early test of maintaining effective continental defence and how Trump May respond to non-American Canadian defence purchases is already brewing with Ottawa’s negotiations to purchase six Saab GlobalEye Airborne Early Warning and Control aircraft.

“If we sign a contract with Saab and integrate the GlobalEye into Norad, this will be huge. The first big test, the first credibility test,” said Massie.

He says GlobalEye will need to show it can securely share data with Canada’s F-35s and Norad, and he believes the technical challenges can be resolved.

Another test will be whether Canada proceeds with purchasing the F-35 or goes with a European alternative, such as the Swedish Gripen.

Canada selected the F-35 a few years back, agreeing to buy 88 of them, and Ottawa has maintained a commitment to an initial 16 jets. But the broader purchase is in question, with Carney having ordered a review in March 2025 that remains underway. Defence Minister David McGuinty said last month that the review would take “all the time it needs,” and Massie and Lagassé suggested that the timing May be linked to a potential trade deal with the U.S.

But should Canada decide to buy European, Massie sees a separate political question: “Will the United States authorize Canada to operate a non-U.S. Awacs aircraft in Norad?” he asked.

“If we went for a non-U.S. combat aircraft, that would create significant … tension with the U.S. government,” he added.

Massie hopes Ottawa addresses those questions with Washington before signing anything.

Keeping U.S. cooperation on side is important, and both Massie and Charron warn that a breakdown in continental defence cooperation could leave Washington acting to protect itself without Ottawa’s consent, including in Canadian airspace.

Charron argues that Norad helps preserve Canadian control because Ottawa decides which military capabilities it contributes and retains authority over their use.

“We get to choose what we cut over. We get to choose if we take action or not,” she said. “And we get the benefit of having a partner to assist us.”

“So let’s not throw out the … Norad baby with the political bathwater.”

Based in the U.S. capital region, Tracy Moran has covered Canada-U.S. relations for National Post since 2025. She previously reported on international news for DW, USA Today, Gzero Media and several online magazines. She holds a master’s degree in international affairs from George Washington University.

Canada selected the F-35 a few years back, agreeing to buy 88 of them, and Ottawa has maintained a commitment to an initial 16 jets. But the broader purchase is in question, with Carney having ordered a review in March 2025 that remains underway. Defence Minister David McGuinty said last month that the review would take “all the time it needs,” and Massie and Lagassé suggested that the timing May be linked to a potential trade deal with the U.S.
But should Canada decide to buy European, Massie sees a separate political question: “Will the United States authorize Canada to operate a non-U.S. Awacs aircraft in Norad?” he asked.
“If we went for a non-U.S. combat aircraft, that would create significant … tension with the U.S. government,” he added.
Massie hopes Ottawa addresses those questions with Washington before signing anything.

Keeping U.S. cooperation on side is important, and both Massie and Charron warn that a breakdown in continental defence cooperation could leave Washington acting to protect itself without Ottawa’s consent, including in Canadian airspace.
Charron argues that Norad helps preserve Canadian control because Ottawa decides which military capabilities it contributes and retains authority over their use.
“We get to choose what we cut over. We get to choose if we take action or not,” she said. “And we get the benefit of having a partner to assist us.”
“So let’s not throw out the … Norad baby with the political bathwater.”

She previously reported on international news for DW, USA Today, Gzero Media and several online magazines. She holds a master’s degree in international affairs from George Washington University.

Washington — American leaders have been criticizing Canada for falling short on defence commitments for decades — a critique that has only intensified in recent years to include “free riding” and “delinquency.”

The recent release of Canada’s first national security strategy in over 22 years comes amid demands that Ottawa contribute more to allied defence as well as worsening security threats, military capability gaps, and concerns about relying too much on the United States. “The Plan for a Stronger Canada” pledges a greater contribution to allied defence and strategic autonomy for Canada.

“To protect Canada’s sovereignty, strengthen our strategic autonomy, and meet our Norad and Nato targets, the Canadian government is changing how we invest in defence,” Ottawa said in announcing the plan. The document calls for a “cooperative, clear-eyed relationship with the United States” and “a robust domestic industrial base.”

While Prime Minister Mark Carney’s defence agenda could strengthen Canadian defence capabilities, it could also test U.S. tolerance for non-American equipment, expanded domestic production and greater Canadian freedom of action. So is the Trump administration likely to applaud this as welcome burden-sharing — or see it as problematic?

Mark Cancian, a senior adviser in defence and security at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said he had not seen a U.S. government response to the strategy, but he predicted Washington would welcome much of it. Ottawa’s push for greater independence, however, could prove politically sensitive.
“(President Donald) Trump prefers acquiescence or acceptance rather than defiance,” he said. “I think that will be an irritant.”
If we went for a non-U.S. combat aircraft, that would create significant … tension

Cancian predicts Washington will appreciate the strategy’s call to hit five per cent of GDP defence spending by 2035. He also noted Carney’s increase to two per cent over the past year, calling it a “pretty substantial increase from where it was before.” Canada’s commitment to Norad and pledges to stop illegal guns, drugs and human smuggling will also be seen favourably, he believes, as will the fact that the strategy avoids discussion of China, particularly as a counterweight to the U.S.
“I think that’s very wise,” he said. “That’s a red line … for the administration.”
The seven references to “strategic autonomy,” however, could be a problem.
“We all know what that means or at least what the implication is,” Cancian said, explaining that it’s seen as “pulling away from the United States and being less dependent on the United States.”

Justin Massie, a politics professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal and co-director of The Network for Strategic Analysis, says it’s less about strategic autonomy and more about Canada “hedging its bets” — adding new partners and creating more opportunities without abandoning the American relationship.

stories.title: Canadians split on withholding public programs from non-permanent residents, poll finds
stories.summary: Responses to national poll closely mirror opinions expressed in Alberta referendum
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Canadians are split on whether they support withholding access to health care, education and other social services to certain non-permanent residents, closely mirroring the opinions expressed by Albertans in last month’s provincial referendum , according to a new poll.

The public opinion poll, conducted by Nanos Research for The Globe and Mail, also shows Canadians share similar levels of support for some of the other proposals that were on the referendum ballot, including abolishing the unelected Senate and requiring proof of citizenship when voting.

Nik Nanos, the company’s chief data scientist, said in an interview that the findings suggest it’s not just Albertans who are split on the issue of whether temporary foreign workers and asylum claimants should be allowed access to public health care and education.

“You’ll see many Canadians that agree with Albertans or have the same degree of divisions or lack of consensus on these issues,” Mr. Nanos said. “Generally, Albertans are not the outliers on this. They might have a different level of intensity, but they’re not outliers.”

The Nanos poll found that 46 per cent of Canadians either support or somewhat support withholding access to provincially funded programs such as health care and education from temporary foreign workers. On the flip side, 51 per cent said they somewhat or fully oppose the idea.

Support for the measure is highest in the Prairies (Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba). Support in Atlantic Canada, Ontario and Quebec ranges between 43 per cent and 48 per cent. In British Columbia, nearly 40 per cent of respondents said they would endorse withholding access.

The results are based on a poll of 1,058 Canadians from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2, with a 3-per-cent margin of error, and are considered accurate 19 times out of 20.

The poll question echoes three proposals that were on Alberta’s referendum ballot last month: limiting provincially funded services to certain non-permanent residents; requiring many of those individuals to live in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for publicly funded social supports; and charging temporary residents fees for health care and education.

In the end, Alberta voters narrowly endorsed the ideas, with support barely scraping past 50 per cent.

In the days after the referendum, Premier Danielle Smith – the architect and proponent of the proposals – said the results indicate she should “proceed with caution” before implementing them.

But the outcome has become part of a broader discussion about provinces having greater control over immigration, currently a shared federal-provincial responsibility.

Saskatchewan and Newfoundland have joined Alberta in asking Ottawa for more immigration powers. Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled openness to the idea, though it’s unclear how much territory he’s willing to cede.

Mr. Carney’s moderate approach to immigration since the record-high levels under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, has appeared to lower public opposition to the issue.

But the topic re-emerged after last week’s federal budget revealed plans to grant permanent residency to 200,000 temporary residents in Canada, in addition to the 380,000 spots previously allocated in 2026. The one-time measure could potentially raise total permanent-resident admissions in 2027 to more than 650,000 people.

Mr. Nanos said the findings in his poll underline how divisive politics around immigration have become – and how the issue is a political minefield.

“If you’re a politician that wants to play in this area – especially if it has to do with taking away provincially funded programs – you’ve got to be prepared to potentially be in the crossfire,” he said.

Christopher Worswick, an economics professor at Carleton University, said the poll question lacks details on how withholding services would play out – such as whether companies would be asked to pay health and education premiums for temporary workers they hire – which could affect how Canadians respond.

But the responses exhibit a reflexive negative opinion to immigration among a significant segment of Canadians, acknowledged Prof. Worswick, who studies immigration policy.

“I don’t think that was the feeling 10, 15 years ago in Canada,” he said.

The Nanos poll also asked about other issues on the Alberta ballot, including some constitutional amendments (all of which voters rejected) and whether proof of citizenship should be required to vote in elections.

Again, the responses to the national poll largely reflect the results in Alberta.

Sixty-one per cent of Canadians said they support requiring voters to supply proof of citizenship in provincial elections, only a few percentage points higher than the 58 per cent of Albertans who voted in favour of the idea.

On the matters of abolishing the Senate; allowing provinces to opt out of federal programs but still receive funding; giving provinces control over certain judicial appointments; and giving provincial law precedence over federal law, Canadians largely rejected the proposals, same as Albertans in the referendum.

stories.title: Time to deal with our waste problem
stories.summary: NIMBYism and woolly thinking are blocking the obvious solution
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
A combination of witless NIMBYism, blinkered environmentalism and political cowardice is making it next to impossible for Ontario to solve what should be a simple problem.

The province has been struggling for years to cope with its garbage. Its existing landfills are running out of space. They could be entirely full in less than a decade.

Ontario already exports 40 per cent of its commercial waste to Michigan and New York, an absurd thing for a sophisticated modern place to do. Now, trash tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump threaten to choke off that safety valve.

The solution is plain as day. Build more landfills and incinerators. Modern landfill sites have little, if any, impact on the environment. Special lining systems keep groundwater from being polluted. Gases emitted by decaying waste are burned to generate electricity. Once full, sites are carefully covered and sealed. Many become parks and nature reserves.

Modern incinerators use a complex of scrubbers, filters and chemical processes to purify their emissions. They, too, produce electricity for the power grid. Many parts of Europe and Asia rely on incineration to cope with their waste.

Despite all this technological progress, most of Ontario is allergic to both systems. Whenever a landfill or an incinerator is proposed, local residents and politicians take up their torches and pitchforks, acting as if nothing had changed since garbage was simply tipped into smelly dumps or set ablaze in a smoky old-school incinerator. Not in my backyard, they say.

Environmentalists, too, are locked in a time warp. Most oppose both solutions. They insist that more recycling is the answer, even though just about all Ontario communities already have extensive programs for the sorts of waste it makes sense to recycle. Recycling programs have even expanded since the provincial government started making companies pay for processing the stuff that goes in the blue box every week.

This is the situation Ontario Environment Minister Todd McCarthy finds himself in. Mr. McCarthy has been warning that with landfills filling and tariffs biting, Ontario has to do something decisive about its waste problem. He is surely right about that. But the government he represents, led by Progressive Conservative Premier Doug Ford , has fumbled the issue.

A few years ago, when rural communities were squawking about the deadly threat of having landfills built in their vicinity, the Ford government caved and gave them a veto over any such new projects. But now, Mr. McCarthy says Ontario must build more landfills or incinerators to avoid a trash crisis.

As part of its Building Ontario Faster Act, the government is proposing to accelerate approvals for both. It is also talking about removing, or at least weakening, the veto power.

Naturally, that has led to more squawking from environmentalists and politicians, both local and provincial. So Mr. McCarthy has been hedging and waffling.

Last month, he said that “municipalities will hold the pen on whether or not they want a landfill site, but there are benefits, obviously, economic benefits, to having a landfill site, an expansion to a landfill or energy from waste site in a community.”

This week he told Globe and Mail reporter Jeff Gray that he is willing to entertain changes – “tweaks,” as he called them – to the legislation getting rid of the local veto. Though “technically, that veto is being removed,” he said, “some consideration will be given to different alternatives.”

Seen through a political lens, his hesitation is understandable. The last thing the PC government wants is a battle with the cities and towns in Ontario’s heartland that form the bedrock of its support. But Mr. McCarthy was on the right path when he started warning about the fix the province is in.

It was bad even before Mr. Trump got involved, but at least his tariffs underline how ridiculous it is for Ontario to export its garbage.

We need to find a better way. We have the space, plenty of it – in empty gravel pits, in underused farmland, in old industrial sites. We have the technology. Landfill and incineration systems are getting cleaner and more efficient every year.

Let’s not let woolly-headed thinking and silly quarrels stand in the way.

Mr. McCarthy has been warning that with landfills filling and tariffs biting, Ontario has to do something decisive about its waste problem. He is surely right about that. But the government he represents, led by Progressive Conservative Premier Doug Ford , has fumbled the issue.

A few years ago, when rural communities were squawking about the deadly threat of having landfills built in their vicinity, the Ford government caved and gave them a veto over any such new projects. But now, Mr. McCarthy says Ontario must build more landfills or incinerators to avoid a trash crisis.
As part of its Building Ontario Faster Act, the government is proposing to accelerate approvals for both. It is also talking about removing, or at least weakening, the veto power.
Naturally, that has led to more squawking from environmentalists and politicians, both local and provincial. So Mr. McCarthy has been hedging and waffling.

Last month, he said that “municipalities will hold the pen on whether or not they want a landfill site, but there are benefits, obviously, economic benefits, to having a landfill site, an expansion to a landfill or energy from waste site in a community.”

This week he told Globe and Mail reporter Jeff Gray that he is willing to entertain changes – “tweaks,” as he called them – to the legislation getting rid of the local veto. Though “technically, that veto is being removed,” he said, “some consideration will be given to different alternatives.”

Seen through a political lens, his hesitation is understandable. The last thing the PC government wants is a battle with the cities and towns in Ontario’s heartland that form the bedrock of its support. But Mr. McCarthy was on the right path when he started warning about the fix the province is in.
It was bad even before Mr. Trump got involved, but at least his tariffs underline how ridiculous it is for Ontario to export its garbage.

We need to find a better way. We have the space, plenty of it – in empty gravel pits, in underused farmland, in old industrial sites. We have the technology. Landfill and incineration systems are getting cleaner and more efficient every year.
Let’s not let woolly-headed thinking and silly quarrels stand in the way.

stories.title: "A positive step" — National Council of Canadian Muslims hopeful after Jays meeting
stories.summary: Toronto - A National Council of Canadian Muslims spokesman said he was feeling hopeful after an initial meeting with the Toronto Blue Jays this week in the wake of the Anthony Santander controversy.
stories.author: Gregory Strong The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A National Council of Canadian Muslims spokesman said he was feeling hopeful after an initial meeting with the Toronto Blue Jays this week in the wake of the Anthony Santander controversy.

Santander shared anti-Muslim posts on Nov. 4 in the aftermath of last week’s U.S. midterm elections and deleted them the next morning.

Steven Zhou, media and communications lead for the Nccm, said the meeting between Blue Jays brass and members of the Muslim community was an important step in trying to turn a negative into a positive.

“I feel more strongly about that now,” Zhou said. “Now that we’ve had a first meeting, we’ve gotten on the same page about why this kind of narrative is not just annoying and upsetting. It poses real dangers in a place like Canada.”

Santander apologized on Friday afternoon, saying the content caused hurt and fell short of his own convictions.

The Blue Jays are the only MLB team in Canada, which has a population of over 1.78 million Muslims, per 2021 census data from Statistics Canada. About 10 per cent of Toronto’s 2.8 million residents identify as Muslim, the agency said.

Santander’s statement came a day after Blue Jays president and chief executive officer Mark Shapiro apologized to the Muslim community and fans following the meeting with community leaders. General manager Ross Atkins said earlier in the week that he asked Santander to publicly address the controversy.

“The Blue Jays’ apology (and) explicit condemnation of Islamophobia and engagement with Muslim community leaders are a good start,” said Morgan McLellan, a managing partner at Sovereign, a Toronto-based strategic, financial and crisis communications advisory firm. “But that clarity should have come immediately.

“After more than a week of backlash, the response looks reactive, driven by mounting pressure rather than a clear commitment to the values the club says it represents.”

In his statement, Santander said reflection and conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful about what he shared and the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.

He expressed respect for the Muslim community and pledged to avoid sharing content that promotes hate.

The posts included a video of a Christian preacher disparaging Muslims and another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the United States after Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the Senate in Michigan.

“There’s no need to perpetuate those dangerous narratives, especially if you’re a public figure,” Zhou said. “There’s just no need for that. And if that does happen, then it’s our job to follow up, to denounce it, to call for denunciations and to work from there.”

It wasn’t clear why Santander, a 32-year-old Venezuelan who signed a US$92.5-million, five-year contract with Toronto in January 2025, waited over a week to apologize.

Messages left in recent days with him and the sports management agency that represents him were not returned.

Santander missed the entire 2026 season because of injuries. He hit 44 homers for the Baltimore Orioles in 2024 but hit just .175 with six homers over 54 games in an injury-plagued 2025 season with Toronto.

He’s expected to be healthy for the 2027 season and become an everyday player again.

It remains unclear whether the team will discipline him over the posts. There are also unanswered questions about how potential social media policy and morality clause contract violations might be handled by the team or club owner Rogers Communications Inc.

Messages left with the team and Rogers on those subjects were not returned.

“With no discipline publicly announced, the Blue Jays and Rogers also leave an obvious question unanswered: what does accountability look like?” McLellan said. “If the organization says this behaviour violates its values, fans deserve to understand what consequences follow.”

Spring training is scheduled to begin in February, but there is a strong possibility an MLB lockout will begin next month when the current collective bargaining agreement expires.

In the meantime, Zhou said the meeting was a “positive step in the right direction.”

“There’s only more opportunities going forward and we’ll be actively seeking those out,” he said. “And I think there’s good reason to think that there will be a positive engagement and response on that.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: 'A terrible mistake': B.C. Isis bride Kimberley Polman, in her own words
stories.summary: Vancouver - In 2015, Kimberly Polman was unemployed and living in low-income housing in British Columbia when she made a life-changing decision — she would move to war-torn Syria and join her husband in the Islamic State terrorist organization.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press

Vancouver - In 2015, Kimberly Polman was unemployed and living in low-income housing in British Columbia when she made a life-changing decision — she would move to war-torn Syria and join her husband in the Islamic State terrorist organization.

It was, she said later, a “terrible mistake.”

Polman’s story — her regrets, the circumstances of her fateful decision, and her fear of retribution from the terror group — are laid out in their most complete form in a statement of facts in her terrorism case.

The signed statement includes a handwritten two-page letter from Polman composed in the Roj refugee camp in Syria after her capture by U.S.-backed forces, as well as two pages of her handwritten notes.

It was obtained by The Canadian Press after Polman pleaded guilty last month to leaving Canada to participate in activities of a terrorist group.

She has not been sentenced.

Polman said in her letter, in which she begged to be allowed to return to Canada, that she “came to Isis believing I could help women and children” as a nurse.

It was a mistake, “which I regret constantly and will for the rest of my life,” she wrote in the letter, dated April 3, 2019.

“Immediately I was thrown into a world of intense fear, unable to leave. My desire to help turned into my own need for help.”

The statement of facts does not explain how authorities obtained the letter, which Polman starts by saying “Dear Canadians.”

But her situation had been highlighted by media reports and interviews she gave in the camp.

In the letter, she asserted she was not a threat and had no history of violence. She said she needed to return to Canada for protection, saying she had “spoken out against Isis.”

“I’m a traitor to them, someone who has betrayed Islam and must be killed, also because I left — something I had been trying to do for 3.5 years.”

Polman, who had converted to Islam in 2003, asked Canadians to “put away the paintbrush that has the world viewing every woman who was within Isis the same.”

“We’re not,” she said. “Under Isis I held openly to my understanding of Islam, which often contradicted theirs. I would come to know imprisonment, torture, rape and sometimes I lost hope that I’d ever get out alive. Bombings, dronings (sic), disease, famine, death were my daily life.”

She said she was “an innocent woman” who simply wanted to “help those in need.”

“The truth is I ended up with bad people, finally escaped and now need to return home, to Canada. Please, I survived Isis. Now I want to live as I am — a Canadian.”

But the statement of facts paints a more nuanced story.

Polman, it said, had converted to Islam in 2003. About a decade later, she began researching Islamic extremist ideology and began communicating with people who held those beliefs.

In 2014, she met a Kenyan man of Somali descent named Suhayb Muhammad Adan and “entered into a marriage” with him that summer.

They continued corresponding online and by July 2015, she had formulated a plan to “leave Canada and emigrate to Syria to join her husband and the Islamic State,” the document said.

It said data obtained from her computer revealed she was aware the Islamic State was a terrorist entity at the time, that Syria was an active war zone and that she could be arrested for attempting to leave Canada to join the group.

She was also aware Adan was an Isis fighter.

In July 2015, Polman, a dual Canadian-U. S. citizen with two adult children in Canada, went to a Flight Centre in Surrey, B.C., and booked return flights to Vienna, Austria.

From there she continued to Turkey to meet Adan.

She would never use the return tickets.

From ‘safe houses’ to syria

The statement offers insights into the mindset of Polman, who had a learning disability, including her goal of gaining work experience with Isis that she hoped could help her pursue a career in nursing.

While in Austria, she stayed with a longtime friend, an American lawyer based in Vienna.

She told him she had married a Somali man living in Syria and she was going to Turkey to join him, and she “wanted to become a nurse in Syria to help women and children there.”

They discussed how she had struggled to achieve her nursing aspirations in Canada because of a disability. ”(She) felt she would be able to obtain experience in Syria that simply would not be available to her in Canada.”

Her friend had attempted to dissuade her and suggested a divorce, but she told him she planned to leave after obtaining nursing experience. She also said she planned to take her husband to a “deradicalization camp” in Denmark.

Polman travelled to Turkey on July 25, 2015, before making her way toward the Syrian border, staying in Islamic State “safe houses” before the group smuggled her across into Syria.

“By August, Ms. Polman had arrived in (Islamic State) controlled territory in Syria. Upon arrival in Syria, Ms. Polman forfeited her U.S. passport to (the Islamic State),” the document said.

She would remain in Syria for about seven years.

Adan divorced her in January 2016 — within about six months of her arrival — before Polman went on to work in the Islamic State hospital in Raqqa, Syria, caring for infants and children until February.

Her time as a single woman did not last long. In October 2016 she married a Trinidadian Islamic State member named Safraz Ali, who “produced explosives and IEDs” for the group.

They would not remain in Raqqa for long — U.S.-backed forces declared the city’s liberation in October 2017, and the couple moved together to different towns in Syria as the group lost territory.

Polman was with Ali until she was captured by coalition forces on Jan. 27, 2019, just outside of the Baghouz, the last Isis stronghold in Syria.

Polman would remain in Syrian detention camps for almost four years. Less than three months after her capture, she wrote her “Dear Canadians” letter.

Global Affairs Canada agreed to repatriate Polman in October 2022, and she arrived in Montreal later that month, where she was arrested.

She was not the only Canadian woman arrested after marrying an Isis fighter and going to Syria.

They have included Oumaima Chouay, who returned to Canada at the same time as Polman, and pleaded guilty in July 2025 to one count of participating in the activities of a terrorist group. The Quebec woman received a one-day custodial sentence, in addition to her time in pretrial custody, as well as three-year probation order.

Chouay was also ordered to undergo “depolarization therapy.”

Polman’s trial had been scheduled to begin on Nov. 9, but the dates were vacated after she pleaded guilty in October.

A spokeswoman for the Public Prosecution Service of Canada said in an email Friday that dates for Polman’s sentencing hearing had not yet been scheduled, but she is set to appear in court next week.

In her letter, Polman distances herself from the Islamic State.

She depicted her capture in Baghouz as a dramatic escape, with Islamic State fighters firing on her, an orphan baby girl in her arms.

She did not want the Canadian way of life, “to ever be poisoned by Isis,” she wrote.

“The truth is I’m an innocent woman, a Canadian with a heart for children and a desire to help those in need,” Polman wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Carney says Canada will only sign a U.S. trade deal that includes viable auto sector
stories.summary: Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney says trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won't accept a deal that doesn't allow for a viable auto sector.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney says trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector.

“Lots of people think that we should just go and take whatever deal,” Carney said Saturday in Manila. “This government will not settle for a deal with the United States that is not consistent with a viable Canadian auto sector.”

stories.title: Carney says Canada will not waiver in Nato support, amid concerns over Ukraine talks
stories.summary: Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will not waiver in its support of Nato allies, as European leaders express concern at Russia seeking a reordering of continental security in negotiations with Ukraine.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Manila - Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will not waiver in its support of Nato allies, as European leaders express concern at Russia seeking a reordering of continental security in negotiations with Ukraine.

“There’s no way that Canada as a Nato member is going to walk away from any other Nato member — ever,” Carney said at a news conference Saturday in Manila.

His comments come amid talks brokered by the U.S. between Russia and Ukraine, aimed at ending Moscow’s incursions into Ukraine in 2014 which expanded into a full-scale invasion in 2022.

American and Russian negotiators have widened the discussions around borders and prisoners to include wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War, in particular how Nato functions.

That has raised fears of pressure to soften the alliance’s stance that it will protect any Nato country that is attacked, including those which border Russia.

Carney said Saturday that Canada wants “more stable outcomes” than repeating historical missteps that involved trying to limit Russian expansionism without adequate deterrence. He cited steps taken in the 1940s, the Minsk agreements, and the French policy of cordon sanitaire.

“The security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and Nato, not by Russia and a redux of the Minsk agreement,” Carney said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is set to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit in Shenzhen, China next week, as will Carney.

The prime minister said he will not boycott the traditional “family photo” of leaders at the summit. “I will participate in the photos, out of respect for the host,” Carney said.

In contrast, last month Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said she would have boycotted a photo at a G20 meeting that included her Russian counterpart in Atlanta, as European peers had done.

Anand said that in any case, she arrived at that meeting after the photo was set to occur. The American hosts ended up cancelling the photo.

Carney said Saturday that Canada’s stance on Russia has been clearly demonstrated through its sanctions policies and a recent announcement of banning athletes competing under the flags of Russia or Belarus at sporting events in Canada.

“Canada stands firmly with Ukraine, firmly with democracy, territorial integrity, rule of law — and all of those put us on the other side of Vladimir Putin’s Russia,” he said.

Moscow has rejected numerous statements and framings from Ottawa, arguing Canada is not serious about dialogue with Russia.

stories.title: Ontario ‘Crypto King’ testifies kidnappers made him kneel for a mock execution — ‘Scared I was going to die’
stories.summary: "You're either going to pay with your money, or you're going to pay with your life."
stories.author: Betsy Powell
stories.content:
Aiden Pleterski , once known as the “Crypto King,” told a packed Toronto courtroom Friday that he was repeatedly beaten and threatened over three days in December 2022 by men demanding millions of dollars in ransom.

“Very scared. Scared I was going to die. Survival mode, essentially,” Pleterski testified after recounting how two gun-wielding men ordered him to kneel in a field while one counted down from 10 and discharged a bullet close to his head.

He was testifying at the trial of Akil Heywood, 42, Rakeem Henry, 26, and Alfredo Paladino, 26, who have all pleaded not guilty to kidnapping and extortion charges. Henry and Paladino also face firearm and assault-related charges.

Pleterski operated a cryptocurrency investment business that attracted substantial sums from investors drawn to the lavish lifestyle he showcased on social media. But by late 2021 he had fallen behind on payments to investors, and by mid-2022 he had filed for bankruptcy protection.

A video taken during the kidnapping, in which Deren Akyeam-Pong fires a gun beside Aiden Pleterski's head.

According to Pleterski, tensions escalated with Akil Heywood, who gave him between $300,000 and $400,000 to invest and was an inspector in the bankruptcy proceedings. Heywood, he said, made threats by text and telephone, including once telling him: “Pay me my money or else. The streets don’t forget.”

Another time, in a downtown nightclub, Heywood pulled him close by wrapping his arm around his neck, Pleterski said, demonstrating the move. Heywood then told him, “I have a stick on me,” which Pleterski assumed was a gun, he testified.

On the night of Dec. 6, 2022, Pleterski said a man he knew as “Slime” — who had pretended to want help with cryptocurrency conversion — lured him to a black Dodge Ram pickup truck parked downtown near a friend’s condo. (Slime is Derek Akyeam-Pong, who is not on trial.) Once seated in the back, he said Slime and Henry, whom he knew as Racks, started pummeling him with their fists and guns. Behind the wheel was Paladino, or “Fredo,” he said, whom he identified in court sitting behind his lawyer.

‘I wouldn’t be calling you begging you for money right now at one o’clock in the morning if it

After they peeled out, a phone call was put on speaker. The call display said “OVO Akil” and “immediately, I knew instantly it was ... Akil Heywood,” Pleterski testified.

Heywood was someone he had known for about two years and had “spoken to him hundreds of times. He said the man’s voice told him, “You’re either going to pay with your money, or you’re going to pay with your life.”

Wearing the grey suit he wore throughout his recent fraud trial, Pleterski recounted the ordeal in a flat, monotone voice, his expression changing little as he described being punched, burned with cigarettes, pistol-whipped, cut with a saw and waterboarded.

It felt “like I was drowning,” he said, describing lying across the back of the pickup truck as his captors doused his towel-covered head with water, which he felt “in my lungs.” The torture stopped, he said, when they ran out of water.

Aiden Pleterski, bottom left, at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel on Dec. 2, 2022 — a few days before the alleged kidnapping — with Rakeem Henry, top left, Deren Akyeam-Pong, bottom right, and another man who was not charged.

Pleterski identified men alleged to be the accused in numerous surveillance videos, still images and intercepted calls. Jurors also watched the infamous “forced confession” video, which surfaced on social media months after his release. Wearing a burgundy Harvard hoodie, with a swollen face, cuts, a black eye and a visibly misaligned jaw, Pleterski followed along with a transcript as it played, telling the court it was “kinda hard to look at.”

In the video, he apologizes to investors for losing “close to $45 million” and accepts full responsibility.

The 27-year-old said he told his captors many lies as he was desperately trying to defuse the situation, at times wearing reusable grocery bags over his head, his hands zip-tied together. That included telling the men that his wealthy landlord, Sandeep Gupta, was hiding some of his money and would step up and help. Gupta put Pleterski’s call through to 911, which played in court earlier this week.

Pleterski recalled one of the most vivid moments of the ordeal as his captors moved him from Hamilton to Pickering. Led into the basement of a home with a shopping bag over his head, he heard a radio crackling with static as Bon Jovi’s “Wanted Dead or Alive” played in the background.

Before testifying Friday, Pleterski read a statement stating that under the Canada Evidence Act, nothing he said on the stand can be used against him in any criminal or bankruptcy proceedings. Earlier, he appeared in a different courtroom to set a date for sentencing. Unlike at his fraud trial, when he was self-represented, Pleterski appeared alongside defence lawyer Marco Sciarra.

The trial resumes Monday when Pleterski will continue to testify “in chief.” After that, he will be cross-examined by defence lawyers.

stories.title: Secret lobbyist texts raise questions about the origin of the Ford government’s controversial Oakville highrise plan
stories.summary: The text exchange, involving a senior political staffer in Premier Doug Ford’s government and the man given the moniker “Mr. X” for his involvement in the Greenbelt scandal, raise questions about the origin of the province’s involvement with the midtown development.
stories.author: Sheila Wang
stories.content:
Between invitations to a Toronto Raptors game and a round of golf at one of Canada’s most exclusive courses, the lobbyist floated an idea to the Ford government staffer on a land development poised to reshape the Oakville skyline.

In a WhatsApp conversation in September 2022, John Mutton messaged the deputy chief of staff to Ontario’s housing minister about the province assigning a special designation to facilitate the development.

The private exchange took place more than a year and a half before the town was blindsided by the Ontario government’s decision to intervene on the project.

In designating the area as a Transit-Oriented Community (TOC), the province overrode Oakville’s vision for the land with a thicket of highrises that town staff have warned will provide “very little to no community benefit.”

Now, the revelation of the back-channel conversation has ignited the anger of local opponents to the controversial project who say the text exchange signals that the plans were on the government’s radar well before they were shared publicly.

“We lost almost two years of time where the residents could have been vocal about it, instead of being surprised when the TOC was announced,” said Michael Reid, president of the Oakville Community Association.

It has also renewed questions about why the province decided to champion a developer’s plan over the town’s.

“It bothers me greatly,” said Oakville Councillor Janet Haslett-Theall. “Respect for the individuals that the public elected was not there.”

Mutton is most recognizable by the moniker “ Mr. X, ” a pseudonym assigned to him in 2023 by the integrity commissioner for his role in the Greenbelt land swap scandal , in which Premier Doug Ford’s government was found to have given preferential treatment to certain developers with close ties to the Progressive Conservatives.

The Oakville TOC, which has not yet broken ground, calls for 11 condo towers with a daycare and Ymca stuffed into an area roughly the size of the Rogers Centre. The TOC designation allows for higher density near the Oakville GO train station, and the province deployed minister’s zoning orders (MZOs) to fast-track the project. The MZOs cannot be appealed.

The project has faced intense pushback from resident groups who allege it will benefit the developer , Distrikt Developments, at the public’s expense.

Emil Toma, president of Distrikt, said the company made public zoning applications on the sites to the town “well in advance of the province advising its interest in selecting the area” for a TOC.

“While we have not been privy to all discussions between the Province and the Town, we do know the process was lengthy and thorough,” Toma said.

Infrastructure Ontario (IO), the agency that manages the province’s TOC program, had no role in the Oakville GO TOC development prior to June 2023, a spokesperson told the Star.

“IO conducts TOC-related development discussions in accordance with conflict-of-interest policies and established oversight and approval processes,” said Brian Buchan, adding that the agency held public engagement sessions and solicited public feedback in its planning process.

A transcript of the WhatsApp conversation between Mutton and Kirstin Jensen, then deputy chief of staff to the minister of municipal affairs and housing, is contained in a 2025 report by the integrity commissioner into Mutton’s unregistered lobbying on behalf of developers.

This version of the report was not publicly released. The Star obtained a copy from Mutton, who said he wanted “truth to be told” about the Greenbelt land swap scandal, in which he says he was made a fall guy while major players weren’t held responsible. The report was first reported by The Trillium.

The integrity commissioner banned Mutton from lobbying the provincial government until April 2027 for his repeated and “serious” violations of lobbying rules.

In the 2022 WhatsApp exchange, Mutton invited Jensen to make use of his season’s tickets to the Raptors, telling her to “pick a game and you can come with me or take a friend.” Mutton then pivoted to business. He explained that he was “PM ing” [project managing] for Distrikt in Oakville on matters of the parkland cash-in-lieu and transit-oriented communities, and wanted a “brief convo” about which direction “May be quickest.”

Jensen told Mutton that the Distrikt matter was “not going to be a quick solution” and “has to be a province wide solution.”

Mutton told the Star that his conversation with Jensen about the Oakville land took place at the time when he was looking to project manage Distrikt’s land in Midtown Oakville with the goal to eventually work as a lobbyist for the project.

Jensen, who is currently working at the Ontario Home Builders’ Association, did not respond to the Star’s questions.

Mutton also provided copies of emails to the Star that showed Distrikt approached another client of Mutton’s who owned land in the same neighbourhood, in an attempt to band together to “preserve development land value” and “intensification potential.”

Developer Emil Toma says his company Distrikt Developments is qualified to help build the transit-oriented community.

Emails in August 2022 show Distrikt invited Mutton’s client to join them in lobbying the province to “immediately give attention to designating Midtown GO Node as a TOC” by way of an MZO. Distrikt was also planning to meet with Metrolinx to discuss the plan and “align on objectives supporting intensification.”

A Metrolinx spokesperson said the agency’s engagement with Distrikt “has been limited to standard adjacent development and safety related reviews and engagement as part of Town-led Midtown Oakville meetings.” Metrolinx took part in no subsequent meetings with Distrikt related to the TOC.

Mutton told the Star that shortly after he chatted with Jensen about the TOC status, he parted ways with Distrikt over “competing objectives” with his other client. He was never paid or formally retained by Distrikt, he added.

Toma told the Star that Distrikt was introduced to Mutton by another landowner in the area, and his company never had any relationship with him. “Any insinuation that a relationship exists here is factually incorrect,” he said.

When the Ford government picked Distrikt’s land for the TOC development, Toma and his partners were struggling to pay back a loan for a Toronto apartment development that eventually fell into receivership.

By that time, Distrikt had hired the former chief of staff of Mayor Rob Ford, the premier’s late brother, to advocate for its Oakville development, according to the lobbyist registry. The firm had assembled more land in the area and co-owned one parcel with developer Christopher Bratty, a personal friend of Doug Ford who attended the premier’s daughter’s wedding.

Oakville Coun. Janet Haslett-Theall was among those who say they were blindsided by the Ontario government’s decision to intervene in the highrise development.

According to Mutton, Rob Burton, who was Oakville mayor at the time, first suggested pitching the TOC status for Distrikt’s land.

“He initiated it,” Mutton told the Star. “He wanted to have the first giant towers around the transit system in Oakville. I think he thought that that was going to be a legacy for the future.”

For years, Burton faced criticism for what residents allege were mixed signals about his position on the TOC.

Burton strenuously denied he ever initiated the TOC idea for Distrikt’s land. He said that he voted against the TOC, and for Oakville’s own plan, “every time it came before council.”

The former mayor called Mutton’s characterization “bull- - - -” and questioned why the Star was spreading “the lies of a liar.” He recalled meeting Mutton once but said he never spoke with him.

Mutton fired back: “The former mayor definitely has a credibility gap… Perhaps that’s why the residents of Oakville sent him packing.”

After five consecutive terms in office, Burton was unseated in October by Jeff Knoll, whose campaign included a promise to stand up to the province’s midtown development.

stories.title: Family appeals for help finding missing Penticton senior with dementia
stories.summary: The disappearance of 72-year-old Penticton resident Lawrence Jerry McAnulty, who goes by Jerry, is especially concerning as the senior has dementia.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A Penticton woman is pleading with the public to help look for her missing father.

“Check your cameras, check your sheds, just please keep eyes out everywhere,” said an emotional Carmen Gee.

The disappearance of 72-year-old Penticton resident Lawrence Jerry McAnulty , who goes by Jerry, is especially concerning as the senior has dementia.

“With him having dementia, so many possibilities are running through my mind and everyone else’s,” Gee said.

Gee, along with other family members, are now scouring Penticton’s downtown area, which McAnulty was known to frequent on foot.

They are putting up posters, talking to operators of businesses McAnulty frequently visited and asking people if they have seen the missing man.

Police say McAnulty was seen the morning of Oct. 23 on security video in the lobby of his apartment building, just a few blocks from downtown.

Gee says she got a text from her dad the next day but nothing since.

“I had gone a little bit of time without contacting, which was not abnormal,” she said. “We would always check in here and there.”

However, after a wellness check at his apartment earlier this week showed no sign of him, McAnulty was reported missing.

Searches for seniors with dementia are not that uncommon.

Officials with Central Okanagan Search and Rescue (Cosar) say they get called out 10 to 15 times a year and in some cases, people have been found a long distance away.

“We had one subject leave Cottonwoods and was found in McKinley Landing, almost 18 kilometres away, ” said Ed Henczel, Cosar’s search manager. “They are just like toddlers when they want to get going; they can go pretty fast.”

Gee is appealing to people on the outskirts of the city to also keep their eyes and ears open.

She says she’s not ruling out her dad potentially heading north to Oyama in Lake Country or Vernon, where he has deep roots.

Henczel says regular check-ins and tracking devices are important, especially at this time of year when the weather turns cold.

“If you could, you know, put on an AirTag on a piece of clothing or something or buy grandpa an iPhone that you can track,” Henczel said.

In McNulty’s case, numerous requests to ping his cell phone’s location have been unsuccessful.

Penticton RCMP say McNaulty has white hair and beard.

His family says he May be wearing a blue toque.

RCMP are urging anyone who May know of his whereabouts to contact them.

Gee says any sightings or information can also be directly sent to her at 250-551-7551.

stories.title: Flights resume in U.S. after hours-long nationwide ground stop halts travel
stories.summary: All commercial flights were grounded for more than four hours, throwing the air travel system in the U.S. into chaos.
stories.author: Bruce Arthur
stories.content:
Philadelphia — Plane departures across the U.S. were allowed to resume Friday night after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop due to “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

All commercial flights were grounded for more than four hours, throwing the nation’s air travel system into chaos in one of the most significant disruptions since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

The initial FAA notice at just before 4 p.m. announcing the ground stop said it was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” An estimated 3,500 planes already in the air were ordered to land at the nearest available airport.

There was widespread confusion over the cause of the outage. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin initially said there were no indications it was the result of a “nefarious attack,” but did not immediately rule out a cyberattack, or a malfunction in the AI system that had been integrated into key FAA systems earlier this week.

The U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there are no indications of an attack against the nation, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon due to communications problems. (Nov. 13, 2026)

“There’s nothing completely certain right now,” Mullin said, adding there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that it appears to be “mechanically driven,” adding that officials were still looking for the cause.

U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy speaks as U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin listens during a press conference at the White House on Friday night.

In a press conference shortly after the ground stop was lifted just before 8:20 p.m., Mullin and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the outage on an antiquated air traffic control system. Mullin said the introduction of new technology overwhelmed it. The system needs funding for a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag and blaming Congress for not providing the money.

“I don’t want to rule out that we didn’t have nefarious activity here,” said Duffy.

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like, by the organization and the team he’s put together. We are built to handle crisis like this,” said Mullin.

“It was an old legacy equipment,” said Duffy. “It failed, and listen, it’s going to continue to fail. But my number one job is America’s safety.”

Duffy did say the outage was caused by an overload of the time delay multiplexing, or TDM copper-wire system, which underpins the American air traffic control system and carries both radar signals and voice information from air traffic control to pilots. Duffy did not say why the system overloaded.

“We’re still working on the details of what went wrong today,” said Duffy. “I’ll be happy to give you more information when we have it.”

Across America airplanes were stranded on tarmacs, airports ground to a halt, and travellers scrambled to rent cars and trains, book hotels, and rebook travel without any clarity on when the system might resume. CNN reported some airports neared saturation points on tarmacs and runways, with too many planes and not enough space. According to flight trackers, some international flights to Europe, Asia, and Hawaii were being allowed to leave from airports on both coasts.

Passengers make calls in front a flight departure board as planes are placed on hold at Philadelphia International Airport on Friday.

This ground stop extended widely, and the chaos spread. The New York Times reported that the FAA asked its European counterpart to suspend flights from 42 European nations. Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST, raising the likelihood of more cancellations and flight diversions.

The American air traffic control system operates on antiquated computer systems. The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fibre optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country. Earlier this year, the FAA fledged to eliminate floppy discs from the air control system by 2028.

The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. (Nov. 13, 2026)

Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it. In the press conference Friday night, he repeatedly asked for $50 billion.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale.

Three days before Friday’s ground stop, the FAA said an AI tool called Smart AI was being integrated into the air traffic control system. In September, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents some 15,000 members nationwide, told Flying magazine it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of Smart and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”

Air Space Intelligence, the company responsible for the Smart AI tool, wrote on X, “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the Smart system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and (Air Traffic Control).”

Both administration officials denied AI caused the outage, but Mullin said, “What it appears to be right now is ... (the) FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology was overwhelming the older system.” Mullin did not specify what technology he was referring to.

Air Canada announced it was cancelling Canadian flights to and from the United States, and said that flights to international destinations that were scheduled to pass through American airspace might be affected. Some flights destined for American destinations were expected to be rerouted to Canadian airports.

“Canada has offered its full assistance to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as it manages the situation, including accommodation of US-bound aircraft as required,” wrote Minister of Transportation Steven MacKinnon in a statement posted on X. “We remain ready to provide support to our American colleagues as the situation evolves.”

Canadian airline systems were not affected although flights to and from the U.S. out of Toronto’s Pearson airport were suspended before also resuming Friday night.

“NAV Canada is aware of the FAA ground stop and is monitoring the situation,” said the air navigation service provider in a statement. “Our systems are operating normally, and there is currently no impact to NAV Canada operations. Safety remains our top priority. NAV Canada continues to support the safe movement of air traffic within our airspace, including any aircraft that May be diverted.”

“Questions regarding the ground stop, including its scope and operational implications, should be directed to the FAA.”
