Three days before Friday’s ground stop, the FAA said an AI tool called Smart AI was being integrated into the air traffic control system. In September, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents some 15,000 members nationwide, told Flying magazine it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of Smart and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”

Both administration officials denied AI caused the outage, but Mullin said, “What it appears to be right now is ... (the) FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology was overwhelming the older system.” Mullin did not specify what technology he was referring to.

Air Canada announced it was cancelling Canadian flights to and from the United States, and said that flights to international destinations that were scheduled to pass through American airspace might be affected. Some flights destined for American destinations were expected to be rerouted to Canadian airports.

“Canada has offered its full assistance to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as it manages the situation, including accommodation of US-bound aircraft as required,” wrote Minister of Transportation Steven MacKinnon in a statement posted on X. “We remain ready to provide support to our American colleagues as the situation evolves.”
Canadian airline systems were not affected although flights to and from the U.S. out of Toronto’s Pearson airport were suspended before also resuming Friday night.

“NAV Canada is aware of the FAA ground stop and is monitoring the situation,” said the air navigation service provider in a statement. “Our systems are operating normally, and there is currently no impact to NAV Canada operations. Safety remains our top priority. NAV Canada continues to support the safe movement of air traffic within our airspace, including any aircraft that May be diverted.”
“Questions regarding the ground stop, including its scope and operational implications, should be directed to the FAA.”

stories.title: Carney wraps up negotiations on trade deal with Philippines
stories.summary: Deal caps expansion of relations with a country that is playing an outsized role in Ottawa’s four-year-old Indo-Pacific strategy
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada has wrapped negotiations on a free trade agreement with the Philippines and has “substantially concluded” a second trade deal with the 11-member group of Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).

He made the announcements on Saturday during his first visit as Prime Minister to the Philippines, a country that is playing an outsized role in Canada’s Indo-Pacific strategy.

The deal to remove barriers to trade with the Philippines, along with the Asean agreement, would be the fourth and fifth trade deals that Mr. Carney’s government has wrapped up since taking office. Canada has been seeking to lessen its dependence on the increasingly protectionist and unpredictable United States under President Donald Trump.

The other deals are with Indonesia, the United Arab Emirates and Ecuador.

While Mr. Carney has issued many declarations of “strategic partnerships” and memorandums of understanding to deepen ties with countries around the globe, those documents do not carry binding obligations on both partners like free-trade deals do.

Free trade deals, backed up by implementing legislation in Parliament, set rules for the ways that economic partners remove restrictions to two-way trade and investment.

“We are developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities for our business and more choice for Canadians, while reducing our reliance on the United States,” the Prime Minister said.

Major powers will join a summit next week of Southeast Asian nations hosted by the Philippines against one of the most complex backdrops for the regional bloc, from the Iran war that has batter…

Mr. Carney said the trade deal with the Philippines will be good for Canadian farmers, ranchers, and food producers as well as businesses and workers in forest products, mining, and energy.

He said this agreement will give Canada a competitive advantage in the Philippines market, saying two-way trade “between our countries expected to triple by 2035 – to more than $10 billion a year.”

Despite Mr. Carney’s efforts, it will be difficult to substitute trade with other countries for exports to the U.S., which totalled more than $560-billion in merchandise goods in 2025. That’s more than 70 per cent of Canada’s goods exports.

Canadian merchandise exports to the Philippines in 2025 amounted to $1.1 billion.

The Ottawa-Manila deal caps a remarkable expansion of relations between Canada and the Philippines, a strategically located country that has playing an outsized role in Ottawa’s four-year-old Indo-Pacific strategy.

In recent years, Canada’s embassy in Manila has quietly grown into one of this country’s biggest worldwide. It’s now No. 2 globally when measured by the number of people, according to Global Affairs Canada.

It does not appear the concluded trade deal, which still must be signed by both countries, will give Canada an exemption from a temporary ban on foreign pork imports being erected by Manila this month.

The Philippines is set to enact a 60-day suspension of imports starting later in November after pressure from domestic producers — one that could potentially be extended. Manila is also planning to hike tariffs on foreign pork.

Kyle Larkin, president and CEO of the Canadian Meat Council, said Saturday his understanding of the Canada-Philippines trade deal is there is no carveout from the import ban for Canada.

But he said he remains hopeful this trade deal will enable Canadian pork to be spared from higher tariffs that the Philippines appears to be planning to impose. “Countries without a free trade agreement are likely to see higher tariff rates.”

Philippines’ tariffs on various type of Canadian pork imports range from 15 per cent to 20 per cent, Mr. Larkin said.

In 2025, Canada exported $229-million of pork products to the Philippines. Mr. Larkin said Saturday’s deal presents an opportunity to deepen trade there.

Mr. Carney, meeting with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., compared leadership in today’s world to navigating a ship in troubled times. He said ships aren’t meant to remain in safe harbours. “It takes a leader to take the ship out of the harbour into choppy waters.”

The Prime Minister said by negotiating a deal to lower trade barriers, Canada and the Philippines are setting an example “for other countries around the world of what is possible when like-minded countries come together.”

The Philippines sits at the edge of some of Asia’s most contested waters, and it has clashed repeatedly with Beijing over competing claims to reefs and shoals in the South China Sea. Its northernmost islands border a vital gateway between those waters and the open Pacific.

Both countries committed to signing the Canada-Philippines trade deal in 2027.

In recent years, Canada’s diplomatic mission in Manila has quietly grown into one of this country’s biggest, with 300 positions. It’s now No. 2 globally when measured by the number of people, according to Global Affairs Canada. This includes locally hired staff and officials from various federal departments, as well as from provincial governments and Crown corporations such as Export Development Canada, which opened an office there in 2024.

Only Canada’s diplomatic mission in Washington is bigger than Manila when it comes to the number of people, figures from Global Affairs show. Canada’s next three largest footprints are in London, Mexico City and New Delhi.

One of the earliest examples of growing Canada-Philippines co-operation under this strategy has been Ottawa sharing satellite data from its Dark Vessel Detection program to help Manila identify illegal fishing craft plying its waters. The data also gives Manila a helping hand in territorial disputes with China.

The Manila embassy has become a hub for Canadian government outreach and operations in the Indo-Pacific region. In 2024, the government opened the Indo-Pacific Agriculture and Agri-Food Office at the embassy to promote Canada’s food exports.

The Immigration Department’s operations in Manila handles immigration and visa matters not only for the Philippines, but also for other nations. The Philippines is among Canada’s largest source of immigrants to Canada, with close to one million people in Canada claiming Filipino ancestry.

Canada and the Philippines have grown closer on the security and defence front, too. This year, Canada appointed a general to represent Ottawa’s security interests in the region: Lieutenant-General Derek Macaulay, the country’s first senior military representative for the Indo-Pacific.

The new post makes him the Chief of the Defence Staff’s envoy to the region’s military leaders. His job is to build relationships from Tokyo to Hanoi to Kuala Lumpur, and to make sure the Canadian Armed Forces’ activities line up with Ottawa’s priorities in the region.

stories.title: Former UBC arts dean testifies about his role in Galloway removal
stories.summary: Gage Averill is the first university decision-maker to appear as a witness in defamation lawsuit launched by author Steven Galloway
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
A handful of University of British Columbia administrators took the unprecedented step in 2015 to publicly announce Steven Galloway’s removal as creative writing program chair because sexual assault allegations against him were spreading at the school and among the public, the former dean of arts, Gage Averill, testified Friday.

Mr. Averill, now Ubc’s provost and vice-president, academic at the institution, is the first and only major decision-maker from the university to testify in the trial more than a decade in the making. But, he told the court, he was travelling as the crisis unfolded and had only a small role in creating the document that he signed and sent out into the world.

Mr. Galloway, who was the chair of Ubc’s creative writing program, launched a lawsuit against almost two dozen defendants in 2018. He claims in this trial that the sexual assault allegations of a woman known only as A.B., because of a trial publication ban – and their repetition online by three other women – ruined his reputation , cost him his job and destroyed his personal life.

Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime but was fired in June 2016.

Mr. Averill testified he was flying to Ottawa when a creative writing faculty member contacted him the Sunday night before the statement went out. They alerted him to the emergency off-campus meeting of colleagues that had just occurred to discuss the allegation against Mr. Galloway.

While on the stand, Mr. Averill was read an e-mail from Annabel Lyon, another creative writing professor: “Our first priority and primary concern is that Steve take a leave immediately so the students will feel the department is a safe environment.”

More than half a dozen UBC administrators worked together to craft the November 2015 statement announcing the suspension of the CanLit star and chair of the creative writing program, which, Mr. Averill testified Friday in provincial Supreme Court, was edited to remove any mention of sexual violence at the behest of the school’s privacy expert.

Still, the university’s online statement noting “serious allegations” against Mr. Galloway made international headlines amid the nascent #MeToo era, with the court hearing Friday how a small group tried and failed to contain a growing public relations nightmare.

Over the next three days, a group of administrators including Mr. Averill exchanged e-mails detailing how to reassure these professors and their students that the university was taking the allegations seriously as well as respecting Mr. Galloway’s privacy rights, the court heard.

Mr. Averill testified he remembered talking to A.B. before the university went public with its suspension of Mr. Galloway, but he said he did not recall whether he discussed the school’s upcoming statement nor if he supplied her a draft.

A.B.’s lawyer Sydney Gomez asked Mr. Averill, who had to be subpoenaed to testify, whether he had ever seen another suspension be announced so publicly during his long tenure at the university.

“I don’t think so,” he replied.

In other parts of his testimony he noted administrators believed at the time that Mr. Galloway’s accuser would go public with the allegations on social media, which also led the school to go “further than we usually do addressing that to make sure that people understood an impartial investigation would be pursued.”

Mr. Averill told the court that four days after the school published Mr. Galloway’s suspension letter, he and his colleagues discussed deleting it from the internet because the professor’s union was incensed.

He agreed with the assertion from Daniel Burnett, a lawyer for Mr. Galloway, that “there was considerable concern expressed by the Faculty Association for Mr. Galloway’s privacy.”

A.B. is not testifying and, at the start of the trial, one of her lawyers told the court that she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment – but denies the accusations that she spread lies about Mr. Galloway, with whom she had a two-year affair. Her lawyers have told the court that she tried to kill herself twice because of the stress of the ordeal.

Soon after Mr. Galloway’s suspension, UBC hired former Supreme Court justice Mary Ellen Boyd to investigate A.B.’s allegations. In 2016 Ms. Boyd found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault, but that he had sexually harassed her and committed other misconduct.

Before Mr. Averill took the stand Friday afternoon, the lawyers for Mr. Galloway and A.B. argued in the morning over whether he could be asked about other issues that May have played into Ubc’s decision to suspend the bestselling author and put out their official statement.

Ms. Gomez, A.B.’s lawyer, argued that Mr. Galloway bears the burden of proving A.B.’s allegation was the legal cause of UBC publishing the statement about his suspension.

Justice Neena Sharma ruled against eliciting testimony from Mr. Averill, which narrowed the scope of the evidence he provided the court.

The testimony has now wrapped, and closing arguments from all parties will begin in the last week of this month.

stories.title: Ottawa stands by Darlington small modular reactor amid delays and rising costs
stories.summary: Project aligns with Canada Growth Fund’s mandate to shoulder risk for tech that can drive economic growth, advance climate goals, Energy Minister says
stories.author: Aya Dufour, Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
The federal government is shrugging off an engineering setback at Ontario’s Darlington small modular reactor project, with Energy Minister Tim Hodgson calling it “a reality in all first-of-a-kind projects.”

Mr. Hodgson defended the Canada Growth Fund’s $2-billion equity investment in the project, saying it aligns with the taxpayer-backed fund’s mandate to shoulder risk for technologies that can drive economic growth and advance climate goals.

“It’s important for Canada that we do not balk on making these important investments,” he said.

Earlier this week, Ontario Power Generation said it would undertake a comprehensive assessment after filings with the Ontario Energy Board indicated the Darlington SMR project is facing cost overruns and delays.

The Crown corporation reported that the overruns reflected the “ongoing engineering” work of its partner, GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, which is responsible for designing the Bwrx-300 reactor and other aspects of the facility.

In a statement, GE Vernova Hitachi spokesperson Jonathan Allen pointed to other factors outside his company’s control.

“While engineering and design maturity are important considerations, as Opg’s update recognizes, there are multiple interconnected contributions across engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”

In quarterly financial statements released Tuesday, OPG said the first reactor unit would not be completed within its previously disclosed $7.7-billion budget.

The utility did not specify the size of the cost overrun or the extent of the delay, although a production forecast included in the filing suggests the project’s timing could slip by at least a year. OPG had previously targeted an in-service date of October 2030.

The delay could ultimately prove shorter than a year, depending on the outcome of an assessment that is expected to be completed by mid-2027.

The project was among the first to be shepherded through the Major Projects Office last year and later received significant equity commitments from the federal and provincial governments via the Canada Growth Fund and the Building Ontario Fund.

In an e-mail, CGF spokesperson Mathieu St-Amand wrote that “the equity commitment is being deployed over time.”

A corporate presentation from the fund said the investment is subject to certain conditions, but Mr. St-Amand declined to say whether those conditions were tied to specific project timelines or cost estimates.

In a separate corporate presentation, the CGF says its capital will be deployed in two tranches: one tied to the first reactor unit and another for the remaining three units, contingent on the achievement of certain milestones.

Asked about whether the investment is a prudent use of public funds, Mr. Hodgson said every project has contingencies built in.

“There are on and off ramps for the CGF to be involved, and I’m confident that it is well structured project-to-project to protect the CGF,” he said.

The Darlington New Nuclear Project (Dnnp), with a total budget of $20.9-billion, involves building four Bwrx-300 reactors and accompanying infrastructure adjacent to the existing generating station in Clarington, Ont.

The project is being watched globally because it’s the first small modular reactor to begin construction in a Group of Seven country. There are also proposals to build Bwrx-300s in several other countries including the U.S., Britain and Poland.

In the U.S., GE Vernova Hitachi has partnered with the Tennessee Valley Authority to build the first single Bwrx-300 on American soil at its Clinch River site. Although no construction date has yet been announced, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission recently issued a construction licence for that project.

“It would be premature to speculate on any direct impact to Tva’s potential projects,” wrote TVA spokesperson Elizabeth O’Connor in a statement.

“TVA remains committed to a disciplined approach to deploying advanced nuclear technology and will continue working through partnerships to ensure costs are managed responsibly to protect TVA customers.”

Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator did not respond directly to questions about how the Dnnp delays might affect plans to supply electricity to Ontarians in the early 2030s.

Ieso spokesperson Michael Dodsworth noted that the Ieso was in the middle of a large competitive electricity procurement known as Long-Term 2, “which was expanded from 5,000 to 7,500 megawatts to meet growing electricity demand.” The organization was also promoting electricity efficiency to reduce peak demand.

He added: “The Ieso will continue to work with OPG as the Darlington New Nuclear Project advances, and relevant information will be considered as part of future system plans to determine if any incremental actions are needed.”

Pierre-Olivier Pineau, chair in energy sector management at HEC Montréal, said the challenges facing the Darlington SMR project “underscore the fact that we need to be very cautious and honest in our energy and electricity policy across Canada.”

He argued governments should take their time to evaluate any potential future investment in the project.

“We should never think because we’ve invested so much, we should keep investing,” he said, describing the initial costs as already more than what anyone would ever want to pay for electricity.

“If they add more billions to this already expensive experiment, then we definitely can take a few more years to think about it.”

stories.title: Carney, Quebec’s St-Pierre Plamondon to meet in Cambodia after weeks of frosty relations
stories.summary: Leaders will meet for 30 minutes in Phnom Penh on the sidelines of the Sommet de la Francophonie
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
After weeks of testy exchanges and thinly veiled jibes, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will meet face to face this weekend for the first time since the Parti Québécois won last month’s provincial election.

They will meet Sunday in Cambodia, after Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon insisted that a meeting on Canadian soil must take place in Quebec City – a demand the Prime Minister’s Office said it was unable to accommodate.

The two leaders will instead meet for 30 minutes in Phnom Penh on the sidelines of the Sommet de la Francophonie, which Mr. Carney will attend as part of a four-summit trip that concludes in China next week.

In the nearly six weeks since the sovereigntist Parti Québécois was elected to form a minority government on Oct. 5, relations between Quebec City and Ottawa have been decidedly frosty. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has accused Mr. Carney of treating his province as a vassal, while the Prime Minister this week appeared to take umbrage at the Quebec Premier’s decision to reach out directly to newly elected officials in the United States.

“We look forward to meeting the Premier on Sunday,” PMO spokesperson Audrey Champoux said Thursday in a brief message.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon campaigned on a promise to hold a third referendum on Quebec sovereignty as early as 2029, though his minority government May not survive that long. Since the election, he has found several occasions to paint Mr. Carney as an adversary.

Still, the Prime Minister remains considerably more popular in Quebec than the new Premier, whose party won just 28 per cent of the vote – a historic low for a party forming government. After the election, Mr. Carney noted to reporters that his Liberals won a 43-per-cent mandate last year.

A back-and-forth over the location of a possible tête-à-tête in Canada played out in public over several days. In an interview with La Presse published late last month, the Prime Minister said he wanted to meet with Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon ahead of the Francophonie summit, either in Montreal or Ottawa.

He extended that olive branch after the Quebec Premier declined to attend a Canada-European Union summit in Montreal because Ottawa refused the province’s request to let him deliver a speech at the event. Mr. Carney said the Premier had chosen to leave an “empty chair.” In turn, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Prime Minister of “vassalization and erasure.”

The Premier responded to Mr. Carney’s invitation in a 1,600-word social-media post on Nov. 1, thanking him for the “change of tone” but adding that any meeting must take place in the provincial capital. In the end, Ms. Champoux said, the leaders’ schedules “didn’t line up” for a trip to Quebec City.

This week, the two leaders also sparred over letters Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon sent to 59 elected officials in the U.S. after last week’s midterms, highlighting the province’s trade relationship with various states.

“As you begin your term in office, Quebec looks forward to working with your team to advance our shared goals,” he wrote in a letter to Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic senator-elect from Michigan.

Asked on Tuesday whether the letters could affect Ottawa’s trade negotiations with Washington, Mr. Carney said trade deals are the purview of the federal government. “In a negotiation, it’s always a good idea to have a single negotiator,” he told reporters in Montreal.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon fired back, telling reporters in Quebec City that the Prime Minister is not his boss. “Mr. Carney would prefer that we not put on our skates and never set foot on the ice because he wants the rink all to himself,” he said. “Over the coming months, expect to see a Quebec that takes its rightful place in the world.”

In an interview, Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said it’s been a “tough start” for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who he said should focus on the economy rather than “symbolic” battles with Ottawa.

“They’re both wrong … they’re both immature,” he said of the two leaders. “Hopefully, now that they’re in Cambodia, it might be easier for them to talk with more respect and with less political pressure.”

The Francophonie summit is Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s first international trip as premier. But his Minister of International Relations, Dieudonné Ella Oyono, told reporters in Phnom Penh on Friday that the Quebec delegation does not intend to focus on sovereignty during the event.

“We don’t need to talk about Quebec independence, because everyone knows a pro-independence government was elected in Quebec,” Mr. Oyono said.

Ahead of the summit on Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron declined to comment on his country’s future relationship with a separatist government in Quebec.

“It is not my place to interfere in Canadian affairs, but to continue to support our common ties, including our cultural and linguistic ties,” he told reporters in Dublin.

With reports from Steven Chase and The Canadian Press

stories.title: How Microsoft’s Outlook outage liberated workers, but hobbled public institutions
stories.summary: Technology outages are ‘the new snow day,’ Concordia professor says
stories.author: Joe Friesen
stories.content:
The disruption that knocked out Microsoft services this week extracted a major toll on workplace productivity and raised questions about Canada’s reliance on U.S.-based tech companies.

But some also saw it as a mixed blessing.

The drumbeat of e-mails that interrupt the lives of office workers everywhere went silent for several hours, creating an opening for extended focus and freeing them from the next task, report or meeting.

“It’s the new snow day,” said Fenwick McKelvey, professor of communication studies at Concordia University.

He described expecting to have an afternoon of answering e-mails on Thursday, only to experience a peculiar kind of delight when the work became impossible, because Microsoft e-mail wasn’t functioning.

“I wasn’t sitting with this constant expectation that an e-mail was going to be coming my way that I needed to respond to,” Prof. McKelvey said.

On Friday, Microsoft apologized, saying it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption the incident had caused. The outage began Thursday around midday in Canada, taking offline a suite of services that millions around the world rely on to communicate, share documents and hold meetings. By Friday morning, many services were being restored.

Microsoft said in a statement that the outage was caused by a technical issue and was not related to “cyber or AI/agents.”

“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said in a statement. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Prof. McKelvey said the extent of the outage provoked a feeling of helplessness. He said it was reminiscent of the July 2022 outage that knocked out services for Rogers wireless customers.

It also raised questions about digital sovereignty, considering how many Canadian institutions rely on U.S. tech companies for crucial services such as communication and data storage.

“To see someone like Microsoft experience an outage that lasts multiple hours is a wake-up call,” Prof. McKelvey said. “You’re left with a lot of questions and not a lot of ways finding answers, so I do think it’s unsettling.”

The list of Canadian institutions that were affected is lengthy and includes schools, hospitals, police and governments.

The University Health Network in Toronto said its e-mail was down Thursday but services were being restored as of Friday morning and that patient care was not affected. The University of British Columbia said its e-mail service was also being restored by Friday morning. The City of Brampton said some online forms and city services were affected.

The Government of Canada had nearly $250-million in contracts with Microsoft for IT software licensing in 2021-2022, according to a contract analysis published by Carleton University’s School of Public Policy and Administration.

The RCMP said some employees had issues using some Microsoft 365 applications, such as Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot, and employees were provided with guidance on mitigating the impact.

“At this time, there were no impacts to RCMP operational policing services or public-facing emergency response capabilities,” said Lisa McDonald-Bourg of national headquarters public affairs.

Emmanuelle Vaast, a professor of information systems at McGill University, said she took advantage of the e-mail silence to do some focused work that otherwise would have been subject to a stream of interruptions.

“At an individual level, it was a little bit of a blessing, although, of course, I realize that at the organizational level, and the collective level, the cost is very high,” Prof. Vaast said.

But the longer the outage went on, she also experienced a mounting sense of anxiety about what would await her when e-mail was eventually restored.

When the system was up and running again Friday morning, there were 78 messages waiting for her, many of them from students who needed a prompt reply.

She said the incident is interesting because it doesn’t appear to have been the work of a malicious actor, which shows that it’s not just cyber attacks that can have serious consequences for IT systems. But it also reveals how dependent our society is on a relative handful of companies.

A discussion about whether that should change is more advanced in Europe, she said. But the ease, availability and low cost that the big players can offer represent a trade-off that many organizations have shown they’re willing to accept.

“The big picture is I don’t foresee this being a huge turn in the history of dependence upon Microsoft,” Prof. Vaast said.

stories.title: Addiction recovery centre completed on Alberta First Nation, but lawsuits remain
stories.summary: A handful of subcontractors allege Melewka Homes Ltd. has not paid them in full for their work
stories.author: Carrie Tait, Tom Cardoso
stories.content:
One of the three addiction-treatment centres swept up in Alberta’s health care procurement controversy expects to open its doors to patients in December, but a handful of subcontractors allege they have not been paid in full for their work.

The Alberta government in late October announced that construction of the maskêkosihk recovery community on Enoch Cree Nation was complete. The First Nation, which abuts Edmonton, selected Melewka Homes Ltd. to build its $35-million provincially funded facility, the type of addiction-treatment centre the government is counting on to address the opioid crisis ravaging communities across Alberta. Two other Indigenous communities, Tsuut’ina Nation and the Métis Nation of Alberta, have been building recovery centres with provincial funding and also hired Melewka.

“Every new recovery community means more people can access the support they need to reclaim their lives from addiction,” Rick Wilson, the Minister of Mental Health and Addiction, said in an Oct. 26 statement about Enoch’s finished facility.

But Melewka’s three recovery centre projects are mired in lawsuits and counterclaims over bills, drawing further attention to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith ’s handling of a broadening procurement controversy that has dogged her government for nearly two years.

Over the last year, Alberta has insisted that while it paid for the projects through grants, each Indigenous community was in charge of selecting a general contractor for their respective facility. Tsuut’ina’s former lawyer, in court documents, alleges the government “ recommended ” Melewka for its recovery project. That has not been tested in court.

Ms. Smith in August said she expects construction on the three recovery projects to be done this year , but the tangle of lawsuits could take much longer to smooth out. Ryan Fournier, a spokesman for Ms. Smith, did not acknowledge messages seeking comment.

Court records show that four subcontractors allege Melewka has not fully paid them for their work on the Enoch facility. Melewka is facing another 11 lawsuits from subcontractors alleging they have not been paid in full for their work on the recovery centre in Tsuut’ina or for Métis Nation projects, including its addictions-treatment facility. The subcontractors are seeking at least $7.4-million across the various lawsuits.

Melewka, in the majority of cases, responded by suing the subcontractors, alleging shoddy craftsmanship and other problems. None of the allegations have been tested in court.

Further, some subcontractors that worked on Enoch’s recovery facility accepted discounted rates rather than pursuing legal remedies. John Schuring, who owns Lana Exteriors Ltd., had submitted a final bill of about $133,000, plus GST, to Melewka. In the end, Mr. Schuring accepted 80 cents on the dollar and ate the tax.

“It sucks,” Mr. Schuring said, noting he is out about $30,000 on the invoice. He subcontracted work to Constant Exteriors Inc. and paid the company what it was owed, save for about $5,000.

“On a government project, this never should have happened,” Erin Constant, who owns Constant Exteriors, said. “There clearly was no one watching what was happening.”

Diablo Fire Protection Ltd. sued Melewka in September, arguing the general contractor failed to pay for roughly $241,000 worth of work on the recovery facilities for Enoch and Tsuu’tina, which abuts Calgary.

Melewka, in a counterclaim filed on Oct. 26, alleges Diablo breached its agreements regarding Enoch and Tsuut’ina by not executing work up to standard, and refusing to return to the projects to complete duties and fix problems.

Further, the counterclaim alleges Diablo refused to fix the deficiencies at Enoch “in an attempt to coerce Melewka into making further payments under the Tsuut’ina Agreement.”

Melewka is seeking at least $498,750, according to the court document. The company alleges it will have to hire others to fix and finish Diablo’s work at Enoch and Tsuut’ina, driving up costs and creating delays.

Diablo’s lawyer declined to comment.

Fancy Doors & Mouldings Ltd. sued Melewka in July for $602,000, alleging the company is behind on bills tied to all three recovery facilities.

Melewka countersued in September, alleging Fancy supplied deficient products, including some in the wrong size.

Fancy has yet to fix the problems tied to the Metis Nation facility, Melewka alleges. And because of the difficulties on the Enoch and Métis Nation projects, Melewka alleges it then cancelled all or part of its Fancy order regarding Tsuut’ina.

Fancy declined to comment.

Sky Light Painting Ltd. alleges Melewka owes it $211,600 for work on the Enoch facility, while Adeer Contracting Ltd. alleges it is out $84,000. Melewka countersued both companies for $150,000 each, alleging Sky Light and Adeer both billed for unauthorized work and did not complete their duties and correct their mistakes. Sky Light and Adeer did not acknowledge requests for comment.

In response to questions from The Globe and Mail, Erin Stroud, a spokesperson for Enoch, directed questions about outstanding bills to the construction company.

“To the Nation’s knowledge, all undisputed amounts owing have been paid,” she said in a statement. “Any outstanding construction-related or payment disputes involving Melewka and its subcontractors would be matters for Melewka.”

Melewka did not acknowledge requests for comment.

The company, owned by Lewis Semashkewich and his son John Semashkewich, is ensnarled in another legal battle which connects the Melewka projects to Alberta’s broader health care procurement controversy.

Melewka is sparring over millions of dollars with former business partner Mohamed Eldassouki and his associates, including his brother-in-law, Sam Mraiche.

Mr. Eldassouki, in court documents, alleges the elder Semashkewich fraudulently took control of his company and a bank account holding about $8.4-million. Conversely, Melewka alleges Mr. Eldassouski’s company inappropriately received more than $11-million tied to Melewka’s projects.

The Semashkewiches also allege that Mr. Eldassouki’s company was secretly controlled by Mr. Mraiche, and that he demanded money while threatening to use his connections to have Melewka removed from construction projects or delay payments.

Mr. Mraiche, in court documents, denies controlling his brother-in-law’s business and said his involvement was limited to giving Mr. Eldassouski “casual, unofficial, and informal business advice.”

None of the allegations have been tested in court. Lawyers for Mr. Mraiche, and Mr. Eldassouski did not acknowledge messages seeking comment.

Mr. Mraiche owns MHCare Medical Corp., the company at the centre of Alberta’s heath care procurement affair – which erupted when Athana Mentzelopoulos sued the provincial government and her former employer, Alberta Health Services, for wrongful dismissal in early 2025.

She alleges Alberta fired her as AHS chief executive to end her investigation into procurement processes and potential conflicts of interest between employees at the public health agency and private businesses, including MHCare. The public health agency paid the company $70-million for generic children’s medication from Turkey, most of which never arrived. Mr. Mraiche was also part of a consortium negotiating for private surgical contracts worth $430-million.

Mr. Mraiche is not party to the lawsuit and has stated his government deals are above board.

Melanie Paradis, a spokeswoman for the Métis Nation, did not address questions about that community’s recovery facility, citing “legal and privacy reasons.”

Tsuu’tina Xàkijí-tii (head chief) Ellery Starlight said in a statement that the nation has paid Melewka in accordance with its grant agreement and “any potential outstanding subcontractor payment issues are matters between the general contractor, Melewka, and its subcontractors.”

He added that the nation believes construction on the facility never stopped and is 80-per-cent complete, through the payment certification process. Tsuut’ina expects to finish on budget, Mr. Starlight said.

The Alberta government in late October announced that construction of the maskêkosihk recovery community on Enoch Cree Nation was complete. The First Nation, which abuts Edmonton, selected Melewka Homes Ltd. to build its $35-million provincially funded facility, the type of addiction-treatment centre the government is counting on to address the opioid crisis ravaging communities across Alberta. Two other Indigenous communities, Tsuut’ina Nation and the Métis Nation of Alberta, have been building recovery centres with provincial funding and also hired Melewka.

“Every new recovery community means more people can access the support they need to reclaim their lives from addiction,” Rick Wilson, the Minister of Mental Health and Addiction, said in an Oct. 26 statement about Enoch’s finished facility.

But Melewka’s three recovery centre projects are mired in lawsuits and counterclaims over bills, drawing further attention to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith ’s handling of a broadening procurement controversy that has dogged her government for nearly two years.

Over the last year, Alberta has insisted that while it paid for the projects through grants, each Indigenous community was in charge of selecting a general contractor for their respective facility. Tsuut’ina’s former lawyer, in court documents, alleges the government “ recommended ” Melewka for its recovery project. That has not been tested in court.

Ms. Smith in August said she expects construction on the three recovery projects to be done this year , but the tangle of lawsuits could take much longer to smooth out. Ryan Fournier, a spokesman for Ms. Smith, did not acknowledge messages seeking comment.

Court records show that four subcontractors allege Melewka has not fully paid them for their work on the Enoch facility. Melewka is facing another 11 lawsuits from subcontractors alleging they have not been paid in full for their work on the recovery centre in Tsuut’ina or for Métis Nation projects, including its addictions-treatment facility. The subcontractors are seeking at least $7.4-million across the various lawsuits.
Melewka, in the majority of cases, responded by suing the subcontractors, alleging shoddy craftsmanship and other problems. None of the allegations have been tested in court.

Further, some subcontractors that worked on Enoch’s recovery facility accepted discounted rates rather than pursuing legal remedies. John Schuring, who owns Lana Exteriors Ltd., had submitted a final bill of about $133,000, plus GST, to Melewka. In the end, Mr. Schuring accepted 80 cents on the dollar and ate the tax.
“It sucks,” Mr. Schuring said, noting he is out about $30,000 on the invoice. He subcontracted work to Constant Exteriors Inc. and paid the company what it was owed, save for about $5,000.
“On a government project, this never should have happened,” Erin Constant, who owns Constant Exteriors, said. “There clearly was no one watching what was happening.”

Diablo Fire Protection Ltd. sued Melewka in September, arguing the general contractor failed to pay for roughly $241,000 worth of work on the recovery facilities for Enoch and Tsuu’tina, which abuts Calgary.

Melewka, in a counterclaim filed on Oct. 26, alleges Diablo breached its agreements regarding Enoch and Tsuut’ina by not executing work up to standard, and refusing to return to the projects to complete duties and fix problems.
Further, the counterclaim alleges Diablo refused to fix the deficiencies at Enoch “in an attempt to coerce Melewka into making further payments under the Tsuut’ina Agreement.”

Melewka is seeking at least $498,750, according to the court document. The company alleges it will have to hire others to fix and finish Diablo’s work at Enoch and Tsuut’ina, driving up costs and creating delays.
Diablo’s lawyer declined to comment.
Fancy Doors & Mouldings Ltd. sued Melewka in July for $602,000, alleging the company is behind on bills tied to all three recovery facilities.
Melewka countersued in September, alleging Fancy supplied deficient products, including some in the wrong size.

Fancy has yet to fix the problems tied to the Metis Nation facility, Melewka alleges. And because of the difficulties on the Enoch and Métis Nation projects, Melewka alleges it then cancelled all or part of its Fancy order regarding Tsuut’ina.
Fancy declined to comment.

Sky Light Painting Ltd. alleges Melewka owes it $211,600 for work on the Enoch facility, while Adeer Contracting Ltd. alleges it is out $84,000. Melewka countersued both companies for $150,000 each, alleging Sky Light and Adeer both billed for unauthorized work and did not complete their duties and correct their mistakes. Sky Light and Adeer did not acknowledge requests for comment.
In response to questions from The Globe and Mail, Erin Stroud, a spokesperson for Enoch, directed questions about outstanding bills to the construction company.

“To the Nation’s knowledge, all undisputed amounts owing have been paid,” she said in a statement. “Any outstanding construction-related or payment disputes involving Melewka and its subcontractors would be matters for Melewka.”
Melewka did not acknowledge requests for comment.

The company, owned by Lewis Semashkewich and his son John Semashkewich, is ensnarled in another legal battle which connects the Melewka projects to Alberta’s broader health care procurement controversy.
Melewka is sparring over millions of dollars with former business partner Mohamed Eldassouki and his associates, including his brother-in-law, Sam Mraiche.

Mr. Eldassouki, in court documents, alleges the elder Semashkewich fraudulently took control of his company and a bank account holding about $8.4-million. Conversely, Melewka alleges Mr. Eldassouski’s company inappropriately received more than $11-million tied to Melewka’s projects.

The Semashkewiches also allege that Mr. Eldassouki’s company was secretly controlled by Mr. Mraiche, and that he demanded money while threatening to use his connections to have Melewka removed from construction projects or delay payments.
Mr. Mraiche, in court documents, denies controlling his brother-in-law’s business and said his involvement was limited to giving Mr. Eldassouski “casual, unofficial, and informal business advice.”
None of the allegations have been tested in court. Lawyers for Mr. Mraiche, and Mr. Eldassouski did not acknowledge messages seeking comment.

Mr. Mraiche owns MHCare Medical Corp., the company at the centre of Alberta’s heath care procurement affair – which erupted when Athana Mentzelopoulos sued the provincial government and her former employer, Alberta Health Services, for wrongful dismissal in early 2025.

She alleges Alberta fired her as AHS chief executive to end her investigation into procurement processes and potential conflicts of interest between employees at the public health agency and private businesses, including MHCare. The public health agency paid the company $70-million for generic children’s medication from Turkey, most of which never arrived. Mr. Mraiche was also part of a consortium negotiating for private surgical contracts worth $430-million.
Mr. Mraiche is not party to the lawsuit and has stated his government deals are above board.
Melanie Paradis, a spokeswoman for the Métis Nation, did not address questions about that community’s recovery facility, citing “legal and privacy reasons.”

Tsuu’tina Xàkijí-tii (head chief) Ellery Starlight said in a statement that the nation has paid Melewka in accordance with its grant agreement and “any potential outstanding subcontractor payment issues are matters between the general contractor, Melewka, and its subcontractors.”

He added that the nation believes construction on the facility never stopped and is 80-per-cent complete, through the payment certification process. Tsuut’ina expects to finish on budget, Mr. Starlight said.

stories.title: Master stickhandler André Lacroix was the Wha’s all-time top scorer
stories.summary: Despite his achievements, he has not been enshrined in the Hockey Hall of Fame, a snub he believed he suffered for abandoning the NHL for an upstart remembered as the Rebel League
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
André Lacroix was an average skater but a brilliant playmaker who survived seven wild and wacky seasons to emerge as the World Hockey Association’s all-time top scorer.

The WHA was launched in the early 1970s as a rival to the well-established National Hockey League. By offering large salaries, the league managed to lure away such stars as Bobby Hull, Gordie Howe, Dave Keon and many others.

The unheralded Mr. Lacroix skated alongside all three of those future Hockey Hall of Famers over seven peripatetic campaigns. He played for franchises that folded, for franchises that changed cities and, memorably, for a franchise in which the coach travelled with wads of cash because hotels would accept the athletes only if the bill was fully paid in advance.

The slight centreman, who stood just 5-foot-8 (1.73 metres) and weighed 175 pounds (79 kilograms), was nicknamed the Magician for the legerdemain of his stickhandling and for the intuitive genius he displayed in passing the puck.

When the remnants of the WHA were rolled into the NHL before the 1979-80 season, Mr. Lacroix held permanent records for most regular-season games played (551), most assists (547) and most points (798).

Mr. Lacroix, who has died at 81, was as savvy in negotiating contracts as he was in making pinpoint passes on the ice. Working without an agent, he earned more than many of his peers by including a clause making him a free agent if a club moved cities or stopped operating. He also got desperate owners to include several bonuses for scoring. He signed to play for a team based in San Diego by cajoling multi-millionaire owner Ray Kroc, who made his fortune with McDonald’s restaurants, into guaranteeing his salary over six seasons even if he retired or played for another team.

“I was probably one of the few guys who never missed a paycheque,” he wrote in After the Second Snowfall , his self-published 2020 memoir.

Often overshadowed by more famous teammates, he proved his talents on the global stage, emerging as one of Canada’s stars in an eight-game showdown against the Soviets held two years after the more famous Summit Series of 1972.

Despite a successful career, he has not been enshrined in the Hockey Hall of Fame, a snub he believed he suffered because he had abandoned the NHL for an upstart remembered as the Rebel League.

He was born in Lauzon, Que., a shipbuilding town now part of Lévis, across the St. Lawrence River from Quebec City, ON June 5, 1945. He was the youngest of 14 children – Lorraine, Raymond, Hervé, Marcel, Bertha, Pierrette, Monique, Colette, Maurice, Françoise, Hélène, Claude and Jacques – born to the former Albéa Lapierre and Alfred Lacroix, who worked at an automobile repair shop, among other jobs.

The boy, who shared a bed with a brother, learned to skate at school at age six and later cleared the ice at a public rink in exchange for not paying a 50-cent admission. He did not play an indoor game of hockey until age 13, when he was bumped up a level to play with and against older teenagers on an area all-star team that won three consecutive provincial championships.

“For me, hockey always came first,” he told the Houston Post in 1978. “During the summer, instead of chasing girls, I would play baseball and tennis so I could keep in shape.”

In junior, a coach insisted he practice skating and stickhandling while blindfolded, a regimen the player credited for developing his superior puck sense.

After a season with the Montreal Junior Canadiens, he spent two seasons of junior with the Peterborough Petes of the Ontario Hockey Association. He led the circuit with 120 points in just 48 games in 1965-66, winning a second consecutive Albert (Red) Tilson Memorial Trophy as the most outstanding player, beating out a promising young defenceman named Bobby Orr.

The centre turned professional with the Quebec Aces, who played across the river from his hometown.

In 1967, the Philadelphia Flyers, one of six NHL expansion teams preparing for their inaugural season, purchased the Aces to serve as a farm team while also getting the rights to 11 players, including Mr. Lacroix, not under contract to NHL teams.

Near the end of the season, the Flyers called up the centre, who scored a goal in his debut and added a goal and three assists in his second game. Quebec wanted him returned for their own playoff run, while the Flyers wanted his scoring punch.

He stayed in Philadelphia, though the team’s home arena, the Spectrum on Broad Street, had to be closed for repairs after strong winds blew off part of the roof. The team played home games at Madison Square Garden in New York and Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto before settling in at the Colisée in Quebec City, where the rookie centre had starred for the Aces. On his return, grateful local fans presented the hometown hero with a new Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme.

Playing on what was called the French Line with Jean-Guy Gendron, of Montreal, and Dick Sarrazin, of Saint-Gabriel-de-Brandon, Que. (the latter later replaced by Simon Nolet, of Saint-Odilon-de-Cranbourne, Que.), Mr. Lacroix scored a respectable 66 goals over three seasons with the Flyers.

When coach Vic Stasiuk ordered the team’s Francophone players to stop speaking French in the dressing room, ON the bench and on the team bus, the ban was leaked to the press while the team was in Montreal for a game against the Canadiens, further distancing the players from management. The team and the league later clarified they wanted the players to speak English during games.

The Flyers adopted a rougher, more physical style, becoming known as the Broad Street Bullies. Mr. Lacroix, known more for finesse than fisticuffs, was dispatched to Chicago for defenceman Rick Foley, a scofflaw who spent 306 penalty minutes in the minors the previous season.

The Blackhawks had no plan for their new acquisition, who was often a healthy scratch.

“He’s the only French-Canadian hockey player I know who can’t skate,” coach Billy Reay said.

The WHA arrived just in time to rescue Mr. Lacroix. He was drafted by the Quebec Nordiques, but they could not match his contract demands. His rights were then sold to the Miami Screaming Eagles, who folded before the season started. New owners purchased the franchise, and Mr. Lacroix returned to Philadelphia as a member of the Blazers, doubling his base NHL salary by signing for $60,000 plus performance bonuses.

The Blazers featured several top NHL players in goalie Bernie Parent, moon-faced winger Johnny (Pie) McKenzie and flamboyant playboy Derek (Turk) Sanderson, a centre whose extravagant contract briefly made him the highest-paid athlete in the world.

Mr. Lacroix led the WHA in scoring in its inaugural, 12-team season with 50 goals and 74 assists to claim the W.D. (Bill) Hunter Trophy. He was also named to the league’s First All-Star team at centre, while linemate Danny Lawson was on right wing and Mr. Hull, who had gained the league credibility by rejecting the NHL in favour of signing a million-dollar contract, ON left wing.

The league’s fate seemed to be captured in the Blazers’ first home game in 1972, a Friday the 13 th , when an ice-cleaning machine cracked the ice, forcing a postponement, an announcement which led to a hail of souvenir pucks being thrown at the club president.

The Blazers sold the team to Canadian businessman Jim Pattison, who moved the franchise to his base in Vancouver. Mr. Lacroix then signed with the New York Golden Blades (formerly the Raiders), who wore leather skates painted white with gold paint on the metal blades. Dismal attendance, numbering in the hundreds, led the new owner to return the franchise to the league, which moved back into the now-abandoned Philadelphia market by playing as the Jersey Knights in Cherry Hill, N.J.

In 1974, a second Summit Series against the Soviet Union was held, with Canada represented by top WHA players. In this eight-game exhibition, Mr. Lacroix centred a line with Mr. Hull and Mr. McKenzie, scoring one goal and six assists. The Soviets emerged victorious with a record of four wins, one loss and three ties.

His next stop in the WHA was in San Diego, where he drove to Mariners practice in a street-legal dune buggy. He led the league in points with 41 goals and 106 assists in 1974-75, but once again, financial troubles overshadowed the game on the ice. A nadir was reached when the team had no money for a bus from the airport, so the trainer’s father operated a shuttle with his mobile home.

At first, Mr. Kroc’s ownership promised stability, but not even his acumen could make the operation profitable. The franchise folded. Mr. Lacroix signed with the Houston Aeros. When they, in turn, folded, he signed with the New England Whalers, where Mr. Howe and his son Mark were linemates.

Mr. Lacroix scored a goal in his final WHA game, a 6-3 loss to the Edmonton Oilers. An 18-year-old Wayne Gretzky scored twice for the Oilers.

With the exhausted league near collapse, the NHL absorbed four teams, including the renamed Hartford Whalers. Mr. Lacroix returned to the NHL for one final season, finishing his NHL career with 79 goals and 119 assists in 325 games. His combined WHA-NHL totals left him four points shy of 1,000.

After hanging up his skates, Mr. Lacroix spent eight years as an analyst and colour commentator for Whalers games alongside legendary play-by-play broadcaster Chuck Kaiton.

During his playing days, he co-owned a rink with Flyers teammate Ed Van Impe. He later operated a sporting goods store and a drywall company before spending a decade directing hockey operations for a rink in Oakland, Calif. He coached youth hockey in Ohio, guiding his daughter’s high school team to a championship.

In 2019, he was presented the Jacques Amyot Award for lifetime achievement by Sports Quebec.

As well, an arena in his hometown carries his name.

Mr. Lacroix died on Oct. 27 at his home in Chagrin Falls, Ohio. He leaves a son, André Jr., and a daughter, Chantal Lacroix Ayers, a college ice and field hockey coach. He also leaves seven grandchildren; a brother, Fr. Jacques Lacroix; and two sisters, Bertha Méthot and Françoise Lemieux. He was predeceased by five brothers and five sisters, as well as by an infant grandson, Joseph Lacroix, who died in 2004. A marriage to the former Suzanne Postus, the daughter of National Football League player Al Postus, ended in divorce.

In New York, he was once invited to a lunch by a businessman only to discover his dining companions were three models representing a new magazine for women called Viva, a risqué companion to publisher Bob Guccione’s adult Penthouse. The hockey player was asked to pose both clothed and unclothed in the shower and other suggestive locations.

“The reason I gave them for not accepting their offer was that I was not brought up that way,” he wrote in his memoir, “my parents would not appreciate it, my wife would not like it, my brother, Jacques, who was a priest, would not agree with it, and I could not face my fans knowing I did something like that.”

Not wishing to offend, he politely suggested they try Mr. Sanderson.

paragraphs: André Lacroix was an average skater but a brilliant playmaker who survived seven wild and wacky seasons to emerge as the World Hockey Association’s all-time top scorer.

The WHA was launched in the early 1970s as a rival to the well-established National Hockey League. By offering large salaries, the league managed to lure away such stars as Bobby Hull, Gordie Howe, Dave Keon and many others.

The unheralded Mr. Lacroix skated alongside all three of those future Hockey Hall of Famers over seven peripatetic campaigns. He played for franchises that folded, for franchises that changed cities and, memorably, for a franchise in which the coach travelled with wads of cash because hotels would accept the athletes only if the bill was fully paid in advance.

The slight centreman, who stood just 5-foot-8 (1.73 metres) and weighed 175 pounds (79 kilograms), was nicknamed the Magician for the legerdemain of his stickhandling and for the intuitive genius he displayed in passing the puck.

When the remnants of the WHA were rolled into the NHL before the 1979-80 season, Mr. Lacroix held permanent records for most regular-season games played (551), most assists (547) and most points (798).

Mr. Lacroix, who has died at 81, was as savvy in negotiating contracts as he was in making pinpoint passes on the ice. Working without an agent, he earned more than many of his peers by including a clause making him a free agent if a club moved cities or stopped operating. He also got desperate owners to include several bonuses for scoring. He signed to play for a team based in San Diego by cajoling multi-millionaire owner Ray Kroc, who made his fortune with McDonald’s restaurants, into guaranteeing his salary over six seasons even if he retired or played for another team.
“I was probably one of the few guys who never missed a paycheque,” he wrote in After the Second Snowfall , his self-published 2020 memoir.

Often overshadowed by more famous teammates, he proved his talents on the global stage, emerging as one of Canada’s stars in an eight-game showdown against the Soviets held two years after the more famous Summit Series of 1972.
Despite a successful career, he has not been enshrined in the Hockey Hall of Fame, a snub he believed he suffered because he had abandoned the NHL for an upstart remembered as the Rebel League.

He was born in Lauzon, Que., a shipbuilding town now part of Lévis, across the St. Lawrence River from Quebec City, ON June 5, 1945. He was the youngest of 14 children – Lorraine, Raymond, Hervé, Marcel, Bertha, Pierrette, Monique, Colette, Maurice, Françoise, Hélène, Claude and Jacques – born to the former Albéa Lapierre and Alfred Lacroix, who worked at an automobile repair shop, among other jobs.

The boy, who shared a bed with a brother, learned to skate at school at age six and later cleared the ice at a public rink in exchange for not paying a 50-cent admission. He did not play an indoor game of hockey until age 13, when he was bumped up a level to play with and against older teenagers on an area all-star team that won three consecutive provincial championships.
“For me, hockey always came first,” he told the Houston Post in 1978. “During the summer, instead of chasing girls, I would play baseball and tennis so I could keep in shape.”
In junior, a coach insisted he practice skating and stickhandling while blindfolded, a regimen the player credited for developing his superior puck sense.

After a season with the Montreal Junior Canadiens, he spent two seasons of junior with the Peterborough Petes of the Ontario Hockey Association. He led the circuit with 120 points in just 48 games in 1965-66, winning a second consecutive Albert (Red) Tilson Memorial Trophy as the most outstanding player, beating out a promising young defenceman named Bobby Orr.
The centre turned professional with the Quebec Aces, who played across the river from his hometown.

In 1967, the Philadelphia Flyers, one of six NHL expansion teams preparing for their inaugural season, purchased the Aces to serve as a farm team while also getting the rights to 11 players, including Mr. Lacroix, not under contract to NHL teams.

Near the end of the season, the Flyers called up the centre, who scored a goal in his debut and added a goal and three assists in his second game. Quebec wanted him returned for their own playoff run, while the Flyers wanted his scoring punch.

He stayed in Philadelphia, though the team’s home arena, the Spectrum on Broad Street, had to be closed for repairs after strong winds blew off part of the roof. The team played home games at Madison Square Garden in New York and Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto before settling in at the Colisée in Quebec City, where the rookie centre had starred for the Aces. On his return, grateful local fans presented the hometown hero with a new Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme.

Playing on what was called the French Line with Jean-Guy Gendron, of Montreal, and Dick Sarrazin, of Saint-Gabriel-de-Brandon, Que. (the latter later replaced by Simon Nolet, of Saint-Odilon-de-Cranbourne, Que.), Mr. Lacroix scored a respectable 66 goals over three seasons with the Flyers.

When coach Vic Stasiuk ordered the team’s Francophone players to stop speaking French in the dressing room, ON the bench and on the team bus, the ban was leaked to the press while the team was in Montreal for a game against the Canadiens, further distancing the players from management. The team and the league later clarified they wanted the players to speak English during games.

The Flyers adopted a rougher, more physical style, becoming known as the Broad Street Bullies. Mr. Lacroix, known more for finesse than fisticuffs, was dispatched to Chicago for defenceman Rick Foley, a scofflaw who spent 306 penalty minutes in the minors the previous season.
The Blackhawks had no plan for their new acquisition, who was often a healthy scratch.
“He’s the only French-Canadian hockey player I know who can’t skate,” coach Billy Reay said.

The WHA arrived just in time to rescue Mr. Lacroix. He was drafted by the Quebec Nordiques, but they could not match his contract demands. His rights were then sold to the Miami Screaming Eagles, who folded before the season started. New owners purchased the franchise, and Mr. Lacroix returned to Philadelphia as a member of the Blazers, doubling his base NHL salary by signing for $60,000 plus performance bonuses.

The Blazers featured several top NHL players in goalie Bernie Parent, moon-faced winger Johnny (Pie) McKenzie and flamboyant playboy Derek (Turk) Sanderson, a centre whose extravagant contract briefly made him the highest-paid athlete in the world.

Mr. Lacroix led the WHA in scoring in its inaugural, 12-team season with 50 goals and 74 assists to claim the W.D. (Bill) Hunter Trophy. Mr. Lacroix scored a goal in his final WHA game, a 6-3 loss to the Edmonton Oilers. An 18-year-old Wayne Gretzky scored twice for the Oilers.

After hanging up his skates, Mr. Lacroix spent eight years as an analyst and colour commentator for Whalers games alongside legendary play-by-play broadcaster Chuck Kaiton.

During his playing days, he co-owned a rink with Flyers teammate Ed Van Impe. He later operated a sporting goods store and a drywall company before spending a decade directing hockey operations for a rink in Oakland, Calif. He coached youth hockey in Ohio, guiding his daughter’s high school team to a championship.
In 2019, he was presented the Jacques Amyot Award for lifetime achievement by Sports Quebec.
As well, an arena in his hometown carries his name.

Mr. Lacroix died on Oct. 27 at his home in Chagrin Falls, Ohio. He leaves a son, André Jr., and a daughter, Chantal Lacroix Ayers, a college ice and field hockey coach. He also leaves seven grandchildren; a brother, Fr. Jacques Lacroix; and two sisters, Bertha Méthot and Françoise Lemieux. He was predeceased by five brothers and five sisters, as well as by an infant grandson, Joseph Lacroix, who died in 2004. A marriage to the former Suzanne Postus, the daughter of National Football League player Al Postus, ended in divorce.

In New York, he was once invited to a lunch by a businessman only to discover his dining companions were three models representing a new magazine for women called Viva, a risqué companion to publisher Bob Guccione’s adult Penthouse. The hockey player was asked to pose both clothed and unclothed in the shower and other suggestive locations.

“The reason I gave them for not accepting their offer was that I was not brought up that way,” he wrote in his memoir, “my parents would not appreciate it, my wife would not like it, my brother, Jacques, who was a priest, would not agree with it, and I could not face my fans knowing I did something like that.”
Not wishing to offend, he politely suggested they try Mr. Sanderson.

stories.title: Historian Carl Berger offered a dramatic new understanding of Canada’s past
stories.summary: The University of Toronto professor wrote a groundbreaking pair of books considered key to the study of this country’s political mechanics and intellectual imagery
stories.author: Michael Valpy
stories.content:
Sometimes a nation’s story gets shaken in such a way as to make its teeth rattle. University of Toronto historian Carl Clinton Berger did just that in 1970. He turned the study of Canada’s past topsy-turvy with his book The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867-1914 . His book, as ordinary Canadians and academics came to see, was not really about Canadians’ attachment to imperialism. It was a masterful introduction to Canadian intellectual history, to the history of ideas and how they develop, spread and transform across time.

The book brought Prof. Berger to the finding that what he was really looking at was not an English-Canadian notion of imperialism but an English-Canadian notion of nationalism. And as historians Douglas Owram and Gerald Friesen wrote in the introduction to Thinkers and Dreamers , their 2011 collection of essays honouring Prof. Berger’s work, The Sense of Power had a huge impact on how Canadian history was thought about, put into words and taught.

The principles of intellectual history, Prof. Berger declared, did not exist in a vacuum; they needed to be understood within the context of their specific political, social, cultural and material environments. And as he laid bare these layers of intellectual history, Prof. Berger revealed that what he was looking at was not really imperialist thought with a maple sugar coating – it was Canadian nationalism.

His approach combined a narrative presentation of history – stories about what people said and thought about their country – with the body of literature dealing with technical historical matters, including techniques, theories and principles of historical research as well as the critical examination of material from primary and secondary sources subject to scholarly criteria.

The dust jacket of Prof. Berger’s book showed a two-cent Canadian stamp from Christmas 1898 (Prof. Berger was a serious stamp-collector), bearing a map of the globe with countries belonging to the then-British Empire coloured red. A big, red blob of Canada was shown at the map’s centre, with the inference that Canada would be a dominant partner in a reorganized British Empire. But really, what the story of the stamp reveals was Prof. Berger’s argument that allusions to imperialism were a form of Canadian nationalism taking place in the country’s intellectual discourse between the seminal dates of Confederation in 1867 and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914.

Prof. Owram and Prof. Friesen wrote in their introduction to Thinkers and Dreamers that whereas earlier work on political history in Canada was primarily limited to depictions of the ideas of politicians, the opinions of journalists and sometimes references to historiography (the study of how history is written and recorded by historians over time), Prof. Berger probed the thinking and utterances of a much broader swath of Canadians. He examined and recorded myths and legends that Canadians had about their country and looked into their origins. He used textual analysis and archival research to figure out what past writers and speakers actually meant to do with their words rather than judging them in the context of modern settings.

In his revisionist interpretation of what was largely considered to be a Canada glued to imperialist thinking, he assembled his findings into what Prof. Owram and Prof. Friesen wrote of as a lucidly constructed, carefully documented and stylishly written argument to the contrary.

It was the groundbreaking academic path he took for the rest of his career – nearly 40 years at University of Toronto – and on which he led others.

He followed The Sense of Power with his 1976 book The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900-1970 , the first in-depth study of Canadian historiography, which garnered critical praise and won the Governor-General’s Award for non-fiction. He was also elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada.

The two books together were unified by a similar preoccupation – the identity of Canada as revealed by its history – and together they examined the pronounced shift of thinking in Canada from British North American to North American, from one century to the next, and were described by academic historians as all that students of history needed to know about the political mechanics and intellectual imagery of how Canada worked.

Prof. Berger died in Toronto on Oct. 1 at the age of 87.

He was born on Feb. 25, 1939, in The Pas, Man., the son of a millworker. He did his undergraduate degree at the University of Manitoba where he proved to be a brilliant student, graduating with the university’s gold medal. He then went to University of Toronto to do a master’s degree in 1961 on a Woodrow Wilson Fellowship and, after obtaining his master’s degree, began a doctorate under the supervision of J.M.S. Careless, one of English Canada’s leading historians.

Carl Berger’s appearance at U of T as a graduate student and his appointment to its history department coincided with the rapid expansion of advanced Canadian historical studies – a heretofore neglected academic discipline – centred in Canada on work being done at U of T. And Prof. Berger’s chosen specialty, the Victorian period in Canada, alongside the framework for study he had built for his early writings, were among the major factors drawing students to the U of T’s program.

Prof. Berger had a tremendous ability to use the study of very specific, often quiet, elite organizations to paint a larger picture of what was being said and thought about in the country. This was not an easy task, as Prof. Owram and Prof. Friesen wrote.

Much intellectual history work foundered like snuffed candles because the chosen groups or organizations for academics to study did not illuminate larger responses. Prof. Berger’s work did not founder; it wasn’t snuffed. Both The Sense of Power and The Writing of Canadian History wrestle successfully with the way in which private groups tried to understand Canada.

“All written history is in a sense a form of autobiography and an essay of self-knowledge,” Prof. Berger once wrote.

Prof. Berger was a modest, private man who could also be wickedly funny. His approach to historical writing was founded on a deep sense of irony. (His close friend, the celebrated late York University historian Ramsay Cook, titled his essay on Prof. Berger for the Owram-Friesen book, Carl Berger: Ironic Man as Historian , and noted that in much of Prof. Berger’s written work, irony dripped from every page.)

Prof. Berger’s essay “The True North Strong and Free” in political scientist Peter Russell’s 1966 collection Nationalism in Canada begins with some truly outrageous purple poetry (“Hail! Rugged monarch, Northern Winter, hail!”) by William Henry Taylor.

The essay illustrates some of the appalling beliefs that many leaders of Anglo-Saxon Canadian society once held, weaving together racism and nationalism. The following passage, for example, looks at the writing of Upper Canada College headmaster George Parkin (1846-1922).

“[Parkin] asserted, we May attribute to the Anglo-Saxon race a unique aptitude for self-government. The special importance of the Canadian climate, therefore, was not merely that it sustained the hardy character of the stronger races, but that it also constituted, in Darwinian terms, ‘a persistent process of natural selection.’”

The essay, it needs to be pointed out, was referring to Canadian attitudes of the previous century and not to Prof. Berger’s own views (a perfect example of the mechanics of intellectual history referring to attitudes of the past often being starkly different from beliefs of the present).

“If Canadian nationalism is to be understood,” Prof. Berger wrote, “its meaning must be sought and appreciated in myths, legend and symbols.” And setting down his thoughts on the differences between French-Canadian and English-Canadian intellectuals, he wrote: “For both the French-Canadian nationalists and the English-Canadian imperialists, history had ordained a special avocation and nationalism was consecrated by the hand of God.”

Prof. Berger leaves his wife, Laurel Sefton MacDowell; his younger sister, Eileen; his daughters, Rachel Berger and Clare Barnett; stepchildren, Jen MacDowell and Lawrence MacDowell; five grandchildren and two stepgrandchildren.
