Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville police force, was stationed outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue Sept. 20 during a Yom Kippur service. There were about 25 people inside.
Editor’s Picks
He was ambushed by 29-year-old Sean Ward and gravely injured when he was shot in the head and body. The attacker yelled “You are going to die for the Jews” as he opened fire.

Smith was joined less than three minutes later by McCurdy, a seven-year veteran of the force. Ward was struck when the officers returned fire, and died in hospital the next day. Neither McCurdy nor anyone inside the synagogue was injured.

“We cannot imagine the stress of Const. Mike McCurdy arriving on scene to an active shooter and to his fellow officer, Const. Smith, who was suffering from multiple gun shot wounds,” Fogel wrote on the GoFundMe page.

She added that McCurdy “fulfilled the most righteous possible deed. In Judaism, we refer to this as Pikuach Nefesh, the preservation of human life. Const. McCurdy’s actions were selfless and nothing short of heroic.”
Smith has since been released from hospital and is “recovering well at home,” the Belleville Police Service said late last month.

“Constable Smith and his family remain incredibly grateful for the overwhelming support shown by the community and beyond over the past several weeks,” police said in a press release. “Every well wish and message of encouragement has been sincerely appreciated.”
National Post has reached out to Belleville Police Services for more information about both officers.

stories.title: National Capital Commission considering artificial freezing for Rideau Canal
stories.summary: Ottawa - The National Capital Commission is considering a plan to artificially freeze a portion of the Rideau Canal as it copes with the effects of climate change.
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The operators of the iconic Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa May turn to artificial cooling to keep it frozen in coming years, as climate change wreaks havoc with the centrepiece of the city’s Winterlude festival.

A feasibility study investigating the option of using refrigeration pipes to help freeze a 900-metre stretch of the canal in Ottawa’s downtown is currently under consideration by the National Capital Commission.

The project would cover just over 10 per cent of the Skateway. The rest would still rely on the co-operation of nature.

The commission, known as the NCC, is the capital’s public lands planner and manages the cultural character of the area. It manages the Rideau Canal Skateway as a part of a parliamentary mandate.

Tobi Nussbaum, NCC chief operating executive officer, told CBC Radio’s Ottawa Morning show this week the study recommends using refrigeration pipes embedded in concrete — a system similar to the ones used to freeze many outdoor rinks.

Bruce Devine, the Ncc’s senior manager of facilities and programs, told The Canadian Press that if the project proceeds, it would be costly.

“It’s significant. It will be in the millions. We will be looking for funding from a federal program. Other sources of funding will be researched,” he said.

He said the number of days the canal is open could triple if the plan goes ahead, but it wouldn’t happen until after 2030.

Devine said an emphasis would be placed on reducing the project’s carbon footprint.

“If such a system is feasible, the project would be aiming for carbon neutrality. And this is true by identifying opportunities to recover and reuse the heat. So that’s a principle that we have with this project,” he said.

The Skateway first opened in 1971 when the NCC cleared a small portion of ice on the canal for skating. It has since expanded to become the world’s largest skating rink, offering 7.8 kilometres of ice for people to enjoy.

The National Capital Commission says it sees 19,000 visitors daily during the winter months.

The Skateway is also a popular feature of Ottawa’s Winterlude festival, which hosts an average of 500,000 visitors over about 2.5 weeks every February.

In 2023, one of the warmest winters on record kept the Skateway from opening at all for the first time in its history. In 2024, another warmer-than-usual winter meant it could open for just 10 days.

Devine says a plan to ensure at least some of the Skateway can open each year could drive tourism at the Unesco World Heritage site.

“I think people will be able to make a clear decision as to which day they would like to come and plan around their visits. That will be known information, ‘Definitely, I can skate and it’s not weather-permitted.’ So no, I think it’s going to sustain and help tourism,” he said.

The Weather Network says this winter is expected to be warmer than the average.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: National Capital Commission considering artificial freezing for Rideau Canal Skateway
stories.summary: Ottawa — The operators of the iconic Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa May turn to artificial cooling to keep it frozen in coming years, as climate change wreaks havoc with the centrepiece of the city's Winterlude festival.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The operators of the iconic Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa May turn to artificial cooling to keep it frozen in coming years, as climate change wreaks havoc with the centrepiece of the city’s Winterlude festival.

A feasibility study investigating the option of using refrigeration pipes to help freeze a 900-metre stretch of the canal in Ottawa’s downtown is currently under consideration by the National Capital Commission.

The project would cover just over 10 per cent of the Skateway. The rest would still rely on the co-operation of nature.

The commission, known as the NCC, is the capital’s public lands planner and manages the cultural character of the area. It manages the Rideau Canal Skateway as a part of a parliamentary mandate.

Tobi Nussbaum, NCC chief operating executive officer, told CBC Radio’s Ottawa Morning show this week the study recommends using refrigeration pipes embedded in concrete — a system similar to the ones used to freeze many outdoor rinks.

Bruce Devine, the Ncc’s senior manager of facilities and programs, told The Canadian Press that if the project proceeds, it would be costly.

“It’s significant. It will be in the millions. We will be looking for funding from a federal program. Other sources of funding will be researched,” he said.

He said the number of days the canal is open could triple if the plan goes ahead, but it wouldn’t happen until after 2030.

Devine said an emphasis would be placed on reducing the project’s carbon footprint.

“If such a system is feasible, the project would be aiming for carbon neutrality. And this is true by identifying opportunities to recover and reuse the heat. So that’s a principle that we have with this project,” he said.

The Skateway first opened in 1971 when the NCC cleared a small portion of ice on the canal for skating. It has since expanded to become the world’s largest skating rink, offering 7.8 kilometres of ice for people to enjoy.

The National Capital Commission says it sees 19,000 visitors daily during the winter months.

The Skateway is also a popular feature of Ottawa’s Winterlude festival, which hosts an average of 500,000 visitors over about 2.5 weeks every February.

In 2023, one of the warmest winters on record kept the Skateway from opening at all for the first time in its history. In 2024, another warmer-than-usual winter meant it could open for just 10 days.

Devine says a plan to ensure at least some of the Skateway can open each year could drive tourism at the Unesco World Heritage site.

“I think people will be able to make a clear decision as to which day they would like to come and plan around their visits. That will be known information, ‘Definitely, I can skate and it’s not weather-permitted.’ So no, I think it’s going to sustain and help tourism,” he said.

The Weather Network says this winter is expected to be warmer than the average.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stelco to recall 175 laid-off workers in Hamilton, Ont. on Dec. 1
stories.summary: Stelco is recalling 175 temporarily laid off workers as it plans to restart its Hamilton, Ont., finishing operations on Dec. 1.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Stelco is recalling 175 temporarily laid off workers as it plans to restart its Hamilton, Ont., finishing operations on Dec. 1.

The company says the move is due to increased customer demand.

Stelco parent company Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. raised the ire of Ottawa when it announced the layoffs in September.

The federal government said the cuts went against conditions it set when it approved the American company’s purchase of the steelmaker.

Cleveland-Cliffs cited US tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products as reasons for the cuts.

However, it says it has now reached agreement with a sufficient volume of its customers to restart the operations and recall all of the laid off workers.

The company noted that it will take several weeks to restart the operations, but that all affected employees will be made whole retroactively for the standard wages they would have received during the period in which they were temporarily laid off.

stories.title: Feds investing $200M in B.C.'s Woodfibre LNG over three years
stories.summary: Vancouver - The federal government says it is investing $200 million in the Woodfibre LNG project in British Columbia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal government is investing $200 million in British Columbia’s Woodfibre LNG project over three years, funding that Energy Minister Tim Hodgson says will help diversify Canada’s energy exports.

Hodgson said during an announcement in Vancouver that Canada’s Pacific coastline gives the country direct access to some of the world’s most dynamic economies.

“We will seize that advantage,” Hodgson said at a news conference also attended by British Columbia’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson.

“We will turn geographic advantage into conditions to attract investment to this country, to build major projects, and to create jobs for British Columbians and Indigenous Peoples, as we grow this industry in partnership with the private sector.”

Woodfibre LNG is a liquefied natural gas export facility seven kilometres southwest of Squamish, B.C.

CEO Luke Schauerte said the project was about 75 per cent finished, with the first exports more than a year away.

Hodgson said the federal investment would support a nearly 25 per cent increase in the project’s capacity to 2.6 million tonnes of LNG per year, from 2.1 million.

He said the project was taking place in collaboration with the Squamish Nation and the facility was the first major industrial site in Canadian history approved through an Indigenous-led environmental assessment, with the First Nation acting as regulator.

“Woodfibre is a project that should make Canadians proud of not only our resources, but in the kind of energy superpower Canadians are building,” Hodgson said.

Doerkson, who will be sworn in later this month after a decisive win by his B.C. Conservatives in October’s snap election, said the federal investment was welcome news for the region and British Columbia’s economy.

“Our resources are the strongest hand that British Columbia holds, and Woodfibre is what it looks like when we play it,” Doerkson said.

He said the project showed British Columbia’s potential, and what governments, First Nations and industry could achieve when they worked together.

“One question that has come up, whether I’m in the Cariboo, whether I’m in the Okanagan, the Island or Metro (Vancouver) is: Can we still build big things in this province? And today is proof that we can,” he said.

Schauerte said that the project “is already bringing benefits to British Columbia and Canada.”

He said construction alone generated more than $13.6 billion in economic output, and contributed nearly $7 billion to Canada’s gross domestic product.

“We have created more than 52,000 job-years through construction, and with more than 1,500 people on-site today, there is more to come,” he said.

Once completed, the project would generate about $11.6 billion in government revenues over the next 40 years, Schauerte said.

But Marc Lee, senior economist with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, questioned the federal investment.

“Why can’t this project go ahead on straight up commercial terms?” he said.

The economist said Woodfibre LNG and other projects would be competing against a “lot of new supply coming on stream” elsewhere in the world, and Ottawa was responding to this competition by pushing Canadian projects across the “finish line” with various subsidies.

“This is just another one of those,” he said.

Criticism also came from the BC Greens. MLA-elect Jeremy Valeriote said in a statement that the federal money represented another “gift for the fossil fuel industry,” when people and communities were struggling with the cost of living.

Valeriote, who is the MLA for the area where the project is under construction, cited a recent spate of extreme weather that has triggered flooding around Squamish in his opposition to the funding.

“On a day, when our communities are reeling from flooding damage and expecting more and more extreme weather, they deserve a government focused on keeping them safe, not on another fossil fuel project that will only increase the climate risk,” he said.

Interim British Columbia NDP leader Jennifer Whiteside praised the federal investment in the project, saying that the work of the out-going government has helped position the province for a more prosperous future.

stories.title: More electric vehicles exempt from luxury tax, Ottawa says
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced that starting Friday, all electric vehicles that cost less than $150,000 would be exempt from the 10 per cent tax.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
More electric vehicles will now be exempt from Canada’s luxury tax , Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said.

In a press release on Friday, the minister said all electric vehicles that cost less than $150,000 would be exempt from the 10 per cent tax.

The price threshold for luxury vehicles subject to the tax was originally set at $100,000 and included electric vehicles over that threshold.

Canada’s luxury tax was originally proposed in the 2021 budget and covers luxury cars , planes and boats bought for personal use and leisure. The tax was rolled out in September 2022 and would amount to either 10 per cent of the taxable amount of the item, or 20 per cent of the amount over the price threshold – whichever is less.

Champagne said by increasing the price threshold for electric vehicles to $150,000, the government “recognizes the higher upfront cost of zero-emission vehicles and supports the global shift to electric vehicles (EVs).”

All other vehicles remain subject to the $100,000 price threshold.

According to the Canadian Automobile Association, the average price of a new electric vehicle in Canada sits around $50,000, but some models from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Cadillac and Tesla cost well over $100,000.

According to Statistics Canada data released in September, zero-emission vehicles made up 3.5 per cent of Canada’s 25.3 million registered light-duty vehicles in 2025. That same year, there were more than 58,000 new registrations of zero-emission vehicles across the country.

The Department of Finance said EVs are projected to account for nearly 40 per cent of global car sales within five years.

Budget 2026 committed $587 million over five years to install more than 55,000 EV chargers which will more than double the availability of federally supported chargers.

“With Budget 2026, we are expanding our electricity system, cutting emissions, and unlocking new investment in clean technologies,” Champagne said in a news release. “By updating this measure to reflect today’s vehicle market, we are supporting the transition to a cleaner, more competitive economy.”

This is not the first time the luxury tax has been amended.

In Nov. 2025, the federal government scaled back the tax on aircraft and boats after budget numbers showed tax revenues for those items did not yield initial government projections.

stories.title: Stelco recalling laid-off Hamilton workers, citing sufficient demand for its steel
stories.summary: Parent Cleveland-Cliffs laid off 175 workers in September, igniting a fight with Ottawa
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Stelco Inc. is recalling 175 laid-off Ontario steel workers effective Dec 1., ending a faceoff that started in early fall between Ottawa and the company’s U.S. parent, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N

Hamilton-based Stelco announced in a statement on Friday that owing to sufficient demand from customers for its steel, it is in a position to bring back all of the laid-off workers.

“Our customers have committed to support our Hamilton finishing operations,” the company said in the statement.

The restart of its Hamilton galvanized steel operations will take several weeks and all impacted employees will be compensated retroactively for any pay missed while off the job, the company said.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005 in an interview said the recall of the workers is a relief.

“We are happy the government held them accountable, enforced the Investment Canada Act, got our members back in a relatively short period of time, and made them whole,” he said.

On Sept. 28, Stelco announced it was laying off up to 500 workers at two plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont. and in the process ignited a political firestorm.

Cliffs said Stelco’s galvanized-steel business was losing money, and it blamed both U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and a deluge of cheap imports into Canada. But almost immediately, Ottawa alleged that the Ohio-based steel maker had violated a series of legally binding commitments made as a condition for being allowed to acquire Stelco in 2024. Most notably, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly pointed to Stelco’s commitment to maintain employment levels of about 2,400 workers for a period of five years after it acquired the Canadian steel maker in 2024.

While Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves maintained the company was onside with its Investment Canada Act (ICA) commitments, Ms. Joly repeatedly pushed back. In multiple letters and in scores of media appearances, she warned Mr. Goncalves that Cliffs risked being sued, facing financial penalties or being forced to divest Stelco if it didn’t recall the laid-off workers. The notion of nationalizing Stelco was even floated by some.

“This fight was absolutely worth it,” Ms. Joly said in a news conference in Hamilton on Friday evening.

“We’re also sending a message this is a country of the rule of the law and that applies to everyone.”

With Stelco bringing back the steel workers, Ottawa avoids the need to launch a legal suit against Cliffs, something that would have been fraught with uncertainty, and likely have taken years to play out.

There had been signs of a détente emerging between Ottawa and Cliffs in recent weeks, with Mr. Goncalves saying he was planning on recalling the laid-off workers by Christmas if market demand was high enough.

But a week ago, Ms. Joly turned up the heat on Cliffs once again, asking the Competition Bureau to investigate whether Mr. Goncalves’s statement in a media interview that he bought Stelco to prevent it from dumping steel into the U.S. warranted enforcement action.

Mr. Goncalves has pressed Ottawa to reach a “Fortress North America” trade deal with President Donald Trump ’s administration that would see the U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel imports dropped. But Mr. Goncalves has also repeatedly thanked Mr. Trump for bringing in the same tariffs, saying they are helping to reduce a deluge of cheap imports from abroad. After acquiring Stelco, Mr. Gonsalves said he put an end to Stelco selling steel into the U.S., which made it easier for Cliffs to compete in its home market.

While Canada last year brought in stringent measures to reduce imports of foreign steel, including a 50-per-cent tariff on imports above a certain level, Mr. Goncalves has argued the crackdown hasn’t gone far enough in galvanized steel.

Stelco in its Friday statement criticized the government for not doing enough to reduce what it characterizes as a “continued flood” of cheap foreign steel into the market.

stories.title: Avril Lavigne gets her happy ending, welcomes first child
stories.summary: Canada's pop-punk princess is now a pop-punk parent.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada’s pop-punk princess is now a pop-punk parent.

Avril Lavigne has become a mother.

The 42-year-old “Sk8er Boi” singer announced the arrival of her first child, a daughter, in an Instagram post on Friday, featuring a series of black-and-white photos.

The images show Lavigne and her partner holding the newborn’s tiny hand, while another captures the singer-songwriter cradling the baby against her chest.

A final photo features three pairs of checkered Vans sneakers — two adult-sized pairs and a miniature set — laid out on a skateboard.

Lavigne has not publicly identified the child’s father.

“Our Mini F–king Princess has arrived,” she wrote in her caption.

Lavigne, who shot to fame with her 2002 debut album “Let Go,” has had several high-profile relationships, though she has kept her current romance under wraps.

She was married to Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley from 2006 to 2010 and Nickelback singer Chad Kroeger from 2013 to 2015. She was also engaged to musician Mod Sun before the pair split in 2023, and was later romantically linked to rapper Tyga.

Earlier this year, the 10-time Juno winner recorded a cover of Alanis Morissette’s “Ironic” for the Canadian rom-com “Mile End Kicks.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta landowners urge farmers, ranchers to resist oil development
stories.summary: Group says province is failing to deal with issues like orphan wells and unpaid municipal taxes by oil and gas companies
stories.author: Amanda Stephenson
stories.content:
An Alberta landowner advocacy organization is urging farmers and ranchers to “actively resist” new oil and gas development on their land, an unprecedented move highlighting growing tensions between industry and rural residents in Canada’s main energy-producing province.

Growing opposition to oil and gas development in a province that has long supported the oil industry could challenge Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to boost oil output, build new pipelines and attract new markets for Canadian energy.

The Alberta Surface Rights Federation, in a letter sent to Premier Danielle Smith on Thursday, said landowners must push back against energy development given what it calls government’s failure to deal with issues like orphan and abandoned wells, delayed reclamation of oil and gas sites, and unpaid municipal taxes owed by oil and gas companies.

Both the federal and Alberta governments are keen to expand domestic oil production in the face of an escalating trade war with the U.S. But the move by Alberta landowners is evidence of pushback by some who believe economic growth is being prioritized over environmental rules and regulatory obligations.

“Some of these politicians clearly don’t have long-term thinking on their minds,” said Bill Heidecker, president of the Alberta Surface Rights Federation, in an interview.

A spokesman for Alberta’s Energy Minister Brian Jean said the province is committed to working with landowners. He said the government will be bringing forward legislation that addresses liabilities and orphan wells, and is working on a framework to assess a company’s financial viability which will ensure landowners, municipal taxes and creditors are paid by companies.

“We recognize there are frustrations that need to be addressed,” the spokesman said in an e-mail.

The federal government declined to comment.

Heidecker, who describes himself as a conservative rancher not opposed to responsible energy development, said there has been a “stunning erosion of support” for the oil and gas industry in rural Alberta in part due to the province’s struggle to cope with thousands of so-called “orphan” wells that dot Alberta’s rural landscape.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, remains popular there and his efforts to appeal to the oil industry likely helped quell a non-binding referendum on separatism last month.

In September, however, a group of landowners launched legal action to argue that the province’s energy regulator has chronically and knowingly underfunded a program meant to protect the public from the cost of cleaning up these abandoned oil and gas wells.

Studies have shown that abandoned oil and gas wells pose many risks, including potential methane leakage, soil and ground contamination, as well as the financial cost associated with cleanup.

Rural residents are also concerned about the impacts of newer forms of energy development including lithium mining and electricity generation for AI data centres and bitcoin mining, Heidecker said.

In Alberta, landowners possess surface rights – giving them the right to farm the land or exploit surface resources like trees, gravel or water – but mineral rights are for the most part owned by the province, which leases them to energy companies.

Those companies then have the right to enter a landowner’s land to extract the resources.

Heidecker said his organization is not recommending that landowners physically bar energy companies from their property, but that they verbally withhold consent and refuse to sign any new surface leases.

Without consent, oil and gas companies then must seek a legal right-of-entry order to access the property.

Heidecker said Alberta must address issues of energy infrastructure liability and environmental regulation before pushing ahead with its proposed one million-barrel-per-day Pacific Link pipeline project, which would increase Canada’s west coast oil export capabilities and potentially pave the way for oil and gas production expansion in the province.

stories.title: ‘It’s heartbreaking’: Defibrillator donation honours fallen OPP officer
stories.summary: Twenty years ago, a beloved Huron County OPP officer died from injuries sustained in a crash while responding to a call for help.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Twenty years ago today, a beloved Huron County OPP officer died from injuries sustained in a crash while responding to a call for help.

“It’s heartbreaking. But I think he’s watching from above,” said Brenda Orr.

Dave Mounsey’s memory lives on through one of the police officers he trained many years ago. Patrick Armstrong is donating defibrillators to community organizations across Ontario in the names of fallen police officers, firefighters and soldiers. Mounsey and Orr were fundraising for a defibrillator for the Blyth Fire Department shortly before he died.

“In a way, I’m carrying on Dave and Brenda’s work. I’m not going to take the credit and say 275. They did the first one, but I think it’s important to recognize that they did do the first one, and they started what became the Memorial Fund without even knowing it,” said Armstrong.

The first defibrillator from the Dave Mounsey Memorial Fund was installed at the Blyth Festival in 2009. To replace that unit, which simply wore out over time, defibrillator No. 274 was donated to the festival on Thursday.

“The mission of the festival, really, we’re here to inspire and to fill people’s hearts, and to know that now we have this instrument here in this building that is here to protect their hearts and save lives, it just means so much,” said Gil Garratt, artistic director of the Blyth Festival.

“It warms my heart because Dave, obviously, being a police officer, he wanted to serve and protect, save lives. And he was a volunteer firefighter too, same sort of mission. And the fact that there’s a defibrillator in his name that could save a life, and he can continue to do the stuff he was doing when he was alive, just makes me very happy,” said Orr, Mounsey’s partner.

Armstrong said eight lives have been saved by defibrillators donated through the Dave Mounsey Memorial Fund. It is a powerful legacy for a man who touched so many lives in Huron County and beyond.

“You think about all of Dave’s teaching. I’m lucky that I was his rookie as a police officer and he taught me about community, about service. I hope that I exemplify that, and I hope that I’m living up to what he had hoped I would be,” said Armstrong.

Dave Mounsey’s memory lives on through one of the police officers he trained many years ago. Patrick Armstrong is donating defibrillators to community organizations across Ontario in the names of fallen police officers, firefighters and soldiers. Mounsey and Orr were fundraising for a defibrillator for the Blyth Fire Department shortly before he died.

stories.title: Two dead, one missing after flood-related boating incident in Squamish, B.C.
stories.summary: Police say all others involved have been accounted for and search is challenging due to elevated water levels and weather conditions
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
The waters of the Squamish River roared under rainy skies Friday, as search and rescue crews recovered the bodies of three people who died when a boat overturned in the swollen waterway north of Vancouver, following days of heavy rain and flooding in the region.

Insp. Robert Dykstra, the officer in charge of the Sea to Sky RCMP, said there were originally about eight people aboard the boat Thursday, and police said no one is unaccounted for.

But Dykstra wasn’t sure why they were on the water or what caused the boat to overturn.

“I do believe that they ran into something. That’s all I really know at this point,” he told reporters on Friday.

Dykstra said he believed the boat was local to Squamish and he wasn’t aware of any injuries among the survivors of the incident.

The tragedy came after southwest British Columbia was drenched by a series of storms that brought more than 300 millimetres of rain to some areas this week.

The Sea to Sky corridor, including Squamish and Pemberton, was among the areas hardest hit.

Dykstra said police got the call at around 1:50 p.m. on Thursday but it took time for responders to gain access to the area because of a road washout and the state of the raging river.

Police initially said two people had died and a third was missing, but a third body was recovered by Friday afternoon.

Three full white body bags were unloaded from a helicopter at the airport in Squamish around 1:30 p.m., as low-lying clouds rolled in.

Police have not released any details about the victims or survivors.

Dykstra called the situation “tragic.”

“You never know exactly why people are doing what they’re doing sometimes,” he said, adding that “there could be any number of reasons” for the boat being on the water.

Dykstra said the best thing for people to do during major weather events is stay home and stay safe, especially around rapidly moving waters.

“These waters are unforgiving when they’re going fast.”

All of the rainfall warnings that had blanketed the region over the past week were lifted by Friday, but as weather conditions eased, effects of the deluge were still being felt.

A third body has been found after a boat overturned Thursday in the Squamish River, north of Vancouver. The Canadian Press

The entire village of Pemberton, about 90 kilometres north of Squamish, remained under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders imposed by the nearby Lil’wat First Nation, and in Zeballos on Vancouver Island, also remained in place, although an order for parts of Pemberton was downgraded to alert status.

A shelter-in-place advisory issued Thursday for some residents about 16 kilometres north of Squamish was lifted Friday. Still, residents were advised not to drive across flooded roads, and RCMP told residents to stay out of flood zones.

BC Emergency Health Services said it received a call at 2:48 p.m. on Thursday about the boat incident near the 15900 block of Squamish Valley Road. No one was taken to hospital, it said.

At the Squamish airport earlier Friday, a white pickup truck pulled an RCMP boat into the parking lot as members of the local search and rescue team gathered inside their headquarters before deploying to recover the third victim.

Legislator Jeremy Valeriote, who represents West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, said he was “devastated” and his thoughts were with the victims’ families.

Valeriote, who was re-elected as the riding’s Green legislator last month, said the Sea to Sky region “is a strong and resilient community.”

“But no one should have to navigate this alone.”

Valeriote said he and his team would support people however they could as the community begins recovering.

At an unrelated event on Friday, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson called the situation “very serious” and said he intended to visit the area.

“It’s pretty serious in our province right now. So (my) heart goes out to those families that are dealing with the losses. Of course the communities as well. These are small communities and everybody is going to feel the pain in those communities,” he said.

Wilson Williams, chairperson of the Squamish Nation, said at the same event that he was “calling upon Mother Nature” to protect those in areas dealing with the hazardous weather.

The province’s River Forecast Centre downgraded warnings it had issued for the south coast to a lower-level high streamflow advisory. It also ended flood watches for Fraser Valley north, the central coast and east Vancouver Island.

Meanwhile, residents of coastal areas of southwest B.C. were facing a new flooding risk, even as rains eased, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.

Environment Canada said the surge could hit low-lying and exposed coastal areas of Metro Vancouver, southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands.

It said elevated water levels surpassing tidal predictions were being driven by high winds and “enhanced wave activity,” and could last into the weekend.

stories.title: Farm truck caught going 92 km/h in 40 km/h zone: OPP
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police say a 49-year-old driver is charged with careless driving after a farm truck was caught going 92 km/h in a 40 km/h zone.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say a 49-year-old driver has been charged with careless driving after a farm truck was caught going 92 km/h in a 40 km/h zone.

The OPP said the incident occurred around 2:15 p.m. on Nov. 11 in Mapleton Township, which is roughly 50 kilometres west of Orangeville, Ont.

Officers pulled over a truck hauling farm equipment after catching it on radar.

“The piece of farm equipment was also observed to be occupying almost both lanes of traffic, posing as a traffic hazard,” the OPP told Global News in an email.

The driver was charged, and the OPP said the tires on the truck had a safety rating only designed to be driving at 40 km/h.

The OPP said Friday in a post on X the speed is more than double the maximum allowed speed for certain types of farm equipment operating on Ontario roads.

stories.title: Fundraiser for officer injured in Belleville synagogue shooting surpasses $1-million goal
stories.summary: Organized as an expression of gratitude from the Canadian Jewish community, the fundraiser met its target on Thursday.
stories.author: Gabriel Hilty
stories.content:
A fundraiser for Const. Jeff Smith, the officer injured in the shootout outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville , has reached and surpassed its goal of raising $1 million.

With congregants gathered inside on the eve of Yom Kippur, shots pierced the air and riddled the place of worship on Sept. 20 amid a shootout between a lone gunman, Sean Ward, and police. Ward died the next day in hospital while Smith was admitted to the ICU.

Organized by members of the Canadian Jewish community, the GoFundMe fundraiser was set up as an expression of “profound gratitude” to Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue, and to support Smith and his family during his recovery, according to organizer Derek Kreindler.

Sons of Jacob congregants returned to the building for the first time since bullets pierced its

Around two dozen people were inside Belleville’s Sons of Jacob synagogue when police say Ward arrived with a stockpile of ammunition and gasoline. Police and Ward exchanged gunfire, between 20 and 30 shots according to some witnesses, and Smith was hit multiple times.

In Judaism, “pikuach nefesh” is the principle of preserving a life, Kreindler wrote, adding that Smith exemplified this in September.

“Const. Smith fulfilled that obligation not through words, but through courage and action. When members of a vulnerable community needed protection, he put himself in harm’s way,” Kreindler said on the GoFundMe.

In an update posted Friday morning, Kreindler said the fundraiser has stopped accepting donations after reaching its target at the request of Smith’s family, and that the money raised will be administered to the family’s designated beneficiary through GoFundMe.

According to an update in late October, Belleville police informed the fundraiser that Smith was released from the hospital and continuing to recover at home.

In a video released by police, Ward was heard saying “you are going to die for the Jews,” as he started his attack, with investigators classifying it as a hate-motivated crime and describing it as a thwarted attempt at a mass killing of Jewish worshippers.

Shima Vigodda, vice-president of the synagogue, said that costly enhanced security measures are necessary to protect congregants.

Speaking at a press conference in Ottawa on Nov. 2, Vigodda said priorities include replacing windows and installing burglar alarms.

He said it has become clear that more expensive measures are also necessary, including bullet-resistant glass, building a safe room and having security personnel or armed police on site.

“These measures are necessary not only to ensure our physical safety, but to deter would-be attackers,” Vigodda said. “For many in our congregation who were there on Yom Kippur, it is also a necessity for them to feel comfortable to return.”

He indicated that money from a federal program to help places of worship improve security would not fully cover the more extensive measures.

stories.title: Alberta changes graduation requirements for high school students
stories.summary: Students will soon be allowed to graduate with fewer math, science and humanities courses under their belts
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
High school students in Alberta will soon be allowed to graduate with fewer math, science and humanities courses under their belts.

Alberta’s government says that starting with students entering high school in 2028, only 47 credits in core classes will be required, down from the current 56.

The government’s new requirements mean that students will only need to complete one senior level course in either English or social studies, while senior level math and science classes will still not be mandatory.

Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides says the new system will allow students to spend more time developing interests or learning hands-on skills for jobs after graduation by taking more optional classes.

While the government is reducing the need for core subjects, it is making physical education classes mandatory throughout high school instead of just Grade 10.

Nicolaides says the government also plans to mandate a new wellness and financial literacy course for all three years of high school.

“These changes will give students more choice to find their passions, prepare for further schooling or rewarding job opportunities,” Nicolaides told reporters in Calgary on Friday.

“More flexibility does not mean lower expectations. Students will continue to build strong basics in core classes and will have to write at least one diploma [exam] to graduate.”

stories.title: E-mail services restored to Toronto hospitals after Microsoft outage caused some disruptions
stories.summary: The City of Toronto has said some services May be temporarily unavailable or delayed as a result of the outage
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hospitals and other health institutions in Toronto say their e-mail services are returning to normal after a global Microsoft 365 outage caused some delays and disruptions.

Unity Health Toronto, which includes St. Michael’s Hospital and St. Joseph’s Health Centre, says staff experienced difficulties sending and receiving e-mails on Thursday but people could reach a clinic or department by calling the main hospital phone line.

The health-care network says patient and resident care is not affected by the outage and its hospitals continue to operate.

University Health Network, which includes Toronto General Hospital, Princess Margaret Cancer Centre and others, also says the e-mail outage didn’t impact patient care.

Sunnybrook Hospital, the largest trauma centre, says it remains open for care as staff experience difficulties sending and receiving e-mails, but people can still reach clinics about upcoming appointments by calling the main hospital phone line.

The outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft said Outlook e-mail service was up and running again for many users in North America as of Friday morning, but warned that some users may still encounter “intermittent access issues or delayed e-mail delivery.”

The City of Toronto has said some services may be temporarily unavailable or delayed as a result of the Microsoft outage.

Meanwhile, Via Rail said its train operations continue normally across its network despite the Microsoft disruption.

“Considering that some passengers may have intermittent access to their emails, we encourage them to use the Via Rail train tracker or to subscribe to SMS notifications through the Via Rail train status and schedules page to get the most up-to-date information about their train,” it said.

stories.title: Quebec won't talk independence at Francophonie summit, minister says
stories.summary: Phnom Penh - The new Parti Québécois government won't be discussing independence at the Francophonie Summit which starts Sunday in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.
stories.author: Caroline Plante The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Phnom Penh - The new Parti Québécois government won’t be discussing independence at the Francophonie Summit which starts Sunday in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

International Relations Minister Dieudonné Ella Oyono told reporters today that he won’t be bringing up the topic on his very first overseas mission.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum on sovereignty by 2030, although not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.

In the event of a “Yes” victory, the province would need to secure international recognition of Quebec as a country.

But Ella Oyono said that’s not an immediate priority, as he spoke to reporters on the margins of a conference on scientific diplomacy in Phnom Penh.

He said the Quebec delegation did not plan to discuss independence or make any dramatic gestures.

“We don’t need to talk about Quebec’s independence, because everyone knows that a pro-independence government was elected in Quebec City,” he said.

“So, do we need to shout it from the rooftops? I don’t think so.”

On Wednesday, in an interview with The Canadian Press, Roxane Milot of Québec solidaire encouraged the government to assert itself and “promote its own vision on the international stage.”

Speaking in Quebec City on Friday, Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said, “If we can avoid talking about separation for two days, that would be fantastic.”

St-Pierre Plamondon is set to meet Prime Minister Mark Carney at the summit for a first in-person meeting since the PQ took power.

Ella Oyono was also reluctant to say whether St-Pierre Plamondon would try to push the case to name Montreal as the headquarters of the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.

“The bank will choose the best location to set up,” he said.

However, that decision rests with Carney, who has the choice between Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, and Ottawa. The competition is expected to be fierce.

The previous Quebec government and Montreal’s mayor had lobbied for the new bank’s headquarters to be in Montreal. Former premier Christine Fréchette’s government had said the institution could create 3,500 jobs over five years and bring in some $620 million in annual economic benefit.

“As far as we’re concerned, we’re not part of those discussions,” Ella Oyono said, while adding, “But there’s no doubt that Montreal has everything it takes to host this institution.”

St-Pierre Plamondon will begin his mission in Phnom Penh on Saturday, where he’ll meet with the business delegation from Investissement Québec International.

He will then deliver a speech at a meeting of entrepreneurs.

Later Saturday, the premier will meet with the current secretary general of the International Organization of la Francophonie, Louise Mushikiwabo.

Mushikiwabo is seeking a third term as head of the OIF, but Quebec has not yet taken a position in the race.

On Sunday, the premier will meet the president of Senegal and visit the Quebec booth at FrancoTech before meeting with Carney.

Tensions arose between the premier and prime minister after St-Pierre Plamondon refused to attend the recent Canada-European Union Summit in Montreal because he had not been granted speaking rights.

St-Pierre Plamondon then insisted that a first meeting between the two leaders take place in Quebec City, instead of in Montreal or Ottawa-Gatineau as Carney initially proposed.

The two men will ultimately have their first in-person meeting in Phnom Penh. According to St-Pierre Plamondon’s official schedule, the meeting is expected to last no more than 30 minutes.

They are expected to discuss homelessness, immigration, and culture, among other topics.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

On Sunday, the premier will meet the president of Senegal and visit the Quebec booth at FrancoTech before meeting with Carney.
Tensions arose between the premier and prime minister after St-Pierre Plamondon refused to attend the recent Canada-European Union Summit in Montreal because he had not been granted speaking rights.
St-Pierre Plamondon then insisted that a first meeting between the two leaders take place in Quebec City, instead of in Montreal or Ottawa-Gatineau as Carney initially proposed.

stories.title: Coroner's inquest begins in case of Jamal Francique, shot by police in Mississauga
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the death of a man shot in the head by police in Mississauga, Ont., is now underway.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The parents of a man shot in the head by police in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago told a coroner’s inquest into his death Friday that while nothing can bring back their beloved son, they hope the proceedings will provide some much-needed answers about what happened that day — and what could have been done differently.

Derek Francique and Ann-Marie White each delivered tearful messages to the jury on the first day of the inquest into the death of Jamal Francique, sharing memories of the man they described as a smart, considerate son and devoted father whose loss forever shattered their lives.

“He always was the glue to our family,” Derek Francique said of his son.

“Our family is destroyed without him. Our family hopes to gain a fuller understanding of police tactics... and the role that anti-Black racism May have played in the police decision-making,” he said.

“Everything should be investigated ... I would like to know how many different non-violent ways this could have turned out.”

White said she still struggles with the reality that her son is no longer there.

“I am not simply grieving an event that happened in the past. I am living with this loss, this pain every single day,”

“No outcome can undo the pain ... and personally I’m consumed by agony and grief and I hope through this inquest the circumstances surrounding my beautiful son’s death will be examined carefully and that the questions that remain will be addressed.”

Jamal Francique’s partner and the mother of his children, Isabel Meira, also expressed her enduring grief in a statement read by her lawyer, saying Francique was ripped out of their lives too early and “did not deserve this ending.”

In his opening remarks, inquest counsel Roger Shallow stressed that Francique was not an incident or a file number.

“He was a grandson, a father, a brother, a member of a family, and a young man whose life ended in circumstances that have had a profound effect on many people and will continue to,” he said.

“Nothing that happens at this inquest will change what happened to him.”

Francique, a 28-year-old Black man, was shot during an attempted arrest outside his home on Jan. 7, 2020, and died in hospital days later.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest said Francique was living with his mother and stepfather at the time. Both were acting as his sureties while he was on bail from drug trafficking and firearm charges he faced in Guelph, the narrative said.

Francique was on house arrest with conditions that allowed him to leave the home only in the company of his sureties, for work or school, for medical emergencies or for prearranged appointments with his lawyer, doctor or physiotherapist, the inquest heard.

Peel regional police had recently received a tip through Crime Stoppers that Francique had a gun and was trafficking drugs, so they secretly observed him over three days, the inquest heard.

By Jan. 7, however, they had found no evidence to corroborate the tip, according to the narrative. Still, the officers believed that Francique was breaching one of his bail conditions and a briefing was held that day to plan his arrest, it said.

Around 5 p.m., not long after sunset, a team of plainclothes officers in unmarked cars made their way to the townhouse complex where Francique lived, the inquest heard. They placed a tire-deflating device behind one of the tires of his car and waited for him to emerge, the narrative said.

At 7:44 p.m., Francique left the home and made his way to his car, an Acura, about 200 metres away, it said. The officer who was supposed to block in the car was late, and Francique reversed out of his parking spot then accelerated around the unmarked cruiser, the inquest heard.

At that point, several officers on foot and in unmarked cars were trying to contain the Acura, the inquest heard. One of the officers on foot fired his gun four times, and one of the bullets hit Francique on the left side of the head, leaving him with what was later deemed an “unsurvivable” injury, jurors heard.

His car veered sharply and crashed into the pillar of a nearby garage, where it came to a stop, jurors heard. The officers notified dispatch and requested a tactical unit. An ambulance was also called to the scene.

The tactical unit arrived at 8:05 p.m., and the ambulance minutes later, the narrative said. Francique was removed from the car and seen by paramedics, then taken to the trauma unit at Toronto’s St. Michael’s Hospital. He was declared brain dead shortly before noon on Jan. 9, jurors heard.

Ontario’s police watchdog later cleared the police officers of wrongdoing, saying the officer who opened fire reported fearing for his life when Francique drove toward him.

The Special Investigations Unit said there were aspects of the officer’s behaviour that gave rise to questions, however, including the decision to place himself near a fleeing vehicle.

The inquest will look at Peel regional police procedures and training, including on use of force when a vehicle is involved, oversight of preplanned arrests, medical care for suspects who are incapacitated and anti-Black racism, among other topics.

Its scope does not include the investigations carried out by various watchdog agencies.

The inquest was initially scheduled to start Thursday but was pushed back by a day. As a result, the schedule needed adjustment, and the first witness is expected to testify Monday.

The inquest is expected to hear from about 12 witnesses over 10 days, including four of the seven officers involved in the operation, police supervisors, a police instructor and a forensic pathologist.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility but May make recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Police in Cape Breton disrupt major, national stolen vehicle trafficking ring
stories.summary: Sydney - Police in Cape Breton say they’ve uncovered a major stolen vehicle trafficking ring following an investigation that began when a stolen vehicle was tracked to a property in a small, rural community.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sydney - Police in Cape Breton say they’ve uncovered a major stolen vehicle trafficking ring following an investigation that began when a stolen vehicle was tracked to a property in a small, rural community.

The regional police force has laid 220 criminal charges against four people, two from Cape Breton and two from Ontario, following a 16-month investigation.

stories.title: TikTok says it has taken down deepfake videos spreading trade falsehoods
stories.summary: Ottawa - TikTok says it has taken down accounts associated with a network that uses deepfakes to spread divisive and false content to Canadians.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The company says it has permanently banned the accounts named in a report released by McGill University’s Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy on Thursday.

TikTok says it also launched its own investigation that removed additional content and accounts that were breaking the platform’s rules on deceptive behaviour and misleading AI-generated content.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The McGill report says the network uses deepfakes of real influencers, and included nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts whose videos were viewed 22.1 million times in the past three months.

The report says many of the videos focused on the U.S.-Canada trade war and the most-watched videos included false information.

It says it’s not clear who is behind the network but it is “almost certainly” run from outside of North America.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Eby seemed inauthentic during failed election campaign, former B.C. minister Brenda Bailey says
stories.summary: She called last month’s crushing defeat a ‘harsh judgment’ on the outgoing premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
One of David Eby’s former top lieutenants said he came across as inauthentic during the BC Ndp’s failed election campaign, calling last month’s crushing defeat a “harsh judgment” on the outgoing premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote.

Brenda Bailey, who served as finance and jobs minister under Eby, delivered her post-mortem on the Oct. 24 election in an interview in which she also said she had successfully undergone cancer treatment and was taking a break from politics to enter the private sector.

Bailey, who did not seek re-election in Vancouver-South Granville, said there had been “a lot of piling on Eby and it feels a little unfair” – but nevertheless contrasted Eby’s campaign persona with premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s, calling the B.C. Conservative leader a “deeply authentic man” and “very likable.”

Doerkson’s appointment as interim leader of the Conservatives, she said, was a “brilliant” move by the party.

“I look at [the election] through the lens of authenticity, and I don’t think Eby came across as authentic,” she said Thursday.

Eby stepped down as NDP leader on election night after the scale of the Conservative victory became clear, having secured a two-thirds majority with 64 seats, while the NDP ranks were decimated from 47 to 27.

It ended nine years of NDP rule, with Eby at the helm since 2022.

Bailey singled out two moments as emblematic of Eby’s authenticity problem – his Sept. 22 announcement of the election outside Government House, and a pre-election appearance where he wore a red-and-black checked jacket and the audience was warmed up by a parody rapper who mocked U.S. President Donald Trump.

She called the election announcement where Eby justified the snap vote by citing the threat posed by Trump “perhaps the weakest presser I’ve ever seen the premier give.”

“It was kind of clear from that very first presser that Eby’s explanation of why to go now wasn’t resonating, even with him,” she said.

Bailey said Eby had “many redeeming qualities,” but the “lumber-jacket-at-the-border version of David Eby, it doesn’t work.”

“Going down to the border and wearing that coat, that’s not who David Eby is and people could tell. So it’s less a criticism of him as a human than what he specifically did during this election run, not having resonated with the public, in my opinion.”

She said Eby used explanations to justify the election that he believed would poll well, rather than what he knew to be true.

She described the election call as “quite defensible” because there was “a real sense of instability” around the government with its one-seat majority, which was hurting its ability to respond to U.S. tariffs.

Bailey said Eby was struggling to “tap dance” to keep the party together at a time when everyone in the caucus effectively had a policy veto.

But Eby’s explanation to the public that he needed to “build a firebreak” against Trump-style politics coming to British Columbia “didn’t work at all” once Doerkson became the Conservatives’ interim leader.

The day that Eby called the vote, Doerkson called Trump an “absolute bully” and said Canada would never be the 51st state.

“I think it was strategically brilliant to put Lorne Doerkson as the candidate,” Bailey said of the Conservatives’ choice after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay two days before the election call.

Bailey also said the decision to go to the polls was made at an NDP caucus meeting held on Sunday, Sept. 20, even though the Conservatives had not yet announced their interim leader.

The former minister said she did not take part in the meeting as she was “quite sick” but the decision was shared with her later.

Bailey also said her cancer treatment “was fully successful.”

“They detected it very early. I had a surgery and the surgery got all the cancer and I’ve just been recovering from surgery. I haven’t had to have chemotherapy, I haven’t had to have radiation,” she said.

“And I would say as of last week, I feel fully back to normal. So I’ve been very, very lucky.”

While she is still a member of the NDP, “time will tell” if she remains in the party, which she said runs the risk of being in opposition for a very long time if it moves too far to the left.

“I struggle with where I live politically,” she said.

“I want to be a member of a party that is fiscally responsible, and has strong social goals,” she said. “That is the party I want and I think that is the party that I think most British Columbians want and often struggle to find.”

Jennifer Whiteside has been named as the BC Ndp’s interim leader.

When Bailey was asked about the odds of her throwing her hat in the ring as leader, she said “absolutely none.”

“You couldn’t make me,” she said.

stories.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ turns Canadian duo Bob Moses’s song into a viral hit
stories.summary: Bob Moses didn’t have to steal a car, pull off a heist, or even pick up a controller to score big with “Grand Theft Auto VI.”
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Bob Moses didn’t have to steal a car, pull off a heist, or even pick up a controller to score big with “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

All the Canadian electronic duo needed was a killer song and an email from Rockstar Games.

They say their 2021 collaboration with British musician Elderbrook, “Inner Light,” has racked up more than 50 million additional streams since being featured in an extended trailer for the game in late August.

Fans have waited more than a decade for “GTA VI,” which finally arrives Thursday. But “Inner Light” has already taken on a life of its own, spreading across social media and reaching listeners far beyond the electronic music scene.

Vancouver’s Tom Howie and Jimmy Vallance, who formed the Grammy-nominated duo in 2012, say their manager emailed them earlier this year with a request from Rockstar to use their song, with few details about how it would be featured.

“We were like, sweet, ‘GTA’ is a big game. And then we sort of forgot about it,” recalls Howie.

Months later, their phones lit up with messages from people they hadn’t heard from in years.

It turned out “Inner Light” had landed a prime spot during the trailer’s climax, its haunting, synth-driven melodies underscoring an emotional speech about living in one’s “glory days.”

“It became the part that everyone clipped and re-shared and kind of made the song go viral,” says Vallance.

Spotify says the track saw a 500 per cent surge in streams since the trailer dropped, with daily additions to listeners’ playlists increasing by more than 3,000 per cent.

The unexpected success comes as musicians face mounting pressure to create viral moments in an increasingly crowded streaming landscape.

Vallance says the experience reinforced something the duo has learned over years of navigating an industry reshaped by TikTok and social media: there’s no reliable formula for a hit.

“You can’t engineer this in a lab,” he says.

“Someone somewhere liked a song that we wrote one day and put it in the trailer, and then that connected with millions of people.”

The duo says they were paid a relatively modest licensing fee.

“I forget how much money it was, but it’s not enough to remember,” says Howie.

“The opportunity is definitely in the potential for the reach, not in the paycheque.”

Toronto music supervisor Heather Gardner says that’s not unusual.

Gardner, president of the Guild of Music Supervisors Canada, says a placement in a gaming behemoth like “GTA” can be valuable even when the licensing payment itself isn’t especially lucrative.

“It’s such a cultural icon,” she says of the franchise.

“No one can pay their bills in exposure, but it really is in an industry that is so saturated musically right now. Everybody is looking for a way to break through and to get eyes and ears on them and a sync, beyond the payment, is absolutely that.”

Music has long been integral to the “GTA” experience, with the franchise’s fictional radio stations introducing generations of players to an eclectic mix of genres as they cruise city streets, mow down pedestrians, and outrun police.

For “GTA VI,” Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice composed the score, while Rockstar plans to release an album of original songs Thursday, featuring SZA, Tame Impala, and Keith Richards. The musical celebrations will continue into the weekend with a “GTA”-themed concert in Miami featuring Travis Scott and Cardi B.

Gardner says video games offer a particularly powerful form of music discovery because players aren’t simply watching or listening.

“You’re an active participant in the media in a way that no other form can do.”

Vallance is a longtime fan of the “GTA” series, recalling playing the original top-down game of the ’90s on a friend’s computer before becoming captivated by the leap to three-dimensional gameplay in “Grand Theft Auto III.”

But it was the 1980s-inspired soundtrack of “Grand Theft Auto: Vice City” that left the deepest musical impression, introducing him to acts such as A Flock of Seagulls and sparking an interest in the synth-pop sounds of that era.

Vallance says it’s a “huge honour” his own music has now become part of the franchise’s cultural orbit. The placement has also given the duo a moment of validation after years of navigating the uncertainties of a music career.

“Every once in a while something happens and you’re like, ‘Oh, we’re a real band.'”

“GTA VI” is estimated to bring in $3.25 billion to $5.2 billion in first-week sales, according to market research firm Newszoo.

Howie believes the game serves as a tastemaker at a time when audiences are increasingly fragmented across countless entertainment platforms.

“There’s not many things that tons of people do all together anymore. We used to all watch the same shows and listen to the same radio stations and read the same things,” he says.

“‘GTA’ is one of the very few things that a lot of people still come around to; that’s a unifying thing on a scale that doesn’t really exist in today’s age.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Saskatchewan hospital safety review complete, but findings won’t be released yet
stories.summary: The six-month review is now in the health ministry's hands, but Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill says he does not want to expose vulnerabilities until they are addressed.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatchewan’s health minister says the independent safety review commissioned by the province earlier this year is now complete, but will not be shared publicly until the ministry addresses its recommendations.

Jeremy Cockrill said Thursday that there is work to be done between the Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) and the Ministry of Health to review some of the “immediate pressures” identified in the report and to work with facilities to implement them.

“I don’t want to put a report out there that May share vulnerabilities that both are there for staff and patients in health care facilities,” said Cockrill at an unrelated press conference in North Battleford, Sask.

The Health Ministry announced in January it was launching a review into hospital safety at the request of the SHA following a string of violent incidents and mounting concerns at facilities across the province.

In May, the province announced it had contracted Buckingham Security Services Ltd. to conduct the six-month review, under the leadership of executive director and former Saskatoon police chief Clive Weighill.

Cockrill said he met with the contracted firm earlier this week for the first time since the report was finalized, adding it did a “really fantastic job” evaluating the current safety status of health care facilities and future opportunities.

The finished review now presents the province with an opportunity to accelerate the work needed to address vulnerabilities, Cockrill said.

“So we’ll be having some discussions with both the ministry and the Saskatchewan Health Authority and many of our site leads right around the province and health care facilities to say, ‘Hey, this specific item was addressed in this facility; this needs to get dealt with in the next 30 days.'”

The review was expected to involve around 30 people and cost the province $1 million , according to the health ministry. It would involve a review of current safety practices at SHA facilities and provide recommendations to improve safety for patients, visitors and staff.

Weighill previously told Global News that his team would talk to a range of stakeholders, including unions, protective services officers, First Nations and new immigrants to Canada.

The announcement of the review also came weeks after the death of 36-year-old Trevor Dubois, who died on Jan. 9 following an altercation with security staff at Saskatoon’s Royal University Hospital.

But Weighill said the review will not investigate the circumstances of that incident and will only be reviewed at a high level, along with other security incidents, to identify trends.

In January, the province responded to the mounting hospital safety concerns by installing metal detectors at emergency department entrances in Saskatoon, Regina, Prince Albert and North Battleford.

The SHA also said it would hire 51 protective service workers to staff the detectors in the province, with the cost of the detectors and staff totalling $3 million.

Alongside these previous investments, Cockrill said the Health Ministry will also bring forward “a more comprehensive plan,” with work to be done on the best way to execute it.

“There’s more work to do, but you’re going to see, out of this report, I think, really a more integrated plan come forward.”

Cockrill did not provide a timeline for releasing the review.

stories.title: Beer recall hits 2 more Canadian products, bringing total to 31
stories.summary: Quebec-based Archibald Inc. issued the recall for its Nuit Blanche White IPA 473 ml cans as well as four packs due to pieces of metal.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A Quebec-based microbrewery and restaurant operator has issued a beer recall for two of its products just three days after more than two dozen alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer products were pulled off the shelves nationwide from other brands.

Archibald Inc. issued the recall for its Nuit Blanche White IPA 473 ml cans as well as four packs.

A notification from the Canadian Food Inspection Agency says the product was recalled due to pieces of metal.

The agency is requesting that all retailers cease the selling, serving or distributing of the affected products.

The recall comes just days after Molson Canada 2005, the official Canadian subsidiary of Molson Coors Beverage Company, issued a recall for 29 of its products due to pieces of metal.

Blue Moon, Black Horse, Brasseur de Montreal, Coors Light, Hop Valley, India Beer and Molson Canadian are the brands affected by the recall.

The affected products include:

Black Horse beer 8 x 355ml

Blue Moon Non-alcoholic Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 6 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Non-alcoholic Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 24 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 24 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 24 x 473 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 4 x 473 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 12 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 473 ml

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour 24 x 473 ml

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour 473 ml

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour 4 x 473ml

stories.title: A condo discount startup, streamlining mortgage applications and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Nov. 13
stories.summary: Plus, house-hunting in St. John’s, N.L.
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: A startup promises condo discounts at a cost, and the CRA could help speed up your mortgage application. Plus, what $442,000 gets you in St. John’s and one property worth a look.

Would you agree to keep quiet to save five- or even six-figures on a new condo? Real estate startup QuietMarket is promising to get individual buyers the major discounts on unsold units usually reserved for large investors buying in bulk. One recent buyer snagged a condo in Toronto’s Annex neighbourhood for $663,000, a 44 per cent discount off the original $1.18-million listing price. But as Salmaan Farooqui reports, the savings the startup promises come at the cost of your silence.

As the condo crash has left developers eager to unload their unsold condos, QuietMarket sprung up to create an online marketplace for units in the Greater Toronto Area at discounted or unlisted prices. Founder Cara Hirsch says the prices of the units on QuietMarket are generally at least 10 per cent cheaper than what’s on offer on the resale market, and discounted up to 50 per cent compared to the units’ 2022 listing prices.

However, to see more than basic details about the roughly 100 units listed, users need to sign a nondisclosure agreement, something we’ve previously written about condo developers turning to but consumer advocates have cautioned against. Read Salmaan’s story about how QuietMarket works , and experts’ advice on how to limit your risk if you do give it a try.

If you’ve been dreaming of moving to St. John’s for years – or just since Netflix’s Newfoundland-set giant-squid thriller Below made a splash last month – you might be wondering how much bang you can get for your buck in Newfoundland and Labrador’s biggest city. St. John’s median detached home price hit $442,000 in September, slightly down from the summer, but as Shane Dingman reports, the province’s market is one of the few in Canada where sale and prices are rising in most categories.

So what does that get you in the city, compared to what the $723,000 national median home price or even $1-million could buy? From an iconic brightly-coloured Jellybean Row house to a million-dollar listing with ocean views, Shane takes you on a tour of St. John’s real estate market at every budget.

Which of the three homes is the best deal? Read Shane’s story , put yourself in a N.L. buyer’s shoes and cast your vote in our reader poll.

If you hate digging up every pay stub, bank statement and tax return just to prove you make what you say you make, know that mortgage lenders enjoy going through all that paperwork even less. That’s why Ottawa is creating a pilot program that could speed up the process for borrowers and lenders – and help crack down on mortgage fraud.

The Canada Revenue Agency will establish and test a system for lenders to quickly verify mortgage applicants’ incomes with the agency in the next three years, according to a proposal in last week’s federal budget. As Salmaan Farooqui reports, this would make it even more difficult for someone to overstate their income to dupe lenders into a mortgage bigger than they can afford. “With the ability of AI to generate these documents, it’s getting harder and harder to confirm whether they’re fraudulent or not,” said Kevin Fettig, president of alternative mortgage lender CMI Financial Group.

And for all you straight-up mortgage applicants, lenders say the administrative savings of the income-verification portal could translate to slightly lower borrowing costs for you. Read Salmaan’s story on how the pilot program might help save money, time and the trees.

This year I finally parted ways with the Ikea pull-out couch that had seen me through nine years and six apartments, and my guests’ backs and necks have thanked me for it. But Matthew Hague writes – and I certainly found out – the only thing harder than sleeping on a bad sofabed is finding a good one .

Double-duty sofabeds have been gaining appeal as homes become smaller, and while they don’t exactly have a reputation for being chic, there’s now hope for finding one that is both stylish and comfortable. From a sleek, armless futon with multiple configurations to the justttt right “Goldilocks of couches,” here are six sofabeds to consider and experts’ advice for choosing wisely. (For what my months-long search is worth, I ended up going with a regular sofa and sleep kit from Cozey that fits one, and the reviews have been raves so far).

5 Undercliffe Ave., Hamilton, Ont. – Full gallery here

This grand mansion is just over a century old, but it’s already lived a millennium’s worth of stories. Built by the prominent diamond-dealing Levy family, it was brought to near ruin by high-flying financier Ron Koval, who abandoned it in the late ’90s when he fled accusations of a massive $100-million fraud. But after he was caught and convicted in 2001, a couple who lived down the street, and their community, conspired to bring the Levy House back to its former glory.

Dr. John Miller and his wife Pat Miller tackled burst pipes, mould, caved-in ceilings and damaged heritage features with a little help from their friends, including a neighbour who restored all the doorknobs and hardware, and another who located an expert to replace the aged ropes and pulleys on the counterweight windows. It took almost a year, but now the century-old Georgian-style home is a faithful reflection of its era with a few modern updates.

Rich, dark-stained oak floors run through the central hall and two wings of the home, and the same wood clads the window trims, crown moldings and staircase with an air of grandeur. In the stunning library, built-in shelves and elaborate, Corinthian-column-inspired carvings fill the walls but were designed to leave gaps for large works from the Levy family’s significant art collection. The kitchen was renovated with white Shaker cabinets and dark floors to be cohesive with the home’s original features, and on the upper floors, a total of seven bedrooms offer plenty of space – though hopefully not for any more scheming.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

a. $1,995,000 b. $2,395,000 c. $2,795,000 d. $3,195,000 b. The asking price is $2,395,000.

stories.title: Two workers hurt, one seriously, at Meaford-area job site
stories.summary: Grey Bruce OPP said officers and paramedics responded to a report of two injured workers at a job site near Highway 26, between 6th Concession Road North and Grey Road 11, shortly after 9 a.m. on Nov. 11.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
An 18-year-old man was taken to hospital and a 16-year-old boy suffered serious injuries in a workplace incident near Meaford, provincial police say.

Grey Bruce OPP said officers and paramedics responded to a report of two injured workers at a job site near Highway 26, between 6th Concession Road North and Grey Road 11, shortly after 9 a.m. on Nov. 11.

Police said the 18-year-old was transported to a local hospital for treatment, while the 16-year-old was taken to a trauma centre with serious injuries.

No further details about the incident have been released.

The investigation is continuing.

Police reminded employers and workers that proper training, safe work practices and compliance with workplace safety regulations are key to preventing serious injuries on the job.
