stories.title: Former top Mountie to be sentenced for assault on teen in B.C. court
stories.summary: Abbotsford British Columbia - A former senior RCMP officer who held a teenager off the floor by their neck while off duty is expected to be sentenced today in a British Columbia provincial court.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ABBOTSFORD BRITISH COLUMBIA - Former RCMP assistant commissioner David Teboul has been given a conditional discharge by a judge in Abbotsford, B.C., after he pleaded guilty to the off-duty assault of a 16-year-old at a lacrosse game last year.

It means if he abides by the court’s conditions he will not have a criminal record, but he’s been ordered to provide a DNA sample, he must abide by a weapons prohibition for his 12-month probation period and has 50 hours of community work to complete.

Provincial court Judge Carmen Rogers read out her reasons for sentencing in an Abbotsford courtroom on Thursday.

Rogers said Teboul committed a “serious assault,” using what her decision said was a judo hold on the teenager.

“Mr. Teboul still has work to do to address the factors that led to the commission of the assault,” the judge said.

“He accepted responsibility for his actions and demonstrated remorse by apologizing to his victims. I accept his remorse and his acceptance of responsibility for this crime.”

Teboul resigned from the force in July and pleaded guilty last month to assaulting the teenager, who the court heard was lifted off the floor by their neck in an unprovoked attack at a lacrosse game attended by Teboul’s son in Abbotsford, B.C.

The ruling said that Teboul, his wife, son and his son’s girlfriend gave statements to Abbotsford police, but their version of events were “not consistent with the video” of the altercation.

The court heard that Teboul suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder from his more than 25 years as a police officer, with a psychological report outlining what he’s been exposed to during his career.

“He has had hundreds of exposures to human remains, decapitations, drownings, hangings, gunshot wounds, and eviscerated bodies,” the report said.

“Although not clearly set out in the report, it seems reasonable to conclude that the trauma described in the report has led to PTSD and that the PTSD is impacting Mr. Teboul’s functioning. Its role in the incident before the court is unknown,” the judge’s ruling said.

Special prosecutor Andi MacKay told the court last month that Teboul’s actions were “gratuitous and opportunistic violence” and she asked that he serve a suspended sentence with 18 months of probation.

An agreed statement of facts said Teboul’s son had an argument with the victim after a game at the Abbotsford Recreation Centre on July 2, 2025, and Teboul grabbed the teen’s neck twice.

The first occasion was brief but Teboul lifted the youth off the floor in the second instance for about 15 seconds as he bent the victim over a low wall, the court heard.

The plea on the single charge comes more than a year after Teboul was charged with two counts of assault and one count of assault causing bodily harm by choking, suffocating or strangling.

His lawyer, Brock Martland, told the court last month that granting his client a conditional discharge was an appropriate sentence for a father who acted on “protective instinct” when his son faced what he viewed as a threat of violence.

Martland said Teboul had no intention of intimidating the youth when he identified himself as a police officer, saying his client “has a duty” to do so during an altercation.

The lawyer said the guilty plea reflected Teboul’s recognition of wrongdoing.

He said his client had lost his career, livelihood, and “his previously outstanding reputation” as a result of the assault that lasted less than a minute.

The RCMP said last month that Teboul voluntarily submitted his discharge document over the summer and retired after 29 years of service.

Teboul, the prosecutor and the victim declined to comment after the sentencing hearing concluded on Thursday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: New designer drug found in Toronto fentanyl supply
stories.summary: Toronto - A new opioid part of an emerging class of designer drugs has been found in fentanyl samples in Toronto, according to a drug monitoring program.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A new opioid part of an emerging class of designer drugs has been found in fentanyl samples in Toronto, according to a drug monitoring program.

It’s the sixth new substance to be found in the city’s fentanyl supply so far this year, as reported by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service, raising concerns about the ongoing contamination and ever-changing nature of the street supply driving Canada’s opioid overdose crisis.

Karen McDonald, executive director of the drug checking service that operates out of St. Michael’s Hospital, said little is known about the new drug that was first found in four fentanyl samples in October. It is so new, it doesn’t even have a generic name yet.

N’-Phenethyl-5-chloro nor-orphine or N’-Phenethyl-6-chloro nor-orphine — the two drugs are so chemically similar the drug checking service said it can’t currently differentiate between them — has also been detected in Vancouver.

The drug is part of the orphine class of opioids, a potent group of designer drugs that have increasingly been on the radar of global monitors.

Late last year, Toronto’s Drug Checking Service started finding cychlorphine, an orphine-class opioid believed to be about 10 times stronger than fentanyl, in the city’s illicit drug supply.

But with next to no available research, the strength and effects of the novel orphine found in Toronto and Vancouver in October is unknown, McDonald said.

“This is a really good example of what we’re dealing with, with the unregulated fentanyl supply. It is just evolving, and the substances that are presenting are incredibly novel,” she said.

Cristiana Stefan, a lab director and clinical biochemist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, has concerns about how the orphine may interact with other drugs.

“It’s never good news whenever there is something else in the supply,” she said.

Stefan and her team, who analyze and identify the drugs collected by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service, spent weeks trying to unmask the unknown substance they were seeing in October’s samples using instruments that blast molecules with intense energy until they break down into fragments.

The biochemist’s concern about the novel orphine’s interactions with other drugs is made all the more salient given that drugs sold as fentanyl in Toronto hardly come as advertised.

The vast majority of “fentanyl” samples collected by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service — 96 per cent in the service’s latest report — were cut with at least one non-opioid drug, usually a veterinary tranquillizer or benzodiazepine, a class of depressants that includes Xanax.

During the same period, 83 per cent of fentanyl samples were found to contain multiple high-potency opioids and more than a quarter contained all three — a high-potency opioid, a vet tranquillizer and a benzodiazepine.

The share of overdose deaths across Canada involving multiple substances has been on the rise, according to the latest data.

From 2018 to 2023, the Public Health Agency of Canada found the percentage of opioid or stimulant overdose deaths involving three or more substances rose to 42 per cent from from 20, representing 491 deaths in 2018 to more than 1,500 in 2023.

When Toronto’s Drug Checking Service first launched, the fentanyl supply was far less contaminated, McDonald said. She speculated there are a number of factors why the cocktail of substances sold as fentanyl is ever-changing.

The availability of precursor chemicals to synthesize opioids is affected by drug laws and scheduling, as governments across the globe attempt to keep up with emerging opioids and drug producers invent new ones to minimize risk and cost, McDonald said.

According to Dan Werb, a substance use epidemiologist and St. Michael’s Hospital Chair in Mental Health and Substance Use Disorders, the drug market has seen “absolute disruption” since fentanyl became the dominant opioid, taking over from heroin before it.

That’s when opioid production shifted from poppy fields in Southeast Asia, Afghanistan and parts of western Mexico, to backyard laboratories across the world, Werb said. Suddenly, anyone with the right precursor chemicals and equipment could be an opioid producer.

Werb said drug producers also change their recipes in response to their clients.

“There’s an incentive for drug traffickers to produce these higher-potency opioid products. They test them, they introduce them, they see what happens. If too many people die, they remove them, maybe they reduce the potency and the cycle continues,” he said.

This vicious feedback loop played out with the rise and fall of carfentanil, an opioid about 100 times more potent than fentanyl.

According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, carfentanil was, at its peak, implicated in 20 per cent of apparent opioid overdose deaths in 2019 before gradually falling to three per cent in 2024.

Werb said drug producers lowering the potency of the illicit opioids they sell has been a driving factor in declining overdose deaths observed in Canada since 2023.

“What keeps me up at night is the fact that we do not control these markets. At any time, new products could be introduced. Now we’ve got orphine opioids, what people call now ultra-potent opioids,” Werb said.

“While we’ve seen these reductions really across most places in North America that have been previously hot spots of overdose mortality, that could change at any moment.”

paragraphs: TORONTO - A new opioid part of an emerging class of designer drugs has been found in fentanyl samples in Toronto, according to a drug monitoring program.

It’s the sixth new substance to be found in the city’s fentanyl supply so far this year, as reported by Toronto’s Drug Checking Service, raising concerns about the ongoing contamination and ever-changing nature of the street supply driving Canada’s opioid overdose crisis.

Karen McDonald, executive director of the drug checking service that operates out of St. Michael’s Hospital, said little is known about the new drug that was first found in four fentanyl samples in October. It is so new, it doesn’t even have a generic name yet.

N’-Phenethyl-5-chloro nor-orphine or N’-Phenethyl-6-chloro nor-orphine — the two drugs are so chemically similar the drug checking service said it can’t currently differentiate between them — has also been detected in Vancouver.
The drug is part of the orphine class of opioids, a potent group of designer drugs that have increasingly been on the radar of global monitors.
Late last year, Toronto’s Drug Checking Service started finding cychlorphine, an orphine-class opioid believed to be about 10 times stronger than fentanyl, in the city’s illicit drug supply.
But with next to no available research, the strength and effects of the novel orphine found in Toronto and Vancouver in October is unknown, McDonald said.
“This is a really good example of what we’re dealing with, with the unregulated fentanyl supply. It is just evolving, and the substances that are presenting are incredibly novel,” she said.
Cristiana Stefan, a lab director and clinical biochemist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, has concerns about how the orphine may interact with other drugs.
“It’s never good news whenever there is something else in the supply,” she said.

stories.title: Chow to shuffle city hall leadership, decide whether to sit on Toronto police board
stories.summary: Olivia Chow is set to shuffle her leadership team at Toronto City Hall as new faces are set to be picked for high-profile committee roles.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Mayor Olivia Chow shuffled her leadership team at city hall on Thursday, tapping a former Liberal MP to head up the housing committee and her Scarborough deputy as transit chair.

The appointments of Nate Erskine-Smith to housing and Paul Ainslie to transit were among the shakeups announced Thursday. Elsewhere, Chow opted for continuity with her last term, sticking to the same roster of deputy mayors and bringing back her budget chief.

“This is the team that will help deliver strong public services and take on the biggest challenges facing our city,” Chow said.

The mayor will look to take more direct control of the homelessness file by consolidating that work into her executive committee, Chow said. Her focus would go beyond temporary shelter, she said, to more lasting solutions with a goal to “significantly reduce” homelessness over the next four years.

“Other big cities have been able to deal with homelessness better than we have and there’s a lot of lessons that need to be learned there, and for me it’s a very, very high priority,” she said.

That work is expected to dovetail with the city’s housing committee, to be chaired by Erskine-Smith, who served briefly as a federal Liberal housing minister. He was elected to council after a failed bid earlier this year for the Ontario Liberal leadership, taking over the Beaches-East York seat vacated by Chow’s rival in the mayoral race, Brad Bradford.

Erskine-Smith, who earned a reputation as an independently minded Liberal on the party’s left flank, will lead the committee alongside vice-chair Diana Chan McNally, a former housing worker and advocate.

In a nod to Scarborough’s public transit frustrations, Chow tapped the area’s deputy mayor Ainslie to head up the transit board. A key issue for him will be advancing work on the Scarborough East LRT, a proposed 18-kilometre line, the mayor said.

Chow, who has overseen consecutive hikes to the police budget, turned down a seat on the police board, as she did in her first term. All post-amalgamation mayors have, at one time, delegated that position, but Chow was routinely criticized by rival Bradford for the move during the mayoral campaign.

It comes as the board is overseeing the service’s response to the explosive Project South scandal, which implicated several officers in a case tied to allegations of bribery, illegal searches and a murder plot.

Chow said the board and the chief had “been able to do good work to keep our city safe” but acknowledged “there’s always improvement.”

“I have confidence in how they have been managing in the last three years,” she said.

Newly elected Toronto Centre councillor Curran Stikuts will replace Lily Cheng on the board. In a statement, a spokesperson for Stikuts said the councillor “believes in transparent and accountable policing that is effective.”

“As a gay man who has spent most of his career working in the Church and Wellesley Village, the councillor is keenly aware of the work required to rebuild trust on our communities’ terms,” his chief of staff Nadine Tkatchevskaia wrote in a statement, which also referred to concerns raised by festival and street fair organizers about the rising policing costs.

Stikuts joins a board with returning councillors Amber Morley and Shelley Carroll.

Carroll expressed her openness on Thursday to return as board chair and is also set to reprise her role as Chow’s budget chief. As the mayor did in her inaugural speech, Carroll, a 23-year council veteran, alluded on Thursday to the city’s looming fiscal pressures. Officials have estimated a roughly $1 billion shortfall in the upcoming budget.

“We have a really tough budget coming this year, but it’s going to need the institutional memory. All the solutions that we’ve ever used are going to be employed here,” she said.

Affordable housing and provincial relations were at top of the mayor’s agenda during Thursday’s council meeting, two issues likely to figure prominently in her second term. Council advanced a program designed to give financial breaks to selected affordable rental housing developers and pushed back on proposed changes by Premier Doug Ford’s government to remove council’s representative from the Toronto Hydro board.

The provincial pushback at city hall Thursday went beyond proposed changes to Toronto Hydro. Mike Layton, newly minted chair of the infrastructure and environment committee, said one of his goals would be defending the city’s bike lane network from the province’s overhaul.

“Wasting taxpayer money was not the mandate that Mr. Ford was given,” said Layton, who sat on council for 12 years before stepping away in 2022 and then returning as University-Rosedale’s representative in last month’s election.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Oxford Youth Invitational Robotics Challenge Today
stories.summary: Each team had to build an autonomous collection and sorting robot using a VEX IQ robotics kit.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Thursday, 19 November 2026 at 05:46

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Each team had to build an autonomous collection and sorting robot using a VEX IQ robotics kit.

WOODSTOCK - Goff Gym will be packed with lots of bright young minds for the 19th annual Oxford Invitational Youth Robotics Challenge.

Twenty teams from Oxford, Norfolk, London-Middlesex, and St. Thomas-Elgin will compete for bragging rights this afternoon. The city says more than 75 students are expected to be there, plus their coaches and supporters.

Brad Hammond, Woodstock Economic Development Officer and the co-chair of this competition, says each team had to build an autonomous collection and sorting robot using a VEX IQ robotics kit, plus provide a written report and a video detailing the whole process.

"This competition gives students an exciting opportunity to explore how robotics and technology are being applied in real-world industries. By working alongside industry mentors and tackling practical challenges, students gain hands-on experience in engineering, technology and skilled trades while developing critical thinking, teamwork and problem-solving skills. It’s a valuable introduction to career pathways that play an important role in our local economy."

They will set up their projects at 2:00 p.m. today and the judging will take place from 5:00 p.m. to 5:30 p.m..

stories.title: Police across region launch Festive Ride checks
stories.summary: Beginning Thursday, drivers will begin to encounter Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (Ride) checks on their travels.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Beginning Thursday, drivers will begin to encounter Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (Ride) checks on their travels.

Police services across the region are launching their annual Festive Ride campaigns.

“Police continue to encounter drivers who get behind the wheel after consuming alcohol or drugs,” said Lambton OPP Insp. Ross Stuart at a kickoff event in Point Edward Wednesday.

A group of representatives from area police and emergency services, as well as a spokesperson from Mothers Against Drunk Driving (Madd) gathered under the Bluewater Bridge for the event.

Erin Pollard, president of the Sarnia Lambton Chapter of Madd says impaired driving is a choice, and too often a tragic one.

“If you injure somebody in drinking and driving, you have to live with that. But there’s a whole family as well that has to live with either a loss or an injury from a choice that you made,” said Pollard.

In last year’s Festive Ride, OPP alone laid nearly 300 charges across Western Region.

“We are doing more Rides every year. We are stopping more vehicles every year. We continue to see impaired driving being one of the leading causes of death on the roadways,” said Insp. Stuart.

Also on hand at the kickoff, chiefs and supervisors from Anishinabek, Walpole Island, and Sarnia Police services.

“And I can’t describe how devastating the event can be. We witness it as professionals, trying to convince people that it just simply isn’t worth it,” said Sarnia Police Chief Mike Frederico.

“If you plan to drink alcohol or consume drugs, please plan ahead and arrange a safe ride home,” said Walpole Island Police Acting Staff Sgt. Rick Mathieson.

Penalties for impaired driving range from license suspension to vehicle impoundment, and a wide range of fines all the way to jail time or imprisonment, depending on the severity of the conviction.

The Festive Ride Campaign begins Thursday, and wraps up on New Year’s Day.

stories.title: Health Canada approves Eli Lilly's GLP-1 pill for weight loss
stories.summary: Health Canada has authorized a new GLP-1 medication for weight loss that is a pill taken every day, rather than weekly injections.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Health Canada has authorized a new GLP-1 medication for weight loss that is a pill taken every day, rather than weekly injections.

Eli Lilly’s Foundayo is approved for adults with obesity as well as those who are overweight and have at least one related medical problem, such as high blood pressure or sleep apnea.

In addition to promoting and maintaining weight loss, the pill is also approved to help treat Type 2 diabetes.

Eli Lilly also makes the injectable drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, which contain the active ingredient tirzepatide. Tirzepatide acts on two receptors associated with insulin production and hunger: GLP-1 and GIP.

Competitor Novo Nordisk manufactures injectables Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain the active ingredient semaglutide. Semaglutide acts on GLP-1 receptors. Several other companies make generic semaglutide sold in Canada.

The class of drugs known as GLP-1s have revolutionized weight-loss treatment and experts say some patients may prefer to take a pill rather than an injection.

There is another GLP-1 pill — Novo Nordisk’s Rybelsus — already on the market in Canada, but it is only approved for Type 2 diabetes management and not for weight loss.

The active ingredient in Foundayo is orforglipron, a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist.

Because it’s a smaller molecule than peptides semaglutide and tirzepatide, orforglipron can be taken orally and absorbed without being broken down by the digestive system, said Dr. Ehud Ur, an endocrinologist in Vancouver who is not associated with either Eli Lilly or Novo Nordisk.

“It seems to be just as good as if not better” for weight loss as semaglutide and tirzepatide, he said.

The most common side effects of GLP-1 medications — both injectable and oral — include gastrointestinal issues, such as nausea or vomiting.

Ur said whether he would prescribe Foundayo depends on the patient, partly because he is still waiting for clinical trial results on whether or not orforglipron has a cardiovascular benefit like semaglutide and tirzepatide do.

Foundayo received Health Canada authorization on Nov. 13. Eli Lilly spokesperson Ethan Pigott said the company expects the pills to be available in pharmacies in January.

There may soon be a second GLP-1 weight-loss pill option in Canada: competitor Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill, which is still awaiting Health Canada approval.

Both Foundayo and the Wegovy pill are approved and available in the U.S.

Even though Wegovy is made of the large peptide molecule semaglutide, Novo Nordisk is able to manufacture it in pill form by adding an ingredient called salcaprozate sodium to protect it from being broken down by digestive enzymes.

Once the pill is swallowed, salcaprozate sodium, or SNAC, temporarily makes the area around it less acidic and helps it pass through the stomach lining into the bloodstream, Novo Nordisk spokesperson Kate Hanna said in an email on Wednesday.

GLP-1 medications should be used in conjunction with diet and exercise for weight loss, experts say.

paragraphs: TORONTO - Health Canada has authorized a new GLP-1 medication for weight loss that is a pill taken every day, rather than weekly injections.
Eli Lilly’s Foundayo is approved for adults with obesity as well as those who are overweight and have at least one related medical problem, such as high blood pressure or sleep apnea.
In addition to promoting and maintaining weight loss, the pill is also approved to help treat Type 2 diabetes.

Eli Lilly also makes the injectable drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, which contain the active ingredient tirzepatide. Tirzepatide acts on two receptors associated with insulin production and hunger: GLP-1 and GIP.

Competitor Novo Nordisk manufactures injectables Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain the active ingredient semaglutide. Semaglutide acts on GLP-1 receptors. Several other companies make generic semaglutide sold in Canada.
The class of drugs known as GLP-1s have revolutionized weight-loss treatment and experts say some patients may prefer to take a pill rather than an injection.
There is another GLP-1 pill — Novo Nordisk’s Rybelsus — already on the market in Canada, but it is only approved for Type 2 diabetes management and not for weight loss.
The active ingredient in Foundayo is orforglipron, a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist.

Because it’s a smaller molecule than peptides semaglutide and tirzepatide, orforglipron can be taken orally and absorbed without being broken down by the digestive system, said Dr. Ehud Ur, an endocrinologist in Vancouver who is not associated with either Eli Lilly or Novo Nordisk.
“It seems to be just as good as if not better” for weight loss as semaglutide and tirzepatide, he said.
The most common side effects of GLP-1 medications — both injectable and oral — include gastrointestinal issues, such as nausea or vomiting.

Ur said whether he would prescribe Foundayo depends on the patient, partly because he is still waiting for clinical trial results on whether or not orforglipron has a cardiovascular benefit like semaglutide and tirzepatide do.
Foundayo received Health Canada authorization on Nov. 13. Eli Lilly spokesperson Ethan Pigott said the company expects the pills to be available in pharmacies in January.
There may soon be a second GLP-1 weight-loss pill option in Canada: competitor Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill, which is still awaiting Health Canada approval.
Both Foundayo and the Wegovy pill are approved and available in the U.S.

Even though Wegovy is made of the large peptide molecule semaglutide, Novo Nordisk is able to manufacture it in pill form by adding an ingredient called salcaprozate sodium to protect it from being broken down by digestive enzymes.

Once the pill is swallowed, salcaprozate sodium, or SNAC, temporarily makes the area around it less acidic and helps it pass through the stomach lining into the bloodstream, Novo Nordisk spokesperson Kate Hanna said in an email on Wednesday.
GLP-1 medications should be used in conjunction with diet and exercise for weight loss, experts say.

stories.title: Quebec Bar Association wants new hotline, tax credit to improve access to justice
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - The professional order of lawyers in Quebec is proposing a new provincial telephone hotline as part of a range of measures to make legal services more accessible to members of the public.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - The professional order of lawyers in Quebec is proposing a new provincial telephone hotline as part of a range of measures to make legal services more accessible to members of the public.

The Barreau du Québec is calling on the province’s new justice minister, Marie-Claude Sarrazin, to take action on its recommendations released in a new report.

The bar association says the hotline could be similar to the province’s 811 service for health care information.

It is also proposing the government introduce a new refundable tax credit for family law fees.

The association says the new measures are needed as the justice system becomes increasingly expensive and difficult to navigate.

The report does not estimate the cost of its proposals, but Marcel-Olivier Nadeau, the elected leader of the order, says failing to act would also come at a price.

“There is also a cost to doing nothing, a cost when people give up on the justice system, a cost in psychological distress,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The report follows a provincewide consultation tour conducted by the Barreau last spring and calls for “putting people back at the heart of the justice system.”

About a dozen forums were held across 11 regions of Quebec, bringing together 450 members of the legal profession, the judiciary and organizations involved in the administration of justice.

Another 45 people who had firsthand experience with the justice system also took part in the forums.

One of the 45 was a man who represented himself in the Court of Québec in a dispute over a hidden defect in a property. He said he felt he had not been taken seriously by a lawyer.

The Canadian Press agreed not to identify the man because he did not want to be publicly associated with having been involved in legal proceedings.

He described the justice system as one that “doesn’t fix anything.” He described the process as “very intimidating,” with language that was “difficult to understand” and made people “feel like idiots.”

Nadeau acknowledged that more needs to be done to provide people with support throughout legal proceedings, adding that people often “feel lost, alone and powerless.”

He said the consultations conducted last spring were intended, in part, to “put a human face to the data and findings.”

Nadeau said lawyers need to be able to discuss their fees “frankly” with clients, calling for greater transparency and predictability in legal costs.

He also urged the province to simplify civil and family law procedures to reduce unnecessary procedural steps that drive up legal expenses.

Nadeau said he is optimistic that Sarrazin will be receptive to the recommendations.

“She knows that the justice system needs some love and needs to be more humane,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario to increase fines against drivers who create excessive noise
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario is set to make it tougher on drivers who wheel around with excessive noise.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says the province will soon table legislation to increase fines for drivers who are revving their engines or installing illegal mufflers.

He says the minimum fine will increase from $60 to $200 while the maximum fine remains at $1,000.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Peel Police Deputy Chief Marc Andrews says they have been conducting targeted enforcement on noise violators for years, but they wanted more teeth in the law to dissuade lawbreakers.

The force has handed out more than 5,000 noise violation tickets as part of Project Noisemaker, which began in 2020.

Police already have the authority and detection tools to enforce current excessive noise laws in the Highway Traffic Act, but Andrews says the increased fines will have an effect that should help quieten communities.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Researchers on B.C. coast use drones to collect whale snot for genome sequencing
stories.summary: Researchers studying humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia used drones to collect "whale snot," allowing scientists to conduct a complete genome sequencing without darts, biopsies or approaching closely with a boat.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Researchers studying humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia used drones to collect “whale snot,” allowing scientists to conduct a complete genome sequencing without darts, biopsies or approaching closely with a boat.

Eadin O’Mahony, lead researcher in the study published in the scientific journal Molecular Ecology Resources this week, said her team spent 2022 and 2023 collecting the samples.

“It was (about) getting the whole genome, but it was getting a whole genome in a non-invasive way,” she said of the project.

Genomic data is an important tool for conservation, she said, letting researchers measure population health, including genetic diversity and inbreeding, and helping them identify individuals and estimate population size.

“To have an understanding of the genetic resilience of a population of animals is really important for their long-term protection, their conservation,” O’Mahony said in an interview from Cork, Ireland.

To collect the DNA, she would pilot a drone from a small vessel or from land at the Fin Island Research Station in a remote location on B.C.‘s northern coast.

Humpback whales forage in the region in the summer before migrating to Hawaii to breed in the winter, she said.

The drone flights were conducted under a Fisheries and Oceans Canada research permit.

O’Mahony said she would be watching through the video feed to ensure the animal was not visually showing any signs of distress as she approached. If any were detected, they would terminate the flight, she said, adding this happened “very rarely.”

The drone carried a sterile petri dish and would hover over the whale, waiting for it to take the typical five to six breaths per surfacing.

“I’m trying to pre-empt the whale’s behaviour somewhat positioning the drone just behind the blowhole so that when she comes up to take that exhale, I’m ready to just fly through the breath covering the petri dishes in these little ‘mucusy’ droplets that’s what is effectively snot,” O’Mahony said.

The drone would then capture a photo of the animal’s tail fluke as it dove below the water’s surface.

She said the tail fluke is similar to a “human fingerprint,” allowing scientists to easily identify each animal.

A second photographer would use a zoom camera to help ensure a “fluke ID photograph” is captured during each collection.

“The actual sampling event is very quick,” she said, noting each flight only takes a couple of minutes.

“The scientific study, on the other hand — science is a slow game,” she said.

They collected 58 blow samples from a total of 26 humpbacks. The study said about 84 per cent of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself.

Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across the two years, gave matching genomes. Blow genomes also matched previously collected biopsy genomes from the same animals, the study said.

Researchers, alongside collaborators from the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow samples was very similar to those of traditional biopsies.

The customary way of obtaining a genetic sample is from a biopsy, which requires getting a boat very close to the animal to dart it to obtain pieces of the whale’s blubber and skin.

The research also determined the population studied shows little evidence of recent inbreeding.

O’Mahony said the humpback whale population declined about 20 per cent between 2012 and 2021, which she called “quite significant and quite worrying.”

“Genetic understanding helps us make management plans for our conservation agencies, to make management plans that are sustainable and protect these animals going forward,” she said.

O’Mahony noted humpbacks were long subjects of commercial hunts, which “brought their numbers to the brink of extinction.”

She said there has been local recovery along B.C.‘s coast, but there are conservation concerns over more expanded vessel traffic from tankers in the region, which increases the chances of fatal ship strikes.

“Getting that baseline information on what their genetic health looks like is really important in that context,” O’Mahony said.

She said there are scenarios where biopsy sampling is not possible, so this provides a non-invasive alternative.

“It’s not so much that the blow sampling will once and for all replace biopsy sampling, but there are a number of places where the blow sampling has its place,” she said.

“It just opens the door to more scenarios in which we might need to get the genetic material, but we haven’t been able to get it to such quality up until this point.”

She said she thinks blow sampling data is “only going to get better from here.”

“This is not the end of the road,” she said.

“It’s just going to open the door to increasingly non-invasive methods of research for conservation genomics.”

paragraphs: Researchers studying humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia used drones to collect “whale snot,” allowing scientists to conduct a complete genome sequencing without darts, biopsies or approaching closely with a boat.
Eadin O’Mahony, lead researcher in the study published in the scientific journal Molecular Ecology Resources this week, said her team spent 2022 and 2023 collecting the samples.
“It was (about) getting the whole genome, but it was getting a whole genome in a non-invasive way,” she said of the project.

Genomic data is an important tool for conservation, she said, letting researchers measure population health, including genetic diversity and inbreeding, and helping them identify individuals and estimate population size.

“To have an understanding of the genetic resilience of a population of animals is really important for their long-term protection, their conservation,” O’Mahony said in an interview from Cork, Ireland.
To collect the DNA, she would pilot a drone from a small vessel or from land at the Fin Island Research Station in a remote location on B.C.‘s northern coast.
Humpback whales forage in the region in the summer before migrating to Hawaii to breed in the winter, she said.
The drone flights were conducted under a Fisheries and Oceans Canada research permit.

O’Mahony said she would be watching through the video feed to ensure the animal was not visually showing any signs of distress as she approached. If any were detected, they would terminate the flight, she said, adding this happened “very rarely.”
The drone carried a sterile petri dish and would hover over the whale, waiting for it to take the typical five to six breaths per surfacing.

“I’m trying to pre-empt the whale’s behaviour somewhat positioning the drone just behind the blowhole so that when she comes up to take that exhale, I’m ready to just fly through the breath covering the petri dishes in these little ‘mucusy’ droplets that’s what is effectively snot,” O’Mahony said.
The drone would then capture a photo of the animal’s tail fluke as it dove below the water’s surface.
She said the tail fluke is similar to a “human fingerprint,” allowing scientists to easily identify each animal.
A second photographer would use a zoom camera to help ensure a “fluke ID photograph” is captured during each collection.
“The actual sampling event is very quick,” she said, noting each flight only takes a couple of minutes.
“The scientific study, on the other hand — science is a slow game,” she said.
They collected 58 blow samples from a total of 26 humpbacks. The study said about 84 per cent of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself.

Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across the two years, gave matching genomes. Blow genomes also matched previously collected biopsy genomes from the same animals, the study said.

Researchers, alongside collaborators from the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow samples was very similar to those of traditional biopsies.
The customary way of obtaining a genetic sample is from a biopsy, which requires getting a boat very close to the animal to dart it to obtain pieces of the whale’s blubber and skin.
The research also determined the population studied shows little evidence of recent inbreeding.
O’Mahony said the humpback whale population declined about 20 per cent between 2012 and 2021, which she called “quite significant and quite worrying.”
“Genetic understanding helps us make management plans for our conservation agencies, to make management plans that are sustainable and protect these animals going forward,” she said.
O’Mahony noted humpbacks were long subjects of commercial hunts, which “brought their numbers to the brink of extinction.”

She said there has been local recovery along B.C.‘s coast, but there are conservation concerns over more expanded vessel traffic from tankers in the region, which increases the chances of fatal ship strikes.
“Getting that baseline information on what their genetic health looks like is really important in that context,” O’Mahony said.
She said there are scenarios where biopsy sampling is not possible, so this provides a non-invasive alternative.
“It’s not so much that the blow sampling will once and for all replace biopsy sampling, but there are a number of places where the blow sampling has its place,” she said.
“It just opens the door to more scenarios in which we might need to get the genetic material, but we haven’t been able to get it to such quality up until this point.”
She said she thinks blow sampling data is “only going to get better from here.”
“This is not the end of the road,” she said.
“It’s just going to open the door to increasingly non-invasive methods of research for conservation genomics.”

stories.title: Chow to lay out vision for new term as Toronto council holds first meeting
stories.summary: Toronto - Mayor Olivia Chow is expected to lay out her vision for her second term as Toronto City Hall hosts its first meeting of the new council.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Olivia Chow laid out her vision for a second term as Toronto’s mayor, underlining her campaign promises to tackle affordability issues while also pointing to the city’s fiscal challenges.

Chow’s speech on Wednesday afternoon punctuated the usual fanfare and formalities of the first meeting of Toronto’s new council. She presided over a council with a boosted progressive bloc and without one of her chief rivals, Brad Bradford, whom she defeated in last month’s election.

Her speech alluded to pledges to build more affordable homes, crack down on bad-faith evictions, expand school nutrition programs and cap transit fares at 10 rides a week.

She connected her own upbringing to the city’s promise as a place where families could afford to “build a better life.” Toronto is a city, she said, where an immigrant child from Hong Kong raised by a hotel maid in a St. James Town apartment could rise through the political ranks and be twice elected mayor.

“I have never forgotten what Toronto gave my family. And I have spent my life trying to make sure other families have the same opportunities,” she said.

Chow also referred to the “enormous fiscal challenge” facing Toronto and other cities across Ontario. The city is facing an estimated $1.1 billion hole in the upcoming budget.

The remarks come after Premier Doug Ford earlier this month shot down the idea of renewing the so-called “new deal” he struck with Chow in the early days of her first term. That three-year deal saw Ontario provide $1.2 billion in operating dollars for transit and shelter costs, while taking on the long-term maintenance costs of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway.

Toronto cannot keep going back to Queen’s Park year after year asking for another agreement, “another Band-Aid solution,” Chow said.

“We need a structured financial solution that is fair, predictable and grows with the economy.”

A new speaker was elected by council for the first time in 16 years, after longtime rules enforcer Frances Nunziata was unseated last month, ending her more than four decades in city politics. Ausma Malik, a close ally of Chow and a deputy mayor during the last term, was elevated to the position.

Last month’s election set the table for a shakeup in Chow’s leadership team, with the retirement of housing chair Gord Perks and the defeat of transit chair Jamaal Myers. The mayor will have seven new councillors to consider for high-profile committee roles, including former Liberal MPs Nate Erskine-Smith and Shaun Chen. Those selections won’t be revealed until Thursday.

Affordable housing is at the top of Chow’s first agenda. When council reconvenes Thursday, she will look to advance a rental housing incentive program dating back to her first term.

The program offers financial breaks to purpose-built rental housing developers who dedicate at least 20 per cent of a project to affordable housing. Those affordable units are exempt from city property taxes and fees, on top of a provincially mandated development charge exemption. For the other market-value rental units, the city offers a 15 per cent property-tax reduction and an indefinite deferral on remaining development charges.

The city has conditionally picked 19 projects for the latest funding round, representing 9,667 homes, including 2,059 affordable units. The city says those incentives add up to about $500 million, made possible by a $1.5 billion federal-provincial deal to offset a reduction in development charges citywide.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

stories.title: House unanimously passes Conservative MP’s bill honouring son who died by suicide
stories.summary: Ottawa — The House of Commons has unanimously adopted a bill introduced by Conservative MP Luc Berthold, in memory of his son, that aims to help young people struggling with addiction.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The House of Commons has unanimously adopted a bill introduced by Conservative MP Luc Berthold, in memory of his son, that aims to help young people struggling with addiction.

The Quebec MP, who also serves as deputy House leader for the Official Opposition, has been championing the legislation while grieving the loss of his son David, who died by suicide after struggling with addiction and encounters with the justice system.

Bill C-231 was given the alternate title “For the Friends of David Law.” It would allow youth courts, in certain circumstances, to delay sentencing for a young person found guilty of an offence, allowing them to participate in a substance abuse treatment program or another type of treatment program.

The bill would amend the Youth Criminal Justice Act to give courts that option.

Shortly before the Commons unanimously adopted the bill on Monday, Berthold addressed his son during an emotional speech that noted it would have been David’s 30th birthday.

“Today, David, the House of Commons is unanimous. Your life, your experiences, your joys, your sorrows, none of it will have been in vain,” he said.

“Your life will serve as an example to perhaps help other young people avoid going through all the hardships you went through, perhaps make different choices, and help young people choose a path that will allow them to be here for their 30th birthday.”

Before Bill C-231 can become law, it must pass through the Senate and receive royal assent from the Governor General.

Speaking to reporters alongside his wife, Caroline, and daughter, Justine, Berthold said he was taking his grief “one day at a time,” with some days more difficult than others.

Berthold, a former mayor of Thetford Mines, Que., was first elected to Parliament in 2015.

“I think we started out with the idea of doing something, of giving meaning to something that makes no sense, in order to help other people,” Caroline said.

Both of David’s parents said that during a period when he was doing better, their son had expressed a desire to help “his friends.”

“He even had plans with his father to give talks to help young people, so I think this bill is, in a way, making the help David wanted to provide a reality,” Caroline said.

Berthold said he hopes the Senate will move more quickly than the House of Commons in advancing Bill C-231.

At the same time, the Conservative MP welcomed the collaboration among lawmakers from all parties during the bill’s consideration.

He also thanked public servants, noting that his original proposal had been broadened to give young people access not only to addiction treatment but also to other forms of care, including mental health treatment.

“We really had great collaboration from everyone to make this bill something that will, I hope, change the lives of many young people,” Berthold said.

Asked what would be needed to ensure provincial and municipal governments have the resources to provide appropriate addiction treatment programs, the Quebec MP said the bill was a first step.

“Our goal is to raise awareness among people, but also among governments, so that when a judge tells a young person to go to a treatment centre, there will be one available to them, and access won’t depend on their parents’ financial means,” he said.

Berthold criticized what he described as a “two-tier system,” in which lower-income families struggle to help their children access the resources and support they need.

He said raising awareness would be “the next step once we’ve completed all the stages of the legislative process here.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Émilie Bergeron, The Canadian Press

stories.title: National Congress of American Indians calls on Trump to reverse Lake Ontario change
stories.summary: The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The organization, which represents American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments in the United States, says the order demonstrates disrespect for Indigenous geographic names and Indigenous cultural, spiritual and historical relationships with lands and waters.

A resolution rejecting the name change, passed at the organization’s October assembly, was introduced by the Seneca Nation of Indians, a community based in Western New York.

Trump directed all arms of the federal government to start calling the body of water Lake America in August, to the dismay of Haudenosaunee communities on both sides of the border whose languages are the source of the name “Ontario.”

Lake Ontario is known in Seneca as “sga:nyodai:yoh,” meaning “beautiful lake,” and in Wendat as “ontari:io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The resolution says unilateral efforts to rename geography risk erasing Indigenous history and calls on the U.S. federal government to suspend its use of the term “Lake America.”

“The National Congress of American Indians opposes the removal, replacement, or erasure of Indigenous names of lakes, rivers, mountains, and other geographic features and calls upon federal, state, and local governments, geographic naming authorities, and public and private entities to preserve and respect those names in consultation with affected Tribal Nations,” it says.

“Lake Ontario is one example of the enduring Indigenous relationships with geographic features that this resolution seeks to protect, having been known to and used by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee peoples since time immemorial for travel, trade, diplomacy, subsistence, and cultural practices, and bearing a commonly used name derived from Indigenous linguistic roots.”

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard told The Canadian Press his nation was “shocked” to hear about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario. He called it an attempt to eradicate their history in the region.

The Wendat occupied parts of the St. Lawrence Valley up to the Great Lakes and the area was rich with both pre- and post-contact trade routes.

The name Lake Ontario predates the founding of both Canada and the United States.

Trump’s move was ridiculed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat. He posted a video of himself at a McDonalds restaurant, signing a fast food napkin to decree that Lake Michigan would now be called “Lake Wisconsin.”

“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the lake remains Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto sees another stretch of warm weather with temperatures in mid-teens
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto and the surrounding areas are getting another stretch of unusually warm weather in the middle of fall.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Toronto and the surrounding areas are getting another stretch of unusually warm weather in the middle of fall.

Environment Canada is forecasting clear and sunny weather and temperatures hitting 13 degrees on Tuesday in Toronto.

A Toronto non-profit is launching a tech week for the city, filling a hole created by the recent departure of the annual Collision conference. The Toronto skyline is seen on Monday, Aug. 5, 2024.

The Canadian Press

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard told The Canadian Press his nation was “shocked” to hear about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario. He called it an attempt to eradicate their history in the region.
The Wendat occupied parts of the St. Lawrence Valley up to the Great Lakes and the area was rich with both pre- and post-contact trade routes.
The name Lake Ontario predates the founding of both Canada and the United States.

Trump’s move was ridiculed by Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat. He posted a video of himself at a McDonalds restaurant, signing a fast food napkin to decree that Lake Michigan would now be called “Lake Wisconsin.”
“See, I can sign napkins that say things, too,” Evers wrote on X at the time.

stories.title: Trillium College students disappointed at selective return to classes
stories.summary: Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Students at one career college are decrying its approach to a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program payments, with the school allowing only those who can pay without the financial aid to continue learning.

Lorraine Eaton, who is in the law and security program at Trillium College, was supposed to graduate in January and had a security guard job lined up. Now, because she was relying completely on Osap loans and can’t pay tuition out of pocket, she has been told she can’t attend class.

“I am frustrated to all hell,” she said.

“I’ve actually had a couple of my classmates tell me they’re in class right now and … (our teacher) has this list of how many people can go into the class and there’s a lot of people not on that list anymore.”

Trillium College, with five campuses around the province, announced last month that it was suspending classes due to uncertainty created by the provincial government’s Osap pause. For many career colleges, Osap-funded tuition makes up a sizable portion of their revenue, and many say they are struggling, having to lay off staff or even consider closing.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced in early October that Osap would not flow for students at private post-secondary institutions during a government-commissioned audit of the sector that Quinn says has uncovered serious and widespread concerns.

He has not offered a timeline for resumption of Osap for career college students other than saying it would be in the new year, and low-interest, third-party bank loans Quinn said he was trying to arrange have not yet materialized.

Now, nearly a month after Trillium paused its classes, they are starting to resume, but only for some students.

Certain cohorts started returning last week, but some students told the school they couldn’t afford a payment plan without their Osap loan.

“Those students will remain on temporary academic pause and will not return with their cohort unless an eligible funding source or approved payment arrangement is confirmed,” Trillium wrote in a note to students.

Students on a payment plan have to pay weekly in advance of the following week’s classes and if a payment is missed, the student’s attendance May be “temporarily paused,” the school wrote.

A spokesperson said in a statement that Trillium is focused on resuming instruction “wherever this can be done responsibly and on helping as many students as possible complete their education.”

“Students and cohorts that are not included in the initial phases of the return will remain on temporary academic pause,” Jennifer Miles wrote.

“They have not been automatically withdrawn from Trillium College. The pause will continue while the college and affected students await an accessible government funding solution or establish another viable arrangement that supports the responsible completion of their programs.”

Jennifer Koster is in Trillium’s law clerk program and was supposed to graduate in February.

She said she could not pay the full amount Trillium had proposed for a payment plan and offered lesser instalments, but the school did not accept that so she remains on academic pause while some classmates have returned.

“I just want somebody to help,” she said. “There’s a lot of students just like me that are stuck in the same position, and we’re not getting what was promised. … It’s us taking responsibility for a mess that we didn’t create.”

Marina Whitehead, a student in Trillium’s community developmental service worker program, is in her program’s placement right now, so she is not attending classes.

But she does still owe the school nearly $6,000 from earlier in the term that Osap was supposed to cover, and she worries she won’t be able to graduate as planned in February if Osap doesn’t come through. Whitehead’s placement involves working 40 hours a week unpaid.

“We’re working for free,” she said. “Where would you like me to pull that much money out of?”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Allison Jones, The Canadian Press

TORONTO - Ontario’s medical regulator is hitting pause on implementing a host of changes to the ways doctors prescribe safer supply drugs after it was served with a legal challenge.

stories.title: Milton, Ont., to swear in first new mayor in 46 years as Gord Krantz leaves office
stories.summary: Milton - The town of Milton is set to swear-in a new mayor for the first time since 1980.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MILTON - The town of Milton is set to swear-in a new mayor for the first time since 1980.

George Minakakis and eight regional and town councillors will take their oaths of office at the council’s inaugural meeting Monday night.

Minakakis takes the reins from Canada’s longest-serving mayor, Gordon Krantz, who held Milton’s top job for 46 years before being defeated in October’s municipal election.

First elected to the town’s council in 1965, Krantz helped steward Milton’s transformation from agricultural community to rapidly growing suburb, negotiating the “Big Pipe” project that brought the town fresh drinking water from Lake Ontario in 2000 and sparked a population boom.

During Krantz’s tenure as mayor, Milton’s population more than tripled and the town was Canada’s fastest-growing municipality for a 10-year stretch.

The 89-year-old told The Canadian Press in an interview before October’s election that he was running again for mayor because he still felt he had more to do.

But ultimately, voters rewarded Minakakis, who ran on a platform of strengthening Milton’s economy and attracting more businesses to the bedroom community to spur local job growth.

The former business executive had served as a Milton town councillor for a year after winning a 2025 byelection.

Krantz told The Canadian Press in October that pragmatism guided his long political career.

“Separating out your wants from your needs for your community is important,” he said of the “delicate” balancing act of expanding services while keeping taxes low as Milton grew.

“As I will often say, there really is no free lunch. You pay me now or you pay me later,” he said.

Krantz said he correctly predicted that Milton would one day be home to highrise buildings when he was a town councillor back in 1965, an idea “way out in left field” at the time.

His next prediction for Milton’s future? Urbanization and a move away from cars.

“You’re going to find places like Oakville, Burlington, Milton, and the region of Halton, York and Durham be part of one great metropolis 100 years from now. Urbanization is here to stay in this part of the world,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

ST. JOHN’S - An airport in a Newfoundland town known for its care of stranded plane passengers was on the ready Friday as flights were grounded for several hours in the United States.

Reg White, chief executive of the airport authority in Gander, N.L., said he called the local hotels for vacancy numbers and made sure the restaurant could stay open if planes were diverted to the town.

stories.title: Busy day at Canadian airports as airlines scramble to recover from U.S. flight stop
stories.summary: Toronto - One of Canada's largest airlines says it will likely take the weekend for schedules to return to normal after officials temporarily grounded flights across the United States on Friday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Dale Flood had booked what he called a once-in-a-lifetime 50th birthday trip with his family to New York City to watch his beloved Buffalo Bills play on Sunday.

After a four-hour freeze on U.S. air traffic resulted in his Saturday morning flight being cancelled, the Vancouver man jumped into action, hoping to salvage the trip for himself, his wife and his 11-year-old son.

But after staying up until 4 a.m. trying to get his family on any flight that could get them to New York on time, he had to concede defeat. Instead, his family will fly on Sunday, landing too late for the much-anticipated NFL game.

“It’s sad,” Flood said in a phone interview. “It’s hard to watch an 11-year-old cry. It’s hard to go through all of October and November really looking forward to this, to that time in New York.”

The ripple effects of a four-hour freeze on U.S. air traffic continued across Canadian airports on Saturday, as airlines issued flight notices and travellers spent hours tethered to their phones waiting for updates.

Airports from Vancouver to Halifax posted on social media that they were facing delays, and the one in Toronto said it even called in more staff to help out.

“A busy day of travel is underway,” said Toronto Pearson International Airport.

Flood acknowledged that the disruption was unforeseen, and that there was likely nothing that could have been done to get him from the West Coast to New York on time. But he’s frustrated by his inability to get through to an agent over the phone.

“You do wish you could at some point talk to Air Canada, like actually talk to a human being,” he said.

Traveller Edward Langer, who is in New York with his 15-year-old daughter, said his Saturday flight back home to Edmonton was postponed by about four days due to the freeze.

He said he and his daughter are facing several missed days of school and work, as well as thousands of dollars in extra hotel costs.

He had not been able to reach Porter Airlines as of Saturday afternoon despite spending hours on hold.

“When you go on some of the travel sites to book hotels, (the price) is just doubling and tripling,” he said.

“It’s crazy.”

Global travel chaos began after the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday that brought air traffic in that country to a halt for more than four hours.

The U.S. government said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused intermittent communications and radar gaps. The matter was under investigation.

Air Canada said Saturday it cancelled approximately 250 flights after the order, which affected some 27,000 passengers.

“This was a significant disruption, and its effects have carried over into today, with additional cancellations as aircraft and crews are out of position across our network,” said Yasmine Mehdi, an Air Canada spokesperson.

“Returning to normal operations will take some time.”

Porter Airlines and WestJet said it would likely take the whole weekend for its flights to return to normal schedules.

Porter said it would refund its customers who can’t accommodate rescheduled flights while Calgary-based WestJet said its policy allowing flexible rescheduling was activated.

Isabelle Rochefort said she had been standing in line at Montreal’s Trudeau International Airport to board her Air Canada flight to Cancun, Mexico, around 5 p.m. Friday when she received word that it was cancelled.

She said the situation was initially confusing because her plane wasn’t touching down in the United States.

“We didn’t know what to do, of course,” she said in a series of Facebook messages.

“The Air Canada staff had no information on what was next except that we had to wait for news.”

She was able to retrieve her bag after leaving the line and call someone to drive her home to Sorel-Tracy, more than an hour-and-a-half away.

She’s since been rebooked on a new flight leaving Sunday, though she’ll have to pay for yet another expensive ride to the airport.

Rochefort believes that both the airport and airline are managing as best as they can.

“The real question now is, will it be possible to be compensated?” she asked.

“That remains to be seen.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

—- By Morgan Lowrie in Montreal, Sarah Smellie in St. John’s, and Fakiha Baig in Edmonton, with files from The Associated Press

stories.title: One person arrested, other suspects at large after overnight home invasion in Mt. Brydges
stories.summary: One person is in custody, and others remain at large after a home invasion in Mt. Brydges, Ont. west of London.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
One person is in custody, and others remain at large after a home invasion in Mt. Brydges, Ont. west of London.

Around 3:55 a.m., officers from the Middlesex County OPP, and officers from Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service (Scps) responded to reports of a break and enter involving possibly armed individuals in the area of Edinburgh Road, Adelaide Road, Parkhouse Drive and Ferne Drive.

“We had a police officer that was on scene within one minute,” said Staff Sgt. Jason Cartwright of the Scps.

“The officer, when she arrived, actually was confronted by one of the suspects who was exiting the residence (on Parkhouse Drive) at that time. She got into a short-foot pursuit with the suspect, at which time the suspect did get away. She returned to the residence and called for more assistance and continued the investigation.”

While the person on foot did get away, an officer who was in the area was able to locate what was believed to be a suspect vehicle.

“He attempted to stop that vehicle, but the vehicle did not stop for police,” said Cartwright.

Police say they don’t have much information on the two outstanding suspects other than they are still searching for two black males between the age of 20 and 30 who were wearing dark clothing.

Hours after the home invasion, police tape surrounded a home on Parkhouse Drive, where a couple was home at the time of the break in.

A contractor was rebuilding the front door which was kicked in and Scps officers along with K9 were searching the area near the residence.

CTV News spoke with a couple of neighbours along Parkhouse Drive who wished to remain anonymous. They said the incident is “very unnerving” and one even went as far as to track down OPP officers and ask them to come double-check the area around her home and under her porch.

Another neighbour told CTV News he plans to upgrade from a doorbell camera to a full security system.

“This is unnerving for sure,” said Cartwright.

“This is a a serious incident that occurred. There will be police presence in Mt Brydges today in the area. We are potentially looking for one or more suspects still. If there’s anything suspicious in the area, call 911 or our emergency line and we will certainly have somebody come out and see them.”

Police say despite early reports, there is no evidence that the suspects had a firearm.

stories.title: Lawyers unsure if extra funding can reduce massive caseload at Federal Court
stories.summary: Ottawa — The recent federal budget included $58 million in additional funding court administration but the Federal Court still doesn't have a clear picture of how it can be used to reduce a massive caseload that has grown rapidly since 2020.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The recent federal budget included $58 million in additional funding court administration but the Federal Court still doesn’t have a clear picture of how it can be used to reduce a massive caseload that has grown rapidly since 2020.

“At the moment, the Federal Court doesn’t have additional details on how the funding confirmed will be distributed among the stated purposes,” Chief Justice Alan Diner told The Canadian Press in an emailed statement on Thursday.

The Federal Court hears immigration-related issues such as visa applications, refugee claims, admissibility cases and removals. It has responsibility for upholding the law in other areas related to federal jurisdiction, like intellectual property, national security and Indigenous rights.

The court asked for additional resources to handle a caseload that’s ballooned to nearly 31,000 proceedings commenced as of Sept. 30 this year — up from about 7,600 in all of 2020.

More than 27,000 of the proceedings started this year are immigration cases.

Diner told The Canadian Press in an August interview that judges and court staff have had to work evenings, weekends and vacation days to handle a caseload that has been growing in large part because of immigration matters.

The budget says the money is earmarked for the Courts Administration Service, which serves the Federal Court, the Federal Appeal Court, the Tax Court of Canada and the Court Martial Appeal Court of Canada.

The single mention of it in the documents published Nov. 5 says the new funding is meant to address the Federal Court caseload and to help the Courts Administration Service with Official Languages Act compliance, a translation backlog and the need to modernize court infrastructure.

The extra $58 million in funding is set to begin in the 2027/28 fiscal year and continue for four years, averaging $14.5 million annually.

Joannie Fogue, spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser, said the funding is meant to “strengthen the national courts,” respond to resource challenges and build workload efficiencies. But exactly how it will be allocated aren’t yet known.

“We are continuing to work through the details and implications of the funding commitment and are awaiting further information on the how allocation will be distributed,” she said in a media statement.

While the court awaits more details, immigration lawyers question whether the additional money from Ottawa will do much to move cases through the court more efficiently, given how the demands have grown.

“Any increase in funding is positive, but it’s a modest increase and the increase in the Federal Court’s immigration caseload has been anything but modest,” said Jacqueline Bonisteel, an Ottawa-based immigration lawyer.

While Bonisteel said the additional funding is welcome, she doesn’t see how $58 million spread over four years will be enough, given the spike in the caseload.

“It’s not going to be enough to cope with the issues that the court’s seeing right now, a 600 per cent increase in immigration caseload since 2020,” she said.

“The current compliment of judges and the current resources that the court has just simply aren’t enough to deal with that magnitude of an increase.”

Bonisteel said it can take “upwards of two years” now to get an immigration case through the court.

Zeynab Moayyed, a Toronto-based immigration lawyer, agreed the problems at the Federal Court go beyond what $58 million could fix.

Moayyed cited a shortage of registry staff in the court and said routine paperwork that used to take about a day to process — like a filing for a judicial review — now takes weeks.

Moayyed attributed the increase in caseload in part to more people filing mandamus applications meant to force a decision from the Immigration Department when people are facing long delays.

But both Moayyed and Bonisteel said the quality of Immigration Department decisions has declined since the feds adopted artificial intelligence tools and new software in a bid to review and process applications more quickly.

The lack of human interaction at the department is turning small problems into large ones and pushing them onto the court’s plate, they said.

“Previously, (lawyers) could reach out to (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada), to program managers, to visa office managers and so on. And … if it was a mistake they would receive a reconsideration and that matter would be reopened, and if it wasn’t a mistake, (the applicant) would understand what they did wrong,” Moayyed said.

“But with the coming into effect of those tools, at the same time we had the shutting down of informal ways of addressing areas that happen in the system, and applicants started turning to Federal Court.”

Bonisteel said the department could ease the Federal Court’s workload by finding a way to streamline requests for reconsideration before they get shunted to the court.

“These are very multi-faceted problems and they need multi-faceted solutions. So it’s not just about court funding. It’s about addressing the systemic issues that are leading to the increase in the court’s caseload,” she said.

The Immigration Department has said it uses AI and advanced analytics tools under human oversight at all times. The department says these AI tools do not make decisions and are meant to assist with tasks like triaging applications, identifying routine cases, generating case summaries and answering client questions through chatbots.

The department’s first AI strategy, released earlier this year, says the goal is to get the technology to reduce application backlogs and wait times.

Moayyed said those long delays are causing “a great deal of distress” for people stuck in the system.

“Our job, in addition to being immigration lawyers, has become confidant and the therapist for a client, listening to them talk about having their life on hold and in limbo until they get a decision,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: CFB Wainwright incident casts spotlight on reserve pay disparities: former bureaucrat
stories.summary: Ottawa — A former director general for the Canadian military's reserves and cadets says the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright casts a spotlight on disparities in pay and benefits for reservists.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — A former director general for the Canadian military’s reserves and cadets says the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright casts a spotlight on disparities in pay and benefits for reservists.

John Milne, a retired major-general, told The Canadian Press reservists on short-term contracts get less compensation than the regular force members they train with. He said the recent training accident at CFB Wainwright shows those short-term reservists face the same risks as their regular force colleagues.

Four soldiers died and 39 others — including several reservists — were injured when a fire suddenly overtook a training area at CFB Wainwright last month.

Military pay is not a straightforward matter and is calculated based on a range of factors.

Unlike regular force members, reservists usually study or work at full-time civilian jobs while they serve under one of a number of different service classes for the military. Those service classes affect how their benefits are determined.

Milne — who has written academic papers on military pay structure — said the formula the federal government uses to calculate daily reservist pay has amounted to an earnings penalty of roughly 32 per cent for part-time reservists compared to the regular force.

He said it’s a “matter of equity” and the daily rate for reservists should be made the same as what regular force members get. He also said the policy governing their benefits should be rewritten to be more fair.

“As the government grows and increases its military commitments and has intentions of using reservists in more dangerous and more complex environments, then it’s a matter of equity that the daily rate for the reservists should actually be the same as the daily rate for the regular,” he said.

Reservists injured in training also normally receive lower-tier compensation and benefits during their recovery, Milne said. He added he believes the military has reclassified the Wainwright reservists’ contracts from short to long-term service classes to improve their access to benefits.

The Department of National Defence did not respond to questions about the reclassification of injured reserve members’ contracts by deadline.

Official information about the Wainwright tragedy has been limited. Three separate investigations are taking place.

Milne sent a submission to the House of Commons national defence committee in the hopes that Parliament would take up the matter. In it, he writes that there is “no justification” for the earnings penalty, which affects other benefits such as disability payment amounts.

He also wrote directly to Defence Minister David McGuinty. A response letter he received from the minister’s office said the military’s pay structure is complex and involves “specific military considerations” different from civilian pay, and denied that Milne had identified pay inequities.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a military pay hike last year, which included a 13 per cent boost for some reserve force ranks. It did not address how pay is structured.

The Canadian Armed Forces Ombud has flagged for years systemic financial inequities and administrative delays with reservist pay as major problems the government must fix, but has reported little progress.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 14, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press
